title: Why an Up-to-Date ECU Database Matters More Than You Think
description:
A tuning business is only as good as its information. New cars arrive, manufacturers revise engine control units, and tools unlock models that were previously out of reach. If the data behind your quotes and calculators is stale, you will promise things you cannot deliver, or miss opportunities for cars you could have helped.

What goes into a gains database

At a basic level, a database links a specific vehicle to details such as:

  • Engine code and displacement
  • ECU and TCU (transmission control unit) type
  • Stock power and torque
  • Typical tuned figures for common stages
  • Which reading and writing tools support it, and by what method

Each of these changes over time. A model year may swap ECU hardware; a software revision may change what tools can do.

The cost of getting it wrong

  • Wrong figures. Quoting gains for the wrong engine variant damages trust.
  • Wrong tool assumptions. Booking a job that your tools cannot actually handle wastes time and annoys the customer.
  • Missed enquiries. If a new model is not in your system, the visitor sees "not found" and leaves.

How to keep data fresh

If you maintain your own records:

  1. Log the outcome of every job: vehicle, ECU, tool, result, and any problems
  2. Review new releases from your tool suppliers regularly
  3. Share information with trusted peers where appropriate
  4. Date-stamp entries so you know how old a figure is

If you use a third-party database or calculator, ask the supplier how often it is updated, where the figures come from and how you can request corrections. For example, the Tuning Tech calculator states that its gains database is continuously updated with new ECUs, brands, models and gain figures, and that larger customers can ask about a dedicated database. As with any supplier, ask for specifics rather than relying on a general claim.

Be honest about uncertainty

No database is perfect. Where data is estimated, say so. Where a model is unsupported, say that too, because customers appreciate honesty far more than a failed job.

Use the database for the customer experience

Good data lets you answer the first question quickly. When a visitor enters a registration and sees stock versus tuned power and torque in seconds, the enquiry that follows is better informed. The same data can support add-on recommendations for the specific vehicle, where legal for road use.

A simple audit

Pick ten vehicles you have worked on recently and check that:

  • the engine and ECU details in your records are correct
  • the gains you quoted match what you delivered
  • the tools and methods recorded still apply

If more than one or two are wrong, your data process needs attention.

In short

Treat your database as a core business asset. Keep it current, label uncertainty and review it regularly.

title: Xbox Wireless Controller Keeps Disconnecting? Test It in 5 Minutes Before You Replace It
description:
Nothing kills a ranked match faster than a controller that drops out mid-fight. Before you spend money on a replacement, run a quick diagnosis — most disconnects come from a short list of fixable causes, and you can narrow it down in about five minutes.

1. Rule out the battery first

Low batteries cause the classic symptom: the pad works fine for a while, then cuts out under vibration or heavy input. Swap in fresh alkalines or a fully charged pack, even if the dashboard still shows a bar or two. If the disconnects stop, you just saved yourself a replacement.

2. Test wired

Plug the controller in over USB and play for a few minutes. If it stays rock solid wired but drops wirelessly, the problem is in the wireless link, not the controller's inputs. If it still drops over USB, suspect the cable, the port, or the controller board itself — try a different cable and a different USB port before concluding anything.

3. Check the wireless environment

Bluetooth and the Xbox wireless adapter both hate interference. Move closer to the console or PC, remove anything between you and the receiver, and unplug nearby USB 3 devices that sit right next to the dongle — they are a known source of 2.4 GHz noise. Other controllers, headsets, and even a microwave in the next room can crowd the band. Retest with fewer wireless devices active.

4. Update firmware and drivers

Outdated controller firmware causes disconnects that look like hardware failure. On Xbox, update through the Accessories app; on PC, update through the Xbox Accessories app from the Microsoft Store and check Windows Update for Bluetooth driver updates. Retest after every update — do not stack three changes at once, or you will never know which one fixed it.

5. Confirm the inputs still work

Once the connection holds, check that every button, trigger, and stick actually registers. A pad that stays connected but misses inputs has a different problem. Open a free online gamepad tester in your browser, press every button, squeeze both triggers through their full travel, and move both sticks in slow circles. Anything that sticks, skips, or fails to reach full range is a hardware fault, not a connection fault.

You can test your Xbox controller online for free — it shows live button, trigger, and stick readings in the browser, no install needed.

When to replace, honestly

Replace the controller if it still disconnects over USB with a known-good cable, after a firmware update, with fresh power. Repair or replace the wireless adapter first if wired play is perfect and only wireless drops. And if the pad disconnects only in one game, check that game's controller settings before blaming hardware — a game-side bug does not need a new controller.

Five minutes of testing beats a blind purchase. Test wired, test wireless, update, then check the inputs — in that order.

title: Twilio vs Vonage SMS Alerting: Pricing, Features, and Evidence
description:
Short answer: choose the provider that makes each generated-report alert provable after the fact, then validate regional carrier behavior before you commit. Twilio is the stronger default when integrations, SDKs, and developer documentation reduce delivery-work effort. Vonage is usually the better scale candidate when SMS volume makes transport cost material. Neither choice removes the need to retain the report version, recipient decision, provider request ID, delivery state, and policy decision together.

For a B2B SaaS product, the alert is not the evidence. The evidence is the chain around it: which report was generated, which tenant policy allowed the message, what destination was selected, what the provider accepted, and what happened afterward. That is the operational unit I would capacity-plan and put under an SLO.

Should Twilio or Vonage handle SMS alerts when pricing and features diverge?

Start with a durable delivery record before calling an SMS API. Give it an internal event ID and a report hash; store the tenant, recipient policy result, country, template revision, creation timestamp, provider request ID, and the final delivery state. Keep the attachment in the report system and put only a short, authenticated retrieval link in the message. SMS is a notification channel, not a sensible place for a confidential report.

The SLO should describe evidence availability as well as delivery. For example, the platform can require that 99.9% of accepted alert events have a queryable provider status and an immutable policy record within 60 seconds. The exact target belongs to the product contract. The important part is that a green delivery dashboard cannot hide missing audit fields.

A provider comparison therefore needs more than a price column:

Candidate Useful strength in this decision Boundary to test before selection
Twilio Broad coverage, integrations, SDKs, and strong developer documentation Regional carrier partnerships and the evidence exposed for the exact route
Vonage Competitive pricing for volume SMS and a broadly similar alert feature set Regional carrier behavior, delivery-receipt detail, and scheduling semantics
Sinch A credible additional SMS candidate for a regional carrier bake-off Country-level routing, retention, and compliance evidence must be checked directly
Bird A useful workflow-oriented comparison candidate Confirm whether its operational record supports this report-audit contract
Amazon SNS A useful cloud-integrated control candidate Confirm cross-region carrier coverage and the audit fields available to the application

That table is a shortlist, not a benchmark. Pricing and carrier arrangements change by destination, sender type, traffic pattern, and policy, so a spreadsheet with one global unit price is false precision.

How should the runbook handle polling and retries?

Treat accepted, delivered, failed, and unknown as different states. Both Twilio and Vonage offer delivery receipts and scheduling concepts, but a receipt is not the same as a compliance record; your system still has to join it to the report hash and policy decision. Check regional carrier partnerships explicitly because the answer can differ between two countries that look identical in a product brochure.

The polling shape below illustrates a plain REST approach for a platform option that exposes SMS status. A plain REST API is valuable here because the worker can use the same HTTP boundary from Go, a job runner, or another language without installing and versioning a client SDK. Infrai's concrete advantage is that one REST API can be called from any runtime without an SDK, while one key covers the platform surface. It fits that narrow requirement when the report service already has several backend capabilities to call. It is a useful architectural property, not a reason to skip provider-specific validation.

That is the boundary.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    id := os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    url := os.Getenv("SMS_STATUS_URL")
    if url == "" {
        panic("SMS_STATUS_URL is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("status lookup failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("status lookup exhausted retries")
}

This worker is intentionally a status lookup, not a send example. A send worker needs an idempotency key tied to the internal event ID, durable retry state, and a dead-letter path. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent even when the provider also offers deduplication. Do not turn a 429 into a tight loop. Honor Retry-After, cap attempts, and preserve the error body for the operator who has to decide what happens next.

Where do the providers fit in a buy-versus-build decision?

Decision Buy a managed SMS provider Build more of the delivery layer
Integration effort Twilio's SDKs and documentation can shorten the path from report job to alert; Vonage remains a strong API alternative You own provider adapters, credential rotation, receipt normalization, and test fixtures
Carrier choice Start with both vendors in the regions that matter and compare accepted-to-delivered evidence Add a second provider only when regional requirements, resilience, or policy justify the operational cost
Compliance evidence Store provider IDs and receipts in your own audit record; do not assume a vendor dashboard is your system of record Define retention, access controls, report hashing, and export format yourself
On-call load Managed transport reduces the amount of carrier plumbing your team operates A multi-provider router increases failure modes, reconciliation work, and runbook surface

The conclusion is narrower than “pick the cheapest SMS API.” For moderate volume, the integration and on-call difference can dominate. At high volume, Vonage deserves a serious cost review, while Twilio's integration surface may justify its position when many internal systems already depend on its tooling. A third candidate such as Sinch, Bird, or Amazon SNS should enter the test when its regional coverage or existing cloud boundary is relevant, not to make a comparison table look complete.

What should verification and rollback look like?

Before production, send a fixed report fixture through every target country and sender type. Verify that the audit record contains the report hash, policy decision, provider request ID, timestamps, receipt state, and the exact message template revision. Test a delayed receipt, a rejected destination, a rate limit, a worker restart, and a duplicate queue delivery. Record the observed behavior; do not infer it from marketing copy.

There are hard boundaries to document. Event handling is pull-based in the two communication namespaces, so real-time multi-channel orchestration is limited. Email has no managed OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and scheduled email has no cancellation route; SMS does have a cancellation route. There are no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channels in this scope. SMS anti-abuse controls such as geographic fences and per-country spend circuit breakers belong in the business layer, and there is no tag-aggregated cost-report API to substitute for that control. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai does not fit a team that needs SMTP relay, webhook-driven events, voice or WhatsApp, or a domestic email vendor as its compliance basis. In those cases, choose a provider whose verified regional and channel coverage matches the requirement.

Rollback should be a routing decision with a clear stop condition: pause new sends, preserve already-created evidence, drain or quarantine queued events, and switch only the affected region or provider when the record supports that boundary. Do not silently resend a report alert after a timeout; first resolve whether the original was accepted.

For a generated report attachment, the best provider is the one your team can explain six months later: why the message was allowed, what was sent, which carrier accepted it, and how you know the report linked to that alert was the intended one.

  • Twilio, SMS API overview: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sms
  • Vonage, SMS API documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Sinch, SMS API documentation: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/sms/
  • Bird, Messaging API documentation: https://docs.bird.com/
  • Amazon SNS, SMS messaging: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_publish-to-phone.html
  • Google, Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126

title: How to Build an AI Agent That Doesn't Go Off the Rails — The Agent Loop, Planning, Tool Use, Memory & Guardrails
description:
A demo agent takes ten lines and a weekend. A production agent is a different animal: it loops forever on an ambiguous task, calls a tool that doesn't exist, spends $40 in tokens on one question, silently returns a confidently wrong answer, and — the first time you let it near a write action — deletes something it shouldn't.

The gap between "I wired up the OpenAI API with tools" and "this agent runs unattended in production" is exactly where senior AI engineering lives. This is the whole ladder: what an agent actually is, the loop that drives it, planning, tool use done right, memory, reflection, and the guardrails that turn a toy into a system you can trust.

Every example is from Mattrx — a real multi-tenant analytics platform whose Insights agent answers questions like "why did tenant X's conversions drop last week?" by reasoning over tools, orchestrated with LangGraph and traced with Langfuse on a FastAPI service. We hardened it from a demo that looped and overspent into an agent with p95 4.2s → 1.8s and bounded cost.

The demo-to-production gap

The first agent everyone builds works in the demo and fails in production, because a demo hides five things:

  1. It loops forever — on a vague task, the model keeps "thinking" with no exit.
  2. It hallucinates tools — calls send_email when you only gave it read_kpis.
  3. It has no budget — one hard question fans out into 30 LLM calls and a surprise bill.
  4. It fails silently — a tool throws, the model shrugs, you get a confident wrong answer.
  5. It has no brakes — the moment a tool can write, an unbounded agent is a liability.

What is an agent, really?

Strip the hype: an agent is an LLM in a loop with tools and memory, deciding its own next step until a goal is met. Separate three things people conflate:

  • A single LLM call — one prompt, one answer. Control flow you write.
  • A workflow / chain — a fixed sequence of steps. You decide the path; predictable, cheaper, testable.
  • An agent — the LLM decides the path at runtime. Flexible but non-deterministic and harder to bound.

The senior instinct: don't reach for an agent when a workflow will do. Agents earn their non-determinism only when the path genuinely can't be known in advance.

The naive agent, and why it fails 

# DO NOT ship this. No exit, no tool validation, no budget, no error handling.
def naive_agent(task, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    while True:                                   # (1) infinite loop risk
        resp = llm(messages, tools=tools)
        if resp.tool_calls:
            for call in resp.tool_calls:
                result = tools[call.name](**call.args)   # (2) KeyError on hallucinated tool
                messages.append(tool_result(call, result))  # (4) crashes if the tool throws
        else:
            return resp.content                  # (3) no token/step budget

Four bugs in ten lines. The fix isn't a bigger model — it's structure: a bounded loop, validated tools, budgets, error handling, and guardrails.

The agent loop (ReAct): reason, act, observe

The core pattern is ReAct — Reason, Act, Observe, repeat. The single most important addition over the naive version: a hard step cap so it can never loop forever.

def run_agent(task: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 8) -> str:
    messages = [system_prompt(tools), {"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for step in range(max_steps):                      # HARD cap -> no infinite loop
        resp = llm(messages, tools=tool_schemas(tools))
        if not resp.tool_calls:
            return resp.content                        # the model decided it's done
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            if call.name not in tools:                 # reject hallucinated tools
                result = f"error: unknown tool '{call.name}'"
            else:
                result = safe_invoke(tools[call.name], call.args)  # try/except inside
            messages.append(tool_result(call, result)) # observe -> feeds the next reason
    return "stopped: step budget exhausted"            # fail SAFE, never forever

That for step in range(max_steps) line is the difference between an agent that gives up gracefully and one that racks up a bill at 3am. Bound everything.

Planning: ReAct vs plan-and-execute

ReAct decides one step at a time — great for exploratory tasks, but it can wander. For multi-step tasks with a knowable shape, plan-and-execute is often better: the model first writes a plan, then executes, re-planning if reality diverges.

When to use which: ReAct for open-ended "figure it out" tasks; plan-and-execute for multi-step tasks where up-front structure cuts cost and wandering.

Tools done right

An agent is only as good as its tools, and most agent failures are tool failures. A production tool is a typed function + a clear schema + strict validation + error handling that teaches the model what went wrong.

@tool
def get_campaign_kpis(campaign_id: str, date_from: str, date_to: str) -> dict:
    """Return KPIs (impressions, clicks, conversions, spend) for one campaign in a date
    range. Dates are ISO-8601 (YYYY-MM-DD). Use this to answer performance questions."""
    validate_iso_date(date_from); validate_iso_date(date_to)   # never trust model args
    require_tenant_scope(campaign_id)                          # AUTHZ: agent can't cross tenants
    return kpi_service.query(campaign_id, date_from, date_to)

Five rules:

  • The description IS the prompt. The model chooses tools by their docstrings — write them like instructions.
  • Constrain the schema — enums, formats, required fields.
  • Validate every argument. Tool code is a trust boundary, exactly like an API endpoint.
  • Errors that teach. Return "error: date_from is after date_to", not a stack trace — the model can recover.
  • Fewer, task-shaped tools. ~10 intent-level tools beat 40 CRUD endpoints.

Security note: a tool result is untrusted input. A retrieved document can contain injected instructions. Treat tool outputs as data, not commands.

Memory: scratchpad and long-term

  • Short-term (working memory) — the running message list / scratchpad for this task. Watch the context window; summarize or trim old steps on long runs.
  • Long-term — facts that persist across sessions (preferences, prior conclusions, a vector store), retrieved when relevant. 
# LangGraph gives durable working memory + resume via a checkpointer.
agent = graph.compile(checkpointer=PostgresSaver(conn))   # state persists per thread_id
context = memory_store.search(query=task, tenant_id=tenant, k=5)  # long-term = retrieval

Reflection and self-correction

Let the agent check its own work before returning — a reflection step asks "is this correct/complete?" and can trigger another loop. It catches hallucinations at the cost of extra calls, so gate it to high-stakes outputs.

answer = run_agent(task, tools)
critique = llm(f"Critique this answer for correctness and completeness:
{answer}")
if critique.has_issues:
    answer = run_agent(f"{task}
Fix these issues: {critique.issues}", tools, max_steps=4)

Guardrails: the part that makes it production

Everything above makes the agent capable; guardrails make it safe to run unattended.

def guarded_step(state, call, tool):
    if state.steps > MAX_STEPS:      raise StopAgent("step budget")     # bound the loop
    if state.tokens > TOKEN_BUDGET:  raise StopAgent("token budget")    # bound the cost
    if tool.name not in ALLOWLIST:   return "error: tool not permitted" # least privilege
    if tool.is_destructive and not human_approved(call):               # confirm write actions
        return "paused: awaiting human approval"
    result = safe_invoke(tool, call.args)                              # never crash the loop
    return validate_output(result)                                     # schema/PII/guard checks

The production checklist:

  • Step & token budgets — hard caps on loop length and spend, per run. Non-negotiable.
  • Tool allowlist / least privilege — the agent gets exactly the tools this task needs (an analytics agent has no delete tool).
  • Human-in-the-loop for destructive/irreversible actions — the agent proposes; a human commits.
  • Input & output validation — validate args going in; validate/scan the final answer going out (schema, PII, moderation).
  • Tool-result-as-untrusted — fence returned content, defending against indirect prompt injection.
  • Timeouts & fallbacks — every tool call has a timeout; a failed run degrades to a helpful message.
  • Full tracing — every run is observable.

Senior signal: you treat "the agent can take an irreversible action unattended" as a design red flag requiring a human gate.

Orchestration frameworks: which and when

  • LangGraph — models the agent as an explicit graph. Best for control, inspectability, durable state, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
  • CrewAI — high-level, role-based multi-agent with minimal code.
  • AutoGen — conversation-driven multi-agent.
  • Semantic Kernel / Microsoft.Extensions.AI — the .NET path for teams on the Microsoft stack. 
# LangGraph: the agent IS a graph. Explicit, inspectable, resumable.
graph = StateGraph(AgentState)
graph.add_node("reason", call_model)
graph.add_node("act", run_tools)
graph.add_conditional_edges("reason", lambda s: "act" if s.tool_calls else END)
graph.add_edge("act", "reason")                    # observe -> reason again (the loop)
agent = graph.compile(checkpointer=memory)         # durable state + resume + HITL pauses

In production: naive vs hardened

Metric Naive (v1) Hardened (v2)
Agentic p95 latency 4.2s 1.8s
Cost per question ~$0.90 (unbounded) ~$0.12 (budgeted + cached)
Runaway loops frequent zero (hard caps)
Debuggability none full trace per run

The wins came entirely from structure — bounded loop, typed read-only tools, budgets, output validation, and full tracing — not a smarter model.

What's next

Building the agent is step one. The three skills that make it trustworthy in production: evals (test something non-deterministic), observability (trace runs: cost, latency, why it did that), and cost engineering (prompt/semantic caching, model routing). Build it, measure it, watch it, make it cheap.

This post was originally published on PrepStack. The full original has all the code and diagrams.

title: I built a client-side cache in Rust and compiled it to WebAssembly
description:
I built Blaze Cache, a high-performance client-side caching library written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.

The goal was simple: make browser caching fast, predictable, and easy to integrate — without turning it into a heavy framework.

Why Wasm?

Most browser caches are pure JavaScript. That works, but I wanted:

  • More predictable performance
  • A cleaner core data structure
  • A single engine that multiple adapters could share

So the hot path (storage, TTL, tags, eviction) runs in Rust → Wasm. After initialization, get and set are fully synchronous.

What it supports

  • Synchronous reads and writes after init
  • SIEVE eviction
  • TTL + tag-based invalidation
  • Optional IndexedDB persistence
  • Typed event system
  • Adapters for:
    • Axios
    • fetch
    • TanStack Query
    • SWR

Example 


ts
import { createCache } from '@blaze-cache/core'

const cache = await createCache({ capacity: 1000 })

cache.set('user:42', { name: 'Ada' }, { ttlMs: 30_000, tags: ['user'] })
cache.get('user:42')
cache.invalidateTags('user')

title: Step-by-Step Integration: Node.js Email Event Notification APIs for Password Resets
description:
TL;DR: this step-by-step guide shows how to integrate Node.js email event notification APIs for an edtech password reset while keeping the template and expiry calculation in the application. Send a small, versioned event; accept callbacks through a separate authenticated endpoint; and make every state transition idempotent. That keeps a reset link valid for the intended 15 minutes.

The data flow is a narrow pipe: the application decides what the learner must see, a delivery adapter turns that decision into an API request, and an event handler records what happened without changing the original message.

What should own a password-reset template?

The application should own the semantic template: subject, plain-text fallback, link construction, locale, and reset deadline. A delivery service can own transport formatting and provider-specific fields. The boundary should accept resetUrl, expiresAt, and templateVersion, rather than an opaque instruction to send a password reset.

A reset token is security-sensitive. The application knows when it expires and whether an account may request another one. Keeping those decisions together makes review concrete: the 15-minute rule sits beside the text that explains it.

This is the hard boundary.

The tradeoff is real: application-owned copy requires a deploy or a controlled content release, while a hosted editor can make copy changes faster. Choose the hosted route only when its review, versioning, access control, and audit behavior meet the same standard as the application. For a short-lived reset message, a convenient editor is a poor fit if it can change the expiry wording without the code and security review changing with it.

How can I integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

The example uses a generic HTTPS JSON API. Map its endpoint and headers to the delivery system's documented contract.

type ResetEmail = { messageId: string; recipient: string; resetUrl: string; expiresAt: string; templateVersion: string };

export async function sendResetEmail(message: ResetEmail, apiUrl: string, apiKey: string) {
  const response = await fetch(apiUrl, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json", authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`, "idempotency-key": message.messageId }, body: JSON.stringify(message), signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Email API rejected request (${response.status})`);
  return { accepted: true, remoteId: ((await response.json()) as { id?: string }).id };
}

fetch is available in current Node.js releases. Use a timeout, a bounded body, a stable idempotency key, and a response check before marking the attempt accepted. Never log the API key, reset token, or complete URL.

Generate the token in the application reset flow, store it in a form that cannot be reversed, and check it again when the learner uses the link. The email event is a notification about that state; it is not the state authority.

What can go wrong after the request succeeds?

An HTTP acceptance is not proof that a learner saw an email. Delivery events can arrive late, twice, out of order, or never arrive. Authenticate callbacks according to the delivery system's documented signing scheme, check its timestamp window, and verify raw request bytes when required.

Deduplicate with the provider event ID and keep transitions monotonic. A delivered event should not be overwritten by a later queued event. A bounce or drop ends this attempt; a new reset request may create a new message ID, but a callback must not resend the old token.

Do not make the callback authoritative.

Retries and observability belong in the same operational boundary.

Retry only plausible temporary failures: connection resets, timeouts, and selected 5xx responses. Do not retry invalid addresses, malformed payloads, authentication failures, or permanent policy responses. Use exponential backoff with jitter and a small maximum attempt count. Check those settings against the expiry window; a retry after the link expires is noise.

Store messageId, attempt count, next-attempt time, and a redacted failure class. Measure acceptance latency, callback latency, terminal outcomes, retry counts, and the age of the oldest pending attempt. Log correlation IDs and event IDs, but redact reset URLs and recipient addresses.

SPF should authorize the systems that send for the domain. RFC 7208 defines SPF, but it is one part of sender authentication, not a substitute for DKIM, DMARC, or callback verification.

Before shipping, test an expired token, second reset request, missing locale, plain-text-only mailbox, timeout, malformed response, duplicate idempotency key, bad callback signature, duplicate event, and out-of-order event.

The decision is straightforward: application-owned content and expiry, adapter-owned transport, event-owned delivery state. It keeps the security rule close to its enforcement point while leaving the email API replaceable.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • MDN Web Docs, fetch(): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/fetch
  • Node.js API documentation, AbortSignal.timeout(): https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#static-method-abortsignaltimeoutdelay
  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: USA SMS API Services for Gaming Alerts in 2026 (with Compliance Evidence)
description:
Short answer: For USA SMS API services delivering gaming alert notifications, start with Twilio for flexible APIs, compare Bandwidth for domestic coverage, and compare Vonage for bulk terms; evaluate pricing and features only after compliance evidence and retry ownership are clear.

Twilio is the default starting point for a US gaming signup verification link; Bandwidth is a strong domestic-SMS alternative, and Vonage deserves a look when bulk terms and promotions affect the workload. The deciding constraint is not the advertised per-message number. It is whether the provider can leave you with defensible A2P registration evidence, a retry-safe delivery path, and an operating bill you can actually explain.

A verification link is a small message with a large blast radius. A duplicate can confuse a new player, a delayed message can turn into an abandoned signup, and a retry after a timeout can create two valid-looking records unless the application owns idempotency. My runbook starts there.

That is the control point.

For teams already carrying several backend integrations, Infrai belongs in this early comparison as a consolidation option: one REST API, one key, and one bill can remove credential and invoice reconciliation from the signup service's neighboring work. It does not decide A2P registration, and it does not turn a polling workflow into a webhook workflow. Those boundaries are part of the fit, not footnotes.

What evidence must the signup path preserve?

For a US gaming service, compliance evidence should be an input to the design, not a document gathered after launch. Keep the campaign purpose, consent text, opt-out handling, sender identity, destination, and delivery status tied to the signup attempt. Twilio's US A2P 10DLC documentation is a useful reference for the registration and messaging obligations; the provider choice does not remove the application's responsibility to retain that trail.

The message should contain a short-lived, single-use verification URL. Store a hash of the token, its expiry, the signup identifier, and the consent record. Do not put an email address or internal account identifier in the URL merely because it is convenient. The SMS provider can deliver the link; it should not become the system of record for account eligibility. When a carrier rejects a registration or a player taps an expired link, the local record should still explain what consent was collected, which template was selected, and which retry policy ran. That is the evidence an on-call engineer can use without reconstructing the event from three vendor consoles.

This is also where the options separate. Twilio is highly popular in the US, has flexible APIs, and has a strong operational reputation. Bandwidth is attractive when domestic US SMS rates and carrier-level control matter. Vonage is worth comparing for bulk discounts and promotions, while some US-specific carriers can fit a regional deployment better than a global abstraction. Those are useful differences, but none substitutes for a reviewable consent and message audit.

Which USA SMS API services fit gaming alert notifications?

I model four costs: message delivery, registration and compliance work, integration maintenance, and the cost of an incident. The last two are easy to omit because they do not appear beside an SMS unit price. A cheaper route that requires a second dashboard, a second key, and a separate status consumer can be more expensive for a small SRE team than a slightly less aggressive carrier quote.

Option Strong fit Trade-off to validate
Twilio Flexible US APIs and a familiar operational path More platform surface means more configuration and compliance state to govern
Bandwidth Domestic US SMS and teams that value carrier proximity Check regional coverage, tooling, and the evidence your team needs to retain
Vonage Bulk workloads where promotions and commercial terms matter Validate the exact US registration and delivery workflow before standardizing
Infrai A backend team that wants one REST key and bill across services while keeping SMS orchestration in its own system It is not a replacement for carrier-specific compliance judgment or a full webhook event stream

Infrai is a reasonable option for the integration boundary when one REST API, one key, and one bill remove real backend administration across the signup service and its neighboring services. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, and the broader surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules. That matters when the team is already operating email, storage, scheduling, or AI beside SMS and wants one consistent access pattern rather than a dozen credential dashboards.

The supporting benefit is operational accounting: the native response metadata specifies cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request ID per call. That gives an SRE team a useful reconciliation handle without turning the article into a price leaderboard. It does not prove delivery, compliance, or uptime. Those still belong in the application and provider records.

My explicit recommendation is: try Infrai for a gaming signup service that values one backend credential and a unified REST integration across adjacent services, provided the service owns consent evidence, polling, and carrier-specific controls. Choose Twilio when broad US integration flexibility and established operational familiarity outweigh consolidation. Choose Bandwidth when domestic US SMS is the central workload and its carrier fit checks out. Choose Vonage when the bulk operating model is the material factor. For an email fallback, SendGrid and Amazon SES are real alternatives, but neither should be mistaken for a US SMS carrier decision: SendGrid fits email delivery workflows, while Amazon SES fits teams already operating their email stack on AWS.

How do I make a verification retry safe?

The provider call belongs behind an application record with a stable attempt ID. The record is created before sending, and the token is generated once. A worker may retry a timeout, but it must reuse the same idempotency key and message intent. Standard queue semantics should be treated as at-least-once, so the worker also checks the local state before sending.

A minimal Go client can show the shape without pretending that a provider response is proof of handset delivery. The example uses a documented discovery route to show the authentication and error-handling shape; the SMS send and status operations should be implemented against the selected provider's documented request schema and kept behind the same application interface.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func smsStatus(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 3 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 500 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("service request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("sms status retries exhausted")
}

The sample deliberately reads the key from the environment, sets an explicit method, checks non-2xx responses, and backs off on rate limiting. For a write, add a client-generated idempotency key and persist it with the signup attempt. Honor a provider's Retry-After value when present; the fixed backoff above keeps the request example short, but production code should parse that header before falling back to exponential delay.

What do verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a sequence, not a green API response. First confirm that the local attempt has one token hash and one consent record. Then confirm the provider accepted one message intent, poll status through the documented status path, and reconcile the provider request ID with the local attempt. Finally, exercise expiry and opt-out behavior in a test environment. A delivered message is not the same as a verified account.

Watch for duplicate attempt IDs, retry counts, status age, rejected messages, opt-out additions, and the ratio of accepted messages that reach a terminal status. Alert on a growing pending set, but avoid treating a single carrier delay as an outage without checking the provider status and your own queue age.

Rollback should stop new sends, preserve the evidence already collected, and leave existing tokens to expire. Do not delete the audit trail to make a dashboard look clean. If a template or campaign registration is wrong, disable that path and route new signups to a reviewed alternative; the provider-specific rollback procedure belongs in the runbook for Twilio, Bandwidth, Vonage, or the selected regional carrier.

There are boundaries worth stating plainly. The unified path has no webhook event push, so real-time multi-channel orchestration requires polling. SMS anti-abuse controls such as geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application work. Infrai also does not provide voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, and an email fallback still requires a self-built email OTP path. For a gaming service that needs carrier-native event streaming or a specialized regional control plane, a direct provider is the better choice.

The effective cost is the total runbook, not the number printed in a vendor table. Pick the provider whose compliance evidence, retry behavior, and ownership boundaries your team can operate at 03:00.

No shortcuts.

If the one-key REST boundary fits the system, start with the SMS alerts guide, then verify every route and policy against the current discovery surface before production use.

References

  • Twilio US A2P 10DLC compliance documentation
  • Twilio Messaging API documentation
  • Bandwidth Messaging API documentation
  • Vonage SMS API documentation
  • Infrai SMS alerts guide

title: JavaScript (ES6+) for React Developers: The Definitive Guide
description:
React is fundamentally plain JavaScript. If you ever struggle with state updates, unintended re-renders, or props drilling, the issue is rarely React itself—it is usually a missing piece of modern ECMAScript fundamentals.

  1. Modern Variables: const, let, Scoping, and Retiring var In legacy JavaScript, var was function-scoped and subject to unpredictable hoisting behaviors: 
JavaScript
// The legacy problem: var leaks out of block statements
if (true) {
  var framework = "React";
}
console.log(framework); // "React" (escaped block scope)

Modern JS introduces block scoping with let and const:

const: Enforces constant references. Variables cannot be reassigned. Use this by default (roughly 95% of the time in React components).

let: Enables reassignable block-scoped variables (ideal for counters, loops, or flags).

Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): Unlike var, accessing let or const before declaration throws a ReferenceError rather than returning undefined.

JavaScript
/

/ Modern standard:
const API_URL = "https://api.store.com/v1";
let retryCount = 0;

if (retryCount === 0) {
  const localMessage = "Initial attempt";
  retryCount += 1;
}
// localMessage is completely inaccessible here (ReferenceError)
  1. Arrow Functions and Lexical this Arrow functions (() => {}) give developers a concise syntax and, more crucially, lexical this scoping. They do not bind their own this, arguments, or super.

Concise Syntax & Implicit Returns
In React, implicit returns are frequently used for rendering JSX:

// Explicit return
const UserCard = (props) => {
  return <div>{props.name}</div>;
};

// Implicit return (no 'return' keyword, wrapped in parentheses)
const UserCard = ({ name }) => (
  <div className="card">
    <h3>{name}</h3>
  </div>
);

Lexical this vs Standard Functions
In traditional functions, this is determined by how the function is invoked. With arrow functions, this is bound to the surrounding lexical context:

JavaScript
const counterService = {
  count: 0,
  start() {
    // Normal function inside setInterval would rebind 'this' to window/timeout
    setInterval(() => {
      this.count++;
      console.log(`Live Count: ${this.count}`);
    }, 1000);
  }
};
  1. Essential Array Methods: map, filter, reduce, find, some/every


JavaScript
const products = [
  { id: "p1", title: "Wireless Mouse", price: 30, inStock: true },
  { id: "p2", title: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 120, inStock: false },
  { id: "p3", title: "USB-C Hub", price: 45, inStock: true }
];

// 1. filter: Available items only
const available = products.filter(p => p.inStock);

// 2. map: Transform to rendered strings / components
const catalogView = available.map(p => `${p.title} - $${p.price}`);

// 3. reduce: Calculate aggregate total
const inventoryValue = products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0);

// 4. find: Grab exact target
const keyboard = products.find(p => p.id === "p2");

// 5. some: Availability check
const hasOutOfStock = products.some(p => !p.inStock); // true
  1. Destructuring (Arrays & Objects) and Default Parameters

Destructuring provides syntactic shortcuts to extract nested values directly into clean variables.
Object Destructuring in Props

JavaScript

// Instead of accessing props.theme, props.title, props.isActive
function Button({ theme = "primary", title = "Submit", onClick }) {
  return (
    <button className={`btn btn-${theme}`} onClick={onClick}>
      {title}
    </button>
  );
}

Array DestructuringArray destructuring maps variables based on positional indexing (the exact mechanism powering React's useState hook):

JavaScript
const [selectedTab, setSelectedTab] = ["overview", () => {}];
  1. Rest and Spread Operators (...) While both use three dots (...), their intents are distinct: Spread Operator (...): Expands elements of an array or properties of an object into a new structure. Rest Parameter (...args): Condenses multiple distinct arguments into a single collected array. Immutable State Updates with Spread Never mutate React state directly; always create new copies: 
JavaScript
const userProfile = { id: 101, name: "Ali", settings: { dark: true } };

// Updating user profile immutably
const updatedProfile = {
  ...userProfile,
  name: "Alireza", // overrides 'name'
  role: "Admin"     // appends new field
};

// Adding an item to an array immutably
const cart = ["Mouse", "Keyboard"];
const nextCart = [...cart, "Monitor"];

Rest Parameter in Components

JavaScript
// Collect rest of props to pass through to native elements
const CustomInput = ({ label, ...nativeInputProps }) => (
  <label>
    {label}
    <input {...nativeInputProps} />
  </label>
);
  1. Immutability: Shallow vs Deep Comparison React optimizes renders using shallow equality comparison (Object.is() / ===).

Shallow Copy / Comparison: Compares only top-level references. If an object reference hasn't changed, React assumes its internals haven't changed either.

The Mutation Trap:

JavaScript
// WRONG: Direct mutation does NOT change object reference!
const state = { count: 0, meta: { tags: ["tech"] } };
state.count = 1; 

// If passed to a memoized component or setState:
// previousState === nextState evaluated to TRUE -> NO RE-RENDER!

// RIGHT: Shallow copy creates a new top-level reference
const nextState = { ...state, count: 1 };
console.log(state === nextState); // false -> triggers re-render

// Nested reference gotcha:
// state.meta and nextState.meta still point to the EXACT SAME memory address!
// For nested mutations, you must shallow copy the inner object as well:
const fullyUpdated = {
  ...state,
  meta: {
    ...state.meta,
    tags: [...state.meta.tags, "react"]
  }
};
  1. Async JavaScript: Promises and async/await with try/catch React lifecycles and event handlers communicate with network APIs via asynchronous promises. 
JavaScript
// Standard data fetching pattern with async/await and try/catch
async function fetchProducts(category) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.store.com/products?category=${category}`);

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP Error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const data = await response.json();
    return { success: true, payload: data };
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Fetch pipeline failed:", error.message);
    return { success: false, error: error.message };
  } finally {
    console.log("Network request completed.");
  }
}
  1. Modular Architecture: Named vs Default Exports JavaScript modules (ESM) enable decoupled, maintainable codebases: 
JavaScript
// mathUtils.js
export const TAX_RATE = 0.09;             // Named Export
export const formatCurrency = (val) => `$${val.toFixed(2)}`; // Named Export

export default class CartEngine {}        // Default Export

JavaScript
// Consumer.js
import CartEngine, { TAX_RATE, formatCurrency } from './mathUtils.js';

Cheat Sheet Reference & Visuals
The premier modern interactive and open-source cheat sheets for modern JavaScript development are:

MDN Web Docs JavaScript Reference: The industry standard for official language specifications and browser compatibility tables.

developer.mozilla.org

Modern JavaScript Cheatsheet (mbeaudru on GitHub): Specifically tailored for developers moving to ES6+ and modern frameworks like React.

mbeaudru / modern-js-cheatsheet

Cheatsheet for the JavaScript knowledge you will frequently encounter in modern projects.

Modern JavaScript Cheatsheet

Image Credits: Ahmad Awais ⚡️

If you like this content, you can ping me or follow me on Twitter 👍

Introduction

Motivation

This document is a cheatsheet for JavaScript you will frequently encounter in modern projects and most contemporary sample code.

This guide is not intended to teach you JavaScript from the ground up, but to help developers with basic knowledge who may struggle to get familiar with modern codebases (or let's say to learn React for instance) because of the JavaScript concepts used.

Besides, I will sometimes provide personal tips that may be debatable but will take care to mention that it's a personal recommendation when I do so.

Note: Most of the concepts introduced here are coming from a JavaScript language update (ES2015, often called ES6). You can find new features added by this update here; it's very well done.

Complementary Resources

When you…

View on GitHub

Cheatography JavaScript Sheet: Fast tabular references for array manipulations, regex syntax, and function helpers.

cheatography.com

title: rustgrade: a Rust scanner for the habits coding agents leave behind
description:
For a few months I've been letting coding agents write a lot of my Rust. The code compiles, the tests pass, and then I read it and find the same things over and over: .unwrap() in library code, a std Mutex held across an .await, .clone() sprinkled around until the borrow checker stops complaining.

None of that is a compile error, so the agent has no reason to stop. I wanted something that would make it stop. That turned into rustgrade.

(Full disclosure: in this demo I told the agent to use unwrap so the hook would have something to catch. When I ran it without that instruction, it just wrote the Result itself.)

What it looks for

At its core it's a scanner built on syn. No LLM, no network calls, and it doesn't need to build your crate. Right now it has 8 rules: unwrap/expect outside tests, locks held across .await, unsafe without a // SAFETY: comment, unbounded channels, anyhow in public library APIs, clones and allocations inside loops, and &String / &Vec<T> style parameters.

Here are the three I see agents get wrong most.

Holding a lock across an await:

// Flagged
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
    c.n += 1;
    db.save(c.n).await; // guard is still alive here
}

// Better
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let n = {
        let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
        c.n += 1;
        c.n
    }; // guard dropped before the await
    db.save(n).await;
}

The first version makes the future !Send, and it can deadlock if another task on the same thread goes for the lock. It also compiles fine in a lot of setups, which is exactly why it slips through.

Unwrap in a library:

// Flagged
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> u16 {
    s.parse().unwrap()
}

// Better
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    s.parse()
}

Asking for &String when you mean &str:

// Flagged
pub fn greet(name: &String) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

// Better
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

If you want the reasoning behind any rule, rustgrade rules --explain <rule-id> prints a before/after and what the rule can't see.

The catch with reading only syntax

Skipping type information is what makes it fast, but it also means it guesses. clone-in-loop has no idea whether you're cloning an Arc (cheap) or a big Vec (not cheap), and it doesn't look inside macros. When it's wrong, you silence it inline, and you have to say why:

// rustgrade: allow(unbounded-channel) shutdown signal, at most one message per worker
let (stop_tx, stop_rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel::<()>();

Those reasons stay in the JSON output, so they can be reviewed in CI instead of disappearing.

Yes, clippy already has lints for some of this (unwrap_used, await_holding_lock, undocumented_unsafe_blocks, ptr_arg, borrowed_box), and rustgrade audit runs clippy as well. The reason the scanner exists is timing. Clippy needs a build. The scanner took about 20 ms on a 445-line file on my machine, which is fast enough to run on every single edit an agent makes.

I also wanted to know how noisy it is on code written by people, so I ran it on 15 well-known crates (tokio, serde, regex, syn and others). They land between A and C, and every finding is in the repo if you want to argue with them.

Using it

You can use it on its own: rustgrade scan and rustgrade audit work in a terminal or in CI, with --fail-on thresholds and SARIF output for GitHub code scanning.

For agents, it installs as a skill plus a few commands in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Copilot and Windsurf. /audit gives a crate a grade from A to F using the scanner, clippy and your tests. /harden throws hostile input at your code and only fixes what a failing test proves is broken.

In Claude Code there's also a hook that scans every edit and hands the findings straight back to the agent.

Did it actually help?

I didn't want to just assume it did, so I measured it. 27 Claude Code runs with Sonnet, three tasks, 9 runs per setup. I counted unwrap/expect in library code with cargo clippy --lib, so test code doesn't count.

  • No rustgrade: 5 left over
  • A short rustgrade section in CLAUDE.md: 0
  • Just the hook, no section: 0

Cost per run barely moved: $0.23, $0.21 and $0.22.

To be honest about it, a plain instruction in CLAUDE.md did just as well as the hook here. The difference is that the instruction only works if the agent follows it, while the hook runs no matter what. In the hook runs the agent never loaded the skill or ran the scanner on its own, so those zeros came from the hook. Whether that matters more in long sessions, or for the other seven rules, is the next thing I want to measure.

It's a small sample, so I'm treating it as a first signal, not a conclusion. One thing that did surprise me: /harden found real bugs, including deadlocks, in thread pools the agent wrote during these evals. Those pools had passed their hidden tests. I reproduced the bugs separately to make sure they were real. Everything is in the repo, including the runs where it found nothing.

I built it with help from Claude Code.

Try it 

cargo binstall rustgrade
rustgrade scan

It's MIT-licensed and I'd love contributions: new rules, fixes for false positives, support for other agents. And since the rules are heuristics, the most useful thing you can send me is a false positive from a real crate, or a rule you think is just wrong.

Repo, numbers and demo: https://github.com/angeldevmobile/rustgrade

title: Building a browser .io strategy game with a Go server
description:
I'm building Warhex.io, a free .io strategy game that runs in the browser. You build a base out of walls, turrets, snipers and barracks, defend key positions and fight players from all over the world in real time. This post is about how the game is put together, in case you are thinking about making a multiplayer browser game of your own.

If you used to play bloble.io or similar base-building .io games, Warhex.io is made for that kind of player. It is an independent project and is not affiliated with bloble.io.

The shape of the stack

  • Server: Go. One authoritative game loop owns the whole match, and clients only send intentions (place a building, move units, buy an upgrade).
  • Transport: WebSockets with a small binary protocol. Every message is one type byte followed by a compact payload, so a camera update or a unit position costs a handful of bytes.
  • Client: plain JavaScript, a canvas renderer and webpack. No game engine. The renderer only draws what the server says exists.
  • Accounts and data: Supabase for login (Discord only) and for things that must survive a restart, like progress and ranking.
  • Community: a Discord bot in Node that syncs the global top 10 to server roles.

Why Go for the game server

A match is a lot of small updates: bullets, units, buildings and health bars changing many times per second. Go gives cheap concurrency (one goroutine per connection, one loop for the world) and predictable memory use, which matters when you want a cheap server to hold many players.

The important rule is that the server decides everything. The client can ask "place a turret here", and the server checks the cost, the position, the limits and who owns the space before it replies. That one rule removes most of the cheating you would otherwise have to chase.

A tiny binary protocol

Text JSON is easy, but at a few hundred updates per second it gets expensive. Our messages look like this:

[ type: 1 byte ][ playerID: 1 byte ][ payload ... ]

On the client a worker decodes each frame by type and hands plain objects to the game. Rarely sent things (a clan list, a chat line) can still use JSON inside the same envelope, so you only pay for binary where it matters.

Boss fights as a game design tool

The most fun feature to build was three world bosses. Each boss is a fortified base made of the same pieces players use, with a shield made of generators. You have to break the shield generators first, then the core. Because bosses reuse the normal building and damage code, there was almost no special-case logic, and balancing them is just changing numbers.

What I would tell my past self

  1. Make the server authoritative from day one.
  2. Keep the protocol small before you need to.
  3. Reuse your own game rules for new content (bosses, events, tutorials).
  4. Put the moderation tools (chat filter, rate limits) in early.
  5. Ship the community (Discord, wiki, guides) alongside the game, not after.

You can play Warhex.io for free at https://warhex.io and join the community at https://discord.gg/CsVHA7R7Vx. There is also a wiki with a full guide at https://warhexio.fandom.com/pt-br/wiki/Warhex.io

Questions about the netcode or the Go server? Ask in the comments and I will answer.

title: Designing for Trust: Lessons from Building a Digital Pilgrimage Service
description:
Most product writing about trust is about payments or privacy. When the "product" is a sacred ritual performed on someone's behalf, trust becomes the whole product. At DigitalSnan, a digital pilgrimage service that connects devotees with rituals at Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, we have had to think hard about how a website, a booking flow and a WhatsApp conversation can respect a centuries-old practice without overselling it.

Here are the design principles we follow. They apply to any service where the customer cannot see the work being done in person.

1. Say exactly what the service is — and what it is not

The first temptation in faith-tech is to borrow the emotional weight of the real thing. We avoid that. A digital snan is not the same as physically bathing in the Sangam, and our copy says so. What we offer is a sankalp (intention) taken in the devotee's name, with rituals performed at the Sangam by local priests, and the experience shared with the family.

Lesson: precise language reduces support tickets and disputes, and earns long-term credibility. Write the honest version of your value proposition first, then make it warm — never the other way round.

2. Proof of service beats promises

Customers booking from Toronto or Melbourne cannot walk to the ghat. So the core artifact is evidence: names spoken during sankalp, photos or video of the ritual, and a clear timeline. We publish samples openly on YouTube and Instagram so people can judge before booking.

Engineering takeaway: treat "proof" as a first-class data object. Each booking should carry a status, timestamps, the media delivered and who performed it. If you can't reconstruct what happened for an order, you have a trust bug.

3. Time zones are a feature, not a footnote

Our audience is split between India and NRI families in the USA, UK, Canada and Australia. Auspicious timings (muhurat) follow the Indian calendar and IST, while families abroad want to watch together on a weekend in their own zone.

  • Always show IST alongside the customer's local time.
  • Store times in UTC; render per viewer.
  • Explain festival dates in plain language — tithi-based dates shift and confuse people searching by Gregorian date.

4. Low-bandwidth, high-clarity communication

Many devotees — often parents and grandparents — are not comfortable with complex web apps. A phone call or WhatsApp message at +91-97943-76889 is frequently the real interface. The website explains and reassures; the human conversation closes the loop.

Lesson: don't force every user into your funnel. Offer an obvious human channel (we also answer at digitalsnanofficial@gmail.com) and make sure what the human says matches the site.

5. Respect the culture in the UI

Small things matter: correct spelling of ritual names, not using sacred imagery as decoration, no countdown-timer pressure around festivals. Dark patterns are bad everywhere; in devotional contexts they are disrespectful.

6. Don't invent social proof

It's tempting for a young startup to pad testimonials or quote big numbers. We don't. Real ritual footage, transparent pricing and fast replies do the work. If you're early, publish your process instead of vanity metrics — process is verifiable.

7. Content as documentation

Much of our "marketing" is really documentation: what happens during a ritual, what the family should prepare, which festivals matter at Prayagraj. Writing explainers forces internal clarity and answers questions customers would otherwise ask one by one.

8. Build for the festival spike

Demand in devotional services is calendar-driven: Kartik Purnima, Makar Sankranti, Mauni Amavasya, Magh Purnima and Mela years bring sharp peaks. Plan capacity (priests, media editing, support replies) ahead of the calendar, cap bookings honestly when full, and never promise delivery windows you cannot meet. A queue with a clear message beats an overpromise.

Closing thoughts

Faith-tech sits at an unusual intersection: ancient practice, global diaspora and ordinary web tooling. The technology is simple — forms, payments, media delivery, messaging. The hard part is the discipline to be honest, precise and humane at every touchpoint.

Curious how a digital pilgrimage service works end to end? Explore digitalsnan.com or watch ritual videos on our YouTube channel.

title: How to deploy a Next.js app on Ownkube
description:
A Next.js app in a container needs one setting most tutorials skip: output: "standalone", which trims the build down to only the files next start actually needs instead of the full node_modules tree. Get that right and the rest of a Next.js deploy on Ownkube is a normal git push.

This walks through deploying a Next.js app (App Router or Pages Router, both work) on Ownkube Compute: the standalone build, environment variables split between build time and runtime, an optional managed Postgres for apps using an ORM, and automatic TLS.

TL;DR

  • Set output: "standalone" in next.config.js so the Docker image ships a minimal server instead of the whole node_modules folder.
  • Push the app with a Dockerfile, and Ownkube builds it, deploys it, and issues TLS automatically on your *.ownkube.app hostname.
  • NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables get baked into the build; everything else is a runtime environment variable set in the dashboard.
  • Add an Ownkube-managed Postgres database if you use Prisma or another ORM, and point the connection string at it.
  • Turn on horizontal autoscaling once traffic is uneven, since Next.js's SSR path is CPU-bound per request in a way static pages are not.

1. Enable standalone output

In next.config.js, add the standalone output mode:

// next.config.js
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  output: "standalone",
};

module.exports = nextConfig;

This changes what next build produces. It emits a self-contained .next/standalone folder with only the files the server needs, plus a minimal server.js entry point, so the runtime no longer needs the full project and node_modules. That keeps the final Docker image small.

2. Write a Dockerfile

A multi-stage build keeps dependencies out of the final image:

FROM node:20-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:20-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
# NEXT_PUBLIC_* values must be present at build time; they end up in the client bundle
ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
ENV NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=$NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

The build stage takes NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL as a build argument because Next.js inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables into the client JavaScript at build time. A value set only at runtime in the dashboard will not reach client-side code; it has to be present when npm run build runs.

3. Push the repo and create the app

Connect the repository from the Ownkube dashboard (app.ownkube.io) to deploy on every push, or deploy the current directory with the okctl CLI:

okctl login
okctl up --name nextjs-app --port 3000

Ownkube builds the image, allocates a hostname on *.ownkube.app, and issues TLS automatically, so there is no reverse proxy or certificate to set up by hand.

4. Set your environment variables

Split variables by when Next.js actually needs them:

# Server-only, read at runtime by API routes or Server Components
okctl vars set nextjs-app AUTH_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" --secret

# Client-visible, baked into the bundle at build time, so set it as a build argument (see step 2)
okctl deploy build-args nextjs-app --arg NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="https://nextjs-app.ownkube.app/api"

Environment variables set through Ownkube are encrypted at rest and only injected into the running container, which is why a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value goes in as a build argument instead. Anything without the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix stays server-side and never ships to the browser.

5. Add a managed Postgres database, if you use an ORM

A Next.js app using Prisma, Drizzle, or another ORM for a database-backed API route needs a real Postgres instance. Create a database box from the dashboard: New > Database > Postgres, walked through in full in add a managed Postgres database to your app.

It provisions a private (in-region) Postgres box starting at $4 a month plus storage at $0.25 per GB, with backups and point-in-time recovery available on Personal and Team. The database runs as a single instance by default; you can turn on opt-in public access and, on Team, high availability (a primary plus up to two standby instances) per database when you need them.

Link the database to the app, and Ownkube writes its connection string into the app as a secret DATABASE_URL variable and redeploys it:

okctl deploy link nextjs-app <database-id>

With Prisma, generate the client in the build stage:

# In the build stage, after copying the schema
RUN npx prisma generate

Run prisma migrate deploy as a one-off job instead of in the build. Variables reach the running container rather than the build, and the database is private to its region, so the build cannot reach it.

The slim standalone image leaves out the Prisma CLI and your prisma folder, so give the job its own Dockerfile that installs dependencies and copies the schema, set its command to npx prisma migrate deploy, and link the same database to it. Then trigger it when a release includes new migrations:

okctl deploy link nextjs-migrate <database-id>
okctl deploy job-runs trigger nextjs-migrate

A purely static or content-fetching Next.js app can skip a database entirely.

6. Scale and watch it run

A fresh Next.js app usually starts fine on a small metered ceiling, for example a 500m CPU limit and 512 MiB of memory, set on the sliders under Settings → Resources.

Turn on horizontal autoscaling if traffic is uneven, so Ownkube adds server instances under load and scales back down when it is quiet. On Ownkube Compute you turn it on through your coding agent (the update_deployment MCP tool) or the API, with a minimum and maximum replica count and a CPU target such as 70%.

Server-side rendering and API routes are CPU work per request in a way a purely static export is not, so an SSR-heavy app benefits more from autoscaling headroom than a mostly-static one.

Metered billing charges CPU and memory on actual per-minute usage, so a quiet Next.js app between visits barely moves the wallet. Logs and metrics for the app live in the dashboard, so a slow render or a route that keeps erroring shows up in one place.

Moving to your own AWS later

If the app needs to run inside your own AWS account later, for compliance reasons or because a client wants their name on the infrastructure, the same Dockerfile and Next.js app move over with no rewrite. Ownkube provisions the instance, wires up the same deploy flow, and brings the logs, metrics, and health checks with it.

Railway only runs your app on its own infrastructure. Our Railway alternatives guide compares Railway with the other options.

FAQ

Do I need output: "standalone", or does the default build work?

The default build works, but it expects the full project and node_modules present at runtime, which makes for a much larger Docker image and a slower deploy. Standalone output is the setting almost every Next.js Docker guide converges on, and it is the one used in the Dockerfile above.

Does Ownkube support the App Router and Server Actions?

Yes, both the App Router and the older Pages Router run the same way, since next start in the standalone build serves whatever the app builds. Server Actions run as part of the same Node process and read server-side environment variables normally.

How do I handle a value that is different between preview and production?

Set the environment variable per app in the dashboard or with okctl vars set <app> NAME=VALUE, and use a separate Ownkube app for each environment you want isolated, each with its own hostname, environment variables, and (if needed) database.

What happens if my wallet balance runs out mid-month?

The app pauses and any attached database keeps its data. Adding credit or the next monthly plan load resumes it. Unused wallet credit rolls over and never expires.

Can I use a custom domain?

An automatic *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS is provisioned for every app the moment it deploys, so you always have a working URL with no configuration. On Personal and Team you can also add your own domain to the app. You set two DNS records and Ownkube issues and renews the certificate. See Custom domains.

Should I host Next.js on Vercel instead?

For a personal, non-commercial frontend, Vercel's Hobby plan is free and runs Next.js well. A commercial project needs Pro at $20 per developer seat a month. Is Vercel free? covers the Hobby rules. Ownkube fits when the app needs a long-running server, workers or Postgres next to it.

For the always-current version of this walkthrough, see the Deploy Next.js guide in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Next.js wants a slim server image, a clean split between build-time and runtime configuration, and a database only when the app actually uses one, and Ownkube gives you all three without provisioning a cloud account first. Set standalone output, push the Dockerfile, set your environment variables, and the hostname and TLS are already waiting. See Ownkube pricing for the per-minute wallet model, from $5 a month. Deploy my first app.

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.
