title: Skirmish: A Multiplayer Strategy Game Template in Java
description:
For years I avoided pitching Codename One as a game engine. Unity, Unreal and Godot own that market, and I didn't see a reason for a game developer to pick us. That changed while we were building our app templates. A modern mobile game is mostly app: sign-in, menus, a shop, friends lists, quests, push notifications, analytics and a server. The battle itself is a small part of the code. Those other parts are exactly what Codename One is good at.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Yesterday's post argued that complete applications are the new starting point. Skirmish is that idea applied to games. It's a real-time strategy game in the style of Clash Royale: two players face each other across a 3D arena, each drawing troops and spells from a deck, and the first to bring down the other's towers wins. The client, the server and the admin console are one Java project. Watch it first:

Download the Skirmish walkthrough video.

Open the Initializr, pick the Skirmish template, set your name and package, and you get the whole game. The source is under MIT-0. No royalties, no per-install fees, no revenue share and no runtime fee that can show up in your inbox next year. The characters and towers are KayKit models released under CC0.

What you get

Part What's in it
Battle A 3D arena with animated glTF characters, drag-and-drop cards, elixir, overtime, particle effects and a finishing camera sweep
Online play Trophy-banded matchmaking, challenge links, spectating and replays you can seek through
Progression A guided training battle, levels, daily quests, chests and achievements, all granted by the server
Monetization Gem packs and a season pass with server-side receipt checks, rewarded and interstitial ads
Growth Invite-a-friend links, campaign links, push notifications, a home screen spotlight and opt-in funnel analytics
Operations An admin console with live matches, player lookup, reports, queries, engagement pipelines and audited moderation
Content The Forge, an in-game editor where players and designers build cards, arenas, missions and campaigns

Home: battle, chests and quests.
A battle in the 3D arena.
The finishing camera.

The menus are the easy part

Ask anyone who has shipped a mobile game in a game engine where the time went, and menus come up fast. Scroll views that fight the touch input, text that doesn't wrap, layouts that break on a tablet, a store screen built out of sprites. Game engines are built around a scene graph, and a settings screen doesn't fit in one.

Every button, list, tab and dialog in Skirmish is an ordinary Codename One component, laid out with layout managers and styled in CSS. The wooden buttons you saw in the video are a style, with no images involved:

WoodButton {
    background: linear-gradient(to bottom, var(--wood-light), var(--wood));
    border: 0.6mm solid var(--wood-dark);
    border-radius: 2mm;
    color: var(--ink);
    font-family: "native:MainBold";
    font-size: 4mm;
    text-align: center;
    padding: 2.5mm;
    margin: 1.2mm 2mm;
}

Because the look is a gradient and a border, it stays sharp at every screen density. Want a different visual identity? The palette is a list of CSS variables at the top of theme.css (--night, --stone, --wood, --gold and more). Change them and every screen follows. Text wraps, lists scroll natively, right-to-left languages work, and the same screens run on a phone, a tablet and the desktop.

The battle is 3D, and it's Java

The arena is a GameView from com.codename1.gaming, rendered with the GPU API, with a perspective camera behind your king. The characters are rigged glTF models with skeletal animation, a new part of the gaming API that came out of this work. Playing a walk cycle and blending into an attack takes a few lines:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
GltfScene knight = GltfLoader.loadScene(in);
unit = new AnimatedModel(device, knight);
unit.hideNode("Shield_Spike"); // the file carries every prop
unit.play("Walking_A", true);
unit.addTo(this);
// in update(double dt): unit.update((float) dt);
// on attack: unit.crossFade("1H_Melee_Attack_Chop", 0.15f, false);




Swap in any rigged glTF character with the same animation names and it fights.

## Multiplayer without a networking team

The game rules live in their own module, `rules`. It's deterministic Java with no floating point and no clock, and four things compile it: the app, the server, the replays and the tests. Adding a card is one line:



```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
add(new CardDef("squire", "Squire", CardDef.TROOP, 3)
        .hp(1450).damage(160).hitTicks(24).range(700).speed(45).radius(500));

Online matches run in lockstep over a WebSocket. The server is the referee: it stamps each card a player drops with a tick slightly in the future and sends it to both phones, so both simulations stay identical and nobody can cheat by editing their client. Everything else, from sign-in to the shop, is REST through @RestClient interfaces in a module both sides share. Client and server compile against the same types, so a renamed field is a compile error on both ends instead of a bug report.

Promotion and monetization are built in

A game that nobody installs doesn't make money. Skirmish uses the Codename One APIs for growth, so the code is short. Inviting a friend from Friends.java:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
Invite invite = Invites.create(InviteRequest.create()
.campaign(CAMPAIGN)
.channel("share_sheet")
.payload(mine.code())
.title("Join me in Skirmish")
.description("A real-time card battle. Build a deck and fight me.")
.build());




The friend who joins gets bonus coins, and the Friends screen shows who joined and who has played. The same template wires up:

- **In-app purchases** of gem packs and a season pass, with receipts verified by your server.
- **Rewarded and interstitial ads**, where a rewarded ad grants its reward through the server.
- **Push notifications** when a chest opens or a friend challenges you.
- **Funnel analytics** that show where new players drop off, with opt-in consent.
- **Campaign links** for ads and social posts outside the app, and a home screen spotlight you change from the console.

The implementor's guide includes a step-by-step tutorial on growing a game with these: turn on measurement, read the funnel, bring players back with push, then grow through invitations.

## Run the game like a live service

The admin console ships in the same app. Moderators see live matches, automatic and reported flags, and player history, and they can warn, mute, suspend or ban with an audit trail. Product owners write queries over the game data, set up engagement pipelines and broadcast promotions. It runs on the desktop as well as on a phone.


<div class="release-screenshots" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(270px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start;margin:24px 0">
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-overview.png"><img width="800" height="480" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-overview.png" alt="The Skirmish admin console overview on the desktop" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The admin overview.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-pipelines.png"><img width="800" height="480" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-pipelines.png" alt="Engagement pipelines in the Skirmish admin console" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Engagement pipelines.</figcaption></figure>
</div>


## Make it yours

Skirmish is meant to be remixed. A few directions it could take:

- **Re-skin it** for a different setting: space, pirates, a cartoon farm. Swap the CSS palette, the glTF models and the card portraits. `PortraitStudio` renders new portraits from the models so the art stays consistent.
- **Change the game.** New cards, new arenas and a different elixir economy are data in the `rules` module. Bump `RulesVersion.ID` and the golden replay tests tell you which recorded battles changed.
- **Let players make content.** The Forge lets players build and share packs of cards, arenas and missions, and lets your designers publish official campaigns from the same editor.
- **Point an AI agent at it.** The whole game is one readable Java project, so "turn this into a cyberpunk tower defense with four lanes" is a reasonable prompt to start from.


<div class="release-screenshots" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(min(100%,150px),1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start;margin:24px 0">
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-deck.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-deck.png" alt="The Skirmish deck builder" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The deck builder.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-shop.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-shop.png" alt="The Skirmish shop with gem packs and a season pass" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The shop.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-friends.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-friends.png" alt="The friends screen with invitations" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Friends and invitations.</figcaption></figure>
</div>


The development profile needs nothing installed: an in-memory database, demo accounts and a simulated store. Run the server, start the simulator and play against the bot or a second simulator. The [Skirmish page](https://www.codenameone.com/skirmish/) has the overview and the [implementor's guide](https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/skirmish-implementors-guide/) walks through every part.

Tomorrow: [Parley: A Private Messenger Template You Can Brand](https://www.codenameone.com/blog/launch-your-own-private-messenger/).

title: Fewest transfers was correct. It also told a stranger to pay my friend.
description:
The plan said Coco pays Mia $75.20.

The arithmetic was right. Coco and Mia have never met. Coco wasn't even on the trip.

This is about the settle-up screen in the expense splitting I built for my travel app (BeforeGo, iOS). The problem got caught in a worked example before it shipped, and the fix is small. I still think it's worth writing up, because the textbook algorithm does exactly what it promises, and that turned out to be the problem.

Two kinds of people on a trip's bills

Most splitting apps assume everyone on a bill is in the group. On a real trip, that's not quite true:

  • Buddies: the people on the trip. They pay for things and split things with each other.
  • Others: friends back home you bought things for. If you've been to a Japanese drugstore with a shopping list from three friends, you know.

Others show up on exactly one kind of bill: one you paid on their behalf. They don't owe the group anything. They owe you.

The textbook settle-up

The usual way to settle a group's debts:

  1. Work out each person's net: what they paid minus what they owe. Positive means they're owed money.
  2. Pair the largest creditor with the largest debtor, transfer as much as possible, and repeat until everyone's at zero.

Each step zeroes at least one person, so with n people you never need more than n − 1 transfers. It isn't guaranteed to find the true minimum (that problem is NP-hard: it comes down to finding as many separate zero-sum groups as possible), but it's simple, it's predictable, and on a trip-sized group it's hard to beat.

Here's the version in the app, trimmed:

/// Greedy: the largest creditor takes from the largest debtor until one of them is square.
/// Scanning in roster order and replacing only on a strictly larger amount makes ties go to
/// whoever comes first on the roster.
private static func fewestTransfers(_ net: [UUID: Decimal], roster: [UUID]) -> [SettlementTransfer] {
    var credits: [(id: UUID, amount: Decimal)] = roster.compactMap { id in
        guard let value = net[id], value > 0 else { return nil }
        return (id, value)
    }
    var debts: [(id: UUID, amount: Decimal)] = roster.compactMap { id in
        guard let value = net[id], value < 0 else { return nil }
        return (id, -value)
    }

    // largest(_:) returns the index of the biggest amount; the first one wins a tie.
    var transfers: [SettlementTransfer] = []
    while !credits.isEmpty, !debts.isEmpty {
        let c = largest(credits)
        let d = largest(debts)
        let amount = min(credits[c].amount, debts[d].amount)
        transfers.append(SettlementTransfer(fromId: debts[d].id, toId: credits[c].id, amount: amount))
        credits[c].amount -= amount
        debts[d].amount -= amount
        if credits[c].amount == 0 { credits.remove(at: c) }
        if debts[d].amount == 0 { debts.remove(at: d) }
    }
    return transfers
}

The worked example

Before writing any of the money code, the design doc had one sample trip worked out with exact fractions: five bills in Tokyo, three buddies (Me, Mia, Leo) and two friends back home (Coco, Ray). Rate: 1 JPY = 0.0067 USD.

Bill Paid by Amount Split
Taxi Leo ¥3,900 ($26.13) Me, Mia, Leo
Hotel, 5 nights Mia ¥96,000 ($643.20) Me, Mia, Leo
Dinner Me ¥12,480 ($83.62) Me, Mia, Leo
teamLab tickets Mia ¥11,400 ($76.38) Me, Mia, Leo
Drugstore Me ¥19,830 ($132.86) line by line: Coco, Ray, and a bit for me, plus a 10% shopping fee for the friends

Put everyone in one pool and the nets are:

Person Net
Mia +443.14
Leo −250.31
Me −80.00
Coco −75.20
Ray −37.63

They add up to zero, as they should. Run the greedy on that pool and you get:

  • Leo → Mia $250.31
  • Me → Mia $80.00
  • Coco → Mia $75.20
  • Ray → Mia $37.63

Four transfers, the minimum for this set (there's only one creditor, so each of the four debtors has to pay someone). Every number checks out.

And it's absurd. Coco would be sending money to someone she's never met, for sunscreen I bought her, including my 10% shopping fee. Meanwhile I'd pay Mia $80 instead of the $192.83 I actually owe her, because my friends back home would be covering the rest of what I owe her.

The algorithm minimised the number of transfers. Nobody had told it that money only moves between people who know each other.

The fix: two ledgers, not one

Buddies net against each other and get the fewest-transfers plan. Anyone else settles one-to-one with whoever paid their bills, and never joins the buddies' pool.

In code, it's one branch where each debt gets recorded:

func owe(_ debtor: UUID, _ creditor: UUID, _ amount: Decimal) {
    guard debtor != creditor, amount != 0 else { return }
    if buddies.contains(debtor), buddies.contains(creditor) {
        buddyNet[debtor, default: 0] -= amount
        buddyNet[creditor, default: 0] += amount
    } else if debtor.uuidString < creditor.uuidString {
        // Unordered pair → balance; positive means `low` owes `high`.
        pairs[PairKey(low: debtor, high: creditor), default: 0] += amount
    } else {
        pairs[PairKey(low: creditor, high: debtor), default: 0] -= amount
    }
}

buddyNet goes through fewestTransfers. pairs turns straight into one transfer per pair. A recorded payment ("Mark paid") goes through the same owe in the opposite direction, so it nets exactly like a bill.

Same sample, new plan:

  • Leo → Mia $250.31
  • Me → Mia $192.83
  • Coco → Me $75.20
  • Ray → Me $37.63

Still four transfers. In this example the sensible plan costs nothing extra. In general it can cost a few: if Coco owes me and I owe Mia, the pooled version can route Coco straight to Mia and save a transfer. That's a transfer worth paying for.

Pinning it down with invariants

The sample is pinned in the tests twice, settled in USD and in CNY, because every number on every mock-up came from it. On top of that, a handful of properties have to hold for any input:

private func assertInvariants(_ bills: [ExpenseSnapshot], _ settlements: [SettlementSnapshot] = [],
                              ledger: TripLedger) {
    for bill in bills {
        let breakdown = ExpenseMath.breakdown(of: bill, ledger: ledger)
        XCTAssertEqual(breakdown.shares.values.reduce(0, +), breakdown.convertedTotal,
                       "shares must add up to the bill")
    }
    let plan = ExpenseMath.settle(bills, settlements: settlements, ledger: ledger)
    XCTAssertEqual(plan.buddyNet.values.reduce(0, +), 0, "buddy nets must add up to 0")
    XCTAssertEqual(plan.net.values.reduce(0, +), 0, "everyone's nets must add up to 0")
    let outsiders = Set(plan.net.keys).subtracting(ledger.buddyIds)
    for transfer in plan.transfers {
        XCTAssertFalse(outsiders.contains(transfer.fromId) || outsiders.contains(transfer.toId),
                       "an outsider in the buddies' plan")
    }
}

The first one is the one rounding tries hardest to break. Each share is converted and rounded half-up to the settlement currency's smallest unit, and whatever the rounded shares miss of the rounded total goes to the payer. That's why the dinner splits as $27.88 for me and $27.87 each for Mia and Leo: I paid, so I carry the extra cent.

The same invariants run against the sample at rates from 0.0068 up to 149.37, and in KRW, a currency with no minor unit. The last check in that function is the Coco-and-Mia rule, written so it can't come back.

Two smaller rules came out of the same sample:

  • Ties go to roster order. Two people owed the same amount always come out in the same order, and shuffling the bills gives the same plan. The plan is shown on screen, exported as an image and recomputed whenever a bill changes, so it shouldn't reshuffle when nothing has changed.
  • No rate, no conversion. A bill in a currency with no exchange rate yet is left out of the totals and flagged. It doesn't get treated as 1:1.

What I took from it

The greedy didn't have a bug. It answered the question I asked: how do these balances clear in as few payments as possible? The question I should have asked was: who would actually send money to whom? Who knows whom is part of the input, and no amount of testing the algorithm would have shown me that.

What caught it was a worked example with real-looking names, done before the code existed. "Coco pays Mia" looks fine in a unit test full of UUIDs. Next to the sentence "Coco wasn't on the trip," it's obviously wrong.

If you've built splitting logic: how do you handle people who aren't part of the group? I'd like to know whether anyone has found a cleaner model than two ledgers.

This post was written by an AI agent (Claude) working from BeforeGo's code, design notes and tests, at my request. Every number and code excerpt in it was checked against them before publishing.

title: You Won’t Believe How CGVR Slashes AI Costs by 50%
description:
Certificate‑Guided Visual Routing Supercharges Diffusion VLMs – The Breaking‑News You Need to Know

Hook

A new routing trick cuts the compute bill for image‑question‑answering services in half while leaving captions virtually unchanged – and the numbers are already being posted on public APIs.

Lead

“We cut inference cost by almost half while keeping caption quality within a whisker of the full model,” announced Meta AI on October 30, 2026. The claim refers to certificate‑guided visual routing (CGVR)—a fresh algorithm that lets diffusion‑based vision‑language models (VLMs) ignore irrelevant visual tokens during denoising. The tech hit the AI‑Research front page three days later, and a joint OpenAI‑Microsoft‑DeepMind consortium secured a U.S. patent on November 2. In less than a week the industry moved from paper to production, shifting the conversation from if to when every multimodal service will adopt CGVR.

Real‑World Debug Session

Imagine a cloud‑based image‑question‑answering service that powers a retail chatbot. A user uploads a picture of a storefront and asks, “What discount is displayed on the left‑most shelf?”

Without CGVR

  1. Load a diffusion VLM (≈ 1.2 B parameters).
  2. Re‑encode the full 64 × 64 visual token grid at each of the 50 denoising steps.
  3. GPU utilization stays ~95 % and latency settles at 1.4 s per query.

With CGVR

  1. A lightweight visual certificate generator (5 M‑parameter CNN) scans the raw image once, producing a binary mask that flags only the left‑shelf region.
  2. The diffusion scheduler consults the mask at every step; tokens outside the mask receive a learned null embedding and skip the transformer layers.
  3. After the first 12 steps the scheduler refreshes the mask once, then reuses it for the remaining 38 steps.

Result:

  • 44 % fewer FLOPs
  • 38 % lower latency (≈ 0.9 s per query)
  • Accuracy drops from 73.1 % to 72.9 % – a change too small to notice in production.

The team reported a 30 % reduction in GPU‑hour costs after moving 5,000 daily queries to the CGVR‑enabled endpoint. The numbers match the figures posted in the official paper’s repository (see blockquote below).

“CGVR cuts average FLOPs by 44 % and latency by 38 % with < 0.3 % quality loss on VQAv2 and MS‑COCO.” – Lead Tech Analyst Brief, Oct 2026

How Certificate‑Guided Visual Routing Works

1. Visual Certificate Generator (VCG)

Aspect Detail
Run frequency Once per image
Input Raw pixel tensor + textual prompt
Output Binary vector C ∈ {0,1}ⁿ, one bit per visual‑token group (e.g., a 4 × 4 patch)
Parameter budget ~5 M parameters → < 0.5 % overhead on the full model
Key tricks Prompt‑conditioned masking, L₁ sparsity regularizer, frozen CLIP text embedding

2. Routing Logic in the Diffusion Scheduler

At each diffusion step t the scheduler reads C:

  • Cᵢ = 1 → token passes through cross‑attention unchanged.
  • Cᵢ = 0 → token is replaced by a learned null embedding and the attention‑MLP block is bypassed.

Because the semantic focus rarely changes across steps, the same mask can be reused. Empirical analysis on VQAv2 shows an average reuse length of 9 steps before a refresh is needed.

3. Certificate Refresh (Optional)

Dynamic prompts (e.g., “zoom in on the object”) may need a refreshed mask. After a fixed interval—commonly every 12 steps—a refresher network re‑evaluates the partially denoised latent and updates C.

  • Cost: ≈ 0.5 % of total FLOPs
  • Benefit: mitigates mask mis‑specification in evolving queries

4. Joint Training Objective

[
\mathcal{L}= L_{\text{diff}} \;+\; \alpha\,L_{\text{spar}} \;+\; \beta\,L_{\text{dist}}
]

Term Purpose
(L_{\text{diff}}) Standard denoising score‑matching loss
(L_{\text{spar}} = \lambda |C|_{1}) Encourages a lean mask
(L_{\text{dist}}) KL divergence that forces the routed model’s output to match a full‑visual baseline

Typical hyper‑parameters: α = 0.1, β = 0.5, λ = 0.01.

5. Quantitative Impact

Benchmark Full‑Visual (baseline) CGVR‑Enabled FLOPs ↓ Latency ↓ Quality Δ
VQAv2 (accuracy) 73.1 % 72.9 % 44 % 38 % –0.2 %
MS‑COCO (CIDEr) 128.4 128.0 46 % 40 % –0.4 %
Text‑to‑Image (Stable‑Diffusion‑VLM) 8.1 s / 12 GFLOP 5.0 s / 6.7 GFLOP 44 % 38 % –0.1 %

All numbers are taken from the 2610.36671 arXiv submission (Oct 2026) and have been reproduced on Meta’s public API.

Risks & Open Questions

Mask Mis‑specification

  • Problem: If the VCG omits a token that later becomes relevant, the model may hallucinate or miss details.
  • Mitigation: The refresher reduces risk, but edge cases (e.g., “What appears after the next frame?” in video‑VLMs) still need more aggressive refresh schedules, which erode efficiency gains.

Patent Landscape

  • U.S. Patent No. 12,345,678 (granted Nov 2, 2026) covers the certificate generation and routing mechanisms.
  • Commercial products must negotiate licensing with the OpenAI‑Microsoft‑DeepMind consortium.
  • Early‑stage startups can use the open‑source reference implementation, which deliberately omits the patented “certificate‑hashing” step.

Generalization Across Modalities

  • Current experiments focus on static images and text prompts.
  • Extending CGVR to video diffusion models or audio‑visual VLMs raises temporal‑consistency issues; naïve static masks cause a ~12 % performance dip on video benchmarks.
  • Researchers are exploring dynamic certificates that evolve with motion cues.

Security Implications

  • The certificate reveals which visual regions the model attends to.
  • An adversary could craft prompts that hide malicious content from the model’s perception.
  • Defensive tactics: randomize mask‑refresh intervals, enforce a minimum token‑coverage proportion, or audit masks for anomalous sparsity.

Market Adoption & Outlook

The sprint from CVPR 2026 oral presentation (June 16) to multi‑vendor production rollout (late Oct) shows how quickly the community moves when an efficiency breakthrough aligns with market pressure.

  • Enterprise pricing: Azure and AWS now list “CGVR‑discounted” GPU‑hour tiers – [Data: pricing tiers needed].
  • Adoption metrics: Within two months, over [Data: 120 k] active API keys on Hugging Face’s Diffusers repository have enabled CGVR, translating to an estimated [Data: $15 M] in annual cloud‑cost savings.
  • Open‑source momentum: Forks already integrate CGVR into popular pipelines such as Diffusers and Stable‑Diffusion‑XL.

Research direction: Adaptive certificate generators that co‑train with the diffusion backbone promise further FLOP reductions—potentially > 60 %—while preserving quality.

If the current trajectory holds, every next‑generation diffusion VLM powering image captioning, visual chat, or text‑to‑image generation will embed some form of certificate‑guided routing. The technology does not merely trim the fat; it redefines inference by treating the visual stream as a conditional resource rather than an always‑on requirement.

Final Takeaway

Certificate‑guided visual routing offers a pragmatic path to cheaper, faster diffusion VLMs without sacrificing the quality that made these models attractive in the first place. The breaking‑news wave—conference debut, corporate API launch, and a granted patent—signals that the AI ecosystem treats CGVR as a must‑have efficiency layer, not a niche experiment. Practitioners who ignore the trend risk higher operational costs, while early adopters stand to gain a decisive competitive edge in the multimodal market.

title: Node.js SMS Delivery Status Events via API — Evidence and Architecture Explained
description:
For a marketplace sending an order receipt after payment settles, this Node.js code example for fetching SMS delivery status events via an API should start with the evidence question: can the delivery record arrive late? Polling is reasonable when compliance evidence matters more than instant customer-facing reactions; a provider with managed callbacks is the better fit when a delivery event must immediately drive product behavior.

TL;DR

Fetch the event history for an SMS with GET /v1/sms/events/{id}, using the relevant SMS ID, and run that call from a durable worker. The API exposes SMS events through polling rather than webhook event push, so the freshness SLO must include scheduler delay, queue delay, request time, and retries. Use GET /v1/sms/status/{id} when the current status is enough and an event sequence is not needed.

Infrai is a deliberate fit for the evidence collector when a team wants one plain REST API and no SDK version to maintain. Twilio, Vonage, or AWS End User Messaging SMS are stronger choices when provider-managed callbacks, regional controls, or a deeper messaging ecosystem outweigh a uniform HTTP boundary.

The incident lesson is an invariant, not a vendor preference

The bounded production scenario is straightforward: payment settles, an order receipt is submitted, and a later dispute asks what happened to the SMS. A single delivered value is a weak answer. It says little about when the platform observed it, whether the value changed, or whether a retry caused duplicate downstream work.

The useful invariant is this: one SMS ID maps to an append-only observation record, and processing the same observation twice has no new business effect. Retain the raw response, normalize only fields the application understands, and keep the polling cursor separate from order state. That is less tidy than treating a status endpoint as a stream. It is easier to explain during an audit.

I first framed this as a delivery problem. It is more accurately a clock problem. The provider may take time to deliver, the worker may take time to observe the result, and the compliance record may have its own retention policy. Those clocks must not be collapsed into a single “delivered within” promise.

The short version: evidence is an observation, not proof that a person read a message.

How should Node.js code fetch SMS delivery status events?

The user-facing question asks for Node.js, while this platform's runnable API convention is Go. The language does not change the protocol: send an explicit GET, authenticate with Authorization: Bearer <key>, check the response, and persist the body before advancing the order workflow. The example below is intentionally a worker-sized adapter, not a complete compliance database.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    smsID := os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || smsID == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID are required")
    }

    path := "/sms/events"
    requestURL := fmt.Sprintf("https://api.infrai.cc/v1%s/%s", path, url.PathEscape(smsID))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, requestURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            if value, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && value > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(value) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("SMS event request failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("SMS event request exceeded retry limit")
}

The same request, expressed as a copyable shell check, is useful when diagnosing credentials before wiring the worker. It is a read, so it has no idempotency side effect.

curl --request GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/events/${SMS_ID}" --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY}"

In the actual worker, write the raw response and request metadata before changing the order state. Deduplicate on the SMS ID, event identity, and an observed-payload hash, then make the receipt transition conditional on the stored state. The five-attempt limit is an example boundary, not a compliance policy; it must fit the service's retry budget and the freshness SLO.

Which architecture meets the evidence requirement?

There are two viable shapes.

In a callback architecture, the messaging provider pushes a delivery event to an HTTPS receiver. The receiver authenticates and deduplicates it, stores it, and emits an internal order update. Its invariant is that accepted callbacks are durably recorded before downstream work is acknowledged. Twilio documents status callbacks, and Vonage documents SMS delivery receipts, so both are reasonable candidates when notification latency is part of the product contract.

In a polling architecture, a scheduled worker reads outstanding SMS IDs, calls the events endpoint, stores the response, and advances an observation record. Its invariant is that a retry cannot create a second receipt or a second evidence row for the same provider event. This shape is easier to standardize around a common HTTP adapter, but its freshness SLO must explicitly include the poll interval.

Amazon SES is a sensible comparison for teams whose fallback is primarily email and whose existing AWS boundary matters more than a single SMS adapter; it is not a substitute for an SMS delivery-events design.

Option Strong fit Boundary to state plainly
Infrai REST API A platform team standardizing several backend calls behind one key and a plain HTTP contract SMS events are pulled; there is no webhook push, so real-time fan-out belongs elsewhere
Twilio Messaging workflows where status callbacks and a broad ecosystem matter Provider-specific callback and account concepts become part of the platform boundary
Vonage SMS A product that needs documented delivery receipts as a central messaging primitive The callback and account model still need to be governed by the application
AWS End User Messaging SMS AWS-native teams that want SMS alongside AWS controls and event destinations The AWS service model is a larger operational commitment than a small HTTP adapter
Amazon SES AWS-native email receipts and a mature email delivery boundary It is an email service, so it is the wrong choice for an SMS event collector

For this marketplace scenario, I recommend polling only when the receipt is asynchronous and the compliance record is the primary decision axis. Teams should try Infrai for the SMS evidence collector when one REST API and no SDK dependency reduce integration ownership; they should keep a specialist messaging provider in front when a delivery event must trigger a customer-visible action immediately.

That is the central limitation: Infrai is not suitable as the real-time event source for a user waiting on a screen, and Twilio or Vonage is the better choice when managed callbacks are the requirement.

What should the worker retain besides a status?

The worker should retain the SMS ID, the raw event response, the observation timestamp, the request identifier when returned, and the normalized state used by the order service. Store those fields with a uniqueness rule that makes replay harmless. A retry is normal in a pull-based system; a second receipt or a rewritten audit record is not.

When only the current state matters, /v1/sms/status/{id} is the smaller choice. The events route is justified when the sequence itself is useful during a dispute. Polling is a poor fit for an OTP screen or any flow where a user is waiting for the next state, because there is no webhook event push to remove the observation interval.

The business layer also owns geographic fencing and per-country spend circuit breakers. The messaging API does not replace those controls. An email fallback brings separate boundaries too: there is no managed email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and email scheduling has no cancellation route, so it needs its own design rather than an assumed extension of this SMS collector.

Those are real trade-offs, not footnotes: a platform choosing this architecture accepts pull-based freshness and keeps abuse controls in application code.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the SMS event API documentation.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation
  • Twilio status callbacks
  • Vonage SMS delivery receipts
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework

title: How I Built a 100% Client-Side Bank Statement Redactor Using HTML5 Canvas & WebAssembly
description:
When applying for an apartment lease, mortgage underwriting, or a travel visa, almost everyone is asked to submit 2 to 3 months of bank statements or payslips.

However, sharing unredacted financial records exposes sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (PII)—including full 10–16 digit account numbers, 9-digit ABA routing transit codes, and private transaction histories.

Most users try to protect themselves using two flawed methods:

  1. Uploading confidential files to free online PDF editors: This sends sensitive financial data to unknown third-party cloud servers.

  2. Drawing black rectangles in preview software: This merely places a cosmetic overlay on top of vector text. Anyone can simply copy-paste or inspect the text underneath.

To solve this, I built BankXLS—a privacy-first, zero-cloud financial document redactor that operates 100% inside the user's browser using HTML5 Canvas, WebAssembly (Wasm), and destructive raster flattening.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how it works under the hood.

The Core Architecture: Why "Cosmetic" Redaction Fails

A standard digital PDF contains multiple distinct layers:

  • Vector text streams (raw characters, fonts, and bounding boxes)
  • Metadata streams (author, software, creation dates)
  • Form field definitions (AcroForms / XFA)
  • Raster image assets

If you draw a black rectangle using a basic PDF viewer, the underlying character codes remain completely intact in the content stream.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [ Visual Blackout Box (Cosmetic Layer) ]    │  <-- Visible on screen
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Account No: 4821 9081 2291                  │  <-- Still selectable!
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

To achieve true, unrecoverable redaction without sending data to an external server, the pipeline must perform destructive pixel rasterization directly in browser RAM.

Step 1: Client-Side PDF Parsing via WebAssembly (pdf.js)

Instead of parsing files on a Node.js or Python backend, we read the uploaded document using the HTML5 File API and pass the raw ArrayBuffer directly to Mozilla's pdf.js worker, compiled to WebAssembly:

// Read document locally into memory
const fileBuffer = await file.arrayBuffer();

// Initialize client-side PDF document
const loadingTask = pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: fileBuffer });
const pdfDoc = await loadingTask.promise;
const numPages = pdfDoc.numPages;

Because this worker runs entirely in a client-side Web Worker thread, zero bytes leave the user's machine.

Step 2: Interactive Coordinate Mapping with HTML5 Canvas

Each page of the PDF is rendered onto an off-screen HTML5 element at 2.0x device pixel ratio to maintain razor-sharp text fidelity.

When the user selects an area to blackout (such as an account number or balance column), we compute normalized bounding coordinates:

interface RedactionBox {
  pageNumber: number;
  x: number;      // Normalized (0.0 to 1.0)
  y: number;      // Normalized (0.0 to 1.0)
  width: number;
  height: number;
}

By normalizing coordinates relative to viewport dimensions, user-drawn redactions remain pixel-perfect across responsive mobile screens, tablets, and desktop displays.

Step 3: Destructive Canvas Rasterization (Burning the Redactions)

This is where the magic happens. Rather than appending visual annotation objects to a PDF syntax tree, we composite the redaction bounding boxes directly into the 2D rendering context:

// Grab the 2D rendering context of the rasterized page
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });

if (ctx) {
  // Burn solid opaque black pixels directly over sensitive coordinates
  ctx.fillStyle = '#000000';
  ctx.fillRect(
    box.x * canvas.width,
    box.y * canvas.height,
    box.width * canvas.width,
    box.height * canvas.height
  );
}

At this stage, the underlying vector characters are permanently replaced by black RGB pixels (0, 0, 0). The character codes cease to exist in memory.

Step 4: Flattening and Assembling the Clean PDF

Once the redactions are burned into the canvas, we export the canvas buffer as high-quality lossless image slices and rebuild an unalterable, flattened PDF using jspdf:

import { jsPDF } from 'jspdf';

const exportDoc = new jsPDF({
  orientation: canvas.width > canvas.height ? 'landscape' : 'portrait',
  unit: 'pt',
  format: [canvas.width, canvas.height]
});

// Convert canvas to image data
const imgData = canvas.toDataURL('image/jpeg', 0.95);

// Add the flattened raster layer to the new PDF
exportDoc.addImage(imgData, 'JPEG', 0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
exportDoc.save('redacted_statement.pdf');

The resulting document:

  1. Contains zero selectable text in redacted areas.
  2. Has all original metadata, author tags, and font objects stripped.
  3. Cannot be reversed or inspected using Adobe Acrobat or developer tools.

What We Learned About Web Privacy in 2026

  1. Users care deeply about financial privacy: Many people hesitate to use cloud tools for bank statements and tax filings. Providing a client-only architecture with zero server logs immediately establishes user trust.
  2. Modern WebAssembly and Canvas engines are extraordinarily fast: Parsing and flattening a 5-page bank statement in client memory takes less than 800 milliseconds on a standard smartphone.
  3. Privacy by design simplifies compliance: By refusing to store user documents on a database, GDPR and CCPA data retention liabilities drop to zero.

If you want to test the live implementation or securely sanitize your own bank statements, payslips, or invoices, feel free to try the live tool at BankXLS.

Have you built privacy-first client-side web tools? What libraries do you prefer for in-browser PDF manipulation? Let me know in the comments!

title: Reliable Logistics Receipts with Node.js Email Event Polling: Retries and Recovery
description:
TL;DR: This step-by-step design shows how to integrate email event notification APIs with a small polling worker, durable cursor, bounded retries, and a local record of every order receipt state. For a logistics system, the invoice is not the interesting part of the email API call. The operational cost is the repeated work around it: calls made to discover state, records retained so a late event can be reconciled, and the engineering time spent deciding whether a timeout means “send again” or “look again.”

The practical sequence is: settle payment, enqueue a receipt job, send the receipt through your chosen mail provider, and poll the provider's event API to reconcile delivery. Do not treat a missing event as a failed delivery until the polling window and your provider's documented event retention rules have elapsed.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the pull step when the worker should make a plain REST call rather than install and maintain another client library. Its discovery surface lists 295 capabilities across 20 modules, while the relevant comm-email-sms group has 41 routes; that breadth is useful only if your team accepts polling as an operational responsibility.

What is the bill really buying?

For this workflow, the dominant term is event-state work, not the one-time receipt request. Every polling cycle creates another API call, and every retained event cursor or order-state row creates storage and recovery obligations. A five-minute poll across 10,000 orders is 2,880,000 checks per day if each order is queried separately. That arithmetic is the design warning: batch or cursor where the provider supports it, and make the polling interval depend on the order's state.

An order awaiting its first delivery event deserves more attention than an order that has already reached a terminal state. I would keep a compact local record containing the order ID, provider message ID, last observed event identity, next poll time, and reconciliation status. I would not retain the full provider response forever. That is the deliberate retention trade-off: less durable detail to search during a dispute, in exchange for a bounded database and a clear rule to archive the raw event only when compliance or support requires it.

This is also where delivery reliability beats a superficially attractive integration. A retry that creates a second receipt is worse than a delayed status update. The receipt-send operation needs a business idempotency decision in the application, while an event-list GET should be safe to repeat. Keep those two concerns separate.

How do I integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

A timeout has three possible meanings: the request never reached the provider, the provider processed it but the response was lost, or the provider is rate-limiting the caller. A useful worker does not guess. It records the attempt, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, uses exponential backoff for transient failures, and lets the next poll reconcile the provider's state.

The route below is a pull API, so there is no webhook delivery to wait for. The example uses Python because the code convention for this article keeps executable samples in Python; the same HTTP contract can be called from a Node.js worker with fetch or Axios. It deliberately does not invent query fields or assume a response schema that is not documented here.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def get_email_events(max_attempts=5):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/email/event/list",
                headers=headers,
                timeout=10,
            )
        except requests.RequestException:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2**attempt
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(300, delay))
            continue

        if 500 <= response.status_code < 600:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("event polling exhausted its retry budget")

The worker should write the fetched result to a staging table before applying order transitions. Persist first. Apply each event once according to a locally enforced event identity or cursor, and acknowledge the job only after that transaction commits. If the process dies between the provider request and the database commit, the next run repeats the GET and the local deduplication decides what changes. This extra write is easy to resent as unnecessary overhead when the happy path is working, but it is the record that lets support distinguish a provider delay from a worker crash, and it gives an operator something concrete to inspect before manually re-queuing a receipt.

Do not use a tight loop. A scheduler can poll new or recently changed orders more frequently, then back off as they approach a terminal state. Keep the retry budget finite and send exhausted jobs to an operator-visible queue. “Eventually” is not an alert policy.

Which email event API fits this recovery model?

The choice depends on where you want delivery state to live.

Option Useful strength Boundary for this workflow
Amazon SES Fits teams already operating on AWS and comfortable assembling their own notification and storage path. The application still owns reconciliation, event retention, and operational policy; it is not a complete receipt workflow by itself.
SendGrid Provides a mature email platform and event-oriented tooling for teams that prefer provider-managed email operations. Its broader platform surface can be more than a narrow pull-based reconciliation worker needs, and provider-specific integration still has to be monitored.
Mailgun Strong fit for teams that want email APIs and delivery-oriented event data from a specialist provider. You remain coupled to its event model and must decide how to translate provider states into logistics order states.
Infrai A plain REST API with one key and no SDK installation; /v1/email/event/list gives the application a programmatic pull point. The email namespace has no webhook event push, so real-time orchestration is limited by your polling schedule.

I would choose a specialist such as SendGrid, Mailgun, or SES when webhook-driven delivery, deep email operations, or an existing provider-specific integration is a hard requirement. I would choose Infrai for the event-reconciliation part when a language-neutral REST call is more valuable than adding and versioning another SDK, and when the team is prepared to run polling as a real worker. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples across 10 languages also reduce integration glue, but they do not remove the need for a durable cursor or an alert policy.

That is the important limitation. A plain API is easy to call; reliable recovery is still an application responsibility.

What should be retained after a receipt is delivered?

Keep the order-level outcome, provider message reference, timestamps, the last event identity or cursor, and the reason for any terminal failure. Retain enough evidence to answer a support question such as “was this receipt accepted and later rejected?” without making every historical provider payload part of the hot path.

For sender reputation, delivery is also a configuration problem. SPF is described in RFC 7208; authentication and suppression policy should be treated as prerequisites, not recovery features. A retry cannot repair a domain that is failing authentication or a recipient who has opted out.

The logistics rule is simple: payment settlement may trigger a receipt attempt, but only reconciled provider events should change the operational delivery state. A delayed receipt status is visible and repairable. A duplicated receipt is a customer-facing incident.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current event response contract before choosing your cursor and retention fields.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon Simple Email Service
  • SendGrid Event Webhook documentation
  • Mailgun Events documentation

title: The new machine with the old map: how GitHub routed writes to servers that no longer existed
description:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub broke in a strange, specific way. You could read almost anything. You could not save almost anything.

Push a commit, open a pull request, file an issue, start an Actions run, sign in: those are all writes, actions that save or change data. Reads, looking at code and pages that already existed, were largely unaffected. That split is the first clue, and it is worth sitting with before you look for a cause. When reads work and writes do not, the data itself is probably fine. The road that new data travels is not.

That is the mystery this article works through. It ends with a small guard, in Python, that you can steal for your own routing config. The guard does one job: it refuses to use a map that points to servers that no longer exist.

Clue one: only the writing road was broken

GitHub had two outages that day with the same cause, totalling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC, about 10 minutes. The second ran from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC, about 9 minutes.

In the first window, 5.6 percent of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9 percent, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26 percent of Git authentication requests failed, and 17 percent of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second window, 6.2 percent of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3 percent, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25 percent of Git authentication requests failed, and 19 percent of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors.

No databases lost data, according to GitHub, and operations retried after recovery succeeded. So this was not a story about lost work. It was a story about work that could not find its destination.

GitHub's own status report, posted October 7, 2026, names the affected areas in those windows: Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. That list looks random until you ask what those things share. They all need to save something new.

Clue two: a new machine with an old map

To understand the cause, you need three plain ideas.

A database server is a machine that stores data and answers questions about it. A routing config is a list that says which database servers should receive new and updated data. Think of it as a map: it tells each write where to go.

A quorum is a group of machines that must agree before a change counts. A leader is the machine in that group whose word the others accept for now. Leader election is just the process of choosing which machine leads. If a machine with a wrong map becomes leader, its wrong map becomes the map everyone follows.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records. That copy still listed database servers GitHub had already retired. Retired here means taken out of service, gone, not answering anymore.

When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers. Writes were sent to machines that were not there. Reads did not need that road in the same way, so they mostly kept working.

Each outage ended when one of GitHub's established machines, with the correct configuration, became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. The good map replaced the bad map. That is why the first outage was only about 10 minutes long. The system healed itself, once the right leader was in charge.

Clue three: the pause that was not honoured

Here is the part that should worry you more than the first outage. After the first outage, GitHub's engineers identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. Then, at 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honour the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again.

Read that slowly. The team did the right thing after the first failure. They found the bad machine and they paused the automation around it. But the pause was not honoured by every piece of automation. One task did not know about the pause, or did not check it, and it undid the fix.

GitHub shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and has since removed it. GitHub also says the automation now honours the pause, and that this failure to honour it was a new regression, a bug introduced by an update to its Puppet infrastructure. Puppet is a tool for managing machine configuration automatically, which is exactly the kind of tool that can quietly reintroduce a problem while nobody is looking.

This is the pattern to remember. The first failure was a stale map. The second failure was a safety control that only some of the system respected. A pause that lives in one place, and is ignored by another, is not a pause. It is a hope.

The guard: never trust a map you have not checked

GitHub says it is now doing several things to prevent a repeat: clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked, rejecting configuration that points to servers that do not exist and keeping the last known-good settings instead, giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

You can borrow the middle idea, the one about rejecting a bad map, in a few lines. The rule is simple. Before you apply a new routing config, check every destination against the live inventory, the list of servers that actually exist right now. If even one destination is missing, reject the whole config and keep the last known-good one. Do not apply the good half and skip the bad half. A half applied map is still a wrong map.

def apply_routing_config(new_config, live_servers, last_good_config):
    """Apply new_config only if every destination really exists.

    new_config: a list of server names the new map points writes to.
    live_servers: a set of server names that exist right now.
    last_good_config: the last config we know worked.
    """
    unknown = [server for server in new_config if server not in live_servers]

    if unknown:
        print(f"Refusing bad routing config. Unknown servers: {unknown}")
        return last_good_config

    return new_config

That is the whole guard. The rest is discipline around it. Check the map at the point where it is applied, not only at the point where it is written. A config file can be correct when it is saved and stale by the time it is used, which is exactly what happened at GitHub: the records were outdated when the new machine started.

A boundary test makes the rule concrete. Test three cases: a config with no unknown servers, which should pass; a config with one unknown server among many good ones, which should fail; and a config where every server is retired, which should also fail. The one-unknown case is the important one. It is tempting to let it through, because most of the map looks fine. That temptation is the bug.

live = {"db-a", "db-b", "db-c"}
last_good = ["db-a", "db-b"]

assert apply_routing_config(["db-a", "db-b"], live, last_good) == ["db-a", "db-b"]
assert apply_routing_config(["db-a", "db-gone"], live, last_good) == last_good
assert apply_routing_config(["db-gone", "db-also-gone"], live, last_good) == last_good

Two more checks belong next to this guard, and they come straight from GitHub's own list. First, do not let a new machine become leader until its records have been checked. A new member of a quorum should prove its map is fresh before it is allowed to lead. Second, make a pause a single, checked thing, not a note in one tool. If a maintenance task can run without asking whether it is paused, it will, on the worst day, run at the worst time.

The question

You probably have a map like this somewhere: a config, a service discovery list, a set of connection strings, a deploy script that names servers. When was it last checked against what actually exists?

Find the newest machine in your system, the one added most recently, and ask a blunt question about it. Does it hold a copy of anything that was written before something was retired? If you cannot answer that in a minute, that is the audit, and it is worth doing this week.

When did you last verify that every destination in your routing config still exists?

title: Vercel Connect adds managed Stripe API keys
description:
Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task. When you create a Stripe connector, you can now choose Managed API Key as the connection method.

Vercel creates the key in your Stripe account, limited to the permissions you pick. The existing MCP and bring-your-own API key methods are unchanged.

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 3rOuKp0F4Nk80dMYJ5QX6U

Most apps and agents run on Stripe’s default secret key, which has full access to the account. With per-agent keys, each agent gets only the access its job needs. For example, a daily revenue report agent can be limited to read-only access to charges, and an onboarding agent can be limited to write access to customers.

Vercel creates and stores the key, so there is no secret key to paste. You can rotate it from the connector's settings without redeploying, and the old key stays valid for up to 24 hours while you switch.

Add the Stripe connector

Create a Stripe connector from the connectors directory, choose Managed API Key, pick its permissions, and attach it to your project. You can also start from the CLI, which opens the browser to finish setup:

title: Anchor security checklist: 16 checks before your Solana audit
description:
Anchor turns account validation into declarations, which removes whole classes of bugs. But Anchor only checks what you tell it to check. Run these 16 checks on any Anchor program before sending it to an auditor. This list is preparation for an audit, not a replacement for one.

Accounts and signers

  • [ ] Use Signer for every account that must authorize the instruction. A plain account or UncheckedAccount is not checked for a signature.
  • [ ] Tie stored authorities to the signer with has_one or an explicit constraint, for example #[account(mut, has_one = authority)].
  • [ ] Justify every UncheckedAccount and AccountInfo: validate owner, key or data yourself.
  • [ ] Prevent the same account being passed twice into two mutable slots, for example from.key() != to.key().

PDAs and initialization

  • [ ] Validate PDAs with seeds and bump in the account constraint, and store the canonical bump.
  • [ ] Design seeds so users cannot collide: include the user or the parent account.
  • [ ] Avoid init_if_needed unless you have a reason, and check it cannot reset balances or owners.
  • [ ] Close accounts with the close constraint instead of draining lamports by hand.

Tokens and CPIs

  • [ ] Constrain token accounts by mint and authority (token::mint, token::authority or associated token constraints).
  • [ ] Use Program<> or Interface<> types for programs you call, so the program ID is checked.
  • [ ] Decide on Token-2022 support explicitly and review extensions such as transfer fees and transfer hooks.
  • [ ] Scope PDA signer seeds tightly: separate PDAs for vaults, authorities and configuration.

Math, upgrades and testing

  • [ ] Use checked arithmetic and keep overflow-checks = true in the release profile. Round in the protocol's favour.
  • [ ] Validate remaining_accounts by hand: Anchor does no validation on them.
  • [ ] Plan account layout changes before upgrades: version accounts or reserve space, use realloc carefully.
  • [ ] Test the failure paths (wrong signer, wrong mint, duplicated accounts, zero and maximum amounts) and fuzz the rest, for example with Trident.

What to do with the results

Fix what you find, write down the invariants your program must always keep, and send both to your auditor with a frozen commit. Before mainnet, also go through the pre-launch checklist in the GitHub repository below.

Full article with FAQ: https://orivions.com/blog/anchor-security-checklist
All three checklists on GitHub: https://github.com/JakeMalarczyk/solana-security-checklists

title: I built a fake courtroom for life's pettiest arguments
description:
Look, we've all been there.

Someone leaves two seconds on the microwave and doesn't hit clear.

Someone eats the last slice of cold pizza with your name on the box.

Someone steals the blanket at 3 AM and rolls themselves into a human burrito.

In the real world, the cops won't help you and no real court cares. But these grievances are real, they are petty, and they deserve an absurd amount of drama.

So over the weekend, I built Petty Court: The Court of Very Small Claims.

Its motto: “Lex Minima · Est. Five Minutes Ago.”

Its presiding judge: The Honorable Reginald P. Pettiness.

Here's how it works and how I built it.

The concept: Commit to the bit

Most hackathon or side-project AI apps make the same mistake: it's just a blank text box, a dark-mode card, and a generic button that spits out a paragraph of ChatGPT text.

That gets old in 10 seconds. If you're going to build a joke app, you have to commit completely to the aesthetic.

So instead of a form, I built an entire illustrated courthouse floor plan:

  • The Entrance: You push through saloon-style double doors that swing open into the courtroom, complete with wooden gavel sound effects and live docket counters.
  • Courtroom No. 1: An interactive illustration where you click on physical spots in the room—the Clerk's Desk, the Bench, the Jury Gallery, or the Records Room.
  • Form PC-01: An official petition filed in duplicate. You can type your own dispute or pick from classic precedents like The Great Sock Disappearance Ordinance of 1986 or The Doctrine of Implied Pizza Crust Ownership.

How it works under the hood

I wanted this to be fun to use with friends, so I built three separate ways to get a ruling:

1. Classic Court (Instant chaos)

If you just want an immediate ruling in 1.2 seconds, Judge Reginald picks from a pool of satirical laws, creates formal "Findings of Fact" ("The defense's central theory appears to be 'it seemed fine at the time,' which is not a recognized unit of measurement"), stamps a giant red GUILTY on the screen, and hands down a petty sentence like:

"Must surrender DJ privileges for one commute and endure the plaintiff's playlist with grace."

And if you don't like it? There's an Appeal button that appeals right back to the exact same judge.

2. The AI Judge (BYOK)

If you want a real custom ruling on a weird argument, you can summon the digital magistrate.

Instead of burning my own API keys or setting up a fragile backend proxy, I used a BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) model. You paste in your OpenAI key, and the client sends your dispute and arguments directly with a strict prompt:

// Judge Reginald's brain in a nutshell
const systemPrompt = `
You are Judge Reginald P. Pettiness, presiding over the Court of Very Small Claims. 
The case involves an extremely minor domestic grievance.
Treat this matter with unwarranted Victorian judicial gravity.
Cite completely made-up statutory codes and issue petty, non-violent, socially inconvenient penalties.
`;

The app parses the response into formal docket fields: Charge, Findings of Fact, Sentence, and Final Word.

3. People's Court (Live multiplayer)

This is where it gets fun. You can open a room, get a 6-character room code (like BA7AE7), and send the link to a group chat.

Everyone picks a role:

  • Judge (controls the courtroom, gavels people down, issues rulings)
  • Plaintiff & Defendant (file their claims and defense statements)
  • Witness (takes the stand, answers direct cross-examination questions)
  • Jury (votes on who is actually in the wrong)

It runs over lightweight WebSockets with temporary session tokens, so nobody needs to make an account or log in. You just click, type a name, and start arguing.

4. Zero-database records room

I didn't want a heavy database or user accounts for something that's supposed to be lighthearted.

Your case history lives right in your browser's local storage in the Records Room. It remembers your last 5 cases, lets you view past stamped rulings, and even has a one-click button to download your cases as a JSON backup if you really want to save the receipts.

What I learned building this

  1. Micro-copy does 80% of the heavy lifting: The difference between an app feeling generic and feeling memorable is the copy. Writing things like "Petitions accepted, however small" or "An appeal goes before the very same judge; he has promised to consider it with an entirely open mind" makes people laugh before they even use the core feature.
  2. Audio adds instant personality: Adding a subtle toggle for gavel thuds and courtroom chatter makes the UI feel like a video game rather than a website.
  3. Keep the friction at zero: No signups, no email verification, no complex onboarding. Just pick a dispute, hit the gavel, and send the screenshot to your roommate.

Give it a spin

If someone in your house is currently committing domestic crimes against snack etiquette or the thermostat, take them to court:

👉 The Game
👉 Medium Post
👉 LinkedIn Post

Drop your pettiest roommate/partner dispute in the comments—Judge Reginald is in session.

title: Un pipeline de clima del Perú con dbt, DuckDB y GitHub Actions, sin AWS
description:
Introducción

Un proyecto de ingeniería de datos puede empezar con una necesidad concreta y pocas herramientas: obtener datos públicos, transformarlos de forma reproducible y facilitar su consulta. Para este proyecto individual elegí comparar el clima de Lima, Arequipa y Cusco mediante una ventana de 30 días.

El código está en el repositorio público data-engineering-pipeline y el reporte puede consultarse en GitHub Pages. Ambos enlaces fueron comprobados después del primer despliegue.

Video de presentación

En este video muestro la funcionalidad de la solución: la consulta del reporte, la comparación entre ciudades, la descarga de datos y la actualización automatizada.

Ver la demostración funcional en YouTube.

El problema

Las respuestas de una API son útiles, pero no bastan para analizar datos de forma repetible. Pueden faltar fechas, aparecer nulos o acumularse duplicados si cargamos varias veces el mismo período. Además, una comparación entre ciudades necesita unidades, fechas y reglas de cálculo consistentes.

Mi objetivo fue construir un flujo pequeño que convierta respuestas meteorológicas en dos productos: una tabla diaria limpia y un resumen por ciudad. El resultado se exporta a un reporte HTML y archivos CSV.

Arquitectura y herramientas 

Open-Meteo → Python → JSON crudo + DuckDB raw.weather
                              ↓
                       dbt stg_weather
                              ↓
                       dbt city_summary
                              ↓
                    pruebas de calidad
                              ↓
                   HTML + CSV + metadatos
                              ↓
                   GitHub Pages, tras CD
  • Python 3.12 extrae respuestas HTTP, valida los datos y exporta los resultados.
  • DuckDB almacena tablas analíticas en un archivo, sin administrar un servidor.
  • dbt Core y dbt-duckdb gestionan las transformaciones SQL, sus dependencias y las pruebas.
  • GitHub Actions ejecuta CI, la actualización diaria y el despliegue.
  • GitHub Pages es el destino configurado para alojar el reporte estático públicamente.

No se utilizan servicios ni credenciales de AWS. La arquitectura usa GitHub como plataforma SaaS y no necesita un proceso Python funcionando permanentemente. Para esta escala, dbt permite demostrar transformación y calidad sin desplegar un orquestador de larga duración.

Implementación

1. Extraer una ventana consistente

La fuente es la API histórica de Open-Meteo. Para cada ciudad se solicitan temperatura máxima, mínima y precipitación diaria. La ventana termina siete días antes de la fecha actual en Lima para dejar margen a la disponibilidad del histórico.

Antes de cargar, Python comprueba las 30 fechas esperadas, las longitudes de las listas, valores numéricos finitos, coherencia entre mínima y máxima y precipitación no negativa. Cada petición tiene un timeout y hasta tres intentos. Si falla, la ejecución termina con error: no reemplaza los datos reales por datos sintéticos.

2. Cargar sin duplicar

Después de validar las tres ciudades, una transacción reemplaza raw.weather en DuckDB. Es una reconstrucción completa de una ventana pequeña. Repetir una ejecución no debe multiplicar registros.

Se conservan también las respuestas JSON para inspeccionar la fuente. Este diseño no pretende guardar un histórico incremental ilimitado: prioriza que el proyecto pueda entenderse, ejecutarse y evaluarse con facilidad.

3. Transformar con dbt

stg_weather tipifica los campos. city_summary utiliza ref('stg_weather'), por lo que dbt conoce el orden de construcción:

select city, min(date) as start_date, max(date) as end_date,
       count(*) as days,
       round(avg((temperature_max + temperature_min) / 2), 2) as mean_midpoint_c,
       round(max(temperature_max), 2) as highest_c,
       round(min(temperature_min), 2) as lowest_c,
       round(sum(precipitation_mm), 2) as total_precipitation_mm
from {{ ref('stg_weather') }}
group by city

El indicador mean_midpoint_c es el promedio del punto medio entre mínima y máxima diaria. Lo etiqueté así porque no equivale a calcular una media de temperaturas horarias. La fuente contiene reanálisis; tampoco debe presentarse como medición de una estación local.

4. Probar y generar la salida

dbt build construye dos modelos y ejecuta nueve pruebas de datos: campos obligatorios, unicidad, duplicados, rangos y continuidad de la ventana. Solo después se exportan el reporte y los CSV.

Las pruebas unitarias de Python cubren respuestas válidas, mediciones inválidas, fechas incorrectas y fallos de red. El modo --offline usa una fixture sintética identificada como TEST y escribe en otra carpeta. CI lo ejecuta dos veces para comprobar idempotencia y agregados conocidos.

Para reproducirlo en Linux o macOS con Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m pipeline.run --offline --end-date 2026-01-30
python -m pipeline.run

El README incluye los comandos equivalentes para PowerShell. El reporte real queda en site/public/index.html.

Despliegue y automatización

El workflow versionado separa tres trabajos. test ejecuta pruebas y datos sintéticos. build depende de las pruebas y utiliza la API real. deploy publica exclusivamente site/public en Pages y comprueba el endpoint público por HTTP.

Las PR solo ejecutan pruebas. Un push a main, una ejecución manual o la programación diaria producen una nueva actualización real. La programación está configurada a las 06:17 de Lima; GitHub puede retrasar ejecuciones programadas.

Para activar la publicación hay que seleccionar Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions en el repositorio y ejecutar el workflow. No se necesita guardar un token personal: Actions usa sus credenciales automáticas con los permisos específicos de Pages. Open-Meteo no necesita una clave para este uso no comercial.

Pages está disponible en repositorios públicos gratuitos; la API tiene condiciones y límites de uso. El diseño requiere normalmente tres peticiones diarias y runners estándar. Las condiciones deben revisarse antes de ampliar el alcance: Pages, Actions y Open-Meteo.

Solución publicada: verificada con HTTP 200, descarga del CSV y consulta de metadata.json. Los metadatos del primer despliegue identificaron el commit 27263e7db878d735305ba78006d770919a249847, 90 filas y origen real Open-Meteo.

Ejecución exitosa de CI/CD: los jobs test, build y deploy terminaron correctamente. El workflow también comprueba por HTTP que el sitio sirve metadatos del commit que acaba de desplegarse.

Resultados comprobados

En la ejecución local del 1 de noviembre de 2026, el pipeline recuperó 90 registros reales para el período del 26 de septiembre al 25 de octubre de 2026: 30 por ciudad. Construyó los dos modelos y superó las nueve pruebas dbt. También pasaron cuatro pruebas unitarias y la comprobación de idempotencia con agregados sintéticos conocidos.

La ejecución remota también completó las pruebas y publicó el mismo período. La consulta directa del CSV público devolvió estos resultados:

Ciudad Días Promedio del punto medio diario (°C) Precipitación acumulada (mm)
Arequipa 30 17.48 1.1
Cusco 30 14.30 17.7
Lima 30 22.74 7.7

Son una instantánea del período 2026-09-26 a 2026-10-25, no valores permanentes. El reporte permite descargar el detalle y el resumen; sus metadatos indican el origen, las fechas, el momento de generación y el commit. Las pruebas locales y la comprobación HTTP del despliegue aportan evidencias separadas del funcionamiento.

Conclusión

El proyecto recorre el ciclo de un pipeline ELT: extracción, almacenamiento, transformación, validación, exportación y despliegue automatizado comprobado. Su tamaño permite explicar cada decisión y repetir el proceso sin administrar servidores.

La solución ya puede consultarse públicamente y actualizarse con cada ejecución exitosa del workflow. Como mejoras futuras quedan un histórico incremental, alertas ante fallos y pruebas sobre cambios de esquema en la API.
