title: Understanding the CAP Theorem
description:
As developers, we often assume that distributed systems can provide everything at once: perfectly consistent data, high availability, and resilience to network failures. Unfortunately, distributed systems don't work like that.

This is where the CAP Theorem comes in, one of the most fundamental concepts in distributed computing.

What Is the CAP Theorem?

Proposed by computer scientist Eric Brewer, the CAP Theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee only two of the following three properties simultaneously:

  • Consistency (C)
  • Availability (A)
  • Partition Tolerance (P)

When a network partition occurs, you must choose between consistency and availability.

Consistency

Consistency means every node sees the same data at the same time.

If you update a user's account balance, every server should immediately return the updated value.

From the user's perspective:

  • Read after write works correctly
  • No stale data
  • Single source of truth

Availability

Availability means every request receives a response, even if some servers are experiencing issues.

The response might not contain the most recent data, but the system remains operational.

Examples:

  • Social media feeds: If User X updates their profile info, it's just fine if User Y sees the old info for a few minutes.
  • Product recommendations
  • Content Platforms
  • Analytics dashboards
  • Review Sites (Yelp etc.)

These systems often prioritize availability over strict consistency.
We can basically ask ourselves "Would it be catastrophic if users briefly saw inconsistent data?" If the answer is yes, choose consistency. If not, choose availability[1]

Partition Tolerance - Not Optional

A partition happens when nodes cannot communicate because of network failures."Partition Tolerance” is the the ability of a distributed system to continue operating even when a partition occurs.

In modern cloud environments, partitions are not hypothetical events.

They happen because of:

  • Network outages
  • Region failures
  • Router issues
  • Infrastructure maintenance

Since partitions are unavoidable, most distributed systems must support partition tolerance. Because you cannot prevent hardware failures or router crashes.The systems should not be affected by network partitions.
Therefore, any distributed system must be partition-tolerant.

A Real-World Example: The ATM

Imagine you have $1,000 in your bank account and two ATMs connected to different bank servers.

You withdraw $200 from the first ATM, but a network failure prevents the second server from receiving the update 🫣 The second ATM still shows your balance as $1,000.

Now, you try to withdraw another $900 from the second ATM.

  • Consistency (CP): The ATM rejects the transaction because it cannot verify your current balance. The system sacrifices availability to protect data consistency.
  • Availability (AP): The ATM continues processing transactions using its outdated balance, potentially allowing you to withdraw more money than you actually have.

Real banking systems use additional safeguards to prevent such situations.

This example illustrates the fundamental CAP trade-off: when a network partition occurs, a system may need to reject or delay requests to maintain consistency, or continue responding despite the risk of serving outdated data.

The Real Trade-off

The CAP Theorem becomes important when a partition occurs.

At that moment you must decide:

CP Systems

Consistency + Partition Tolerance

The system rejects or delays requests to ensure data remains correct.

Examples:

  • Banking transactions
  • Inventory management
  • Financial systems

Correctness matters more than availability.

AP Systems

Availability + Partition Tolerance

The system continues serving requests even if some nodes have outdated information.

Examples:

  • Social networks
  • Messaging systems
  • Content platforms

Availability matters more than immediate consistency.

What About CA Systems?

Technically, CA systems exist only when partitions never happen.

In real distributed environments, partitions are inevitable.

This is why most cloud-native systems end up choosing either CP or AP behavior during failures.

CAP in Modern Databases

Different databases make different trade-offs:

Database Typical Preference
MongoDB CP
Apache Cassandra AP
DynamoDB AP-oriented
PostgreSQL (single node) CA-like
CockroachDB CP

Understanding these trade-offs helps architects choose the right database for their workload.

Why Developers Still Need CAP

Many developers learn CAP Theorem during interviews or reviewing the interview questions and then forget about it😀

But CAP influences real-world decisions:

  • Designing microservices
  • Choosing databases
  • Building global applications
  • Handling outages
  • Architecting cloud-native systems

Whenever someone says, "Why can't we just keep everything available and perfectly consistent?", they are usually running into the limitations described by CAP.

I think CAP Theorem is not like a database rule. It is a reminder that distributed systems require trade-offs.

As systems scale across regions, clouds, and continents, understanding those trade-offs becomes more important than memorizing any specific technology.

Resources & Further Reading
[1]- Cap Theorem

Understanding CAP Theorem: Basics and Real-World Examples

title: Anatomy of 32 Days
description:
Every number here was cheap to collect and late to arrive. That gap is the whole story.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer working mostly in PHP/Symfony and Go, currently carving a live PHP monolith into Go services. The seven parts before this one each took one angle on a single write path that left the monolith. This one is the ledger: the same 32 days read as one timeline, with every figure in one place and a link to the part that unpacks it. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

This is how I do it right now, with the price attached - maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way.

The path in one paragraph

A user saves a set of matching rules; every domain under that account gets marked by them. Four participants: the Go API gateway as the only door from outside, the rule-set-markup service which takes the write and folds the cascade, the domain-rule-map service which owns rule-set identity and recalculates the map, and PostgreSQL behind them - the monolith's database for the rule data, the identity service's own for identity.

One user action, four processes, two databases. Accepting that as working took 32 days, and this is what was inside them.

What "32 days" actually contains

The headline number is the least useful one in the set, so it is worth breaking before anything is built on it.

  DAYS   32 ┤████████████████████████████████  the acceptance timeline
            │        ▼ −21  automated verdicts only: pass/fail per case, no numbers, no traces
         11 ┤███████████
            │        ▼ −2   two days with no verdict at all — the wrong thing was under test
          9 ┤█████████
            │        ▼ −2   days inside the detailed window with no runs
          7 ┤███████  ◄ days with detailed, traced runs
  ──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  MINUTES inside those 7 days — 985 total = 16 h 25 min
    day 1 ██████████████████ 178      day 5 ██████████████████ 179
    day 2 ███████████████    150      day 6 ███████            77
    day 3 ██████████         102      day 7 ████████           89
    day 4 █████████████████████ 210   ◄ one run alone = 120

34 runs across the period, 28 of them numbered. Duration was recorded for 29 of the 34: mean 34 minutes, longest 2 hours, shortest 2 minutes. So the honest version of the headline is not "32 days of testing" - it is 16 hours 25 minutes of measured work, spread over 7 days, inside a 32-day window.

I am starting here because every ratio later in this article has one of these denominators in it, and the wrong denominator turns a modest finding into a dramatic one for free.

Three windows, three instruments

The 32 days are not one measurement. They are three, taken with different instruments, and no line crosses between them honestly.

  window 1   before day 0        no acceptance artefacts exist at all
                                 behaviour reconstructed from migrations, commits, docs
  window 2   day 0 … day 21      automated verdicts per case, per deploy tag
                                 pass / fail, and nothing else — no timings, no traces
  window 3   day 21 … day 32     traced runs: timings, state dumps, statement text
                                 the numbered defect registry starts on day 25

Which produces the reading rule I put on every chart in this material:

Comparing across those windows compares methods of observation, not states of the system.

Two more caveats travel with it, and they are in every part of this series for the same reason: round-trip time to the environment sits at a steady 220-260 ms regardless of endpoint, so it is never part of anyone's work; and a share is never published without its absolute value - 440.0 ms · 61 %, never 61 % on its own.

Day one of the detailed window: three objects, everything passes

For the first weeks the checks ran against a playground of three objects. The runs were honest - real requests, real assertions, real data written and read back - and everything passed.

Then a run went across everything the environment held:

  playground              3 objects        everything passes
  full sweep            276 objects        the active-set registry is EMPTY for 210 of them
  later sweeps          392 objects        392 of 392 covered; 129 map rows of 2 329
                                           carry neither rule set nor priority (5.5 %)

Nothing was fixed between the first two lines. The system was in the same state; what changed is that it could be asked - the services had grown read endpoints that describe state: the input snapshot, the rule set in effect, the pointer to the active set, the stored map page by page.

That is Part 2 - A Service That Cannot Explain Itself Can Only Be Guessed At. It is the earliest thing in this timeline in the causal sense: nothing else here was findable before those four reads existed.

The argument about who was slow

The next thing the traced window settled was an argument that had been running on opinions. A single write, end to end: 121 spans, four services, 1 256.9 ms on the client's stopwatch. The blame sat on the write service, because that is the address on the envelope.

Read as nesting rather than as a sum:

  client wait                                       1 256.9 ms   100 %
  ├── transport, client ↔ environment                  244.9      19.5 %   not ours
  └── four services at work                          1 012.0      80.5 %
      └── the suspected service, own zone                87.4       7.0 %
          ├── own work                                    1.4
          └── waiting on PostgreSQL                      86.0      98.4 % of its zone

87.4 ms of 1 256.9 - 7.0 %, and 98.4 % of that is waiting on the database. The code itself accounts for 1.4 ms.

The cheapest confirmation in the whole set came from a request that was rejected as invalid: server work 6.6 ms, database 0.0 ms, client stopwatch 231.8 ms. Nothing computed, nothing stored, and 97.2 % of the call still happened outside our code.

And when the shape of one read was fixed, the same three-build comparison showed why the unit matters: database round trips went 92 to 7, database time 440.0 to 31.8 ms - a factor of 14 - while the network never moved. By share alone the network went from a third of the call to 88 % of it and reads as a catastrophe. In milliseconds, everything we own fell and the rest stood still.

Full breakdown, including the zone we still cannot measure: Part 1 - Most of Your Latency Is Not Your Code.

The account that did not fit

The same instrument answered a question nobody had asked before shipping: how much work is one caller allowed to order?

One object addressed directly is 121 spans and 53 database round trips, 11 of them repeats. One account addressed at the top, with 366 children below it, is 10 822 spans - roughly 30 spans per child, derived by dividing one measured total by one measured count.

The deadline on that call is a constant 20 seconds. The work behind it is a line. On one observed run the caller was cut off at 20.26 s and the work carried on for another 8.7 s, committing successfully at 28.96 s:

  0 s                                  20.26 s               28.96 s
  ├───────────────────────────────────────┤───────────────────┤
  │  work in progress                     │  8.7 s more work  │
                                          │
                          caller is told: the call failed
                                                              │
                                          database holds: the write landed

Around 253 children is where the endpoint stops fitting, and how many accounts sit above that line is a product fact nobody had written down. In aggregate it showed up as deadline failures on 13 of 76 objects, then 27 of 76 after a change meant to help. The whole slope, and why optimisation moves the crossing point rather than removing it, is Part 5 - The Client Decides How Much Work You Do.

The value nobody owned

The longest-lived defect of the period had no code to blame. A rule is saved, the response is 200, the read shows the new set - and the engine keeps marking by the old one. Eight rounds thirty seconds apart, four minutes of the two answers disagreeing, no error anywhere.

Six iterations, the record of the whole timeline. The analysis that explained it took an afternoon:

  • the value lives in four carriers across two databases, and there is no foreign key between them - there cannot be, they belong to different services;
  • the right to write it had moved seven times in 48 days;
  • in one of those states, two days long, it belonged to nobody;
  • and the state was produced by two commits, same day, two repositories, each correct on its own, which together formed a circle: a freshly written set has no map rows, so it can never become active.

No review inside either repository could have caught it: each diff was right, and the contradiction lived on the seam. Part 3 - Nobody Owned the Value is that afternoon written out, including the detector that catches the class forever: two reads and an equality check, run on all 392 objects.

The contract that could not say zero

While that ran, a second class was producing numbers of its own. A priority that was stored, correct and impossible to present, because the strongest priority in this system is written as 0 and on the wire 0 looks exactly like a field nobody set. Both sides were locally correct: the producer omits zero values by the rules of the format, the consumer treats an absent field as unset.

Eight of the 26 numbered defects were defects of contract shape - the largest single class in the registry, and not one of them was a computation error. The same field's own history: removed from the contract, put back about 45 days later, and pinned down with an explicit meaning for zero on day 91.

What made it observable was not an assertion on a response - every response was correct throughout - but a count over stored state: map rows carrying no priority at all, 27 to 41 to 0.

And its quieter twin: when two rules tie, which wins? Nobody had ever decided. The behaviour was deterministic - first match in array order - and it had held as a norm for 17 months as a property of how a loop was written. Part 6 - Zero Is Not Absent, and Nobody Wrote the Order Down.

The baseline that moved

The method for accepting the new write path was parity: run both implementations on the same input, compare field by field. That is a sound method exactly once - when the reference stands still.

On one day the same input went through nine iterations, and the size of the cascade the two sides produced went 2, then 258, then 2, then 8 rows. The reference was changing its own definition mid-day, and it was internally inconsistent too: one identifier came back as a number in one field and as a string in another. Three times out of nine the new implementation turned out to be the correct one.

Underneath sat the same failure in three different disguises:

  • a 502 returned after the row was committed;
  • a 200 completed on a row that had been silently deleted;
  • a 504 at 20.26 s on a write that went through.

None of them is a lie by the transport. With two storages and no shared transaction, a response code reports that the call arrived and its own transaction closed - and nothing about what is in the database. Then the parity work was erased in one line by a correct decision: the old write endpoint would be removed entirely. Part 4 - Parity Against a Moving Baseline has the full accounting, including the one thing that was missing - the date the comparison would expire.

The ledger

Everything above, as counts.

  26 numbered defects
     16   closed as real defects            (by subtraction from the four rows below)
      5   declared normal behaviour
      3   still open at the end of the period
      2   withdrawn as false

  39 defect-iterations between those 26 numbers      longest single defect: 6 iterations
   8 false alarms in total, of which one is a false PASS - a check that ran zero comparisons

Two rows are worth more than the rest.

Three still open at the end of the period, and their wording is the giveaway: rule order is not provable; cursor paging says "more" and returns no token; an asynchronous rebuild lands in tens of seconds - or does not. None of them is "the code is wrong". All three are "the system cannot demonstrate the property being asked about".

One false PASS. A probe sent a single value to an endpoint that requires a list, got a 422, took the empty decision list as agreement and printed PASS 24, FAIL 3. Two builds were accepted on a line that had performed zero comparisons. A false FAIL creates work. A false PASS removes the check and leaves the report looking identical.

What a document would have caught

This is the number I keep from the whole period, and the one I am least comfortable with.

   26 numbered defects
   ████████████████████████████████████████████  26
             │
             ▼  step 1 — the specification names WHO WRITES this value
   ██████████████████████████████                18  left
             │
             ▼  step 0 — endpoint and fields taken from the contract, not from memory
   ████████████████                              13  left
             │
             ▼  steps 2/3/4/6 — actual measurement against a live system
   ██                                             2  ◄ one conditional, one unobservable

24 of 26 - 92 % - would have been removed by acceptance written before the code, and 21 of 39 defect-iterations die on one question: who is allowed to write this value? That question is answered by reading a document. It is an estimate over the registry rather than an experiment, and I publish it as one - but even halved it says the same thing.

What it cost, and the number I never took

The bill is not "we wrote buggy code". It is the cost of finding out what was wanted:

  requirements with two defensible readings            23
  reversals of decisions already implemented            7      in 5 of 6, the code matched
                                                               the specification of its day
  iterations spent finding out rather than fixing   ~13 of 27  (estimated over intervals)
  iterations of briefs written and discarded            15     within a day
  brief files accumulated in the repository            289     137 of them in 33 numbered sets
  write-ups of my own acceptance mistakes               28     5 of them repeated, 1–6 days apart
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  days with a measurement of money or tokens             0

The last row is the one I would fix first if I were starting again. Every duration in this article was recorded; not one day carries a figure for what the automated work cost in tokens or money. That means everything here is a claim about what the arrangement found, and nothing here is a claim about whether it was worth it. Those are different claims and I can only make the first.

The row above it is the second-cheapest lesson: 5 of 28 mistakes repeated within one to six days, every one of them already written up in prose. A rule that lives only in a postmortem is re-derived by whoever reads it next, which is to say never - and an automated executor never reads it at all. What stopped the repeats was moving each rule into the two places that are read on every run: the brief, as a numbered constraint, and the check, as an assertion that fails.

The arrangement that produced most of the numbers above - one automated pass pointed at the output of another, told to instrument the zone with no spans and report back - is Part 7 - One Executor Checking Another Executor's Work.

Seven readings, one per part

If the timeline collapses to seven sentences, these are the seven:

  1. A service is judged by its own span, not by the client's stopwatch. 87.4 ms of 1 256.9 - and 97.2 % of a rejected call is not our code. -> Part 1
  2. A service that cannot state what its answer should be can only be guessed at. Three objects passed; 276 objects had 210 empty registries, and nothing had changed in between. -> Part 2
  3. A value with no named owner does not have a bug - it has an unfinished analysis. Four carriers, two databases, seven moves of the write right in 48 days, two of those days belonging to nobody. -> Part 3
  4. A comparison is a test only while the reference stands still. Nine parity runs in one day, a cascade of 2, 258, 2 and 8 rows for the same input, and a comparison with no expiry date. -> Part 4
  5. A synchronous answer over work the caller sizes is a promise the caller gets to break for you. A constant 20-second deadline against a cost that is linear in 366 children. -> Part 5
  6. A field that cannot separate "absent" from "zero" is two facts sharing a slot. Eight of 26 defects were contract shape; a tie-break rule held as a norm for 17 months because it lived in a loop. -> Part 6
  7. A second automated pass earns its cost only if it can add a measurement the first one never had. 92 database round trips on a call that needs 7, reported as 200 OK in every column. -> Part 7

And the one that only appears when they are read together: the split did not create these defects, it made them expressible. A single process can hold an unstated ownership rule, an unstated tie-break and an unstated capacity limit indefinitely, because there is no boundary at which the omission has to be declared. Two services cannot.

What none of this proves

Being explicit, because a ledger invites conclusions it cannot support.

It does not say microservices are worse than a monolith, or better. It does not say anything got faster after the split - the instruments changed inside the window, and the earlier stretch has no numbers to compare against. It does not price anything: no money, no person-hours, no token counts. It does not say anything about the reliability of anyone's production system; every figure here comes from a test environment.

What it does support is narrower: on this path, in this period, 24 of 26 defects were answerable before anything ran, and the four questions that would have answered them fit on one page.

The multiplier line

Nine parity runs in a day, a sweep of 392 objects per build, a trace folded into a table and diffed against yesterday's - all of that was cheap because it was automated, and none of it would have been affordable by hand. What automation never supplied was a single one of the sentences that were missing: who may write this value, what absent means for this field, how large a caller is allowed to be, which side of a comparison is entitled to be right. Fast iteration multiplies the definitions that exist in writing. Where a definition is missing, it multiplies the circling instead - and produces, very precisely and very confidently, 39 iterations of a description where four written sentences would have done.

Anatomy of a service split - Part 8. That closes this set. The obvious hole in it is the last row of the bill: 985 minutes of recorded duration and not one day with a cost figure attached. The next thing I measured was exactly that - what the automated work itself bills, per session, in tokens and in money, before any of it produces a line of output.

If you do this better, tell me which of your defects you can honestly say a document would have caught. If you have been through this, what did your own ledger look like when you counted the iterations rather than the tickets? If you see it differently, say where writing the requirement down first costs more than it returns. How is it solved on your side, and what broke there?

title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: What Cloud Computing Actually Is: The Honest First Lesson
description:
TL;DR: Cloud computing is hardware and software reached over the Internet instead of run locally, rented by the hour from someone else’s data centers.

  • NIST SP 800-145, from September 2011, supplies the reference definition and the field’s arithmetic in NIST’s own count: five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models.
  • The plant is countable: 1,136 hyperscale data centers operated worldwide at the end of 2024, and AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud held about 59 percent of hyperscale capacity.
  • IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS order the renting by how much the provider takes over, and XaaS names the packaging grown up around them.
  • Security is a division of labor: the provider keeps the infrastructure side, and the customer’s side grows with control, down to patching an operating system at IaaS.
  • The timeline runs from 1960s time-sharing through a 1994 metaphor and a 1996 compound noun to a commercial opening in 2006, Amazon’s S3 and EC2.

Drawings of the cloud point up, at a soft shape in the sky, and explain nothing. The real answer has a standards-agency definition, a countable number of buildings behind it, and a history whose dates you can check. This article accompanies the Whiteboard Architect lesson that opens the cloud computing series: watch the full episode on YouTube for the boards drawn in real time, or read on: every number below links to the page it was verified against.

The opening board: everyday services on the left, a crossed-out cloud for the usual explanation, and the promise of one checked sentence.

Cloud computing, defined without the sky

The industry says the cloud when it means the network, and the network in question is the Internet; cloud computing is the arrangement in which the machines and the software live elsewhere and you reach them across it. Your side shrinks to whichever device and browser is at hand.

The catalog of what cloud computing rents out runs the full height of the stack. Servers arrive as virtual machines or as dedicated hardware; storage, networking, and databases come alongside them; above those sit development platforms, and at the top entire applications that a team never installs at all, provisioned while you wait.

The NIST definition of cloud computing, and its arithmetic

Vendors describe the field in whatever way flatters their product, so the sentence worth memorizing comes from a standards body. NIST Special Publication 800-145, dated September 2011, calls cloud computing “a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources.” The paper then does the counting that keeps the field organized, and its numbers are exact: five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models.

Treat the enumeration as a checksum: a tutorial advertising four characteristics has slipped against the definition it means to teach. The five characteristics are deep enough material for their own episode later in this series; the present lesson carries the definition, the models, and the corrections.

What are the five essential characteristics?

The paper lists them: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. In its own definitions, a consumer can provision computing capabilities automatically, without human interaction with the provider; the network carries the capabilities to thin or thick client platforms; the provider’s pool serves multiple consumers on a multi-tenant model; provisioning scales outward and inward with demand; and usage is monitored, controlled, and reported.

The buildings behind the joke

Behind cloud computing sits physical plant, and the plant has a size. The buildings are hyperscale data centers: 1,136 were operating worldwide at the end of 2024, twice the count of five years earlier, typically thousands of servers to a building. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud hold roughly 59 percent of all hyperscale capacity between them.

Numbers of that size are why an old joke lands. People say the cloud is just someone else’s computer, and the ownership half of the gag is accurate: the machines, the buildings, and the staff running them all belong to the provider. The alternative to renting is on-premises computing, in which an organization finances its own hardware in advance, installs it, and replaces it as it ages. AWS’s definition page compresses the difference into a swap of up-front capital expense for a metered bill.

Why do people repeat the joke that the cloud is someone else’s computer?

Because the ownership half of the sentence is true. The servers, the buildings, and the people who maintain both belong to the provider, at a scale few single organizations can match: a hyperscale facility typically packs in thousands of servers and operates as a building with its own physical security. Where the gag misleads is the implication that nothing else changed. A machine room rented by the hour arrives wrapped in professional operations, and the scale of those operations is what moves the unit price below anything one organization reaches alone.

The board in the video draws the same split: a crossed-out cloud on one side, the promise of a checked sentence on the other.

IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: a ladder built on control

NIST’s three service models describe how much of the machine work a customer hands over, and the useful mental image is a ladder with control running up one rail. Every rung upward moves another layer into the provider’s hands.

Model The provider’s side Your side
IaaS, infrastructure as a service Raw pieces: networking, compute, storage An operating system to choose and patch, plus every task that follows from it
PaaS, platform as a service The whole runtime: supply code and the platform executes it, hardware and base software included Code, data, and configuration
SaaS, software as a service An application delivered finished and maintained end to end The content you put in: mail, meetings, records

Gmail is email as a service, Zoom is meetings as a service, Salesforce runs customer relationships as a service, and in each case the customer never touches an operating system.

Around the three core models clusters a growing acronym family, XaaS, meaning anything as a service. Its current roster includes network, database, function, security, disaster recovery, and desktop entries. Handy labels, and none disturbs the count: NIST’s three stand, the additions are packaging.

Board 5 of 16: the ladder starts at IaaS, the rung where the customer keeps control and carries the chores.

Where does serverless sit if it is not a fourth model?

To the side, as a delivery pattern. Serverless hands a provider raw code and lets the provider worry about every machine underneath: AWS Lambda, the pattern’s best-known instance, takes a function, provisions what it needs, and charges for the requests it actually serves. Idle functions cost nothing, which is what the phrase scale to zero describes. The acronym family files the pattern under function as a service, and the filing is honest: it names a way of buying compute, not a peer of the three NIST models. Listing serverless as a fourth model is the error corrected further down this page.

The pattern has a precise boundary: the provider owns provisioning, scaling, and the servers themselves, and the customer owns the code and what it does.

Public, private, community, and hybrid

The service ladder says what you rent. A second axis, the deployment models of cloud computing, says who is allowed in, and NIST lists four of them.

Model Its audience Its home
Public Anyone, on published terms The provider’s own infrastructure
Private A single organization Infrastructure set aside for that organization
Community Several organizations with requirements in common Infrastructure they share for that purpose
Hybrid Any mixture of the above Part dedicated, part rented

Hybrid carries the clearest use case. A workload with privacy constraints lives on the dedicated side; when traffic surges past what that side holds, the surplus runs in the public cloud, and the surge is billed only for as long as it runs. One step further sits multi-cloud, an organization deliberately split across providers, a pattern young enough that the 2011 paper does not name it.

The benefits ledger, asterisk included

The claimed benefits of cloud computing are checkable, so treat them as line items. The scalability and elasticity rows sound alike and do different jobs, and the performance row carries the asterisk.

Benefit What it means
Provisioning speed Capacity that once waited on a procurement cycle arrives in minutes
Money Usage-based billing converts an owned-hardware budget into a metered one
Sizing Allocations follow demand upward and downward, so a system built for the December peak no longer idles through June
Scalability A customer adjusts allocations deliberately
Elasticity The platform adjusts allocations automatically as load changes, all the way down to nothing when the load disappears
Durability and recovery Providers run backup and disaster-recovery machinery at prices few private setups reach, and instances placed in several separate locations tolerate one of those locations going dark
Staff time Patching, capacity planning, and hardware maintenance move onto the provider’s payroll
Performance The asterisk: distance still governs latency, so an application placed near its audience responds faster than the same application placed far away

Board 10 of 16: the ledger, three ruled rows, with the pair worth remembering boxed at the lower right: scalability you move, elasticity follows.

How do regions and availability zones contain a failure?

Geography is the tool. AWS carves the world into Regions, and its EC2 guide names closeness to specific customers among the reasons to pick one. Within a Region sit availability zones, isolated locations arranged so that a failure in one leaves the others serving; an instance group split across zones therefore survives the loss of a single zone.

The definition page compresses the global version of the offer into four quoted words, “deploy globally in minutes,” and Local Zones extend it by placing capacity close to individual metro areas. None of the placement happens automatically; the Region menu is where that choice is made.

Virtualization: the mechanism under the price

Renting by the hour pays because of one technology. Virtualization divides a physical computer into several logically independent ones, which keeps the hardware busy and the unit cost low. The supervisor program that manufactures and runs those virtual machines is the hypervisor. A virtual machine presents itself as a complete computer, with processors, memory, and disks of its own, while underneath it shares one physical box with its neighbors.

The series leans on two more terms from here on. A container isolates at the level of the operating system: the application travels together with its libraries and settings, every container on a host shares that host’s kernel, and the package weighs less than a virtual machine as a result. Cloud storage keeps data in pooled space on the provider’s machines, with availability and environmental security as the provider’s deliverables.

Why does a container weigh less than a virtual machine?

Because of where each one draws its line. A virtual machine brings its own kernel, its own operating system files, and its own slice of the hardware’s resources, since the hypervisor fences off a complete computer. A container fences off only the application and its dependencies, then borrows the kernel the host is already running. One therefore ships an operating system per workload, the other ships one per host, and the difference shows up in startup times and in how many of each fit on the same machine. Later episodes of this series return to both patterns.

Corrections the first lesson usually skips

Four mistakes recur across introductory cloud computing material, and the costliest comes first. Security is work divided between two parties, each with a fixed share. The provider’s infrastructure side covers the machinery and the buildings; the customer side varies with the service and reaches deepest at IaaS, where it includes the operating system, the firewall, the data, and who may reach either. A public deployment is not automatically the weaker of the two. The settings decide which deployment is safer, and the customer writes them.

Which half of security does a provider actually own?

AWS’s page on the subject draws the line as security of the cloud against security in the cloud. On the company’s side, its own listing runs hardware, software, networking, and facilities, together with the physical protection of the buildings. Everything above that line is the customer’s, and the page names the parts: patching the guest operating system, configuring the firewall rules, and handling data, encryption, and access permissions.

The size of the customer’s share tracks the service model, shrinking to account settings under SaaS and growing to a full operating system under IaaS. Reading the page retires the idea that security arrives with the subscription.

The second mistake is the count again: three models, with a delivery pattern promoted into a fourth, as the serverless deep dive above explains. The third is a slogan about speed. The claim that moving to the cloud shortens response times holds when the workload ends up near its users and fails otherwise; it reduces to the placement choice from the ledger.

The fourth is chronology. Cloud computing did not exist as a phrase in 1950, whatever a centenary graphic implies. Time-sharing on mainframes, starting in the 1960s, is the genuine ancestor; the network metaphor called the cloud appeared in 1994; the full term spread from a 1996 Compaq business plan; and the commercial form opened when Amazon put S3 and EC2 on the market in 2006. The series gives that road its own third episode.

How much of cloud computing predates Amazon’s 2006 launch?

Most of the lineage. Time-sharing in the 1960s ran the same bargain at mainframe scale: many remote users, one costly machine, access over wires. General Magic gave the metaphor its name in 1994, describing the Telescript world of mobile software agents in terms of the places an agent could travel to, and Compaq’s 1996 plan supplied the compound noun.

The time-sharing users of that era handed jobs to the machine’s operators and waited for output; the browser crosses the same distance today, more cheaply and more often. Amazon’s contribution was making the thing purchasable: S3 opened storage for rent, and the EC2 beta announcement is dated August 25, 2006, four decades after time-sharing put many remote users on one costly machine.

Settled, then: cloud computing is rented infrastructure reached over the Internet, 1,136 hyperscale buildings strong at the end of 2024, defined in one NIST sentence from September 2011. Three service models arrange the renting by control, four deployment models arrange the renters, the benefits arrive as a ledger with an asterisk on latency, and security splits along a line the customer half maintains. The dates close the lesson: 1960s time-sharing, a 1994 metaphor, a 1996 name, a commercial opening in 2006 with S3 and EC2.

Board 16 of 16, the recap. Its first line, “buildings of standard servers”, is the video’s shorthand: as described above, a hyperscale facility holds thousands of servers, but this article does not claim they are all one standard kind.

Continue learning

  • Cloud Computing Interview Questions for 2026: test yourself on the service models, deployment models, and vocabulary from this lesson.
  • AWS Interview Questions and Answers for 2026: the follow-up once the questions turn to one named provider.
  • What Artificial Intelligence Actually Is: the first lesson of the AI fundamentals series, in the same checked format.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI from the script of my video lesson, then checked against its sources before publishing.

This lesson first appeared on iqraa.tech.

More whiteboard lessons on the Whiteboard Architect YouTube channel.

title: Self-Hosted WhatsApp E-Commerce & Automated Client Proposals in Pure Python + SQLite (Zero SaaS Fees)
description:
Running an online store or a freelance consulting business in 2026 often feels like a slow bleed of monthly SaaS subscriptions.

You pay $29/month for a basic Shopify tier, another $15/month for a proposal signing app, $20/month for an invoice generator, and another $30/month for automated WhatsApp messaging plugins. Before making your first dollar in profit, your business is saddled with over $1,000 a year in fixed recurring overhead.

Worse, your customer data, order history, and client contracts sit locked inside third-party walled gardens that can hike prices, change terms, or suspend your account at any moment.

Over the past year at Antigravity Dev Studio, we set out to prove a different thesis: You can build a high-performance, self-hosted e-commerce checkout engine and client proposal portal using only the Python standard library and SQLite.

No Django, no Celery, no Redis, and no monthly fees.

In this deep-dive tutorial, we will walk through the exact architecture and runnable code for three mission-critical components:

  1. Generating pre-filled, structured WhatsApp checkout URLs with zero API gateway fees.
  2. Building an atomic, collision-free invoice numbering system on SQLite WAL mode.
  3. Securing client proposal digital acceptance links using cryptographic HMAC signatures.

1. Zero-Fee WhatsApp Checkout URL Builder

In emerging e-commerce markets across Latin America, the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is the dominant communication channel. Customers often abandon traditional multi-step checkout funnels that force account creation or require complex payment gateways.

Instead of paying a third-party WhatsApp Business API provider hundreds of dollars in monthly platform fees, you can use the official https://wa.me/ direct URL protocol. When a customer clicks "Place Order via WhatsApp", your Python backend formats their entire shopping cart, customer notes, delivery address, and order code into an encoded message.

When the customer taps the link on mobile or desktop, WhatsApp opens instantly with a perfectly structured, ready-to-send message:

import urllib.parse
from typing import Any, Dict, List

def build_whatsapp_order_url(
    business_phone: str,
    order_code: str,
    customer_name: str,
    customer_phone: str,
    delivery_address: str,
    items: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    subtotal: float,
    discount_amount: float,
    delivery_fee: float,
    total: float,
    currency: str = "USD"
) -> str:
    """
    Constructs an official, encoded WhatsApp Web/App direct checkout URL.
    Works natively on iOS, Android, macOS, and Windows.
    """
    # Clean phone number (strip spaces, dashes, plus signs)
    clean_phone = "".join(ch for ch in business_phone if ch.isdigit())

    # Build clean line items breakdown
    item_lines = []
    for item in items:
        qty = item.get("qty", 1)
        name = item.get("name", "Product")
        price = item.get("price", 0.0)
        item_lines.append(f"• {qty}x {name} — {currency} {price * qty:,.2f}")

    items_block = "\n".join(item_lines)

    # Formatted customer message
    message = (
        f"🛍️ *NEW ORDER: #{order_code}*\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"👤 *Customer:* {customer_name.strip()}\n"
        f"📞 *Phone:* {customer_phone.strip()}\n"
        f"📍 *Delivery Address:* {delivery_address.strip()}\n\n"
        f"📦 *Ordered Items:*\n"
        f"{items_block}\n\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"💰 *Subtotal:* {currency} {subtotal:,.2f}\n"
    )

    if discount_amount > 0:
        message += f"🏷️ *Discount:* -{currency} {discount_amount:,.2f}\n"

    message += (
        f"🚚 *Delivery Fee:* {currency} {delivery_fee:,.2f}\n"
        f"✅ *TOTAL AMOUNT:* {currency} {total:,.2f}\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"Please confirm availability and dispatch details!"
    )

    # Encode message safely for URL transmission
    encoded_text = urllib.parse.quote(message)
    return f"https://wa.me/{clean_phone}?text={encoded_text}"

Testing the Output 

sample_items = [
    {"name": "Mechanical Keyboard Pro", "qty": 1, "price": 89.00},
    {"name": "USB-C Braided Cable", "qty": 2, "price": 12.50},
]

url = build_whatsapp_order_url(
    business_phone="+1 (555) 019-2834",
    order_code="ORD-78241",
    customer_name="Alex Mercer",
    customer_phone="+1 555 982 1102",
    delivery_address="742 Evergreen Terrace, Springfield",
    items=sample_items,
    subtotal=114.00,
    discount_amount=10.00,
    delivery_fee=5.00,
    total=109.00
)

print(url)

The resulting link is clean, works without any third-party gateway dependencies, and provides customers with an immediate human connection to your store.

2. Atomic SQLite WAL Invoicing & Sequential Numbering

When building an invoicing engine for clients, sequential and collision-free document numbering (such as INV-2026-001, INV-2026-002) is legally required in most jurisdictions.

If two users or background tasks generate an invoice at the exact same millisecond, a standard SQL query without proper locking will generate duplicate invoice codes or trigger database locked errors.

By leveraging SQLite Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and an explicit write-transaction loop, you guarantee zero collisions and sub-millisecond execution:

import contextlib
import datetime as dt
import pathlib
import sqlite3
from typing import Generator

class InvoiceDatabase:
    def __init__(self, db_path: pathlib.Path):
        self.db_path = pathlib.Path(db_path)
        self.db_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        self._init_schema()

    def _connect(self) -> sqlite3.Connection:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(str(self.db_path), timeout=15.0)
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        # WAL mode enables concurrent readers while writing
        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;")
        return conn

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def session(self) -> Generator[sqlite3.Connection, None, None]:
        conn = self._connect()
        try:
            with conn: # Enters transaction: BEGIN IMMEDIATE on writes
                yield conn
        finally:
            conn.close()

    def _init_schema(self) -> None:
        with self.session() as conn:
            conn.executescript("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS invoices (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    invoice_code TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
                    client_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                    amount REAL NOT NULL CHECK(amount >= 0),
                    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UNPAID',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
                CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_invoices_code ON invoices(invoice_code);
            """)

    def generate_next_invoice(self, client_name: str, amount: float) -> str:
        """
        Atomically queries the current year's highest invoice sequence
        and inserts the next consecutive record in an isolated transaction.
        """
        year = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).year
        now_iso = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0).isoformat()
        prefix = f"INV-{year}-"

        with self.session() as conn:
            # Find the highest existing sequence for the current year
            row = conn.execute(
                """
                SELECT invoice_code FROM invoices 
                WHERE invoice_code LIKE ? 
                ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1
                """,
                (f"{prefix}%",)
            ).fetchone()

            if row:
                last_code = row["invoice_code"]
                try:
                    last_num = int(last_code.split("-")[-1])
                    next_num = last_num + 1
                except ValueError:
                    next_num = 1
            else:
                next_num = 1

            invoice_code = f"{prefix}{next_num:04d}"

            conn.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO invoices (invoice_code, client_name, amount, status, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'UNPAID', ?)
                """,
                (invoice_code, client_name.strip(), round(amount, 2), now_iso)
            )

            return invoice_code

Because SQLite serializes writes at the file level inside with conn:, concurrent invoice generations will wait their turn cleanly rather than colliding.

3. Cryptographic Proposal Approvals via HMAC Tokens

When sending proposals or fee quotes to clients, you do not want to force them to create a username and password just to approve a scope of work. At the same time, you cannot use easily guessable sequential URLs (like /proposals/42/accept), as anyone could guess the URL and fake an approval.

Using standard library hmac and hashlib, you can generate tamper-proof signed authorization URLs. When the client clicks "Accept & Sign", your backend verifies that the token was signed with your server's secret key before marking the proposal as legally accepted:

import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets
import time

SERVER_SECRET_KEY = secrets.token_bytes(32) # Store securely in env / config

def generate_proposal_approval_token(proposal_id: str, client_email: str) -> str:
    """
    Generates a cryptographically signed URL token valid for client signature.
    """
    timestamp = str(int(time.time()))
    payload = f"{proposal_id}|{client_email.strip().lower()}|{timestamp}".encode("utf-8")

    # Generate HMAC-SHA256 signature
    sig = hmac.new(SERVER_SECRET_KEY, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

    # Token structure: timestamp.signature
    return f"{timestamp}.{sig}"

def verify_proposal_approval_token(proposal_id: str, client_email: str, token: str, max_age_days: int = 30) -> bool:
    """
    Verifies that the proposal token was signed with the server key and has not expired.
    """
    try:
        timestamp_str, candidate_sig = token.split(".", 1)
        created_time = int(timestamp_str)

        # Check expiration
        max_age_seconds = max_age_days * 86400
        if time.time() - created_time > max_age_seconds:
            return False # Token expired

        expected_payload = f"{proposal_id}|{client_email.strip().lower()}|{timestamp_str}".encode("utf-8")
        expected_sig = hmac.new(SERVER_SECRET_KEY, expected_payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

        # Constant-time comparison prevents timing attacks
        return hmac.compare_digest(candidate_sig, expected_sig)
    except Exception:
        return False

When verified, the system records the client's IP, acceptance timestamp, and digital signature string, instantly locking the proposal into a frozen state.
