title: Fast simulation code is slow to write, so generators write it
description:
I want to talk about code generators, domain specific languages (DSL), and simulating interactions.

Me personally, I am a fan of games like Dwarf Fortress, Age of Empires and Might and Magic, and Role Playing Games in the broader sense. Now, no matter how you look at them, they all boil down to having a "state" (like a chess board), some "actors" (the little ants you interact with), and "the rules and relationship" they form to each other.

Initially this idea started being explored by looking into cache optimized Go data structures after reading a blog post by Serge Skoredin, and trying to encode them as annotations for generating code out of them. I like meta programming, not gonna lie.

Ecclesia is an isometric pilgrimage through a world of countries drawn as Orthodox icons. It is written as annotations on Go structs, about ten lines per entity. Seven code generators, stacked, turn those lines into cache-friendly memory pools, behaviour, the world, the drawings, the network frame, the screens and the rules. The simulation runs on one thread, at 0.21 ms per tick on an Intel i7-9750H.

Twenty frames from tick 60 to tick 2,340, rendered headless by the game's own tool, with the camera following the shepherd.

The goal

How many classic Reynolds boids can you run on 1 CPU at 60 FPS, without using any goroutines? I managed to get around 8192, using Serge Skoredin's approach from the blog post last year.

My goal for this experiment was to encode the optimal cache data structures into metaprogramming generators, such that Claude can write a high-level DSL and generate down to this level of simulations.

If I had to output the code myself, it would take around 8 hours of constant writing to get around 1k LoC of code. I treat the low-level tasks as building blocks. You need a grasp and understanding of what is possible with them, but you do not need to remember the exact byte order and syntax.

The stack

I went full meme, and stacked like 3 levels of generators on top of each other.

Level 1: A basic generator does the same stuff: raw structs to SoA + wire codecs + bitfields to not waste space. And runs benchmarks to see how many allocs/ops per entity there are. And one more fun thing: it encodes the gamestate on 1400 bytes, in order to fit on a UDP datagram, such that it can support networking.

Level 2: Then on top of this one, I got a generator for relations between entities. Level 3: And on top of this one, one for "game" design and schema behavior. And then all this runs on the simulator engine that handles collision, flow fields, events, genetic algorithms, networking, etc.

Ecclesia added four more levels. Each generator reads its own annotations and writes Go that the level above calls.

Generator Describes Writes
gameframegen Memory Struct-of-arrays pools, wire codecs, bitfield accessors
simgen Behaviour Actants, relations, and the state machines that move each relation forward
gamegen The world Species, spawns, world rules
icongen What a thing looks like Each asset as a list of operations over parametric forms, plotted to an 8-bit indexed sprite by integer arithmetic. No image files.
netgen What a client is told, and in what order Which pool goes first into the 1,400-byte frame when the world is busy
shellgen Everything around the game Screens, render order, layout, typed settings, a versioned save format
rulegen Who a person is, and how what they do turns out Hidden dice. Every probability is computed by exact enumeration of the 216 outcomes of three dice.

Two checks sit outside the chain. simcheck emits nothing. It refuses a relation that nothing spawns, and an actant that nothing fills, because both generate valid code and never happen. netgen's budget check fails the build when a schema promises more than a frame holds, and it prints the arithmetic.

From a story to a running world

The flow is something like this. You ask Claude to read a story, a novel, whatever, and extract relations, entities, etc. Then it edits a Schema.go with the high-level DSL annotations, like 10 lines per entity. Then I run the Level 2 generator: that creates the primitives and a high-level API. Then it combines the high-level API rules in main.go and just compiles it to the final gamestate.

1. A story: "fairies that glow and heal deer".
2. Annotations on Go structs, about 10 lines per entity:
     simgen:actant  affordances=Flee,Graze        (the deer)
     simgen:relation Heal actors=Fairy,Creature   (the healing)
3. Seven generators write the Go code.
4. simcheck and the frame budget refuse what can never happen.
5. go build, and the world runs.

The page view and the eye view

The world is drawn from the page, isometric, as in the first animation. The same state can also be seen through the shepherd's eye.

There is also a first-person view, similar to the original Might and Magic.

Twenty-four frames at tick 600, the eye turning 360 degrees in steps of 15.

Threads

For all this + networking + disk I/O, it works on 4 cores (threads) only. But the simulation in itself is on 1 core, 1 thread. The networking is offloaded to 1 core (1 thread), disk I/O to a different core (thread), and the painting on screen to a different core (thread).

Measured per tick on an Intel i7-9750H, default world, 600 ticks, rendered headless: simulation 0.21 ms, culling 0.28 ms, ground 1.33 ms, sprites 1.14 ms, overlay 0.49 ms.

MMORPGs with a local agent

It is quite wild, as at some point you realize you can hot swap the views of a running program, and end up letting people create their own fantasy game by prompting on the same gamestate and rules shared by other people.

I think we will end up having MMORPGs that ship a small local agent, that allows you to fill in the gaps and build the world and game system tailored to you, but at the same time interact and be a live part of the other people's own game fantasy. I would love to play such games.

Limits. The per-tick numbers come from one machine and one world, over 600 ticks; a busier world costs more. The 8,192 boids figure is a separate experiment, one thread at 60 FPS. The engine and the game are not published.

Originally published on keibisoft.com: Fast simulation code is slow to write, so generators write it

title: How to Create an SVG Icon Sprite for Your Website
description:
Build a small navigation example with Home, Search, and a dismiss button using three icons from the same set. You will paste SVG code into the free SVG Sprite Generator, copy its output, and use the resulting symbols in a web page. No framework or build plugin is needed.

Once the generated sprite is included in your page, a visible icon needs only a reference to its symbol. Here is the Home link used in this example:

<a href="#home">
  <svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
    <use href="#icon-home"></use>
  </svg>
  Home
</a>

.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; }

This short snippet assumes icon-home is already defined in the document. The steps below create that definition; section 3 contains the complete page you can copy.

When a sprite fits

A sprite defines each icon once inside a <symbol>. An <svg> containing <use> draws an instance wherever you need it. This is useful for repeated icons in plain HTML, server templates, and documentation. A small, deliberately chosen set is easier to maintain than a bundle of every available icon.

Sprites can reduce repeated markup, but they do not always improve performance. An inline sprite adds bytes to each HTML document; an external sprite needs a request but can be cached. Unused symbols still cost bytes. Measure your own pages. Separate SVGs or components may fit better when icons need different animations, per-instance path changes, or individual imports.

1. Choose three matching icons

Use the 24-pixel solid variants from HeroIcons: home-solid, magnifying-glass-solid, and x-mark-solid. Keep the same variant and grid rather than mixing outline, 16-pixel, and solid artwork.

On each icon page, use the basic Copy to Clipboard → SVG action. Basic SVG copying is available without signing in; the separate download action requires a verified Member account. Neither an account nor Pro is required to use this generator. See Copy SVG code for that workflow.

The reproducible inputs below come from the same set's official Heroicons v2.2.0 sources. They use a 0 0 24 24 viewBox. Heroicons is distributed under the MIT license; retain its copyright and permission notice with redistributed copies. Save a copy of the linked license alongside your example as LICENSE-heroicons.txt. The generator does not create a license manifest for you.

For an exact reproduction, paste these complete SVG documents into separate input blocks:

Name: home 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path d="M11.47 3.841a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0l8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.06-1.061l-8.689-8.69a2.25 2.25 0 0 0-3.182 0l-8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.061 1.06l8.69-8.689Z"/>
  <path d="m12 5.432 8.159 8.159c.03.03.06.058.091.086v6.198c0 1.035-.84 1.875-1.875 1.875H15a.75.75 0 0 1-.75-.75v-4.5a.75.75 0 0 0-.75-.75h-3a.75.75 0 0 0-.75.75V21a.75.75 0 0 1-.75.75H5.625a1.875 1.875 0 0 1-1.875-1.875v-6.198a2.29 2.29 0 0 0 .091-.086L12 5.432Z"/>
</svg>

Name: magnifying-glass 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M10.5 3.75a6.75 6.75 0 1 0 0 13.5 6.75 6.75 0 0 0 0-13.5ZM2.25 10.5a8.25 8.25 0 1 1 14.59 5.28l4.69 4.69a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06l-4.69-4.69A8.25 8.25 0 0 1 2.25 10.5Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
</svg>

Name: x-mark 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0L12 10.94l5.47-5.47a.75.75 0 1 1 1.06 1.06L13.06 12l5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06L12 13.06l-5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1-1.06-1.06L10.94 12 5.47 6.53a.75.75 0 0 1 0-1.06Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
</svg>

2. Generate the sprite

  1. Open the SVG Sprite Generator. It starts with two blocks named icon-1 and icon-2.
  2. Replace the first name with home and paste the home SVG. Name the second magnifying-glass and paste its SVG.
  3. Click Add SVG Icon +. Name the new block x-mark and paste the third SVG. Use Remove for unwanted blocks; a named empty block prevents generation.
  4. Under Options, keep ID prefix as icon, Default size as 24, and HTML mode as Decorative. Leave Hide sprite by default and currentColor CSS helper checked.
  5. Click Generate Sprite. Check the previews and any errors or warnings. The output should contain icon-home, icon-magnifying-glass, and icon-x-mark.
  6. Select the Sprite tab and click Copy output. The other tabs are HTML snippet, CSS, and React. Copy each snippet you need.

This interface accepts pasted SVG markup, not uploaded files or a selection from Collections. It processes the markup in your browser. There is no file download button: you copy text and save files yourself. Load example set replaces the inputs with the tool's own samples; Clear restores two empty blocks. After editing names, SVGs, or options, click Generate Sprite again before copying to avoid stale output.

3. Use the output in a web page

Save the following as index.html. The hidden SVG is the actual generated sprite. It belongs once inside the document body; the visible SVGs reference its symbol IDs. The Home and Search icons repeat link text, so they are decorative. The icon-only dismiss button has its accessible name on the button and actually hides the notice.

Complete example: index.html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>SVG sprite demo</title>
  <style>body { margin: 2rem; font: 18px/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; color: #163b66; background: #fff; }
nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }
a { color: inherit; }
button { font: inherit; color: inherit; background: #eef4ff; border: 1px solid #7c94ad; border-radius: .5rem; padding: .6rem; cursor: pointer; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #b45309; outline-offset: 4px; }
.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; vertical-align: -.125em; }
.icon-button .icon { width: 24px; height: 24px; }
.large { font-size: 32px; color: #9f1239; }
.dark { margin-top: 1rem; padding: 1rem; color: #e2e8f0; background: #172033; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<!-- Heroicons v2.2.0, MIT; see LICENSE-heroicons.txt. -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" style="position: absolute; width: 0; height: 0; overflow: hidden;">
  <symbol id="icon-home" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path d="M11.47 3.841a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0l8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.06-1.061l-8.689-8.69a2.25 2.25 0 0 0-3.182 0l-8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.061 1.06l8.69-8.689Z"/>
        <path d="m12 5.432 8.159 8.159c.03.03.06.058.091.086v6.198c0 1.035-.84 1.875-1.875 1.875H15a.75.75 0 0 1-.75-.75v-4.5a.75.75 0 0 0-.75-.75h-3a.75.75 0 0 0-.75.75V21a.75.75 0 0 1-.75.75H5.625a1.875 1.875 0 0 1-1.875-1.875v-6.198a2.29 2.29 0 0 0 .091-.086L12 5.432Z"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
  <symbol id="icon-magnifying-glass" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M10.5 3.75a6.75 6.75 0 1 0 0 13.5 6.75 6.75 0 0 0 0-13.5ZM2.25 10.5a8.25 8.25 0 1 1 14.59 5.28l4.69 4.69a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06l-4.69-4.69A8.25 8.25 0 0 1 2.25 10.5Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
  <symbol id="icon-x-mark" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0L12 10.94l5.47-5.47a.75.75 0 1 1 1.06 1.06L13.06 12l5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06L12 13.06l-5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1-1.06-1.06L10.94 12 5.47 6.53a.75.75 0 0 1 0-1.06Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
</svg>

<h1>SVG sprite demo</h1>
<nav aria-label="Demo navigation">
  <a href="#home"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-home"></use></svg> Home</a>
  <a href="#search"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> Search</a>
  <button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Dismiss notice"
    onclick="document.getElementById('notice').hidden = true"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-x-mark"></use></svg></button>
</nav>
<p id="notice">This is a dismissible demo notice.</p>
<section id="home"><h2>Home</h2><p>One sprite, three reusable symbols.</p></section>
<section id="search"><h2>Search</h2><p>This link is a navigation example, not a search engine.</p></section>
<p class="large"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-home"></use></svg> A larger, differently colored instance</p>
<div class="dark"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> The same icon on a dark background</div>
<p>Icons: Heroicons by Tailwind Labs / Refactoring UI Inc, MIT. Keep LICENSE-heroicons.txt with redistributed copies.</p>
</body>
</html>

The generator produces the sprite and small snippets, not the surrounding page, navigation, or dismiss behavior. The example above supplies those parts. The generated wrapper is absolutely positioned with zero width and height, keeping referenced definitions available; its symbols are referenced by the visible SVG instances. Test this pattern with your target browsers, especially if you introduce gradients or filters.

4. Control size and color

The viewBox describes the artwork's coordinate system, not its displayed pixel size. Keep it on each symbol. The CSS helper sets width and height to 1em, so these icons follow their element's font size. The 24-pixel width and height attributes in a generated snippet are overridden by that CSS. Our button deliberately overrides the helper with 24-pixel dimensions; the larger paragraph uses a 32-pixel font size.

fill: currentColor makes this solid artwork follow CSS color. Change the surrounding text color to recolor its icons. The helper does not rewrite hard-coded colors inside paths, and it is a fill helper, not a stroke conversion. Keep intentional multicolor artwork unchanged. See MDN's currentColor reference.

Outline icons keep their paint settings. Supported root presentation attributes, including fill="none", stroke="currentColor", and stroke-width, are preserved on an internal group. Child shapes can still override them. Paste the complete SVG; no manual group wrapper is needed. The fill helper does not turn a preserved outline into a filled icon.

The preview renders the generated symbol. Root style and class are not copied; use explicit SVG presentation attributes. Root viewport effects such as clip-path, mask, filter, transform and vector-effect are not transferred and produce warnings. Review those warnings and the final appearance for complex artwork.

5. Optionally save an external sprite

Save the copied Sprite output as sprite.svg next to your HTML. Remove the inline sprite from that page and use a filename plus a fragment:

<svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
  <use href="sprite.svg#icon-home"></use>
</svg>

Keep the same CSS. Serve both files from the same origin using your project's local development server. Do not test external references by double-clicking the HTML file: file:// restrictions can prevent the SVG from loading. If Python is installed, run this command in the folder containing both files:

python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/index.html. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. An external sprite requires deployment of the asset as well as the HTML; check its URL, response type, caching, and your browser support. Do not assume a sprite on another domain will work just by enabling CORS. MDN documents external use references and same-origin restrictions.

Common problems and fixes

  • No output: remove unused empty blocks and paste one complete, valid SVG document per input. Fix the reported XML error before generating again.
  • Blank icon: compare the exact href fragment with the generated ID. A name like “Home Icon” becomes icon-home-icon, not icon-home. Keep input names unique and inspect final IDs; do not rely on suffixing to resolve every possible collision.
  • Wrong size or clipping: preserve the source viewBox and check CSS dimensions. The tool can infer a viewBox from positive numeric width and height (including px), but it cannot recover arbitrary missing coordinate information.
  • Black or missing outline: check the source fill and stroke settings and any generator warnings. A fixed fill on a child path will also override inherited color. Verify both light and dark backgrounds.
  • Broken gradients or masks: review rewritten internal IDs and every reference. This tool removes some obvious unsafe content but is not a comprehensive sanitizer for untrusted SVG. Use reviewed sources.
  • External sprite missing: use HTTP, check the request succeeds, and keep the asset on the same origin. Recheck the deployed path after moving files.
  • Repeated or missing accessible labels: hide decorative SVGs and name their controls. If you choose Labelled mode for a meaningful standalone icon, adapt its title and make title IDs unique for every repeated instance. The generated title IDs are based on symbol names. See the WAI button pattern and SVG icon accessibility guide.

Keep the workflow small

Start with three icons, review their actual use sites, and keep the source SVGs and license notice beside your generated output. Try the SVG Sprite Generator with your next small set of interface icons.

For more options, read the generator documentation. If your project needs automated generation, see Build an SVG Sprite for Modern Vite, React, and Vue Apps. For per-icon components, see Use SVG Icons in React with Vite and SVGR or the [SVG to Component Converter](https://svgicons.com/tools/svg-

title: October 06, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve compute resources for creating GPU instances through your account team, you can include a Hyperdisk pool in the same request or in a subsequent request. This option helps ensure that your artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) workloads have the storage resources that they require close to your GPU instances. For more information, see Reserve capacity through your account team.

Agent Platform Workbench

Change

M153 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

BigQuery

Feature

Conversational analytics in BigQuery now supports the AI.CAUSAL_EFFECT function to quantify the impact of specific interventions on time series data. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud Monitoring

Feature

Bulk registration of discovered services and workloads to an App Hub application is generally available (GA). For more information, see Register one or more discovered services or workloads.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Change

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports up to 100,000 concurrent connections for Private Service Connect enabled instances created on or after September 30, 2026 with 16 or more vCPUs.

For more information, see Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Change

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports up to 129,024 concurrent connections for Private Service Connect enabled instances created on or after September 30, 2026 with 16 or more vCPUs.

For more information, see Configure Private Service Connect.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve compute resources for H4D instances through your account team, you can include a Hyperdisk pool in the same request or in a subsequent request. This option helps ensure that your high performance computing (HPC) workloads have the storage resources that they require close to your compute instances. For more information, see Reserve capacity through your account team.

Config Connector

Announcement

Config Connector version 1.158.0 is now available.

Feature

New Alpha Resources (Direct Reconciler):

  • AgentRegistryBinding

    • Manage Agent Registry bindings to connect agent tools and authentication configurations.

  • AIPlatformPersistentResource

    • Manage Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform persistent resources for cluster computing and training jobs.

  • AssuredWorkloadsWorkload

    • Manage Assured Workloads to enforce security and compliance controls for regulated workloads.

  • BigtableSchemaBundle

    • Manage Bigtable schema bundles for storing protocol buffer (protobuf) schemas in Bigtable.

  • CloudNumberRegistryRegistryBook

    • Manage Cloud Number Registry registry books to organize IP address management (IPAM) information and discovered IP address ranges.

  • EventarcMessageBus

    • Manage Eventarc message buses to route events from publishers to subscribers.

  • ModelArmorFloorSetting

    • Manage Model Armor floor settings at project, folder, or organization scope to enforce baseline safety and security filters for LLMs.

Feature

New Fields:

  • BackupDRBackupPlanAssociation

    • Added spec.resource.sqlInstanceRef field to support backing up Cloud SQL instances.

  • ComputeNetworkFirewallPolicyRule

    • Added spec.match.srcNetworkContext and spec.match.destNetworkContext fields.

  • ComputeRegionNetworkEndpointGroup

    • Added INTERNET_IP_PORT, INTERNET_FQDN_PORT, and GCE_VM_IP_PORTMAP values for spec.networkEndpointType.

  • RedisCluster

    • Added spec.clusterEndpoints and status.clusterEndpoints fields.
    • Added spec.gcsSource field.
    • Added spec.managedBackupSource field.

  • SQLInstance

    • Added spec.settings.databaseReplicationEnabled field.

Feature

New Features:

  • Added support for pausing and unpausing actuation at the individual resource level by using the cnrm.cloud.google.com/actuation-mode annotation.

Change

Reconciliation Improvements:

Added support for direct reconciliation to more resources, with opt-in behavior. The API is unchanged. To use the direct reconciler, add the alpha.cnrm.cloud.google.com/reconciler: direct annotation to the corresponding Config Connector object. The following resources now have direct reconciliation support:

  • FilestoreInstance
    • Added support for direct reconciliation (opt-in).

Fixed

Bug Fixes:

  • BigQueryDataset (#12383)

    • Fixed a reconciliation failure in projects with a project ID that contains a colon (such as domain-scoped projects example.com:my-project), where creation previously failed with an invalid ID format error and resourceID and selfLink were not populated.

  • ComposerEnvironment (#12795)

    • Fixed infinite reconciliation loops, false drift, and HTTP 400 errors when using empty map fields (envVariables: {}, labels: {}), partial workloadsConfig blocks, or disabling scheduledSnapshotsConfig.

  • ComputeRouterNAT (#12813)

    • Fixed reference validation and resolution in the direct controller so that spec.routerRef accepts both short router names and canonical long paths.

  • Removed empty status.observedState fields from v1alpha1 CRDs to align with Kubernetes structural schema requirements (#12627).

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge
Week 4: Ghost in the
Machine.

What I Built

Afterlight: The Memory Keeper is a privacy-first, local-first AI
memory preservation platform created individually for Hacktoberfest Week
4: Ghost in the Machine.

Afterlight helps people preserve and rediscover meaningful stories,
photographs, voice recordings, family traditions, and personal memories.
It brings together two interpretations of the challenge theme:

  1. Ghost in the Machine: Forgotten stories and recordings can feel like voices trapped in old photographs, tapes, and folders. Afterlight uses local AI to transcribe, organize, search, and creatively reinterpret saved memories.
  2. Día de los Muertos: The Virtual Ofrenda offers a customizable digital space to honor loved ones through photographs, remembrance messages, favorite foods, songs, flowers, traditions, and associated stories.

Afterlight is designed around a simple principle:

Your memories belong to you. Your stories should not depend on a
server you do not control.

The Problem

Family stories and personal histories are often scattered across paper
notes, old photographs, audio recordings, phones, and disconnected
folders. Finding a particular detail can be difficult, and valuable oral
histories may remain inaccessible because they have never been
transcribed or organized.

At the same time, sending intimate memories, photographs, and voice
recordings to third-party AI services can create privacy and
data-ownership concerns. Hosted AI services can also introduce recurring
usage costs and dependence on a provider's availability, pricing, and
terms.

The Solution

Afterlight brings memory preservation and AI-assisted discovery into a
local-first application:

  • Memory Vault: Preserve stories, photographs, dates, people, locations, tags, and personal experiences in an organized archive.
  • Voice of the Past: Transcribe uploaded oral-history recordings with locally running speech recognition, review the transcript, and save it with related memories.
  • AI Memory Companion: Ask natural-language questions about saved memories. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds relevant records and presents the supporting sources.
  • Virtual Ofrenda: Create a customizable Día de los Muertos-inspired remembrance altar with portraits, candles, marigold-inspired decorations, offerings, and tribute messages.
  • Ghost Echoes: Create atmospheric fictional stories inspired by selected memories, with a clear notice that generated stories are creative fiction---not real communications from deceased people.
  • Memory Timeline: Explore saved stories and events chronologically.
  • Privacy & Model Control Center: Inspect the local AI runtime, available models, local data controls, export options, and setup status.

The application is designed to keep personal records and AI inference on
the user's machine. Any offline claims in this submission should reflect
the exact features verified with the network disconnected.

AFTERLIGHT — THE MEMORY KEEPER

"Some stories deserve to live beyond a lifetime."

📖 Executive Summary

AFTERLIGHT is a privacy-first, locally powered AI memory preservation platform developed for the Hacktoberfest Week 4 Challenge — "Ghost in the Machine".

It unifies two poignant themes:

  1. The Ghost in the Machine: Awakening forgotten family memories, cassette recordings, and heirloom photographs through local open-source AI retrieval and atmospheric creative storytelling.
  2. Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead): Honoring departed ancestors through an interactive, culturally reverent virtual altar (ofrenda) adorned with flickering candlelight physics, golden cempasúchil petals, traditional offerings, and printable tribute keepsakes.

Every AI capability in Afterlight—from speech-to-text audio transcription and dense semantic vector retrieval to conversational memory companion RAG—runs 100% locally on your own machine using open-weight models (Qwen2.5 3B, faster-whisper, ChromaDB).

Core Philosophy: "Your memories belong to you. Your stories should…

How I Built It

Afterlight uses a modular, local-first architecture. The frontend
communicates with a local FastAPI backend. The backend manages
persistent records, local files, retrieval, transcription, and requests
to the local model runtime.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+

1. Frontend & Experience

  • Framework: React with TypeScript and Vite.
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS with a dark, cinematic visual identity.
  • Visual direction: Midnight backgrounds, warm amber and candlelight accents, marigold-inspired details, framed photographs, and restrained atmospheric animation.
  • Interface: Responsive pages for the dashboard, Memory Vault, Voice of the Past, AI Memory Companion, Virtual Ofrenda, Ghost Echoes, Memory Timeline, and privacy controls.

2. Backend & Local Persistence

  • Backend: Python and FastAPI for local REST APIs.
  • Database: SQLite for structured memory records, people, photographs, recordings, transcripts, ofrendas, stories, and related metadata.
  • File storage: Photographs and audio are stored as local files; the database stores their metadata and local references rather than Base64 copies.
  • Validation: Pydantic schemas and file validation are used at API boundaries.
  • Data ownership: Local records can be backed up and exported by the user.

3. Open-Weight AI & Local Inference

  • Runtime: Ollama provides a local interface for running compatible open-weight language models.
  • Default model target: qwen2.5:3b (or another compatible model selected in the application).
  • Model flexibility: The AI service is separated behind a model adapter so compatible local models can be changed without rewriting feature logic.
  • AI tasks: Memory summaries, contextual question answering, categorization, remembrance-writing assistance, and fictional story generation.
  • No mandatory hosted LLM: The core AI design does not require OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, or another hosted LLM API.

Model availability, model licenses, and actual tested model names should
be confirmed against the implementation before publishing.

4. Local Speech Recognition

  • Engine: faster-whisper, using a locally available Whisper model.
  • Workflow: Upload audio → transcribe locally → review/edit transcript → save transcript and associate it with a memory.
  • Formats: Support depends on the installed FFmpeg configuration and the formats enabled by the application.
  • Privacy: Audio is processed locally when the local transcription pipeline and model are installed.

5. Semantic Search & Grounded Memory Companion

  • Embeddings: A locally installed sentence-transformers model, such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  • Vector store: ChromaDB for semantic retrieval.
  • Retrieval flow: Embed the question → retrieve relevant memory chunks → load their source records → provide context to the local LLM → return an answer with source references.
  • Grounding: The assistant should state when saved memories do not contain enough information. It should not present unsupported model-generated details as facts.
  • Source visibility: Responses should link to the memory records used as context, allowing users to inspect the original material.

6. Creative Storytelling & Remembrance

  • Ghost Echoes: Generates original atmospheric fiction inspired by user-selected memories.
  • Virtual Ofrenda: Provides a customizable digital remembrance space for portraits, stories, offerings, and messages.
  • Ethical boundary: Generated stories are clearly labeled as fiction. The application does not claim to contact, recreate, or speak for deceased people.
  • Cultural respect: Ofrenda elements are customizable; the experience does not assume that every user follows the same traditions.

7. Testing & Verification

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For Afterlight, open innovation is directly connected to privacy,
ownership, accessibility, and long-term control.

Memories can include intimate family stories, personal photographs, and
recordings of people who trusted us with their words. A
memory-preservation tool should not require those materials to be sent
to a third-party AI provider.

1. Privacy & Data Sovereignty

Local inference allows supported AI operations to run on the user's own
machine. Afterlight is designed to keep its memory archive, photographs,
recordings, and local database under the user's control rather than
making a hosted AI service the default destination for personal
material.

2. Model Choice & Freedom to Experiment

A local model adapter makes it possible to test and switch between
compatible models. Developers can compare model quality, hardware
requirements, languages, and response behavior without redesigning the
entire application around one provider.

3. Offline Access & Independence

Once the application dependencies, model weights, and required assets
have been downloaded, supported local workflows can operate without an
internet connection. This reduces dependence on a hosted service being
available whenever someone wants to revisit a memory.

4. Accessibility Without Per-Request AI Fees

Local inference avoids mandatory per-request hosted LLM charges. It does
not mean the application has no costs: users still need suitable
hardware, storage, electricity, and initial downloads. However, it gives
people another way to use AI without a recurring API bill.

5. Community Adaptation & Longevity

An open implementation can be inspected, modified, extended, and adapted
by contributors. Communities can experiment with language support,
oral-history workflows, accessibility improvements, and culturally
appropriate remembrance experiences.

Honest Technical Trade-offs

  • Hardware: Local inference performance depends on RAM, CPU/GPU, quantization, and model size.
  • Storage: Model weights, audio recordings, photographs, and vector indexes require disk space.
  • Initial setup: Ollama, Python packages, frontend dependencies, and model assets generally need to be installed or downloaded before offline use.
  • Performance: CPU-only transcription and LLM inference may take longer than hosted GPU services.
  • Model licensing: Each model has its own license and usage conditions. Check and document the exact license of every model distributed or recommended.
  • Offline scope: Do not describe the entire application as offline unless every claimed workflow has been tested without network access.

What Worked Better With an Open-Based Approach?

The local-first architecture makes privacy and model choice design
properties rather than optional settings in a hosted service. It also
allows the project to keep working with locally installed models without
requiring a particular commercial AI provider's API.

title: Module Federation (Webpack 5)
description:
Taming the Monolith: How Webpack 5's Module Federation is Revolutionizing Frontend Development

Remember the good old days? We’d all pile our frontend code into one giant, glorious monolith. It was simple, it was contained, and it was… a nightmare to manage as it grew. Updates became a game of Russian roulette, teams tripped over each other, and deployment felt like a high-stakes gamble. Thankfully, the frontend world has evolved, and one of the most exciting advancements is Webpack 5's Module Federation.

Think of Module Federation as a secret handshake for your microservices, but for your frontend applications. It’s a powerful feature that allows you to split your application into independent bundles that can be dynamically loaded at runtime. This means different parts of your application can be developed, deployed, and even versioned independently, all while feeling like a single, cohesive unit to the end-user. Pretty cool, right?

Let's dive deep into this game-changer and see how it can help you tame your frontend monoliths.

The "Why": Why Bother with Module Federation?

Before we get our hands dirty with code, let's understand the problems Module Federation aims to solve. Imagine you're working on a large e-commerce platform. You have a product listing page, a shopping cart, a checkout process, and a user profile section.

  • Monolith Headaches:
    • Slow Builds: As the codebase grows, build times can become excruciatingly long. Waiting an hour for a full rebuild? No thank you!
    • Team Dependencies: Multiple teams working on the same large codebase are constantly stepping on each other's toes. A change in one area might inadvertently break another, leading to endless debugging sessions.
    • Deployment Nightmares: Deploying a new feature often means redeploying the entire application. This increases the risk of introducing regressions and makes rollbacks a complex operation.
    • Code Duplication: Sharing common UI components or utility functions across different parts of the application can lead to duplicated code, increasing bundle sizes.
    • Framework Lock-in: Migrating a large monolith to a new framework is a monumental task.

Module Federation swoops in like a superhero, offering a solution to these woes.

Setting the Stage: What You Need to Get Started

Before we start federating, let's ensure you have the right tools in your arsenal.

  • Webpack 5 (Obviously!): This is the bedrock of Module Federation. Make sure your project is using Webpack 5 or a later version.
  • Node.js and npm/yarn: Standard JavaScript development environment.
  • Basic Understanding of Webpack: Familiarity with Webpack concepts like entry points, output, loaders, and plugins will be incredibly helpful.
  • A Willingness to Experiment: Like any powerful tool, there's a learning curve. Be prepared to tinker and explore!

The Core Concepts: Remote & Host

Module Federation revolves around two key players: the Host and the Remotes.

  • Host Application: This is your primary application. It's the one that will dynamically load modules from other applications. Think of it as the conductor of the orchestra, orchestrating the loading of different musical pieces.
  • Remote Application: These are your independent modules or applications. They expose specific components or functionalities that the Host can consume. They are the individual musicians playing their part.

The magic happens when the Host application requests a module from a Remote application. Webpack, with its Module Federation plugin, handles the dynamic loading and integration seamlessly.

Let's Get Our Hands Dirty: The module-federation-plugin

The heart of Module Federation is the webpack.config.js. Here's where we'll configure our federated applications.

1. Installing the Plugin:

npm install --save-dev webpack-cli webpack-dev-server @babel/core @babel/preset-env babel-loader

(Note: You'll also need Babel configured for your project to transpile modern JavaScript.)

2. Configuring the Host Application (webpack.config.js):

Let's imagine our Host application is our main e-commerce website.

// webpack.config.js (Host)
const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require('html-webpack-plugin');
const ModuleFederationPlugin = require('webpack-module-federation-plugin');

module.exports = {
  mode: 'development',
  devServer: {
    port: 3001, // Host runs on port 3001
  },
  plugins: [
    new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: 'host', // The name of this application (optional, but good practice)
      remotes: {
        // This tells the host about available remotes.
        // The key 'remote_app' is how we'll refer to it.
        // The value is the URL where the remote app's manifest is served.
        remote_app: 'remote_app@http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js',
      },
      shared: {
        // This is crucial! It defines dependencies that will be shared between
        // the host and remotes. This prevents duplicate libraries and ensures
        // consistency. 'react' and 'react-dom' are common examples.
        'react': {
          singleton: true, // Ensures only one instance of react is loaded
          import: 'react',
          shareKey: 'react',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0', // Specify the expected version
        },
        'react-dom': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react-dom',
          shareKey: 'react-dom',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
      },
    }),
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({
      template: './public/index.html',
    }),
  ],
};

3. Configuring the Remote Application (webpack.config.js):

Now, let's create a remote_app that exposes a "Hello World" component. This remote application will run on a different port (e.g., 3002).

// webpack.config.js (Remote)
const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require('html-webpack-plugin');
const ModuleFederationPlugin = require('webpack-module-federation-plugin');

module.exports = {
  mode: 'development',
  devServer: {
    port: 3002, // Remote runs on port 3002
  },
  plugins: [
    new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: 'remote_app', // The name of this remote application
      filename: 'remoteEntry.js', // The name of the entry file
      exposes: {
        // This maps a module name ('./HelloWorld') to its path in the remote app.
        // We'll use './HelloWorld' to import this component in the host.
        './HelloWorld': './src/components/HelloWorld.js',
      },
      shared: {
        // Important: Remotes also need to declare shared dependencies.
        // This allows the host to potentially use the same shared instance.
        'react': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react',
          shareKey: 'react',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
        'react-dom': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react-dom',
          shareKey: 'react-dom',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
      },
    }),
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({
      template: './public/index.html',
    }),
  ],
};

4. Creating the Remote Component (src/components/HelloWorld.js):

// src/components/HelloWorld.js (Remote App)
import React from 'react';

const HelloWorld = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Hello from the Remote App!</h2>
    </div>
  );
};

export default HelloWorld;

5. Consuming the Remote Component in the Host (src/App.js):

This is where the magic of dynamic import comes into play.

// src/App.js (Host App)
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import './App.css';

// Dynamically import the HelloWorld component from the remote_app
const RemoteHelloWorld = React.lazy(() => import('remote_app/HelloWorld'));

function App() {
  return (
    <div className="App">
      <h1>Welcome to the Host App!</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading remote component...</div>}>
        <RemoteHelloWorld />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

To run this:

  1. Build and run both the host and remote applications in separate terminals.
    • Remote: cd remote_app && npm start (or your build/start command)
    • Host: cd host && npm start (or your build/start command)

You should see "Welcome to the Host App!" followed by "Hello from the Remote App!". This is Module Federation in action!

Key Features and Benefits: Beyond the Basics

Module Federation is more than just dynamic imports. It unlocks a suite of powerful features:

  • Independent Deployments: Each federated application can be deployed independently. Need to update the "product listing" micro-frontend? Deploy only that, and the rest of your application remains unaffected. This drastically reduces deployment risk.
  • Code Sharing and Collaboration: Imagine a design system team building a library of UI components. This library can be exposed as a remote, and all other applications can consume these components, ensuring a consistent look and feel across your entire ecosystem.
  • Dynamic Versioning: You can have different versions of shared libraries (like React) running in different federated applications. This allows for gradual upgrades and migration strategies.
  • Technology Agnosticism (Partially): While the examples use React, Module Federation itself is framework-agnostic. You could have a Vue application consuming a React component, or vice versa, as long as they agree on shared dependencies.
  • Performance Improvements: By splitting your application into smaller, independent chunks, you can achieve faster initial load times. Users only download the code they need for the current view.
  • Team Autonomy: Teams can own and manage their specific micro-frontends with minimal dependencies on other teams, fostering agility and faster development cycles.

Shared Dependencies: The Secret Sauce to Efficiency

The shared option in the ModuleFederationPlugin is arguably one of the most important features. When you declare dependencies as shared, Webpack ensures that only one instance of that dependency is loaded across all federated applications. This:

  • Reduces Bundle Size: Instead of each application shipping its own copy of React, only one copy is loaded.
  • Ensures Consistency: All applications use the same version of shared libraries, preventing subtle bugs due to version mismatches.
  • Enables Runtime Updates: If you update a shared library, all applications using it will automatically benefit from the update without needing to be rebuilt or redeployed themselves (within compatible version ranges).

Example of complex sharing:

// webpack.config.js
...
shared: {
  'react': {
    singleton: true,
    import: 'react',
    shareKey: 'react',
    requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
    packageDir: './node_modules/react', // Optional: Can help Webpack find the shared package
  },
  'lodash': {
    singleton: true,
    import: 'lodash',
    shareKey: 'lodash',
    requiredVersion: '^4.17.21',
  },
},
...

Potential Pitfalls and Disadvantages

While Module Federation is incredibly powerful, it's not a silver bullet. Here are some things to be mindful of:

  • Increased Complexity: Setting up and managing a federated architecture is inherently more complex than a monolith. You'll need to think about how applications communicate, how dependencies are managed, and how to handle errors across different modules.
  • Build and Deployment Orchestration: While individual deployments are easier, orchestrating builds and deployments across multiple repositories can become challenging. You might need CI/CD pipelines that can handle multiple independent deployments.
  • Debugging Can Be Tricky: Debugging across federated applications can sometimes be more involved, especially when issues arise from interactions between modules.
  • Learning Curve: As mentioned, there's a learning curve associated with understanding the concepts and effectively configuring Module Federation.
  • Runtime Errors: If a remote module fails to load or throws an error at runtime, it can impact the user experience of the host application. Robust error handling and fallback mechanisms are essential.
  • Network Latency: Dynamically loading modules introduces network requests. If the network is slow, users might experience delays in seeing content.

Advanced Features and Considerations

  • shareScopeMap: This advanced option allows you to explicitly control how shared modules are exposed and consumed. It offers finer-grained control over versioning and dependency resolution.
  • eager loading: By default, modules are loaded lazily. You can set eager: true for specific exposes entries to load them eagerly, which might be beneficial for critical components.
  • Remotes as Hosts: A remote application can also act as a host to other remotes, creating a hierarchical structure of federated applications.
  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Integrating Module Federation with SSR requires careful consideration and additional setup to ensure modules are rendered correctly on the server.

When is Module Federation a Good Fit?

Module Federation shines in scenarios like:

  • Large, complex web applications: Where breaking down the codebase into smaller, manageable pieces is a necessity.
  • E-commerce platforms: Where different sections (product pages, cart, checkout) can be developed and deployed independently.
  • SaaS applications with distinct modules: Think of a CRM with modules for contacts, deals, and reporting.
  • Organizations with multiple frontend teams: Where teams can own and manage their respective micro-frontends.
  • Applications requiring gradual migration to new technologies: You can gradually introduce new frameworks by migrating parts of your application as remotes.

Conclusion: Embrace the Future of Frontend Architecture

Webpack 5's Module Federation is a paradigm shift in frontend development. It empowers us to break free from the limitations of monolithic applications and embrace a more modular, scalable, and maintainable architecture. While it introduces its own set of complexities, the benefits of independent deployments, enhanced collaboration, and improved performance are undeniable.

By understanding the core concepts, carefully configuring your Webpack setup, and being mindful of potential pitfalls, you can leverage Module Federation to build more robust, agile, and future-proof frontend applications. So, go forth, experiment, and start taming your monoliths! The future of frontend architecture is here, and it's federated.

title: The home screen of our app stores nothing about itself, and two of its panels can delete themselves
description:
The first screen behind the login in Nakodo is a list of campaigns with a few panels around it: what is waiting on you, how much of your plan you have used, and a getting-started checklist. It is 255 lines of server component, and the thing I like about it is that none of those panels has any state of its own. There is no onboarding_steps table, no dismissed_checklist column, no last_seen_tips JSON. Every tick, every bar and every empty state is computed from rows that exist for another reason.

That is a decision with costs, and the costs are more interesting than the benefits.

The checklist has no table 

const steps: Step[] = [
  { label: "Start a campaign", done: true, href: inSetup(latest) ? `/campaigns/new/${latest.id}` : base, hint: "" },
  {
    label: "Review and launch",
    done: launched,
    href: inSetup(latest) ? `/campaigns/new/${latest.id}` : `${base}/brief`,
    hint: `Check the proposal and anything Nakodo guessed, then launch. Nakodo starts finding ${many}.`,
  },
  ...(launched && !campaigns.some((c) => c.hasOffer)
    ? [{ label: "Save your proposal", done: false, href: `${base}/outreach/proposal`, hint: "..." }]
    : []),
  {
    label: `Wait while Nakodo finds ${many}`,
    done: campaigns.some((c) => c.conversations > 0),
    href: base,
    hint: "It writes to the best fits on its own as they turn up, a few each day.",
  },
];

Four steps, sometimes five. "Start a campaign" is done: true as a literal, because the checklist only renders when at least one campaign exists, so the first step is a fact about the page rather than a question. "Review and launch" is launchedAt !== null. "Wait while Nakodo finds creators" is conversations > 0. The fifth step, approving the first emails, is pushed on only when the account has turned automatic sending off.

The third step is the one worth reading twice. Saving a proposal is normally part of the setup wizard, so for almost everybody it is not a step at all. It only appears for a campaign that was launched without one, which happens if the setup flow was interrupted. A stored checklist would have had to decide at signup whether that row exists. A derived one answers the question at render time and the answer is simply the truth.

Then the whole thing is conditional on two lines:

const next = steps.findIndex((s) => !s.done);
if (next < 0) return null;

and, at the top:

if (!latest || campaigns.some((c) => c.contacted > 0)) return null;

Nothing dismisses it. It disappears when there is nothing left in it, or as soon as anyone has actually been contacted, because at that point the account is past getting started and a tutorial panel on the main screen is noise.

next does double duty: it is the early return, and it is which row gets the ring, the background tint, the hint text and an sr-only "(next)". Only one hint is ever on screen, which is the difference between a checklist and a wall of advice.

The honest cost of deriving it

A derived checklist can come back.

Delete every campaign, start a new one, and you are a beginner again as far as this panel is concerned. A dismissed_at column would have made that impossible: once gone, gone for ever. I think the derived version is right, because the panel answers "what is the next thing to do with this account" and after deleting everything the honest answer is "launch something". But it is a real difference in behaviour that falls out of where the state lives, not out of any product decision, and it is the kind of thing that surprises you in a support thread six months later.

The progress bar has the same property. It is done / steps.length as an inline width, so adding the conditional fifth step moves the bar backwards: four of four becomes four of five when a campaign turns out to need a proposal. Percentages computed from a list whose length can change are always a little bit of a lie, and the alternative, a stored denominator, is a worse lie.

The panel that is rendered twice

The same component appears in two places in the tree:

{/* On phones, anything waiting goes above the campaigns rather than below them. */}
{list.length > 0 && waiting.length > 0 && <WaitingOnYou waiting={waiting} className="lg:hidden" />}

...

{list.length > 0 && (
  <WaitingOnYou waiting={waiting} className={waiting.length > 0 ? "max-lg:hidden" : undefined} />
)}

On a wide screen, "waiting on you" belongs in the right column next to the usage meters. On a phone there are no columns, and a panel in the second column renders under a list of campaigns that can be any length, which is the wrong place for the only thing on the page that needs a human. Moving it with CSS order was not available: the two positions are in different grid children, not siblings in one flow.

So it is rendered twice with mutually exclusive visibility, which costs some duplicated HTML and gains a layout nobody has to scroll to. The display: none means only one copy is in the accessibility tree at a time, so a screen reader hears it once.

The asymmetry in the second line is the part I had to think about. When there is nothing waiting, the phone copy is not rendered at all and the desktop copy loses its max-lg:hidden, which means the empty state exists only in the sidebar. The empty state is a sentence and a drawing of our mascot asleep:

{/* Nothing to do, so Alcy naps. */}
<AlcyAsleep size="m" className="mx-auto -mb-3" />

On a phone, "nothing is waiting on you" is worth zero pixels, because the absence of the panel says it. On a desktop the sidebar would otherwise have a hole in it, and a napping bird is a nicer answer than a hole. Same component, same data, two different judgements about whether nothing is worth saying.

One link, three destinations

Every campaign card is a link, and where it goes depends on how far the campaign got:

const href = inSetup(c)
  ? `/campaigns/new/${c.id}`
  : c.status === "draft" || c.status === "failed"
    ? `/campaigns/${c.id}/brief`
    : `/campaigns/${c.id}`;

with

export const inSetup = (c: { status: string; launchedAt: Date | null }) =>
  c.status === "draft" && c.launchedAt === null;

A campaign still in the wizard reopens the wizard where it left off. One whose research failed opens its brief, which is where the error and the retry live. Everything else opens its results. The rule is "put me back where the work is", and it is three lines of ternary rather than a status-to-route map, because there are three answers and a map of three entries reads worse than the question it answers.

Five queries and one write

The page does its reads in parallel, including the search params, which in Next 16 are a promise like any other:

const [listed, account, waiting, daily, sp] = await Promise.all([
  campaignsNow(),
  accountForPage(user.id),
  threadsNeedingYou(user.id),
  shareCampaigns(user.id),
  searchParams,
]);

and then does something I am still slightly uneasy about:

// Research cut off mid-run is put right only when the list shows some, so
// the page doesn't write on every visit.
const list = listed.some(researchIsStale) && (await recoverStaleResearch(user.id)) > 0 ? await campaignsNow() : listed;

A render that repairs data. The guard is that the write only happens when the already-fetched rows prove there is something to repair, so the common path is a pure read, but a GET that can update rows is still a GET that can update rows. The alternative is a cron that sweeps for interrupted research, and the reason it is here instead is latency: the person looking at the screen is the one who cares that a campaign stopped mid-research, and they are looking at it now.

What the public page says

The how it works page explains eight things the product does. The checklist asks the customer for four, and three of those four are "look at this and press launch". That gap is the whole design brief for a screen like this: the product can be complicated, the list of what you have to do cannot be.

title: batching in react
description:
Optimizing UI Updates for Performance

Introduction

React is known for its efficient rendering process, and one of the key techniques it utilizes is batching. Batching refers to the process of combining multiple
updates into a single update, minimizing the number of times the real DOM needs to be updated. In this article, we will explore how batching works under the
hood in React and its impact on performance. We will also provide examples to demonstrate the concept.

Understanding Batching

When React renders a component, it doesn’t immediately apply every change to the real DOM. Instead, it batches the updates together and performs them all at
once, resulting in better performance and a smoother user experience. React achieves batching through a technique called “transaction,” which groups related
operations and executes them as a single unit of work.

Example: Updating State with Batching:

Let’s consider an example where a component updates its state multiple times in quick succession. Without batching, React would update the real DOM for each
state change separately, even if the actual value changed only once. This approach would be inefficient.

However, due to batching, React combines these updates into a single transaction. As a result, the real DOM is updated only once after all the state changes
have been processed. This reduces unnecessary DOM updates and improves performance.

To demonstrate this, let’s modify the example code to log the current transaction state:

import React from "react";

function Example() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    const handleClick = () => {
        console.log("before ", React.__SECRET_INTERNALS_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED.ReactCurrentOwner.currentDispatcher);
        setCount(count + 1);
        setCount(count + 1);
        setCount(count + 1);

        console.log("after ", React.__SECRET_INTERNALS_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED.ReactCurrentOwner.currentDispatcher);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Count: {count}</p>
            <button onClick={handleClick}>Increment</button>
        </div>
    );
}

In this modified example, we log the current transaction state before and after the state updates. By observing the logs, we can see that React batches the
updates together into a single transaction.

Common Pitfall: Event Handlers and Batching: React’s batching behavior can sometimes lead to confusion, especially when dealing with event handlers. Consider an
example where a component updates its state and logs the count immediately after the state update. Due to batching, the logged count will always be one less
than the actual value at that moment.

This happens because React schedules a batch of updates to the real DOM, deferring the actual application of changes. Therefore, when the log statement is
executed, the state update might not have been processed yet.

Fiber Architecture and Incremental Updates

React Fiber, introduced in React 16, is a re-implemented rendering engine that offers enhanced efficiency and flexibility. It introduces incremental updates to
the virtual DOM, enabling the browser to handle user input and other events without blocking the UI.

With React Fiber, updates are broken down into smaller chunks, allowing for prioritization and interleaving of different tasks. This approach enhances
responsiveness and ensures that the user interface remains interactive even during intense rendering processes.

Conclusion

Batching is a fundamental mechanism in React that optimizes UI updates for improved performance. By combining multiple updates into a single transaction, React
minimizes the number of DOM manipulations and delivers a smoother user experience. Understanding batching and its impact on event handling and performance is
crucial for developing efficient React applications.

In this article, we discussed the concept of batching in React, its implementation through transactions, and its benefits in terms of performance. We provided
examples to illustrate how batching works and explained the significance of React Fiber’s incremental updates. By leveraging batching effectively, developers
can build highly performant and responsive React applications.

Thank you for reading! ❤️

title: Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now in public beta
description:
Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now available in public beta on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. It isn’t tied to a single sandbox, so you can reuse the same Drive across runs and different sandbox instances.

Use Drives to preserve an agent's workspace or on-disk memory, or to reuse datasets, models, and dependency trees.

Create and mount a Drive

Create or retrieve a Drive and mount it at a path when starting a sandbox. Read and write files through the sandbox filesystem at that path.

Anything stored under /data remains on the Drive after the sandbox stops.

Share Drive data across sandboxes

A Drive supports one read-write mount at a time. After the Drive has been written to, multiple sandboxes can read from it concurrently by mounting point-in-time, read-only snapshots.

Each snapshot reflects the Drive at the moment it's mounted. Later writes aren’t included; mount a new snapshot to access them.

Limits and pricing

Each sandbox can mount up to four Drives at separate paths. Drives default to a maximum size of 1 TiB (1 GiB on Hobby) and can be configured up to 16 TiB, with higher limits available by request.

Drives are available in every Sandbox region. Each Drive stays in the region where it was created. Sandboxes that mount it must run in that region and can’t use failover regions.

Drive pricing is based on storage, reads, and writes, with rates varying by region. In iad1, storage costs $0.05 per GB-month, reads $0.0015 per GB, and writes $0.004 per GB. Hobby includes 15 GB of Drive storage and 30 GB each of reads and writes per month. See Sandbox pricing for regional rates and plan details.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Building Bilgo: Cross-Platform Real-Time State Sync Between Android and React Web
description:
Overview

When building real-time multiplayer web applications, supporting mobile users seamlessly is one of the most critical challenges. For Bilgo, our interactive trivia and competitive learning platform, we recently bridged the gap between our native Android app and our React + TypeScript web client.

While the Android version is currently in the Google Play review pipeline, we rolled out a standalone, signed APK distribution channel coupled with full cross-platform synchronization.

Here is a breakdown of the architectural challenges we solved and how we structured the solution.

  1. The Challenge: Divergent Schemas Across Platforms

During the early stages of development, the Android client and the web frontend stored gameplay progress slightly differently in Cloud Firestore:

Web Client: Stored achievements as key-value maps (achievements: { [id]: { unlocked: boolean, progress: number } }).
Android Client: Persisted achievements as an array of unique identifier strings (unlockedAchievements: ["first_win", "streak_3", ...]).
Streak Telemetry: The mobile app stored streak metadata inside nested objects (streak: { count: number, best: number }), while web aggregations previously expected flat counters.

As a result, mobile players who accumulated significant streaks saw their count display as zero on the web leaderboard, and unlocked mobile medals did not register on the web profile.

  1. The Solution: Unified Ingestion and Non-Destructive Merging

Instead of forcing a destructive migration on active player databases, we introduced a resilient aggregation pipeline on the web client:

Multi-Source Streak Extraction: A normalized extraction utility inspects all candidate structures (streak.count, streak.best, streakCount, and stats.bestStreak) and returns the true mathematical maximum across data sources.
Non-Destructive Document Merging: When fetching global and weekly leaderboards across Firestore instances, documents from publicProfiles and users collections are merged symmetrically using Math.max across scores, wins, XP, and streak counts.
Dual-Write Achievement Unlocks: When an achievement unlocks on the web, we invoke arrayUnion to append the achievement ID to unlockedAchievements while concurrently recording the structured map. This ensures future mobile sessions immediately recognize the unlocked badge.

  1. Real-Time Download Telemetry

To measure user adoption prior to the official Google Play rollout, we implemented an in-house telemetry pipeline:

Environment Detection: Client-side detection identifies OS (Android, Windows, iOS, macOS) and device category (mobile, tablet, desktop).
Event Logging: Each APK download registers an atomic increment and writes an event log entry inside Firestore, preserving audit trails without requiring external third-party tracking scripts.
Real-Time Admin Panel: An administrative dashboard listens via onSnapshot to display real-time counters for total downloads, unique devices, and registered active mobile players.
Tech Stack Summary
Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite
Backend & Database: Google Cloud Firestore, Firebase Modular SDK (v10)
Mobile: Native Android APK distribution
Hosting: Netlify Edge
Check It Out
Web Application: https://bilgo.netlify.app
Android Download Hub: https://bilgo.netlify.app/download

Developed by the team at PixelGroup. Feedback and technical discussions are always welcome!
