title: Node.js 26 LTS: planning the Lambda upgrade
description:
Node.js 26 LTS has been official since October 28, 2026, under the codename “Lithium”. For me, an LTS switch like this is always the moment to stop eyeing the next release and write an upgrade plan instead. If you only touch your Lambda functions once the deprecation email from AWS lands in your inbox, you work under time pressure. And time pressure is a pretty bad advisor for runtime upgrades.

On AWS Lambda, the nodejs26.x runtime is already available as a public preview, and according to the documentation AWS is targeting general availability for November 2026. That window is valuable: you can test today without having to switch production today. I will show you what Node.js 26 brings, what breaks when you move from Node.js 22 or 24, and how a small probe function for a fictional bike rental tells you what the new Lambda runtime can really do.

In short

Node.js 26 became LTS on October 28, 2026 and receives updates until the end of April 2029, while nodejs26.x on Lambda is still a preview with a planned launch in November 2026. The most useful addition for everyday work is the Temporal API for dates and times. The biggest pitfall: what works under Node 26 on your laptop is not necessarily enabled the same way in the Lambda runtime, so check features there directly instead of assuming them.

What you will learn in this article

  • What Node.js 26 LTS means for your support timeline on Lambda
  • Which additions such as Temporal and Map.getOrInsert you can use right away
  • Which changes can break when you upgrade from Node.js 22 or 24
  • How to test nodejs26.x next to nodejs24.x with AWS CDK
  • How to find every Node runtime in your AWS account

What Node.js 26 LTS means for your timeline

LTS stands for Long Term Support: a version receives security and bug fixes over a long period, and new features only arrive cautiously. Release 26.13.0, which officially starts Node.js 26 LTS, is purely formal. According to the release notes, it only switches metadata such as process.release to LTS and contains nothing else beyond 26.12.1. Updates for Node.js 26 LTS continue until the end of April 2029.

The Node.js project is also changing its rhythm. Until now, only even-numbered versions became LTS, while odd ones such as Node.js 25 were done after six months (25 reached EOL, or “end of life”, at the end of March 2026). Starting with Node.js 27, there will be one major version per year, and each of them becomes LTS after its six-month Current phase. For teams, that means fewer versions and a predictable cadence.

Here is where Lambda stands at the end of October 2026:

Runtime Node.js line Status on Lambda
nodejs22.x LTS “Jod” Deprecated on Apr 30, 2027, updates blocked from Aug 31, 2027
nodejs24.x LTS “Krypton” Deprecated on Apr 30, 2028
nodejs26.x LTS “Lithium” Public preview, general availability planned for November 2026

For many teams, the date that matters most is the end of nodejs22.x in April 2027.

My take: for many teams, the real deadline is not the launch of Node.js 26 but the deprecation of nodejs22.x. That leaves roughly six months. If you plan now, you can fit the upgrade into your normal sprint cadence.

Node.js 26 LTS features you will notice day to day

Coming from Node.js 24, you get not only the changes in Node.js 26 LTS but also everything from Node.js 25. That intermediate version was never LTS, so many teams skipped it. A few points stand out for daily work.

Temporal: dates and times without the headache

Node.js 26 LTS ships the Temporal API enabled by default, no flag required. Temporal is the new standard for dates and times in JavaScript and fixes the weaknesses of Date: months that start at 0, no real time zone arithmetic, and objects you can mutate by accident. Instead, you get clear types. Temporal.Instant is an exact point in time, Temporal.ZonedDateTime is a point in time in a specific time zone, and Temporal.PlainDate is a plain calendar date.

const pickup = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T10:00[Europe/Berlin]");
const due = pickup.add({ days: 2 });

console.log(due.toString());
// 2026-10-26T10:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (same wall-clock time, even though the DST change happens in between)

We will use exactly this example in the probe function later. With Date and “plus 48 hours”, you end up at 9 a.m. instead of 10 a.m. on October 26, because the clocks go back during the night before October 25. I cover how to use Temporal day to day for deadlines, time zones and DynamoDB in detail in Temporal API in TypeScript: deadlines and time zones.

Small helpers: getOrInsert, Iterator.concat and Base64

V8 14.6 adds two small but pleasant functions. Map.prototype.getOrInsert() and getOrInsertComputed() read a value or create it if it is missing. The classic “does this key exist yet?” pattern for grouping shrinks to a single line. Iterator.concat() chains several iterators without building intermediate arrays.

const rentals = [
  { station: "Central Station", bikeId: "city-bike-17" },
  { station: "Old Town", bikeId: "e-bike-03" },
  { station: "Central Station", bikeId: "cargo-bike-02" },
];

const byStation = new Map<string, string[]>();
for (const rental of rentals) {
  byStation.getOrInsert(rental.station, []).push(rental.bikeId);
}
// Map { "Central Station" => ["city-bike-17", "cargo-bike-02"], "Old Town" => ["e-bike-03"] }

Node.js 25 contributed, for example, Uint8Array.fromBase64() and toBase64() (plus hex variants) and a noticeably faster JSON.stringify. In Lambda functions that build lots of JSON responses or encode binary data for API Gateway, that is a nice bonus for free. One observation from my test: with "lib": ["esnext"], TypeScript 7.0.2 already knows the types for Temporal, getOrInsert and fromBase64, but still reports an error for Iterator.concat.

Platform: Undici 8, Web Storage and permissions

Undici, the built-in HTTP client behind fetch, moves to version 8. Since Node.js 25, the Web Storage API is enabled by default, but in Node.js 26 localStorage returns undefined as long as no storage file is configured. Since Node.js 25, the permission model also knows --allow-net, which lets you restrict a process’s network access. On Lambda, that matters more for local tools and CI scripts, because isolation there is handled by IAM and VPC anyway.

What breaks when you move to Node.js 26 LTS

Most projects keep running after the upgrade to Node.js 26 LTS. Still, there are a handful of changes worth checking deliberately before you switch the runtime:

  • The old internal modules _stream_readable, _stream_writable and their siblings are removed in Node.js 26. Older libraries sometimes still import them directly.
  • http.Server.prototype.writeHeader() is gone, use writeHead().
  • Since Node.js 25, fs.F_OK, fs.R_OK, fs.W_OK and fs.X_OK are no longer exported directly from the module. The constants live under fs.constants.
  • SlowBuffer and assert.CallTracker have reached end of life since Node.js 25.
  • Corepack is no longer bundled since Node.js 25. If you enable pnpm or Yarn via Corepack, install it separately in CI.
  • module.register() emits a runtime deprecation warning in Node.js 26, and --experimental-transform-types was removed.
  • Native addons need a rebuild, because NODE_MODULE_VERSION changes to 147.
  • Since Node.js 25, the official Linux binaries are linked against libatomic. Slim container images for CI may be missing that package.

On top of that on Lambda: what has applied since nodejs24.x

If you jump from nodejs22.x straight to 26, you also pick up the Lambda-specific changes AWS introduced with nodejs24.x. Callback handlers are no longer supported, context.callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop is removed, and so are context.succeed, fail and done. In addition, Lambda no longer waits for pending promises once your handler returns. Anything you still want to finish has to be completed with await first.

// Before: callback handler (no longer works from nodejs24.x)
export const handler = (event, context, callback) => {
  loadBike(event.bikeId)
    .then((bike) => callback(null, bike))
    .catch((err) => callback(err));
};

// After: async handler, every piece of work is awaited
export const handler = async (event: { bikeId: string }) => {
  const bike = await loadBike(event.bikeId);
  await auditLog.write({ action: "lookup", bikeId: bike.id }); // without await this would get lost
  return bike;
};

One more point is easy to miss: Lambda disables experimental Node.js features by default, such as require() of ES modules and automatic module detection. You can turn them back on via NODE_OPTIONS, but AWS covers such cases with neither support nor the SLA.

nodejs26.x on Lambda: the state at the end of October 2026

The nodejs26.x runtime is available as a public preview, both as a ZIP runtime and as the container base image public.ecr.aws/lambda/nodejs:26-preview. Preview means no SLA, no technical support, and breaking changes are possible. It is explicitly not meant for production workloads. AWS names November 2026 as the launch of the stable version, but only as a non-binding estimate.

The feedback issue for the preview on GitHub is revealing. Users report, among other things, that Temporal is missing in the preview and that process.features.require_module is false. These are community observations, not an official AWS statement, and a lot can change before the stable release. I still think the lesson matters: a Lambda runtime is not automatically identical to the Node.js on your machine. So let us check directly in Lambda.

🎬 Probe function on two Lambda runtimes – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: testing nodejs26.x next to nodejs24.x

Our example is a fictional bike rental. A function calculates when a rented bike has to be back: same time of day, a given number of days later, in the time zone of the rental station. It also returns a small report on which features the runtime really provides. If Temporal is built in, the function uses it, otherwise a polyfill steps in. A polyfill is a retrofitted implementation of a standard API for environments that do not support it yet.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22 or newer locally (thanks to the polyfill, the tests run without Node.js 26 too)
  • AWS CLI v2 with credentials for a test or sandbox account
  • An account bootstrapped with npx cdk bootstrap in your region
  • A region where nodejs26.x is already selectable. You can see that in the Lambda console when creating a function.

Step 1: create the project 

mkdir bike-rental-runtime-check && cd bike-rental-runtime-check
npm init -y
npm install @js-temporal/polyfill@0.5.1
npm install -D typescript@7.0.2 @types/node@26 @types/aws-lambda tsx esbuild aws-cdk-lib@2.275.0 constructs aws-cdk@2.1146.1
mkdir -p bin lib src test

Switch package.json to ES modules and add a few scripts:

{
  "name": "node26-lambda-upgrade",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit -p .",
    "test": "node --import tsx --test test/*.test.ts",
    "synth": "cdk synth",
    "deploy": "cdk deploy"
  },
  "license": "MIT",
  "devDependencies": {
    "@types/aws-lambda": "^8.10.164",
    "@types/node": "^26.6.6",
    "aws-cdk": "^2.1146.1",
    "aws-cdk-lib": "^2.275.0",
    "constructs": "^10.8.1",
    "esbuild": "^0.28.2",
    "tsx": "^4.23.15",
    "typescript": "^7.0.2"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "@js-temporal/polyfill": "^0.5.1"
  },
  "private": true,
  "type": "module"
}

Step 2: configure TypeScript

With "lib": ["esnext"], TypeScript knows the new APIs such as Temporal. noEmit is enough, because esbuild bundles during deployment and tsx runs the tests directly.

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2024",
    "lib": ["esnext"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["bin", "lib", "src", "test"]
}

Step 3: write the runtime report

The function checks every feature directly instead of inferring it from the version number. That is more reliable, because a runtime can have a feature disabled despite a matching version.

// src/runtime-report.ts
// Reports which runtime features are actually available in the current Node.js environment.

export interface RuntimeReport {
  nodeVersion: string;
  ltsName: string | null;
  temporal: boolean;
  mapGetOrInsert: boolean;
  iteratorConcat: boolean;
  uint8ArrayBase64: boolean;
  requireModule: boolean;
  lambdaRuntime: string | null;
}

export function collectRuntimeReport(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = process.env): RuntimeReport {
  const g = globalThis as Record<string, unknown>;
  const iteratorCtor = g.Iterator as { concat?: unknown } | undefined;

  return {
    nodeVersion: process.version,
    ltsName: process.release.lts ?? null,
    temporal: typeof g.Temporal === "object" && g.Temporal !== null,
    mapGetOrInsert: typeof (Map.prototype as { getOrInsert?: unknown }).getOrInsert === "function",
    iteratorConcat: typeof iteratorCtor?.concat === "function",
    uint8ArrayBase64: typeof (Uint8Array as { fromBase64?: unknown }).fromBase64 === "function",
    requireModule: process.features.require_module === true,
    // In Lambda, AWS_EXECUTION_ENV looks like this, for example: AWS_Lambda_nodejs24.x
    lambdaRuntime: env.AWS_EXECUTION_ENV?.replace("AWS_Lambda_", "") ?? null,
  };
}

Step 4: load Temporal with a fallback 

// src/temporal.ts
// Uses the built-in Temporal if the runtime provides it, otherwise the polyfill.

export type TemporalApi = typeof Temporal;

export async function loadTemporal(): Promise<{ api: TemporalApi; source: "runtime" | "polyfill" }> {
  const builtIn = (globalThis as { Temporal?: TemporalApi }).Temporal;
  if (builtIn) {
    return { api: builtIn, source: "runtime" };
  }
  const polyfill = await import("@js-temporal/polyfill");
  return { api: polyfill.Temporal as unknown as TemporalApi, source: "polyfill" };
}

The dynamic import ensures that the polyfill is only loaded when it is needed. esbuild still bundles it, which makes the package about 150 KB larger. Once Temporal is reliably available in the stable runtime, you can remove the fallback.

Step 5: the rental logic 

// src/rental.ts
// Fictional bike rental: when does a bike have to be back?

import type { TemporalApi } from "./temporal.js";

export interface RentalRequest {
  bikeId: string;
  pickupAt: string; // pickup time as an instant, e.g. "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z"
  days: number; // number of rental days
  timeZone: string; // time zone of the rental station, e.g. "Europe/Berlin"
}

export function validateRental(input: Partial<RentalRequest>): RentalRequest {
  const { bikeId, pickupAt, days, timeZone } = input;
  if (!bikeId || !pickupAt || !timeZone) {
    throw new Error("bikeId, pickupAt and timeZone are required");
  }
  if (typeof days !== "number" || !Number.isInteger(days) || days < 1 || days > 30) {
    throw new Error("days must be an integer between 1 and 30");
  }
  return { bikeId, pickupAt, days, timeZone };
}

// With Temporal, "2 days" means the same wall-clock time two calendar days later, even across a DST change.
export function returnDeadline(T: TemporalApi, req: RentalRequest): string {
  return T.Instant.from(req.pickupAt)
    .toZonedDateTimeISO(req.timeZone)
    .add({ days: req.days })
    .toString({ smallestUnit: "minute" });
}

// The classic Date approach just adds milliseconds. Across a DST change it is off by one hour.
export function naiveReturnDeadline(req: RentalRequest): string {
  const start = new Date(req.pickupAt).getTime();
  return new Date(start + req.days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();
}

Step 6: the Lambda handler 

// src/handler.ts
// Lambda handler: returns the runtime report and the return deadline for a rental.

import { collectRuntimeReport } from "./runtime-report.js";
import { loadTemporal } from "./temporal.js";
import { naiveReturnDeadline, returnDeadline, validateRental, type RentalRequest } from "./rental.js";

const DEMO_RENTAL: RentalRequest = {
  bikeId: "city-bike-17",
  pickupAt: "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z",
  days: 2,
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin",
};

// Deliberately async without a callback: since nodejs24.x, Lambda no longer supports callback handlers.
export const handler = async (event: Partial<RentalRequest> = {}) => {
  const rental = validateRental({ ...DEMO_RENTAL, ...event });
  const { api, source } = await loadTemporal();

  return {
    runtime: collectRuntimeReport(),
    temporalSource: source,
    rental: {
      bikeId: rental.bikeId,
      returnAt: returnDeadline(api, rental),
      naiveReturnAtUtc: naiveReturnDeadline(rental),
    },
  };
};

Step 7: tests with the Node test runner

The tests cover the interesting case: a rental across the DST change on October 25, 2026. This shows in black and white why Temporal is worth the switch.

// test/rental.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { loadTemporal } from "../src/temporal.js";
import { naiveReturnDeadline, returnDeadline, validateRental } from "../src/rental.js";

const overDstChange = validateRental({
  bikeId: "city-bike-17",
  pickupAt: "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z", // 10:00 in Berlin (summer time)
  days: 2,
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin",
});

test("Temporal keeps the wall-clock time across the DST change", async () => {
  const { api } = await loadTemporal();
  assert.equal(returnDeadline(api, overDstChange), "2026-10-26T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
});

test("Date arithmetic ends up one hour early after the DST change", () => {
  // 08:00 UTC on Oct 26 is 09:00 winter time in Berlin, not 10:00
  assert.equal(naiveReturnDeadline(overDstChange), "2026-10-26T08:00:00.000Z");
});

test("without a DST change both approaches agree", async () => {
  const { api } = await loadTemporal();
  const normalWeek = { ...overDstChange, pickupAt: "2026-11-02T09:00:00Z" };
  assert.equal(returnDeadline(api, normalWeek), "2026-11-04T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.equal(naiveReturnDeadline(normalWeek), "2026-11-04T09:00:00.000Z");
});

test("invalid rental duration is rejected", () => {
  assert.throws(() => validateRental({ ...overDstChange, days: 0 }), /days must/);
  assert.throws(() => validateRental({ ...overDstChange, days: 1.5 }), /days must/);
});

// test/runtime-report.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { collectRuntimeReport } from "../src/runtime-report.js";
import { handler } from "../src/handler.js";

test("report contains the Node version and detects the Lambda runtime", () => {
  const report = collectRuntimeReport({ AWS_EXECUTION_ENV: "AWS_Lambda_nodejs26.x" });
  assert.match(report.nodeVersion, /^v\d+\./);
  assert.equal(report.lambdaRuntime, "nodejs26.x");
});

test("outside of Lambda, lambdaRuntime is null", () => {
  assert.equal(collectRuntimeReport({}).lambdaRuntime, null);
});

test("handler returns report and return deadline", async () => {
  const result = await handler({ days: 3 });
  assert.equal(result.rental.bikeId, "city-bike-17");
  assert.equal(result.rental.returnAt, "2026-10-27T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.ok(["runtime", "polyfill"].includes(result.temporalSource));
});

Step 8: the CDK stack with two runtimes

The installed version of aws-cdk-lib (2.275.0) does not ship nodejs26.x as a ready-made constant yet. That is not a problem, because new Runtime(...) lets you define any runtime yourself. The stack creates the same function twice. If you have not used AWS CDK with TypeScript before, my introduction Lambda function with CDK and TypeScript will help.

// lib/runtime-check-stack.ts
import * as path from "node:path";
import { CfnOutput, Duration, RemovalPolicy, Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Architecture, Runtime, RuntimeFamily } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda";
import { NodejsFunction, OutputFormat } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs";
import { LogGroup, RetentionDays } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-logs";
import type { Construct } from "constructs";

// aws-cdk-lib does not ship a constant for nodejs26.x yet, so we define it ourselves.
const NODEJS_26_PREVIEW = new Runtime("nodejs26.x", RuntimeFamily.NODEJS, { supportsInlineCode: true });

export class RuntimeCheckStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    const variants = [
      { name: "Node24", runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_24_X, target: "node24" },
      { name: "Node26", runtime: NODEJS_26_PREVIEW, target: "node26" },
    ];

    for (const variant of variants) {
      const logGroup = new LogGroup(this, `${variant.name}Logs`, {
        retention: RetentionDays.ONE_WEEK,
        removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
      });

      const fn = new NodejsFunction(this, `RentalCheck${variant.name}`, {
        entry: path.join(import.meta.dirname, "../src/handler.ts"),
        handler: "handler",
        runtime: variant.runtime,
        architecture: Architecture.ARM_64,
        memorySize: 256,
        timeout: Duration.seconds(10),
        logGroup,
        bundling: {
          format: OutputFormat.ESM,
          target: variant.target,
          minify: true,
          sourceMap: true,
          // esbuild needs a require function in the ESM bundle for CommonJS dependencies
          banner: "import { createRequire } from 'module'; const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);",
        },
        environment: {
          NODE_OPTIONS: "--enable-source-maps",
        },
      });

      new CfnOutput(this, `${variant.name}FunctionName`, { value: fn.functionName });
    }
  }
}

// bin/app.ts
import { App } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { RuntimeCheckStack } from "../lib/runtime-check-stack.js";

const app = new App();
new RuntimeCheckStack(app, "BikeRentalRuntimeCheck", {
  env: { region: process.env.CDK_DEFAULT_REGION ?? "eu-central-1" },
});

// cdk.json
{
  "app": "npx tsx bin/app.ts"
}

Step 9: check, deploy and compare 

npm run typecheck
npm test
npx cdk synth
npx cdk deploy

After the deployment, CDK prints both function names. Call both with the same request and compare the responses:

aws lambda invoke --function-name <Node24FunctionName> \
  --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload '{"days":2}' node24.json
aws lambda invoke --function-name <Node26FunctionName> \
  --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload '{"days":2}' node26.json
diff <(jq .runtime node24.json) <(jq .runtime node26.json)

This is the response when I call the bundled package locally under Node.js 22. Under nodejs26.x you expect a 26.x version, and exactly this report tells you which features are true there:

{
  "runtime": {
    "nodeVersion": "v22.23.4",
    "ltsName": "Jod",
    "temporal": false,
    "mapGetOrInsert": false,
    "iteratorConcat": false,
    "uint8ArrayBase64": false,
    "requireModule": true,
    "lambdaRuntime": "nodejs24.x"
  },
  "temporalSource": "polyfill",
  "rental": {
    "bikeId": "city-bike-17",
    "returnAt": "2026-10-26T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]",
    "naiveReturnAtUtc": "2026-10-26T08:00:00.000Z"
  }
}

The rental field is what matters: the Temporal calculation returns 10 a.m., while the naive Date calculation lands at 9 a.m. local time. On both runtimes, returnAt has to be identical, no matter whether Temporal is built in or the polyfill does the math.

Common mistakes

  • Runtime rejected: if your region does not offer the preview yet, the deployment fails. For the test, switch to a region where nodejs26.x is selectable in the console.
  • “Dynamic require … is not supported”: this message appears when an ESM bundle contains a CommonJS dependency. The banner with createRequire in the stack prevents it.
  • Callback handlers: old code with (event, context, callback) no longer works from nodejs24.x. Switch to async first.
  • Green locally, different in Lambda: your tests may run with the polyfill locally and with built-in Temporal in Lambda, or the other way round. That is exactly why the report checks every feature in the real runtime.

Cost and security

Two small 256 MB functions that you call a few times cost practically nothing and usually stay within the free tier. With the Lambda cost calculator you can do the math for your real load profiles. Logs are deleted after one week, and npx cdk destroy removes everything again. Do not process real customer data in the preview runtime, since there is neither an SLA nor support for it.

Upgrade checklist for your team

Find the Node runtimes in your account

Before you plan, you need a list. This command shows every function with a Node runtime per region:

for region in eu-central-1 eu-west-1; do
  aws lambda list-functions --region "$region" \
    --query "Functions[?starts_with(Runtime, 'nodejs')].[FunctionName, Runtime]" \
    --output text | sed "s/^/$region\t/"
done

Update TypeScript, bundler and CI

Bump @types/node to version 26, set the matching target in esbuild or on NodejsFunction, and add a Node.js 26 entry to your CI test matrix. Rebuild native addons. And if you use pnpm or Yarn via Corepack, install Corepack explicitly in the pipeline, since it is no longer bundled.

Roll out gradually

Once nodejs26.x is generally available, do not switch all functions at once. I would start with non-critical functions and use an alias with weighted routing to send only part of the traffic to the new version. New runtimes often have somewhat longer cold starts at launch, so keep an eye on error rate and init duration. How to build alarms and dashboards for that is covered in Monitoring Lambda with CDK.

My take

Testing: yes, now. Production on the preview: no. That is my position in a nutshell. The preview is a gift, because you find the surprises while nobody is rushing you yet. If you still run on nodejs22.x today, though, I would not wait for November. The move to 24 brings the biggest Lambda-specific breaks, namely callback handlers and promises that are not awaited. Those affect 26 just the same. Once that is done, the step from 24 to Node.js 26 LTS is small in most projects.

Temporal is what I am looking forward to most. I would rather not count how many time zone and daylight saving bugs I have seen in my career. At the same time, the preview shows that Lambda runtimes are deliberately more conservative than upstream Node.js. For stability, I think that is right, but it can catch you off guard. So my advice: check features in the runtime where your code will actually run. And while you are at it, take a look at your patch routine, because security updates like the one for the Node.js vulnerability CVE-2026-111497 arrive regularly for LTS versions too.

By the way, I like the new annual cadence starting with Node.js 27. A team can schedule one LTS upgrade per year instead of debating every time which version to skip.

FAQ

When will Node.js 26 be generally available on AWS Lambda?

AWS names November 2026 as the planned launch for nodejs26.x, explicitly as a non-binding estimate. Until then, the runtime is a public preview without SLA or support.

How long is Node.js 26 LTS supported?

According to the Node.js project, the 26.x line receives updates until the end of April 2029. When AWS will deprecate the Lambda runtime has not been announced yet.

Can I already use Temporal in Lambda?

Yes, via a polyfill such as @js-temporal/polyfill on any Node runtime. Whether Temporal is built in and enabled in nodejs26.x is best checked with feature detection as in the example.

Do I have to upgrade from Node.js 22 to 24 first?

No, you can go straight to 26. But then you have to handle all changes from 24 and 26 at once. Since nodejs22.x is deprecated in April 2027, going through 24 now is often the more relaxed path.

Your next step

Run the command from the checklist today and count how many functions still run on nodejs22.x. Then deploy the probe function to a sandbox account and check in the report what Node.js 26 LTS really brings in nodejs26.x. I would like to know: which Node runtime are your Lambdas on right now, and what slows you down most when upgrading? Let me know in the comments.

Sources

  • Node.js blog: Node.js 26.0.0 (Current), May 5, 2026
  • Node.js blog: Node.js 25.0.0 (Current), Oct 15, 2025
  • Node.js: releases and release schedule
  • AWS Lambda Developer Guide: Lambda runtimes
  • GitHub: feedback issue for the Node.js 26 preview runtime
  • AWS Compute Blog: Node.js 24 runtime now available in AWS Lambda
  • Tested with Node.js 22.23, TypeScript 7.0.2 (tsc --noEmit), aws-cdk-lib 2.275.0 (cdk synth), @js-temporal/polyfill 0.5.1 and the Node test runner (7 tests). A deployment to AWS and a run under Node.js 26 were not possible in my test environment.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: You're Writing Mouse and Touch Handlers. Pointer Events Does Both.
description:
The demo went great. Drag the card, it follows your cursor, drop it anywhere — smooth, on every laptop in the room. Then someone picks up their phone, drags a thumb across the card — and nothing happens. No movement, no feedback, like the card isn't even listening.

You didn't write a buggy drag handler. You wrote half of one.

box.addEventListener('mousedown', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  offsetX = e.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = e.clientY - box.offsetTop;
});

box.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  box.style.left = `${e.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${e.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

box.addEventListener('mouseup', () => {
  dragging = false;
});

This is correct, tested, and works on exactly one category of device.

The "fix" that just adds a second bug

The instinct is to bolt on touch support: copy the three listeners, swap mouse* for touch*, convert e.clientX/e.clientY to e.touches[0].clientX/e.touches[0].clientY, and call it done.

box.addEventListener('touchstart', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  const t = e.touches[0];
  offsetX = t.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = t.clientY - box.offsetTop;
});

box.addEventListener('touchmove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  const t = e.touches[0];
  box.style.left = `${t.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${t.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

box.addEventListener('touchend', () => {
  dragging = false;
});

Now it works on a phone, in isolation. But you're maintaining the same drag math twice, in two event systems that don't agree on anything — touch events report an array of active touch points (because a screen can have more than one finger on it at once), mouse events report exactly one cursor. And both paths share a bug neither the original mouse-only version nor this touch-added version ever fixed: drag fast enough, or past the edge of the box, and the "end" event stops firing, leaving the card stuck mid-drag.

That's not a mobile-only bug. It's the same bug on both input types, because mousemove and touchmove share the same design flaw.

Why the drag "sticks"

mousemove only fires on the element it's attached to while the cursor is actually over that element — it's hit-tested live, every event. Flick the mouse fast enough, or drag past the edge of the box, and the browser stops delivering mousemove (and eventually mouseup) there at all; those events go to whatever's now under the cursor instead, which has no idea your drag was in progress. The card is left believing it's still being dragged, because the one event that was supposed to tell it otherwise was never sent to it.

Touch has a related but distinct failure mode: if the OS decides your drag gesture is actually a scroll or a browser gesture (a mid-drag notification pull-down, a back-swipe), it can cancel the touch sequence outright, firing touchcancel instead of touchend — and if you only wired a touchend listener because "that's how the drag ends," it never gets a chance to clean up.

Two input systems, two different reasons, one shared symptom: dragging gets stuck true, because neither API gives the element a reliable way to say "tell me how this interaction ends, every time, no matter what."

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

One event model, built to not have this bug

The Pointer Events API replaces mouse* and touch* with a single stream — pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel — that fires identically whether the input is a mouse, a finger, or a stylus. You write it once:

box.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  offsetX = e.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = e.clientY - box.offsetTop;
  box.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
});

box.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  box.style.left = `${e.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${e.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

function endDrag() {
  dragging = false;
}

box.addEventListener('pointerup', endDrag);
box.addEventListener('pointercancel', endDrag);

Three things changed, and each one closes a specific gap the old code had:

  1. One set of listeners, no branching on input type. e.clientX/e.clientY work the same for mouse, touch, and pen — no more reading e.touches[0] on one path and e.clientX directly on the other.
  2. box.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId) is the actual fix for the stuck-drag bug. Once an element captures a pointer, every event for that pointer — including pointermove and pointerup — keeps firing on that element, even when the pointer moves outside its boundaries or off the page entirely. The box can't lose track of the drag because the browser is now routing events to it directly, not based on where the pointer happens to be.
  3. pointercancel is the cleanup path the old code didn't have. It fires when the browser interrupts the interaction for its own reasons — a touch sequence hijacked into a system gesture, for instance. Listening for it alongside pointerup means dragging always gets reset, instead of staying stuck on true forever.

One more line matters for touch devices specifically: add touch-action: none in CSS on the draggable element.

.box { touch-action: none; }

Without it, the browser's own scroll/zoom gesture handling can still compete with your drag for the same touch input before your JavaScript gets a say. touch-action: none tells the browser "this element handles its own gestures," which is exactly what you're asking Pointer Events to do.

What you get that mouse-plus-touch never gave you

  • e.pointerType tells you "mouse", "touch", or "pen" when you actually need to branch — for a stylus app that wants pressure (e.pressure) and tilt (e.tiltX/e.tiltY) only from a pen, for instance. You branch when the behavior should differ, not just to read the coordinates.
  • Multi-touch stays sane. Each contact point gets its own pointerId, so a canvas handling two fingers at once tracks two independent pointer streams instead of indexing into a shifting touches array.
  • It's been safe to rely on for years. Pointer Events shipped in every major engine — Safari was the last holdout and added support in 2019 — so this isn't a progressive-enhancement decision anymore; it's the default way to handle pointing input.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Pointer Events quietly fixes two separate bugs with one API. The "nothing happens on a phone" bug goes away because there's only one set of listeners to remember to wire up, not two. And the "drag freezes mid-gesture" bug — the one that was hiding in the mouse-only version from the start, then rode along into the touch-added version unchanged — goes away because setPointerCapture() finally gives the element what neither old API did: a guarantee that it keeps hearing from the pointer until the interaction is actually over.

Go find the component in your codebase with a mousedown handler and a near-identical touchstart handler sitting a few lines apart. How much of that duplication would pointerdown alone have deleted? Tell me what you find.

title: Accept or Revert: Designing AI Edits as Reviewable Patches on a Real Video Timeline
description:
By Sagar Dey, founder of MirrorCut

Most AI features ship with an all-or-nothing contract. The model does a thing, and you either keep the result or throw it away.

That works for a one-line autocomplete. It falls apart for a video edit, where a single "AI pass" might contain dozens of independent decisions: cut this pause, drop that filler word, keep the second take, caption this line.

When I built MirrorCut, an AI video editor that runs in the browser, I made one rule early: every AI change is a patch on the timeline, and every patch can be accepted or reverted on its own.

This post is about why, and the design constraints that rule creates. It's written for developers building any kind of AI-assisted editor: video, docs, code or design.

Note: the code below is a simplified illustration of the pattern, written for this post. It is not MirrorCut's production code.

The problem with "re-render and replace"

The simplest way to add AI to an editor looks like this:

  1. Send the current state to the model.
  2. Get back a new state.
  3. Replace the old state.

It's easy to build. It's also hostile to the user, for three reasons:

  • No granularity. If the model made ten good decisions and one bad one, the user can't separate them.
  • Lost work. Anything the user did by hand can get silently overwritten.
  • No explanation. The user sees a different result, not what changed or why.

In video, there's a fourth problem: re-rendering is slow and expensive. Throwing away a whole pass because of one bad cut costs real time.

The alternative: edits as small, named patches

Instead of returning a new timeline, the agent proposes a list of small changes against the existing one. Conceptually, each patch carries:

// Illustrative only
type EditPatch = {
  id: string;
  kind: "cut" | "caption" | "reframe" | "graphic";
  range: { start: number; end: number }; // seconds on the timeline
  summary: string; // one human-readable line
  status: "pending" | "accepted" | "reverted";
};

The summary matters more than it looks. In MirrorCut, every AI change is explained in one line, for example "Removing a 0.6 s pause at 0:54". If you can't describe a change in one line, it's probably several changes and should be split.

Rule 1: Show every patch where it happens

Each pending change is outlined on the timeline itself, not buried in a side panel. The user's eyes are already on the timeline, so that's where the review should happen.

This also forces a useful discipline on the agent: every change has to map to a visible location. "Improved the pacing" isn't a patch. "Removed 2.1 s of dead air at 3:12" is.

Rule 2: Accept and Revert are per patch

The whole point is granularity. A pass with ten patches gives the user ten decisions, not one.

// Illustrative only
function revert(patchId: string) {
  const patch = timeline.patches.get(patchId);
  timeline.apply(inverse(patch));
  patch.status = "reverted";
}

The hard part isn't the button. It's making sure patches are independent enough that reverting one doesn't break the others. Cutting 0.6 s at 0:54 shifts everything after it, so later patches need to be expressed in a way that survives earlier ones being reverted.

Rule 3: One undo history for humans and AI

This is the rule people find most surprising.

In MirrorCut, AI edits and manual edits share one undo history. There's no separate "AI layer" or "AI mode." If you trim a clip by hand, then the agent removes a pause, then you press undo, you undo the pause removal, exactly like you'd expect.

Why not keep them separate? Because two histories create two mental models. Users end up asking "which undo do I need?" And they lose trust when the AI's changes behave differently from their own.

A cut is a cut, whoever made it.

Rule 4: Follow-ups patch, they don't restart

When the user asks for a follow-up, like "make the intro faster and add captions", the agent edits the existing timeline instead of regenerating from scratch.

This protects everything the user already accepted or adjusted by hand. A restart would quietly throw that away.

It also keeps responses small and reviewable. The site shows this flow: "Done. Intro trimmed from 4s to 2s and captions added." That's two patches, not a new video.

Rule 5: Expensive operations ask first

Some patches are cheap to preview. Others, like a full-resolution render, take real compute.

In MirrorCut, expensive steps ask before running. The general pattern: separate proposing a change from paying for it. Let the user review the plan before the costly part kicks off.

There's a pricing angle too. On MirrorCut's plans, each request to the agent uses AI credits based on the work it takes, while editing by hand on the timeline uses no credits. That makes "do it yourself" a real, free option for small fixes, and it keeps the agent honest about when it's worth calling.

Where this pattern applies beyond video

Strip out the video specifics and you get a reusable checklist for any AI-assisted editor:

  1. Return patches, not replacement states.
  2. Give each patch a one-line explanation and a visible location.
  3. Make accept/revert granular, and design patches to survive each other's reversal.
  4. Use one undo history for human and AI changes.
  5. Patch on follow-up; never silently restart.
  6. Ask before expensive work.

Try it on your own footage

MirrorCut, AI video editor (mirrorcut.ai), runs in the browser. It cuts dead air, filler words and retakes, adds word-timed captions, reframes to 16:9, 9:16, 1:1 and 4:5, finds Shorts, and adds motion graphics, all as reviewable patches on a real timeline. Exports are MP4 up to 4K, plus SRT and VTT captions.

Every account starts with 7 days of the Creator plan free (card required). After that, it's Creator $10, Pro $30 or Studio $60 a month. MirrorCut launches publicly in November 2026: https://www.mirrorcut.ai

I'd love to hear how you handle review flows for AI output in your own tools. Drop it in the comments.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA).     • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

Vertex AI Search

Change

Agent Search: Update to the stable model

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

title: stageshow skill: How to Make Clean Product UI Demos With Your AI Coding Agent
description:
The stageshow skill is a new add-on for AI coding agents that helps them build "faux UI": simplified product screens, feature cards, bento grids and short cursor animations for landing pages and docs. It was released on 31 October 2026 by designer Benji Taylor, and if you run a small product or make content about software, it's worth a look. This is a research-based walkthrough based on the project's GitHub repo and the author's launch write-up.

What problem it solves

Most small teams need product visuals: a hero animation, a feature card, a "here's how it works" clip. You can ask an AI agent to mock one up, but as the author puts it, the results "often look sloppy and heavy-handed." Stageshow writes down the many small design decisions so the agent can make them too.

The skill is built around one rule from its SKILL.md: "It reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause." It also lists five common failures to avoid: too much detail, a bare wireframe, a whole window "boxed" into a card, a flat layout where nothing stands out, and a bland look that ignores the brief.

How to install it

From your project, run:

npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow

The author says this works with common coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini. Then ask for something small: one interaction, in one product, at one size. The write-up's own example prompt is:

A small looping demo for our homepage hero: someone assigns an issue to a teammate.

The agent reads the skill, starts from the closest example, builds the demo, then films it and fixes what it finds. What you get is an ordinary React component you can drop into your site.

What's inside

  • SKILL.md: the core idea, the failure list and a seven-step workflow (medium and place, look, story, start from an example, and so on).
  • kit/: a small set of React parts (stage, windows, phones) that supports React 18 and later, with no third-party animation runtime.
  • examples/: dozens of "gold" examples, including studies of real products like Figma, Linear, Slack and Raycast.
  • scripts/: film.mjs records a demo and makes a contact sheet so the agent can check its own work, plus checks for one-frame jumps and text that doesn't fit.

There's also a local playground. It needs Node 20.19 or later:

npm install
npm run dev

A practical setup for a small team

  1. Install the skill in the repo where your marketing site lives.
  2. Pick one feature you explain often, like booking, invoicing or a dashboard view.
  3. Ask for a 10 to 16 second loop (the length the skill recommends) at the size it will actually appear.
  4. Ask for a compact phone version too; the skill designs a separate 358px-wide layout rather than squeezing the desktop one.
  5. Review the motion yourself. The README is clear: "No automated clean result replaces watching the motion."

Honest caveats

The author warns it "still may not nail it in one shot," and most demos take a few rounds of feedback. These are illustrations, not automation: a scripted click only draws the cursor pressing. And the repo notes that each skill carries its own licence and third-party asset notices, so check those before using real brand marks.

We cover new AI tools for small businesses and creators in plain English at AI News. If you'd rather have the automation built for you, see AIFix.

title: Step-by-Step Email Event Notification APIs Explained — Auditable Compliance Records
description:
Short answer: a B2B SaaS compliance notice needs a small Node.js intake service that authenticates event notifications, writes an immutable evidence record, and keeps message content on a separate retention schedule. A delivery event is evidence of a downstream observation, not proof that a person read the notice.

The bill is usually shaped by retention, not by the outbound request. Duplicated raw payloads, rendered bodies, indexes, attachments, and logs outlive their purpose unless their life is designed. An example policy might retain normalized evidence for 30 days, raw event envelopes for 7 days, and no body after its hash and required metadata are recorded. Those are policy examples; legal requirements set the real window.

What is the bill actually storing?

Data Purpose Retention question
Notice metadata Links a notice to tenant and policy Is an ID enough?
Event envelope Preserves what the source reported When is the original shape no longer needed?
Normalized status Supports reports and reconciliation Can it outlive the raw payload?
Message content Supports review or discovery Is a hash sufficient?
Operational logs Explains retries and failures Can identifiers be logged without addresses?

Store the notice ID, tenant ID, recipient fingerprint, event type, source event ID, observed time, and content hash in durable evidence. Keep the raw payload in short-lived object storage only when investigation requires it. Keep message bodies in a separately governed store with a tested deletion job.

This is a trade-off. Expiring raw data can remove fields that were never promoted into the evidence schema. Expiring the body can leave an auditor able to prove what happened without reconstructing the prose. Define the evidence contract first. Retention is a data-model decision.

A delivered event can mean that a downstream system accepted a message; it does not establish that the recipient read it. A bounced event needs its reason and the time observed. Keep the system's notice ID beside the external event ID so a repeated notification does not become a second compliance notice.

Consider a 30-day audit window. On day one, the normalized record can answer which tenant issued the notice, which recipient fingerprint was targeted, which event source reported the outcome, and when the service observed it. On day eight, the raw envelope may be gone. That is acceptable only if the normalized schema already captured the event type, source identity, timestamps, content hash, and verification result. If the investigation needs a field that was left in the expired envelope, the retention policy has saved storage by spending auditability. This is the kind of failure that appears months after an apparently successful integration, when the team has forgotten which adapter supplied which field. Write the contract while the payload is still in view.

{
  "notice_id": "notice_01J9EXAMPLE",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_42",
  "recipient_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
  "event_type": "delivered",
  "provider_event_id": "evt_7f2",
  "observed_at": "2026-10-31T08:15:00Z",
  "content_sha256": "sha256:...",
  "raw_payload_expires_at": "2026-11-07T08:15:00Z"
}

Use a uniqueness rule on the source identity you trust. Record late events, but do not silently let them rewrite a newer terminal state. Do not put a full recipient address into ordinary logs. A fingerprint supports correlation, but it remains sensitive when the input and hashing process are available to an attacker.

How should the Node.js intake be wired?

This step-by-step integration has four boundaries: authenticate, parse and validate, normalize, and persist idempotently. Email APIs belong at the edge; the rest of the application should receive a narrow internal event shape.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

function fingerprintRecipient(address, secret) {
  return "sha256:" + crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(address.trim().toLowerCase()).digest("hex");
}

function normalizeEvent(payload, secret) {
  if (!payload.notice_id || !payload.type || !payload.event_id) {
    throw new Error("missing event identity");
  }
  return {
    notice_id: String(payload.notice_id),
    tenant_id: String(payload.tenant_id),
    recipient_fingerprint: fingerprintRecipient(String(payload.recipient), secret),
    event_type: String(payload.type),
    provider_event_id: String(payload.event_id),
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
    content_sha256: payload.content_sha256 ?? null
  };
}

export async function acceptEvent(request, deps) {
  const payload = await request.json();
  await deps.auth.verify(request, payload);
  const event = normalizeEvent(payload, deps.secrets.recipientFingerprint);
  await deps.evidence.insertIfAbsent(event, { rawPayload: payload, expiresInDays: 7 });
  return { status: 202 };
}

202 means accepted for processing, not delivered. Parsing and signature checks need a bounded body size, replay protection where supported, and a defined malformed-event response. Write the original only after verification. If a write fails after success is returned, the service has lied; if an error follows a successful write, the sender may retry. Idempotency is correctness.

Which failure mode does each boundary contain?

Failure mode Containment Evidence
Duplicate delivery Unique source event ID and replay-safe insert First-seen time and duplicate count
Late event State ordering rule or event timeline Event time and observed time
Signature mismatch Reject before normalization Redacted request ID and reason
Database outage Bounded backoff or durable queue Attempts and final disposition
Unknown event type Quarantine for review Type and schema version
Accepted without delivery Separate accepted and delivered states Transition history

The subtle case is a retry storm. Separate permanent validation failures from transient infrastructure failures, cap attempts, and expose queue age. A dead-letter record should identify human work without becoming another uncontrolled payload copy.

SPF concerns a sending domain's authorization model. It does not define a webhook schema or prove that a recipient read a message. The intake still needs an authenticated event channel, replay protection, and a record of the verification decision.

Measure acceptance rate, verification failures, duplicate rate, time from receipt to durable evidence, queue age, and notices with no terminal observation after a chosen window. Measure by tenant too; a healthy aggregate can hide one tenant with a consistently wrong domain policy.

Test duplicate delivery, reordered events, unknown types, expired signatures, oversized bodies, and a database timeout after insert. Assert both the response and the evidence left behind. Add a schema version and preserve the old reader until the retention window closes. The cleanup job should count candidates, deletions, and failures.

How can I integrate email event notification APIs step-by-step?

Start with the evidence contract, then connect the email APIs, then exercise the failure paths. The order matters: integrating first and defining evidence later usually leaves a provider-shaped record that cannot answer a compliance question cleanly.

The first design often keeps every payload forever because storage feels cheap and evidence feels valuable. Access review later shows that the system retained more personal data than the audit question required. Promote the fields that answer that question, shorten the rest, and document what cannot be reconstructed after expiry.

One short rule is enough: preserve proof, expire copies.

The least complex implementation is a thin adapter, an idempotent evidence store, and an explicit retention policy. Add queues, reconciliation, or extra channels only when they remove a demonstrated operational burden, because each state transition must also be audited.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5322, Internet Message Format: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322
  • RFC 3339, Date and Time on the Internet: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339

title: Seventeen words for eight database values, and a dot that only pulses when work is actually running
description:
Nakodo does its work while nobody is watching: it reads a brand's website, finds creators and businesses who fit, writes the first email and handles the replies. The how it works page is the public version of that. The private version is a screen that has to answer, in about four words per row, what is happening right now.

That answer lives in three small files totalling 106 lines. None of them touches the database, and none of the words in them is stored anywhere.

Eight values, seventeen words

The conversation table has a status column and a closed_reason column. Both are plain text with a TypeScript enum over them, because this app has no pgEnum anywhere. The words a human reads are a pair of records:

export const STATUS_LABELS: Record<OutreachStatus, string> = {
  drafting: "Writing",
  review: "To approve",
  queued: "Scheduled",
  contacted: "Contacted",
  talking: "Talking",
  needs_you: "Needs you",
  handed_off: "Introduced",
  closed: "Closed",
};

export const CLOSED_LABELS: Record<OutreachClosedReason, string> = {
  no_reply: "No reply",
  declined: "Declined",
  opted_out: "Opted out",
  bounced: "Address bounced",
  complained: "Marked as spam",
  cancelled: "Stopped",
  suppressed: "Can't be contacted",
  no_email: "No email",
  failed: "Failed",
};

export function threadLabel(t: { status: OutreachStatus; closedReason: OutreachClosedReason | null }): string {
  return t.status === "closed" && t.closedReason ? CLOSED_LABELS[t.closedReason] : STATUS_LABELS[t.status];
}

Seventeen words for what the machine thinks of as eight states, and the reason is the three-line function at the bottom. A closed conversation that knows why it closed never shows the word "Closed", because "Closed" is a true statement that answers nothing. "No reply" and "Marked as spam" and "Opted out" are the same state to a scheduler and three completely different things to the person whose brand sent the email: one is normal, one is a deliverability problem, and one is a person telling you to stop.

Typing both as Record<Union, string> rather than Record<string, string> is the whole safety net. Add a ninth closed reason to the schema and the build fails in this file until it has a word. That is the cheapest possible test for "no state reaches the UI without a human writing a sentence for it".

Five views over eight statuses

The same file groups them, in display order, with satisfies doing the checking:

export const THREAD_VIEWS = [
  { key: "attention", label: "Needs you", statuses: ["needs_you", "review"] },
  { key: "active", label: "In progress", statuses: ["drafting", "queued", "contacted", "talking"] },
  { key: "introduced", label: "Introduced", statuses: ["handed_off"] },
  { key: "closed", label: "Closed", statuses: ["closed"] },
  { key: "all", label: "All", statuses: null },
] as const satisfies readonly { key: string; label: string; statuses: readonly OutreachStatus[] | null }[];
export type ThreadView = (typeof THREAD_VIEWS)[number]["key"];

as const satisfies is the pairing I reach for most often in this codebase: as const keeps the literal types, so ThreadView is "attention" | "active" | ... derived from the data, and satisfies checks every status string against the schema union without widening anything. A plain type annotation would have given me string for the keys and no union to derive.

Two things in that array are decisions rather than data. "Needs you" collapses two statuses, because a first email waiting for approval and a reply the model would not answer are both "a human has to look", and a product that makes you learn the difference before you can act has failed at the one job. And statuses: null for "All" means absent rather than a list of everything, so adding a status never silently drops it out of the one view that promises completeness.

The badge is not a traffic light 

// A conversation's state. Introduced is the one stamp; anything waiting on
// the brand is ochre-outlined; work in flight is plain ink; closed stays
// quiet. No traffic-light colours.
const TONE: Record<OutreachStatus, string> = {
  drafting: "border-dashed border-ink-400 text-muted-foreground",
  review: "border-mark-outline text-foreground",
  queued: "border-dashed border-foreground/50 text-foreground",
  contacted: "border-foreground/60 text-foreground",
  talking: "border-cyano-700 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:text-cyano-200",
  needs_you: "border-mark-outline bg-mark/30 text-foreground",
  handed_off: "border-cyano-700 bg-cyano-50 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:bg-cyano-950 dark:text-cyano-200",
  closed: "border-ink-400/60 text-muted-foreground",
};

Eight tones, two hues, and no red or green anywhere. The brand document is blunt about why: ochre is "used only for attention marks", so the moment a colour means "danger" or "success" it stops meaning "look here". A closed conversation is not a failure, a reply is not an alarm, and three quarters of the states are neither good nor bad, so the axis the colours actually encode is "does this need you", not "is this going well".

The signals are also doubled on purpose. Only two states get a fill, filled is "waiting on you" and "introduced", and the attention dot used elsewhere carries its own text:

export function AttentionMark({ label, className }: { label: string; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <span className={cn("inline-flex", className)}>
      <span className="inline-block size-[7px] rounded-full border border-mark-outline bg-mark" aria-hidden="true" />
      <span className="sr-only">{label}</span>
    </span>
  );
}

Seven pixels of ochre and a screen-reader sentence. The dot is decoration, the sr-only text is the information, which is the only arrangement that survives WCAG 1.4.1 and a colourblind reader.

The dot that tells you whether anything is happening

A campaign gets a different treatment: one word and a dot, where the dot answers a question the word cannot.

export function LiveDot({ live, label, className }: { live: boolean; label: string; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <span className={cn("inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[13px] text-muted-foreground", className)}>
      <span className="relative inline-flex size-1.5">
        {live && (
          <span className="absolute inset-0 rounded-full bg-cyano-600 motion-safe:animate-[live-pulse_2.4s_ease-out_infinite]" />
        )}
        <span className={cn("relative inline-flex size-1.5 rounded-full", live ? "bg-cyano-600" : "bg-ink-400")} />
      </span>
      <span className={cn(live && "text-foreground")}>{label}</span>
    </span>
  );
}

A solid dot with a pulsing copy behind it, motion-safe so it is a static dot for anybody who has asked for less motion, and the label's own colour as the second channel so the state is legible without the animation.

And then the function that decides live, which is 32 lines and the densest product thinking in the app:

// Campaign status as a live dot and a word. Only running work pulses: a
// campaign with only its emails paused is still searching, and one with
// enough good leads waiting may still be checking what it found.
export function campaignStatus(
  status: string,
  working: boolean,
  pauseMode: PauseMode | null = null,
  enoughLeads = false,
): { live: boolean; label: string } {
  switch (status) {
    case "researching":
      return { live: true, label: "Reading website" };
    case "draft":
      return { live: false, label: "Brief to review" };
    case "active":
      if (enoughLeads) return { live: working, label: "Enough leads" };
      return working ? { live: true, label: "Surveying" } : { live: false, label: "Up to date" };
    case "paused":
      return pauseMode === "emails"
        ? { live: working, label: "Emails paused" }
        : pauseMode === "finding"
          ? { live: false, label: "Finding paused" }
          : { live: false, label: "Paused" };
    case "failed":
      return { live: false, label: "Research failed" };
    default:
      return { live: false, label: status };
  }
}

Four inputs, nine possible labels, six database statuses. The two branches worth staring at are the ones that return live: working rather than true or false.

"Emails paused" with a pulsing dot looks wrong until you remember that pause here has a reason column and three answers: a campaign can be paused for sending while it carries on searching. The word tells you what is stopped, the dot tells you that something is still moving. If live were hardcoded false for every paused campaign, the screen would claim nothing is happening while jobs run, and the next thing that appears would be unexplained.

"Up to date" versus "Surveying" is the same trick with the opposite emphasis: same status, same plan, and the only difference is whether any job is open right now. "Idle" would have been a worse word, because nothing is wrong, and "Active" would have been a worse word, because nothing is happening.

The branch that should not exist 

default:
  return { live: false, label: status };

That line prints a raw database value into the interface. active instead of "Surveying", in lower case, in a dot label. It exists because the first parameter is typed status: string and not the schema's union, so TypeScript cannot see that the switch is exhaustive and insists on a return.

Printing the raw value is the right behaviour for a branch that should be unreachable: it does not crash, it does not say "Unknown", and anybody who sees active on a card knows immediately that a status was added and this file was not told. But the honest fix is one word in the signature. Narrow status to the union, the switch becomes exhaustive, the default goes away, and the next person to add a status gets a compile error in the same place the conversation labels already give them one.

Three files, 106 lines, 26 words, and not one of them in the database. The nearest public equivalent is the glossary, where the same discipline is applied to the words customers meet before they sign up: one definition each, written once, and never two names for one thing.

title: I Built IntentChord to Bring Human Control to AI Coding Agents — Contributors Welcome
description:
AI coding agents can write code, modify files, and report that a task is complete.

But a successful-looking response doesn't necessarily answer some important questions:

  • Was the agent working on the correct source?
  • Was the change within the approved scope?
  • Is the reported result supported by actual evidence?
  • Who decides whether the work is accepted?

These questions led me to build IntentChord.

What is IntentChord?

IntentChord is a local-first, human-governed development workflow that connects an owner's intent to workspace context, confirmed scope, agent-specific execution contracts, evidence-based review, and a final human decision.

Its central principle is simple:

An AI agent's report is not the same as verified execution evidence, and an agent's claim of success is not the owner's approval.

What's in the project?

The repository includes:

  • Task and scope authority management
  • Workspace discovery, indexing, and source-context foundations
  • Governed execution contracts for Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI
  • Execution evidence and report-verification logic
  • Human review and decision workflows
  • A Next.js, React, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL-based application

The project is still evolving and is not presented as a production-certified system.

I'm opening the project to contributors

I've made the source public because I'd like to develop IntentChord with other developers.

I'm particularly interested in contributions involving code quality, testing, developer onboarding, architecture discussions, and improvements to the human-in-the-loop workflow.

There are already beginner-friendly and documentation tasks available in GitHub Issues.

Repository: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord

Contribution opportunities: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord/issues

The project is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, rather than an OSI-approved open-source license. Please review the repository's license and contribution guidelines before contributing.

I'd be interested to hear how other developers handle agent authority, scope changes, and evidence verification in their AI-assisted development workflows.

What would you improve or challenge in this approach?

title: RunPod em reais: o que custa a hora, a sessão de 4 horas e o pod que ninguém desligou
description:
R$ 134, R$ 239, R$ 480. São três contas de GPU alugada na RunPod que ninguém quer receber: o que se paga ao deixar um pod ligado por 48 horas numa RTX 3090, numa 4090 e numa A100.

Os preços saíram da tabela de preços da RunPod (marcada como atualizada em 28/10/2026, consultada em 31/10/2026). Converti com US$ 1 = R$ 5,397 e 3,5% de IOF, ou R$ 5,59 por dólar; o spread do seu banco não está incluído. Não rodei teste na plataforma, é conta sobre a tabela.

A hora, em reais

A 3090 de 24 GB custa US$ 0,50 por hora, R$ 2,79. A 4090 (24 GB), US$ 0,89, R$ 4,97. A L40S de 48 GB, US$ 1,09, R$ 6,09. A A100 de 80 GB, US$ 1,79, R$ 10,00. A H100 PCIe, US$ 2,89, R$ 16,14. Uma sessão de 4 horas fica entre R$ 11 (3090) e R$ 65 (H100).

Memória é o que você está comprando

Entre a 4090 e a A100 há R$ 5 de diferença por hora e 56 GB de memória. Se o seu modelo cabe nos 24 GB, esses 56 GB ficam parados. Começaria numa 3090 ou 4090 e só subiria para a L40S (48 GB) quando o erro de memória aparecesse.

Se for criar a conta, este é o meu link de afiliado da RunPod. Eu rodaria primeiro um script pequeno para ter certeza de que ele funciona antes de alugar hora cara.

O disco, que o pod parado não desliga

A tabela de armazenamento mostra o Volume Disk a US$ 0,10 por GB por mês com o pod rodando e US$ 0,20 com ele parado. Para 100 GB de modelos, são R$ 112 por mês parado. O Network Storage padrão, a US$ 0,07 por GB abaixo de 1 TB, daria R$ 39 pelos mesmos 100 GB; leia na documentação o que diferencia os dois antes de decidir.

Quando nem vale alugar GPU

Se o seu código só chama API de terceiros, o que você precisa é de um servidor pequeno, como a VPS da Hostinger (comparei promoção e renovação aqui). GPU só quando o modelo roda na máquina alugada.
