description:
Foreword: After the AI Agent Goes Online, What is the Next Bottleneck?

Welcome back to the "Agent Platform in Action" series! In the previous six articles, we took the LINE AI Card Assistant (kkdai/line-card-assistant) through the complete five stages from a standalone prototype to production-grade cloud deployment:

  1. [Agent Platform in Action (1)] Building LINE AI Card Assistant with Go and Google ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow: Using google.golang.org/adk/v2/workflow to build a 13-node directed graph featuring Vision OCR, AddFanOut / AddFanIn parallel background investigation, and NewRequestInputEvent HITL interaction loops.
  2. [Agent Platform in Action (2)] From Monolithic Cloud Run to Google Cloud Agent Runtime: Completed Phase 1 (PR #10), standardizing the project into an agents-cli (adk_go) dual-channel architecture.
  3. [Agent Platform in Action (3)] Implementing Cross-Instance Business Card Recognition and Pause/Resume with ADK 2.0 GCS Artifact Service and Agent Platform Sessions: Completed the first half of Phase 2 (PR #11), solving the HITL "amnesia" of stateless containers and the issue of binary image data explosion.
  4. [Agent Platform in Action (4)] Completing the Architecture Puzzle with Cloud Run LINE Webhook Gateway, Agent Runtime, and Cloud SQL PostgreSQL: Completed the second half of Phase 2 & Phase 3 (PR #12), upgrading the business card database to Cloud SQL PostgreSQL and achieving two-layer stateless decoupling.
  5. [Agent Platform in Action (5)] Establishing Automated Evaluation Benchmarks with agents-cli eval and ADK 2.0 Go: Completed Phase 4 (PR #13), establishing a golden test set and a quality flywheel.
  6. [Agent Platform in Action (6)] Building a Full-Stack Observable LINE AI Card Assistant with agents-cli deploy, Terraform IaC, GitHub Actions CI/CD, and Cloud Trace: Completed Phase 5 (PR #14), adding OpenTelemetry Spans (workflow.node.*) to all 13 Graph Nodes and deploying to the cloud via Terraform and GitHub Actions.

Additionally, we have planned advanced Graph Workflow primitives for future ADK v2.6+ (such as Parallel dynamic dispatch, MultiRoute multi-way fan-out, reflection-repair loops, and strongly typed nodes) into the Future Roadmap Issue #15.

However, now that our Agent possesses Phase 4 Automated Evaluation and Phase 5 Full-Node Tracing (OpenTelemetry Spans), a deeper question emerges:

When evaluations find that the Agent performs poorly in certain real-world cases (e.g., Japanese-English bilingual cards, searching for colloquial nicknames in the Taiwan tech industry, multi-clause colloquial HITL modifications, or financial compliance icebreaker letters), must engineers manually check logs, manually modify Prompt strings in the Go source code, and then recompile and redeploy every single time?

Can we let a Meta-Agent (Engineer Agent) automatically read our evaluation results and OpenTelemetry execution trajectories, diagnose the reasons for lost points, write new Skills and Long-Term Memory itself, and complete a closed-loop self-evolution?

This is precisely the core proposition addressed by Google Research's recently published and open-sourced google-research/harness2 (Harness²: Recursive Harnessing for LLM Agents, arXiv:2610.14224)!

This series will consist of three articles (corresponding to Issue #16, Issue #17, Issue #18, and PR #19), guiding you through the complete integration of Google Research Harness² into our Go ADK 2.0 project:

  • Part 1 (This article, Issue #16): What is Google Harness²? What can it do? Inventorying the existing architecture before modification and decoupling hardcoded configurations in the Go binary into a c1..c8 editable Harness file tree.
  • Part 2 (Issue #17): Encapsulating Phase 4's eval/datasets/ and Phase 5's OpenTelemetry Spans into a LineCardAdapter for Harness², and analyzing why "Zero-Leakage Barriers" and "High-Resolution Behavioral Trajectories" are both indispensable.
  • Part 3 (Issue #18): Complete testing tutorial, disclosure of Parallel vs Sequential + LongTermMEMORY two-layer recursive experimental data (accuracy jumping from 62.5% to 100.0%), and outlook on the future development of Agents.

1. What is Google Research Harness²? What can it do?

1. From "Fine-tuning Model Weights" to "Optimizing Agent Harnessing"

In the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), the success of an AI Agent is often determined not just by the underlying model (like Gemini 2.5 Flash / Pro) itself, but by the "Agent Harness" layer wrapped around the model—namely, System Prompts, formatting and safety Guardrails, Long-Term Memory, Tool Descriptions, Sub-Agent settings, and On-Demand Skills.

Past automated prompt optimizations (like PromptBreeder, TextGrad, or DSPy) mostly targeted mutations of a single Prompt string. However, in a real enterprise-grade Agent, if you stuff all edge-case patching rules into the same System Prompt, it quickly leads to "Context Bloat": the number of Always-On Tokens increases, which not only squeezes the model's Output Token Budget but also causes different rules to interfere with each other!

Google Research's Harness² (Recursive Harnessing for LLM Agents, arXiv:2610.14224) breaks this limitation. It defines the entire Agent's equipment as a structured c1..c8 Editable Component Tree and automatically evolves this file tree through Two-Level Recursion:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Outer["Outer Recursion: Harnessing-Level Recursion (Experience accumulation across rounds k=1..K)"]
        Reflector["Experience Reflector\n(ReflectorPrompt)\nDistilling success and failure patterns across rounds"]
        Memory["c3: LongTermMEMORY.md\nPersisting domain experience across iterations"]
        Reflector -->|Write long-term rules| Memory
    end

    subgraph Inner["Inner Recursion: Task-Level Recursion (Closed-loop diagnosis and patching within a single round)"]
        Propose["1. Propose (Diagnostic Proposal)\nRead trajectory.md\nLocate behavioral defects and propose N candidate Patches"]
        Probe["2. Probe (Sandbox Probing)\nExecute N candidate Harnesses in parallel\nCompare trajectory and score changes before and after modification"]
        Compose["3. Compose (Conflict Resolution and Synthesis)\nRetain positive-gain Patches, discard negative interference\nSynthesize the next-generation best Harness H^(k)"]
        Propose --> Probe --> Compose
    end

    Memory --> Propose
    Compose --> Reflector

2. The c1..c8 Eight Harness Components and the 24KB Budget Limit

In google-research/harness2/harness.py, a standard Agent Harness consists of 4 Always-On Components (c1..c4) and 4 On-Demand Components (c5..c8):

Component Code File Path Rule Loading Mode Responsibility in Harness²
c1 systemprompt.md Always-On Defines core roles, node responsibilities, and indexing rules for triggering c6 skills (Skill Trigger Lines).
c2 guardrails.md Always-On Defines non-violable output formats (e.g., pure JSON constraints), E.164 normalization invariants, and security/PII guardrails.
c3 LongTermMEMORY.md Always-On Domain lessons and industry compliance memories written across rounds by the outer Experience Reflector.
c4 tool_descriptions/*.md Always-On Tool parameter descriptions, search strategies, and normalization details (e.g., Japan long-distance prefix (0) cleaning rules).
c5 sub_agents/<name>/AGENT.md On-Demand Exclusive Instructions and YAML Frontmatter (mode: subagent) for delegated sub-agents (e.g., company_enrich).
c6 skills/<name>/SKILL.md On-Demand Professional skills dynamically injected only for specific domains or tasks (e.g., Japanese card OCR, Hsinchu Science Park colloquial search expansion).
c7 scripts/*.py On-Demand Auxiliary verification or data conversion scripts.
c8 plugin/*.ts On-Demand Runtime lifecycle and OpenTelemetry diagnostic hooks.

Important

Why distinguish between c1..c4 (Always-On) and c5..c8 (On-Demand)? Harness² sets an iron rule in OPENCODE_SURFACE: The total byte count of c1..c4 always-on files must never exceed 24,000 bytes (AlwaysOnMaxBytes = 24000)! When Harness² finds that a failure case requires lengthy domain knowledge (e.g., a department title mapping table for Japanese corporate cards or a colloquial abbreviation dictionary for Taiwan semiconductor parks), it won't force these rules into systemprompt.md causing Context explosion. Instead, it will automatically create an on-demand c6 skill file (skills/<name>/SKILL.md) and leave only a lightweight Trigger Line in systemprompt.md!

3. How Does Two-Level Recursion Work?

The Harness² evolution engine (harness2/core/recursion.py) includes two levels of recursion:

  1. Level 1 (Inner): Task-Level Recursion (Propose $\rightarrow$ Probe $\rightarrow$ Compose):
    • Propose (Diagnostic Proposal): The optimizer (Harvester LLM) observes tasks that lost points in the benchmark, the final output (Deliverable), and the execution trajectory (trajectory.md). It diagnoses which step the Agent made a wrong decision on and proposes multiple independent candidate patches (Candidate Patches, each being a set of additions or modifications to c1..c8).
    • Probe (Sandbox Probing): The system mounts each candidate Patch into a sandbox and runs the task once, collecting new scores and new execution trajectories to form a "Before vs. After" Behavioral Contrast.
    • Compose (Conflict Resolution and Synthesis): The optimizer compares the actual performance of all candidate Patches, merges modifications that truly bring positive score improvements into the new generation Harness $H^{(k)}$, and discards ineffective or side-effect-inducing modifications.
  2. Level 2 (Outer): Harnessing-Level Recursion (Experience Reflector):
    • Between multiple iterations ($k = 1 \dots K$), the outer ReflectorPrompt reviews the evolution history from $H^{(0)} \to H^{(1)} \to \dots \to H^{(k)}$: Which types of modifications succeeded? Which cross-domain constraints (e.g., financial industry compliance headers and personal data protection regulations) need to be remembered at a global level?
    • Distilled high-level experiences are written into c3: LongTermMEMORY.md, guiding the next round of Propose and Agent execution.

2. Inventorying the Current Architecture: Why Phase 1~5 Go Implementation Cannot Be Directly Optimized by Harness²?

Let's compare the left side (Before: Hardcoded Go Binary Architecture) of the architecture diagram at the beginning of the article and review the system architecture we completed in Phase 1 to Phase 5:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Before["Before: Phase 1~5 Solid Compilation Architecture (Hardcoded Go Binary)"]
        direction TB
        N1["nodes_ingest.go\nHardcoded VisionOCR / CleanAndDedup /\nCompanyEnrich / ApplyEdit Prompts"]
        N2["nodes_search.go\nHardcoded QueryIntent /\nEmailDraft Prompts"]
        N3["graph.go\nFixed SubAgent Instruction"]
        E["eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json\nPhase 4 Golden Test Set"]
        T["telemetry.go\nPhase 5 OpenTelemetry 13-Node Spans"]
    end

    Problem["Pain Points:\n1. Prompts hardcoded in .go string constants; re-go build required for every adjustment\n2. Lack of on-demand c6 Skills mechanism\n3. Phase 4 Eval and Phase 5 OTel Spans not yet connected into an automated optimization loop"]
    Before --> Problem

In the code before modification:

  1. All Prompt templates for VisionOCRNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ApplyEditNode (located in internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go), as well as QueryIntentNode and EmailDraftNode (located in internal/workflow/nodes_search.go), are hardcoded as fmt.Sprintf(...) string constants in the Go code.
  2. The llmagent.Config{Instruction: ...} for CompanyEnrichAgent (located in internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go) is also a fixed string hardcoded in a Go function.
  3. When we want the Harness² Python evolution loop to modify system prompts, add a Japanese business card recognition skill (skills/jp_card_ocr/SKILL.md), or adjust phone number normalization guidelines (tool_descriptions/tool_guidance.md), it is impossible for Harness² to rewrite our .go source code and go build again for every single task!

Therefore, the first step in introducing Harness² (Issue #16) is to completely decouple the Go compilation phase from the Harness equipment phase:

  • Go Binary is responsible for "Graph Topology and Dual-Channel Execution Engine": RouterNode, parallel Fan-Out/Fan-In, HITLConfirmNode pause/resume, Cloud SQL and GCS Artifact access, OpenTelemetry instrumentation.
  • External c1..c8 Harness file tree is responsible for the "Evolvable Brain and Skill Equipment": Dynamically hot-reloaded at runtime via the environment variable LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR!

3. Implementation Part 1: Building internal/harness Loader and harness/base/ Initial Equipment Tree

To make the Go ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow natively understand the Harness² c1..c8 specification, we added two core directories to the project:

  • harness/base/: Stores the initial unevolved ($k=0$) c1..c8 baseline file tree.
  • internal/harness/harness.go: Responsible for loading the c1..c8 file tree, validating OPENCODE_SURFACE 24KB limits and YAML Frontmatter rules, and dynamically combining always-on context with on-demand skills for each Graph Node.

1. Establishing the harness/base/ Baseline c1..c8 File Tree

We extracted the basic settings previously scattered in nodes_ingest.go and nodes_search.go into the harness/base/ directory:

harness/base/
├── systemprompt.md # c1: Core roles and overview of Graph Node responsibilities
├── guardrails.md # c2: JSON output format and phone normalization guardrails
├── LongTermMEMORY.md # c3: Cross-round long-term memory (initially empty, to be written by Reflector)
├── tool_descriptions/
│ └── tool_guidance.md # c4: Guidance for google_search and format_company_profile
├── sub_agents/
│ └── company_enrich/
│ └── AGENT.md # c5: CompanyEnrichAgent delegated sub-agent definition
├── skills/ # c6: On-demand skills directory (to be generated by Propose-Probe-Compose evolution)
├── scripts/ # c7: Auxiliary scripts directory
└── plugin/ # c8: Diagnostic plugin directory

For example, harness/base/sub_agents/company_enrich/AGENT.md uses a YAML Frontmatter format fully compatible with google-research/harness2:

---
mode: subagent
description: Searches Google to summarize company background and industry tags.
---
You are a professional business analysis assistant. Please use the google_search tool to query the company name provided by the user, then call the format_company_profile tool to return a two-sentence Traditional Chinese company profile and 3 to 5 technical or industry tags (e.g., AI, Cloud, SaaS, FinTech, Semiconductor).

2. Implementing internal/harness/harness.go: 24KB Always-On Budget Validation and On-Demand Skill Injection

In internal/harness/harness.go, we implemented the validator Validate() and node prompt synthesizer ComposeNodePrompt() fully aligned with the Python version of OPENCODE_SURFACE.validate():

// AlwaysOnMaxBytes matches google-research/harness2 OPENCODE_SURFACE.always_on_max (24,000 bytes).
const AlwaysOnMaxBytes = 24000

// AlwaysOnFiles lists the four c1..c4 always-on files mounted into the agent context.
var AlwaysOnFiles = []string{
    "systemprompt.md",
    "guardrails.md",
    "LongTermMEMORY.md",
    "tool_descriptions/tool_guidance.md",
}

// Validate enforces Google Research Harness² OPENCODE_SURFACE invariants on the c1..c8 tree.
func (h *Harness) Validate() error {
    var problems []string
    for _, reqFile := range AlwaysOnFiles {
        if strings.TrimSpace(h.Files[reqFile]) == "" {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("missing or empty always-on component %q", reqFile))
        }
    }
    if total := h.AlwaysOnBytes(); total > AlwaysOnMaxBytes {
        problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf(
            "always-on c1..c4 byte count %d exceeds cap %d (every token here competes with the agent's output budget)",
            total, AlwaysOnMaxBytes,
        ))
    }

    combinedAlwaysOn := h.SystemPrompt + "\n" + h.Guardrails
    for dirName, skill := range h.Skills {
        if skill.Name != dirName {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("%s frontmatter name %q must match directory name %q", skill.RelPath, skill.Name, dirName))
        }
        if strings.TrimSpace(skill.Description) == "" {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("%s must include a non-empty description in YAML frontmatter", skill.RelPath))
        }
        if !strings.Contains(combinedAlwaysOn, dirName) {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("skill %q is never referenced in systemprompt.md or guardrails.md; add a trigger line naming `%s`", dirName, dirName))
        }
    }
    // ...
}

There are two very critical engineering details here:

  1. Mandatory Skill Trigger Reference Check: If Harness² adds a skill in skills/jp_card_ocr/SKILL.md but forgets to write when to trigger jp_card_ocr in systemprompt.md or guardrails.md, Validate() will directly report an error and intercept it, avoiding the creation of "Orphan Skills" that will never be called.
  2. Node-Level Dynamic Skill Matching (MatchSkills + ComposeNodePrompt): When the Graph Workflow executes VisionOCRNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ApplyEditNode, QueryIntentNode, or EmailDraftNode, it only injects c6 skills related to that node and automatically attaches adk.harness.skills and adk.harness.always_on_bytes attributes to the OpenTelemetry Span: 
// composeHarnessPrompt enriches a node's base prompt with the active Harness² c1..c8 tree
// and records the active harness metadata onto the node's OpenTelemetry span.
func composeHarnessPrompt(span trace.Span, nodeName, basePrompt, taskInput string) (string, *harness.Harness) {
    h := harness.LoadActive()
    composed, skills := h.ComposeNodePrompt(nodeName, basePrompt, taskInput)
    if span != nil {
        span.SetAttributes(
            AttrHarnessRoot.String(h.RootDir),
            AttrHarnessAlwaysOnBytes.Int(h.AlwaysOnBytes()),
        )
        if len(skills) > 0 {
            span.SetAttributes(AttrHarnessSkills.StringSlice(skills))
        }
    }
    return composed, h
}

We can directly use the CLI to verify the always-on byte count and structural validity of harness/base:

$ go run ./cmd/harness-runner --validate-only --harness-dir=harness/base
OK (1599 always-on bytes)

4. Summary and Next Article Preview

In this article (Part 1), we completed the goals of Issue #16:

  1. Gained a deep understanding of how Google Research Harness² (arXiv:2610.14224) automatically evolves Agent capabilities through a c1..c8 editable file tree and two-level recursion (Task-level Propose-Probe-Compose + Harnessing-level Experience Reflector), without recompiling the main program or bloating the always-on context.
  2. Inventoried the architectural bottlenecks of Phase 1~5 where prompts and normalization logic were hardcoded in the Go binary.
  3. Implemented internal/harness/harness.go and harness/base/, allowing the 13 nodes of the ADK 2.0 Go Graph Workflow to support dynamic mounting of the c1..c8 equipment tree via LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR.

With a hot-reloadable c1..c8 equipment tree in place, the next article [Agent Platform in Action (8)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 2): Turning Phase 4 Eval Datasets and Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into LineCardAdapter will enter Issue #17: revealing why we need to encapsulate Phase 4 test sets and Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into a LineCardAdapter, and how the "Zero-Leakage Barrier" prevents the AI optimizer from cheating!

title: How I Measure a Server: The Knee, Percentiles That Lie, and Little's Law
description:
I did not trust latency numbers until I could make a server slow down on purpose. This post is what came out of three small experiments in my system-design-challenges repo. Each one changed how I read a metric I reach for every day. The code is real, and the numbers below are what the scripts actually measured on this machine, not what I hoped they would be.

Side note: this is the first challenge in a repo I keep for hands-on system design. It starts with the tools for measuring a service before it moves on to architecture, storage, and distributed systems. I work through it by running things, not just reading about them.

The setup: one worker, about 10 ms of work per request

The server is deliberately boring. Every request does roughly 10 ms of CPU-bound work in a spin loop that blocks the event loop, so the whole thing behaves like a single worker: a request that arrives while another is being served waits its turn.

// server.js: a tiny server with a simulated service time
const SERVICE_MS = Number(process.env.SERVICE_MS ?? 10);
const SLOW_CHANCE = Number(process.env.SLOW_CHANCE ?? 0);
const SLOW_MS = Number(process.env.SLOW_MS ?? 0);

function busyWork(ms) {
  const end = performance.now() + ms;
  while (performance.now() < end) { /* spin: this loop is the work */ }
}

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (random() < SLOW_CHANCE) await sleep(SLOW_MS);
  busyWork(...);
  res.end("ok\n");
});

One worker doing 10 ms of work has a rough capacity of 1000 / 10 = 100 requests per second. Call that an estimate. Scheduling, random service times, and bursts change the measured result, and that uncertainty is the whole point of the first experiment.

Big word: utilisation. The fraction of a worker's capacity that is currently demanded, usually written as a percentage. At 70 requests per second, this server is about 70% busy.

Experiment 1: the knee, or where a queue stops being polite

The obvious way to load-test a server is to send more traffic and watch the average. The problem is that the average is the last number to admit something is wrong.

As incoming work approaches the server's maximum rate, a queue starts forming before every request becomes slow. The high percentiles move first, because the most recent arrivals wait the longest. The experiment ramps the request rate and looks for the point where tail latency bends sharply upward. The knee.

request/s p99
60 69.4 ms
70 157.6 ms

At 70 requests per second the server is about 70% busy. Not full. Yet the slowest 1% of requests have already more than doubled to 157.6 ms. The M/M/1 estimate W = 1 / (mu - lambda) gives 33.3 ms average at that rate, and the measured mean tracked it early on, then drifted as the run got noisier near the knee.

Where the easy answer is not the full truth: people say "a server is fine until it's 100% busy, then you scale it." Not really. A queue forms well before that, and the tail feels it first. The knee is usually a fair bit below full utilisation. Your headroom is yours to choose; the knee just tells you where the comfortable margin ends.

Experiment 2: percentiles that lie, or how fan-out magnifies a small problem

A mean is one number: add every latency, divide by the count. It is easy to compute and easy to quote. It is also very good at hiding the rare, slow call that decides what a real user experiences. Percentiles show the boundary the slower traffic actually crosses: p95 is the latency that 95% of requests meet or beat.

Fan-out makes the problem worse, because a page is only as fast as its slowest parallel dependency. Every extra call is another chance to pick up a slow one. This experiment gave each dependency a 2% chance of taking 200 ms, then drove pages at 40 requests per second with increasing fan-out.

calls per page mean p95 slow pages observed
1 4.0 ms 1.5 ms ~2%
20 63.1 ms 202.1 ms 31%

Read the mean column and the load test "sounds manageable": 4 ms to 63 ms. Read the p95 and the story inverts: 1.5 ms to 202.1 ms. And observe that about 31% of 20-call pages hit the 200 ms wall. The prediction 1 - (1 - 0.02)^20 ≈ 33% matches what the run observed. A 2% dependency, fanned out 20 ways, becomes a roughly one-in-three page failure.

Pros and cons of averaging. A mean gives you one stable number you can graph and compare. Its cost is that it averages away the rare slow calls that shape actual experience. Useful for spotting drift over time; dangerous as your only performance number.

Experiment 3: Little's law as a reality check on your own measurements

Little's law says the average number of requests in the system is L = lambda times W: the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system. The interesting bit is that it holds for almost any stable queue, so it works as a consistency check on your measurements.

rate/s L measured lambda x W M/M/1 L
50 0.95 0.95 0.89
70 2.06 2.06 2.00
80 3.50 3.50 3.41
90 9.11 9.11 6.94

Measured L matched lambda x W across all four rows. The M/M/1 prediction stayed close at low load and drifted farthest at 90 requests per second, which is exactly where you would expect the classroom model to wobble.

Big word: Little's law. The relationship L = lambda x W between requests in flight, arrival rate, and time in the system. Because it holds for almost any stable system, when your measured L and your lambda x W stop agreeing, something is off with your measurement or your model. Investigate.

What I take away

  1. Watch percentiles, not just the average. The mean hid the real damage in both the knee and the fan-out experiments.
  2. Account for fan-out in your tail budget. A 2% dependency turns into a 31% page failure when it is 20 calls wide.
  3. Queues grow before the server looks bad. Latency is the earliest signal of saturation; the knee marks the end of comfortable headroom.
  4. Use Little's law as a sanity check. When L and lambda x W stop agreeing, trust the mismatch and dig in.

Things that may matter, with no over-claiming on my part: these are finite runs on one machine. Event-loop scheduling, a seeded random source, and the load generator all add noise, and the M/M/1 formulas are a teaching model, not a promise. Treat the charts as tendencies and the relationships as intuition, not as a spec you can copy into a capacity plan.

Try it yourself

Clone system-design-challenges and run node challenges/challenge-1-measure-a-server/part-1-the-knee/knee.js, part-2-percentiles-lie/tail.js, and part-3-littles-law/little.js from the repo root. npm test from the root runs the checks. The repo grows module by module, and the numbers on your machine will be a little different, which is part of the lesson.

title: What Is React?
description:
What Is React?

React is a JavaScript library used to build user interfaces (UI).

It is mainly used to create interactive and dynamic web applications.

For example, websites and applications often have:

  • Buttons
  • Forms
  • Navigation bars
  • Product cards
  • User profiles
  • Interactive pages

React helps developers build and manage these user interfaces more easily.

Why Do We Use React?

When building a large website using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, managing the code can become difficult.

React helps by dividing the user interface into smaller, reusable parts called components.

For example:

Website
   │
   ├── Navbar
   ├── Product List
   │      ├── Product Card
   │      ├── Product Card
   │      └── Product Card
   │
   └── Footer

Each part can be created as a separate component.

What Are Components?

A component is a reusable piece of the user interface.

For example:

function Welcome() {
    return <h1>Hello, World!</h1>;
}

This creates a simple React component.

We can use components to build different parts of a website.

React Uses JSX

React commonly uses JSX.

JSX allows us to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript.

Example:

function App() {
    return <h1>Hello, React!</h1>;
}

Although it looks similar to HTML, JSX is written inside JavaScript.

React Can Update the UI

React helps update the user interface when data changes.

For example, if a user clicks a button and a value changes, React can update the relevant part of the screen.

This makes it useful for building interactive applications.

Popular Uses of React

React can be used to build:

  • E-commerce websites
  • Social media applications
  • Dashboards
  • Portfolio websites
  • Single-page applications
  • Interactive web applications

title: How to Learn CSS Flexbox and Grid (and Stop Guessing Which One to Use)
description:
For about two years my approach to CSS layout was trial and error. I'd type display: flex, add justify-content: center, watch nothing happen, swap it for align-items: center, and keep toggling properties in DevTools until the box landed roughly where I wanted. It worked, sort of. I just couldn't have told you why.

What fixed it wasn't another cheat sheet. It was learning a few ideas properly, in the right order, and then reviewing them until they stopped leaking out of my head. Here's the order I'd follow if I were starting again.

Learn the one idea that explains Flexbox

Flexbox has a main axis and a cross axis. That's most of it.

flex-direction sets the main axis. By default it's row, so the main axis runs left to right. justify-content moves items along the main axis. align-items moves them along the cross axis.

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between; /* along the row */
  align-items: center;            /* up and down */
}

The reason I kept mixing up justify-content and align-items is that I'd memorized them as "horizontal" and "vertical". That's only true for rows. Switch to flex-direction: column and they swap. Once I stopped thinking in left/right and started thinking in main/cross, the guessing mostly stopped.

Then learn what flex: 1 actually means

The second thing that confused me was sizing. flex: 1 is shorthand for three properties:

.item {
  flex-grow: 1;
  flex-shrink: 1;
  flex-basis: 0%;
}

flex-basis is the starting size. flex-grow says how much of the leftover space an item takes. flex-shrink says how much it gives up when space runs out. If you've ever had an item refuse to shrink below its text, the fix is usually min-width: 0, because flex items default to min-width: auto. That one line has saved me more time than anything else in this post.

Grid is for two directions at once

Here's the rule I use now, and it's simple enough to remember. Flexbox is for laying things out in one direction, a row or a column. Grid is for rows and columns together.

A nav bar, a row of buttons, a card's header with a title on the left and an icon on the right: Flexbox. A page layout with a sidebar, header and main area, or a gallery where cards should line up in both directions: Grid.

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

That one declaration gives you a responsive gallery with no media queries. I'd suggest learning fr, repeat(), minmax() and gap before anything else in Grid. Named grid areas are nice too, and they read almost like a picture of the layout:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main";
}

You can skip subgrid, grid-auto-flow: dense and explicit line numbering until a real layout asks for them.

Practice on things you'd actually build

Games help. Flexbox Froggy and Grid Garden are free and take an evening each. They're good for the first pass, but I forgot most of what I learned from them within a few weeks because I never used it on anything real.

What worked better was rebuilding layouts from sites I use. Pick a page, open it in DevTools with the layout overlays turned on (both Chrome and Firefox show Flexbox and Grid overlays), and try to recreate one section from scratch without looking at their CSS. Then compare. Doing this with five or six sections taught me more than the games did.

Josh Comeau's interactive guides on Flexbox and Grid are also worth reading once you've struggled a bit. They make far more sense after you've hit the problems they explain.

The part nobody talks about: forgetting it

My real problem wasn't understanding. I'd watch a good video on minmax(), get it completely, and three weeks later be back to guessing because I hadn't touched a grid since. CSS layout is a thing you use in bursts, so it fades between projects.

So I started reviewing. I keep a short list of the ideas that tripped me up (main vs cross axis, min-width: 0, auto-fill vs auto-fit, when to reach for Grid) and look at it again after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it's boring, and it works.

I ended up building Recl partly because of this. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "CSS", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. If you'd rather not use an app, a plain notes file you reread on a calendar reminder gets you most of the way there. What matters is seeing it again before it's gone.

A one-week plan

If you want something concrete:

  1. Day one: Flexbox Froggy, then rebuild a nav bar with Flexbox.
  2. Day two: build a card with a header, body and footer using flex-direction: column, and make the footer stick to the bottom.
  3. Day three: Grid Garden, then make a responsive gallery with repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...)).
  4. Day four: build a sidebar layout with grid-template-areas.
  5. Day five: rebuild one section of a real site you like, with DevTools overlays on.
  6. Weekend: write down the three things that confused you most, and review them next week.

You'll still open DevTools and fiddle. Everyone does. But you'll know which property you're fiddling with and why it moves things the way it does.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: Node.js Example OpenAI GPT API Integration for Product Text Summarization
description:
The hard part of using a Node.js example to integrate the OpenAI GPT API for text summarization is not producing one short paragraph. It is keeping the catalog pipeline portable when a provider changes its client library, authentication model, or output behavior. My default is to isolate summarization behind a small adapter, use a chat-completion interface for the first useful result, and keep the input contract provider-neutral.

For a team already standardized on OpenAI, the direct OpenAI API is the shortest path. For a team testing several vendors, Infrai is a reasonable integration layer to try because its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is required. That matters when adding a capability should involve inspecting one contract rather than learning another SDK. It is a fit for the adapter boundary, not a reason to pretend every model is interchangeable.

What does portability require in a catalog pipeline?

Start with the data boundary. A catalog record should hand the model a bounded description and a precise instruction: preserve factual attributes, remove sales language, and return a concise summary. The application should own truncation or chunking for long descriptions; letting an SDK silently decide what to drop makes later provider comparisons hard to interpret.

The output should be treated as generated text, not as the source of truth for price, dimensions, or compliance claims. Store the original description beside the summary, record the provider and model selected, and validate the result before publishing it. This is more operational work than calling a model once. It is also what makes a migration measurable.

The useful first test is deliberately small: one record, one bounded prompt, one summary, and a saved request identifier. I initially thought the provider choice would dominate the design. The adapter contract does. If the rest of the catalog service knows a vendor-specific message shape, portability has already been lost.

Keep it boring.

The first failure mode I test is silent truncation: a 12,000-character bound can remove a specification table, while a 45-word output limit can hide a required attribute. I keep those numbers in application configuration, preserve the original description, and compare a direct result with a chunked result before changing providers. That is a concrete boundary, not a benchmark claim.

Which integration path reaches a useful summary fastest?

Option Credentials and setup SDK surface Boundary
OpenAI API One OpenAI API key and the OpenAI client pattern A focused chat-completion call Best when the catalog team already owns this provider and wants the fewest moving parts
Anthropic API A separate provider credential and its messages-oriented client pattern A different request and response contract Good for teams willing to maintain a second adapter and evaluate its output separately
Google Vertex AI Google Cloud project and platform authentication Cloud-platform configuration plus model invocation Useful when identity, governance, and deployment already live in Google Cloud
Infrai One Infrai key for the unified surface A plain REST surface with public discovery and runnable examples Useful when provider portability and capability discovery outweigh direct-vendor simplicity

These are different operational choices, not four interchangeable model names. Direct OpenAI has the cleanest match to the question this article starts from: authenticate with an OpenAI key, instruct a chat model to summarize, and tune temperature and max_tokens. Anthropic and Vertex AI are credible alternatives, but each adds a distinct credential or client contract that the adapter must absorb. Infrai reduces that particular discovery friction across a broad surface: its live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with schemas and runnable examples exposed per capability.

The trade-off is worth stating plainly. A unified layer adds one more boundary to understand, and a direct provider may be preferable when a team needs provider-specific controls or the specialist's native feature set. Portability is valuable only if the boundary preserves the controls the workload actually needs.

How should a Node.js service integrate OpenAI GPT API text summarization?

The following example keeps the provider-specific work in one function. A Node.js service can use axios or the openai npm package against the same contract; this Python sample keeps the HTTP method, URL, headers, status handling, and retry behavior visible. The model name is a configuration choice; do not treat it as a promise that every model has identical context or output behavior.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


def summarize_description(description: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    bounded_description = description[:12000]
    prompt = (
        "Summarize this product description in 45 words or fewer. "
        "Keep factual product attributes, remove promotional claims, and "
        "do not invent missing information.\n\n"
        f"Product description:\n{bounded_description}"
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions",
                headers={
                    "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                    "Content-Type": "application/json",
                },
                json={
                    "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash",
                    "messages": [
                        {
                            "role": "system",
                            "content": "You produce factual e-commerce catalog summaries.",
                        },
                        {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
                    ],
                    "temperature": 0.2,
                    "max_tokens": 180,
                },
                timeout=60,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429:
                if attempt == 3:
                    response.raise_for_status()
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
                time.sleep(delay + random.random())
                continue
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"Summarization failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: "
                    f"{response.text}"
                )
            content = response.json().get("choices", [{}])[0].get("message", {}).get("content")
            if not content:
                raise RuntimeError("The provider returned no summary text")
            return content.strip()
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise
            time.sleep((2**attempt) + random.random())

    raise RuntimeError("Summarization retry loop ended unexpectedly")

This is intentionally not a bulk-ingestion worker. For long descriptions, split on meaningful boundaries, summarize chunks, then summarize the chunk summaries; otherwise a truncation rule can silently remove the specifications that customers care about. For a large catalog, queue the records, make the consumer idempotent, and retain the original input so a prompt or provider change can be replayed.

Where does the unified layer help, and where does it stop?

The strongest argument for the unified layer here is integration friction. Its API is self-describing, and the discovery result includes request schemas, response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples. That lets an engineer inspect a capability before installing a vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is a consistent credential and REST boundary while the catalog service experiments with providers, instead of distributing provider keys and client conventions through every worker.

I would recommend Infrai to a catalog team that expects to test multiple AI providers and wants discovery plus a runnable request to be part of the integration workflow. I would choose direct OpenAI for a single-provider implementation whose main requirement is the OpenAI chat-completion contract, and I would choose a specialist when its native controls or model behavior are a hard requirement.

The capability boundary also matters. Audio transcription is listed but currently unavailable; real-time voice session keys are pending and limited to the western region; there is no dedicated moderation endpoint, so text or image moderation needs a chat model with a JSON schema fallback; and image upscaling is limited to Lanczos. None of those blocks catalog summarization, but they are reasons to keep capability selection explicit instead of assuming the unified surface covers every adjacent workload.

A controlled rollout is the portability test

Begin with a small evaluation set containing short descriptions, long descriptions, missing attributes, and aggressively promotional copy. Compare summaries for factual retention, length, and unacceptable invention. Keep the prompt stable while changing providers; otherwise a provider result and a prompt change become one indistinguishable experiment.

Then ship the adapter behind a feature flag. Record the chosen provider, model, latency, and failure class, but do not publish generated text before validation. A 429 should delay and retry; a malformed or empty response should be visible as a failed record, not converted into a blank catalog field. The operational detail is unglamorous. It is also where portability either survives or disappears.

For one product record, that means retaining the raw description, the normalized prompt version, the provider name, the model name, the response text, and the validation result as separate fields. If the response is too short, contains a missing required attribute, or arrives after a retry, the worker should preserve the response and mark the record for review rather than overwrite the last accepted summary. If a provider is unavailable, the adapter can route the next attempt according to an explicit policy, but the policy must be visible in the record so a later comparison does not confuse provider selection with prompt quality. I would also keep the chunking decision beside the input: a single bounded request and a multi-chunk reduction are different transformations, even when they produce similar prose. That small amount of bookkeeping is the difference between a portable pipeline and a collection of irreproducible calls.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the capability manifest and inspect the available contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • OpenAI Batch API guide
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic Messages API
  • Google Vertex AI generative AI documentation

Sources

  • Infrai AI-readable capability manifest
  • OpenAI Batch API guide
