title: A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data
description:
A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data

Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. A CI job creates an inbox, a verification message arrives, a test reads the link, and the inbox is forgotten. In practice, those messages can contain names, account identifiers, reset tokens, invite URLs, and enough product detail to reconstruct a user journey.

The useful question is not “Which disposable inbox should we use?” It is “How much email data does this test actually need, for how long, and who can see it?” That is a privacy budget: a small, explicit limit on exposure that still lets engineers diagnose failures.

This framing is helpful for teams building web applications because it joins Privacy and Security with maintainability. The cheapest data to protect is the data we never retain.

Why email test data deserves a budget

Test email has a strange lifecycle. It starts as synthetic data, becomes a delivery artifact, then turns into a log attachment or a screenshot. Each copy has a different audience and retention period. A mailbox that is safe for a local smoke test may be a poor fit for a shared staging environment.

I use four questions to set the budget:

  1. Content: Does the test need the whole message, or only a token and delivery timestamp?
  2. Lifetime: Is the message needed for seconds, one CI run, or a week of investigation?
  3. Reach: Which people and systems can read the inbox, traces, logs, or artifacts?
  4. Reuse: Can one inbox accidentally reveal another test's message?

If the answer is vague, the data budget is already too large. The implementation get messy when a test stores a complete email simply because the assertion was easier to write that way.

Define the budget before choosing a tool

For a normal verification test, a reasonable default might be:

  • one generated address per test or isolated worker;
  • one expected message, with a bounded wait;
  • a retention period no longer than the CI run;
  • logs containing message ID, subject hash, and timing, but not the body;
  • a failure artifact containing a redacted excerpt only when the test fails.

This is not a universal policy. An OAuth flow may need a link target, while a rendering test needs HTML and CSS. The point is to name the minimum capability instead of granting an entire persistent mailbox.

Teams also need a vocabulary for search terms and operator mistakes. A developer may type tempail while looking for a temporary inbox, but that typo should never become a reason to broaden a production allowlist or retain more data. Small details like this prevent a test utility from quietly becoming an identity system.

A practical retention and access model

Separate the data plane from the evidence plane:

  • Data plane: the temporary inbox and message body, accessible only to the test worker.
  • Evidence plane: a small JSON receipt with correlation ID, delivery state, elapsed time, and a redacted failure reason.

The receipt should be enough to answer “Did delivery happen?” and “Where did it wait?” without answering “What did the user receive?” If debugging needs more, make the expansion deliberate, time-limited, and visible in the run record.

For flaky tests, Playwright traces for flaky email tests show why a timeline can be more useful than saving every message. The same principle applies to scheduled jobs: self-explaining cron runs make the outcome inspectable without preserving unrelated inputs.

Make failures useful without keeping everything

A test harness can emit a compact receipt like this:

{
  "correlation_id": "ci-1842-verify",
  "mailbox_scope": "worker-7",
  "message_seen": true,
  "delivery_ms": 842,
  "token_checked": true,
  "body_retained": false
}

The message_seen and delivery_ms fields help distinguish a provider delay from an application bug. token_checked confirms the assertion without printing the token. When the test fail, the harness can attach a redacted subject and the last polling event, then delete the inbox as part of cleanup.

Cleanup should be defensive, not aspirational. Put it in a finally block, make deletion idempotent, and record cleanup failure separately from the original assertion. A small ledger make retries understandable: created, message observed, assertion passed, deleted. It also makes a leak visible when deletion did not happen.

Checklist for the next review

Ask these questions in the next email-test review:

  • Does each parallel test have an isolated mailbox scope?
  • Are verification tokens absent from ordinary logs and traces?
  • Is the default retention shorter than the investigation window?
  • Can an engineer diagnose timing without opening the message body?
  • Does cleanup run after assertion failures and cancellations?
  • Are screenshots and CI artifacts covered by the same policy?

The goal is not to make testing slower or less observable. It is to make observability proportional. A privacy budget gives the team a shared tradeoff: retain the smallest evidence that explains the behavior, and require a reason before retaining anything more.

That small boundary usually improves reliability too. Fewer shared inboxes means fewer cross-test races, fewer misleading retries, and less uncertainty about which message belongs to which run. The test become easier to trust because its evidence has a clear owner and an intentional lifetime.

title: Where is this month's Azure cost heading? A month-end estimate you can do by hand
description:
Halfway through the month, someone asks: "Where will we land?" The invoice will not tell you for weeks, and Cost Management's built-in forecast is a line on a chart that is hard to explain to a team. Here is a month-end estimate you can do by hand in a spreadsheet, explain in one sentence, and check against your budget. Then how we automated it.

1. Get the recorded daily cost

In the Azure portal, open Cost Management > Cost analysis for the subscription, choose the Daily costs view for the current month, and download it as CSV. You now have one row per day with its cost.

Two things to know before you use it:

  • Cost arrives a day or two late. The last day or two in the file are usually incomplete. Find the latest day you trust; call it the latest recorded day. Everything after it is "remaining".
  • Keep one currency. If your scope is billed in more than one currency, do the estimate per currency. Adding USD and EUR without a rate gives a number that means nothing.

2. Average the latest seven days

Take the latest seven days with recorded cost and average them. Seven days covers a full week, so weekend dips and weekday peaks cancel out. If the month has fewer than seven recorded days, average what you have.

Example: the latest seven days cost 120, 118, 131, 125, 90, 88, 128. The average is 114.29 a day.

3. Add a trend once you have two weeks

With 14 or more recorded days, compare the average of the latest seven days with the average of the seven before them. If the earlier week averaged 107.14, the daily cost rose by about 7.14 a week, or about 1.02 a day. Add that daily step to each day ahead: day one is 115.31, day two 116.33, and so on. Never let a day go below zero.

Without a trend, a cost that is climbing steadily is underestimated every time.

4. Add up the month

  • Recorded so far: the sum of the recorded days this month.
  • Forecast for the remaining days: the sum of your forecast days, from the day after the latest recorded day to the last day of the month.
  • Forecast to month end: the two added together.

Then put two numbers next to it:

  • Your monthly budget, in the same currency: the forecast as a share of it, and how much over or under.
  • Last month's recorded cost for the same subscriptions: the change as an amount and a percentage.

5. Put a band around it, and say what it is

Add 10% either side of each forecast day and sum again, with the recorded cost in front. That gives a low and a high month-end figure. Be clear with your team about what this is: not a probability, and not a confidence interval. It shows how far a 10% miss on every remaining day would move the month. Early in the month the band is wide, because most of the month is still forecast; near the end it is narrow.

The automated way

(I build CostGuard, an Azure cost tool sold on Azure Marketplace.) Its Forecast overview page automates this on the Pro plan: the cost recorded so far plus a Baseline forecast for the remaining days, made from the latest seven days with a daily trend once fourteen days are recorded, refreshed about once an hour, held against the budget of the scope and against last month.

It also says which subscriptions the forecast covers and which it leaves out, and why, so "Covers 2 of 4 subscriptions in scope" is never hidden inside a total. The day-by-day table shows the recorded days first, then a forecast amount for each remaining day.

Honest limits

  • It is an estimate from recorded cost, not a bill. The invoice can differ.
  • A seven-day average does not know about the batch job you plan for the 28th. A one-off spike in the last seven days also inflates it.
  • The band is fixed at 10% by the method; it does not measure how likely the forecast is.
  • Amounts in different currencies are never added or compared, and no exchange rate is applied.
  • In CostGuard, forecasting is a Pro feature; each subscription needs an active Baseline forecast scenario before it is covered. CostGuard only reads your Azure cost; nothing in Azure is changed.

The full walkthrough of the page, figure by figure:
https://hoshebartar.com/en/help/forecast-overview?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=kb-forecast-overview

How do you answer "where will we land this month": the portal forecast, a spreadsheet, or a gut feeling?

title: New Package Release
description:
Hey everyone!

I've been independently working on a TypeScript PostgreSQL database package called @oneunit/database, and I'm now preparing it for its first external release candidate.

The goal is to provide more than just a database query interface. It includes:
PostgreSQL query and model APIs
Connection pooling and transaction management
Schema and migration management
Multiple database sharding strategies
Distributed transactions (Two-Phase Commit)
Shard management and online resharding
Recovery mechanisms, health checks, and metrics

I've already completed extensive internal testing, including tests with multiple independent PostgreSQL instances and distributed transaction crash recovery.

Now I'd like to get feedback from developers who have experience with Node.js, TypeScript, or PostgreSQL.

I'm particularly interested in feedback about:
Installation and setup experience
API design and developer experience
Documentation clarity
Real-world integration issues
Bugs, unexpected behavior, and compatibility problems

I'm building this project independently, so getting feedback from other developers would mean a lot and help me improve the package before its stable release.

You don't need to contribute code. Simply trying it out and sharing your experience would be extremely helpful.

Package: @oneunit/database

GitHub: https://github.com/oneunitjs/database

Documentation: https://github.com/oneunitjs/database/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md

This is an early release candidate, so it's not being presented as production-ready yet.

Thanks to anyone willing to take a look or share feedback!

title: Node Runs .ts Files Natively. Inside node_modules It Refuses, on Purpose
description:
• Book: TypeScript in Production
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You stop compiling. Your package's exports points straight at ./src/index.ts, every script in the monorepo runs with plain node, and the tests are green. Then someone installs the package from the registry, runs their app, and Node stops with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING.

No flag turns it off. The Node.js TypeScript docs give the reason in one sentence: "To discourage package authors from publishing packages written in TypeScript, Node.js refuses to handle TypeScript files inside folders under a node_modules path."

The refusal makes sense once you see how little Node does to a .ts file.

How Node runs a .ts file without compiling it

Type stripping landed in v22.6.0, became the default in v23.6.0 and v22.18.0, and was marked stable in v25.2.0 and v24.12.0. Current releases of every LTS line on the Node releases page (22, 24 and 26, with v26.13.0 the newest LTS release listed there at the time of writing) have it on by default. You opt out with --no-strip-types.

The mechanism is deliberately dumb. Node doesn't compile anything. It finds the TypeScript syntax and overwrites it with spaces. This is the example from the node:module docs:

import { stripTypeScriptTypes } from 'node:module';
const code = 'const a: number = 1;';
const strippedCode = stripTypeScriptTypes(code);
console.log(strippedCode);
// Prints: const a         = 1;

The = 1 is still in the column where you typed it. An interface that spans twelve lines becomes twelve blank lines. Because nothing moves, a stack trace points at the right line of your .ts file, and the docs note that "source maps are unnecessary for correct line numbers in stack traces; and Node.js does not generate them." The parser doing this is Amaro, a wrapper around SWC's TypeScript parser compiled to WebAssembly.

Being dumb has consequences, and they're all in the docs. There is no type checking. Node ignores tsconfig.json, so paths aliases don't work. Imports need their real extension (./user.ts, not ./user). Type-only imports must say import type, or Node treats them as values and fails at runtime. .tsx is unsupported.


Type stripping removes the annotations and leaves the gaps, so every line and column stays where it was.

The syntax whitespace can't erase

If stripping is "replace with spaces", anything that needs Node to write new JavaScript is out. The Node docs list the main cases: enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases. Hitting one throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

The reason is visible in what tsc emits for them. An enum is a real object at runtime, so the compiler has to generate the code that builds it. A parameter property is shorthand for an assignment the compiler writes into the constructor. Neither exists in your source as JavaScript, so blanking characters can't produce it.

// Rejected by type stripping
class User {
  constructor(public name: string) {}
}

enum Role { Admin, Viewer }

The erasable versions say the same thing in syntax that's already JavaScript once the types are gone:

class User {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const Role = { Admin: 0, Viewer: 1 } as const;
type Role = (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role];

You don't want to find these one runtime crash at a time. TypeScript 5.8 added erasableSyntaxOnly for exactly this: with it on, tsc errors on enums, namespaces and modules with runtime code, parameter properties, import = and export =. The tsconfig reference adds <number>value-style assertions to the list. The Node docs recommend TypeScript 5.8 or newer with erasableSyntaxOnly, verbatimModuleSyntax and rewriteRelativeImportExtensions turned on.

There used to be an escape hatch. --experimental-transform-types arrived in v22.7.0 and was removed in v26.0.0, along with the transform mode of stripTypeScriptTypes. On Node 26 the built-in path is strip-only. For full TypeScript, the docs point you to a third-party runner such as tsx.

Reproduce the refusal (your monorepo hides it)

Here's a two-package npm workspace where the library ships raw TypeScript:

greet-demo/
├── package.json          "workspaces": ["packages/*"]
└── packages/
    ├── greet-ts/
    │   ├── package.json
    │   └── src/index.ts
    └── app/
        ├── package.json
        └── main.ts

The library's manifest points exports at source:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": "./src/index.ts"
}

// packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `hello, ${name}`;
}

// packages/app/main.ts (app has "type": "module")
import { greet } from "greet-ts";
console.log(greet("ada"));

Run npm install at the root, then node packages/app/main.ts, and it should run. That's because npm symlinks each workspace into node_modules. By default Node dereferences symlinks and uses the module's "real path" as its identity. As Jake Bailey points out in nodejs/typescript#14, the "is this in node_modules" check looks at that real path. So Node sees packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts, with no node_modules anywhere in it, and strips it happily.

Your consumers don't get a symlink. They get a copy. Pack the library the way the registry would and install the tarball somewhere else:

cd ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts
npm pack
mkdir ~/code/consumer && cd ~/code/consumer
npm init -y
npm install ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts/greet-ts-1.0.0.tgz

Copy main.ts over as main.mts (.mts always runs as ESM, whatever npm init wrote into type) and run node main.mts. The library's index.ts now lives at node_modules/greet-ts/src/index.ts. That is the case the errors reference describes for ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING: "Type stripping is not supported for files descendant of a node_modules directory." I haven't run this exact repro myself; the error code and its trigger come straight from those docs. npm's install-links setting, which packs file: dependencies (not workspaces) instead of symlinking them, is another way to get the same copy-not-link setup in CI.


A symlinked workspace package resolves outside node_modules and runs. The same files installed from a tarball sit inside node_modules and are refused.

Why Node says no

The request to lift the restriction is nodejs/typescript#14, and it was closed as not planned. The issue's author makes a fair case: Bun, Deno and JSR already run or host TypeScript source, so Node holding out alone won't stop the trend. Replies in the thread explain the other side. Matteo Collina wrote that "TypeScript is designed so that only .d.ts files are shared across projects." Jake Bailey raised the problem that a published .ts file gets type-checked under the consumer's tsconfig, not the author's. Jordan Harband added that, as he understood it, the TypeScript team opposes the idea too, because it would mean they could never make breaking changes to TypeScript's syntax again.

TypeScript's own compiler options guide shows the type-checking cost. A separate outDir is "necessary for libraries that publish their input files. Otherwise, extension substitution will cause the library's consumers to load the library's .ts files instead of .d.ts files, causing type errors and performance problems." Raw .ts in node_modules hands the consumer's compiler your source and your strictness assumptions.

If you control both ends, there is a workaround. One commenter in the thread shares a loader built on module.registerHooks() and stripTypeScriptTypes(), both "release candidate" stability. That loader calls stripTypeScriptTypes() in transform mode, which Node 26 removed, so on current Node the same idea would have to use the default strip mode and handle erasable syntax only. That fits an internal app. It isn't something to ask the users of a public package to install.

What your package still ships

Your own scripts and tests can run the .ts files directly. The thing you publish is still compiled JavaScript plus declarations. One tsconfig covers both, combining the Node recommendations with the library settings from the TypeScript guide:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

rewriteRelativeImportExtensions (TypeScript 5.7) is what lets one source tree serve both: you write import { x } from "./x.ts", Node runs it as-is, and tsc rewrites it to ./x.js in dist. Then the manifest points at the build output:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"],
  "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json" }
}

Key order matters in conditional exports: "earlier entries have higher priority," and the types condition "should always be included first." Node doesn't type-check, so keep a tsc --noEmit step in CI.

JSR: the registry that compiles for you

JSR is the one registry where publishing TypeScript source is the expected path. It "supports and encourages publishing TypeScript source code rather than pairs of .js + .d.ts files." The catch is what reaches Node. Through JSR's npm compatibility layer, "this source code is transpiled to JavaScript," and .d.ts files "are generated for all TypeScript files." A Node user who runs npx jsr add, or installs with pnpm 10.9+ or Yarn 4.9+, gets JavaScript in node_modules.

That's also why JSR enforces its "slow types" rule on exported functions, classes and variables: explicit types are what let it generate declarations for the npm layer.

If this was useful

Getting a package from "it runs in my repo" to "it runs in yours" is most of what TypeScript in Production covers: tsconfig choices, build tools, monorepos, exports maps, dual ESM/CJS and publishing to JSR. If your team has started running .ts directly and is wondering what still needs a build, that book is the one to grab.

It's the fifth book in The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you're coming from the JVM or PHP, swap in book 3 or 4 for those. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work, which, if you read this far, is probably you.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: Why I don't automatically retry timed-out AI video requests
description:
A request times out. The obvious next step is to try again.

For a video generation request, that can be an expensive guess. The provider may already be rendering the first video. You just didn't receive its task ID.

I'm working on AI Effect Studio, where people choose an effect, upload photos, and get a short video. The generation backend has to deal with this gap between sending a paid request and knowing what happened to it.

Here's how the current implementation handles it, including the part that still needs manual review.

The timeout doesn't tell you enough

Imagine this sequence:

  1. Our server sends a generation request.
  2. The provider accepts it and starts work.
  3. The connection drops before our server receives the response.

From our side, the request failed. From the provider's side, there's a video being generated.

Sending the same payload again doesn't necessarily resume that work. Unless the provider supports a documented idempotency mechanism, it may create another paid task.

Exponential backoff changes when that second request happens. It doesn't make the second request safe.

Record the attempt before sending it

Each local job stores a submission timestamp separately from its provider task ID. Before calling the generation API, the worker records that it's about to submit.

That gives the next worker enough information to distinguish these cases:

What the job has What the worker does
No submission marker and no provider ID Claim the job, record the attempt, then submit
A provider ID Query that existing task
A submission marker but no provider ID Hold the job for support review
An output URL already recorded Continue processing or saving that video

The database updates are conditional, and processing uses a short lease so overlapping workers don't casually pick up the same job. The submission marker is checked and written in the database before the external call.

There's an awkward consequence here. If the worker crashes after writing the marker but before sending the request, the job also ends up waiting for review. It might never have reached the provider.

I accept that tradeoff for the expensive generation step. The marker prevents an automatic second submission, but it cannot prove that the first one happened. This is a conservative fallback, and it leaves some real work for support.

A provider-side idempotency key would be a better way to close that gap. A local timestamp can't give us exactly-once execution across two systems.

Retry the stage that failed

A video job keeps going after the model finishes. Depending on the effect, there's a soundtrack step, followed by saving the output to our own storage.

If storage fails, generating another video would be a costly way to retry a file transfer. The job records the source video URL so recovery can continue from the output it already has.

The soundtrack step has a different retry policy. It's much cheaper than generation, so it gets bounded retries. If those are exhausted, the delivery path can fall back to the silent footage. That is a product compromise: the user gets a video, but the soundtrack may be missing. The interface and product description need to make that possibility clear.

Credits need the same care. A confirmed generation failure restores the user's allowance. An ambiguous submission stays reserved while it's investigated, because a timeout alone doesn't tell us whether paid work is still running.

The question I use when reviewing these paths is pretty mundane: if this line runs twice, do we check the same work, or buy more work?

Polling an existing task, copying an existing output, and starting a fresh render deserve different answers. Putting all three behind one generic retry helper would hide the distinction I most need to see.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

Speakers including technology and human rights researcher Maya Woluczem and environmental and public health activist Hillary Flynt discussed the growing discontent among residents.

The main concerns are deals made in secret between local authorities and technology companies, building codes that hide construction plans, environmental and health risks, and the loss of control by the community itself. While some labor unions support data centers because of the temporary construction jobs, critics point out that permanent local jobs are limited.

title: How to Reconcile Logistics Platform Usage and Internal Counters for Billing in Go — 2026
description:
Bill from the platform's usage record; use your own counter to explain the bill. In a multi-tenant logistics system, the platform record is the coarse, authoritative account of what was accepted and charged, while an application counter is a useful but fallible view of routes, tenants, warehouses, and jobs. Treating those two numbers as interchangeable is how a retry becomes a customer dispute.

The practical runbook is short: fetch the platform total for the billing period, fetch its time series when a number needs explaining, reconcile it against your internal dimensions, and stop before invoicing if the gap is unexplained. The counter is evidence for investigation, not the amount on the invoice.

Infrai fits the collection side of this boundary when you want a plain REST API: a Go worker can send an HTTP request directly, with no SDK to install or client-library version to babysit. That is useful operationally because the same access pattern works across languages, while the platform record remains the thing you audit.

It also keeps the backend boundary to one key and one account bill. That does not replace reconciliation, but it removes a class of month-end work in which an operator has to map several service credentials and invoices back to the same logistics tenant before investigating a gap.

The operational advantage is one key, one bill for the platform boundary, not a claim that local counters become trustworthy.

The public discovery surface is another useful detail: an operator can inspect the documented capability surface without a key before wiring the reconciliation worker, which makes endpoint and schema review part of the change rather than an outage-time guess.

Use the first record.

Should platform usage records or internal counters drive the invoice?

Invoice from the platform record. Your own counter can drift when a worker crashes after accepting an event but before incrementing its metric, or when a retry increments a metric twice while the platform deduplicates the request. Those are normal failure modes in an event pipeline, not proof that the platform is wrong.

The distinction matters during an outage. A dashboard can show that a tenant produced 9,998 shipment-label events while the platform reports 10,000 billable events. The two missing events might be sitting in a queue, or they might have completed just before a process died. At 3am, the useful question is not “which graph looks cleaner?” It is “what page fired, and which record can the customer independently verify?”

Keep the internal dimensions anyway. The platform cannot see a warehouse ID, carrier, route, or your retry class unless you put that information into your own system. Those dimensions make a bill explainable and help locate the broken part of the pipeline. They do not turn an application counter into an authoritative ledger.

The distinction is the boundary.

Keep that boundary visible.

A small reconciliation worker in Go

The worker below retrieves the account usage total and its time series, retries a rate-limited request with exponential backoff, honors Retry-After when it is present, and fails loudly on other non-success responses. It deliberately treats the response as JSON data rather than inventing field names that the endpoint may change; the reconciliation service can persist the raw responses alongside its period, tenant mapping, and decision.

Set INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END before running it. The dates are sent as query parameters because the account usage API is the boundary for the platform record; validate the period against the billing calendar in the calling system.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func getUsage(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, path, start, end string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        u, err := url.Parse(path)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        q := u.Query()
        q.Set("start", start)
        q.Set("end", end)
        u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            if attempt == 4 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after retries: %s", strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    start := os.Getenv("USAGE_START")
    end := os.Getenv("USAGE_END")
    if key == "" || start == "" || end == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    usage, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    timeseries, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage/timeseries", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("usage=%s\ntimeseries=%s\n", usage, timeseries)
}

The decision after collection is intentionally boring. Store the platform payload as the invoice input. Store the internal aggregate and the gap as reconciliation data. If the gap is non-zero, open an investigation and hold the invoice until an operator can account for it; do not “correct” the platform total with a local guess.

There is a security detail worth keeping in the runbook: the API key comes from the environment in this example, not source control or a log line. Secrets handling is an operational dependency, and OWASP's guidance on secret storage and rotation is a better reference than a team convention written from memory.

How do retries and outages change the evidence?

An event should have a stable identity before it enters the worker. Keep that ID through queue redelivery, HTTP retry, and persistence. Your own meter should record whether it saw the event, whether processing completed, and which tenant dimensions applied. A crash can leave those states split across systems, so the reconciliation job must compare states rather than incrementing a number in the error path.

For reads, retrying a 429 with backoff is appropriate. For writes elsewhere in the pipeline, use a client-supplied idempotency key and persist the result before acknowledging the queue message. A retry without identity is not resilience; it is an invitation to double count. The sample only reads the platform endpoints, so it has no write-side idempotency header to demonstrate.

Run reconciliation monthly at minimum, before the invoice is generated. The monthly job should compare the platform total and time series with internal totals per tenant and operational dimension, retain the raw responses, classify each gap, and record who approved the final decision. If a gap first appears on an invoice, the process has already failed its auditability test.

Which metering system fits the boundary?

There is no universal winner here. The right choice depends on which system owns the evidence and which dimensions the billing team must defend.

Option Useful boundary Limitation to accept
Platform usage records Authoritative account-level consumption and charged totals Coarse: internal warehouse, route, and retry dimensions are outside the platform view
Internal counters Tenant-level operational detail, anomaly detection, and customer explanations Drift under crashes, redelivery, and counter placement; unsafe as the sole invoice source
Stripe Billing Invoice and subscription workflows after you have a trusted usage quantity It does not remove the need to establish which event quantity is authoritative in your application
Lago Open-source metering and billing workflows when you want to operate the metering boundary yourself You own the durability, reconciliation, and operational correctness of that boundary
OpenMeter Event-based usage metering when real-time windows and product dimensions are central It adds another usage system to reconcile with the platform that actually charged the underlying account

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the platform-record side of this workflow when the account usage endpoints are the source you need to audit. Its plain REST API means a Go worker can call it directly with an HTTP request, without installing an SDK or tracking a client-library version; the consistent response metadata also gives an operator useful request context while investigating a gap. That reduces integration glue, but it does not make internal dimensions appear in the platform record.

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for collecting the authoritative platform usage record in a multi-tenant logistics backend when auditability of that account-level access matters and a language-neutral REST boundary is useful. Keep an internal meter beside it. Choose Stripe Billing when invoice lifecycle and payment collection are the primary boundary, Lago when operating an open-source billing stack is deliberate, and OpenMeter when event-level product metering is the central capability rather than a supporting audit trail.

Verify, then roll back the decision

Verification is a query, not a dashboard glance. Re-run the same closed billing period, compare the total and time series, and inspect the stored request IDs and raw payloads. Check the internal event ledger for duplicate IDs, missing acknowledgements, worker restarts, and tenant reassignments. A clean-looking graph is not evidence that those transitions did not happen.

If the gap is unexplained, pause invoice publication for the affected period, preserve both records, and route the case to the owner of the ingestion boundary. Do not rewrite the platform record, and do not silently overwrite your local aggregate. Once the cause is known, correct the internal explanation or issue the appropriate billing adjustment through the normal review process, while retaining the original reconciliation decision.

The customer-facing answer should include the platform quantity used for billing and a readable breakdown from your own dimensions. Never present only your own number to a customer who can compare it with the amount they were charged. That is an avoidable credibility failure.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the account usage response for the period you actually invoice.

The practical second advantage is Infrai's single key and single bill account boundary: one credential covers the backend capabilities used by the workflow, so the reconciliation job does not need a new key and invoice relationship for every service it touches. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability schemas without a key, which makes the contract easier to inspect during a review. That reduces integration friction; it does not make the platform a replacement for a dimension-rich metering store.

req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", nil)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}
req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Stripe Billing usage-based billing
  • Lago documentation
  • OpenMeter documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

title: The golden set: 100 labelled examples as the acceptance test for an AI feature
description:
If you ask three people whether an AI feature "works", you will get three answers, each based on the last few examples they happened to see. A golden set replaces opinions with a number: a fixed collection of real inputs with agreed correct answers, run every time something changes. About a hundred items is enough to start.

Why a hundred

With 100 items, one mistake moves the score by one point, and you can still read every failure by hand. That is the point of the first set: not statistical perfection, but a measurement the whole team can inspect. As the feature matures you grow it; you do not start with thousands.

A caution on precision: with 100 items the uncertainty is wide. A 95% score can plausibly hide a true rate anywhere from roughly 89% to 98%. Treat it as a tripwire, not a guarantee, and say so in the acceptance document.

What goes into it

Sample from real data from the process, not from examples someone invented. Then deliberately cover:

  • The typical case, in proportion to how common it is (most of the set).
  • The boring variations: different phrasings, formats, languages, typos.
  • Known hard cases: the pairs people confuse, the odd layouts.
  • Things that must be refused or escalated: out-of-scope questions, missing fields, items the system should hand to a human.
  • A few adversarial ones: instructions hidden in the input, empty input, absurdly long input.

Tag each item with its category so you can report per-category results, not just one average that hides a weak spot.

Who labels it

The process owner, or someone they trust, decides the correct answer. Two people labelling independently, then discussing disagreements, finds the ambiguous items early. Ambiguity found at this stage is a requirements problem, and it is cheaper to fix now than after launch.

How to use it

  1. Freeze it. The set is not training data. Never tune on it after you start reporting from it, or the score only reflects what you memorised.
  2. Run it on every change: a new prompt, a new model version, a new threshold.
  3. Write the pass bar before the first run, as a number per category. Example: "at least 95% correct on automated items, and every must-refuse item refused".
  4. Read the failures, all of them. Each one is either a bug, a labelling error, or a missing rule.
  5. Keep a changelog of scores per version so regressions are visible.

A minimal runner is a few lines:

def evaluate(system, items):
    results = [(it, system(it["input"])) for it in items]
    ok = [r for it, r in results if r["answer"] == it["expected"]]
    return len(ok) / len(items), [it for it, r in results if r["answer"] != it["expected"]]

Refresh it slowly

Every month or so, add 10 to 20 fresh real items, especially ones that came out of the review queue as corrections. Retire items that no longer reflect the process. Keep a separate untouched holdout if you tune a lot.

Takeaways

  1. Start with about 100 real, labelled items.
  2. Cover typical, hard, and must-refuse cases and tag them.
  3. Freeze it, write the pass bar first, run it on every change.
  4. Be honest about the uncertainty that comes with a small set.

title: Why Most Directories Fail Developers with 14-Day Queues (And How We Engineered an Instant-Live Launchpad)
description:
If you’ve ever launched a developer tool or side project, you know the dread of the Directory Holding Pattern.

You spend months building your product. You polish the UI, fix the edge cases, write clean docs, and submit your link to five different software launchpads.

Then, you wait.

One directory asks for $49 to "skip the queue." Another takes 17 days to approve your listing. And the third one silently goes live on a random Sunday night while your entire audience is asleep — completely burning your launch momentum.

Makers shouldn't be penalized because an admin queue is backed up.

That’s why I spent the last few months building Astro Discover — an open, hype-free product launchpad with a guaranteed 24-hour spotlight and zero queue delays.

💡 The Core Problem: The Launch Day Limbo

Traditional launchpad moderation models have two major flaws:

  1. The Ghosting Trap: Submissions get buried in queues for weeks. By the time the product is approved, the maker has already moved on to other marketing initiatives.
  2. The Pay-to-Win Fast Track: Platforms create artificial delays just to monetize expedited review tiers.

We wanted to engineer a platform where the maker’s launch day is sacred and protected.

🛠️ The Architectural Solution: 24–48 Hr Turnaround + The "Pending Review" Fail-Safe

Here is the exact mechanism we implemented on Astro Discover:

1. 24–48 Hour Maximum Human Verification

Every submission is screened by a human to prevent malicious phishing, direct executable downloads, and broken links. We keep our queue lean and mean with a 24 to 48-hour SLA.

2. The Auto-Live Fail-Safe (No Lost Launches)

Here’s our biggest innovation: Makers schedule their exact launch day in advance.

If your scheduled launch day arrives and manual review is still in queue over a weekend or holiday, your project still goes live automatically on Today's Launches with a transparent "Pending Review" badge.

  • You never lose your 24-hour spotlight window.
  • The 24-hour spotlight starts cleanly at 12:01 AM IST.
  • Early adopters can still test your project and inspect your tech stack.
  • Once verified, the badge seamlessly flips to approved.

3. Tech Stack Transparency Over Marketing Hype

Developers don't care about corporate buzzwords. Every card on Astro Discover directly exposes:

  • The actual tech stack (React, TypeScript, Go, Python, Rust, etc.)
  • Open-source licensing (MIT, Apache, AGPL)
  • Direct GitHub repository links
  • Verified maker socials

⚡ Zero-Delay Performance & Architecture

We built the frontend on React + Vite + Tailwind CSS with real-time reactive Firestore listeners.

To eliminate "Soft 404" indexing issues and ensure search engine crawlers (Googlebot, Perplexity, ChatGPT) never see an empty screen, we pre-hydrate the baseline tools at zero milliseconds and stream live Firestore upvotes in the background.

🌐 Try Astro Discover

The directory is completely free, open, and requires zero login to browse:

👉 Explore Live Launches: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio

👉 Submit Your Tool & Lock Your Launch Day: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio/submit

title: Gradle Under the Hood: Fighting Incremental Cache Misses in Bytecode Processing
description:
If you have ever written a custom Gradle task to analyze or process compiled bytecode (like custom linters, schema validators, or metadata generators), you have probably encountered a hidden, silent performance killer: the aggressive compiler erasure.

In this first article of our Gradle Under the Hood series, we’ll explore how we re-engineered the incremental tracking of JPersist (a zero-boilerplate JPA build automation suite) to achieve bulletproof UP-TO-DATE execution states, even when the Java compiler tries to destroy your task's cache.

The Naive Approach to Bytecode Tasks

When building a task that processes compiled .class files, the most intuitive setup is to declare the compiler's output directory as your task's @InputDirectory:

abstract class MyBytecodeTask extends DefaultTask {
    @InputDirectory
    abstract DirectoryProperty getCompiledClassesDir()

    @TaskAction
    void execute(InputChanges inputChanges) {
        // Process altered files...
    }
}

You then wire it in your plugin by binding it to the JavaCompile task:

task.getCompiledClassesDir().set(compileJavaTask.flatMap { it.destinationDirectory })

Why this fails in the real world:
Gradle has a magnificent incremental build engine. However, JavaCompile is highly defensive. When a developer alters even a single line of Java source code, JavaCompile often wipes out its entire destination directory (build/classes/java/main) before rebuilding to guarantee no stale classes remain.

For your downstream bytecode task, this folder deletion is catastrophic. Even though you are using Gradle's InputChanges API, the engine sees that the root directory was destroyed and recreated. It panics, concludes that the historical file snapshot graph is non-linear, and forces inputChanges.incremental to evaluate to false. Your task is forced into a heavy, full-pass execution loop on every minor code tweak.

The Solution: Source-Driven Incremental Tracking

To make our query linters and schema validators truly incremental and immune to compiler erasures, we shifted our architectural paradigm: We stopped tracking the volatile compiler output folder and started tracking the stable source code repository layout instead.

Instead of listening to the .class directory, our tasks now listen to sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories as a flat @InputFiles collection wrapper:

abstract class ValidatePersistenceSchema extends DefaultTask {
    @Incremental
    @InputFiles
    @PathSensitive(PathSensitivity.RELATIVE)
    abstract ConfigurableFileCollection getSourceFiles()

    @InputDirectory // Kept as standard non-incremental input
    abstract DirectoryProperty getCompiledClassesDir()
}

Inside our plugin wiring loop, we feed it lazily while filtering out any intermediate or generated build directories:

task.getSourceFiles().from(project.provider {
    sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories.asFileTree.matching {
        exclude { element ->
            element.file.absolutePath.replace('\\', '/').contains(project.layout.buildDirectory.get().asFile.absolutePath.replace('\\', '/'))
        }
    }
})

Mapping Source Deltas to Bytecode Outputs

Because source directories are managed by the developer and are never aggressively wiped out by a compiler task, Gradle's file system snapshot engine maintains a perfect, unbroken lineage of mutations.

When a developer modifies an entity, InputChanges accurately catches exactly one modified .java file. Inside our @TaskAction, we intercept this .java path, compute its relative package structure, and translate it on-the-fly to find the corresponding compiled .class file inside the freshly compiled folder:

@TaskAction
void validate(InputChanges inputChanges) {
    List<String> affectedEntities = []

    if (inputChanges.incremental) {
        inputChanges.getFileChanges(getSourceFiles()).each { change ->
            if (change.file.name.endsWith('.java')) {
                String relativePath = change.normalizedPath
                // Translate com/example/model/User.java -> com.example.model.User
                String className = relativePath.substring(0, relativePath.lastIndexOf('.java')).replace('/', '.')

                if (change.changeType != ChangeType.REMOVED) {
                    affectedEntities.add(className)
                }
            }
        }

        // Fast-Exit Pass: If no active entities were touched, skip heavy DB bootstrapping!
        if (affectedEntities.isEmpty()) return
    } else {
        affectedEntities.addAll(fullDiscoveredEntityList)
    }

    // Submit isolated work wrapper with precisely filtered entity subsets...
}

The Engineering Win

By decoupling task delta tracking from the volatile compilation output graph, we achieved major engineering victories for the JPersist v1.8.0 release pipeline:

  1. Immunity to Directory Purges: Even if JavaCompile erases and rewrites 5,000 class files, our tasks compare the stable source metadata signatures. If only 1 file changed, we only process 1 class binarized stream via ASM.
  2. The Fast-Exit Optimization: If a developer edits a standard Service, Controller, or Utility class that doesn't hold JPA annotations, our tasks process the change stream in under 5 milliseconds and exit before ever spawning database connections or heavy classloaders.

Stay tuned for Part 2, where we’ll dive into ClassLoader Harvesting and how we forced isolated Gradle workers to run seamlessly on headless CI nodes without ever hitting network lookups or requiring mavenLocal() fallbacks!

What are your thoughts on handling aggressive compiler tasks in custom Gradle plugins? Let's discuss in the comments below!

🔗 Check out the JPersist open-source architecture: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: Ảnh mà Google không thấy: CSS background, lazy load sai cách và cách audit thẻ img
description:
Developer thường tối ưu ảnh theo hướng hiệu năng: nén, lazy load, chuyển sang ảnh nền cho dễ căn chỉnh. Một số lựa chọn trong đó làm ảnh biến mất khỏi Google Hình ảnh mà không ai để ý. Bài này đi qua những gì tài liệu Google Search Central nói về cách Google tìm và hiểu ảnh, và một script audit thẻ img trên trang.

Google tìm ảnh ở đâu

Google tìm ảnh trong thuộc tính src của thẻ <img>, kể cả khi thẻ đó nằm trong <picture>. Ảnh đặt bằng CSS background-image thì Google không lập chỉ mục. Đây là lỗi hay gặp ở theme bán hàng: ảnh sản phẩm trong lưới danh mục được render bằng div có ảnh nền để dễ cắt khung.

<!-- Google không lập chỉ mục ảnh này -->
<div class="thumb" style="background-image:url(ao-thun-den.webp)"></div>

<!-- Dùng img với object-fit để có cùng hiệu ứng cắt khung -->
<img src="ao-thun-den.webp" alt="Áo thun nam cổ tròn màu đen, mặt trước"
     width="600" height="600" style="object-fit:cover" loading="lazy">

object-fit: cover cho kết quả hiển thị gần như giống ảnh nền, mà ảnh vẫn nằm trong img có alt.

Google hiểu ảnh bằng gì

Theo hướng dẫn SEO cho Google Hình ảnh: văn bản thay thế (alt) cùng thuật toán thị giác máy tính và nội dung trang; thông tin từ chú thích và tiêu đề trang; còn tên file chỉ là "gợi ý rất nhẹ". Hệ quả cho cấu trúc HTML: dùng figure và figcaption để chú thích gắn rõ với ảnh, và đặt ảnh gần đoạn chữ liên quan thay vì gom hết vào một gallery cuối trang.

<figure>
  <img src="yoast-o-seo-title-va-meta.webp"
       alt="Ô SEO title và meta description trong Yoast SEO trên WordPress">
  <figcaption>Thanh xanh cho biết title và mô tả nằm trong giới hạn hiển thị.</figcaption>
</figure>

Script audit ảnh trên một trang 

import re
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

DUOI_HOP_LE = {"bmp", "gif", "jpg", "jpeg", "png", "webp", "svg", "avif"}
TEN_CHUNG = re.compile(r"^(img|image|dsc|screenshot|pic|anh|hinh)[-_ ]?\d*", re.I)

def audit_anh(html: str) -> list:
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    loi = []
    for el in soup.select("[style*=background-image]"):
        loi.append(f"Ảnh nền CSS (không được lập chỉ mục): {el.get('class')}")
    for img in soup.find_all("img"):
        src = img.get("src") or ""
        ten = src.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].split("?")[0]
        if not src or src.startswith("data:"):
            loi.append(f"img không có src thật (lazy load?): {img.get('data-src') or img}")
            continue
        if img.get("alt") is None:
            loi.append(f"Thiếu thuộc tính alt: {ten}")
        if TEN_CHUNG.match(ten):
            loi.append(f"Tên file chung chung: {ten}")
        duoi = ten.rsplit(".", 1)[-1].lower() if "." in ten else ""
        if duoi and duoi not in DUOI_HOP_LE:
            loi.append(f"Định dạng lạ: {ten}")
    return loi

Kiểm tra src rỗng hoặc data: bắt một lỗi lazy load phổ biến: thư viện cũ để ảnh thật trong data-src và chỉ gán vào src khi cuộn tới. Nếu Google không render tới bước đó, ảnh không có src thật. Thuộc tính loading="lazy" gốc của trình duyệt không gặp vấn đề này, và WordPress đã tự thêm nó cho ảnh trong nội dung.

Định dạng và kích thước

Google hỗ trợ BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG và AVIF, và đuôi file phải khớp với loại ảnh. WordPress tự sinh nhiều kích thước và khai báo srcset, nên phần cần làm thủ công là cắt ảnh về đúng kích thước hiển thị trước khi tải lên. Với ảnh đại diện, Google khuyên rộng ít nhất 1200 pixel cho Discover.

Phần dành cho người viết nội dung, gồm vai trò của 4 ô alt, title, caption, description trong WordPress và ví dụ metadata theo ngành, có trong bài Tối ưu hình ảnh chuẩn SEO trên Onic.vn.

Bài gốc: https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/toi-uu-hinh-anh-chuan-seo/
