title: Next.js 16: Fixing "cookies() can't be read inside 'use cache'" (and Caching Public Data Without It)
description:
You turn on Cache Components, add 'use cache' to a data function, and the build fails:

Error: Route "/broken": `cookies()` can't be read inside `"use cache"`. Read it outside the cached function and pass what you need as an argument.
Learn more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache
    at h (lib/server-client.ts:6:29)
    at i (app/broken/page.tsx:7:24)

The confusing part is that your cached function might never call cookies() itself. In this example, the call is inside a helper that creates a "server client", the kind of cookie-aware factory that many auth and database SDKs ship for the App Router. The rule follows the call stack, so a cookie read anywhere below a 'use cache' boundary breaks it.

This post shows why that happens and the four patterns that fix it, each built and run on Next.js 16.4.3.

What you'll learn

  • Why cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed in 'use cache'
  • How to cache public data when your SDK's default client reads cookies
  • How to pass a cookie value into a cached function safely
  • Where per-user data should go instead (and the Suspense rule that comes with it)
  • When 'use cache: private' is the right tool, and what it does not do

Prerequisites and versions

  • Next.js 16.4.3 with the App Router
  • React 19.3.1
  • TypeScript
  • Cache Components enabled (below)

Since Next.js 16.0, cacheComponents is a top-level config option. The current docs recommend setting partialPrefetching explicitly alongside it. Leaving it unset logs a warning:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

Background: why the rule exists

A 'use cache' function's output is stored and reused across requests and users. Its cache key is built from the build ID, a hash of the function's identity, and its serializable arguments (see the use cache reference).

Cookies and headers aren't arguments. If a cached function could read them, the cache key wouldn't reflect them, and one user's cookie-dependent result could be served to someone else. So Next.js forbids request-time APIs inside the cached scope:

Cached functions and components cannot access runtime APIs like cookies(), headers(), or searchParams, and the restriction follows the call stack: a helper the cached function calls that reads one of these fails the same way.

The docs also warn that on a dynamically rendered route this "can pass next build and fail under next start". Don't treat a green build as proof.

Reproducing the error

Here's a stand-in for a cookie-aware SDK factory. Real ones (for example, an auth or database "server client" for the App Router) usually take the cookie store so they can attach the user's session:

// lib/server-client.ts
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

// Stand-in for a cookie-aware SDK factory such as an auth or database
// "server client". The important part: it calls cookies() internally.
export async function createServerClient() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies()
  const token = cookieStore.get('session')?.value ?? null
  return {
    async getPublicPosts() {
      return [{ id: 1, title: 'Hello' }, { id: 2, title: 'World' }]
    },
    async getMyDrafts() {
      if (!token) return []
      return [{ id: 99, title: `Draft for ${token}` }]
    },
  }
}

And a page that caches "public" posts with it:

// app/broken/page.tsx
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'
import { createServerClient } from '@/lib/server-client'

async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  const client = await createServerClient() // calls cookies() inside the cache scope
  return client.getPublicPosts()
}

export default async function Page() {
  const posts = await getPublicPosts()
  return <ul>{posts.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>)}</ul>
}

next build fails with the error at the top of this post. The stack trace points to the cookies() call in the helper and to the cached function that called it. That's the fastest way to find the culprit in a real codebase.

The fix, in four patterns

All four patterns below live on one page. Together they built cleanly. Next.js marked the route as Partial Prerender (◐) with Revalidate 1h and Expire 1d, which come from the hours profile.

Pattern 1: Public data uses a client that never touches cookies

If the data is the same for everyone, it shouldn't go through a cookie-aware client at all. Create a separate client for public reads. With real SDKs, this usually means the plain client created with a public/anon key, not the App Router "server client" helper.

// lib/public-client.ts
// Stand-in for a cookie-free client (for example a plain SDK client created
// with a public/anon key). It never touches cookies() or headers().
export function createPublicClient() {
  return {
    async getPublicPosts() {
      return [
        { id: 1, title: 'Hello' },
        { id: 2, title: 'World' },
      ]
    },
  }
}

// 1. Public data: cookie-free client, safe to share across all users.
async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('posts')
  const posts = await createPublicClient().getPublicPosts()
  return { posts, generatedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

generatedAt is there to show the caching. With the page served by next start, two requests without cookies and one request with Cookie: locale=fr; session=alice all returned the same generatedAt value. The entry was filled during the build and reused for everyone.

Security note: Only do this for data that really is public. If your database enforces row-level security based on the user's session, a cookie-free client sees what an anonymous user sees. That's correct for public data and wrong for anything personal.

Pattern 2: Read the cookie outside and pass the value in

This is the pattern the error page recommends. The value you pass becomes part of the cache key, so each distinct value gets its own entry.

// 2. Data that depends on one small cookie value: read the cookie outside,
//    pass the value in. The value becomes part of the cache key.
async function getGreeting(locale: 'en' | 'fr') {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('days')
  return locale === 'fr' ? 'Bonjour' : 'Hello'
}

async function Greeting() {
  const raw = (await cookies()).get('locale')?.value
  const locale = raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en'
  return <p id="greeting">{await getGreeting(locale)}</p>
}

The response without cookies showed Hello. With Cookie: locale=fr it showed Bonjour.

Two design choices here matter:

  • Normalize the value before passing it. raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en' limits the cache to two entries. If you pass a raw cookie straight through, any client can create a new cache entry by sending a random value.
  • Prefer low-cardinality values such as locale, theme, plan tier or feature-flag variant. Passing a session token or user ID technically works (one entry per user), but at that point you're building a per-user cache. That's usually better handled by Pattern 3 or 4.

Pattern 3: Per-user data stays uncached, inside Suspense

Personal data, like "my drafts", can just stay dynamic. Use the cookie-aware client outside any cache scope:

// 3. Per-user data: not in a shared cache at all. Rendered at request time
//    inside a Suspense boundary.
async function MyDrafts() {
  const client = await createServerClient()
  const drafts = await client.getMyDrafts()
  return (
    <ul id="drafts">
      {drafts.map((d) => (
        <li key={d.id}>{d.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

The full page puts it all together:

// app/fixed/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
import { createPublicClient } from '@/lib/public-client'
import { createServerClient } from '@/lib/server-client'

// 1. Public data: cookie-free client, safe to share across all users.
async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('posts')
  const posts = await createPublicClient().getPublicPosts()
  return { posts, generatedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

// 2. Data that depends on one small cookie value: read the cookie outside,
//    pass the value in. The value becomes part of the cache key.
async function getGreeting(locale: 'en' | 'fr') {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('days')
  return locale === 'fr' ? 'Bonjour' : 'Hello'
}

async function Greeting() {
  const raw = (await cookies()).get('locale')?.value
  const locale = raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en'
  return <p id="greeting">{await getGreeting(locale)}</p>
}

// 3. Per-user data: not in a shared cache at all. Rendered at request time
//    inside a Suspense boundary.
async function MyDrafts() {
  const client = await createServerClient()
  const drafts = await client.getMyDrafts()
  return (
    <ul id="drafts">
      {drafts.map((d) => (
        <li key={d.id}>{d.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

export default async function Page() {
  const { posts, generatedAt } = await getPublicPosts()
  return (
    <main>
      <p id="generated">{generatedAt}</p>
      <ul id="posts">
        {posts.map((p) => (
          <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading greeting…</p>}>
        <Greeting />
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading your drafts…</p>}>
        <MyDrafts />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  )
}

The test results: without a session cookie the drafts list was empty. With session=alice it contained Draft for alice. The public posts and their timestamp were identical in both responses.

Why the Suspense boundaries matter. With Cache Components, reading cookies() outside <Suspense> blocks prerendering. This page fails the build:

// app/nosuspense/page.tsx — fails the build with Cache Components
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

export default async function Page() {
  const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value
  return <p>{session ?? 'anonymous'}</p>
}

Error: Route "/nosuspense": Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data during prerendering.
`fetch(...)`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, `params`, `searchParams`, or `connection()` accessed outside of `<Suspense>` prevents the route from being prerendered, blocking the page load and leading to a slower user experience.
Ways to fix this:
  - [stream] Provide a placeholder with `<Suspense fallback={...}>` around the data access
  - [cache] For uncached data (`fetch`, database calls): cache the access with `"use cache"` (does not apply to `connection()`)
  - [block] Set `export const instant = false` to allow a blocking route

Wrapping the cookie-reading component in <Suspense> (as Greeting and MyDrafts are above) is the "[stream]" option. The static shell, which includes the cached public posts, is served right away, and the personal parts stream in.

Pattern 4: 'use cache: private' when you can't refactor

Sometimes the cookie read is buried in code you can't change easily. 'use cache: private' allows cookies(), headers() and searchParams inside the cached scope:

// app/private/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'

async function getDashboard() {
  'use cache: private'
  cacheLife({ stale: 60 })
  const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value ?? 'guest'
  return { session, at: new Date().toISOString() }
}

async function Dashboard() {
  const { session, at } = await getDashboard()
  return <p id="dash">{session} @ {at}</p>
}

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}>
      <Dashboard />
    </Suspense>
  )
}

The important thing is what "private" means. From the docs: "In production, matching calls within one request can reuse the same result, but Next.js does not store it in a server cache across production requests." The client router can keep the output in browser memory for the stale time.

The test confirmed this. Under next start, consecutive requests with the same session=alice cookie got a different at timestamp every time. So 'use cache: private' deduplicates within a request and feeds the browser's router cache. It does not make repeated server requests cheaper. If you need that, use Patterns 1–3.

Other limits from the docs:

  • connection() is still not allowed inside it.
  • You can't configure custom cache handlers for it.
  • Its stale time feeds the route's client cache. It must be at least 30 seconds for per-link prefetching and at least 5 minutes to be included in the route's App Shell.

Choosing a pattern

Your data Pattern
Same for everyone 1: cookie-free client inside 'use cache'
Varies by a small, known set of values from a cookie/header 2: read outside, normalize, pass as argument
Specific to the signed-in user 3: uncached, in a component wrapped in <Suspense>
Per-user, and the cookie read can't be moved 4: 'use cache: private', but no cross-request server cache

Common mistakes and troubleshooting

  • "My function doesn't call cookies()." Something it calls does. Check the stack trace. The first frame is the actual cookies() call, and the next frames show the path back to your cached function.
  • The build passes, production throws. On dynamically rendered routes, the error shows up when the route runs. Exercise the route under next start before deploying.
  • Passing the whole cookie store or headers() object. Arguments must be serializable, and class instances aren't. Extract the plain values you need.
  • Passing unbounded values. Each distinct argument creates a cache entry. Validate and normalize anything that comes from the client.
  • Using React.cache to smuggle values in. React.cache is isolated inside 'use cache' boundaries. Values set outside aren't visible inside. Use arguments.
  • Module-level promise caches. The error page notes that a cached function can stall if it awaits a promise stored outside the function (for example, in a module-scoped Map). 'use cache' already deduplicates calls with the same arguments, so remove the extra layer.
  • Draft Mode. You can read draftMode().isEnabled inside 'use cache', but cookies() and headers() are still off-limits, even in draft mode.

Limitations and alternatives

  • With the default in-memory cache handler on serverless platforms, runtime cache entries "typically don't persist across requests", although build-time caching works normally. Self-hosted servers keep entries in memory. If you need a shared runtime cache, look at 'use cache: remote', which uses a platform-provided handler and has network and cost trade-offs.
  • Cache entries don't survive a new deploy, because the build ID (or deploymentId) is part of the key.
  • Cache Components needs the Node.js runtime and doesn't support the runtime route segment config. Remove export const runtime = ... from routes when you adopt it.
  • Don't wait for plain 'use cache' to start accepting cookies()/headers(). A reply in discussion #82873 (August 2025) says "There's no plan to allow use cache to access cookies/headers" and suggests using 'use cache' as much as possible and the private variant only rarely. The current docs take the same position.

Conclusion

The error is Next.js protecting you from serving one user's data to another. Most of the time the fix is structural. Keep public reads on a cookie-free client inside 'use cache'. Read cookies at the edge of your component tree, normalize the values, and pass them in as arguments. Keep personal data uncached behind <Suspense>. Use 'use cache: private' only when you can't move the cookie read, and remember that it doesn't give you a cross-request server cache.

Next step: search your codebase for helpers that call cookies() or headers() and check whether any of them run below a 'use cache' boundary. Then run the affected routes under next start, not just next build.

References

  • use cache directive: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
  • Error: Cannot access request data in use cache: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache
  • use cache: private: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private
  • use cache: remote: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote
  • cacheComponents config: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents
  • Caching guide: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/caching
  • Blocking prerender error: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-prerender-dynamic
  • Next.js discussion #82873, "Allow cookies() or headers() in use cache": https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/82873
  • Next.js 16.4 release post: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-4

title: Cutting LLM Calls in Incident Triage: Sliding Windows, Log Reduction, and a pgvector Cache
description:
A Kafka-to-WebSocket pipeline where the model is the last resort, not the first step.

The problem

The obvious way to add an LLM to log monitoring is to send logs to a model and ask what is wrong. That breaks quickly. Most log lines are not errors. During an outage, the same error repeats thousands of times with only timestamps, UUIDs and counters changing. A raw stack trace with framework frames is mostly noise. And the same database timeout will show up on orders today and inventory tomorrow, so you pay for the same diagnosis again.

I built telemetry-incident-dashboard around one rule: every step before the model must be cheaper than the model, and must be able to stop the pipeline.

It is a working prototype. I'll say clearly later what has and hasn't been exercised.

Architecture 

flowchart TD
    A[Apps / log shipper] --> K[Kafka topic app-logs]
    K --> C[Spring Boot consumer<br/>virtual threads]
    C -->|every log| W[STOMP /topic/logs]
    C -->|ERROR only| D[Per-service sliding window<br/>10+ errors in 60s]
    D -->|below threshold| X[Stop: no tokens]
    D -->|burst| R[LogPayloadReducer]
    R --> E{Exact fingerprint<br/>in cache?}
    E -->|yes| H[CACHE_EXACT]
    E -->|no| V{pgvector cosine<br/>>= 0.90?}
    V -->|yes| S[CACHE_SEMANTIC]
    V -->|no| L[LLM call via LangChain4j]
    L --> P[(PostgreSQL + pgvector<br/>diagnosis_cache)]
    H --> I[(incidents hypertable)]
    S --> I
    L --> I
    I --> A2[STOMP /topic/alerts]

Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.3, Apache Kafka (KRaft), PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB and pgvector, LangChain4j with OpenAI (gpt-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small by default), and a React + Vite dashboard.

Step 1: detect bursts without a model

Each service gets its own ErrorWindow. It holds the errors from the last 60 seconds, fires when the count reaches the threshold (default 10), and then stays quiet for a cooldown (default 120 seconds).

synchronized List<LogEvent> record(LogEvent event, long nowMs, long windowMs, int threshold,
                                   long cooldownMs, int maxBuffered) {
    errors.addLast(new Stamped(nowMs, event));
    while (!errors.isEmpty() && nowMs - errors.peekFirst().arrivalMs() > windowMs) {
        errors.pollFirst();
    }
    while (errors.size() > maxBuffered) {
        errors.pollFirst();
    }
    if (errors.size() < threshold || nowMs - lastAlertMs < cooldownMs) {
        return List.of();
    }
    lastAlertMs = nowMs;
    return errors.stream().map(Stamped::event).toList();
}

Info, debug and warning logs never get here. They are counted and streamed to the dashboard, capped at 200 non-error events per second. A malformed Kafka record is counted and dropped. The listener never rethrows, so one bad record can't stall a partition.

Visual instruction: Capture this exact code section in VS Code using the OneDark-Pro theme. Use a readable font size and crop unnecessary editor UI.

The cooldown matters. Without it, a long outage would trigger analysis on every incoming error once the window is full.

Step 2: shrink the burst

LogPayloadReducer turns a burst into a short context string:

  • strips ANSI codes, ISO timestamps, UUIDs and hex addresses
  • drops framework frames (java.base/, jdk.internal., Tomcat, Spring AOP and CGLIB, JUnit)
  • keeps the top 12 stack lines and notes how many were cut
  • groups identical errors by fingerprint and prints them as xN
  • caps the whole thing at 2,000 characters and 5 distinct errors

The fingerprint is a SHA-256 of the text after volatile parts are normalised. Numbers become <n>, so Timeout after 3001ms and Timeout after 9999ms hash the same:

private static String normalize(String s) {
    return NUMBER.matcher(scrub(s)).replaceAll("<n>");
}

For the 15-error connection-pool burst in sample-data/02-db-timeout-burst.ndjson, the README reports the model input going from 8,415 characters (about 2,100 tokens) to 506 characters (about 127 tokens). That is one synthetic burst and the token count is a four-characters-per-token estimate, so treat 94% as an illustration, not a benchmark.

The reduced output looks like this:

service=orders errors=15 distinct=1
[1] x15 ERROR HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30001ms
java.sql.SQLTransientConnectionException: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30001ms
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.createTimeoutException(HikariPool.java:696)
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:197)
    at com.shop.orders.Repository.save(Repository.java:48)
    at com.shop.orders.Service.handle(Service.java:71)

Step 3: a two-level cache

LogAnalysisEngine.resolve goes cheapest first.

Exact match. One UPDATE ... RETURNING both bumps the hit counter and fetches the stored diagnosis:

List<String> exact = jdbc.queryForList(
        "UPDATE diagnosis_cache SET hits = hits + 1 WHERE fingerprint = ? RETURNING diagnosis",
        String.class, fingerprint);

Semantic match. If there's no exact hit, embed the context and ask pgvector for the nearest row. A cosine similarity of 0.90 or more counts as a hit. This is what lets a database timeout on inventory reuse the diagnosis made for orders:

SELECT id, diagnosis, 1 - (embedding <=> ?::vector) AS similarity
FROM diagnosis_cache
WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector
LIMIT 1

The table uses an HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops. The schema is 1536 dimensions to match text-embedding-3-small. If you change the embedding model, you change docker/init.sql and EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS together. The engine checks the returned vector length and skips the vector cache on a mismatch instead of failing.

LLM call. Only on a miss. The prompt asks for under 150 words in three headings (root cause with confidence, impact, fix) and says not to invent details. The answer and its embedding are written back, so the next occurrence is free.

Visual instruction: Capture this exact code section in VS Code using the OneDark-Pro theme. Use a readable font size and crop unnecessary editor UI.

Engineering decisions

Single-flight for identical bursts. Two services can hit the same failure at once. diagnoseOnce keeps a ConcurrentMap<String, CompletableFuture<Diagnosis>> keyed by fingerprint. The first caller does the work; the rest join() its future. That avoids paying for duplicate LLM calls in the gap before the first answer lands in the cache.

Never throw from the pipeline. If the cache query, the embedding call, the database or the LLM fails, the incident is still recorded with source FALLBACK and the raw condensed telemetry attached. A flaky dependency degrades the diagnosis, not the stream.

Virtual threads. Each Kafka consumer loop and each analysis task runs on a Java 21 virtual thread. Analysis is blocking I/O (HTTP to a model, JDBC), which is the case virtual threads fit. The analysis is also submitted off the consumer thread so a slow model call can't hold up log ingestion.

Timescale for history. Cached diagnoses live in diagnosis_cache. Every incident, including cache hits, goes into an incidents hypertable with its source, similarity and tokens used, so you can see how often the model is actually needed.

Testing

There are two unit test classes, five tests:

  • ErrorWindowTest: fires at the threshold, respects cooldown, and expires old errors from the window.
  • LogPayloadReducerTest: truncates stacks to 12 lines plus a marker, collapses 200 repeated errors to x200 under the 2,000-character budget, and gives two events with different numbers and UUIDs the same fingerprint.

Nine NDJSON scenarios in sample-data/ cover normal traffic, bursts (DB timeout, NPE, OOM, upstream 502, JWT failures), a similar failure on a second service, malformed lines, and a below-threshold case.

Limitations

I'd rather list these than have you find them:

  • The successful LLM path (real diagnosis written to the cache and then served as a hit) has not been run against a funded OpenAI account. The fallback path, reducer, window logic and the dashboard demo have been run.
  • The dashboard's live mode hasn't been tested against the backend.
  • Kafka offsets auto-commit, so a crash mid-analysis can lose that burst.
  • No auth on the WebSocket endpoint. No cache eviction. Single Kafka broker.
  • No throughput or latency benchmarks.

Try it 

cp .env.example .env            # optionally set OPENAI_API_KEY
docker compose up -d            # Kafka (KRaft) + TimescaleDB with pgvector
set -a; source .env; set +a
mvn spring-boot:run             # http://localhost:8080, STOMP at /ws

cd dashboard && npm install && npm run dev   # http://localhost:5173

scripts/send-sample-logs.sh sample-data/02-db-timeout-burst.ndjson

Without an API key the app still starts, and bursts are stored as FALLBACK. There is also a browser-only demo that simulates the same rules with hand-written diagnoses and is labeled as a simulation. Click "Play the story" to see an LLM call, a below-threshold burst, a similar-error hit and an exact hit.

What's next

Not implemented yet, but the obvious gaps: manual offset commits after analysis, cache eviction, authentication on the WebSocket, and a real run of the LLM path with measured cache hit rates.

Code is on GitHub: axololtos/telemetry-incident-dashboard

If it's useful, a star helps. Issues and PRs are welcome (there's a CONTRIBUTING guide). Follow me here on DEV for more write-ups like this.

title: Skip sending request bodies to Routing Middleware
description:
You can now skip sending client request bodies to Routing Middleware with skipMiddlewareRequestBody. This reduces incoming Fast Origin Transfer usage for middleware invocations and can improve time to first byte, especially for requests with large bodies.

Enable this option only if your Routing Middleware doesn’t read request bodies. Vercel Functions and rewrite targets still receive the body, so you can read and process it there.

Set skipMiddlewareRequestBody to true in your project’s JSON configuration file, vercel.json:

If you use a TypeScript configuration file, add the same setting to vercel.ts instead. This example assumes @vercel/config is installed:

Redeploy your project for the change to take effect. The option defaults to false, so existing projects are unchanged unless you enable it.

Read more in the skipMiddlewareRequestBody documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now accepts service submissions
description:
Vercel Connect now lets you submit your own service to the connectors directory, so you no longer need to wait for Vercel to build a connector for it.

Submitting a service takes four steps:

  1. Describe your service.

  2. Add one or more connection methods, using OAuth or an API key.

  3. Verify each OAuth method by requesting a real token through a test connector.

  4. Send the submission for review.

Vercel reviews each submission before publishing it to the directory.

Get started from Submit a Service in the dashboard, or read what your service needs to support in the documentation.

title: Secure Amazon S3 Buckets Using IAM Policies and Bucket Policies
description:
Introduction

Amazon S3 is one of the most widely used AWS services, and also one of the most common sources of data leaks. Almost every S3 breach in the news comes down to one thing: a misconfigured access policy.

In this article, I'll explain the two main ways of controlling access to S3, IAM policies and bucket policies, show when to use each, and walk through a hands-on example you can try in your own account.

How S3 Access Is Evaluated

Before writing any policy, it helps to know how AWS decides whether a request is allowed:

Everything is denied by default.
An explicit Allow in a relevant policy grants access.
An explicit Deny always wins, no matter what else says Allow.
For requests within the same account, access is granted if either the IAM policy or the bucket policy allows it (and nothing denies it).

Remember this rule: Explicit Deny > Allow > Default Deny.

IAM Policies vs Bucket Policies
Feature IAM Policy Bucket Policy
Attached to IAM user, group, or role The S3 bucket
Answers the question "What can this identity do?" "Who can access this bucket?"
Has a Principal element No Yes
Cross-account access Needs help from the other side Supported directly
Best for Managing permissions for your users and roles Bucket-wide rules, cross-account access, enforcing conditions
Size limit 2 KB (users), 6 KB (groups), 10 KB (roles) 20 KB

Simple way to remember it:

IAM policy = identity-based ("what can I do?")
Bucket policy = resource-based ("who can touch this bucket?")
Hands-On: Secure a Bucket Step by Step
Step 1: Create a Private Bucket
Open the S3 console and choose Create bucket.
Give it a unique name, for example vishal-secure-demo-bucket.
Keep Block all public access turned ON.
Enable Bucket Versioning.
Enable Default encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Choose Create bucket.

Tip: Block Public Access is your first line of defense. Leave it on unless you have a very specific reason to turn it off.

Step 2: Create an IAM Policy (Least Privilege)

Let's give a user read and write access to only one bucket, nothing more.

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "ListBucket",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "s3:ListBucket",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket"
},
{
"Sid": "ReadWriteObjects",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

Why two statements? s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket itself, while GetObject and PutObject apply to the objects inside it (/*). This is a very common mistake for beginners.

To apply it:

Go to IAM → Policies → Create policy → JSON and paste the policy.
Name it S3-DemoBucket-ReadWrite.
Attach it to a user, group, or (better) a role.
Step 3: Add a Bucket Policy to Enforce HTTPS

Now let's add a rule at the bucket level. This policy denies any request that doesn't use HTTPS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:",
"Resource": [
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket",
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
],
"Condition": {
"Bool": {
"aws:SecureTransport": "false"
}
}
}
]
}

To apply it: S3 → your bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy → Edit → paste → Save.

Step 4: Restrict Access to a Specific IAM Role

You can also lock the bucket so that only one role can access it. Replace the account ID and role name with your own:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "AllowOnlyAppRole",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Principal": {
"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AppServerRole"
},
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

This is useful when an EC2 instance or Lambda function needs access to the bucket. Use roles instead of long-term access keys.

Step 5: Require Encryption on Upload

This policy blocks any upload that isn't encrypted with SSE-KMS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyUnencryptedUploads",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:PutObject",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/",
"Condition": {
"StringNotEquals": {
"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"
}
}
}
]
}
Step 6: Test Your Setup
Try uploading a file with the IAM user: it should succeed.
Try accessing the bucket over plain HTTP: it should be denied.
Try accessing the bucket with a different user that has no permissions: you should see Access Denied.
Use the IAM Policy Simulator or IAM Access Analyzer to validate your policies.
S3 Security Best Practices
Enable Block Public Access at both the bucket and account level.
Follow least privilege. Grant only the actions and resources that are needed.
Use IAM roles, not long-term access keys.
Enforce HTTPS with aws:SecureTransport.
Encrypt data at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Enable versioning and consider MFA Delete for critical data.
Turn on logging with S3 server access logs and CloudTrail data events.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to find buckets shared outside your account.
Avoid "Principal": "" with Allow unless you really mean public access.
Review policies regularly and remove permissions that are no longer used.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Using "Action": "s3:" and "Resource": "" in IAM policies.
Forgetting the / on the resource ARN for object-level actions.
Making a bucket public "temporarily" and forgetting about it.
Hardcoding access keys in application code.
Not testing policies before applying them in production.
Conclusion

Securing S3 isn't about picking IAM policies or bucket policies. The strongest setups use both:

IAM policies control what your users and roles can do.
Bucket policies enforce rules at the bucket itself, like HTTPS-only access, encryption, and cross-account permissions.
Block Public Access, encryption, and logging add extra layers of protection.

Start with least privilege, test your policies, and review them regularly. Your data will be much safer for it.

title: Character limits have two numbers: building an ad preview around warnings and blocks
description:
Disclosure up front: I run Maestro, a B2B paid media company, and this post is about a free tool we built, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup. Nothing here needs you to use it. The problems are the same for anyone building a form, an editor or a preview against a platform's published limits.

The tool does one narrow job. You enter a LinkedIn single-image ad (company name, intro text, image, headline, optional description, CTA and destination URL), compare desktop and mobile views, and export a mockup plus a production brief for whoever approves the ad. It runs in the browser, needs no sign-in, and doesn't upload your creative.

Most of the interesting engineering wasn't in drawing the card. It was in deciding what the tool is allowed to say. This post walks through those decisions: how to model a limit, how to count characters when the platform doesn't tell you how it counts, how to show truncation you can't reproduce exactly, and how to test all of it.

A field has two limits, not one

LinkedIn's single image ad specifications publish two numbers for most text fields: a shorter length to avoid truncation and a hard maximum.

Field Avoid truncation Hard maximum
Introductory text 150 characters 3,000 characters (up to 10 emojis)
Headline 70 characters 200 characters
Description 100 characters 300 characters
Destination URL n/a must start with http:// or https://; up to 2,000 characters
Ad name (optional) n/a 255 characters

A single maxLength can't represent that. Set it to 3,000 and people ship intro text that gets cut off after the first line. Set it to 150 and you block copy LinkedIn would accept, which is worse, because the writer now has a tool telling them something false.

So the tool treats the two numbers as different kinds of rule:

  • Past the recommendation: show a warning. The copy may be fine. A longer intro can be a deliberate choice, and the writer decides.
  • Past the published maximum: block the review export until the field is fixed. This copy can't work.

That split, "you should look at this" versus "this can't ship", is the single most useful idea in the tool. It applies to any field with a soft and a hard limit: meta descriptions, SMS segments, push notification titles, app store subtitles.

Model the limit as data, with its source

Constants scattered through components break the first time the platform changes a number. Limits are facts with a source and a date, so they belong in one table that the UI, the validator and the export all read. Here's a simplified sketch of that shape:

type Severity = "warning" | "error";

type Rule = {
  field: "introText" | "headline" | "description" | "destinationUrl" | "adName";
  kind: "recommendation" | "maximum";
  limit: number;
  unit: "characters" | "emoji";
  source: string;      // URL of the published spec
  checkedAt: string;   // ISO date the spec was last read
};

type Finding = {
  field: Rule["field"];
  severity: Severity;
  count: number;
  limit: number;
  method: CountMethod;  // see the Unicode section
  message: string;
};

const severityFor = (rule: Rule): Severity =>
  rule.kind === "maximum" ? "error" : "warning";

Two details matter more than they look.

First, kind drives severity, not the number. Nobody has to remember that 150 is a warning and 3,000 is an error. A recommendation can never block, by construction.

Second, every rule carries checkedAt. Our page states that the limits were checked against LinkedIn's specs on September 27, 2026, and the exported brief carries the same date. If a refresh of the source fails, the honest state is "Unknown currency", not a silent pass on old numbers.

One green check is a lie: keep the states separate

The most common failure in review tools is a single status that quietly means several things. "Ready" might mean the preview renders, or the copy is within limits, or someone approved it, or the platform accepted it. Those are four different questions with four different owners.

The tool keeps them apart:

  • Preview: can the draft be pictured, with any missing fields labeled?
  • Technical check: do the supplied copy, URL and image pass the supported rules?
  • Production handoff: is the record complete enough for a named reviewer to check?
  • LinkedIn: has the intended Campaign Manager account supplied dated approval and native-rendering evidence?

Sketched as types:

type PreviewState = "Preview available" | "Preview incomplete";
type TechnicalState = "Pass" | "Needs changes" | "Unknown" | "Unsupported";
type HandoffState = "Ready for review" | "Hold";
type PlatformState = "Not checked" | "Externally verified";

type ReviewStates = {
  preview: PreviewState;
  technical: TechnicalState;
  handoff: HandoffState;
  platform: PlatformState;
};

Nothing inside the tool can set platform to "Externally verified". That value only arrives with dated, account-scoped evidence from someone who looked in Campaign Manager. A mockup can be ready for production review while LinkedIn is still Not checked, and the UI says exactly that instead of collapsing it into a checkmark.

If you build anything that previews a third-party platform, I'd start here. Write down which states your tool can know and which it can only record from someone else, and make the second group impossible to set from local code.

What counts as a character?

This is where most counters quietly go wrong. In JavaScript, "ðŸ‘ðŸ½".length is 4. A user sees one thing.

I ran a handful of strings through Node 20 to show how far the common methods drift apart:

Input .length (UTF-16 units) Code points Grapheme clusters
Hello 5 5 5
ðŸ‘ 2 1 1
ðŸ‘ðŸ½ (thumbs up + skin tone) 4 2 1
ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’» (ZWJ sequence) 5 3 1
ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ (regional indicator pair) 4 2 1
Ã© (precomposed) 1 1 1
Ã© (e + combining accent) 2 2 1
1ï¸âƒ£ (keycap) 3 3 1

The two Ã© rows look identical on screen and count differently under two of the three methods. Normalizing to NFC first collapses the second one to length 1, which is worth doing before you count anything.

Grapheme clusters are the closest match to what a person thinks of as a character. Browsers expose them through Intl.Segmenter, which MDN lists as available across browsers since April 2024:

const segmenter = typeof Intl !== "undefined" && "Segmenter" in Intl
  ? new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" })
  : null;

export function countCharacters(text) {
  const s = text.normalize("NFC");
  if (segmenter) {
    let n = 0;
    for (const _ of segmenter.segment(s)) n++;
    return { count: n, method: "grapheme (Intl.Segmenter)" };
  }
  return { count: [...s].length, method: "code point fallback" };
}

Note the return shape. The count travels with the method that produced it. If an older runtime falls back to code points, the export says so.

The part you can't know

Here's the honest problem: LinkedIn doesn't publish every detail of its Unicode counting logic. It says 150 characters "including spaces, emojis, and punctuation" and a limit of 10 emojis, but not whether a skin-toned thumbs up is one character or two.

So our count is a local review count, and the tool labels it that way. Copy that lands near a boundary gets a note to test it in Campaign Manager before launch. I'd rather show an honest "approximately 150, check natively" than a confident number that turns out to be wrong at exactly the point where it matters.

Counting emoji is its own trap

The 10-emoji limit needs an emoji detector, and the obvious regex doesn't agree with itself. Testing the same strings against two Unicode properties in Node 20:

  • /\p{Extended_Pictographic}/u matched ðŸ‘ and ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», missed ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, and matched a plain Â© with no emoji presentation selector.
  • /^\p{RGI_Emoji}$/v (the newer v flag) matched ðŸ‘, ðŸ‘ðŸ½, ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, did not match a bare Â©, and did match Â©ï¸ with the variation selector.

The v-flag version is closer to what a person would call an emoji, but neither is guaranteed to match LinkedIn's rule. The approach I'd use: segment into graphemes first, test each grapheme, record the counting and emoji-sequence method in the export, and treat an emoji count near 10 as a boundary to check natively.

Truncation you can't reproduce exactly

The point of the 150 and 70 recommendations is truncation, so people want the preview to show where the "â€¦see more" lands. You can't get that exactly right from outside the platform. Truncation depends on fonts, viewport width, line height and rules the platform doesn't publish.

What we did instead:

  1. Pick fixed, documented card widths. The preview uses a 552 CSS-pixel desktop card and a 358 CSS-pixel phone card inside a 390px model, and stays responsive down to 320px. Those are product decisions, written down, not claims about LinkedIn's layout.
  2. Clamp by lines in CSS, not by slicing characters. Cutting the string at character 150 is wrong for two reasons: you might split a grapheme cluster, and the platform truncates visually, by lines. A line-clamp with a More/Less toggle is closer to the real behaviour and never corrupts text.
  3. Keep the text selectable and complete. The collapsed state is presentation. The exported brief always contains the full copy, even when the preview is collapsed.
  4. Label every export. Mockup images carry the caption "Approximate feed preview â€” check the final ad in Campaign Manager", plus the mode and variant. Production artwork is exported separately, with no card chrome or crop guides on it.

If a stakeholder screenshots the mockup and forwards it, the caption goes with it. That's cheaper and more honest than chasing pixel-perfect truncation.

Don't fake unsupported states

LinkedIn's spec says paid vertical (4:5) images serve on mobile devices only. A desktop/mobile switch could squeeze a portrait image into the desktop frame anyway, and it would look plausible. It would also show a placement that doesn't exist.

So the desktop view renders an explicit unsupported state for portrait creative. The same thinking applies to the description field. LinkedIn says the description shows on LinkedIn mobile and desktop when the image is less than 200 pixels wide, or when the ad runs beyond the feed through the LinkedIn Audience Network. For a normal large feed image, the tool doesn't promise the description will be visible.

A rule of thumb I took from this: if the honest answer is "this doesn't render here", render that answer. An empty state that explains itself is better than a convincing picture of something that won't happen.

Validate images against published ranges, and stop there

The image rules come from the same LinkedIn page:

Ratio Recommended Minimum Maximum
Landscape 1.91:1 1200 Ã— 628 640 Ã— 360 7680 Ã— 4320
Square 1:1 1200 Ã— 1200 360 Ã— 360 4320 Ã— 4320
Vertical 4:5 720 Ã— 900 360 Ã— 640 2430 Ã— 4320

LinkedIn accepts JPG, PNG or GIF up to 5 MB. Our first version takes JPG and PNG only. Animated GIFs are rejected with a clear message rather than silently frozen on their first frame, because a frozen frame would misrepresent the ad.

Two things we deliberately did not do:

  • Infer a ratio tolerance. LinkedIn publishes rows, not a tolerance. Is 1200 Ã— 630 "close enough" to 1.91:1? The spec doesn't say, so the tool doesn't guess. It offers the recommended presets and Fit/Crop controls, and records the crop rectangle and focal point in the export.
  • Pretend our caps are LinkedIn's. The tool has its own limits, 5,000,000 bytes in and out and 24,000,000 decoded pixels, to keep the browser responsive. The UI calls them tool limits, not platform rules.

URLs: validate syntax, keep everything

Destination checks are simple on paper: an http:// or https:// prefix and up to 2,000 characters. LinkedIn also warns that some special characters in the query string, such as < > # % { } [ ], can cause errors.

export function checkDestination(raw) {
  const findings = [];
  let url;
  try { url = new URL(raw); } catch {
    return [{ severity: "error", message: "Not a valid URL." }];
  }
  if (!/^https?:$/.test(url.protocol))
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: "Must start with http:// or https://." });
  if (raw.length > 2000)
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: `Over 2,000 characters (${raw.length}).` });
  const query = raw.includes("?") ? raw.slice(raw.indexOf("?")) : "";
  if (/[<>{}\[\]]/.test(query))
    findings.push({ severity: "warning", message: "Query string contains characters LinkedIn says can cause errors." });
  return findings;
}

Note that the query check reads the raw string. new URL("https://x.com/?a=<b>").search comes back as ?a=%3Cb%3E in Node 20, so testing url.search would miss the characters the user actually typed.

Two cautions. Store the raw string exactly as entered, including every tracking parameter. Normalizing it through URL and writing back url.href can re-encode characters and change what gets launched. And syntax validity proves nothing about the page. The brief records the destination headline and next action separately, so a reviewer can judge whether the ad's promise matches the page.

Edits invalidate checks, presentation doesn't

Once there are reviews in the record, every edit raises a question: which checks does this edit invalidate?

We split inputs into two groups:

  • Content: image, crop, copy, CTA, destination and evidence. Changing any of these invalidates the checks and exports that depend on it, while unrelated evidence survives.
  • Presentation: desktop/mobile mode, collapsed/expanded copy, theme, crop overlay. Changing these changes what you see and nothing else.

One simple way to implement it: store, with each review, a hash of the content fields it covered. On edit, recompute the hashes and drop any review whose hash no longer matches. That's easier to reason about than event-driven invalidation, and it makes "why did my approval disappear?" answerable: the field it covered changed.

Import is all or nothing

Users can export a structured JSON record and import it later. The record embeds the original, delivered and logo image bytes with hashes, so a file that only contains a path isn't treated as lossless.

Import validates the whole record first: schema, embedded assets, hashes and size caps. Only then does it replace the current work, in one step. If anything fails, the current work stays as it was. A half-imported record is worse than a failed import, because it looks fine.

How to test it

These are the tests I'd write for any tool like this. Each one maps to a behaviour our tool's page commits to:

  • Boundary triplets for every rule. 149, 150 and 151 characters of intro text should give no finding, no finding and a warning. 2,999, 3,000 and 3,001 should give a warning, a warning and an error. Same pattern for 70/200 and 100/300. A 151-character intro must never produce an error.
  • A Unicode fixture file. The strings in the table above, plus the two forms of Ã©, run through countCharacters, with expected counts per method. When a runtime changes its segmentation data, this file is where you'll find out.
  • State-separation tests. Load the worked example, and no real approvals come with it. The sample ships with clearly labeled simulated review records, and loading it into the editor clears them, so it opens on Production handoff: Hold. Assert that no code path sets the platform state to verified.
  • Invalidation tests. Approve, change the headline, assert the copy review is gone and the asset review survives. Toggle desktop/mobile, assert nothing is gone.
  • Import round-trips. Export, import, and compare byte-for-byte. Then corrupt one embedded image hash and assert the import fails with the current work intact.

What I'd tell someone building one of these

  • Put limits in data, with the source and the date they were checked.
  • Give recommendations and maximums different kinds, so severity follows from type.
  • Count graphemes, say which method you used, and label the number as local.
  • Clamp visually, never slice strings, and caption every exported image as approximate.
  • Render unsupported states instead of plausible fakes.
  • Keep "we checked it" and "the platform accepted it" in separate fields that local code can't merge.

The tool isn't an official LinkedIn preview and can't predict approval, delivery or performance. It's a review step before Campaign Manager, and the final check still happens there. If you want to poke at the decisions above, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup is free and runs entirely in your browser.

Disclosure: I'm Tim Keen and I run Maestro, the B2B paid media company that makes the tool. LinkedIn limits in this post were taken from LinkedIn's single image ad specifications page; the tool's page records them as checked on September 27, 2026. Unicode results come from Node 20.

title: Debug Malformed JSON Response from Email Send API — Four Clinical Signup Gates
description:
Validate the outgoing payload before blaming the email API for malformed JSON. For a healthtech signup flow, the useful result is an evidence chain: the payload passed the documented schema, the request returned an explicit status, and the raw response can be inspected without exposing a verification token.

Short answer: treat the problem as a contract failure until the evidence proves it is a transport or delivery failure. Validate the exact object for POST /v1/email/send, reject non-success status codes before deserializing, and retain a redacted request fingerprint, status, and bounded response body. A 400 identifies a bad request branch; it does not prove that a message was rejected by a recipient mailbox.

The rest of this article is an architecture decision record for sending an account-verification link. The primary decision is compliance evidence, not a prettier exception message.

The parser is not the arbiter.

What does a malformed JSON response actually tell you?

Very little on its own. A client may report malformed JSON because it received an HTML error page from a proxy, because it expected one response envelope and got another valid JSON object, or because it tried to parse a 400 body as a success response. The request can also be wrong before the provider has a chance to create a send attempt.

I split the critical path into four gates:

Gate Evidence to retain Boundary it isolates
Intent signup event ID, consent result, template revision The application created a send request
Payload schema result and redacted payload fingerprint The client produced the documented shape
Transport HTTP status and bounded raw body The API accepted or rejected the request
Audit request timestamp, retry count, and correlation ID The evidence can be reconstructed later

Do not put the verification token or a complete recipient address into ordinary application logs. A SHA-256 fingerprint of the normalized, redacted payload is enough to show which request was checked, provided the retained audit record can be joined to the signup event under the organization’s access policy.

The order matters. Parse the body after checking the status. Preserve the raw bytes when parsing fails. A JSON validator is useful before the network call, but it cannot tell you whether the recipient’s mailbox accepted the message.

There is a subtle audit trap here. Suppose validation succeeds, the worker mutates the recipient object to add a display name, and the request then receives a 400. If the stored fingerprint was calculated before that mutation, the audit record proves the wrong payload. Calculate the fingerprint immediately before the request, after all transformations, and retain the same event identifier through retry. This is why the sample validates a file-loaded object and sends that object without a second hand-built dictionary: the code path stays inspectable. The evidence should answer a narrow question precisely: what did this worker attempt to send, and what status did the API return?

Which four checks should sit between signup and send?

First, load the current request schema and validate the exact JSON object that the worker will send. “It looks like JSON” is not a schema check. Wrong nesting, an incorrect type, a missing required property, or an extra property rejected by the contract can all turn a verification-link request into a 400.

Second, make the HTTP method and endpoint explicit. The route in this decision is POST /v1/email/send; do not infer a different path from a prose description or from a stale client wrapper. Third, branch on the status before decoding the success shape. Fourth, record enough bounded response data to distinguish an API validation error from a proxy-generated page, while redacting secrets.

Here is a deliberately small Python harness. It expects the request object and its current schema as local JSON files, so the contract being checked is visible in code review. The schema file must come from the provider’s documented schema; the harness does not guess email fields.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

from jsonschema import validate


BASE_URL = os.environ["EMAIL_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def read_json(path: str) -> object:
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def post_email(payload: dict, idempotency_key: str) -> tuple[int, str]:
    request_body = json.dumps(payload, separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE_URL}/email/send",
        data=request_body,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        response_headers = {}
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
                status = response.status
                response_headers = response.headers
                body = response.read(4096).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            status = error.code
            response_headers = error.headers
            body = error.read(4096).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

        if status == 429:
            retry_after = response_headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue

        if not 200 <= status < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"email API returned {status}: {body}")

        return status, body

    raise RuntimeError("email API remained rate-limited after four attempts")


def send_verified_email(payload_path: str, schema_path: str, signup_event_id: str) -> dict:
    payload = read_json(payload_path)
    schema = read_json(schema_path)
    validate(instance=payload, schema=schema)

    payload_bytes = json.dumps(
        payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")
    ).encode("utf-8")
    fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(payload_bytes).hexdigest()
    status, raw_body = post_email(
        payload,
        idempotency_key=f"signup:{signup_event_id}:verification-email",
    )
    try:
        parsed_body = json.loads(raw_body)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        parsed_body = {"raw_body_prefix": raw_body}

    return {
        "signup_event_id": signup_event_id,
        "payload_sha256": fingerprint,
        "status": status,
        "response": parsed_body,
    }

The retry branch is intentionally narrow. A 400 is surfaced for correction and is not retried. A 429 backs off, and the same idempotency key is reused so a process restart does not create a second send intent. The response body is capped at 4096 bytes in this example; the production retention limit should follow the organization’s policy. The code also preserves a non-JSON body as text, which is often the quickest clue that a gateway or intermediary answered the request.

The 15-second client timeout and four-attempt cap are operational boundaries, not delivery measurements. They keep a worker from waiting forever while leaving the final decision in the audit record.

One implementation detail deserves scrutiny: the code must validate the exact payload it later sends. Validating one object and mutating another between validation and the request creates a false audit trail. If the payload contains a token, hash or redact it before durable logging, and keep the original request out of general-purpose logs.

Where do sender policy and API evidence meet?

They meet at different layers, and conflating them causes bad incident reports. A schema-valid request can still fail because the sending domain has not completed its required authentication or policy work. SPF is one documented part of sender policy, not proof that a verification message reached an inbox. Conversely, a 400 from the API is evidence about the request contract, not about SPF.

For compliance review, I would keep these records separate but joinable: signup consent, template revision, payload-validation result, API status, bounded response, and the delivery event available from the mail system. The account-verification token belongs in the protected application store, not in the evidence index. This separation makes a reviewer’s question answerable without making the audit log a second credential store.

The failure boundaries are also different. The email capability has no hosted email OTP interface, so an email-code fallback is an application responsibility. It also has no email cancellation route for a scheduled send. If the product needs revocation, invalidate the token in the signup system and make the link one-time and time-bounded; do not claim that cancellation of a pending email is available. SMS has a separate cancel route, but that does not change the email contract.

Which provider boundary best preserves the evidence trail?

There is no universal winner. Amazon SES is a strong fit when the team wants close control over domain identity and delivery configuration. SendGrid is a broader email platform with templates and event tooling. Postmark is focused on transactional mail and message activity. Resend is a focused email API that teams often pair with a separate job runner. Those are real differences, but none removes the need to validate the outgoing object and retain a defensible signup record.

Option Good fit Boundary the application still owns
Amazon SES Teams comfortable owning email identity and delivery configuration Payload evidence, scheduling, and signup correlation
SendGrid Teams that need a broad email platform and operational tooling The join between template, event, consent, and retention records
Postmark Transactional mail where message activity is the central concern Scheduling and any cross-channel workflow
Resend plus a job runner Teams that prefer focused services with separate orchestration Two credentials, two failure domains, and the glue between them
One REST surface for backend work Teams prioritizing one credential boundary and a shared request trail Vendor readiness, access control, retention, and schema ownership

I would reject an unexamined “email provider plus random scheduler” design for this healthtech flow, not because the individual products are poor, but because it often loses the correlation ID between accepted work and the email attempt. That design is valid when independent scaling or specialist vendor controls outweigh a unified evidence path. The choice should be explicit.

The unified option has two verified advantages that matter here. One key and one bill reduce credential rotation and reconciliation across the backend worker. Separately, the API is plain REST and self-describing: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That reduces the specific friction in this problem: a reviewer can inspect the contract without installing an SDK, and a Python, Go, or Java worker can follow the same HTTP boundary.

For this narrow evidence-first workflow, I would consider Infrai when one credential boundary and a public schema discovery surface matter more than a mail-only product. Infrai’s second advantage is one REST API for the backend: the worker uses plain HTTP with no SDK, so a Python, Go, or Java implementation can send the same documented request and keep the validation path consistent. That is a fit judgment, not a blanket recommendation.

The limitation is just as concrete. This is a poor fit when the organization requires a domestic email vendor as its compliance basis, an SMTP relay, or a hosted email OTP interface; the documented Tencent email vendor is still pending, and those capabilities are not substitutes for a policy review. In that case, choose the email provider whose regional and protocol requirements are already approved, even if it means maintaining a separate scheduler.

The breadth is also concrete: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That can keep account workflow infrastructure in one operational boundary, but it is not a compliance certification and it does not supply the missing email OTP interface, SMTP relay, or a domestic Tencent email vendor. SMS anti-fraud controls such as geographic fencing and per-country circuit breakers remain application work. A broad surface is useful only when its access controls, vendor readiness, retention, and failure handling pass review.

Decision

For a healthtech signup verification link, choose the provider boundary that makes these four facts easy to prove: the exact payload was schema-valid, the API returned an explicit status, retries were idempotent, and the retained evidence excludes secrets. The self-describing REST option is a reasonable fit when one credential boundary and cross-language access reduce workflow friction. Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, or Resend remain sensible choices when their email-specific controls fit the organization better.

The debugging rule is less glamorous and more durable than a vendor preference: validate first, inspect status second, preserve the raw failure third. A malformed-looking response is a clue. The contract and the evidence trail tell you what actually happened.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • SendGrid API documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/api-reference
  • Postmark Developer Documentation: https://postmarkapp.com/developer
  • Resend API Reference: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/emails/send-email

title: Architecture Firm Website Redesign Guide
description:
Architecture Firm Website Redesign Guide

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have witnessed numerous architecture firms struggle to create an effective online presence. The primary culprit behind this struggle is the reliance on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which fail to capture the unique essence and complexity of architectural services. These templates often lack the nuance and customization required to showcase an architecture firm's distinctive style, expertise, and portfolio.

The limitations of generic templates are multifaceted. Firstly, they are designed to cater to a broad range of industries, resulting in a lack of specificity and depth in their design and functionality. Secondly, they often prioritize aesthetics over user experience, leading to confusing navigation and poorly optimized conversion paths. Lastly, these templates rarely provide the flexibility and scalability needed to accommodate the evolving needs of a growing architecture firm.

To overcome these challenges, it is essential to adopt a more tailored and engineering-driven approach to website redesign. Here are three concrete takeaways to consider:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: Develop a bespoke information architecture that reflects the firm's unique services, projects, and values. This involves creating a clear and intuitive navigation system, as well as a robust filtering and search functionality to facilitate easy access to relevant content.
  2. High-Performance Visual Storytelling: Leverage high-quality visuals and immersive storytelling techniques to showcase the firm's portfolio and expertise. This can include interactive 3D models, virtual tours, and responsive image galleries that adapt seamlessly to various devices and screen sizes.
  3. Data-Driven Conversion Optimization: Implement a data-driven approach to conversion optimization, using tools like A/B testing, heat mapping, and analytics to identify areas of improvement and measure the effectiveness of design iterations. This enables architecture firms to refine their website's user experience, enhance engagement, and drive more conversions.

By embracing these engineering principles and moving away from generic templates, architecture firms can create a website that truly reflects their brand and expertise. A well-designed website can serve as a powerful marketing tool, attracting new clients, and showcasing a firm's capabilities to a wider audience.

title: Queues: at-least-once means never exactly-once
description:
The most useful sentence I've read about queues: at-least-once delivery is easy, exactly-once processing is a property of your handler, not the broker.

Which means every consumer needs to survive a duplicate. The ways I do that, in order of preference:

  1. Idempotent writes. UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected instead of blind writes.
  2. A dedupe key with a unique index. Cheapest and most explicit.
  3. A processed table with a TTL, for handlers with side effects.

The failure mode to design for isn't the duplicate, it's the poison message: one bad event that blocks the partition because the handler retries forever. Give every consumer a max attempt count and a dead-letter queue you actually read.

One more: make the retry delay grow. A flat 1-second retry turns a small outage into a stampede.

What's your dead-letter policy?

Introducing Strongcopy, a macOS App That Confirms Your Copies
description:
What is this article about?

I recently released Strongcopy.

Strongcopy is a macOS app that lets you confirm that something was actually copied to the clipboard. Copy-and-paste mistakes are hard to notice in time. Sometimes you only realize that you failed to copy something when you go to paste it.

Strongcopy is a tool to prevent such mistakes. When data lands on the clipboard, a small badge appears for a moment so you can confirm the copy.

User experience

The Strongcopy landing page shows the small badge that appears when you copy something. You can see the Copied badge next to the mouse pointer.

The badge flashes beside the mouse pointer the moment the clipboard contents change, then disappears in under a second. The menu bar icon tells you that the app is running, and the badge tells you that your copy has just gone through.

Privacy and safety

Strongcopy doesn't read, log, or retain your clipboard contents. It needs neither Accessibility nor notification permission, and it makes no network connections. In fact, Strongcopy's codebase is small enough that you can read and understand it yourself. The source code is available on GitHub.

Strongcopy runs as a background accessory app.

It has no Dock icon; all you see is a single icon in the menu bar. Its menu offers little more than About, Open at Login, and Quit. It's a simple little app.

Feedback and requests

If you'd like, please take a look at the Strongcopy page and let me know if anything catches your attention or if there's something you'd like improved.

title: Making a WPF Expander Faster with UI Reuse and Virtualization
description:
Working with large collections in WPF can introduce performance issues that aren't always obvious at first.

Recently, I worked on optimizing an Expander in our application that contained around 1,000 sequences. Opening it was noticeably slow, so I started investigating what was happening behind the scenes.

The Problem

We had an Expander that displayed approximately 1,000 sequences.

Each sequence also had a three-dot (⋮) button that provided additional actions.

The problem was in how the UI was structured.

In the existing XAML implementation, a separate three-dot button was created for every sequence item.

This meant WPF had to create and manage a large number of additional UI elements when loading the collection.

With around 1,000 sequences, this introduced unnecessary UI creation overhead and affected the Expander's opening performance.

Finding the Bottleneck

I started examining the XAML structure and how the sequence items were being rendered.

I found that the three-dot button was being repeatedly created for individual items, even though its functionality and structure were reusable.

This was unnecessary work that could be optimized.

The Solution

I approached the problem in two ways:

  1. Reusing the Button

Instead of repeatedly creating the same button structure, I changed the implementation to reuse the button reference and avoid unnecessary repeated creation.

  1. Implementing UI Virtualization

I also implemented virtualization so that WPF would create UI elements only for the items needed for the visible portion of the collection rather than creating everything upfront.

This reduced the number of UI elements that needed to be generated and managed at once.

The Result

The Expander now opens significantly faster, even with approximately 1,000 sequences.

The improvement came from reducing unnecessary UI element creation and using virtualization to manage a large collection more efficiently.

What I Learned

This was another reminder that UI performance is not just about how much data an application handles.

It's also about how efficiently the UI framework creates, manages, and renders that data.

When working with large collections in WPF, consider:

  • Avoiding unnecessary UI element creation.
  • Reusing common UI definitions and resources.
  • Implementing UI virtualization.
  • Investigating DataTemplates and visual tree complexity.
  • Understanding when UI elements are actually created and rendered.

Sometimes, optimizing the UI structure can make a bigger difference than optimizing the underlying data operations.
