title: AWS Cloud Practitioner CLF-C02 Study Guide: Domains, Free Labs and Exam Tips
description:
The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) exam has 65 questions in 90 minutes, a minimum passing score of 700 out of 1,000, and four domains weighted from 12% to 34%. The most efficient plan is to study from the official exam guide's task statements: Cloud Technology and Services (34%) and Security and Compliance (30%) together account for nearly two thirds of scored content.

This guide is for people new to AWS who want a structured way to prepare, such as career changers, sales and support staff, project managers, and early-career IT staff. By the end you will know exactly what the exam covers, which official free and low-cost resources to use, how to spread your study over four weeks, and what to do in the exam. All exam facts come from AWS's own exam guide and certification page, checked on 31 October 2026. Exams are revised, so confirm details on the official page before you book.

If you are deciding between this and a Microsoft fundamentals exam, read AWS Cloud Practitioner vs AZ-900: which to take first. For the next step up, see the AWS Solutions Architect Associate study guide.

Who this is for and what you will have at the end

You have a few hours a week and no requirement for prior AWS experience. After following this guide you will have a domain-by-domain checklist drawn from the official guide, a four-week schedule, a safe way to practice hands-on without surprise bills, and a clear picture of how the exam behaves.

Exam facts

Item Detail
Level Foundational
Questions 65 (50 scored, 15 unscored)
Duration 90 minutes
Question types Multiple choice (one correct, three distractors) and multiple response (two or more correct from five or more options)
Passing score 700 on a scaled 100 to 1,000 score
Cost 100 USD, plus possible costs such as foreign exchange rates
Delivery Pearson VUE testing center or online proctored
Validity 3 years
Prerequisites None listed

The exam guide adds that unanswered questions are scored as incorrect and there is no penalty for guessing, so answer everything. Scoring is compensatory: you do not have to pass each section, only the exam as a whole. Section-level feedback on your score report is general information, and the guide advises caution when interpreting it.

For recertification, AWS lists three options: complete the AWS Cloud Quest: Recertify Cloud Practitioner course, pass the latest version of the exam, or pass an Associate or Professional exam. The certification page lists 12 languages, noting that the Italian and German versions will be retired after December 31, 2026.

What the exam covers

The official guide lists four content domains.

Domain Weight
1. Cloud Concepts 24%
2. Security and Compliance 30%
3. Cloud Technology and Services 34%
4. Billing, Pricing, and Support 12%

The guide says it is not a comprehensive list of exam content, and that coding, designing cloud architecture, troubleshooting, implementation and load testing are out of scope for the target candidate.

Domain 1: Cloud Concepts (24%)

The four task statements are benefits of the AWS Cloud, design principles, migration, and cloud economics. Study:

  • The value of global infrastructure, high availability, elasticity and agility.
  • The six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability, and how they differ.
  • The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework and migration strategies.
  • Fixed versus variable cost, on-premises costs, Bring Your Own License versus included licenses, rightsizing, automation and economies of scale.

Domain 2: Security and Compliance (30%)

  • Shared responsibility model: who is responsible for what, and how responsibility shifts depending on the service, with the guide's examples of Amazon RDS, AWS Lambda and Amazon EC2.
  • Governance and compliance: where to find compliance information (AWS Artifact), encryption in transit and at rest, and the roles of CloudWatch, CloudTrail and AWS Config. Know what Amazon Inspector, Security Hub, GuardDuty and Shield do.
  • Access management: IAM users, groups, roles and policies, least privilege, protecting the root user, tasks only the root user can perform, MFA, IAM Identity Center, federation, and storing credentials with services such as Secrets Manager. See AWS IAM basics.
  • Security resources: AWS WAF, Firewall Manager, Shield, GuardDuty, the AWS Marketplace for third-party security products, and Trusted Advisor.

Domain 3: Cloud Technology and Services (34%)

This is the largest domain, with eight task statements:

  1. Deployment and operating methods: console, API, SDK, CLI and infrastructure as code, plus cloud, hybrid and on-premises models.
  2. Global infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations, and when to use multiple Regions (disaster recovery, latency, data sovereignty).
  3. Compute: EC2 instance types, containers (ECS, EKS), serverless (Fargate, Lambda), auto scaling and load balancers.
  4. Databases: RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, and the migration tools DMS and SCT.
  5. Networking: VPC components, network ACLs and security groups, Route 53, VPN and Direct Connect.
  6. Storage: S3 storage classes and lifecycle policies, EBS and instance store, EFS and FSx, Storage Gateway and AWS Backup.
  7. AI/ML and analytics: SageMaker AI, Lex, Athena, Kinesis, Glue and Amazon Quick.
  8. Other categories: EventBridge, SNS, SQS, Amazon Connect, SES, developer tools such as CodeBuild, CodePipeline and X-Ray, end-user computing such as WorkSpaces and AppStream 2.0, Amplify, and IoT Core.

Because the exam asks you to identify the right service for a use case, build a one-line "what it is for" note for every in-scope service. The guide links the in-scope and out-of-scope AWS services lists, which tell you which services you can safely ignore.

Domain 4: Billing, Pricing, and Support (12%)

  • Compute purchasing options: On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Spot, Savings Plans, Dedicated Hosts, Dedicated Instances and Capacity Reservations, and when to use each. See AWS EC2 pricing explained.
  • Data transfer costs: incoming versus outgoing, between Regions and within a Region.
  • Storage options and tiers.
  • AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, Pricing Calculator, Organizations consolidated billing and cost allocation tags. See AWS Budgets and billing alerts setup.
  • Support plans, Trusted Advisor, the AWS Health Dashboard, AWS Partner Network and technical resources such as re:Post and the Knowledge Center.

Official free and low-cost resources

AWS's certification page links these preparation resources:

  • Exam Prep Plan on AWS Skill Builder, a four-step plan.
  • Official Practice Question Set, Official Pretest and Official Practice Exam.
  • The exam guide itself in AWS documentation.
  • Hands-on practice: AWS Builder Labs, AWS Cloud Quest, AWS Jam, AWS SimuLearn and AWS Escape Room.
  • Digital courses to fill knowledge gaps.
  • AWS Training Live on Twitch for free live and on-demand training.

The certification page does not say which of these are free, so check the Skill Builder page for what your account includes before you plan around a particular resource. This article does not quote Skill Builder prices or subscription contents.

Practice safely in your own AWS account

For hands-on practice outside guided labs, AWS's Free Tier page describes a Free plan for new customers: $100 in credits immediately, with up to $100 more by exploring key services, for up to $200. On the Free plan you are not billed unless you upgrade or activate paid-only services. More than 30 services stay free within monthly usage limits. The page states that the account "closes on its own 6 months after you open it or when your credits run out, whichever comes first." Because the account closes, do not put anything you want to keep in a Free plan account. Set a budget alert if you use the paid plan.

A four-week study plan

This assumes 4 to 6 hours a week. Adjust to your schedule.

Week 1: Cloud concepts and billing. Read Domain 1 and Domain 4 task statements. Make notes on the Well-Architected pillars and the compute purchasing options. Take the official Pretest to see where you stand.

Week 2: Security. Study Domain 2. Draw the shared responsibility model for EC2, RDS and Lambda from memory. Complete a hands-on lab on IAM users, MFA and the root user.

Week 3: Services. Work through Domain 3 by category: compute, storage, databases, networking, then the rest. For each, write what it is, when to choose it, and its closest alternative.

Week 4: Practice and review. Take the Official Practice Exam under timed conditions: 65 questions in 90 minutes is about 83 seconds per question. Review every wrong answer and also the right ones you guessed. Revisit your weakest domain and re-read the in-scope services list.

Exam tips

  • Answer every question. Unanswered ones are scored wrong and guessing has no penalty.
  • Treat each question as scored. The 15 unscored questions are not marked.
  • Read multiple-response questions for how many answers they ask for.
  • Eliminate distractors. The guide notes they are plausible responses that match the content area, so look for the option that fits the scenario's exact requirement (cost, availability, security or ease).
  • Flag long questions and return to them, keeping time for a final pass.
  • If you test online, check the proctoring requirements and test your equipment ahead of time on the booking site.

Troubleshooting your preparation

You keep mixing up similar services

Make comparison tables: S3 versus EBS versus EFS; Security Groups versus network ACLs; SQS versus SNS versus EventBridge; GuardDuty versus Inspector versus Shield. Questions often turn on one distinguishing feature.

Practice scores are not improving

Review why distractors are wrong rather than memorizing answers. Then return to the task statement behind the question in the exam guide.

You are unsure whether a service is in scope

Check the in-scope and out-of-scope lists linked from the exam guide.

Unexpected charges on your AWS account

Check Billing and Cost Management, shut down any resources you created, and keep a budget alert active.

Checklist

  • Read the official exam guide and the in-scope services list.
  • Book a date to create a deadline.
  • Complete the four-week plan.
  • Take the Official Pretest first and the Official Practice Exam last.
  • Practice hands-on in a guided lab or a Free plan account with budget alerts.
  • On exam day, answer every question and manage the clock.

References

  • AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) exam guide
  • Domain 1: Cloud Concepts
  • Domain 2: Security and Compliance
  • Domain 3: Cloud Technology and Services
  • Domain 4: Billing, Pricing, and Support
  • AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification page
  • AWS Free Tier

This guide was researched and drafted with AI assistance and checked against the vendor documentation listed in its References. Read the maintained version and related guides on EpiFive.

title: Run Claude Managed Agents with Chat SDK
description:
You can now run Claude Managed Agents with Chat SDK.

Claude Managed Agents handles the agent loop server-side, including the model, tools, session state, and sandboxed web research. That means you can ship a Slack research bot built on Claude Managed Agents and Chat SDK, with one persistent session per thread and streamed briefs with sources.

What you get

  • Token-by-token streaming: Replies render as the model writes them, over a single streamed response.

title: Adding a whole team as request participants in Jira Service Management
description:
A request comes in and a whole team needs to follow it: finance on every invoice question, facilities on every move request. In Jira Service Management that is more awkward than it should be, because request participants are individual people. There is no field for a group. Here is what you can do with the built-in options, and where each one stops.

How request participants work

  • Request participants is a field on service requests. Everyone in it gets the request's customer notifications and can see and comment on it in the portal.
  • It holds people, not groups. Adding a group means adding each member by hand.
  • Only people who may raise requests in that service project can be participants. On sites where customers need explicit access, group members without it are rejected.

Atlassian's request for group participants, JSDCLOUD-1268, has collected hundreds of votes over the years and has not been built.

Option 1: organizations

  1. In the service project, go to Customers and create an organization, or use an existing one.
  2. Add the people to it.
  3. Customers in the organization can share requests with it, and agents can share a request with an organization.

The catch: sharing with an organization makes the request visible to its members, but it does not make them participants. Members get one "Organization added" email, and later updates only if they turn notifications on for that request. Organizations are also separate from Jira groups, so somebody has to keep both lists in step.

Option 2: Jira Automation

A rule can set the Request participants field when a request is created.

  1. Trigger: Work item created, with a condition on the request type.
  2. Action: Edit work item, and set Request participants to the people who should follow it.

That works for a fixed list of people. Automation has no simple built-in way to turn a Jira group into its current members, so the list lives inside the rule and someone updates it when people join or leave. Requests that are already open do not change when the list does. And every rule run counts towards your site's monthly Automation usage, which is limited by plan.

If you are comfortable with the REST API, there is a more flexible route: the service desk API can add participants to a request with one call listing several account IDs, and you can read a group's members with the group/member endpoint. Wire that into a scheduled rule or a script and you get something close to group behaviour. It is also more moving parts to maintain, and it won't remove leavers unless you write that part too.

Option 3: ask the requester

Requesters can add participants from the portal. Fine for one-off requests, unreliable for "this team must always be on it".

Decide these before you automate anything

  • Which requests? Usually a few request types per project, not everything.
  • New requests only, or open ones too? When someone joins the team, should they be added to requests that are already open?
  • What about leavers? Come off open requests, or stay until it is closed?

Option 4: an app that works from Jira groups

Full disclosure: we build Group Participants, so take this one with that in mind. Group Participants for Jira Service Management works with the Jira groups you already have:

  • Rules per service project and request type: new requests get everyone in the chosen groups as participants.
  • An agent action adds any group to a request from the work item's actions menu.
  • An hourly sync adds people who join a group to matching open requests. Removing people who leave is optional, and someone still covered by another rule stays on.
  • It stores only its settings and member snapshots, and makes no calls outside Atlassian.
  • It runs as its own Forge app, so it does not use your Automation rule runs.

Other Marketplace apps do the same thing, some of them cheaper. I compared a few here: https://kayabyte.dev/atlassian/guides/jsm-group-request-participants-apps-compared

For a fixed team and a couple of request types, an Automation rule is probably all you need. Once the team changes regularly, keeping a hand-written list current is the part that starts to hurt.

title: Designing Photo Slots for Multi-Person AI Video Templates
description:
A photo-to-video interface becomes more complicated as soon as a template supports two people or a group. A generic upload box does not tell users which photo belongs to which performer.

Dame Hombro AI is the product example here: fourteen dance and freestyle templates cover solo adults, duos, groups of three, cats and dogs. Outputs are 15-second, 720p MP4 clips with generated audio. The following is a practical interface design checklist for this kind of workflow, rather than a claim about any particular model architecture.

Treat each upload as a role assignment

A template should define its required cast before the user chooses files. Label the slots with the same role names used in the preview. For a duo, two distinct slots are easier to inspect than a single gallery of attachments. For a pet preset, make the expected animal type explicit.

Keep the selected template and its photo assignments together. If a user switches from a solo scene to a group scene, show the newly required roles before allowing generation. Do not silently treat a missing performer as an optional input.

Separate preparation from generation

Choosing a file, preparing an upload and starting a paid generation are different actions. The interface should make those boundaries visible. A useful review screen answers four questions: which template is selected, which photo fills each role, which aspect ratio will be generated, and what the request costs.

Dame Hombro AI offers 9:16 and 16:9 output and charges one credit per video. Its credit packs are one-time purchases; unused credits do not expire, and failed generations restore the credit. These are product rules worth showing before a request starts.

Validate the brief, then review the result

Input validation can confirm required slots and file constraints. It cannot guarantee that a generated face, hand or dance movement will look right. Completion therefore needs a second review step: watch the whole clip, including its audio, before downloading or sharing it.

For this product, photos must be authorized. Human subjects must be adults, and minors, celebrities and public figures are excluded. The result is a new AI interpretation, so the UI should not promise exact identity preservation or frame-by-frame replacement.

Describe audio independently

A dance template can evoke a movement style without including a commercial recording. This service creates new audio; it does not promise the original song, lyrics or an artist's voice. Dame Hombro AI is independent of Bulin 47 and Kevin Wai.

For builders, the useful design boundary is between the reference, the request and the generated result. Make each one inspectable, and users have a clearer basis for deciding what to create and what to share.

title: CV0-004 Exam Guide: Cost, Format and Study Plan
description:
The CV0-004 exam is the test for CompTIA Cloud+. It proves you can deploy, secure, run and troubleshoot cloud environments, and it is not tied to one vendor. Our voucher costs $224.99, and most people with some admin experience can prepare in about eight weeks.

What CV0-004 proves and who should take it

Cloud+ shows that you can work with cloud services across providers. It covers design, deployment, security, operations, DevOps basics and troubleshooting. It is a practical, job-focused exam, not a theory test.

It fits systems administrators, cloud and network engineers, and support staff who are moving into cloud roles. CompTIA commonly recommends some hands-on experience in systems or network administration, plus a basic grounding such as Network+ or Server+. These are recommendations, not hard requirements.

It is a poor fit if you have never touched a server or a cloud console. In that case, start with a fundamentals exam such as AWS Cloud Practitioner or browse our entry-level certifications first.

Exam format and price at a glance

The figures below are the commonly published CV0-004 details. Confirm them on CompTIA's exam page before you book, because formats and list prices can change.

Item Detail
Exam code CV0-004
Certification CompTIA Cloud+
Question types Multiple choice and performance-based
Maximum questions 90
Time limit 90 minutes
Passing score 750 on a scale of 100 to 900
Prerequisites None required; hands-on experience recommended
Our voucher price $224.99 (USD), checked 2026-11-01

Performance-based questions put you in a simulated task, such as fixing a configuration or ordering steps. They often take longer than multiple-choice items, so they affect your pacing.

Skills measured and how much each domain weighs

CV0-004 is organized into six domains. The weights below are the commonly published ones. The takeaway is simple: architecture, deployment and security together make up over 60% of the exam.

Domain Weight
1.0 Cloud Architecture 23%
2.0 Deployment 19%
3.0 Security 19%
4.0 Operations 17%
5.0 DevOps Fundamentals 10%
6.0 Troubleshooting 12%

DevOps Fundamentals is the newer, smaller domain. Expect questions on infrastructure as code, CI/CD pipelines, containers and version control. Do not skip it just because it is only 10%, since those points are easy to win with a weekend of practice.

Download the official objectives PDF from CompTIA and use it as your checklist. Every bullet in it is fair game.

An eight-week study plan with weekly hours

This plan assumes you already know basic networking and have used a server or a cloud console. It totals about 64 hours. If you are newer to IT, stretch it to ten or twelve weeks.

Week Focus Hours
1 Cloud models, service types, shared responsibility, objectives review 8
2 Architecture: storage, compute, networking, high availability 8
3 Deployment: provisioning, migrations, templates, sizing 8
4 Security: IAM, encryption, network controls, compliance 8
5 Operations: monitoring, backup, patching, cost control 8
6 DevOps: IaC, CI/CD, containers, Git 8
7 Troubleshooting methodology and scenario drills 8
8 Timed practice exams, weak-area review 8

Worked example: turning a practice score into a plan

Say you score 68% on your first timed practice test. Break the result down by domain. If Security is at 55% and Operations at 80%, spend most of week 8 on Security. Security is worth 19% of the exam, so a 25-point gap there costs you more than a small gap in a 10% domain.

Commands worth running yourself

Reading about cloud tools is not enough for performance-based questions. Spend a few evenings in a free-tier account and run commands like these:

terraform init
terraform plan
terraform apply
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
kubectl get pods
dig example.com
traceroute example.com

These cover infrastructure as code, containers, orchestration and basic network troubleshooting. Destroy resources when you finish, so you do not pay for idle services.

Common mistakes that cost points

  • Memorizing one provider. Cloud+ is vendor-neutral. Learn the concepts, then map them to AWS, Azure and Google Cloud names.
  • Using only dumps or question banks. Questions get reworded, and performance-based items need real understanding. Use practice tests to find gaps, not to memorize answers.
  • Ignoring troubleshooting order. Scenario questions often reward the first sensible step: identify the problem, check what changed, then test a fix.
  • Spending too long on early questions. With about 90 minutes, flag performance-based items and return to them if you are stuck.
  • Skipping cost and capacity topics. Right-sizing, reserved capacity and tagging show up in operations scenarios.
  • Booking before you have a date plan. Pick a test date about eight weeks out, then work backward.

Buying the voucher: delivery, redemption and refunds

Our CV0-004 CompTIA Cloud+ voucher is $224.99. One voucher covers one exam attempt. The code is emailed within 12 hours of payment and also appears in your account.

You can cancel an order for a full refund before delivery. A delivered code is non-refundable unless the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use. In that case, contact support within 14 days with your order number and a screenshot, and we will replace or refund the code. Details are on the refund policy and delivery policy pages.

Before you pay, check CompTIA's current list price and exam details on its own site, since we cannot show a verified list price here.

After you pass

Update your resume and professional profiles the same week. Cloud+ pairs well with a vendor certification, so many people add an AWS or Azure exam next. Our cloud computing certifications page lists options.

CompTIA certifications are commonly valid for three years and can be renewed through continuing education activities. Check your CompTIA account for the exact renewal rules that apply to your certification.

title: Before You Ship a Task App, Test Its Data Export
description:
A task app can look great during a demo. You create a task, assign it to someone, add a deadline, and move it across a board.

Then you click Export.

The download contains task titles and dates. The comments are missing. Attachments are only links. Completed work has disappeared because a filter was active.

The file opens, but it does not contain everything the team expected.

For developers, this is a useful reminder: an export button is a feature with its own requirements. Downloading a file is only the first step.

I run WhatsOnTech, where we publish guides about software and everyday business technology. This article looks at a question that matters to both software buyers and developers: can people take their work with them in a form they can actually use?

The example below uses a fictional task app. It is a suggested testing approach, not a claim that I tested every product mentioned.

Disclosure: I run the website linked in this article. This article was prepared with AI assistance.

Decide What the Export Is Supposed to Do

Before choosing a file format, decide why someone needs the export.

A manager preparing a weekly report may only need task names, owners, deadlines, and status.

A team moving to another app may need much more: descriptions, comments, checklists, attachments, and the relationships between records.

Someone recovering from data loss needs a tested restoration process.

These are different jobs.

An export designed for reporting can be useful without recreating an entire workspace. The problem starts when the interface calls that file a complete backup.

Write a clear description of the feature before building it:

Export the selected tasks and their main fields for spreadsheet reporting. Comments and attachment files are not included.

That explanation may sound less impressive than “Export everything,” but it sets an expectation the product can meet.

Understand the Work Before Choosing the Fields

A personal reminder and a shared project do not carry the same amount of information.

“Send the invoice” might need a title, deadline, and completion status.

“Prepare the new website homepage” could involve several people, review comments, image files, subtasks, and approval history.

This difference also matters when choosing software. Our Microsoft To Do vs Trello comparison explores the distinction between simple lists and work organised into stages.

For developers, the lesson is to export the information that gives a task its meaning.

A card titled “Update the page” is not very useful after migration if the page address, feedback, and assigned person have been lost.

Start by listing the fields people rely on during normal work. Then decide which export includes each field.

Use a Small Dataset With Deliberate Edge Cases

Testing with three tasks called “Task 1,” “Task 2,” and “Task 3” will miss many problems.

Instead, create a small test workspace with records that challenge the export.

Include:

  • Two tasks with the same title but different IDs.
  • One completed task and one archived task.
  • A task without a deadline.
  • A description containing commas, quotation marks, and line breaks.
  • Text in more than one language.
  • A task with several checklist items.
  • Two attachments that share the same filename.
  • A task with more than one comment.
  • A deadline with a specific time.
  • A date-only deadline with no time attached.

Record what you expect before downloading anything.

For example, your fictional workspace might contain 12 tasks, 7 comments, 4 checklist items, and 3 attachments.

Those counts give you something concrete to compare against. They are not proof of completeness by themselves, but they make missing data easier to notice.

Use invented information for this test. Real customer records are unnecessary.

Make Export Scope Visible

A common source of confusion is the difference between “what I can see” and “everything in the workspace.”

If a user filters the screen to show open tasks, should Export include only those tasks?

Either behaviour can be reasonable. It needs to be explicit.

The export screen could offer:

  • Current filtered view.
  • All tasks I am allowed to access.
  • Include completed tasks.
  • Include archived tasks.

Show a summary before the download:

This export includes 12 tasks, including completed tasks. Archived tasks are excluded.

For larger systems, the export should also explain its timing. If a team changes records while a long export is running, the resulting file may contain information collected at different moments.

Use a consistent snapshot where practical, or document how the export handles changes during generation.

The user should not have to guess what “all” means.

Choose CSV or JSON for a Clear Reason

CSV is useful for rows and columns. People can open it in a spreadsheet, sort tasks, and create simple reports.

JSON can represent nested information such as a task with several comments and checklist items.

Neither format guarantees completeness.

Format Useful for What needs attention
CSV Spreadsheet reports and simple transfers Nested records, text formatting, dates, and spreadsheet interpretation
JSON Structured records and custom migration tools Schema documentation, relationships, and importer compatibility
ZIP package Records plus attachment files File organisation, missing files, and a contents summary
PDF A readable snapshot Limited usefulness for importing structured data

A well-documented CSV may be more useful than an unexplained JSON file.

For a structured export, include a format version, export time, field descriptions, and a clear explanation of how records connect.

Keep stable identifiers. Two tasks with identical titles should remain distinguishable after export.

Learn From a Real Export Limitation

Trello provides a practical example of why these details matter.

According to Atlassian’s export documentation, board members can export raw JSON, while boards in Premium Workspaces can also be exported as CSV. Comments are not included in the CSV export.

For Workspace exports, including raw attachments is a separate option. Without it, the export links to attachments hosted on Trello.

Atlassian also states that importing the exported JSON or CSV to recreate a Trello board is not currently supported.

That does not make the exports useless. It means exporting, reporting, migration, and restoration are separate capabilities.

When evaluating any app, check the documentation for the exact export option you plan to use. Different formats and export levels can include different information.

Check Attachment Files, Not Just Their Names

An attachment entry may contain a filename and a web address without containing the file itself.

That can work while the original account remains available. It may fail later if permissions change, the file is removed, or the link expires.

If an export promises attachment files, check that they are actually present.

Download a sample package, disconnect from the original service, and try opening the included documents and images.

Also test duplicate filenames. Two different files named “brief.pdf” should not overwrite each other.

A package can keep files in separate folders based on task or attachment IDs. A contents list can connect each file to its original record.

If a file could not be included, report it clearly. A successful download message should not hide skipped attachments.

Keep Dates and Text Meaningful

Dates deserve more attention than they usually receive.

“05/06/2026” can mean different dates depending on the reader’s locale.

A date-only deadline should remain a date. Converting it unnecessarily into a timestamp can make it appear on a different day in another time zone.

For timed events, use a documented representation with a time-zone offset or UTC convention. Where local scheduling matters, preserve the relevant time-zone information too.

Text needs similar care.

Check that:

  • Commas stay inside the correct field.
  • Quotation marks survive the export.
  • Multiline notes remain attached to one record.
  • Urdu and other non-English text remains readable.
  • Identifiers with leading zeros stay intact.

A file that opens without an error can still contain changed values.

Compare actual field values, not just the appearance of the first few rows.

Separate Export, Sync, and Backup

These three features are related, but they serve different purposes.

An export provides a copy of selected information.

Sync carries changes between connected locations.

Backup is intended to support recovery under defined conditions.

A team may use all three.

For example, syncing a folder can make an exported file available on another computer. It does not automatically protect that file from a deletion that also syncs.

Our guide to cloud backup versus sync explains this distinction from the user’s perspective.

For your own app, describe recovery in practical terms:

  • Which records can be recovered?
  • How old can the recovery point be?
  • How long are copies retained?
  • Are attachment files included?
  • What access is required to restore them?
  • Has the recovery process been tested?

An occasional manual export can contribute to a backup plan. Its value depends on its coverage, storage, age, and whether someone can use it to recover the information they need.

Test the Return Journey

If your app promises restoration, test the complete journey.

Create a test workspace, export it, and restore it into a separate empty test environment.

Then compare the result with the original.

Check record counts, field values, attachment contents, and relationships. Make sure comments belong to the correct tasks and checklist items retain their completion status.

If the destination creates new IDs, verify that the relationships are mapped correctly rather than expecting every ID to remain unchanged.

Repeat the import.

Does it create duplicates? Update existing records? Refuse to continue? The behaviour should be deliberate and documented.

If your app supports export but not import, say so. Do not describe a readable archive as a tested restore package.

Never delete the original workspace just to find out whether restoration works.

Treat Spreadsheet Export as a Security Feature

User-entered text may behave differently after it leaves your application.

Some spreadsheet programs interpret values beginning with certain characters as formulas. This creates a risk known as CSV or formula injection.

Correctly escaping commas and quotation marks does not, by itself, solve that problem.

OWASP notes that protections depend on the spreadsheet application and how the file is opened, saved, and reopened.

For a related DEV discussion, see spreadsheet exports and formula-injection controls.

Keep the original data unchanged in your application. Apply suitable handling when creating a spreadsheet-facing export, and test it with the applications you support.

A separate machine-readable export may be appropriate when users need exact original values.

Export permissions also matter. The download must not reveal private fields or other users’ records simply because the export query has fewer restrictions than the normal screen.

Make Large Exports Honest About Failure

A small workspace may export quickly. A large one may require background processing.

Give the job clear states such as preparing, ready, failed, or completed with omissions.

If only part of the data was exported, say so. Provide a useful summary of what was included and what failed.

Avoid giving every download the same filename. A descriptive name with an export date makes older copies easier to distinguish.

Protect the generated file appropriately. A private workspace should not become a publicly accessible download.

If download links expire, tell users when they need to create another export.

Use a Release Checklist

Before releasing an export feature, check more than the download button.

Check What a useful result looks like
Export scope Included and excluded records are clear
Record counts Counts match the selected scope
Text Quotes, line breaks, and different languages survive
Dates Date-only values and timed events retain their meaning
Attachments Promised files are present and open correctly
Relationships Comments and subtasks remain linked correctly
Permissions Restricted records and fields stay restricted
Spreadsheet behaviour Untrusted text is handled for supported applications
Repeated import Duplicate handling follows the documented rule
Partial failure Missing items are reported
Restoration Tested if recovery is promised

Keep the test dataset so you can run these checks again when the data model changes.

A newly added field is easy to display in the app and easy to forget in an export.

Build the Exit Alongside the Entrance

Onboarding helps people bring their work into an app. Export helps them keep control of that work later.

Both deserve careful design.

Start with a clear purpose, test with realistic sample records, and explain the limits of each format. If you promise recovery, test recovery.

The goal is not to produce the largest possible download. It is to give people a copy they can understand and use for the purpose you promised.

Before shipping another task feature, try taking the existing work out of your app. What survives that journey tells you a great deal about the quality of the export.

title: I wanted Copier in Rust, so I wrote rootstock
description:
I write Rust for a living, and over the last couple of years the tools around me quietly turned into Rust too. On the frontend, Biome does what ESLint and Prettier used to. In Python land it's Ruff and uv. They're fast, they ship as one binary, and there's nothing to set up besides the binary itself.

Project templates were the exception. The best tool I know for them is Copier, and it's genuinely good. But it's Python, so every machine and every CI job that touches a template needs Python and pipx first. I wanted the same thing as one binary. That's rootstock.

Creating a project is the easy part

Plenty of tools can create a project from a template: cargo-generate, kickstart, cookiecutter. They render the files and that's it. From then on the project and the template live separate lives.

That's fine for a one-off. It hurts when the template keeps changing. Think shared CI workflows, lint configs, a service skeleton your team uses everywhere. Someone fixes the CI in the template, and now there are twenty projects with the old version, each with its own local edits. Copying the fix by hand gets old fast.

Copier's answer is to remember how the project was made and replay the template's changes on top of it. rootstock does the same.

What an update looks like

rootstock new renders the template and writes a small record, .rootstock.toml, next to your files: the template source, the tag and exact commit, your answers, and the list of files it wrote.

$ rootstock new gh:acme/service-template my-app --data project_name=my-app --defaults
created my-app from gh:acme/service-template v1.0.0

Later the template ships v1.1.0. It bumps actions/checkout in CI and adds --all-targets to the test and lint targets in the Makefile. Meanwhile you've added a fmt target and made clippy stricter.

$ rootstock update
updated to v1.1.0
markers Makefile
1 conflict

The CI bump and the new test line went in on their own. Your fmt target is still there. The one line you both changed is marked:

lint:
<<<<<<< project
    cargo clippy -- -D warnings
=======
    cargo clippy --all-targets
>>>>>>> template v1.1.0

You fix it, run rootstock check, commit. The update is a plain diff in git, so it's easy to review and easy to throw away.

How the merge works

Under the hood rootstock renders the template twice in temp directories: the old version with the answers from the record (the base), and the new version with the current answers (the target). Then it goes path by path and compares base, target and what's in your project.

If only the template changed a file, you get the template's version. If only you changed it, nothing happens. If both did, the text goes through git merge-file, which is what Copier uses too. I picked the git CLI over a merge library on purpose: the result matches Copier, the markers look like the ones everyone already knows, and your own git config doesn't leak into it.

Some cases can't be merged at all, and rootstock doesn't pretend they can. A binary file you edited keeps your copy and gets the template's version next to it as name.rootstock-new. A file you deleted but the template changed stays deleted and gets reported. Files marked as starter (a README, say) are written once and never touched again.

Want to change an answer later? rootstock update --data ci=false renders the base with the old answers and the target with the new ones, even when the version stays the same.

Conflicts are an exit code

Every case that needs a human ends with exit code 2 and one line per problem on stdout: markers Makefile, binary logo.png and so on. Everything else goes to stderr.

That makes it easy to automate. My harness template (agent tooling, hooks and CI for my projects) has a daily workflow in each project that runs rootstock update, opens a PR and labels it when the exit code is 2. Clean minor and patch updates merge themselves once CI is green. The conflicting ones wait for me.

rootstock check runs in CI without network access and fails on leftover markers or side files, so a half-resolved conflict can't slip into main.

Coming from Copier

rootstock import-copier converts a Copier template, a project generated by Copier, or both if they live in the same directory. It writes nothing unless the whole conversion succeeds. Old template tags don't need converting – update reads versions that only have copier.yml and converts them in memory.

For harness I checked that the converted template renders byte for byte like Copier 9.19 for every combination of its answers. That was my bar for calling the import done.

What it doesn't do (yet)

rootstock supports the part of Copier my templates use. _migrations, Jinja extensions and some question types aren't there, and the import stops with the full list if your template needs them. It's v0.1.0, so expect rough edges.

Try it 

cargo install rootstock --locked

There are also prebuilt binaries for Linux (static, musl), macOS and Windows on GitHub Releases. The only thing it needs at runtime is git.

If you maintain templates and something here doesn't fit how you work, open an issue. I'd like to hear about it.

bodasooqa / rootstock

Create projects from versioned git templates and update them by three-way merge, without losing the project's edits. A single Rust binary, like Copier.

Project templates that keep growing after you use them.

Create a project from a versioned git template, then update it to every new template version
with a real three-way merge: your edits stay, the template's improvements arrive, conflicts are never silent.

Website · Install · Quick start · How updates work · Commands · Writing a template · Coming from Copier

In grafting, the rootstock is the root system, and the scion is the branch grafted onto it. The scion grows its own way, and the root keeps feeding it. A rootstock project works the same way. The template is the root and the project is the scion: the project goes its own way, and improvements to the template keep reaching it.

Why rootstock

Most scaffolding tools stop once the project is created. That is fine for a one-off, but not for a template that keeps changing: shared CI, lint…

description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

title: Why I replaced looping MP3s with live Web Audio API math for my focus timer (Cadenzato)
description:
Every developer knows the pain of trying to get into a deep coding flow state, throwing on a 3-hour rain or brown noise stream, and getting hit with two problems:

  1. A sudden loud mid-roll ad that shatters your mental stack right when you are debugging a race condition.
  2. Audio loop fatigue. Most ambient focus apps and streams just loop a 60-second MP3 file. Because the human auditory cortex is wired to detect patterns, the moment your ear subconsciously catches the loop seam repeating, your brain wakes up on alert.

On top of that, most visual study timers run unthrottled canvas loops in the background, eating 25% of your GPU and spinning up your laptop fans while your IDE is open.

So I built Cadenzato (https://cadenzato.com), a free, zero-signup focus sanctuary in the browser that solves both problems using pure math and the Web Audio API.

How the procedural audio engine works:

Instead of fetching and looping static audio files, Cadenzato synthesizes every sound wave live in the browser using a custom Web Audio API graph:

  1. Live Brownian Noise (-6dB/octave):
    White noise has equal energy across all frequencies, which sounds like a harsh high-pitched hiss after 20 minutes. By integrating white noise samples over time inside a Float32Array buffer (with a leaky integrator to prevent DC offset drift), we get deep Brown Noise that rolls off high frequencies at -6dB per octave. Because the samples are calculated dynamically, it never repeats a loop.

  2. Procedural Rain & Hearth Fire:
    Rainfall is synthesized by routing pink-filtered noise through dual BiquadFilterNode bandpass stages with randomized micro-transients for individual droplet acoustics. Hearth fire layers low-frequency rumble below 180Hz with stochastic high-passed crackle envelopes.

  3. 40Hz Gamma Binaural & Isochronic Pulse:
    For heavy architectural work, a pair of precision Sine Wave OscillatorNodes (200Hz left ear, 240Hz right ear) creates a gentle 40Hz gamma frequency differential without fatiguing the ear.

How we kept background CPU/GPU at 0%:

A focus tool should never slow down your compiler or IDE. Cadenzato includes 5 live 60fps HTML5 Canvas scenes (Warm Cafe, Botanical Grass, Ocean Drift, Rainfall, and Obsidian), but listens to the browser Page Visibility API (document.hidden). The instant you Alt+Tab back to VS Code or switch windows, the canvas render loop suspends completely to 0% GPU usage while the Web Audio synthesizer continues running on its dedicated audio thread.

No accounts, no ads, no paywalls:

You can open it, press Space to start a 50/10 or 90/15 deep work block, mix your audio channels, and get straight to coding.

Live app: https://cadenzato.com

I would love to hear what timer intervals (25/5 vs 50/10 vs 90/15) and audio setups other devs here use when writing code!

title: Case Converter: Batch-Renaming PascalCase React Components to kebab-case Without Breaking Imports
description:
Last Tuesday we agreed on a file naming rule. Components move to kebab-case, so ChatWidget.tsx becomes chat-widget.tsx, and the old PascalCase files disappear.

The trigger was mundane. Two teammates on macOS kept hitting broken checkouts because DateRange.tsx and daterange.tsx are two files in CI on Linux, but a single file on their laptops. Same repo, two views of it.

Eleven components. Sounds like one slow afternoon.

I spent most of that afternoon on three problems that have nothing to do with converting case: imports pointing at old paths, Git refusing to notice half my renames, and XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx coming out of my first script as xmlhttprequestpanel.tsx.

Here is what worked, in Python 3.11.1 and Node v22.13.1, plus the shortcut for small batches.

Method 1: a Python 3.11.1 script that keeps Git history

Plain mv loses the fact that a rename happened. git mv keeps it. My script runs git mv per file, then rewrites every import that points at an old name.

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SPLITTER = re.compile(r"(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])")

# Digits next to acronyms: the splitter cannot guess these.
OVERRIDES = {
    "UserAvatar2FA": "user-avatar-2fa",
    "OAuth2Callback": "oauth2-callback",
}

root = Path(sys.argv[1])
plan = {}
for src in sorted(root.glob("*.tsx")):
    target = root / f"{OVERRIDES.get(src.stem) or '-'.join(p.lower() for p in SPLITTER.split(src.stem))}.tsx"
    if target.name != src.name:
        plan[src] = target

for src, dst in plan.items():
    subprocess.run(["git", "mv", str(src), str(dst)], check=True)
    print(f"{src.name:26} -> {dst.name}")

edited = 0
for path in root.glob("*.tsx"):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for old, new in ((s.stem, d.stem) for s, d in plan.items()):
        text = re.sub(rf"([./]){old}(?=\")", rf"\g<1>{new}", text)
    if text != path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"):
        path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        edited += 1

print(f"\nrenamed {len(plan)} files, rewrote imports in {edited} files")

Run it against the component folder, then check that nothing still refers to the old paths.

$ python3 rename_components.py src
ChatWidget.tsx             -> chat-widget.tsx
DateRange.tsx              -> date-range.tsx
Grid2Col.tsx               -> grid2-col.tsx
HTTPClientErrors.tsx       -> http-client-errors.tsx
InvoiceLineItemV2.tsx      -> invoice-line-item-v2.tsx
OAuth2Callback.tsx         -> oauth2-callback.tsx
PDFViewer.tsx              -> pdf-viewer.tsx
SideNavBar.tsx             -> side-nav-bar.tsx
UserAvatar2FA.tsx          -> user-avatar-2fa.tsx
Utils.tsx                  -> utils.tsx
XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx    -> xml-http-request-panel.tsx

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 11 files

$ grep -rn 'from "./[A-Z]' src/*.tsx || echo "(none)"
(none)

Every import got rewritten, so the grep comes back clean, and git mv keeps the batch as 11 renames rather than 11 deletions plus 11 untracked files.

The splitter does the real work. (?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z]) cuts between a lowercase letter or digit and an uppercase one. (?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z]) cuts before the last capital of an acronym run, which is what turns XMLHttp into XML-Http. Both are zero-width assertions, documented in the Python re reference.

Two names refuse to cooperate. UserAvatar2FA splits into user-avatar2-fa and OAuth2Callback into o-auth2-callback, because the digit rule cannot tell whether a digit attaches forward (2FA) or backward (OAuth2). I gave up on solving that inside the regex and pinned both names in OVERRIDES.

Method 2: the same batch rename in Node v22.13.1

No Python on the machine? The logic ports over directly.

import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { readdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const root = process.argv[2] ?? "src";
const OVERRIDES = new Map([
  ["UserAvatar2FA", "user-avatar-2fa"],
  ["OAuth2Callback", "oauth2-callback"],
]);
const SPLIT = /(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])/;
const toKebab = (stem) =>
  OVERRIDES.get(stem) ?? stem.split(SPLIT).map((p) => p.toLowerCase()).join("-");

const candidates = readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })
  .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".tsx"))
  .sort();

const mapping = new Map();
for (const name of candidates) {
  const stem = name.slice(0, -4);
  const target = `${toKebab(stem)}.tsx`;
  if (target === name) continue;
  execFileSync("git", ["mv", path.join(root, name), path.join(root, target)]);
  mapping.set(stem, target.slice(0, -4));
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(26)} -> ${target}`);
}

let edited = 0;
for (const name of readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })) {
  if (!name.endsWith(".tsx")) continue;
  const file = path.join(root, name);
  const before = readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  let after = before;
  for (const [from, to] of mapping) {
    after = after.replaceAll(new RegExp(`([./])${from}(?=")`, "g"), `$1${to}`);
  }
  if (after !== before) {
    writeFileSync(file, after);
    edited += 1;
  }
}

console.log(`\nrenamed ${mapping.size} files, rewrote imports in ${edited} files`);

String.prototype.split accepts lookbehind in V8, so both assertions work unchanged (MDN covers the lookbehind syntax). The output matched Python line for line: 11 renames, 11 files rewritten, zero leftover imports.

Spot-check the odd names against the Utilvy case converter before trusting either script. If it disagrees with your expectation, the script is usually the wrong one.

Method 3: convert names in a browser tab

Two or three files? Skip the script entirely. Paste the component names into a free case converter, pick kebab-case, copy the result, and pair them up by hand.

It handles whole lists in one paste, so ten names are no slower than one. It runs locally in the tab, which matters on an unreleased branch.

Above a handful of files, go back to a script. The browser gives you the new names, but someone still has to rewrite eleven import blocks, and a web page cannot do that part.

Three things that cost me the afternoon

Straight lowercasing destroys acronym boundaries

My very first line was this:

>>> "XMLHttpRequestPanel".lower()
'xmlhttprequestpanel'

Same for HTTPClientErrors turning into httpclienterrors and PDFViewer into pdfviewer. Every word boundary vanishes, and there is no way back from a flattened string. This browser-based tool keeps those boundaries intact, which makes it a decent oracle when you want to argue with your own regex. Split first, lowercase second.

Renaming the file is only half the job, and the failure is silent

My first rewrite used a guard I thought was clever:

text = re.sub(rf'(?<!/){old}(?=")', new, text)

Every import path in a TypeScript file starts with ./. The guard rejected all of them, and the script printed:

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 0 files

Eleven renames, zero rewrites, exit code 0. Nothing broke visibly until the next build. Use a capture group instead of a lookbehind, then grep for from "./[A-Z] before you commit.

Case-insensitive filesystems hide case-only renames

Utils.tsx to utils.tsx changes nothing but case. Fine on Linux, invisible on macOS and Windows, where Git is configured with core.ignorecase. Here is the reproduction on an ext4 disk:

$ git config core.ignorecase true
$ mv Utils.tsx utils.tsx
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx

Only a deletion. git ls-files still lists Utils.tsx, while import Utils from "./utils" points at a file Git no longer tracks. Flip the flag and Git sees both halves:

$ git config core.ignorecase false
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx
?? utils.tsx

On macOS, step through a temp name: git mv Utils.tsx tmp-utils.tsx && git mv tmp-utils.tsx utils.tsx. Or do the whole batch in CI where the filesystem takes casing seriously.

Pick your approach

Scenario Approach Handled 11 files in
Whole repo to migrate Python 3.11.1 script + git mv one run, imports rewritten
Python unavailable Node v22.13.1 equivalent one run, identical output
Two or three names Browser-based kebab conversion under a minute

Verify in this order: grep for leftover PascalCase imports, then read git status on a case-sensitive filesystem, then commit.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

title: Introducing Vedha: New Testing framework for Agentic World. Test your web app with an AI agent in 5 minutes (and catch the bugs it would miss)
description:
AI agents are good at clicking through a web app. They're bad at knowing whether it actually worked. An agent sees "Order placed" on the screen and reports success, even when the API behind it returned 500 and saved nothing.

This tutorial sets up an AI agent that tests your app in a real browser and checks what the server did. You'll go from zero to a test you can keep in CI in about five minutes.

We'll use Vedha, an open-source MCP server built on Playwright. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and any other MCP client.

Step 1: Add Vedha to your agent (1 minute)

In Claude Code:

claude mcp add vedha -- npx -y @vedhajs/mcp --allow-domain localhost --out ./vedha-out

For Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop, add this to your MCP config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "vedha": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@vedhajs/mcp", "--allow-domain", "localhost", "--out", "./vedha-out"]
    }
  }
}

Two things to note:

  • --allow-domain localhost is required: the agent can only browse the domains you list. Point it at your dev server, not the open web.
  • If you've never used Playwright on this machine, run npx playwright install chromium once.

Optional: install the agent skill, which teaches the agent how to test with Vedha (declare checks, mark writes, never retry an unknown outcome):

npx skills add HMAKT99/VEDHA

Step 2: Ask the agent to test something (1 minute)

Start your app, then ask:

Test the checkout on localhost:3000: place an order for Ada and confirm it worked.

The agent opens the page and works through the flow with vedha_act. Each call is one browser action, and it can say what success looks like. Here is the call an agent sends to fill the form and submit it:

{
  "op": "fill", "intent": "enter name", "target": { "label": "Name" }, "value": "Ada",
  "then": [{
    "op": "click", "intent": "place the order",
    "target": { "role": "button", "name": "Place order" },
    "mutating": true,
    "expect": { "text_contains": "Order placed" }
  }]
}

mutating: true tells Vedha the click changes data, so it should check what the server did, not just the page.

On a healthy app, this is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: verified
effect: server confirmed (POST /api/orders 201; read-back /api/orders confirms POST /api/orders)
changed on the page (3 added, 3 removed):
  + status: Order placed

Vedha saw the 201, then read the order list back to confirm the order is really there.

Step 3: Watch it catch a bug the page hides (1 minute)

Now the same test against a broken backend: the API returns 500, but the frontend still shows "Order placed". This is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: failed (health_check_failed): declared checks passed, but the page reported: POST /api/orders returned 500
hint: treat this action as failed: the server or page reported an error even if the page looks fine
requests: POST /api/orders 500
  + status: Order placed
open failure: "place the order" - declared checks passed, but the page reported:
POST /api/orders returned 500. Do not report success unless a later step fixed it.

"Order placed" is on the page, and the agent's own check passed. Vedha still reports the step as failed, says why, and reminds the agent not to claim success. A browser tool that only checks the screen would have reported a pass.

Two more things Vedha does here without being asked:

  • If a submit times out and Vedha can't tell whether the order went through, it reports outcome_unknown and refuses to click "Place order" again until a read-only check settles it. No duplicate orders from a retrying agent.
  • The agent can check server state without leaving the page with vedha_probe (for example GET /api/orders).

Step 4: Turn the run into a Playwright test (1 minute)

Once a flow is verified, ask the agent:

Save that as a Playwright test.

It calls vedha_promote, which writes a plain @playwright/test spec from the verified steps. This is the real output for the order flow above:

// Generated by Vedha from an explored session. Review before committing.
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("places an order", async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step("open the shop", async () => {
    await page.goto("/");
  });
  await test.step("enter name", async () => {
    await page.getByLabel("Name", { exact: true }).fill("Ada");
  });
  await test.step("place the order", async () => {
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Place order", exact: true }).click();
    await expect(page.locator("body")).toContainText("Order placed");
    await expect.poll(async () => {
      const res = await page.request.get("/api/orders");
      const body = await res.json();
      const items = Array.isArray(body) ? body : [body];
      return items.some((it) =>
        Object.entries({ name: "Ada", qty: 1, product: "Widget" }).every(([k, val]) => it[k] === val),
      );
    }).toBe(true);
  });
});

Notice the last assertion: because Vedha confirmed the order on the server during the run, the generated test checks the server too, not just the text. It also lists its assumptions at the top, so review it before committing.

Step 5: Keep it honest in CI (1 minute)

Commit the spec and run it with your normal Playwright setup. One more line makes the rest of your suite safer too:

npm install -D @vedhajs/playwright-test

import { test, expect } from "@vedhajs/playwright-test"; // instead of "@playwright/test"

With that import, any test whose own checks pass while the app answers with a 5xx, or a write request fails, fails instead of going green. That covers tests written by your agent and by people. (More on guard mode here.)

What you get

  • An agent that tests in a real browser and reports verified, failed or unknown, never "looked fine".
  • Bugs caught that the screen hides: 5xx behind a success message, rejected writes, writes that weren't stored (where the API allows a read-back).
  • Plain Playwright tests to keep, with server checks included.

How much difference does it make? In a small pilot (one model, held-out tasks, 3 trials each), the agent missed 9 seeded bugs with Vedha against 26 with Playwright MCP, using about 30% fewer tokens. Details and limits here.

Try the demo without your own app 

git clone https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA && cd VEDHA
pnpm install && pnpm build
npx tsx examples/demo/run.ts

Repo, docs and benchmark data: https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA (Apache-2.0)

If you try it on your app, I'd like to hear what it caught, and anything it got wrong.

title: Building an Asynchronous WhatsApp Cloud API Webhook Gateway with Sub-50ms Latency
description:
When building production enterprise messaging applications, handling real-time incoming events from the Meta WhatsApp Cloud API requires speed, resilience, and strict cryptographic verification.

Many engineering teams default to legacy Business Solution Providers (BSPs) that introduce intermediate aggregator servers, per-message markups, and artificial queue bottlenecks. At AIsoule, engineered by PrimeSkill Solutions Private Limited (Scheme No. 51, Indore, MP 452006, India), we architected our platform directly on Meta's native Cloud API infrastructure, bypassing all third-party aggregators to achieve 0% markup and sub-50ms event processing latency.

In this deep dive, we'll walk through the implementation of a high-throughput, event-driven WhatsApp Cloud API webhook gateway with HMAC SHA-256 signature verification and real-time audio signaling.

1. The Core Architecture Challenge

Every incoming WhatsApp event—whether it's an inbound customer text, message delivery status (sent, delivered, read), button click, or media upload—is dispatched by Meta's servers as an HTTPS POST request to your configured webhook URL.

┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Meta WhatsApp Cloud API │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ HTTPS POST (JSON Payload + X-Hub-Signature-256)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   AIsoule Edge Gateway  │ ──► Verify HMAC Signature (<2ms)
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ Fast-Ack: HTTP 200 OK (<15ms)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Async Processing Worker │ ──► CRM Routing & Live WebRTC Signaling
└─────────────────────────┘

If your server takes longer than 3,000 milliseconds to respond with an HTTP 200 OK, Meta considers the request timed out and begins aggressive exponential retry loops. Under heavy broadcast spikes (thousands of replies per minute), synchronous database writes will quickly exhaust your connection pool and cause cascading failures.

2. Step 1: Webhook Challenge Verification (GET Request)

When first registering your webhook in the Meta Developer Portal, Meta sends a GET request with challenge query parameters. Here is the verification logic:

const crypto = require("crypto");
const express = require("express");
const app = express();

const VERIFY_TOKEN = process.env.WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN || "aisoule_secure_webhook_token_2026";

app.get("/api/whatsapp/webhook", (req, res) => {
  const mode = req.query["hub.mode"];
  const token = req.query["hub.verify_token"];
  const challenge = req.query["hub.challenge"];

  if (mode === "subscribe" && token === VERIFY_TOKEN) {
    console.log("[AIsoule Gateway] Webhook successfully verified by Meta.");
    return res.status(200).send(challenge);
  }

  return res.sendStatus(403);
});

3. Step 2: Cryptographic HMAC SHA-256 Signature Validation

Security is paramount. You must verify that incoming POST payloads originate from Meta and were not spoofed or intercepted. Meta attaches an X-Hub-Signature-256 header formatted as sha256=<hash>.

// Middleware to capture raw buffer for HMAC hashing
app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req, res, buf) => {
    req.rawBody = buf;
  }
}));

const APP_SECRET = process.env.META_APP_SECRET;

function verifyMetaSignature(req, res, next) {
  const signature = req.headers["x-hub-signature-256"];
  if (!signature) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Missing X-Hub-Signature-256 header" });
  }

  const expectedSignature = "sha256=" + crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", APP_SECRET)
    .update(req.rawBody)
    .digest("hex");

  if (!crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(signature), Buffer.from(expectedSignature))) {
    console.error("[Security Alert] Invalid webhook HMAC signature!");
    return res.status(403).json({ error: "Invalid signature" });
  }

  next();
}

Using crypto.timingSafeEqual prevents timing attacks that could reveal secret bits.

4. Step 3: Fast-Ack Asynchronous Queue Pattern

To guarantee sub-50ms latency and prevent Meta webhook retries, your gateway should return res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED") immediately after cryptographic verification, offloading the event payload to a worker queue:

const { Queue } = require("bullmq");
const messageQueue = new Queue("whatsapp-messages", {
  connection: { host: "localhost", port: 6379 }
});

app.post("/api/whatsapp/webhook", verifyMetaSignature, async (req, res) => {
  // FAST-ACK: Return 200 OK immediately
  res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED");

  const body = req.body;
  if (body.object === "whatsapp_business_account") {
    for (const entry of body.entry || []) {
      for (const change of entry.changes || []) {
        if (change.value && change.value.messages) {
          // Push to asynchronous worker queue
          await messageQueue.add("process-message", {
            businessAccountId: entry.id,
            data: change.value
          }, {
            removeOnComplete: true,
            attempts: 3
          });
        }
      }
    }
  }
});

5. Bridging Chat to Live WebRTC Voice Calling

One of the standout architectural innovations we built into AIsoule is native in-browser WebRTC voice calling.

Traditionally, when a high-intent customer chatting on WhatsApp needs immediate human support, agents must dial an international PSTN number, incurring telecom carrier fees. With our architecture, agents can generate a secure single-use WebRTC voice signaling session link directly inside the WhatsApp chat thread:

  1. Agent generates a session token via our multi-agent conversational CRM.
  2. The customer receives an interactive WhatsApp action button.
  3. Clicking the button opens a secure, browser-native WebRTC audio call connected directly to the agent's live browser desk—delivering HD audio with zero telecom toll charges.

6. Real-World Cost Benchmarks: Zero Markup vs Legacy BSPs

By implementing a direct Meta Cloud API pipeline, organizations eliminate aggregator markups entirely:
