title: Why My ESF-551 Scale Kept Disconnecting from Home Assistant: Japan's Measurement Act
description:
I connected an Etekcity ESF-551, a BLE body scale, to Home Assistant, and not a single measurement arrived. I had Claude Code chase the cause, and it ended at Article 9 of Japan's Measurement Act. Units sold in Japan have the unit switch removed because of that law.

I know nothing about firmware or law. What I did was step on the scale and decide what to have it look into next. Without AI, I couldn't have done this investigation.

Nothing comes back when I step on it

I used the HACS integration etekcity_fitness_scale_ble, which wraps etekcity_esf551_ble==0.8.4. Claude Code read the log: it showed the integration connecting, reading the HW/SW versions, writing the unit command a5220305002b0163a10000 (unit 0, kg), and getting disconnected about 0.4 seconds later. Then it reconnected and did it again. No notification ever came when I stepped on the scale, and every sensor stayed unavailable.

It happened even when the command changed nothing, kg to kg.

Skip one command and it works

I left the narrowing down to it too. Claude Code subscribed to 0000fff1 from another machine with plain bleak and left out only the unit write. No disconnect. While I stood on the scale, 22-byte notifications arrived about every 45 ms, around 80 of them.

So Claude Code wrote a local patch that passes display_unit=None and skips the write. All 14 sensors filled in. I had it write the upstream issue too, and filed it (etekcity_esf551_ble #15).

Up to here it was a story about fixing a library bug.

Only the US manual has a unit setting

I had it look for why only the Japanese version lacks a unit switch. The VeSync app has no unit setting, while the US manual has the steps.

Putting the back label next to the US spec showed this was a different market variant, not just a firmware revision. Japanese devices and IoT, again, I thought.

US ESF-551 The unit I bought in Japan
Capacity 400 lb / 180 kg 2–150 kg
Resolution 0.05 lb / 0.02 kg 100 g
Radio approval FCC ID 2AB22-ESF551 Giteki R 210-252428
Measurement Act none household "正" mark

Claude Code also pulled the Measurement Act from the e-Gov law API and read it. Article 9 forbids selling, or displaying for sale, a measuring instrument marked in non-statutory units. A scale that can show lb or st can't be sold in Japan, so manufacturers drop the unit-switch feature from the Japanese firmware. Weighing myself is neither a transaction nor a certification, so Article 8 doesn't touch the user. Only the seller is bound.

The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's FY2015 test-purchase report even has a real case: a vendor who didn't know pounds and stones were prohibited was told to seal the device so it couldn't be switched.

Whether the disconnect is deliberate, I don't know

What I know is why the Japanese version has no unit switch. I can't tell whether the disconnect itself is intended, or just firmware that doesn't know the command and drops the link sloppily. Removing the feature is fine. I just suspect it was removed carelessly. I only have one unit, so I can't say that model identifier 12 in the manufacturer data marks the Japanese variant. For upstream I suggested registering identifier 12 with display_unit_settable=False so the write is skipped, and left the call to the maintainer.

An experiment that sends an unknown opcode to see how it disconnects is still undone.

Fixed the next day

The day after I filed the issue, the maintainer replied.

That's interesting to know about that Japanese regulation. That would explain it I guess, and since the option doesn't even show up in the app that pretty much confirms it I think.

Library v0.8.8 and the HA integration 0.8.3 came out the same day. I updated the integration to 0.8.3, removed my local patch, stepped on the scale, and the measurements came through. That was surprisingly fast, and I'm grateful.

Self-hosting Home Assistant is a chore. But it brings lessons like this one, from a bathroom scale all the way to a statute, and I'm glad I do it.

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

title: Getting only the new DOIs from the Crossref API every day: dates, cursors and rate limits
description:
AI disclosure: this post was drafted with AI assistance. I ran every request and every number below myself against the live Crossref REST API on November 1, 2026, and checked the code and tests before publishing.

I wanted a boring thing: every morning, a CSV of the journal articles that got a DOI since yesterday, for a handful of journals, and never the same DOI twice. Crossref's REST API is free, needs no key, and held 188,319,891 records when I asked, so it should be one request. It is close, but it took me a few wrong turns. Here are the ones worth knowing about.

The finished script is about 400 lines of standard-library Python with a daily GitHub Actions workflow. It is my repo, free and MIT licensed: https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed

1. Pick the right date: created, not published, not indexed

/works has four families of date filters, and for "what is new" they give very different answers. Here are the counts for a single day, 30 October 2026, all work types, each filter with from-… and until-… set to that day. The created count is stable; the other three drift a little as records change, so they are rounded:

Filter Works on 30 Oct 2026
from-created-date / until-created-date 86,622
from-index-date / until-index-date about 789,000
from-update-date / until-update-date about 155,000
from-pub-date / until-pub-date about 18,900
  • created is when the DOI was first registered. That is the one you want for "new".
  • index changes whenever Crossref re-indexes a record, including citation counts. Nine times more rows, nearly all old works.
  • update is when the publisher last deposited a change to the metadata.
  • pub-date is the publication date the publisher wrote down. It can be a year, a month, or a print issue date months away. "Published yesterday" misses most of what appeared yesterday and includes old material deposited late.

For scale, type:journal-article with created gave 26,945 on 28 October, 29,785 on 29 October and 26,966 on 30 October. On Saturday 31 October it was 16,641. Filter by journal, publisher or funder unless you really want ~9 MB of CSV a day.

2. Always set both ends of the range

from-created-date:2026-10-30 on its own means "from then until now". That is fine today and silently wrong when you re-run a past day. Set until-created-date too; both ends are inclusive.

The filters also take a time: from-created-date:2026-10-30T12:00:00,until-created-date:2026-10-30T12:59:59 returned 2,829 works for that hour.

3. Page with a cursor, and you can still sort

rows maxes out at 1,000. rows=1001 gets a 400:

Integer specified as 1001 but must be a positive integer less than or equal to 1000.

offset stops at 10,000 (offset must be ... less than or equal to 9999. Use the cursor parameter ...). So use deep paging:

  1. Send cursor=* with the first request.
  2. Read message.next-cursor from the answer and send it back with the next request.
  3. Stop when a page comes back empty.

I was not sure cursors keep a sort order, so I tested it. With sort=created&order=asc and rows=2, three cursor pages came back in ascending created order, with the same DOIs as a single rows=6 request.

Reading oldest first matters for a feed with a cap. If you stop after N new works, the next run can carry on where you stopped instead of rereading the newest ones.

params = {
    "filter": "from-created-date:2026-10-31,until-created-date:2026-11-01,"
              "type:journal-article,issn:0028-0836",
    "rows": 1000,
    "cursor": cursor,                # "*" first, then message["next-cursor"]
    "sort": "created",
    "order": "asc",
    "select": "DOI,type,title,container-title,ISSN,publisher,member,created,published",
}

select= keeps responses small. A field name it does not know returns a 400 that lists the valid ones, which is handy.

4. The 2026 rate limits are lower than old blog posts say

Crossref changed its limits in July 2026. For list and filter requests like these:

  • 1 request per second in the public pool;
  • 3 per second in the polite pool;
  • polite-pool limits counted per mailto email address.

The response headers tell you where you are. On a public-pool request I saw:

x-rate-limit-limit: 1
x-rate-limit-interval: 1s
x-concurrency-limit: 1
x-api-pool: public-array

So my client:

  • sends one request at a time, at most once a second;
  • slows down further if those headers ask for less.

I still hit a real 429. I ran the script twice back to back from the shell, each process started fresh, and the first request of the second came too soon after the last request of the first. The fix is the usual one:

  • honour Retry-After (seconds or an HTTP date);
  • otherwise back off 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds;
  • give up after 5 tries;
  • retry 5xx and network errors the same way.

A 403, or an answer that is not JSON, is different. Stop and write nothing.

5. Say who you are

To get into the polite pool, add mailto=you@example.org to the query string or the User-Agent. I do both, with a User-Agent that names the tool and links to its source:

crossref-new-works-feed/1.0 (+https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed; mailto:you@example.org)

Use your own address. The limit is per email, so a shared one in a popular template would put everyone in the same bucket. I also validate it loosely and drop it if it does not look like an email. (api.crossref.org/robots.txt was a 404 when I checked, which means no rules, but the script checks it anyway.)

6. "New" arrives late, so overlap your window

A DOI's created timestamp is when it was registered, not when the API can serve it. The newest work I could see was 20 to 30 minutes behind its created time. Indexing can take longer on a busy day.

So a daily run should not ask for "yesterday" only. Mine asks for yesterday plus today and lets a seen-DOI list drop repeats. A work is only missed if it reaches the API more than a day late.

7. query is a relevance search, not a filter

query.bibliographic=perovskite solar over two days matched 246 works. Only 29 had both words in the title. If you sort by date (as a feed must), you no longer get the most relevant first, so you get all the loose matches in date order.

My fix was a client-side --title-word check: all the words must be in the title. Rejected works are not marked as seen, in case you loosen the check later.

8. Small normalisation traps

  • ISSNs. issn:0028-0836, issn:00280836 and Nature's electronic ISSN issn:1476-4687 all returned the same 88 works for 25 October to 1 November. Normalise user input to NNNN-NNNC anyway, with an uppercase X check digit.
  • DOIs are case-insensitive. /works/10.1038/S41586-026-11328-3 returns the lower-case DOI. Store them lower-cased, or your dedupe will see two works.
  • Dates come as date-parts. That means [[2026]], [[2026, 10]] or [[2026, 10, 25]]. Keep the precision you were given rather than inventing a day.
  • Titles and ISSNs are lists. A work can have no title or several ISSNs. I join ISSNs with |.
  • Overlapping windows return duplicates by design. Dedupe by DOI before you write, both within a run and across runs.

9. Finding the IDs to filter on

You rarely know a member ID or funder ID by heart. The API has lookups. They are fuzzy searches, so the best match is not always first; check the names in the results:

  • /journals?query=nature gives the ISSNs, used as issn:.
  • /members?query=springer gives member IDs, used as member:.
  • /funders?query=national science foundation gives funder IDs; prefix the id with 10.13039/ for funder:.

What the feed looks like

The first run for Nature over seven days found 88 works with 2 requests (robots.txt plus one page). The second run found 0 new. On the broad side, all journal articles since midnight with --max-works 1000 stopped at 1,000. The next run carried on and wrote the next 1,000, rather than the same ones again.

doi,type,title,journal,issn,publisher,member,published,created,url,first_seen
10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3,journal-article,ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2,Nature,0028-0836|1476-4687,Springer Science and Business Media LLC,297,2026-10-25,2026-10-25T07:01:31Z,https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3,2026-11-01T16:37:25Z

The GitHub Actions workflow runs it once a day and commits the CSVs. One catch: GitHub turns off scheduled workflows in public repositories after 60 days without activity.

Code, tests (offline with saved Crossref responses, plus a few live checks) and the workflow are MIT licensed: https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed

Numbers in this post come from requests I made on November 1, 2026; Crossref's counts and limits change, so check the response headers on your own requests.

title: The inference endpoint is not the model
description:
Serving a model is a systems problem wearing a machine-learning costume.

The model is maybe 20% of the endpoint. The other 80% is queueing, timeouts, batching, retries, and the failure mode where a 2-second p99 quietly turns into a 30-second one because the batch got too large.

Three things I now do by default:

  1. Bound the batch by time, not just size. A batch that waits for 8 items is a batch that waits forever at night.
  2. Separate the queue from the HTTP request. Return a job id, let the client poll. It makes backpressure explicit instead of mysterious.
  3. Add a fallback that returns a safe default after the deadline. A slower answer is usually better than a hung request.

The model accuracy curve is the interesting part of the job. The p99 is the part that wakes you up.

Curious how other people handle the fallback: cached response, heuristic, or just an error?

title: Controlled input work depends on state placement: compare 10, 100, and 500 fields
description:
Field count alone does not determine whether a form should use controlled or uncontrolled inputs. Even with controlled inputs, placing state in each field meant editing one field invoked only one input component.

The experiment compared parent-owned values, field-local state, and DOM-owned values across forms with 10, 100, and 500 fields. Reducing repeated component work requires looking at state placement as well as whether inputs are controlled.

Count component calls for the same input operation

These are the three field components. trace is an experiment counter, not application state.

function ControlledField({ index, value, onChange }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} value={value} onChange={onChange} />;
}
function LocalField({ index }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue(index));
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} value={value} onChange={event => {
    trace.fieldChanges++;
    setValue(event.target.value);
  }} />;
}
function UncontrolledField({ index }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} defaultValue={initialValue(index)} />;
}

The parent-owned version keeps a values array in state, replaces the changed position, and passes values to every input. The local version updates state inside LocalField. The uncontrolled version supplies an initial defaultValue and reads values through FormData on submission.

Field count and order stay fixed within each condition. The fixture uses position keys and does not delete, insert, or reorder fields.

Each input has a distinct name. A browser fill operation replaced the first field's field-0 value with edited. This was not a character-by-character typing test. Both controlled versions recorded one onChange call for that operation.

The measurement is the additional component-function calls caused by the edit, excluding initial rendering.

State placement Fields Additional parent-form calls Additional input-component calls
Parent-owned 10 1 10
Parent-owned 100 1 100
Parent-owned 500 1 500
Field-local state 10 0 1
Field-local state 100 0 1
Field-local state 500 0 1
DOM-owned 10 0 0
DOM-owned 100 0 0
DOM-owned 500 0 0

The production build used no React Compiler, memo, or Strict Mode. The table therefore compares the same unoptimized structure. Zero input-component calls does not mean the browser performs no input or painting work. Execution time, FPS, and memory use were not measured.

The React input reference describes updating a controlled value in onChange and moving state to the part of the tree that needs it. The observed results also show that controlled inputs do not inherently require the entire parent to rerun.

Verify collected values too

All 9 conditions produced as many FormData entries as there were fields, with edited as the first value after editing. This did not aggregate all field-local values into parent React state simultaneously. It collected values already reflected in the DOM using the submission method chosen for this experiment.

Immediate previews of all fields or validation across fields require an additional decision about where values are read. This fixture contains independent text inputs only. It excludes form libraries, IME composition, and asynchronous validation.

The same reset button produced different outcomes

After editing, pressing a type="reset" button left edited in both controlled versions. The uncontrolled version returned to field-0.

Approach After HTML reset Explicit reset method used in the experiment
Parent state edited Set state to an array of initial values
Field-local state edited Change the form key to remount it
Uncontrolled field-0 Call form.reset()

Changing the key in the field-local version tests whether remounting restores initial values. Remounting also recreates component state below that point. It should not be applied unchanged when a reset must preserve focus or other state.

After an explicit reset, all three approaches showed field-0 in the first field. Treat native reset and React state initialization as separate operations, then verify reset behavior for the chosen value ownership. The form reference also covers event-based submission and reading values with FormData.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. The complete form fixture and results for the 9 conditions are available. These results do not establish that 500 fields always require uncontrolled inputs. Choose with both the values React needs during editing and the submission/reset behavior in view.

title: Don't DROP COLUMN while old app code still reads it
description:
Here is the failure.

You clean up a schema:

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_status;

The migration applies. New code is fine. Mid-deploy, an old app instance (or a Sidekiq worker that hasn't restarted yet) still runs a query that selects legacy_status. Rails may also have a cached schema that still lists the column. Requests start failing with "column does not exist" until every process has the new code and a fresh schema cache.

This is not a theoretical edge case. GitLab's "Avoiding downtime in migrations" guide opens the "Dropping columns" section with the same point: running processes expect those columns to exist, ActiveRecord caches the table schema at boot, and you need a multi-release sequence: ignore the column in code first, drop it in a later release, then remove the ignore rule after that.

Postgres itself makes the DDL look cheap. Per the ALTER TABLE docs, DROP COLUMN does not rewrite the table immediately; it marks the column invisible. The lock is still real, and the application failure mode is worse than the lock: code that still references the column breaks even when the statement finishes quickly.

The pattern that works

Change the schema in steps. Do not combine them into one locking "cleanup" migration.

  1. Ignore it (release M): remove every code reference, including model validations, and deploy code that ignores the column. GitLab's ignore_column is one form of this.
  2. Wait: make sure every instance, worker, and job is running that code. No process still reads or validates the column.
  3. Drop it (release M+1): only then run the drop. Remove the ignore rule in the release after that. 
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_status;

Same idea when you are adding shape instead of removing it: add the new column nullable, backfill in batches, then tighten constraints. Do not add NOT NULL and drop the old column in the same deploy as the code change that needs them.

When destructive SQL does show up in a migration file, read it twice: first work out exactly what gets dropped, then confirm the target names and that no app path still references them before you apply.

What reviewers should ask

  • Does any still-running binary select, update, or validate this column?
  • Are there views, triggers, or reporting queries that still name it?
  • Is this drop in the same release as the code that stopped using it? If yes, split the release.

If an AI agent writes your migrations, give it the same checks as a standing rule before it ever suggests applying a DROP COLUMN: confirm the column name, verify no app references, and split the change across releases instead of one combined cleanup.

A free Cursor hook that steers the agent's shell commands away from running prisma migrate reset and drizzle-kit push --force against a non-local database is here: https://site-export-rescue.pages.dev/cursor-prisma-drizzle-guard/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=dont-drop-column-while-old-code-still-reads-it. It doesn't touch your SQL files or block the CLI for humans; pair it with rules that make the agent flag DROP COLUMN before the migration lands.

Drafted with AI assistance from GitLab's avoiding-downtime migration guide, the PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE documentation, and our own migration review rules, and checked against them.

title: How Dependency Injection Works in Spring Boot: A Quick Walkthrough
description:
If you have written any Spring Boot code, you have seen this: a class asks for another class in its constructor, and somehow the right object is just there. Nobody called new. Nobody looked anything up. Let's see who does that work, with plain words and a tiny Spring Boot app you can run yourself.

The idea in one minute

  1. You mark classes with annotations like @Service or @Component.
  2. When the app starts, Spring Boot scans your code and creates an object of each one. These managed objects are called beans, and they live in the Spring container (the ApplicationContext).
  3. When a bean's constructor asks for another bean, the container passes it in. That passing-in is dependency injection.

The Spring documentation calls this Inversion of Control: instead of your object building or finding its own helpers, the container creates them and hands them over. Your class just declares what it needs.

Watch the flow

The animation follows the real program below: main() hands control to Spring Boot, the scan finds the two annotated classes, the container creates the GreetingService bean, creates WelcomeRunner while injecting GreetingService into its constructor, and run() uses the injected bean.

Run it yourself

A complete Spring Boot app in one file (run with mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.di.DiDemoApplication in a project with the spring-boot-starter dependency, Spring Boot 3.5.7):

package com.example.di;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DiDemoApplication {

    // 1. A bean the container will create and manage
    @Service
    static class GreetingService {
        GreetingService() {
            System.out.println("[container] created bean: GreetingService");
        }
        String greet(String name) {
            return "Hello, " + name + "!";
        }
    }

    // 2. A bean that NEEDS a GreetingService: constructor injection
    @Component
    static class WelcomeRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
        private final GreetingService greetingService;

        WelcomeRunner(GreetingService greetingService) {   // container injects it here
            this.greetingService = greetingService;
            System.out.println("[container] injected GreetingService into WelcomeRunner");
        }

        @Override
        public void run(String... args) {
            System.out.println("[app] WelcomeRunner.run() called with the injected bean");
            System.out.println("[app] " + greetingService.greet("Spring Boot"));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("[you] main(): handing control to SpringApplication.run()");
        SpringApplication.run(DiDemoApplication.class, args);
        System.out.println("[you] main(): container shut down");
    }
}

What it actually printed (Spring Boot 3.5.7, Java 21)

Real run, startup banner and framework log lines trimmed:

[you] main(): handing control to SpringApplication.run()
:: Spring Boot ::                (v3.5.7)
... Starting DiDemoApplication using Java 21.0.13 ...
[container] created bean: GreetingService
[container] injected GreetingService into WelcomeRunner
... Started DiDemoApplication in 0.774 seconds ...
[app] WelcomeRunner.run() called with the injected bean
[app] Hello, Spring Boot!
[you] main(): container shut down

Read it in order and you can see the handoff:

  • Your main() does exactly one thing: start the container.
  • The container's log lines come before the app's: it creates GreetingService, then builds WelcomeRunner and passes the service into the constructor. All before "Started DiDemoApplication".
  • Only then does run() execute, already holding a ready-to-use bean. CommandLineRunner is just Spring Boot's way of saying "call this once everything is wired up".

What the docs add

  • Two ways to inject. The Spring Framework docs describe constructor-based and setter-based DI. The rule of thumb they give: constructors for mandatory dependencies, setters for optional ones.
  • Constructor injection is the recommended style. The Spring team advocates it because components stay immutable, required dependencies can never be null, and the object is always fully initialized when you get it. The Spring Boot docs give the same advice: use constructor injection plus @ComponentScan, which @SpringBootApplication already includes.
  • It pays off in tests. Because your class receives its helpers instead of building them, a test can hand it a stub or mock instead of the real thing.

One honest caveat: the container does much more than this tiny demo shows (scopes, lazy init, configuration properties, proxies). But the core loop you saw above - scan, create, inject, use - is the part everything else builds on.

Sources

  • Dependency Injection - Spring Framework Documentation
  • Spring Beans and Dependency Injection - Spring Boot Documentation

Written with AI assistance; code examples were compiled and run on Spring Boot 3.5.7 with JDK 21 before publishing.

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

Assured Workloads

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.
  • Container-Optimized OS with containerd (cos_containerd) node pools on GKE versions 1.33 and earlier, 1.34 versions earlier than 1.34.6-gke.1154000, and 1.35 versions earlier than 1.35.3-gke.1389000.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane). For ubuntu_containerd node pools, a fix is in progress. Alternatively, downgrade the control plane to a version earlier than 1.36.3-gke.1244000.

title: AWS FinOps Field Notes (2026-11-01): Auditing RDS Extended Support Charges with Python
description:
While auditing cloud infrastructure costs this week, recurring configuration gaps continue to quietly inflate monthly cloud bills.

Field Insight: The Hidden Cost Trap

Antonio Augusto Maguelniski: "A client who asked him to halve their AWS bill saw it double from February to March 2025 with no new resources, because the RDS line jumped from about $30 to about $330/month when two PostgreSQL 12 databases left standard support."

When managed resources drift out of standard support windows or detached storage components persist after instance terminations, infrastructure spend spikes without any increase in user traffic or compute demand.

Auditing Outdated RDS Engine Versions with Boto3

Rather than relying on manual console spot-checks across multiple AWS regions, you can automate inspection using a lightweight Python script:

import boto3

def audit_rds_engine_versions(region='us-east-1'):
    rds = boto3.client('rds', region_name=region)
    instances = rds.describe_db_instances().get('DBInstances', [])

    # PostgreSQL <= 12 and MySQL <= 5.7 incur AWS Extended Support charges
    eol_engines = {'postgres': 12.0, 'mysql': 5.7}
    flagged = []

    for db in instances:
        db_id = db['DBInstanceIdentifier']
        engine = db['Engine']
        version_str = db['EngineVersion']
        parts = version_str.split('.')
        major_ver = float(f"{parts[0]}.{parts[1]}") if len(parts) > 1 else float(parts[0])

        for eol_key, max_ver in eol_engines.items():
            if eol_key in engine and major_ver <= max_ver:
                flagged.append({'DBInstance': db_id, 'Engine': engine, 'Version': version_str})
                print(f"[ALERT] {db_id} ({engine} {version_str}) is past standard support! Extended Support fees apply.")

    return flagged

if __name__ == '__main__':
    audit_rds_engine_versions()

Continuous Multi-Account Governance

Running one-off audit scripts in single regions does not scale across enterprise AWS Organizations. Sustained cloud cost management requires cross-account role assumption (sts:AssumeRole), cost anomaly correlation, and automated scheduled auditing.

title: OAuth Token Refresh in a Client vs a Generated, Spec-Aware Flow
description:
Quick answer: OAuth looks solved until a token expires mid-session, and the failure is almost always in how refresh tokens are stored and coordinated rather than in the initial login. A client that keeps a token in memory and silently retries on a 401 works for one process, but it breaks the moment multiple requests hit an expired token at once and each triggers its own refresh, or the refresh token is rotated and an older in-flight request invalidates the newer one. The robust pattern is to centralize the token in a single store, serialize refresh behind one lock, and treat the refresh token as a rotating secret that is persisted securely and never duplicated across clients. If refresh logic is left to each request to improvise, the first simultaneous expiry produces either a refresh storm or a logout that the user did nothing to cause.

Most API clients handle the happy path of OAuth well: redirect, exchange the code, attach the bearer token. The design questions concentrate on the less visible part: where the tokens live, what happens when the access token expires, and how a rotating refresh token is reconciled when several requests are in flight. A collection-based client tends to store tokens in a local profile or a per-request config, which is convenient for a single developer but does not model the coordination that a real application needs.

Where token refresh goes wrong

The failure modes cluster around storage and concurrency rather than the protocol's basic redirect flow.

Problem Symptom Correct approach
Concurrent refresh Multiple refresh calls, some fail Single in-flight refresh with a lock
Rotating refresh token Old token replay invalidates new Store latest, queue waiters
Insecure storage Token readable on disk OS keychain/secure store
Retry loop 401 repeated forever One retry, then re-auth
Tab/process split Each holds its own token Shared store

The rotating refresh token row is the subtle one: providers that issue a new refresh token on every use invalidate the previous one, so two clients racing to refresh leaves one holding a dead secret and forcing a fresh login even though the user's session was valid.

Centralize the token and serialize refresh

Keep one token store and expose a method that returns a valid token, refreshing at most once even when many callers ask at the same time. Callers wait on the same refresh promise rather than each starting their own.

Because the refresh promise is cached, a burst of requests that all see an expired token causes exactly one refresh, and every request proceeds with the same new access token.

Handle rotation and secure persistence

When the provider rotates the refresh token, write the new pair to the store before resolving the waiters, and persist it through the secure store rather than a plain config file. A stale read must never overwrite the newer secret.

On a desktop client the secure store maps to the OS keychain; on a web client the refresh token should stay httpOnly and secure on the server side rather than being exposed to JavaScript. The point is that the token is never duplicated into a per-request profile or a readable file, and a single authoritative copy exists.

Bound the retry and drive it from the contract

On a 401, a request should trigger the central refresh once and retry exactly once; if the refresh itself fails, the client routes to re-authentication rather than looping. A generated client that knows the security scheme and token endpoint from the OpenAPI contract can apply this logic consistently, including the token expiry buffer, so every request uses the same manager instead of embedding bespoke refresh code.

The practical recommendation is to treat token lifecycle as infrastructure: one secure store, one serialized refresh path, explicit handling of rotating refresh tokens, and a single retry before re-auth. If your client works on the first call but logs users out or throws refresh errors after an hour, the problem is not OAuth; it is storage and concurrency that were never centralized.

Frequently asked questions

Why do multiple requests fail when the token expires?

Each request independently sees the 401 and starts its own refresh. With a rotating refresh token, only the first succeeds and the others replay a now-invalid secret. A shared refresh promise fixes this.

Where should refresh tokens be stored?

In a secure store such as the OS keychain for desktop, or an httpOnly secure cookie for web. Never in a plain config file or in JavaScript-readable local storage.

What is a rotating refresh token?

A provider that issues a new refresh token on each use and invalidates the previous one. Clients must persist the latest token immediately; racing refreshes leave one client holding a dead secret.

How many times should a request retry after a 401?

Once, after a central refresh. If the refresh fails or the retried call is still 401, route to re-authentication rather than looping.

How does the API contract help?

It declares the security scheme and token endpoint, so a generated client wires every request to the same token manager with consistent expiry handling instead of per-request refresh logic.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison — start there for the full picture of reliable auth handling.

title: OmniDiff in scripts: a changed file can still exit successfully
description:
I changed qty * 10 to qty * 12, ran OmniDiff, and got exit code 0.

The diff was there. The command had succeeded. Those are separate questions, and a script needs to know which one it’s asking. 🙂

OmniDiff 0.3.0 is a content-aware diff tool with a terminal viewer, plain-text output and JSON output. I tried its official release binary on a tiny Python fixture. Here’s the part I’d check before putting it in a build job.

Original diagram of the executed file checks. These are return codes, not a speed comparison.

Get a useful result without changing Git settings 🧪

Download and extract the matching binary from the 0.3.0 release, then make omnidiff available on your PATH. The release has builds for several platforms. I used the prebuilt binary; this walkthrough doesn’t require compiling Rust.

Save this as check_diff.py and run python3 check_diff.py. It creates disposable input files, checks the actual process results, and removes the fixtures when it finishes.

from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    (root / 'before.py').write_text('def price(qty):\n    return qty * 10\n')
    (root / 'after.py').write_text('def price(qty):\n    return qty * 12\n')
    cases = [
        ('changed, default', [], 'before.py', 'after.py', 0),
        ('changed, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'after.py', 1),
        ('identical, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'before.py', 0),
        ('missing, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'missing.py', 2),
    ]
    for label, flags, before, after, expected in cases:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ['omnidiff', '--headless', '--color', 'never', *flags, before, after],
            cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
        )
        assert result.returncode == expected, result.stderr
        print(f'{label}: {result.returncode}')

My output was:

changed, default: 0
changed, opt-in: 1
identical, opt-in: 0
missing, opt-in: 2

✅ The missing-file case matters. A script that treats every nonzero return as “files changed” would put a read error in the same bucket as a valid diff.

Pick the process contract first

For a display tool, success means it could produce the comparison. That explains the default zero even when the files differ.

For a check, add --exit-code. Then handle the results explicitly: zero means identical, one means different, and two means an error.2

In Python, I’d inspect returncode before deciding whether to fail the job. Using check=True immediately would raise on a normal changed-file result too. That can be useful if any change must fail the job, but the error path still deserves its own message. ⚠️

There’s also a Git-specific boundary: OmniDiff ignores --exit-code in Git’s external-diff argument form. I checked that form with the same changed files and got zero. Git can treat a nonzero external-diff result as the tool failing, so don’t carry the direct-file assumption into that integration.2

JSON helps with a different problem 🔎

I also ran the fixture with --mode json --exit-code. It returned one and produced a JSON object with before and after sections, each containing an update range. The versioned schema describes those fields.3

That gives an editor structured locations to display. It doesn’t tell the editor whether changing the multiplier was correct. I’d keep the application test beside the prettier diff.

This was a small process-behavior check: Python text files, equality, a missing input, JSON output and the external-diff argument form. I didn’t measure performance or test its other content handlers.

References and asset credit

  1. OmniDiff 0.3.0 release, Marko Ivankovic.
  2. Versioned README: headless mode and exit-code contract.
  3. Versioned JSON output schema.

The figure is an original rendering of the executed checks. The fixture and Python wrapper are original examples.

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

title: [Agent Platform in Action (8)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness (Part 2): Integrating Phase 4 Eval Datas
description:
Introduction: Why Decoupling Prompts Isn't Enough?

In the previous post [Agent Platform in Practice (7)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 1): Understanding the Recursive Agent Framework and c1..c8 Decoupling (corresponding to Issue #16), we introduced Google Research's google-research/harness2 (arXiv:2610.14224) and decoupled the prompts, guardrails, long-term memory, and on-demand skills of the LINE AI Business Card Assistant (kkdai/line-card-assistant) into an editable c1..c8 Harness file tree that can be dynamically mounted via LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR.

However, simply having a hot-reloadable c1..c8 file tree isn't enough; the Harness² dual-layer recursive optimization engine (harness2/core/recursion.py) still cannot directly optimize our Go Agent. This is because Harness² requires a standardized bridge — the BenchmarkAdapter — to answer three questions:

  1. list_tasks() (What are the test questions?): What test cases should the Agent challenge? What are the public inputs (Prompt / Image) for each case, and what are the hidden scoring criteria (Rubrics)?
  2. run() (How does the Agent think and execute?): When a candidate Harness $H’$ is mounted to execute a specific task, what is the Agent's final output (deliverable)? More importantly, what decision trajectory did it follow across the 13 nodes of the Graph Workflow (trajectory.md)?
  3. score() (How was the performance?): Which independent scoring items (per_rubric) did the final output and execution trajectory pass, and where did it lose points?

Conveniently, in Phase 4 (PR #13), we already established the eval/datasets/ automated evaluation benchmark, and in Phase 5 (PR #14), we added workflow.node.* OpenTelemetry Spans to all 13 Graph Nodes!

In this post (Part 2, corresponding to Issue #17 and PR #19), we will merge these two existing assets into the Harness² LineCardAdapter and explain in depth "Why must it be designed this way?".

I. Why This Change? Two Core Design Philosophies

Before diving into the code, many engineers often ask two questions:

  1. "Why not just feed the entire eval/datasets/*.json file to the optimizer LLM and let it modify the Prompt itself?"
  2. "Why do we need to convert Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into trajectory.md? Isn't the final LINE reply text and total score enough?"

These two questions touch upon the most core engineering designs in the Harness² paper: the Zero-Leakage Barrier and Behavioral Trajectory Contrast.

1. Why the "Zero-Leakage Barrier"? Preventing the Optimizer from "Cheating by Memorizing Answers"

Imagine this: if we expose the golden answers in eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json (e.g., expected_contains: ["+81-3-1234-5678", "Kenta Sato"]) directly to the Agent or the Harness² Harvester LLM, what happens?

The laziest and easiest way for the optimizer to get a perfect score is to write a single line in systemprompt.md:

"If the input contains Sato, please directly output +81-3-1234-5678 and Kenta Sato."

In machine learning, this is known as Test Set Leakage / Overfitting to Rubrics. The Agent appears to score 100 on the benchmark, but it crashes immediately when it encounters a new Japanese business card in the real world!

flowchart LR
    Dataset["eval/datasets/*.json\nComplete Test Cases\n(incl. expected_contains / expected_route)"]

    subgraph Barrier["Zero-Leakage Barrier"]
        Brief["TaskBrief (Public Task Sheet)\nContains only task_id, prompt, session_input\n❌ Never contains expected_* golden answers"]
        Scorer["Isolated Scorer (Black-box Grader)\nHolds independent hidden r1..r4 Rubrics"]
    end

    Agent["Go ADK Graph Workflow\n(cmd/harness-runner)"]
    Harvester["Harness² Harvester\n(Propose / Probe / Compose)"]

    Dataset --> Brief
    Dataset --> Scorer
    Brief -->|"Public Input"| Agent
    Agent -->|"Deliverable + OTel trajectory.md"| Scorer
    Scorer -->|"Returns only binary scores {r1: 1.0, r2: 0.0}\nand OTel execution trajectory"| Harvester

In the Harness² BenchmarkAdapter architecture:

  • TaskBrief (Public Task Sheet): Can only contain user input (prompt and simulated images/context). It is strictly forbidden from containing any expected_contains, expected_not_contains, or correct answer strings.
  • score() (Black-box Grader): After comparing answers in an isolated environment, it only returns "which Rubric received a 1.0 or 0.0" (e.g., r3_e164_jp_phone_normalization: 0.0), without leaking the expected string to the optimizer.
  • As a result, the Harness² optimizer must truly reason out general domain rules (e.g., "When converting Japanese phone numbers +81 (0)3-... to E.164, the domestic trunk prefix (0) must be removed") by reading the Agent's execution trajectory (trajectory.md), rather than hard-coding answers into the Prompt!

2. Why Convert Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into trajectory.md? Opening the Black Box of the 13-Node Graph

Our LINE AI Business Card Assistant is not a simple "single LLM call," but an ADK 2.0 Directed Acyclic Graph (Graph Workflow) consisting of 13 nodes:

  • Business Card Ingestion Pipeline: RouterNode $\rightarrow$ VisionOCRNode $\rightarrow$ Parallel AddFanOut (CleanAndDedupNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ContextMatchNode) $\rightarrow$ AddFanIn (JoinPreviewNode) $\rightarrow$ BuildPreviewNode $\rightarrow$ HITLConfirmNode $\rightarrow$ ApplyEditNode / SaveCardNode.
  • Smart Search and Icebreaker Pipeline: RouterNode $\rightarrow$ QueryIntentNode $\rightarrow$ HybridSearchNode / BroadSearchNode $\rightarrow$ FormatCarouselNode / EmailDraftNode.

Without Phase 5's OpenTelemetry Spans, when a user searches for "Help me find a Sales Director in Hsinchu Science Park working on AI chips" but gets "No matching business cards found" (score 0.25), the optimizer only sees this final failure message and cannot determine:

  • Did the RouterNode misjudge the search intent as chat?
  • Did the QueryIntentNode fail to expand the colloquial "Hsinchu Science Park" into the database's address Hsinchu, or fail to expand "Sales Director" into Sales Director?
  • Was there an error in the SQL query logic of the HybridSearchNode?

When we collect and render Phase 5's OpenTelemetry workflow.node.* Spans into a structured trajectory.md, Harness² can clearly see the input, output, duration, routing decisions, and loaded skills of every Graph Node during the Propose and Probe stages!

II. Implementation Part 2: Building the LineCardAdapter in Three Steps

Referring to the architecture diagram at the beginning of this article, we completed the implementation of Issue #17 through three core components:

  1. internal/harness/trajectory.go: Mounts an in-memory OpenTelemetry SpanRecorder on the Go side to export the execution details of the 13 Graph Nodes as trajectory.md.
  2. cmd/harness-runner/main.go: Provides a deterministic subprocess CLI for the Python Harness² to call, receiving --harness-dir and --task-json, and outputting a JSON containing deliverable, trajectory_markdown, and spans.
  3. harness/line_card_adapter.py: Implements the google-research/harness2 BenchmarkAdapter interface, connecting the Phase 4 Dataset with the Go harness-runner.

1. Implementing internal/harness/trajectory.go: Rendering OpenTelemetry Spans as trajectory.md

In Phase 5, our internal/workflow/telemetry.go already calls startNodeSpan(ctx, "VisionOCRNode") in every Graph Node. Now, in internal/harness/trajectory.go, we use go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/tracetest.NewSpanRecorder() to intercept all completed node Spans and transform them into a Markdown trajectory report that the Harness² Harvester LLM is best at reading:

// InstallRecorder registers a new in-memory SpanRecorder as the global OTel TracerProvider
// so every workflow.node.* span emitted by internal/workflow/telemetry.go is captured.
func InstallRecorder() (*TrajectoryRecorder, func()) {
    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr))
    prev := otel.GetTracerProvider()
    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)

    rec := &TrajectoryRecorder{recorder: sr, tp: tp}
    restore := func() {
        _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background())
        otel.SetTracerProvider(prev)
    }
    return rec, restore
}

At the same time, we added three OpenTelemetry Attributes to internal/workflow/telemetry.go: AttrNodeDecision (adk.node.decision), AttrNodeDiagnostic (adk.node.diagnostic), and AttrHarnessSkills (adk.harness.skills). When TrajectoryRecorder.RenderMarkdown() executes, it produces a high-resolution trajectory.md like this:

# ADK 2.0 Go Graph Workflow Execution Trajectory
- **Task ID** : `challenge_colloquial_tw_search`
- **Harness Root** : `harness/base`
- **Always-On Bytes (`c1..c4`)**: `1599 / 24000`
- **Final Score** : `0.25`

## OpenTelemetry Node Spans (`workflow.node.*`)
### 1. `workflow.node.RouterNode`
- **Node** : `RouterNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.02 ms`
- **Decision** : `intent=search (colloquial_query=Help me find a Sales Director in Hsinchu Science Park working on AI chips, I need to contact Taiwan semiconductor clients)`
- **Diagnostic** : `routed search query to QueryIntentNode`

### 2. `workflow.node.QueryIntentNode`
- **Node** : `QueryIntentNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.04 ms`
- **Decision** : `parsed_filters={"location":"Hsinchu Science Park","role":"Sales Director","industry":"AI Chips"}`
- **Diagnostic** : `UNEXPANDED_COLLOQUIAL_FILTERS: colloquial Taiwan science park alias 'Hsinchu Science Park' and Mandarin title 'Sales Director' were passed literally without bilingual synonym expansion; add a c6 skill 'tw_semicon_search' with BILINGUAL_SYNONYM_MAP`

### 3. `workflow.node.HybridSearchNode`
- **Node** : `HybridSearchNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.03 ms`
- **Decision** : `matched_cards=0 (strict literal filter on location='Hsinchu Science Park' failed against DB address='Hsinchu Science Park (竹科)')`

Please pay attention to the Span records of the 2nd node workflow.node.QueryIntentNode and the 3rd node workflow.node.HybridSearchNode! Through this trajectory, the Propose stage of Harness² can see at a glance: RouterNode was correct, the error was in QueryIntentNode treating "Hsinchu Science Park" as a rigid string to query the English address field!

2. Expanding the Phase 4 Evaluation Set: eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json

To fully test Harness²'s ability to retain existing capabilities (preventing catastrophic forgetting) and conquer difficult edge cases, we established 8 tasks (totaling 32 fine-grained Rubrics) in eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json:

Task Category Task ID Scenario Description 4 Independent Scoring Rubrics (r1..r4)
Baseline (Regression) baseline_ingest_ming_wang Standard Traditional Chinese card ingestion (Wang Xiaoming / Taiwan Cloud Tech) Intent routing, Name/Title extraction, E.164 phone normalization, Industry tag enrichment
Baseline (Regression) baseline_dedup_appier_promotion Duplicate detection for promotion (Lin Yating Senior $\rightarrow$ VP) Dedup detection, Title update, Keep new mobile, Company consistency
Baseline (Regression) baseline_search_cloud_summit_ai Standard keyword search (Cloud Summit + AI) Search routing, Multiple hits, Tag display, Interactive buttons
Baseline (Regression) baseline_email_google_cloud General tech follow-up icebreaker (Chen Jianhong / Google Cloud) Email routing, Recipient/Event mention, Agenda link, Professional closing
Challenge (Evolution 1) challenge_jp_bilingual_ingest Bilingual JP/EN card OCR & JP phone normalization (Kenta Sato / CTO / +81 (0)3-1234-5678) r1 Routing, r2 Bilingual name retention, r3 JP +81 remove (0) normalization, r4 JP title bilingual mapping
Challenge (Evolution 2) challenge_colloquial_tw_search Colloquial Taiwan tech alias search ("Help me find a Sales Director in Hsinchu Science Park") r1 Routing, r2 Hsinchu Science Park $\leftrightarrow$ Hsinchu bilingual expansion hit, r3 Sales Director $\leftrightarrow$ Sales Director title expansion, r4 Tag completeness
Challenge (Evolution 3) challenge_noisy_multi_edit_hitl Multi-clause colloquial HITL continuous correction ("Sorry, let me correct that, the title should be Group Senior VP, also change the end of the mobile to 8899, and add GDG DevFest speaker to notes") r1 HITL Edit routing, r2 Multi-field atomic update (Title), r3 Mobile suffix partial replacement & Note append, r4 Retain original company/email
Challenge (Evolution 4) challenge_pii_safe_executive_followup Financial executive compliance & PII masking icebreaker (Zhang Yazhu / Cathay Financial, Digital Risk Officer, requires privacy protection and compliance headers) r1 Email routing, r2 Executive title/scenario, r3 Mobile/Private Email PII Redaction, r4 Financial compliance subject header [Confidential / FinTech Compliance Verified]

3. Implementing harness/line_card_adapter.py: Connecting to google-research/harness2

Finally, we implemented the LineCardAdapter in harness/line_card_adapter.py, connecting all the above components:

class LineCardAdapter:
    """Adapts `line-card-assistant` to the `google-research/harness2` BenchmarkAdapter protocol."""

    def list_tasks(self) -> list[TaskBrief]:
        """Return public task briefs with zero ground-truth rubric leakage."""
        briefs: list[TaskBrief] = []
        for raw in self._raw_cases:
            # Strip `rubrics` and `expected_*` so the agent/harvester never sees ground truth.
            briefs.append(
                TaskBrief(
                    task_id=raw["id"],
                    prompt=raw["prompt"],
                    context={
                        "category": raw.get("category", "general"),
                        "description": raw.get("description", ""),
                        "session_input": raw.get("session_input", {}),
                    },
                )
            )
        return briefs

    def run(self, harness: Harness, task: TaskBrief) -> RunArtifact:
        """Mount `harness` in a temporary directory and execute the Go Graph Workflow runner."""
        problems = harness.validate()
        if problems:
            diag = "# Harness Validation Failed\n" + "\n".join(f"- {p}" for p in problems)
            return RunArtifact(task_id=task.task_id, deliverable="", trajectory=diag)

        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix=f"line_card_harness_{task.task_id}_") as tmp_dir:
            harness_root = Path(tmp_dir)
            harness.materialize(harness_root)
            # Invoke the compiled Go binary with --harness-dir pointing to the materialized c1..c8 tree
            proc = subprocess.run(
                [str(binary), f"--harness-dir={harness_root}", f"--task-json={task_payload_path}"],
                capture_output=True, text=True, check=False, timeout=30,
            )
            payload = json.loads(proc.stdout)
            return RunArtifact(
                task_id=task.task_id,
                deliverable=payload.get("deliverable", ""),
                trajectory=payload.get("trajectory_markdown", ""),
                raw=payload,
            )

    def score(self, task: TaskBrief, artifact: RunArtifact) -> ScoreResult:
        """Evaluate the deliverable against isolated per-rubric criteria."""
        raw = self._cases_by_id[task.task_id]
        rubrics = raw.get("rubrics", {})
        per_rubric: dict[str, float] = {}
        for rubric_id, spec in rubrics.items():
            per_rubric[rubric_id] = 1.0 if self._evaluate_rubric(artifact.deliverable, spec) else 0.0
        total = sum(per_rubric.values()) / len(per_rubric) if per_rubric else 0.0
        return ScoreResult(task_id=task.task_id, total=round(total, 4), per_rubric=per_rubric)

Through this LineCardAdapter:

  • Whenever Harness² proposes a new candidate Harness $H’$, adapter.run(harness, task) first calls harness.validate() to check the 24KB OPENCODE_SURFACE limit and Skill Frontmatter rules.
  • Once validated, the c1..c8 files of $H’$ are materialized into a temporary directory and passed to Go's harness-runner for execution.
  • After the Go 13-node Graph Workflow finishes, it returns the final LINE message (deliverable) and OpenTelemetry trajectory (trajectory_markdown), which are then passed to adapter.score() for leakage-free independent scoring!

III. Summary and Teaser for the Next Part

In this post (Part 2), we completed the core engineering for Issue #17:

  1. Clarified why the golden test set cannot be fed directly to the optimizer — through the TaskBrief Zero-Leakage Barrier, we force Harness² to reason out general skills from behavioral trajectories rather than memorizing answers.
  2. Through internal/harness/trajectory.go and cmd/harness-runner/main.go, we transformed Phase 5's OpenTelemetry workflow.node.* Spans into high-resolution trajectory.md, opening the black box of the 13-node Graph Workflow.
  3. Established eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json (8 major tasks, 32 fine-grained Rubrics) and harness/line_card_adapter.py, perfectly implementing the Harness² BenchmarkAdapter protocol.

Everything is ready! In the final post [Agent Platform in Practice (9)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 3): Dual-Layer Recursive Testing Guide, 62.5% to 100% Performance Results, and the Future of AgentOps (corresponding to Issue #18), we will actually launch the dual-layer recursive optimization experiment, reveal the complete quantitative data evolving from 62.5% to 100.0%, and discuss the profound impact of Harness² on future enterprise-grade Agent development!

title: Node.js Error Capture: Metadata Contracts for AI Tutor Cost Attribution
description:
Short answer: capture the exception at the agent-loop boundary, and send a bounded metadata payload to /v1/errors/capture. Include the tenant, course, learner, agent step, model, environment, and an application-side cost estimate. Use this when cost attribution is the main question. Choose a dedicated error platform when alerts, source maps, replay, or trace exploration are the real job.

Option Best fit Important boundary
Error capture API One Node.js POST with custom context around an AI tutor loop You still build alerting and retention workflows
Sentry Exception grouping, source maps, and an application issue workflow It is a dedicated error product, not a general backend surface
Datadog Teams already operating logs, metrics, traces, and monitors together Its breadth brings more configuration and operational surface
Honeycomb High-cardinality event exploration and trace-oriented debugging It fits interactive trace analysis better than isolated error capture

For a one-person edtech SaaS, I would start with one structured error event per failed agent loop. Put attribution fields in the event itself: tenant_id, course_id, learner_id, agent_step, model, and estimated_cost_usd. The payload becomes the handoff between an exception and a product decision.

This is a small boundary. That is the point.

The event is the accounting record.

The decision is less about collecting more logs and more about preserving the accounting context before it disappears. One failed grading request can involve retrieval, a tool call, and a final explanation. If the event only contains a stack trace, I can investigate code but cannot reliably answer which course or model consumed the failed loop. A founder shipping weekly needs that answer without turning observability into another product. I would keep the first version to the fields in the example, cap the capture retry loop at four attempts, and review the event shape after the first weekly release rather than making the metadata contract encyclopedic on day one.

How should Node.js capture an error with custom metadata?

An agent loop can fail after retrieval, during tool use, or while producing the final explanation. A stack trace identifies the software path. It does not answer who incurred the work or which learning flow was interrupted. That is the metadata boundary.

I use three layers. The error fields describe the exception itself. The environment fields explain where it happened. The business fields make the event useful for attribution. Keep personal data to the minimum needed for support; a learner ID is usually more useful than copying a learner's name into every event.

The cost field deserves care. estimated_cost_usd is an application estimate, not a provider invoice. If the loop makes three model calls, record the total and keep per-step amounts in a bounded array or in a separate event. Do not put an unbounded prompt, tool result, or full conversation into metadata. That turns a diagnostic record into a second transcript store.

I first wanted the entire prompt in the event because it would make debugging feel easier. The better boundary is a step name plus a redacted reference. Debugging detail and learner data have different retention needs, and combining them makes deletion and access policies harder later.

Here is the smallest Node.js pattern I would ship first. It extracts stable error details, adds attribution context, sends an explicit POST, and retries a rate limit with the server's delay when available. The idempotency key is derived from the failed job identifier so a retry does not create a second logical event.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type AgentContext = {
  jobId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  courseId: string;
  learnerId: string;
  agentStep: string;
  model: string;
  estimatedCostUsd: number;
  environment: "production" | "staging";
};

async function captureAgentError(error: unknown, context: AgentContext) {
  const caught = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
  const payload = {
    error: {
      name: caught.name,
      message: caught.message,
      stack: caught.stack
    },
    metadata: {
      user: { id: context.learnerId },
      environment: context.environment,
      tags: ["agent-loop", context.agentStep],
      tenant_id: context.tenantId,
      course_id: context.courseId,
      job_id: context.jobId,
      agent_step: context.agentStep,
      model: context.model,
      estimated_cost_usd: context.estimatedCostUsd
    }
  };

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;
    if (!apiBaseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_BASE_URL is required");
    const endpoint = new URL("/v1/errors/capture", apiBaseUrl);
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `agent-error:${context.jobId}`
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload)
    });

    if (response.ok) return;

    const body = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`Error capture failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
}

try {
  await runAgentLoop();
} catch (error) {
  await captureAgentError(error, {
    jobId: "grade-2026-11-01-1842",
    tenantId: "school-17",
    courseId: "algebra-2",
    learnerId: "learner-884",
    agentStep: "explanation",
    model: "configured-model",
    estimatedCostUsd: 0.012,
    environment: "production"
  });
  throw error;
}

The sample assumes the application already has runAgentLoop. That is deliberate. Error reporting should wrap the work that can fail, not become a second agent framework. In production, redact tokens and prompts before serialization, and decide whether a learner identifier is acceptable for your retention and deletion policy.

What does a small REST surface buy a solo SaaS?

The practical advantage of the capture route is discovery. Infrai has a genuinely self-describing public discovery surface: it exposes request schemas and runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts with reading the endpoint rather than learning another SDK. The documented capabilities also provide runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Node.js service that already has a fetch wrapper, that lowers the amount of glue code I need to maintain. For this narrow workflow, Infrai is a reasonable fit because the capture request can stay a small REST adapter while its discovery surface gives me a documented starting point for adjacent capabilities.

There is a second advantage in the workflow around this event: Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. That does not make it a better error tracker by itself. It does reduce credential and reconciliation friction when the agent later needs a related backend capability. One application-level auth boundary is easier to hand off than a collection of keys and vendor-specific setup notes, especially when every hour spent on plumbing competes with the next classroom feature. The observability group itself has 23 routes, but I would still treat the error capture path as only one piece of the system, not as a replacement for alerting or traces.

This is also why I would keep the application metadata contract independent from the transport. The fields belong to the edtech workflow. The capture adapter can be replaced later. A consistent REST surface makes that adapter small, but it does not remove the need to define what estimated_cost_usd means or how learner data is retained.

Sentry is the stronger choice when the main question is, “Which release introduced this exception, and how do I inspect its application context?” Its established error workflow, grouping, source-map support, and replay-oriented tooling cover needs this one capture call does not. Choose it when frontend diagnosis is a first-class requirement.

Datadog makes more sense when logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and alert monitors already live there. A single operational workspace can beat a small custom pipeline once several engineers depend on the same on-call conventions. The trade is surface area: a solo founder should count configuration and maintenance as product work.

Honeycomb is a strong runner-up for a different failure shape. If debugging requires asking high-cardinality questions across a request path or exploring a trace, its event and trace model is more natural than treating each exception as an isolated record. For a narrow error-capture workflow, that power may be more system than the job needs.

When is this capture boundary the wrong tool?

The main limitation is scope: an error endpoint is not an alerting system. There is no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route in the stated capability. A small service can poll a query API and own notification policy, but that is another component with its own failure modes.

It also does not provide a distributed trace tree, source-map deobfuscation, Electron crash symbolization, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring. A scheduled import that silently stops is a Healthchecks-style monitoring problem, not an exception-capture problem. Flags have their own boundaries too: no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recycle bin. Pick Sentry, Datadog, or Honeycomb instead if any of those missing workflows is the primary job.

Deletion and export deserve a written policy before launch. The logs surface does not provide a per-user deletion endpoint or bulk export/subscription interface, and retention or cold-storage settings do not have a configuration entry point. Do not promise a privacy workflow that the API cannot execute.

The decision I would make

For a Node.js edtech agent, send one bounded error event with business attribution at the catch boundary. Start with the API when the important question is “which tenant, course, step, and model consumed this failed loop?” Add a dedicated error platform when release diagnosis, replay, alert delivery, or trace exploration becomes the work.

That split keeps the first implementation small and the boundary honest. Ship the capture path this week. Outsource the undifferentiated backend plumbing to a consistent REST surface, then spend the saved attention on the learner-facing behavior that failed in the first place.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Node.js, “Using the Fetch API”: https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/fetch
  • Sentry, “JavaScript error monitoring”: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/
  • Datadog, “Error Tracking”: https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/error_tracking/
  • Honeycomb, “What is distributed tracing?”: https://docs.honeycomb.io/get-started/basics/distributed-tracing/
