title: In Cloud Security, Good Enough is Indistinguishable From Failure
description:
✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading.

Cloud failures come from systems that are good enough until they aren't.

The IAM role was good enough for 18 months. Then someone discovered the trust chain it created. The S3 bucket policy was good enough until the VPC endpoint was removed and the condition clause failed silently. The security tooling was good enough. It detected 95% of individual misconfigurations. The 5% it missed were the compound paths where breaches happened.

Good enough is the most dangerous state a safety system can be in. Good enough: functioning well enough that nobody prioritizes replacing it, while silently accumulating the conditions for catastrophic failure.

In cloud systems, good enough safety is indistinguishable from failure that is just delayed. The delay makes it invisible. The failure makes it catastrophic.

The convergence pattern

Every product category goes through the same cycle. Many good enough tools → structural pressure → convergence into one integrated solution:

Domain Good enough era Convergent era
Mobile phones (1990s) Phone + MP3 player + GPS unit + wallet + pager + camera. Each "good enough" at its job. Smartphone subsumes all of them. Not by being better at any one — by being the integrated solution.
Browser plugins (2000s) Flash + RealPlayer + ActiveX + Java applets. Each solving one media problem. Native browser (HTML5/JS). The plugins disappeared not because they stopped working — because the integrated solution made them unnecessary.
Build automation Make + autoconf + custom shell scripts. Each solving one piece of the build. Integrated CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI). The scripts didn't break — they became unnecessary.
Configuration management SSH + custom scripts + tribal knowledge. Each "good enough" for its scope. IaC + GitOps. The scripts were still correct — but the integrated approach was structurally superior.
Cloud security (today) CSPM + SIEM + WAF + IaC scanners + OPA + dashboards. Each "good enough." (Convergence pending)

The pattern is the same every time. The good enough tools work. They work at the wrong level. The convergent solution subsumes them by solving the higher-order job.

The smartphone didn't have a better camera than a dedicated camera. It solved "capture and share a moment" better than camera + USB cable + computer + email. The job was higher-order than any individual tool addressed.

The most dangerous state

For most product categories, good enough is fine. A good enough MP3 player plays music adequately. The worst case: slightly worse audio quality.

For safety systems, good enough is structurally dangerous:

Non-safety system:
    "Good enough" → acceptable → stays acceptable → no problem

Safety system:
    "Good enough" → acceptable today → margin tested over years 
    → margin fails at an unpredictable moment → catastrophic

This is the temporal version of Lamport's safety/liveness distinction. A safety property must hold at ALL TIMES. A good enough safety margin will be tested by every possible configuration, composition and interaction continuously, for years. The margin that was good enough for the first 10,000 configurations meets configuration #10,001 and fails.

The three outages of Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, AWS are each a good enough margin that failed:

  • Cloudflare's feature-file validation was "good enough" until a file exceeded the size the proxy could handle
  • CrowdStrike's schema checking was "good enough" until a file had 20 fields instead of 21
  • AWS's plan versioning was "good enough" until a race condition applied a stale plan

Each system worked correctly for years. The transition from good enough to catastrophic was instant.

The job customers want

The cloud security industry has been selling MEANS:

"We scan!"     → a means, not a job
"We alert!"    → a means, not a job
"We block!"    → a means, not a job  
"We visualize attack paths!" → a means, not a job
"We auto-remediate!"         → a means, not a job

The job customers want:

"Operate distributed systems safely, continuously, and without surprise."

No customer wakes up wanting more scans, alerts, or dashboards. They want the job done: the system stays safe, continuously, without requiring constant human attention.

The means-vs-job distinction separates pre-convergence tools from convergent-era solutions. Pre-convergence tools sell means ("we scan 47 resource types!"). Convergent solutions deliver the job ("the invariant holds against every snapshot, deterministically, before deployment").

Once a credible job-fit product appears, customers switch, but because the new tool solves the job they were hiring the old tools to do.

Perfection

Perfect means: achieving the safety function with zero unnecessary harm.

Function Perfect direction
Safety Always enforced — not "mostly" or "usually"
Cost Only when needed — not running continuously if per-commit is sufficient
Latency Before damage — not after deployment, not after detection
Scope Smallest possible — not "scan everything always" but "evaluate what's changing"
Human effort Near zero — not "faster triage" but "no triage"
Recovery Reversible — not "auto-fix production" but "block the merge before it's irreversible"

Each row is a direction. The product moves toward each direction with every release. "Always enforced" is the limit. Currently, Stave enforces on every CI run, not on every API call. "Near zero human effort" is the limit. Currently, the operator selects a profile and reads an exit code. Each is closer to the perfect direction than the industry default, without claiming perfection.

The Innovator's Dilemma

Incumbent tools look at the convergent-era product and see inferiority:

Incumbent: "We manage 300+ resource types across 5 clouds with runtime monitoring,
            auto-remediation, attack-path visualization, and AI-powered triage."

Convergent product: "We evaluate invariants against snapshots. No runtime monitoring.
                     No auto-remediation. No visualization. No AI."

The incumbent's feature list is longer. The convergent product looks inferior by every metric the incumbent measures.

This is the Innovator's Dilemma. The convergent solution doesn't compete on the incumbent's metrics. It solves a different job at a different level:

Historical parallel Why the "inferior" solution won
VOIP beat telecom Solved "talk to people remotely" at a fraction of the cost. Worse call quality. Didn't matter.
Flash storage beat spinning disks Solved "store data portably." Less capacity initially. Didn't matter.
GitOps beat manual ops Solved "reproducible deploys" at the right abstraction. Less flexibility. Didn't matter.

Each inferior solution won because it solved the higher-order job better than the superior incumbent. The incumbent's features were means. The convergent solution delivered the job.

The cloud-security version:

Incumbent job (means):     "Scan, alert, triage, remediate"
Convergent job (outcome):  "The invariant holds. Deterministically. Before deployment."

The convergent product doesn't scan (the operator's collectors do). Doesn't alert (exit codes replace alerts). Doesn't triage (the verdict is binary). Doesn't remediate (the CI pipeline blocks the merge). Each missing feature is a means the convergent product doesn't need. Because it solves the job differently.

Seven commitments for the convergent era

Each commitment looks suboptimal from the pre-convergence competitive frame. Each is optimal for the convergent-era job:

1. Self-checking yes; self-healing no

Pre-convergence view: "Why can't it auto-fix? Every competitor auto-remediates."

Convergent-era reason: Perfection advances in small reversible steps, not leaps. Auto-remediation is an irreversible mutation of production state. One wrong fix is worse than the misconfiguration it corrected. The convergent product evaluates and blocks. The operator's existing pipeline fixes.

2. Invariants, not rules

Pre-convergence view: "Rules are more flexible. Invariants are rigid."

Convergent-era reason: Invariants compose (Alpern-Schneider theorem). Rules accumulate. 3000+ invariants compose into a global safety guarantee by mathematical theorem. 3000+ rules accumulate into a maintenance nightmare. The convergent product scales through composition.

3. Transitions, not just snapshots

Pre-convergence view: "Just tell me what's wrong right now."

Convergent-era reason: The convergent system asks about CHANGE, not just state. "Does this proposed transition violate an invariant?" is a different question from "is this resource misconfigured?" The first prevents breaches. The second detects them after the fact.

4. Bounded mitigation, not full remediation

Pre-convergence view: "Why doesn't it fix the problem end-to-end?"

Convergent-era reason: Stay outside the runtime mutation path. A product that modifies production state has the same blast-radius risk as the misconfigurations it's supposed to prevent. The convergent product gates. The existing pipeline remediates through the existing change-management process.

5. No replacement of existing tools

Pre-convergence view: "We need a platform that replaces our fifteen tools."

Convergent-era reason: Additive adoption beats rip-and-replace. The convergent product adds one step to the existing pipeline (the CI gate). The fifteen existing tools keep running as the reactive safety net. Adoption friction kills convergent products; zero-friction adoption is the only path.

6. Open-source embedded catalog

Pre-convergence view: "Why give away the controls? That's the IP."

Convergent-era reason: The catalog becomes the convergence substrate like HTTP or the Kubernetes API. When every operator runs the same 3000+ controls, the catalog is the standard. The value accrues to the entity that defined the standard.

7. "One invariant closer" — not "we solve cloud security"

Pre-convergence view: "You need a bigger vision statement."

Convergent-era reason: Engineering claims beat marketing horizon-claims. "We evaluate 3000+ invariants deterministically" is testable. "We solve cloud security" is a hostage to fortune. The convergent product advances step-wise with each invariant added, chain defined, schema extended and the claim is always verifiable.

Four refusals

Each refusal looks like a weakness from the pre-convergence frame. Each is an advantage in the convergent era:

Refusal Why it's correct
Don't replace existing tools Adoption friction kills convergent products. Add one CI step, not a platform migration.
Don't auto-remediate cloud state Irreversible runtime mutation compromises the trust the product is built on.
Don't claim "we solve cloud security" Maximalist claims are hostages to fortune. The claim must be verifiable at every moment.
Don't optimize for current customer feature requests Current requests target the pre-convergence era. The convergent product builds for the job that doesn't have a name yet, until it's the only job that matters.

The strategic dichotomy

"The only strategic choice is whether you lead that convergence or get displaced by it."

There is no third option. Once the structural conditions for convergence are present (the good enough tools have saturated, the failure cost has crossed the threshold, the higher-order job is nameable), convergence happens. The empirical record such as VOIP, Flash storage, GitOps, smartphones, HTML5 is decisive. Incumbent excellence at the pre-convergence job is no defense against displacement when the convergent era arrives.

The conditions are present now in cloud security:

"Good enough" tools have saturated      → 15+ tools per organization, breach rate unchanged
Failure cost has crossed the threshold  → Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, AWS are billion-dollar outages
Higher-order job is nameable            → "The invariant holds, deterministically, before deployment"
Structural forcing function has arrived → Agentic era removes the human from the loop

All four conditions met. The convergence is coming. The question is which product leads it.

The good enough test for your own stack

Look at your cloud security toolstack. For each tool:

1. Is it solving a MEANS or a JOB?

We scan is a means. The system stays safe, continuously, without surprise is the job. If the tool solves a means, it's pre-convergence.

2. Is it "good enough" — or is it structurally sound?

Good enough means: it works for the configurations you've tested. Structurally sound means: it works for every configuration that could exist, by mathematical guarantee (safety composition). Good enough fails at configuration #10,001. Structurally sound doesn't fail.

3. Would the tool survive the removal of humans from the loop?

When agents deploy infrastructure and humans aren't triaging alerts at 3am: does the tool still work? If it requires a human to interpret its output, it's pre-convergence. The convergent-era tool produces machine-readable verdicts that agents and pipelines act on.

Good enough is the state your toolstack is in right now. It works. It detects things. It alerts people. It has worked for years.

It's indistinguishable from failure that is just delayed. The delay makes it invisible. The convergence makes it inevitable.

Built for the convergent era with invariants that compose (not rules that accumulate), transitions evaluated before deployment (not states scanned after), bounded mitigation (not runtime mutation), additive adoption (not rip-and-replace), open catalog as convergence substrate, step-wise verifiable claims. Stave is an open-source Risk Reasoner. The convergence is coming. This is the product built for after it arrives. Try it: bash examples/demo-ai-security/run.sh

title: rspec-wasm v0.2.0: Testing Ruby Code That Integrates with JavaScript and WebAssembly
description:
In September 2026, I released rspec-wasm, a tool for running RSpec tests on ruby.wasm, and introduced it in my previous DEV article:

Stop Writing Ruby Tests in JS Template Literals: Meet rspec-wasm

I've now released rspec-wasm v0.2.0, which adds support for asynchronous JavaScript setup and teardown around RSpec execution.

One of the great advantages of building applications with WebAssembly is the ability to combine functionality from different Wasm modules.

However, until now, rspec-wasm had no way to asynchronously initialize an external runtime before running RSpec tests or clean it up afterward.

With v0.2.0, we can initialize external JavaScript or Wasm runtimes before running RSpec, making it possible to test Ruby code that interacts with them.

In this article, I'll demonstrate the new functionality by testing Ruby code that uses a WebAssembly-based MP3 decoder.

Why Use External Wasm Modules with ruby.wasm?

When developing applications with ruby.wasm, building a custom Wasm binary can expand what's possible.

However, if we want to use existing gems with a prebuilt ruby.wasm runtime, we're currently limited to pure Ruby gems.

This can lead to a few challenges:

  • An appropriate pure Ruby gem might not exist for the functionality we need.
  • A pure Ruby implementation might not provide the performance we expect.
  • Our application might be designed to combine multiple Wasm modules from the beginning.

In these situations, using external Wasm modules alongside ruby.wasm can be a practical solution.

For example, we might want to integrate:

  • Image and video processing libraries
  • Databases such as SQLite
  • Python/Wasm runtimes
  • Compression and cryptography libraries
  • Numerical computing or machine learning runtimes

But how can we test Ruby code that depends on these external runtimes?

That's where the new functionality in rspec-wasm v0.2.0 comes in.

Example: Decoding MP3 Audio with WebAssembly

Let's build a small example that initializes a WebAssembly-based MP3 decoder, calls it from Ruby, and verifies the decoded audio information using RSpec.

We'll use the following:

  • Node.js 18 or later
  • rspec-wasm 0.2.0
  • mpg123-decoder 1.0.3

Both ruby.wasm and RSpec are included in rspec-wasm, so we don't need to install them separately.

mpg123-decoder is an MP3 decoder that runs mpg123 through WebAssembly.

1. Create the Project

First, create a new project and install the dependencies.

mkdir rspec-wasm-mp3-example
cd rspec-wasm-mp3-example
npm init -y
npm install mpg123-decoder@1.0.3
npm install --save-dev rspec-wasm@0.2.0

Add the test command to package.json.

{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "rspec-wasm"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "mpg123-decoder": "1.0.3"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "rspec-wasm": "0.2.0"
  }
}

Our project will have the following structure:

.
├── lib/
│   └── audio_probe.rb
├── spec/
│   ├── fixtures/
│   │   └── tone.mp3
│   └── audio_probe_spec.rb
├── package.json
└── rspec-wasm.config.mjs

2. Prepare an MP3 File for Testing

For this example, we'll use a stereo MP3 file with a sample rate of 44.1 kHz.

Download the test file using the following commands:

mkdir -p spec/fixtures
curl -L https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders/raw/refs/heads/main/test/data/44100.stereo.cbr.mp3 \
  -o spec/fixtures/tone.mp3

This file comes from the test data in eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders, which is distributed under the MIT license.

If you use a different MP3 file, adjust the expected sample rate and channel count in the tests accordingly.

3. Initialize the Wasm Decoder Before Running RSpec

Now comes the main feature introduced in v0.2.0.

Create rspec-wasm.config.mjs to define the setup and teardown operations.

import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";
import { MPEGDecoder } from "mpg123-decoder";

let decoder;

function summarize(decoded, encodedBytes) {
  const peakLevels = decoded.channelData.map((channel) => {
    let peak = 0;

    for (const sample of channel) {
      peak = Math.max(peak, Math.abs(sample));
    }

    return peak;
  });

  return {
    encoded_bytes: encodedBytes,
    sample_rate: decoded.sampleRate,
    channels: decoded.channelData.length,
    samples_per_channel: decoded.samplesDecoded,
    duration_ms: Math.round(
      decoded.samplesDecoded / decoded.sampleRate * 1000
    ),
    peak_levels: peakLevels,
    errors: decoded.errors.map((error) => error.message),
  };
}

export default {
  async setup({ workspaceRoot }) {
    decoder = new MPEGDecoder();
    await decoder.ready;

    globalThis.audioCodec = {
      async inspect(relativePath) {
        const root = path.resolve(workspaceRoot);
        const filePath = path.resolve(root, relativePath);
        const relative = path.relative(root, filePath);

        if (relative.startsWith("..") || path.isAbsolute(relative)) {
          throw new Error("Audio file must be inside the workspace");
        }

        const encoded = await fs.readFile(filePath);

        try {
          const decoded = decoder.decode(encoded);
          return JSON.stringify(
            summarize(decoded, encoded.byteLength)
          );
        } finally {
          await decoder.reset();
        }
      },
    };
  },

  async teardown() {
    decoder?.free();
    delete globalThis.audioCodec;
  },
};

The setup function initializes the Wasm decoder and waits until it's ready before RSpec starts.

We expose the initialized API through globalThis.audioCodec, allowing Ruby code to access it through the JavaScript bridge.

After the tests finish, teardown releases the decoder.

The execution flow looks like this:

Create Ruby VM
      |
      v
Asynchronously initialize
the MP3 Wasm decoder
      |
      v
Run RSpec tests
      |
      v
Release the decoder

This lifecycle management is particularly useful for external Wasm modules that require asynchronous initialization.

4. Await a JavaScript Promise from Ruby

Next, create lib/audio_probe.rb.

require "json"
require "js"

class AudioProbe
  def self.inspect(path)
    result = JS.global[:audioCodec]
      .call(:inspect, path)
      .await
      .to_s

    JSON.parse(result, symbolize_names: true)
  end
end

The JavaScript inspect function returns a Promise, so we use .await on the Ruby side to wait for the result.

In v0.2.0, rspec-wasm executes RSpec through RubyVM#evalAsync, allowing Ruby code inside specs to await JavaScript Promises.

Another important detail is that the MP3 binary data and decoded PCM data remain on the JavaScript/Wasm side.

Only a small JSON summary is returned to Ruby.

This avoids unnecessarily transferring large binary data across the Ruby–JavaScript boundary.

5. Write the RSpec Tests

Now let's create spec/audio_probe_spec.rb.

require "audio_probe"

RSpec.describe AudioProbe do
  it "decodes MP3 metadata with a WebAssembly codec" do
    result = described_class.inspect("spec/fixtures/tone.mp3")

    expect(result[:encoded_bytes]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:sample_rate]).to eq(44_100)
    expect(result[:channels]).to eq(2)
    expect(result[:samples_per_channel]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:duration_ms]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:peak_levels].first).to be_between(0.0, 1.0)
    expect(result[:errors]).to be_empty
  end

  it "rejects parent-directory traversal" do
    expect {
      described_class.inspect("../outside.mp3")
    }.to raise_error(JS::Error, /inside the workspace/)
  end
end

The first test actually decodes an MP3 file using WebAssembly and verifies properties such as the sample rate, channel count, and audio duration.

The second test verifies that the JavaScript API rejects attempts to access files outside the workspace using ../.

JavaScript exceptions are exposed as JS::Error on the Ruby side, so we can test them using the usual RSpec matchers.

A note about path validation: This example uses lexical path validation with path.relative. If you need to enforce workspace boundaries even when symbolic links are involved, you should also validate the resolved paths using fs.realpath.

For this demonstration, we'll keep things simple.

6. Run the Tests

Finally, run:

npm test

The output should look similar to this:

AudioProbe
  decodes MP3 metadata with a WebAssembly codec
  rejects parent-directory traversal

Finished in 0.10502 seconds (files took 1.3 seconds to load)
2 examples, 0 failures

2 examples, 0 failures!

We've successfully tested Ruby code that calls JavaScript, invokes a WebAssembly MP3 decoder, and returns the result to RSpec.

And we can use ordinary RSpec matchers throughout the process.

What's New in rspec-wasm v0.2.0?

Version 0.2.0 introduces the following features:

  • Configuration through rspec-wasm.config.mjs — Define JavaScript-side initialization and cleanup behavior.
  • Asynchronous setup and teardown — Initialize external runtimes before tests and release resources afterward.
  • Promise support in Ruby specs — Call JavaScript functions that return Promises and wait for their results using .await.
  • Reliable cleanup — Run teardown operations whether RSpec tests pass or fail.
  • Initialization failure handling — If setup fails, RSpec won't start, and the process exits with a non-zero status.

The MP3 decoder example demonstrates the first three features directly.

Conclusion

With rspec-wasm v0.2.0, we can now test more than just Ruby code running entirely inside ruby.wasm.

We can also test Ruby applications that use JavaScript as their host environment and integrate functionality from external WebAssembly modules.

I think combining multiple Wasm modules is one of the interesting possibilities of WebAssembly-based application development.

By supporting asynchronous runtime initialization and Promise handling, rspec-wasm makes it easier to write RSpec tests for these applications without moving test logic into JavaScript.

If you're building applications with ruby.wasm and other Wasm modules, give rspec-wasm a try!

References

  • rspec-wasm on npm
  • ruby.wasm on GitHub
  • RSpec
  • mpg123-decoder on npm
  • My previous DEV article: Stop Writing Ruby Tests in JS Template Literals: Meet rspec-wasm

title: React Use Mobile Hook: SSR-Safe, No Hydration Mismatch
description:
TL;DR

A React use mobile hook returns false on the server because the server has no screen: it renders the HTML before any browser reports a width, and hydration has to repeat that guess. Switch visible layout with CSS breakpoints, which apply at first paint, and keep the hook for behavior after an interaction, such as opening a bottom sheet instead of a dialog. Build the hook on useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot, so hydration matches and every later mount reads the real value on its first render.

Sooner or later, a Next.js app that has to work on phones grows a React use mobile hook: a useIsMobile() that returns true below 768px, copied from a starter or from shadcn/ui. It works in the browser, then surprises you three ways: it returns false on the server, a careless version throws a hydration error, and a phone can briefly see the desktop version of whatever the hook controls. This tutorial explains where each one comes from, which jobs belong to CSS breakpoints, and how to write an SSR-safe media query hook on useSyncExternalStore that hydrates cleanly.

Why is useIsMobile false on the server?

Because the server has no screen. React renders the HTML before any browser has reported a width, so a hook that reads matchMedia has nothing to read and must return a fixed guess. In the Next.js App Router the gap is wider still: a page that uses no request-time APIs is prerendered once at build time, with no request and no visitor at all.

The guess itself is harmless. The trouble is hydration: the first client render has to produce the same markup as the server, so the browser repeats the guess, and the value may only change after hydration. On a phone, the server's answer stays on screen from the first paint until the JavaScript has downloaded, parsed and hydrated, and on a slow connection that takes a while. Anything visible that depends on the hook is wrong for that whole window.

So the useful question is which jobs can live with a guess for that window.

Why does a useIsMobile hook cause a hydration mismatch?

Only when it reads window during render: the browser's first render then disagrees with the server's HTML. Search for a React is mobile hook and you find three shapes, and only the first one does that. We server-rendered each one with renderToString from React 19.3, hydrated it with hydrateRoot in Chromium at 390px through Playwright, and mounted a second copy 300ms later, the way a dialog, a lazy panel or a client-side route mounts after hydration:

Pattern Hydration at 390px First render of a later mount
typeof window check in render Text: an error, the tree is rebuilt on the client. A class: no error, the server's class stays true
useState + useEffect No error: false, then true after the effect false, then true
useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot No error: false, then true right after hydration true

The first shape is the obvious one:

// wrong: the server says false, a phone says true during hydration
const isMobile = typeof window !== "undefined" && matchMedia("(max-width: 767.98px)").matches;

When the hook changes text, React 19 reports "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" and rebuilds that tree on the client, which throws away the work SSR did. The Next.js hydration error page lists this exact check as a common cause.

When the hook only picks a className, nothing fails, and that is worse. In development React 19 logs "A tree hydrated but some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't match the client properties. This won't be patched up." A production build logs nothing. In our test the phone kept class="desktop" after hydration in both builds, and nothing corrects it while the value stays the same.

The second shape is the shadcn use-mobile hook that ships with the shadcn/ui Sidebar. As of October 2026 its source keeps undefined in state, measures in an effect and returns !!isMobile:

const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = React.useState<boolean | undefined>(undefined)

React.useEffect(() => {
  const mql = window.matchMedia(`(max-width: ${MOBILE_BREAKPOINT - 1}px)`)
  // ...subscribes to mql, then:
  setIsMobile(window.innerWidth < MOBILE_BREAKPOINT)
}, [])

return !!isMobile

It never mismatches, because every first render returns false. The catch is the word every: a component that mounts long after hydration also renders as a desktop once, then corrects itself in the effect. An autoFocus={!isMobile} on a field in that component is true on the first commit, and React focuses the field during that commit, so a phone can still get the keyboard you meant to avoid.

The shadcn Sidebar gets away with the false start for a good reason. The desktop markup it renders on the server carries hidden md:block, so a phone never sees it, and on a phone the correction swaps in a Sheet that stays closed until someone opens it. That is the pattern to copy, and the next section spells it out.

When should you use CSS breakpoints instead of a hook?

For everything visible before the first interaction. CSS media queries apply at first paint, before any JavaScript runs, so they are already right in the server's HTML. Render both versions and let a breakpoint hide one:

// app/orders/page.tsx: a server component, no hook to correct
import { getOrders } from "@/lib/orders";
import { OrderCard } from "./order-card";
import { OrderRow } from "./order-row";

export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const orders = await getOrders();
  return (
    <>
      <ul className="flex flex-col gap-2 md:hidden">
        {orders.map((order) => (
          <OrderCard key={order.id} order={order} />
        ))}
      </ul>
      <table className="hidden w-full md:table">
        <tbody>
          {orders.map((order) => (
            <OrderRow key={order.id} order={order} />
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </>
  );
}

Both trees are in the DOM, which costs little for a nav or a page of 20 rows. When the switch depends on the space a component gets rather than the window, Tailwind v4's @container and @md: variants do it in CSS with no hook at all.

Keep the hook for decisions that start after the person does something, or that never show on the first paint:

  • which overlay opens: a bottom sheet below 768px, a popover or a dialog above it
  • the edge a panel slides in from
  • whether a field takes focus when a panel opens, since focusing it on a phone pops the keyboard over the content
  • where a click goes: a full page on a phone, a side panel next to the list on desktop

A closed overlay renders only its trigger, and the trigger is usually the same button in both modes, so the hook can switch the overlay freely. The shadcn responsive dialog tutorial builds that switch for a dialog, and the mobile-first React components guide applies the same rule across a whole component library.

How do you write an SSR-safe useMediaQuery hook?

Read the query through useSyncExternalStore, React's API for values that live outside React, and give it a server snapshot. That is the whole fix for useMediaQuery SSR problems:

// hooks/use-media-query.ts
import { useCallback, useSyncExternalStore } from "react";

// the complement of Tailwind's md: variant, in the same unit
export const MOBILE_QUERY = "(width < 48rem)";

const lists = new Map<string, MediaQueryList>();

function getList(query: string) {
  let list = lists.get(query);
  if (!list) {
    list = window.matchMedia(query);
    lists.set(query, list);
  }
  return list;
}

export function useMediaQuery(query: string, serverFallback = false) {
  // stable per query, or React unsubscribes and subscribes again on every render
  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onChange: () => void) => {
      const list = getList(query);
      list.addEventListener("change", onChange);
      return () => list.removeEventListener("change", onChange);
    },
    [query],
  );
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => getList(query).matches,
    // the server and the hydration render
    () => serverFallback,
  );
}

export function useIsMobile() {
  return useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY);
}

// the same check in event handlers and effects; false on the server
export function matchesMedia(query: string) {
  return typeof window !== "undefined" && getList(query).matches;
}

Here is what React does with it:

  • Server and hydration. React calls the third function, so the server HTML and the hydration render agree. Leave it out and the React docs are blunt: "rendering the component on the server will throw an error."
  • Right after hydration. Once the effects run, React compares the server snapshot with the browser's answer and, when they differ, re-renders synchronously. That is the false, then true in the table above.
  • Every later mount. React calls the second function during the first render, so a sheet that opens on a phone renders as a phone from its first frame.
  • Updates. A MediaQueryList fires change only when the query flips, so dragging the window edge costs no renders until it crosses the breakpoint, unlike a resize listener. The lists are cached per query because matches is read on every render.

If the shadcn Sidebar added hooks/use-mobile.ts to your project, point that file at the new hook. The Sidebar keeps its import, and its hidden md:block desktop markup now flips at the same width as the hook:

// hooks/use-mobile.ts
import { MOBILE_QUERY, useMediaQuery } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export const useIsMobile = () => useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY);

Event handlers do not need the hook at all. Read the query at the moment of the click:

// app/orders/use-open-order.ts
"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { useState } from "react";
import { MOBILE_QUERY, matchesMedia } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export function useOpenOrder() {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  function openOrder(id: string) {
    // phones get a full page, desktops a panel next to the list
    if (matchesMedia(MOBILE_QUERY)) router.push(`/orders/${id}`);
    else setSelected(id);
  }

  return { selected, openOrder };
}

Which serverFallback should you pass?

The answer whose mistake costs least during the hydration window. For useIsMobile, false is usually right, because the decisions it drives start after a tap and by then the real value is in. For a query that changes something visible, pick the answer that works on every device. With (hover: hover) that is false: the server renders the always-visible version of a control, and a mouse user gets the hover polish a moment later.

Should the query use px or rem?

Use the unit of your CSS breakpoints. Tailwind v4 defines --breakpoint-md: 48rem, and our build compiles md: to @media (min-width: 48rem). Media Queries Level 4 says relative units in media queries are "based on the initial value", so 48rem follows the default font size set in the visitor's browser and ignores your html { font-size }. A hook written in px does not move with it.

We checked this in Chromium through Playwright, with a 900px window and the default font size set to 20px. (min-width: 48rem) stopped matching, so Tailwind showed the phone layout, while (max-width: 767.98px) did not match either, so a px hook still reported a desktop. (width < 48rem) matched, in step with the CSS. Range syntax also retires the .98px trick that Bootstrap's docs explain with "viewports with fractional widths". As of October 2026, MDN's compatibility data lists range syntax from Chrome 104, Firefox 102 and Safari 16.4.

Breakpoints are tokens like colors and radii, so keep them in one place: the Tailwind v4 design tokens guide shows how to layer them. A caveat about our own code: as of October 2026 the MOBILE_QUERY in Wingo UI is still (max-width: 767.98px), so it has the gap described above. With a 20px default font size, md: classes switch at 960px while the Drawer and the Sheet, which call useIsMobile(), switch at 768px. In your own components, call useMediaQuery("(width < 48rem)") where the hook and your classes have to agree.

Can Next.js detect mobile on the server?

It can guess from request headers, and only on routes rendered per request. Most ways to make React detect mobile or desktop on the server read the User-Agent header. Next.js parses it with userAgent() from next/server, whose device.type is "mobile", "tablet" and a few others, or undefined for desktop browsers. Pass the guess down as the server snapshot and hydration still matches, because the prop travels with the page:

// app/orders/page.tsx
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { userAgent } from "next/server";
import { OrdersScreen } from "./orders-screen";

export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const { device } = userAgent({ headers: await headers() });
  return <OrdersScreen phoneGuess={device.type === "mobile"} />;
}

// app/orders/orders-screen.tsx
"use client";

import { MOBILE_QUERY, useMediaQuery } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export function OrdersScreen({ phoneGuess }: { phoneGuess: boolean }) {
  // the server and the hydration render both use the guess, then the real value takes over
  const isMobile = useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY, phoneGuess);
  return <p>{isMobile ? "Tap an order to open it" : "Select an order to see it on the right"}</p>;
}

Know the cost before you add it:

  • Dynamic rendering. headers() is a request-time API, so the page renders on every request instead of once at build time, and any shared cache has to vary by user agent. With Cache Components turned on, the read also has to sit inside a <Suspense> boundary, or next build fails.
  • It names a device. The header stays the same for a desktop browser narrowed to 600px, a tablet app in split screen and a phone turned to landscape, so it cannot tell you the window width. Since Safari 13, Safari on iPad sends the same user agent as Safari on macOS by default, so most iPads read as desktops.
  • Client hints cover Chromium only. Sec-CH-UA-Mobile arrives without opting in, but as of October 2026 MDN's compatibility data lists it in Chrome and Edge and not in Firefox or Safari.

It pays off on app pages that are dynamic anyway, such as a signed-in dashboard, and rarely on marketing pages you want served from a CDN.

How do the Wingo UI Sheet and Drawer use the hook?

Only for behavior, and their closed state renders the same markup at every width. The free useMediaQuery hook is built the same way, with the same serverFallback parameter, plus useIsMobile, useIsTouch for (pointer: coarse), useBreakpoint and matchesMedia. Resize this window across 768px, or open the page on a phone:

Live demo: useMediaQuery. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Resize the window across 768px: the useIsMobile() card and the (width < 48rem) card flip together at the default font size, and the ruler moves to the widest Tailwind breakpoint that matches). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the useMediaQuery docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query

The Drawer calls useIsMobile() in its root. Phones always get the draggable sheet; from 768px the desktop prop picks a centered sheet, a side panel or a dialog. Its trigger is the same Radix Dialog trigger in every mode, so the server's guess changes nothing on screen, and the open state lives in the root, so a tablet rotated across 768px keeps the drawer open.

Live demo: Drawer. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap Filters: below 768px the drawer slides up as a sheet you can drag down to close; on a wider screen the same component opens a centered dialog). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Drawer docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer

The Sheet does the same for side panels. mobileSide="bottom" turns a filter panel from the right into a bottom sheet on phones, and the side only matters once the sheet is open:

import { SlidersHorizontal } from "lucide-react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Sheet } from "@/components/ui/sheet";

export function OrderFilters() {
  return (
    <Sheet
      side="right"
      mobileSide="bottom"
      title="Filters"
      description="Status, date and amount"
      trigger={
        <Button variant="soft" leftIcon={<SlidersHorizontal />}>
          Filters
        </Button>
      }
    >
      <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">Pick the orders you want to see.</p>
    </Sheet>
  );
}

What should you do next?

Paste the hook above into hooks/use-media-query.ts, or install ours with npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query. Then search your codebase for useIsMobile and sort every call: visible layout moves to md: classes, behavior stays on the hook. More posts on the same stack live in Next.js and Tailwind CSS.

Components in this post

  • useMediaQuery (Free): SSR-safe hooks for media queries, phone widths, touch screens and the current Tailwind breakpoint. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query
  • Sheet (Free): A panel that slides in from any edge on a spring: filters, a cart, an inspector or the phone navigation menu, swipeable to close on touch. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add sheet
  • Drawer (Free): The library's bottom sheet on vaul: drag to dismiss, snap points, nesting, and a side panel or dialog on desktop. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer

FAQ

Why does useIsMobile return false on the server?

The server renders the HTML before any browser reports a screen width, so the hook has nothing to measure and returns a fixed guess. Hydration has to repeat that guess, and the real value arrives right after it.

Does the shadcn useIsMobile hook cause a hydration mismatch?

No. The shadcn use-mobile hook keeps undefined in state and measures the screen in an effect, so its first render returns false on the server and in the browser alike. The cost is that a component mounted after hydration also renders as a desktop once, until the effect corrects it.

How do I fix a hydration mismatch caused by useMediaQuery?

Stop reading window during render and read the query through useSyncExternalStore, with a getServerSnapshot that returns the same value on the server and during hydration. React then corrects the value right after hydration, with no mismatch.

Can Next.js detect a mobile device on the server?

It can guess from the User-Agent header with userAgent() from next/server, which makes the route render per request. The header names a device and says nothing about the viewport width, so use the guess as the server snapshot only and keep layout in CSS.

Why does my useIsMobile hook disagree with Tailwind's md breakpoint?

Tailwind v4 breakpoints are in rem (md is 48rem), and media queries resolve rem from the browser's default font size, while many hooks, shadcn's included, hard-code 768px. When a visitor raises that font size the two disagree; write the hook's query as (width < 48rem) and both flip at the same width.

Is the Wingo UI useMediaQuery hook free?

Yes. useMediaQuery, useIsMobile and the rest of the hook file are free, and so are the Sheet and the Drawer that use it. Install the hook with npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Use Mobile Hook: SSR-Safe, No Hydration Mismatch. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Humanize OpenRouter Output in Java: A Zero-Dependency Linter for Bold-Label Bullets, Emoji and Title Case + 5 Free Tools (2026)
description:
Last verified November 2026. Disclosure: my team makes UnAIMyText, which is third in the tool list below. The Java is free to copy.

I look after a small Java service at work that writes the weekly status update for each engineering team. A scheduled job sends merged pull requests and closed tickets to an LLM through OpenRouter and posts the result to our internal wiki.

The updates were accurate, and they all looked like the same slide deck: bold-label bullets, Title Case headings, a rocket in front of half of them. Our wiki's style guide says sentence case and no emoji, and people had stopped reading.

So I wrote a linter. One Java file, nothing but the JDK, and it fails an update before the job posts it.

What the linter checks

My earlier checkers in this series looked at wording and punctuation. This one looks at Markdown structure:

  1. Bold-label bullets. - **Faster Builds:** CI now caches... once is fine. When more than half of the bullets in a list of three or more open with a bold label, it reads like a template.
  2. Emoji. More than one emoji fails. The count skips fenced code and inline code, so a deploy script that prints a rocket doesn't count.
  3. Title Case headings. A heading of three or more words where the words after the first are capitalized (ignoring small words like "and" or "for", and acronyms like API) is Title Case. More than one fails, because our house style is sentence case.

The exit code is 0 for a pass, 1 for a rewrite and 2 when the API call fails. --json prints a machine-readable report.

The request

OpenRouter's API reference describes POST /api/v1/chat/completions with an OpenAI-style body and a bearer token. A few details from it shaped the code:

  • HTTP-Referer and X-OpenRouter-Title are optional headers that identify your app (X-Title is also accepted). The linter only sends them if you set OPENROUTER_APP_URL.
  • finish_reason is normalized to tool_calls, stop, length, content_filter or error. Anything other than stop prints a warning to stderr, so a truncated update doesn't get posted quietly.
  • A choice can carry its own error object, and message.content can be null. Both count as a failed request.

The default model is openai/gpt-oss-20b, which is a reasoning model. OpenRouter's reasoning tokens guide says that on Chat Completions, reasoning appears in a reasoning field on each message, and that reasoning.exclude omits it from the response (the tokens are still billed). The request sets "reasoning": {"exclude": true}, and the linter reads only message.content either way, because that's what gets posted.

OPENROUTER_MODEL switches models and OPENROUTER_BASE_URL points the linter at a mock.

The code

Java 17 or newer. Run it straight from source with java StatusLint.java; there's no build step.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Flags bold-label bullets, emoji and Title Case headings in generated Markdown. */
public class StatusLint {
    // House style knobs.
    static final int MIN_BULLETS = 3;
    static final double MAX_BOLD_SHARE = 0.5;
    static final int MAX_EMOJI = 1;
    static final int MAX_TITLE_CASE_HEADINGS = 1;

    static final Pattern FENCE = Pattern.compile("(?ms)^```

.*?^

```[ \\t]*$");
    static final Pattern HEADING = Pattern.compile("^\\s{0,3}#{1,6}\\s+(.+?)\\s*#*\\s*$");
    static final Pattern BULLET = Pattern.compile("^\\s*(?:[-*+]|\\d+[.)])\\s+(.*)$");
    static final Pattern BOLD_LABEL = Pattern.compile("^(?:\\*\\*|__)[^*_]{1,40}(?::(?:\\*\\*|__)|(?:\\*\\*|__):)");
    static final Pattern SMALL_WORDS = Pattern.compile(
            "a|an|and|as|at|but|by|for|in|nor|of|on|or|the|to|vs|via|with");

    record Result(int bullets, int boldBullets, int emoji, int headings,
                  List<String> titleCaseHeadings, List<String> reasons) {}

    static Result check(String markdown) {
        String text = FENCE.matcher(markdown).replaceAll("");
        int bullets = 0, bold = 0, headings = 0;
        List<String> titleCase = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String line : text.split("\\R")) {
            var h = HEADING.matcher(line);
            if (h.matches()) {
                headings++;
                if (isTitleCase(h.group(1))) titleCase.add(h.group(1));
                continue;
            }
            var b = BULLET.matcher(line);
            if (b.matches()) {
                bullets++;
                if (BOLD_LABEL.matcher(b.group(1)).find()) bold++;
            }
        }
        String noInlineCode = text.replaceAll("`[^`\\n]*`", "");
        int emoji = (int) noInlineCode.codePoints().filter(StatusLint::isEmoji).count();

        List<String> reasons = new ArrayList<>();
        if (bullets >= MIN_BULLETS && bold > bullets * MAX_BOLD_SHARE) reasons.add("bold-label bullets");
        if (emoji > MAX_EMOJI) reasons.add("emoji");
        if (titleCase.size() > MAX_TITLE_CASE_HEADINGS) reasons.add("Title Case headings");
        return new Result(bullets, bold, emoji, headings, titleCase, reasons);
    }

    /** Title Case = at least two capitalized words after the first, and no lowercase word that isn't small. */
    static boolean isTitleCase(String heading) {
        String[] words = heading.replaceAll("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}'\\s-]", " ").trim().split("\\s+");
        if (words.length < 3) return false;
        int capped = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < words.length; i++) {
            String w = words[i];
            if (w.isEmpty() || !Character.isLetter(w.charAt(0))) continue;
            if (Character.isUpperCase(w.charAt(0))) {
                if (!w.equals(w.toUpperCase())) capped++; // skip acronyms like API
            } else if (!SMALL_WORDS.matcher(w).matches()) {
                return false;
            }
        }
        return capped >= 2;
    }

    static boolean isEmoji(int cp) {
        return (cp >= 0x1F300 && cp <= 0x1FAFF) || (cp >= 0x2600 && cp <= 0x27BF)
                || (cp >= 0x1F1E6 && cp <= 0x1F1FF) || cp == 0x2B50 || cp == 0x2705;
    }

    static String askOpenRouter(String prompt, String key) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        String base = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_BASE_URL", "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1");
        String model = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_MODEL", "openai/gpt-oss-20b");
        String body = "{\"model\":" + Json.quote(model)
                + ",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":" + Json.quote(prompt) + "}]"
                + ",\"reasoning\":{\"exclude\":true}}"; // keep thinking out of the reply

        var req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base.replaceAll("/+$", "") + "/chat/completions"))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
                .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json");
        String appUrl = System.getenv("OPENROUTER_APP_URL"); // optional attribution
        if (appUrl != null) req.header("HTTP-Referer", appUrl).header("X-OpenRouter-Title", "statuslint");

        HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build();
        HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req.POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build(),
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        if (res.statusCode() / 100 != 2) {
            String snippet = res.body().substring(0, Math.min(200, res.body().length()));
            throw new IOException("HTTP " + res.statusCode() + ": " + snippet);
        }

        Object choices = Json.get(Json.parse(res.body()), "choices");
        if (!(choices instanceof List<?> list) || list.isEmpty()) throw new IOException("no choices in reply");
        Object choice = list.get(0);
        if (Json.get(choice, "error") != null) throw new IOException("provider error: " + Json.get(choice, "error"));
        Object finish = Json.get(choice, "finish_reason");
        if (finish != null && !"stop".equals(finish)) System.err.println("warning: finish_reason=" + finish);
        // Only message.content is checked; a "reasoning" field, if any, is ignored.
        Object content = Json.get(Json.get(choice, "message"), "content");
        if (!(content instanceof String s) || s.isBlank()) throw new IOException("reply had no content");
        return s;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        List<String> rest = new ArrayList<>(List.of(args));
        boolean asJson = rest.remove("--json");
        String prompt = String.join(" ", rest).trim();
        String key = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "");

        String raw;
        try {
            raw = key.isEmpty() || prompt.isEmpty()
                    ? new String(System.in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
                    : askOpenRouter(prompt, key);
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException | IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.err.println("request failed: " + e);
            System.exit(2);
            return;
        }

        Result r = check(raw);
        if (asJson) {
            System.out.println(Json.write(Map.of("bullets", r.bullets(), "bold_bullets", r.boldBullets(),
                    "emoji", r.emoji(), "headings", r.headings(),
                    "title_case_headings", r.titleCaseHeadings(), "reasons", r.reasons())));
        } else {
            System.out.printf("bullets: %d (%d bold-label), emoji: %d, headings: %d (%d Title Case)%n",
                    r.bullets(), r.boldBullets(), r.emoji(), r.headings(), r.titleCaseHeadings().size());
            System.out.println(r.reasons().isEmpty() ? "verdict: ok"
                    : "verdict: rewrite (" + String.join("; ", r.reasons()) + ")");
        }
        System.exit(r.reasons().isEmpty() ? 0 : 1);
    }

    /** Just enough JSON for one request and one response; no dependencies. */
    static final class Json {
        private final String s;
        private int i;

        private Json(String s) { this.s = s; }

        static Object parse(String text) {
            Json p = new Json(text);
            try {
                Object v = p.value();
                p.ws();
                if (p.i != text.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("trailing data at " + p.i);
                return v;
            } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("truncated JSON");
            }
        }

        static Object get(Object node, String key) {
            return node instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? m.get(key) : null;
        }

        static String quote(String v) {
            StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder("\"");
            for (char c : v.toCharArray()) {
                switch (c) {
                    case '"' -> b.append("\\\"");
                    case '\\' -> b.append("\\\\");
                    case '\n' -> b.append("\\n");
                    case '\r' -> b.append("\\r");
                    case '\t' -> b.append("\\t");
                    default -> b.append(c < 0x20 ? String.format("\\u%04x", (int) c) : String.valueOf(c));
                }
            }
            return b.append('"').toString();
        }

        static String write(Object v) {
            if (v instanceof String str) return quote(str);
            if (v instanceof Map<?, ?> m) {
                List<String> parts = new ArrayList<>();
                new java.util.TreeMap<>(m).forEach((k, val) -> parts.add(quote(k.toString()) + ":" + write(val)));
                return "{" + String.join(",", parts) + "}";
            }
            if (v instanceof List<?> l) {
                return "[" + String.join(",", l.stream().map(Json::write).toList()) + "]";
            }
            return String.valueOf(v);
        }

        private void ws() {
            while (i < s.length() && Character.isWhitespace(s.charAt(i))) i++;
        }

        private Object value() {
            ws();
            if (i >= s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected end of JSON");
            char c = s.charAt(i);
            if (c == '{') return object();
            if (c == '[') return array();
            if (c == '"') return string();
            if (s.startsWith("true", i)) { i += 4; return Boolean.TRUE; }
            if (s.startsWith("false", i)) { i += 5; return Boolean.FALSE; }
            if (s.startsWith("null", i)) { i += 4; return null; }
            int start = i;
            while (i < s.length() && "+-0123456789.eE".indexOf(s.charAt(i)) >= 0) i++;
            if (start == i) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad JSON at " + i);
            return Double.parseDouble(s.substring(start, i));
        }

        private Map<String, Object> object() {
            Map<String, Object> m = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            i++;
            ws();
            if (s.charAt(i) == '}') { i++; return m; }
            while (true) {
                ws();
                String k = string();
                ws();
                expect(':');
                m.put(k, value());
                ws();
                if (s.charAt(i) == ',') { i++; continue; }
                expect('}');
                return m;
            }
        }

        private List<Object> array() {
            List<Object> l = new ArrayList<>();
            i++;
            ws();
            if (s.charAt(i) == ']') { i++; return l; }
            while (true) {
                l.add(value());
                ws();
                if (s.charAt(i) == ',') { i++; continue; }
                expect(']');
                return l;
            }
        }

        private String string() {
            expect('"');
            StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder();
            while (s.charAt(i) != '"') {
                char c = s.charAt(i++);
                if (c != '\\') { b.append(c); continue; }
                char e = s.charAt(i++);
                switch (e) {
                    case 'n' -> b.append('\n');
                    case 't' -> b.append('\t');
                    case 'r' -> b.append('\r');
                    case 'b' -> b.append('\b');
                    case 'f' -> b.append('\f');
                    case 'u' -> { b.append((char) Integer.parseInt(s.substring(i, i + 4), 16)); i += 4; }
                    default -> b.append(e); // \" \\ \/
                }
            }
            i++;
            return b.toString();
        }

        private void expect(char c) {
            if (i >= s.length() || s.charAt(i) != c) throw new IllegalArgumentException("expected " + c + " at " + i);
            i++;
        }
    }
}

A few notes:

  • Why a hand-rolled JSON reader? I wanted a single file that runs on a bare JDK. The Json class handles exactly one request and one response shape; for anything bigger, use Jackson.
  • Emoji detection is approximate. It counts code points in the main emoji blocks. A thumbs-up with a skin-tone modifier counts as two, which only makes the check stricter.

A mock OpenRouter server

The JDK ships a small HTTP server in com.sun.net.httpserver, which is enough for tests. Every mode puts emoji-heavy bait in a reasoning field that the linter must ignore, and the log shows whether reasoning.exclude and the attribution header were sent.

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

/** java MockOpenRouter.java 8091 robotic|clean|length */
public class MockOpenRouter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int port = Integer.parseInt(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "8091");
        String mode = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "robotic";
        String finish = mode.equals("length") ? "length" : "stop";
        String content = !mode.equals("robotic")
                ? "## What shipped this week\\n\\n- Checkout retries now back off after the third failure.\\n"
                  + "- The refunds report loads in about two seconds instead of nine.\\n"
                  + "- Priya fixed the timezone bug in the invoice footer.\\n\\n## Next week\\n\\nWe start on saved cards."
                : "## \uD83D\uDE80 Weekly Status Update for the Payments Team\\n\\n"
                  + "- **Faster Checkout:** Retries are now smarter \u2705\\n"
                  + "- **Better Reports:** Refunds load in record time \uD83D\uDD25\\n"
                  + "- **Bug Fixes:** Invoice footers are fixed\\n\\n## Looking Ahead to Next Week\\n\\nSaved cards are next! \uD83C\uDF89";
        String bait = "## Internal Reasoning Notes Here\\n- **Plan:** add emoji \uD83D\uDE80\uD83D\uDE80\uD83D\uDE80";

        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", port), 0);
        server.createContext("/", ex -> {
            String req = new String(ex.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            System.err.println("mock got " + ex.getRequestMethod() + " " + ex.getRequestURI().getPath()
                    + " exclude=" + req.contains("\"exclude\":true")
                    + " referer=" + ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("HTTP-Referer"));
            int status = 200;
            String out;
            if (!ex.getRequestURI().getPath().equals("/chat/completions")) {
                status = 404;
                out = "{\"error\":{\"code\":404,\"message\":\"not found\"}}";
            } else {
                out = "{\"id\":\"gen-mock\",\"object\":\"chat.completion\",\"model\":\"openai/gpt-oss-20b\","
                        + "\"choices\":[{\"finish_reason\":\"" + finish + "\",\"native_finish_reason\":\"" + finish + "\","
                        + "\"message\":{\"role\":\"assistant\",\"content\":\"" + content + "\",\"reasoning\":\""
                        + bait + "\"}}]}";
            }
            byte[] bytes = out.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            ex.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "application/json");
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(status, bytes.length);
            ex.getResponseBody().write(bytes);
            ex.close();
        });
        server.start();
        System.err.println("mock listening on " + port + " (" + mode + ")");
    }
}

Running it 

javac -Xlint:all -Werror -d /tmp/build StatusLint.java MockOpenRouter.java

# lint an exported update
java StatusLint.java < updates/platform-team.md

# generate with OpenRouter, then lint
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...
java StatusLint.java "Write this week's status update from these merged PRs: ..."

# point at the mock
java MockOpenRouter.java 8091 robotic &
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=test OPENROUTER_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8091 java StatusLint.java "anything"

Test results

Both files compiled with javac -Xlint:all -Werror and no warnings. I ran the same test script on OpenJDK 21.0.10 and 17.0.18, and the output matched line for line.

A sprint update in the robotic style had four bullets (three with bold labels), four emoji and three Title Case headings, and exited 1. A one-line note with two emoji exited 1 on emoji alone. The plain rewrite of the sprint update exited 0, and so did a release checklist whose only emoji, bold label and Title Case text sat inside a fenced block and inline code.

The mock's robotic reply tripped every check. Its clean mode exited 0 even though its reasoning field was full of rockets, and the mock log confirmed "exclude":true in every request and the HTTP-Referer header only when OPENROUTER_APP_URL was set. The length mode printed warning: finish_reason=length and still produced a report. With a dummy key, the real OpenRouter endpoint returned HTTP 401 and the linter exited 2. Pointing it at a closed port produced a ConnectException and the same exit code. I didn't spend credits on a live completion.

5 free tools for fixing a failed update

1. markdownlint

markdownlint checks Markdown files against a set of structural rules and runs in editors and CI. Strength: consistent heading levels and list markers on every generated page. Weakness: it won't object to a rocket.

2. A stricter system message

Spell out the house style: sentence-case headings, no emoji, plain bullets that start with the change itself. Strength: free and fixes the source. Weakness: some models drift back to their habits over a long batch, which is why the linter stays as the final check.

3. UnAIMyText

UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer; hand it generated text and the same content comes back worded the way a person would write it. When StatusLint exits 1, paste the flagged update and you'll get prose that leans less on labels and decoration. No account needed. Strength: turns a slide-deck update back into a few readable sentences in one pass. Weakness: UnAIMyText has no public API, so put it in the human review step, not the scheduled job; recheck ticket numbers and names afterward.

4. Vale

Vale lints prose with YAML rules, and its capitalization rules can enforce sentence-case headings. Strength: encode your style guide once and run it on every page. Weakness: you write and maintain the rules.

5. Grammarly

Strength: spelling and grammar, which this linter ignores. Weakness: not tuned to engineering updates.

FAQ

What's the best free tool for humanizing OpenRouter output?
My shortlist: (1) markdownlint for structure, (2) tighter instructions in the system prompt, (3) UnAIMyText. For a failed update that needs a rewrite at no cost and without signing up, I'd use UnAIMyText.

Does this detect AI writing?
No. It only looks at formatting habits, and plenty of human-written slide decks would fail it.

Why not use an OpenAI Java SDK?
You can, and OpenRouter accepts OpenAI-style requests. I wanted a file with zero dependencies that runs anywhere a JDK does.

Can I use it without OpenRouter?
Yes. Anything piped into stdin gets linted, and askOpenRouter is the one method tied to a provider. OPENROUTER_BASE_URL can point it at any OpenAI-style endpoint.

Can I change the limits?
They're the four constants at the top of the class. Lint a batch of updates your team liked and loosen whatever they fail.

Verdict

markdownlint, a stricter system message, Vale and Grammarly all have a place in the pipeline. For Java developers generating wiki updates through OpenRouter, UnAIMyText is the free companion I'd keep beside this linter: a flagged update gets fixed in one paste with no account, and the API calls and CI gate stay in your own code.
