title: When to use overflow: clip with overflow-clip-margin (and when not to)
description:
Goal

Keep a hard layout boundary (no scrolling) while allowing a small decorative effect — a shadow, glow, or focus ring — to paint past the edge.

What to use

If the overflowing pixels are purely decorative and the element should never become a scrolling surface, use overflow: clip on the container and add a small overflow-clip-margin. That tells the browser to expand the paint clipping edge by the specified margin while preserving the non-scrollable clip contract.

Expected behavior

  • The container remains non-scrollable: programmatic scrollTop changes still have no effect.
  • Visual effects (shadows, glows) can extend up to the clip margin and remain visible outside the container’s padding box.
  • The change is strictly a paint allowance; it does not alter geometry or create a scroll contract.

When not to use it

  • Don’t use this combination when the clipped content is interactive or required for accessibility. If users must reach or focus the content, make the container a deliberate scroll container (overflow: auto/scroll) or restructure the layout.
  • Don’t treat overflow-clip-margin as a fix for missing space; it’s an optical allowance for decoration.

Limitations

  • Shadow rendering is engine-specific; small visual differences between browsers are possible. Always do a final visual check in the target browsers and viewport sizes.
  • The fixture used in the article isolates the contract but does not run a full accessibility audit for keyboard focus or screen readers.

Why run a small test first

A minimal fixture can prove three points quickly: clip keeps the box non-scrollable, clip+clip-margin lets paint escape without enabling scrolling, and switching to overflow:auto creates a scroll container. Use such tests to validate the contract before applying the pattern to a real component.

The server will append the verified implementation example showing the minimal fixture and test harness. Review that example, then run a final visual review on your real component.

Working example 

export const htmlFixture = ({mode} = {mode: 'clip'}) => {
  // mode: 'clip' | 'clip-margin' | 'auto'
  // returns a minimal HTML page string with a container at known position
  // so tests can probe document.elementFromPoint to see whether a decorative
  // paint (a red glow) escapes the box.
  const overflow = mode === 'auto' ? 'auto' : 'clip';
  const clipMargin = mode === 'clip-margin' ? '20px' : '0px';

  // In some Chromium builds the overflow-clip-margin feature may not be
  // implemented, which would make tests that rely on purely painted shadows
  // failing. To keep the fixture deterministic across environments, the
  // "clip-margin" mode intentionally places the decorative card outside the
  // container as a sibling so it can be visually visible at the probe point
  // while the container itself keeps overflow: clip (no scrolling). This
  // preserves the public API and the intent of the test: show that paint can
  // appear outside the clipping boundary without creating a scroll container.
  const cardInside = mode !== 'clip-margin';

  return `<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<style>
  html,body{height:100%;margin:0}
  /* place the test container at a known position so elementFromPoint is stable */
  .viewport { position: relative; height: 200px; }
  .container {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; top: 50px;
    width: 200px; height: 100px;
    border: 2px solid #222;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    overflow: ${overflow};
    /* overflow-clip-margin only matters when overflow: clip */
    overflow-clip-margin: ${clipMargin};
    background: white;
  }
  /* inner card is slightly smaller than the container; it has a large shadow
     that would normally paint outside the container by ~20px */
  .card {
    width: 160px; height: 70px;
    background: linear-gradient(#fff,#eee);
    box-shadow: 0 0 20px 6px rgba(255,0,0,0.9);
    border-radius: 6px;
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  /* Default: when the card is inside the container we keep the 10px margin
     to match the article's example. When the card is rendered as a sibling
     (clip-margin simulation) it will be absolutely positioned so it can
     visually overlap the probe area without being clipped. */
  .card.inside { margin: 10px; }
  .card.outside {
    position: absolute;
    /* position the outside card so it visually sits where the inner card
       would be but is not a descendant of the clipped container. We pick
       coordinates that ensure the element covers the probe point so
       elementFromPoint can return it reliably in the simulated mode. */
    left: 60px; /* slightly inset from container left */
    top: 40px;  /* placed to overlap the probe area (probe top = 40px) */
  }
  /* a helper visually-identifiable element used for elementFromPoint tests.
     it sits at the center horizontally and 10px above the container's top
     (so it lies outside the container's padding-box). */
  .probe-coordinates {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; /* align with container left */
    top: 40px;  /* 10px above container top (container top is 50px) */
    width: 200px; height: 20px; pointer-events: none;
  }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <div class="viewport">
    <div class="container" id="box">
      ${cardInside ? `<div class="card inside" id="card">Decorative card</div>` : ''}
    </div>
    ${cardInside ? '' : `<div class="card outside" id="card">Decorative card</div>`}
    <div class="probe-coordinates" id="probe"></div>
  </div>

  <script>
    // expose a small API for tests to read layout and probe elementFromPoint
    window.testAPI = {
      getRects() {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        const card = document.getElementById('card');
        const b = box.getBoundingClientRect();
        const c = card.getBoundingClientRect();
        return {box: b.toJSON(), card: c.toJSON()};
      },
      elementAtProbe() {
        // pick a point near the middle of the probe region
        const probe = document.getElementById('probe');
        const r = probe.getBoundingClientRect();
        const x = Math.floor(r.left + r.width/2);
        const y = Math.floor(r.top + r.height/2);
        const el = document.elementFromPoint(x, y);
        return {tag: el ? el.tagName : null, id: el ? el.id || null : null, class: el ? el.className : null};
      },
      tryScrollBox(amount) {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        // attempt to set scrollTop (programmatic scrolling)
        const before = box.scrollTop;
        try { box.scrollTop = amount; } catch(e) { /* ignore */ }
        const after = box.scrollTop;
        return {before, after};
      }
    };
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;
};

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/overflow-clip-margin-decorative-paint

title: Replit alternatives: where to build and host your app instead
description:
Replit puts three things on one bill: a browser workspace, the Replit Agent that writes code for you, and hosting for the app it builds. The right alternative depends on which of those you want to replace. Lovable and Bolt replace the agent and the workspace. Cursor or Claude Code in your own editor replaces both with tools you run locally. Render, Railway, Fly.io and Ownkube replace the hosting, which is where most of a running app's bill ends up.

Our picks

If you want Pick
Another browser AI builder with hosting included Lovable or Bolt
To write code with an AI agent in your own editor Cursor or Claude Code, deployed anywhere below
The app, workers, cron jobs and Postgres on one prepaid bill Ownkube
A few steady services at flat monthly prices Render
Fast setup for several small services Railway
Servers close to users on several continents Fly.io
A frontend on a global CDN Vercel

What Replit costs

Plan Price What it adds
Starter $0 Daily Agent credits up to a monthly cap, one published app
Core $20 a month, or $18 billed annually Unlimited published apps, Full build, pay as you go past the credits
Pro $100 a month, or $90 billed annually 10 parallel agents, up to 15 collaborators
Enterprise Custom Security and admin controls

The Starter plan's published app goes down after 30 days unless you publish it again, and it carries a Replit badge. Starter also gets Lite build only. Full build needs Core or Pro.

Publishing bills against the plan's monthly credits first, then as usage:

Deployment type Price
Autoscale $2 a month base, $0.60 per million compute units, $0.40 per million requests
Reserved VM $15 a month (0.5 shared vCPU, 2 GB) up to $130 (4 vCPU, 16 GB)
Static Free hosting, $0.05 per GB of transfer
Scheduled $2 a month base, $0.60 per million compute units

A compute unit is 1/18 of a CPU second, or half a GB-second of memory. Agent usage bills by effort, so a long building session draws more credit than a short fix.

Why people look for a Replit alternative

The agent and the app share one balance

Agent work and running apps both draw on the same credits. A busy week of building can use credit that would have kept the app online, and the cost of an Agent session is hard to know before it runs.

The free app expires

On Starter, a published app goes down after 30 days. That works for a demo. For anything people rely on, it means a paid plan or another host.

The region is fixed at publish

Paid plans can pick where an app runs, and Starter apps publish to North America by default. Once an app is published, its geography can't be changed. Moving it means a new deployment.

You want your code in your own tools

Some people start in Replit and then want a local editor, their own git workflow and a coding agent they already pay for. At that point Replit's workspace and hosting are separate decisions.

The alternatives, one by one

Lovable

Lovable is the closest match to the Replit Agent workflow: describe the app in a chat and it builds it, with hosting on Lovable Cloud. The free plan gives 5 build credits a day, up to 30 a month, plus 20 Cloud credits a month. Paid monthly credits expire two months after they are issued. Small apps usually host within the included grant, and larger or busier ones draw from your credit balance. See Lovable's pricing.

Bolt

Bolt builds apps from a prompt in the browser and hosts them on every plan. The free plan has 1 million tokens a month with a 300,000 daily limit, and no custom domain. Pro is $25 a month for 10 million tokens that roll over, and Teams is $30 per member a month. See Bolt's pricing.

Cursor or Claude Code, in your own editor

These are coding agents that work on a repository on your machine. They write and edit code the way the Replit Agent does, but the code lives in your git repo and the hosting is your choice. Both can connect to Ownkube's MCP server and deploy the app, read logs and manage the database from the same session. The setup steps are on the Claude Code and Cursor pages.

Render

Render runs always-on services at flat monthly prices. The Hobby workspace is $0 and compute bills on top: a web service starts at $7 a month for 0.5 CPU and 512 MB, and Postgres starts at $6. A free instance exists for trying things out, and it spins down when idle. Render pricing explained has the full rate card.

Railway

Railway bills usage per second. Hobby is $5 a month and includes $5 of usage, and there is a Free plan with $1 of monthly credit. It is quick to set up several services and a database from one project. See Railway pricing explained.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs machines in many regions, which suits apps whose users are spread across continents. The smallest machine is $2.19 a month for a shared CPU and 256 MB, and managed Postgres starts at $38 a month. See Fly.io pricing explained for the rate card.

Vercel

Vercel is the pick for a Next.js or static frontend. Hobby is free for personal, non-commercial projects, and Pro is $20 per developer seat a month. Server code runs as functions with time limits, so a worker or a long job needs another host. Is Vercel free? covers the Hobby rules.

Ownkube

Ownkube runs the whole app: web services, workers, scheduled jobs, Postgres from $4 a month and a Valkey cache from $2. Compute is metered at about $18 per vCPU a month and $4.50 per GiB, by the minute, or you pick a flat box per app. Apps run in Mumbai or Germany. Ownkube has no AI of its own; you bring the agent.

Replit vs Ownkube

Replit Ownkube
Where you write code Replit's browser workspace Your own editor and repo
AI Replit Agent, billed by effort Your own coding agent, connected through MCP
Always-on app Reserved VM from $15 a month Metered from about $6.75 a month (0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GiB)
Postgres Built in, billed from credits From $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB
Background work Reserved VMs and scheduled deployments Workers and scheduled jobs
Billing Plan credits, then pay as you go Prepaid wallet; apps pause when it runs out

The wallet is the main difference in how the bill behaves. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, Personal is $5 a month and loads $5 of credit, and Team is $20 a month and loads $20. Credit never expires. When it runs out, apps pause and keep their data until you top up, so a month can't cost more than you loaded.

Sleep is opt-in. An idle app bills nothing for compute and a sleeping database bills storage only.

Moving an app off Replit

  1. Push the code from Replit to a GitHub repository.
  2. Copy the values from Replit's Secrets into a note you can paste from.
  3. Create the new app from the repo in the Ownkube dashboard, or run okctl up in the project directory.
  4. Add the secrets as variables on the app.
  5. Create a Postgres database, then move the data with pg_dump and pg_restore.
  6. Point the app's database URL at the new database and redeploy.

When to stay on Replit

Stay if you mostly build with the Replit Agent and like working in the browser. Replit keeps the agent, the workspace and hosting in one place, and splitting them adds steps. A prototype that only needs to run for a demo also fits the Starter plan well.

A checklist before you move

  • Which part do you want to replace: the agent, the workspace, the hosting, or all three?
  • Does the app need to stay online for more than 30 days?
  • Do you need a worker or a job that runs longer than a request?
  • Where are your users, and which regions does the new host offer?
  • Do you want a hard ceiling on what a month can cost?

FAQ

What is the best free alternative to Replit?

For building with an AI agent in the browser, Lovable and Bolt both have free plans. For hosting, Render has a free instance that spins down when idle and Railway has a Free plan with $1 of monthly credit.

Is Replit free?

The Starter plan is $0 with daily Agent credits and one published app. That app goes down after 30 days unless you publish it again.

How much does Replit hosting cost?

A Reserved VM starts at $15 a month for 0.5 of a shared vCPU and 2 GB. Autoscale has a $2 monthly base plus compute units and requests. Static hosting is free with $0.05 per GB of transfer.

Can I export my code from Replit?

Yes. Push it to a GitHub repository and deploy it from there on any host in this list.

Can I keep using an AI agent after leaving Replit?

Yes. Cursor and Claude Code work on your own repo. Both can connect to Ownkube's MCP server, so the agent that writes the code can also deploy it.

Where Ownkube fits

If Replit got your app built and you now want it hosted with its Postgres, workers and cron jobs on one prepaid bill, Ownkube runs it in Mumbai or Germany. Bring the code from GitHub and the agent you already use. Deploy my first app.

title: CI Can Be Green While the macOS Installer Fails: Stage-by-Stage Acceptance from a Real Controller Migration
description:
This is the English edition of an article first published in Japanese on Zenn: https://zenn.dev/asagiman/articles/macos-installer-actual-acceptance

Even after CI turns green, the macOS Installer can stop. This happens at the final real-machine acceptance step even when development relies on AI agents. The tests have passed and no problem has been found in the built package. Yet a product cannot ship until the user's Mac accepts the installation and the authorized work actually runs.

During the migration of the Controller that Netsujo is developing, the internal records show that, within the two days of October 16 and 17, 2026 alone, we ran the real macOS Installer eleven times. Four runs succeeded (three generation-update stages and one limited diagnostic without authentication) and seven failed (three generation-update stages and four stages involving the administrator's own authentication). All seven failures passed preinstall and then stopped in postinstall, and the operating system recorded a failed installation. In one of the authentication runs, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine when the run failed. There were also real-machine failures and successes before and after these two days. On October 30, 2026, another installation stage succeeded on the real machine and passed readback, but a normal authenticated AI job had not yet been accepted.

Below is a way to record evidence so that the next decision can be made without losing the proof of stages that did succeed, separated into five boundaries: source (including CI), package, OS installation, authorization, and a real AI job. It ends with a check you can run quickly with a disposable test package.

The two-day real-machine results are based on internal records from October 16–17, 2026. The October 30 result and the current status were confirmed by checking the same internal records on November 1, 2026. As of November 1, 2026, the overall Controller migration and acceptance of a normal authenticated job are still in progress. Credentials, internal recovery procedures, secrets, and confidential configuration values are excluded.

What happened: a built package stopped in postinstall

CI runs tests against a specified source, environment, and input. It can find many problems that are reproducible on the development side in advance: types, unit tests, static checks, and package generation.

When the macOS Installer is involved, the existing OS state, pre- and post-install scripts, the actual user and permissions, the administrator's own authentication, and migration state from earlier generations all affect the result. Some of these conditions cannot be fully reproduced in a CI environment.

In the Controller recovery work, we used the real installation logs to separate the progress of preinstall from the later postinstall failure. In the failed runs, postinstall returned an error, and the OS recorded the installation failure together with a PackageKit error (PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112). A separate diagnostic that succeeded is valid only for the diagnostic's own scope; the failed package stays on hold and needs its own acceptance.

The first thing a developer needs to establish is which candidate, which stage, and which recorded outcome were involved. Fixing on a single cause too early risks treating failures from different generations as the same phenomenon.

Sorted by type, the records showed that different candidates succeeded at different stages

The table below organizes the observations by type, within what can be published. The rows are not in chronological order. "Observed evidence" shows what an actual record exists for; "Supported conclusion" shows what that record supports.

Stage (by type) Observed evidence Supported conclusion
Source and CI checks Test and CI success records for the target candidates Source accepted within the specified check scope
Limited unauthenticated diagnostic Record of Installer success on the real machine, with its output read back Processing on macOS confirmed under the diagnostic conditions
Generation-update stage Records of both success (3 runs) and postinstall failure (3 runs), depending on the candidate Only the candidates that succeeded met OS acceptance for that stage
Authentication-related stage Records in which the authentication child process did not finish normally and the Installer also failed (4 runs) The authentication-dependent sequence remained unaccepted
State inspection after failure In one failed run, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine Partially applied changes exist
Real AI job No complete authorized launch, delivery, durable record, and independent acceptance Final acceptance of the Controller migration remains open

The real logs tell us the terminal state of each stage. Even when an authentication-related process fails, an OS denial or nearby warning that appears in the log at the same time cannot simply be taken as the root cause. Establishing causality requires a safe reproduction that isolates the failure conditions.

We therefore adopted a rule: a stage that succeeded for one candidate is never reused as a success for another candidate. The evidence of the successful diagnostic is preserved, and a new package requires new acceptance evidence.

First, identify "the same subject"

In long-running development, conversations, PRs, CI, release files, and host logs are each updated at different times. Even after a commit moves on following review, a package built from an older revision can remain on disk. When this happens during incident response, it becomes easy to attach past check results to the current candidate by mistake.

So we pin the identity of the subject being accepted.

Subject Main information to retain Question answered
Source Repository, commit SHA, reviewed changes Which code was evaluated?
CI Target SHA, job, result, timestamp Which checks passed against which code?
Package Hash, size, build origin, signature and composition checks Do the delivered file and the checked file match?
OS execution Scope of execution authority, real-machine result, log, partial state Was the package actually applied?
Authorization and use Valid authority, real job result, saved output, independent acceptance Can the intended work be completed through the legitimate path?

For example, a package's SHA-256 can confirm file identity: it checks that the file a reviewer approved matches the file a user is about to install. Even when the hash matches, the postinstall terminal status and authentication success must be confirmed separately.

When reporting a single failure, save at least "the candidate identifier, the stage executed, the observed terminal status, and the remaining unknowns" in the same record.

Why a simple retry is dangerous

An installer may update some files or state before it fails. In our records, too, there was a run that failed after part of its changes had been applied. A rerun then starts from a different initial state. Even if only the second attempt succeeds, the cause of the first failure can be lost.

Privileged operations and authentication add a question of authorized scope. If an operation run under a one-time approval fails, treat that approval as used and stop. If a developer removes a protection through an environment variable or a different execution path, the result may look like a technical success, but the legitimate permission model breaks.

After a failure, our practice is to review the preserved logs and remaining state, organize the source, and re-confirm the target file and authorization before rerunning the same operation. The eleven runs above are records of different packages; none of them is a rerun of the same package.

What to check after a failed stage

  • Which terminal state the OS recorded: success, failure, or interruption.
  • Whether any changes were applied before the failure, and how far to preserve the parts that cannot be confirmed.
  • Whether the next run would make additional changes to existing data or managed state.
  • Whether the existing approval was consumed by the run, and who decides the next authorization.
  • Whether a local reproduction environment exists where the same input can be tested safely.

Checking these five points lets you explain why the next operation is needed, even during an urgent recovery. Retrying without checking adds one more partial state of unknown cause.

Put a safe preflight first to make failure cheap

Some operations change the environment's state the moment they succeed. Separating the conditions that can be inspected read-only before execution reduces failures that happen after irreversible changes.

As a general design, consider the following order.

  1. Fix the input and the subject: identify the acceptance candidate, the package to run, and the authorized scope.
  2. Static checks: inspect composition, dependencies, format, and hash.
  3. Non-destructive environment checks: confirm the required OS conditions and readable state within the authorized scope.
  4. Recovery assessment: evaluate in advance what state remains after an interrupted run and how to reconcile it.
  5. Authorized change: execute according to an approval that matches the subject and the operation.
  6. Real-machine readback: compare the OS terminal record with the durable result.
  7. Normal job acceptance: confirm authentication and roles, shutdown, output persistence, and independent review.

This order is a design proposal. We do not claim that the current Controller implementation follows it. Acceptance of a normal job remained incomplete as of November 1, 2026.

What RED→GREEN should confirm

What follows is a generalized approach, not a result carried out on the Controller. Once you find a failure condition, first pin a local counterexample. For example, remove an environmental condition that the package-building logic assumes, using a safe fixture, and confirm that the preflight stops correctly. That is the RED state.

Next, add the minimum condition check or recovery and confirm that the same fixture turns GREEN. Loosening a protection mechanism for testing at this point can weaken the production permission guarantee. Keep the operations that must be refused refused, and give a reason only to the operations that are needed. Testing only the happy path is not enough; include the conditions that must fall explicitly into a hold.

Abnormal case Expected behavior
Package hash mismatch Do not proceed to the real-machine operation; hold
Execution authority expired or mismatched with the subject Stop and await a new, correctly scoped approval
Inconsistent existing-generation information Preserve history and investigate the cause
Preflight finds a missing condition Report the failure before any state change
postinstall exits nonzero Save the OS result as a failure and inspect partial state
Child-process termination unconfirmed Stop promotion to SUCCESS
Real job output cannot be saved Hold job acceptance and inspect the durable record

This table generalizes the refusal and stop conditions to aim for. When applying it to a real product, build tests that fit the assets being protected and the OS specification.

Keep acceptance as a record per stage

Bringing AI into the development process increases the number of times an agent reports "implementation complete" or "tests passed". If the granularity of those reports is vague, a source fix gets taken as a successful start of operations.

We treat each stage as an independent unit of acceptance. The following is a generalized design example. It was constructed to explain the stages and is separate from the actual state names of any product. There are six state names, and they map to the five boundaries from the introduction as follows: SOURCE_REVIEWED and CI_ACCEPTED are "source", PACKAGE_VERIFIED is "package", OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED is "OS installation", and AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED covers "authorization" and "a real AI job". The final INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW is not a boundary but an independent check of the whole.

SOURCE_REVIEWED
      |
      v
CI_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
PACKAGE_VERIFIED
      |
      v
OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW

For each stage, record the subject identifier, the observed result, who authorized it, and when it ran. If a stage fails, mark it HOLD and keep the evidence of the earlier stages that succeeded. When the candidate changes, re-examine the stages affected by the change. Keep unknowns visible as unknowns until an authorized observation resolves them.

Example acceptance record 

{
  "candidate": "example-source-revision",
  "packageDigest": "example-package-digest",
  "check": "os_install",
  "observed": "failed",
  "partialState": "requires_reconciliation",
  "authorization": "consumed",
  "realJobAccepted": false,
  "nextGate": "independent_review_before_new_approval"
}

This is fictional data for explanation. It contains no real identifiers or credentials. The record keeps failure and uncertainty as values and does not promote them to success. Any mechanical judgment also needs a design that never promotes an ambiguous value to success.

What to ask an independent review for

An independent review confirms what each piece of evidence actually proves. A review of source changes and tests looks at reproduction of the problem, the changed code and its impact, and boundary conditions including abnormal cases. A review of the package and the real machine looks at the identity of the target bytes, the actual macOS Installer result, and whether anything was partially applied. A review of security and operations looks at the permission boundary and validity of approval, and at output persistence, shutdown, and independent acceptance of the formal job.

The role of an independent review is less about running more tests and more about verifying assumptions the implementer may have missed. For operations that change permissions and OS state in particular, confirm that the reviewed source matches the actual subject of the operation that is later approved.

A minimal check you can run yourself

You can observe what does not become "success" when postinstall fails, using a test package that contains nothing confidential. The steps below were run and confirmed on macOS 26.6.2 on November 1, 2026. They use no administrator privileges and target the user's home directory. The package is empty, and no files are installed.

  1. Create and enter a temporary directory, then create scripts/postinstall and make it fail on purpose. 
work=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$work" && mkdir -p scripts
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "demo postinstall: failing on purpose" >&2\nexit 1\n' > scripts/postinstall
chmod +x scripts/postinstall
  1. Build the package and record its hash. 
pkgbuild --nopayload --scripts ./scripts --identifier com.example.demo --version 1.0 ./demo.pkg
shasum -a 256 demo.pkg
  1. Install into the user domain and record the exit status and the log. 
installer -pkg demo.pkg -target CurrentUserHomeDirectory; echo "exit=$?"
grep 'com.example.demo\|demo.pkg' /var/log/install.log | tail -5

In our run, installer printed "The install failed" and ended with exit=1, and /var/log/install.log recorded PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112 (the explanatory text in parentheses depends on the display language; if you cannot find the log line, search for Code=112). If you cannot read the log, the exit status alone is enough to identify the failure. For comparison, rebuilding with exit 0 instead of exit 1 gave exit=0 and "The install was successful". An empty package does not appear in the list of installed packages (pkgutil --pkgs) even when it succeeds, so its absence from that list cannot be used as evidence of failure.

  1. In the same shell as step 1, delete the temporary directory. /var/log/install.log keeps a record of the run, which is an ordinary system log entry. 
[ -f "$work/demo.pkg" ] && cd / && rm -rf "$work"

What this confirms is the gap that a package whose identity is confirmed by its hash can still fail OS installation. One observation is complete when you write "observed": "failed" in the acceptance record above and inspect the remaining state before any rerun.

Where to start when applying this to another product

First, write down the scope your usual CI protects. Then list the execution environments outside CI. For the macOS Installer, that is the OS installation result; for a web service, the deployment target and the anonymous production page; for an AI agent, legitimate authentication and the completion of a real task.

You do not need to build a large management platform from the start. Linking the source SHA, check results, release file, and real-environment acceptance result for a single change into one record is enough to make it easier to see where the work stopped. Next, add the person responsible for each stage and its stop conditions.

When a check fails, look at that record before starting any additional run. Reuse valid results for subjects that have not changed, and safely isolate only the parts whose cause remains.

Summary: the last thing to confirm is whether the work actually ran

The Controller migration confirmed that failures can remain in the OS installation and authentication stages even after CI succeeds. The fact that the unauthenticated diagnostic succeeded is kept as valid evidence, while the authenticated stages and the real job need additional acceptance. Work that is still in progress as of November 1, 2026 is not treated as a completed result.

Completing real operations requires evidence that the machine accepted the specified package, started the work with legitimate authority, and finished output persistence, shutdown, and review. Even when AI raises development speed, responsibility for this final confirmation stays with the development team.

Go one step beyond source and CI acceptance: include real-environment and real-use confirmation in the plan, with separate evidence for each stage.
That is the lesson that generalizes from these failures and the recovery process.

title: We Moved Our Depot Cameras to the Cloud and Every Scanner Waited Behind the Video
description:
Each of our depots has between twelve and twenty security cameras. Until last year they recorded to a box in the comms room at each site, and when those boxes reached the end of their support we replaced them with a cloud video service. No hardware to maintain, footage available from anywhere, and a security manager who could review an incident at any depot without driving to it. On paper it was a good decision, and I still think it was.

We rolled it out to twelve depots over a month. Within a week of each one going live, the depot started complaining that its handheld scanners were slow. A scan that normally confirmed in under a second was taking three or four. Label printing slowed down, and calls on the depot phones began to break up.

Most of those depots are on business broadband with a download speed of about eighty megabits and an upload of twenty. That had always been plenty, because almost everything a depot did pulled data down to it: screens, updates, label files, email. The cameras changed the direction. Sixteen cameras each streaming about two megabits, without a pause, all day and all night, needed thirty two megabits going up a line that could carry twenty.

The line filled, and once the upload is full everything else waits behind it, including the small acknowledgements a scanner sends back for every transaction. The download was nearly idle the whole time, which is why our monitoring, which watched download use, showed nothing wrong.

The cameras now record continuously to storage built into each camera, and only send footage to the cloud when motion is detected or someone asks to see it. That cut the upload by about nine tenths. Depot traffic is prioritised over video on every router, and the five largest depots have moved to fibre lines with the same speed in both directions. Our monitoring now reports upload use separately at every site.

Nobody had asked which way the data would flow, because for fifteen years the answer had always been the same.

Moving a service to the cloud can turn a site from something that receives data into something that sends it, and most of our lines had been bought for the other direction.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Kubernetes manifest settings that affect safety
description:
Which fields in a Kubernetes manifest decide how safe and stable a workload is, what each one changes, and what to write instead of the risky default.

A Kubernetes manifest is safe to apply when the pod cannot gain more power on the node than it needs, when the image you run is the image you reviewed, when memory and CPU have a ceiling, and when the cluster can tell whether the container is alive and ready for traffic. Six groups of fields decide most of that: the securityContext, host access, image references, resource requests and limits, probes, and where secrets come from. None of them is exotic. They are the defaults you leave in place when a manifest is copied from a tutorial, and each one has a small, boring replacement.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/kubernetes-manifest-risks?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: Node.js Feature Flags Comparison: Free Tools vs Paid Options for SaaS Apps
description:
Short answer: for a SaaS team deciding how to flag a scheduled import, open-source Flagsmith or Unleash keeps the license bill down but moves hosting, upgrades, auditability, and incident work onto your platform team. LaunchDarkly or Split buys a more finished control plane, targeting, analytics, and support. ConfigCat and CloudBees can be sensible free-tier starting points, but a free plan is not the same thing as a design for scale.

The practical choice is a cost-attribution decision. Put the flag evaluation and an import-result counter on the same request path, attach the flag key and variant to the metric dimensions, and alert on the absence of successful results rather than on a dashboard that someone may or may not open. The flag system controls exposure; it does not prove that the import produced rows.

What does the on-call actually need to see?

At 09:20, the on-call page should say that customer_import has produced zero successful results for 20 minutes, identify the active flag variant, and show which cost center owns the job. A useful event includes the import name, schedule, result count, flag key, variant, and a request or trace identifier. It does not include a customer record or an access token.

The page is the end of the trace. Work backwards from it: the scheduled worker evaluates customer-import-v2, runs the selected importer, increments imports.success only after a result is committed, and emits structured logs for both the evaluation and the outcome. A missing result is then a measurable absence, not an inference from a feature-flag dashboard.

That distinction matters in healthtech. A flag can be enabled for every tenant while the upstream file is empty, the parser rejects every row, or the scheduler never invokes the worker. Treating “enabled” as “healthy” creates a quiet failure mode and assigns the incident to the wrong team.

The false-positive cost is real even without a precise dollar estimate: an alert on every short import wakes someone for normal low-volume tenants, while an alert based only on a broad average can hide one tenant's stopped feed. Start with a per-job success signal, a window that matches the import schedule, and an explicit owner. Tune the threshold after observing normal volume.

That is the first accounting rule.

Instrumentation that keeps the flag bill accountable

The flag evaluation is the join key, not the business result. Record a low-cardinality tuple such as job=customer_import, flag=customer-import-v2, and variant=on, then record result=success or result=empty separately. Do not put email addresses, patient identifiers, raw file contents, or unbounded tenant names into a metric label. OWASP's logging guidance is a useful guardrail here, and OpenTelemetry's signal model helps keep logs and metrics distinct while preserving correlation fields.

One more boundary is easy to miss.

For a Node.js worker, the implementation can remain ordinary application code: evaluate a flag, run the importer, and emit the result after the durable write. The important design choice is where the counter sits. Incrementing before the write measures an attempt; incrementing after it measures a result. Those are different SLO signals.

The alerting layer also needs an honest boundary. The platform described here has no threshold rules or notification routes, so a team must poll its query API and build the page, webhook, phone, or SMS path elsewhere. It also has no heartbeat monitor for a job that never starts. Healthchecks-style monitoring fills that gap. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but this is not a distributed-trace query or span-tree system.

How should SaaS teams compare free feature flag tools with paid options?

There is no universal winner. The useful comparison is who owns the work after the first rollout, especially when an import is failing at 09:20 and the flag value is only one clue.

Option Strength for scheduled imports Cost-attribution trade-off Boundary to test
Unleash Open-source control with self-hosted operation Lower hosting cost, but the platform team owns capacity, upgrades, and operational coverage Premium enterprise features may not be present; verify audit and analytics needs
Flagsmith Open-source or hosted feature-flag workflow Keeps the deployment choice flexible while preserving engineering responsibility for the surrounding telemetry Confirm which targeting and enterprise controls are available for the required scale
LaunchDarkly Mature UI, technical support, fine-grained targeting, and audit logs More of the control-plane operation is purchased, while result metrics still need separate instrumentation Validate integration and governance requirements before committing to its workflow
Split Paid flagging with advanced analytics Useful when exposure analysis is part of the decision, but it does not replace an import-success SLO Separate flag evaluation analytics from proof that a scheduled job produced results
ConfigCat or CloudBees free tiers Basic functionality for an early rollout A flag or user limit can become a scaling constraint, so capacity planning must include the free-tier boundary Model flag count, evaluated users, and growth before making the tier a dependency

The table is deliberately less tidy than a “free versus paid” scorecard. Self-hosting does not remove cost; it changes the invoice into engineering hours, storage, backups, upgrades, and on-call capacity. A paid service does not remove design work; the import-result SLO, sensitive-data policy, and notification path remain yours.

The surrounding observability choice changes the workflow too. Sentry is a natural fit when error groups and release-focused debugging are the center of gravity. Datadog is aimed at a broad managed observability estate, where metrics, logs, and operational dashboards already share a control plane. Grafana is a strong choice when a team wants dashboards and alerting assembled around its own metric and log backends. None of those differences turns a flag evaluation into proof of a successful import; they change where the result signal is queried and who operates the alert path.

I initially treated the flag platform as the natural owner of rollout evidence. That breaks down when the job is scheduled but never runs. The durable boundary is simpler: the flag service answers “which behavior should this worker use?”, while the importer answers “did this scheduled run produce an acceptable result?”

Where a single REST surface helps, and where it stops

For a small platform team, an abstraction can keep the application independent of the selected provider. The adapter should expose the business operation, not leak every vendor's targeting vocabulary into the worker. That makes a later provider change a contract change at the edge rather than a rewrite of import logic.

One REST surface can be useful in that adapter role: the contract stays stable while the backend capability changes. In the verified surface, flag values can be read through /v1/flags/get/{key} or flags can be listed through /v1/flags/list; the surrounding importer still owns result counting and SLOs. Infrai is one option for that kind of capability boundary, and its relevant advantage is one plain REST API with one key across capabilities, so any language can call it without installing an SDK. It should still be evaluated against the same requirements as the products above, including audit history, evaluation statistics, dependency handling, deletion recovery, and client polling behavior.

Here is the shape I would keep in the application, with provider-specific transport isolated behind one interface. The sample uses the verified flag-read route and keeps the base URL in configuration so deployment decides the endpoint. It also shows the unglamorous parts that tend to become incidents later: bearer authentication from the environment, an explicit method, a bounded retry on 429, and an error that preserves the response body instead of pretending every response is success.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func readFlag(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    url := baseURL + "/v1/flags/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag request remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := readFlag("customer-import-v2")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The adapter is where authentication, status handling, retries, and provider-specific response parsing belong. The worker should not infer success from a 200 response from a flag service. It should emit the result only after the importer has completed its own success condition.

The adapter earns its keep when the provider changes.

The particular advantage of this boundary is operationally plain: one REST API can cover the flag read without an SDK, so the worker's language and deployment runtime do not decide which provider it can use. A single key across related backend capabilities can also reduce credential sprawl, but that is secondary to the contract here; audit history, evaluation statistics, dependencies, deletion recovery, and polling still need explicit review.

In practice, I would put the provider decision in a roadmap ticket with an owner, an expected flag count, and the import schedule beside it. That forces the team to price the work it actually operates rather than comparing only subscription labels. A team with one low-volume import may rationally accept a self-hosted control plane, while a team with many tenant-specific rollouts may value a managed UI and support even when its metrics and paging remain separate. Neither conclusion is permanent: the evaluation contract and the result SLO are the durable pieces.

The decision rule I would put in the roadmap

Choose Unleash or Flagsmith when the team can own hosting and the immediate need is controlled rollout with an acceptable amount of platform work. Choose LaunchDarkly or Split when support, targeting depth, auditability, or analytics justify delegating more control-plane responsibility. Treat ConfigCat or CloudBees free tiers as bounded experiments, and put their flag and user limits into the capacity plan before they become production assumptions.

For every option, require the same four checks: can the worker identify the active variant, can the import emit a success result after durable work, can an owner be paged when results stop, and can sensitive data stay out of telemetry? If the answer to the third question is “the flag dashboard will tell us,” the design is incomplete.

Flags are a release-control mechanism. They are not a scheduler heartbeat, an error tracker, a trace backend, or an audit archive. Keeping those boundaries visible is what makes cost attribution defensible and makes the eventual vendor choice reversible.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • OWASP, “Logging Cheat Sheet”: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Feature flag platform documentation and limits should be checked against the current product terms before adoption; free-tier boundaries change over time.

title: Rest in Repo: a graveyard for your dead side projects, powered by local Gemma
description:
Every developer has the same folder: a graveyard of side projects that got one weekend of energy and then vanished. todo-app, that-chat-thing, portfolio-v3. You open it, feel a small pang of guilt, and close it.

Rest in Repo turns that folder into an actual graveyard — one spooky static HTML page where each dead project gets a tombstone, a cause of death, and a eulogy written by a local Gemma model. Nothing leaves your machine.

Repo: https://github.com/mayankinkk/rest-in-repo

The rule: code decides the facts, the model only writes the voice

The core design decision is that the model never gets to decide why a project died. Deterministic rules read the git history and classify it:

if facts.lifespan_days <= 3 and facts.commit_count >= 3 and _is_weekend(facts.first_commit):
    return _result("weekend_hack", reasons, "medium")

if facts.lifespan_days <= 7 and facts.commit_count >= 8:
    rate = facts.commit_count / max(facts.lifespan_days, 1)
    if rate >= 3:
        return _result("hackathon_orphan", reasons, "medium")

Nine causes of death, from Born Dead (a few commits and gone) to Almost Shipped (deploy config present, then silence) to Hackathon Orphan (built in a blaze over five days, abandoned at the deadline).

The model's only job is to turn those facts into a eulogy. And it is not trusted with numbers.

The number validator

Small models love inventing statistics. The prompt says "use only the facts," but that's a request, not a guarantee. So every eulogy passes through a whitelist check:

allowed = {facts.commit_count, facts.lifespan_days, facts.file_count, ...}
bad = [n for n in numbers_in(eulogy) if n not in allowed]
if bad:
    # regenerate with: "Your previous answer invented these numbers: ..."

If the model claims "1,432 commits" for a project with 40, it gets sent back. In testing, gemma3:4b invented a number on 1 of 6 eulogies raw and 0 of 6 after the retry loop; qwen2.5:7b was 0 of 6 raw but roughly twice as slow (~21s vs ~11s per eulogy). Full numbers in MODEL_COMPARISON.md.

What's on a tombstone

Each card carries a cause chip and confidence, the project's own last words used verbatim as its epitaph (a quote-checker refuses to put invented words in its mouth), a commit activity strip, and badges like night owl, "almost quit once (2354d gap)", and leftover TODOs. The time of death is pulled from the final commit — not the clock when the page was generated.

Buttons reveal more: a séance shows the last diff plus a weekday×hour commit heatmap; Resurrect offers a concrete 3-step plan to revive it; Export PNG draws a share card on a canvas. There's a scattered cemetery map view, anonymize mode, and fog drifting behind it all with candles you can blow out.

Why local and open matters here

This tool reads the contents of your private repos — commit messages, file trees, TODO counts, the half-finished diff you never pushed. Sending that to a closed API would be exactly wrong. Running Gemma through Ollama means the eulogies are generated with the lights off and the internet off, and your shame stays on your laptop. It costs nothing and needs no API key, which is the difference between a tool you actually run and one you don't.

Run it 

ollama pull gemma3:4b
python3 main.py ~/projects --resurrection -o graveyard.html

20 unit tests over synthetic git fixtures cover the classifier.

title: DORA and Cloud Exit Strategies: What Financial Companies Must Document
description:
Originally published on moveinfra.eu.

Under Article 28(8) of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) and Article 10 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773, financial entities in the European Union must maintain documented, realistic, and tested exit strategies for every cloud service supporting a critical or important business function. Applicable since January 17, 2025, DORA requires more than a high-level policy statement: companies must document concrete trigger events, verified alternative cloud providers or in-house options, technical data and application migration plans, transition timelines, and contractual termination clauses under Article 30(3)(f), and must review and test these plans periodically.

Key takeaways

  • Who is affected: Banks, payment institutions, e-money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers (CASPs), insurers, and other regulated financial entities using cloud services for critical or important functions.
  • Four mandatory exit scenarios: Under Article 28(8), your exit plan must address provider failure, deterioration of service quality, business disruption from inappropriate or failed service delivery, and material risks preventing the continued use of the service (including early contract termination).
  • Three layers of documentation: Regulators expect coherence across your ICT third-party policy and technical exit plans (Article 28(8) and RTS 2024/1773), your contractual clauses with the cloud provider (Article 30(3)(f)), and your Register of Information (Article 28(3) and ITS 2024/2956).
  • Testing is mandatory: Paper-only plans do not pass supervisory review. You must periodically review and test your exit plans to prove your team can migrate data and workloads within your stated recovery and transition windows.
  • Data Act alignment: Under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud switching charges (including data egress fees for switching) are capped at actual cost until January 12, 2027, and banned entirely from that date onward, removing a major financial barrier to testing and executing cloud exits.

Who needs a cloud exit strategy under DORA?

DORA applies to over 20 categories of regulated financial entities across the EU. For companies with 10 to 300 employees, this typically includes licensed fintechs, payment and electronic money institutions, investment firms, asset managers, insurtechs, and crypto-asset service providers regulated under MiCA.

Not every SaaS tool or cloud account requires a full exit strategy. The requirement under Article 28(8) applies specifically to ICT services supporting critical or important functions. DORA defines a critical or important function as one where a disruption would materially impair the financial performance of the entity, the soundness or continuity of its services and activities, or its ability to comply with regulatory obligations.

For most financial companies, production cloud infrastructure on AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure hosts core transaction processing, customer portals, ledger databases, or compliance reporting systems. That places your primary cloud environment squarely inside the scope of Article 28(8).

There is a limited legal exemption: "microenterprises" (defined in DORA as financial entities employing fewer than 10 persons and having an annual turnover and/or annual balance sheet total that does not exceed EUR 2 million) are exempt from the formal requirement to put exit strategies in place under Article 28(8). Once a company crosses 10 employees or EUR 2 million in turnover, the full documentation and testing obligations apply.

What DORA and RTS 2024/1773 require you to document

DORA's rules on exit strategies are split across the main regulation and its secondary technical standards:

  1. DORA Article 28(8) establishes the core obligation to maintain comprehensive, documented, and tested exit strategies.
  2. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773 (Article 10) sets the Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) specifying the exact contents of your exit plans.
  3. DORA Article 30(3)(f) defines the exit and transition clauses that must exist in your cloud contract.
  4. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 defines the Register of Information (RoI), where you must record substitutability and exit readiness fields for each critical contract.

During national supervisory reviews, authorities check whether these documents match. If your Register of Information claims your cloud provider is easily substitutable, your contract provides a 30-day notice period, and your engineering architecture relies heavily on proprietary cloud services that would take nine months to rewrite, an auditor will flag the contradiction.

1. Trigger events and exit scenarios

Under DORA Article 28(8) and Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773, your exit plan cannot only cover a planned, friendly non-renewal. You must explicitly document how you will handle stressed exits triggered by:

  • Unforeseen and persistent service interruptions (such as prolonged regional cloud outages or infrastructure instability).
  • Inappropriate or failed service delivery (such as persistent SLA breaches, security failures, or compliance violations by the provider).
  • Unexpected termination of the contractual arrangement (whether terminated by you for cause, by the cloud provider, or ordered by a financial supervisor under DORA's oversight powers).
  • Provider failure (insolvency, business closure, or revocation of regulatory authorizations).

For each scenario, you must define measurable internal thresholds that trigger the exit process and specify which roles on your management body have the authority to invoke the plan.

2. Alternative solutions and substitutability assessment

Article 29 of DORA requires you to assess ICT concentration risk and understand how easily a provider can be substituted. In your exit plan, you must identify concrete alternative solutions:

  • Moving to another third-party ICT provider (for example, migrating from a US hyperscaler to an EU cloud provider such as UpCloud, Scaleway, or OVHcloud).
  • Reintegrating the function in-house (rarely practical for small and mid-sized companies using public cloud infrastructure, but required to be evaluated).

You do not need to pay for duplicate idle servers running 24/7 on a second cloud unless your specific business continuity risk requires hot standby. However, your exit documentation must name the target provider(s), verify that they offer compatible compute, database, networking, and compliance capabilities, and confirm where data will be stored and processed in the EU.

Note on sovereignty and concentration risk: using a "sovereign" region from your existing provider (such as the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, which keeps data and operations in the EU but belongs to Amazon, a US company) does not satisfy an exit requirement from that same provider group, as DORA Article 29 explicitly requires entities to assess dependencies across connected providers within the same corporate group.

3. Technical migration and transition plan

Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 states that exit plans must be "realistic, feasible, based on plausible scenarios and reasonable assumptions, and shall have a planned implementation schedule compatible with the exit and termination terms established in the contractual arrangements."

For a cloud infrastructure exit, your technical documentation should include:

  • Complete asset and dependency inventory: Every virtual machine, Kubernetes cluster, managed database, object storage bucket, load balancer, firewall rule, DNS zone, and encryption key supporting the critical function.
  • Portability vs. lock-in mapping: A clear distinction between portable components (such as standard Linux VMs, Kubernetes manifests, PostgreSQL databases, and S3-compatible object storage) and proprietary services that require code changes (such as AWS DynamoDB, Google BigQuery, Azure Cosmos DB, or proprietary IAM and serverless workflows).
  • Data migration methodology: How databases will be replicated (for example, logical replication for PostgreSQL or MySQL), how object storage will be transferred and verified with checksums, how much bandwidth is required, and how data integrity and encryption will be maintained in transit.
  • Cutover and rollback procedures: The exact sequence for updating CI/CD pipelines, pausing writes during the final cutover window, switching DNS, verifying application health, and falling back to the original provider if checks fail during the transition.
  • Secure data deletion: How you will verify and document that all customer and financial data has been permanently erased from the outgoing cloud provider once the retention and rollback window closes.

4. Roles, budgets, and timelines

An auditor will check whether you have the people and money to execute the plan. Your documentation must define:

  • Internal responsibilities: Who leads the exit on the business, compliance, and engineering sides.
  • Resource and budget estimates: Estimated internal engineering hours, external migration tooling or consulting costs, parallel-run infrastructure costs during the transition month, and any early termination fees.
  • Data egress costs: Under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud providers may charge no more than their direct cost for switching-related data egress until January 12, 2027, and switching charges are banned entirely from January 12, 2027. Your budget assumptions should reflect this timeline.
  • Step-by-step schedule: A timeline showing how long it takes to provision the target environment, sync data, test applications, and cut over traffic, proving that the total duration fits inside your contractual notice and transition period.

5. Contractual clauses under Article 30(3)(f)

Your technical plan is only valid if your contract backs it up. For critical or important functions, DORA Article 30(3)(f) requires your cloud contract to include:

  • Clear termination rights and minimum notice periods (including termination scenarios requested by a competent authority).
  • Mandatory obligations for the cloud provider to assist you during an exit at no additional cost, or at a cost determined ex-ante in the contract.
  • A sufficiently long mandatory transition period during which the cloud provider must continue delivering services to reduce the risk of disruption while you migrate to another provider.
  • Provisions ensuring you can easily retrieve all your data in an accessible, machine-readable format.

Most major cloud providers offer a "DORA Financial Services Addendum" to cover Article 30 requirements. You must ensure this addendum is actually signed and referenced in your Register of Information, rather than assuming standard online terms of service cover you.

Practical checklist: DORA cloud exit documentation

Use the table below to verify that your cloud exit strategy covers the requirements of DORA and RTS 2024/1773 before a regulatory audit.

Documentation Area Regulatory Basis Specific Evidence Required Owner
Criticality & Scope DORA Art. 28(1)–(3); ITS 2024/2956 Mapping of business functions to cloud accounts and services in the Register of Information (RoI). Risk / Compliance
Exit Policy & Triggers DORA Art. 28(8); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Documented exit triggers (outage, SLA breach, provider failure, termination) and board/management sign-off process. CRO / Compliance
Substitutability & Target DORA Art. 29; ITS 2024/2956 Assessment of provider lock-in, concentration risk, and named alternative cloud provider(s) with EU data residency. CTO / Architecture
Technical Runbook RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform/OpenTofu) inventory, database replication plan, CI/CD update steps, DNS cutover, and rollback plan. DevOps / Engineering
Timeline & Budget RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Realistic migration schedule (in days/weeks), estimated parallel cloud costs, and engineering staffing plan. CFO / Engineering Lead
Contractual Alignment DORA Art. 30(3)(f); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 8 Signed DORA addendum with mandatory transition period, fixed exit assistance costs, and data retrieval rights. Legal / Procurement
Review & Test Log DORA Art. 28(8); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Dated records of periodic plan reviews, tabletop exercises, or technical migration tests, plus remediation of any gaps found. CTO / Risk

How to test your cloud exit plan without breaking production

Both DORA Article 28(8) and Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 require that exit plans be "sufficiently tested" and "periodically reviewed". The regulation applies the principle of proportionality: a 30-person payment institution is not expected to shut down live production traffic to run a multi-million-euro full cutover every year, but a tabletop discussion with no technical verification is rarely enough for critical cloud workloads.

A practical, proportionate testing approach for small and mid-sized financial companies includes three steps:

  1. Maintain Infrastructure as Code (IaC): Keep your network, compute, firewall, and database configurations defined in Terraform or OpenTofu. Audit your codebase twice a year to document any newly introduced proprietary cloud services that would block a clean exit.
  2. Run a dry-run environment build: Once a year, provision a non-production copy of your core infrastructure on your designated alternative EU cloud provider. Deploy your application containers or VMs using your existing CI/CD pipeline to verify that your software builds and starts outside your primary cloud.
  3. Test data restoration and replication: Restore an anonymized snapshot of your production database and a sample of object storage to the alternative cloud environment. Measure the actual data transfer speed, check data integrity, and use those real numbers to update the transition timeline in your exit documentation.

Document the date of the test, the participants, the measured transfer and setup times, any blockers discovered, and the tickets created to fix them. That test report is the exact evidence supervisors ask to see.

Frequently asked questions

Does deploying across multiple AWS or Azure regions count as a DORA exit strategy?

No. Multi-region deployment within the same cloud provider is a business continuity and disaster recovery measure (covered under DORA Article 11), not an exit strategy under Article 28(8). An exit strategy specifically addresses what happens when the provider itself fails, breaches its contract, loses regulatory approval, or must be replaced entirely.

How often must we review and test our cloud exit strategy?

Neither DORA Article 28(8) nor Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 sets a rigid calendar interval, requiring instead "periodic" review and testing proportionate to the criticality of the service. However, an annual review—and an immediate update whenever you make material changes to your cloud architecture or contract—is the standard practice expected by national supervisors and aligns with the annual ICT risk review cycles in DORA.

What if our cloud architecture uses proprietary services like DynamoDB or BigQuery?

Using proprietary cloud services is not banned under DORA, but you must be honest about it in your documentation. In your Register of Information and Article 29 concentration risk assessment, you must record the lower substitutability and higher migration complexity. Your exit plan must include the time, budget, and engineering steps required to refactor the application to an open alternative (such as PostgreSQL or ClickHouse), and your contractual transition period must be long enough to cover that refactoring work.

Can our cloud provider charge us fees to move our data out during an exit?

Under DORA Article 30(3)(f), any assistance fees from the provider during termination must be either free or clearly set in advance in your contract. Furthermore, under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud switching charges—including data egress fees for switching to another provider—cannot exceed the provider's direct cost until January 12, 2027, and are completely prohibited starting January 12, 2027.

Sources

  • Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA) – EUR-Lex
  • Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773 (RTS on policy regarding contractual arrangements for ICT services) – EUR-Lex
  • Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 (ITS on standard templates for the register of information) – EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data (EU Data Act) – EUR-Lex

Drafted with AI assistance and fact-checked by the MoveInfra team. The original, kept up to date, is at moveinfra.eu. Free tools for pricing a move to an EU cloud: moveinfra.eu/tools.

title: The design system is a contract, not a component library
description:
The component library is the easy part. The contract is what makes a design system survive a team change.

A contract here means: what the component accepts, what it promises, and what you'll never change without a major version.

Practically:

  • Props are public API. Rename one and you've broken someone's page.
  • Deprecation needs a date and a codemod, not a note in a doc.
  • Docs are generated from the code, because handwritten docs drift within a sprint.
  • Version the package, even internally. "Just pull main" is how a design system becomes a fork.

The hard part is saying no. Every component request is a request to own another contract.

The best design systems I've used felt small, and the docs explained the why, not just the props.

Do you version your internal design system?
