title: Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3: 4 Rules for User Uploads
description:
Start with private, direct-to-object uploads, then make the export worker the only component that reads a tenant's prefix. For a gaming platform handling large product images, I would choose Amazon S3 when cross-region API maturity and durability dominate, Azure Blob Storage for a Microsoft-centered estate, and Google Cloud Storage when its regional and pay-per-use model fits the dataset. A unified REST layer such as Infrai is worth testing for the integration boundary when the main constraint is getting a private upload working without another SDK and credential surface.

The deciding number is not request count. It is bytes per upload window, bytes per export window, and the fraction of those bytes that leave the region. Treat those as capacity inputs before comparing storage tiers. A 15-minute export SLO is a planning input, not a benchmark.

The byte rate is the part people under-test.

What should the upload path protect first?

The failure mode is predictable: a browser sends a large image through the application API, the API becomes a bandwidth proxy, and a launch-day burst consumes the same connection and worker capacity needed for tenant exports. Direct upload avoids that coupling. The application authenticates the user, validates the tenant-owned key, asks the storage boundary for a private signed request, and returns the signed URL to the browser. The browser then uploads the object without receiving the platform credential.

I plan this path in two independent rates. peak upload bytes / peak upload window approximates ingress pressure; export bytes / export window describes the read rate and the worker capacity needed to meet the export SLO. Keep a separate case for the largest file class. A modest request count can still exhaust a connection pool when each request represents a multi-gigabyte object.

The short operational sequence is:

  1. Allocate a tenant-scoped object key and keep the object private.
  2. Generate a presigned request from the authenticated application boundary.
  3. Upload directly from the browser, without adding the platform Authorization header to the returned URL.
  4. Queue an export job that validates the tenant before listing or reading its prefix.
  5. Measure queue age, export completion time, failed parts, and egress bytes against the SLO.

This is where CORS becomes part of the storage decision. A signed URL does not make a browser policy correct. Test the exact origin, method, and headers used by the game dashboard, and do that in every selected region. Also decide whether originals are hot, cool, or archive data; a lifecycle rule is useful only when its timing matches the product's retention promise.

Should Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3 handle uploads?

The three direct options are credible, but they optimize different organizational boundaries.

Option Strong fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A global-facing service that values API robustness and durability across regions Cross-region behavior, egress destinations, and the AWS credential and policy surface remain the platform team's responsibility
Azure Blob Storage A company already organized around Microsoft business systems The surrounding identity, region, and export workflow should justify another storage-specific integration
Google Cloud Storage Large datasets where Google Cloud regions and pay-per-use consumption fit the workload Validate the browser upload policy, tier behavior, and the path by which exports leave the region
Infrai storage A private upload and tenant export boundary where discovery and a plain REST interface reduce setup work It is not a replacement for specialist replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or cross-cloud migration controls

For the developer-experience part of this comparison, Infrai has a concrete advantage: its public discovery surface is self-describing, so an engineer can inspect the request and response schema for a capability before obtaining a key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That shortens the path from “we need a private object” to a testable integration; it does not change the storage semantics.

The broader platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but breadth is not a throughput guarantee. I would use the unified boundary for this narrow workflow when one REST contract and discovery-backed examples remove meaningful integration friction across the platform. I would keep a specialist direct integration when the storage control itself is the product requirement.

How do you make the smallest safe call?

The first call should be discovery, not a guessed SDK method. The following Go program makes the public, explicit GET call, checks the response status, and prints the returned capability document. It uses no credential because the discovery surface is public. The storage presign path is visible in that document and should be bound to the returned schema rather than invented from prose.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For the authenticated write that follows discovery, use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, set the HTTP method explicitly, and give the request an idempotency key where the documented operation supports it. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and back off exponentially. Do not send that platform header to the presigned upload URL. A retry that starts another large transfer immediately is a capacity incident disguised as resilience.

The export worker should be idempotent too. Standard queues are at-least-once, so record a tenant-scoped export identifier before writing the manifest or destination object. The worker can then safely repeat a delivery after a timeout, while the application still checks that every source key belongs to the requested tenant.

Where does the unified boundary stop being enough?

The direct recommendation has hard limits. The storage capability does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or a public image-hosting pattern. It has no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not automatically recoverable and a financial-grade immutable record needs an external design.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another boundary. Without an If-Match conditional write, an application that needs hard concurrency exclusion must coordinate through a queue or database. Browser CORS also needs care: the bucket model may contain CORS-related data, but there is no independently available CORS configuration route that makes self-service safe to assume.

There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration in this capability. The stated vendor coverage does not include Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2. Lifecycle handling has a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side search index because listing is prefix-oriented. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. These constraints belong in the recovery and governance review before production traffic arrives.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the private upload and tenant-scoped export portion when discovery-backed schemas and runnable examples remove SDK and credential setup, then choose S3, Blob, or Cloud Storage directly when replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or specialist migration tooling is required. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is the wrong choice when the storage control itself is the product requirement, because the unified boundary does not provide those specialist controls. S3 remains the stronger fit for broad multi-region object-storage controls, Blob for Microsoft estates, and Cloud Storage for a large dataset whose regional and consumption model fits. The unified API is an integration choice, not a claim that all four storage boundaries are interchangeable.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage object presign discovery documentation and verify the returned schema before wiring the worker.

How do you verify and roll back the path?

Verification starts with a mixed load, not a single successful upload. Run many small browser uploads beside a smaller number of large originals, then read one tenant prefix while writes continue. Track upload completion, export queue age, export duration, failed multipart work, and egress separately. Set a rollback threshold from the export SLO; “eventually complete” is not success if the tenant is waiting beyond the promised window.

The rollback should be boring. Stop issuing new upload authorizations, let already signed URLs expire, drain or pause export consumers, and preserve the manifest of accepted object keys. Do not delete source objects as a rollback shortcut. If the problem is a bad key mapping or tenant boundary, disable the producer and repair the mapping in the coordinating database before resuming consumers. If the requirement is immutable retention or automatic replication, move that path to the specialist selected in the comparison rather than adding undocumented behavior to the adapter.

References

  • AWS, Presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blobs-introduction
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/introduction
  • Infrai discovery for storage object presigning: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: How Cloud Computing Helps Reduce IT Infrastructure Costs
description:
Introduction

Managing IT infrastructure can be expensive for businesses. Companies need to invest in servers, hardware, software, maintenance, security, electricity, and IT support. As businesses grow, these expenses can increase significantly.

Cloud computing offers a smarter way to manage IT resources without investing heavily in physical infrastructure. Businesses can use cloud services to store data, run applications, manage workloads, and access computing resources over the internet.

But how exactly does cloud computing help reduce IT infrastructure costs?

In this blog, we will explore the key ways cloud computing helps businesses save money, improve efficiency, and manage their IT operations more effectively.

What Is Cloud Computing?

Cloud computing is a technology that allows businesses to access computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking, and software through the internet.

Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical servers, businesses can use cloud platforms to access the resources they need.

Popular cloud platforms include:

Amazon Web Services (AWS)

Microsoft Azure

Google Cloud Platform (GCP)

These platforms offer flexible pricing models, allowing businesses to pay for the resources they use.

7 Ways Cloud Computing Helps Reduce IT Infrastructure Costs

  1. Reduces Hardware Investment

Traditional IT infrastructure requires businesses to purchase physical servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and other hardware.

These investments can be expensive, especially for startups and small businesses.

With cloud computing, businesses do not need to purchase all these physical resources. They can access computing infrastructure through cloud service providers.

Key benefits:

Lower initial investment

Less spending on physical servers

Reduced hardware replacement costs

Better use of IT budgets

  1. Reduces Maintenance and Support Costs

Physical IT infrastructure requires regular maintenance, software updates, hardware monitoring, and technical support.

Businesses may also need dedicated IT teams to manage servers and fix technical problems.

Cloud service providers manage much of the underlying infrastructure, including hardware maintenance and platform availability.

This allows businesses to reduce their infrastructure management workload and focus more on their core operations.

  1. Pay Only for What You Use

One of the biggest advantages of cloud computing is its flexible pricing model.

Traditional infrastructure often requires businesses to purchase hardware based on expected future demand. This can lead to unused resources and unnecessary expenses.

Cloud platforms allow businesses to increase or decrease computing resources based on their requirements.

For example, an e-commerce company may need additional computing resources during festival sales. After the sales period, it can reduce those resources.

Key benefits:

Flexible resource usage

Better budget management

Reduced unnecessary spending

Easier business expansion

However, businesses must monitor their cloud usage to avoid unexpected charges.

  1. Reduces Electricity and Cooling Expenses

Running physical servers requires electricity for power, cooling systems, and other data centre operations.

As infrastructure grows, electricity and cooling expenses can become a significant part of the IT budget.

By moving workloads to cloud infrastructure, businesses can reduce the need to operate their own server rooms and maintain cooling equipment.

Cloud providers operate large data centres and manage the associated infrastructure.

This can help businesses reduce their direct energy and facility expenses.

  1. Improves Business Scalability

As businesses grow, their IT requirements also increase.

With traditional infrastructure, expanding server capacity may require purchasing additional hardware, installing equipment, and spending more money.

Cloud computing makes it easier to scale resources based on business needs.

For example, a growing software company can increase its cloud storage and computing capacity without purchasing additional physical servers.

Key benefits:

Easy resource expansion

Flexible computing capacity

Reduced hardware investment

Better support for business growth

  1. Reduces Software and Infrastructure Management Costs

Managing traditional IT infrastructure involves several responsibilities, including software updates, server monitoring, backup management, and system maintenance.

Cloud services can reduce some of these responsibilities through managed services and automated tools.

Depending on the cloud service model, providers may manage operating systems, databases, application platforms, or underlying infrastructure.

This helps businesses reduce manual IT management work and improve operational efficiency.

  1. Reduces Disaster Recovery Costs

Unexpected events such as hardware failures, cyberattacks, and natural disasters can affect business operations and cause financial losses.

Traditional disaster recovery systems may require additional servers, backup facilities, and dedicated infrastructure.

Cloud platforms offer backup, data replication, and disaster recovery solutions.

Businesses can use these services to protect important data and support faster recovery when problems occur.

The overall cost depends on storage requirements, recovery targets, data transfer, and service configuration.

Traditional IT Infrastructure vs Cloud Computing

Understanding the difference between traditional infrastructure and cloud computing helps businesses identify potential cost-saving opportunities.

Factors

Traditional IT

Cloud Computing

Initial Investment

High

Often lower

Hardware

Purchased by business

Provided by cloud provider

Maintenance

Managed internally

Some responsibilities handled by provider

Scalability

Requires hardware expansion

Flexible resource scaling

Payment Model

Mostly upfront investment

Usage-based or subscription pricing

Infrastructure Management

More manual work

Managed and automated options

Disaster Recovery

Additional infrastructure may be needed

Cloud-based recovery options

Cloud computing does not automatically make every IT operation cheaper. The right solution depends on business requirements, resource usage, and cloud management.

Real-World Example: How a Growing Business Can Save Money

Imagine an e-commerce company that manages its website, customer information, product database, and online transactions using physical servers.

As customer traffic increases, the company needs additional servers, storage, electricity, and maintenance support.

This increases its IT infrastructure expenses.

By migrating suitable workloads to the cloud, the company can:

Reduce its investment in physical servers.

Increase resources during high-traffic periods.

Reduce the need to maintain its own server room.

Use cloud backup solutions to protect business data.

Monitor usage and optimise monthly infrastructure expenses.

This approach can help the business manage IT costs more effectively while supporting future growth.

Important Things to Consider Before Moving to the Cloud

Although cloud computing offers several cost advantages, businesses should plan their migration carefully.

Here are some important factors to consider:

  1. Cloud Migration Costs: Moving applications, databases, and business data to the cloud may involve migration expenses.

  2. Data Transfer Charges: Some cloud providers charge for transferring data out of their platforms.

  3. Security Requirements: Businesses must select suitable security controls to protect sensitive information.

  4. Resource Management: Unused cloud resources can increase monthly expenses.

  5. Right Cloud Platform: Choosing the right cloud provider and service model is important for cost efficiency.

A proper cloud migration strategy helps businesses avoid unnecessary expenses and achieve better results.

How Cloud Migration Helps Businesses Reduce IT Costs

Cloud migration is the process of moving applications, databases, workloads, and IT resources from on-premise infrastructure to a cloud environment.

A well-planned cloud migration can help businesses reduce hardware dependency, improve resource utilisation, and simplify infrastructure management.

Businesses can choose different migration approaches based on their requirements:

Rehosting: Moving applications to the cloud with minimal changes.

Replatforming: Making selected improvements before moving applications.

Refactoring: Redesigning applications to take advantage of cloud-native services.

Repurchasing: Replacing existing software with a cloud-based solution.

Retaining: Keeping selected applications in the existing environment.

The right approach depends on application complexity, business goals, budget, and technical requirements.

Conclusion

Cloud computing provides businesses with a flexible way to manage IT infrastructure without depending entirely on expensive physical hardware.

From reducing initial hardware investments and maintenance expenses to improving scalability and disaster recovery, cloud computing offers several opportunities to optimise IT spending.

However, achieving real cost savings requires proper planning, the right cloud platform, and continuous resource monitoring.

For businesses looking to modernise their IT infrastructure, cloud migration can be an important step towards better cost management and long-term business growth.

title: USA SMS API Services: Alert Notifications with Go, Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage
description:
Short answer: for USA SMS API services and alert notifications, choose Twilio for a flexible US default, Bandwidth for domestic USA SMS, or Vonage for a bulk-oriented fit; select by delivery-state SLOs and peak-load behavior, not price alone.

For USA SMS API services handling a healthtech alert, delivery state matters more than a successful submission. Infrai's one key, one bill, and plain REST API reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation for this support queue, while Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage remain the primary provider choices to test. The signal is late.

One plain HTTP contract lets a Go worker call capabilities without installing an SDK. Fewer handoffs are useful; vendor concentration still needs an explicit SLO and outage review. In 2026, the platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, a breadth claim that does not remove the need for delivery testing.

A healthtech contact form should create one alert contract, attach verified identity context, and hand work to a delivery worker with an SLO. Twilio is a strong default for USA API flexibility and operational reputation; Bandwidth fits domestic USA SMS workloads where rates and carrier depth fit; Vonage is worth testing when bulk discounts and promotions match the send pattern. Keep any provider behind an adapter so a swap changes delivery code, not patient-support routing.

Short answer: choose on terminal delivery states, registration, support, and peak-load behavior. Price is one input, never the reliability argument.

I initially treated an accepted provider request as the milestone. The correction is operational: measure terminal delivery state and queue age, then page only when the SLO is at risk.

Which USA SMS API services fit alert notifications?

The page fired after a support form was submitted, but the useful signal arrived earlier: pending alerts grew faster than the worker could establish delivery status. The on-call could not tell whether identity verification, carrier delivery, or a stopped consumer was responsible. Set an SLO for the whole path, with a separate promise that every other alert is persisted for retry or rejected with a reason. A successful HTTP response is not handset delivery. Page on queue age and unresolved-status fraction, not every carrier delay; low thresholds create false pages, high ones hide a stopped worker.

How should identity hand off to SMS?

The identity response should feed a local alert object, while the SMS adapter receives only the approved recipient and message. Both calls can use one bearer key and base URL, but the responsibilities remain explicit. The event model is pull-based, so status polling needs bounded backoff and a terminal timeout.

package main
import ("context"; "fmt"; "net/http"; "os"; "time")
const baseURL = os.Getenv("API_BASE_URL")
func call(ctx context.Context, method, path string) error {
 key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); if key == "" { return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
 req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, nil); if err != nil { return err }
 req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
 resp, err := (&http.Client{Timeout: 10*time.Second}).Do(req); if err != nil { return err }; defer resp.Body.Close()
 if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return fmt.Errorf("API returned %s", resp.Status) }; return nil
}
func routeAlert(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) error {
 if err := call(ctx, http.MethodGet, "/auth/session/verify/"+sessionID); err != nil { return err }
 // The policy layer builds the schema-validated SMS request after verification.
 return call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/sms/send")
}
func main() { ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second); defer cancel(); if err := routeAlert(ctx, "verified-session-id"); err != nil { panic(err) } }

The route names are real, but the SMS request schema must come from live discovery; inventing fields would be worse than leaving that boundary visible. Production writes also need an idempotency key derived from the alert ID, and 429 responses need exponential backoff honoring Retry-After. An Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify stack means two signups, two credential sets, and glue to connect identity state to notification state, with separate status and billing views. A single-key backend removes that handoff, but creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That concentration risk is real.

Which provider fits the delivery contract?

Provider Good fit Boundary
Twilio Flexible, popular USA APIs and a strong reliability reputation. Test A2P 10DLC registration and carrier policy for the exact traffic.
Bandwidth Domestic USA SMS where rates and carrier depth fit capacity. Test status tooling, escalation, and regional behavior.
Vonage Bulk sends where promotions and discounts match the plan. Test delivery-state semantics against the SLO.
Regional carrier API A deliberately regional workload. A narrower footprint may constrain growth.
Amazon SES An adjacent email fallback, not an SMS choice. It cannot replace an SMS provider for urgent text alerts.

Capacity is peak accepted forms per minute multiplied by retry and polling demand, with room for carrier delay. If that number is unknown, measure it before choosing. The worker should persist an alert ID, apply suppression and policy checks, submit once, then poll with bounded backoff. Metrics should distinguish accepted, submitted, rate-limited, rejected, and terminally resolved states.

SMS cancellation exists, but scheduled email has no cancellation route. There is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, no managed email OTP, no tag-aggregated cost report, and no SMS-template list route. Geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country pricing circuit breakers belong in the business layer.

When is one contract the right trade?

The practical gain is a single credential and a single bill across the platform, plus one plain HTTP contract that a Go worker can call without an SDK. That removes a class of handoff work from this flow: rotating several provider keys, reconciling separate invoices, and translating different request shapes before the support alert even reaches the delivery worker. The trade is vendor concentration, so the convenience is only justified when that concentration fits the outage and compliance model.

A unified REST layer such as Infrai fits when the application contract should stay fixed while the backend capability changes, and when the identity-to-SMS seam matters more than separate control planes. The concrete advantage is one key, one wallet, one bill, and one plain REST API: no SDK is required, so a Go worker can call it directly. The public self-describing discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages reduce the first integration pass. The platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same contract can cover identity and communications as the system grows.

The trade-off is concentration: a unified service is the wrong choice for an organization that requires independent outage domains or provider-specific compliance ownership, so choose separate services there. It is also a poor fit if the team needs webhooks, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, or managed email OTP. Those capability boundaries are operationally important, not marketing fine print. Select the adapter whose failure states, registration, and support model fit peak-load alerting; keep identity, queueing, and routing independent of it.

title: Prism: Building a Zero-Chromium Browser Engine in Rust — Architecture, Internals, and Implementation
description:
Modern web browsers are among the most intricate software systems in computing history. A functional browser cannot simply display markup; it must ingest network streams, tokenize and parse non-standard HTML, construct a mutable object tree, parse and cascade stylesheets, execute scripting runtimes, compute geometric layouts across multiple rendering paradigms, rasterize primitives into pixel buffers, register spatial interactions, and maintain strict process-level security boundaries.

The vast majority of modern browsers bypass this complexity by wrapping existing engines, predominantly Google’s Chromium codebase or occasionally Apple’s WebKit. Prism takes an entirely different route.

Prism is an independent, modular browser engine written from scratch in Rust. Rather than embedding an existing rendering core, Prism implements its own decoupled pipelines for resource handling, document object model creation, style calculation, display-list generation, software rasterization, and extension sandboxing. Where external technologies are integrated — such as Boa for ECMAScript interpretation and Wasmtime for WebAssembly extension containment — they are isolated within custom coordination layers rather than serving as black-box rendering backends.

The browser engine recently crossed a critical threshold: bootstrapping an end-to-end rendering loop on a live production website (Hacker News), successfully loading network dependencies, building a sanitized DOM, hydrating JavaScript structures, calculating multi-column table layout, and flushing an 800 by 600 framebuffer with hundreds of painted glyphs.

This document breaks down the internal architecture of Prism, tracing how each distinct subsystem is constructed, how data transitions across boundary layers, and where the current limitations lie.

  1. Browser Shell and Application Architecture The browser shell acts as the entry point and supervisor process for Prism. It handles high-level application lifecycles, tab orchestration, navigation events, and the display output interface.

At startup, the shell initializes tab managers and coordinates thread barriers between window events and engine processing tasks. For native display targets, Prism interfaces with the winit crate to manage platform windows, surface creation, and system event loops.

A central engineering requirement for Prism is environment resilience. When executed inside environments devoid of an active display server or Wayland/X11 socket — such as a remote development container or automated Linux CI pipeline — the native compositor path fails gracefully. Prism automatically falls back to an embedded HTTP-based frame-streaming server bound locally to port 3000. This fallback mechanism ensures that the engine can execute its full layout and rasterization sequence headlessly, piping the generated framebuffer bytes directly to a web interface for visual inspection and regression testing without requiring virtual framebuffers like Xvfb.

  1. Network and Resource Loading Pipeline The rendering pipeline cannot operate on isolated markup. A modern web document requires synchronous and asynchronous retrieval of external assets, including stylesheets, external scripts, and vector or raster imagery.

Prism’s resource subsystem is built on top of native Rust asynchronous networking primitives. When a navigation event is dispatched by the shell:

The root document is retrieved, following any HTTP redirects to resolve the final canonical base URL.
The tokenizer and parser run a discovery pass to extract resource dependencies linked via standard tags (, , <img src="...">).<br> Relative resource paths are canonicalized against the base navigation URL.<br> Assets are fetched concurrently through an internal asset-preloading broker.<br> Asset resolution operates symmetrically across HTML attributes and CSS property declarations. Because styles frequently declare resources via url() tokens (such as background graphics), the resource loader maintains an internal registry keyed by both original relative paths and canonical absolute URLs. When layout and rasterization stages demand image bytes, they resolve them directly from this memory-backed asset pool without blocking on redundant network I/O.</p> <ol> <li>HTML Tokenization The entry point of the document pipeline resides in components/dom/src/tokenizer.rs. This component transforms raw incoming UTF-8 byte streams into discrete syntactic tokens without intermediate allocations where possible.</li> </ol> <p>The tokenizer operates via an incremental next_token() interface, supporting both push-based streaming and batch processing over whole documents. It defines a rigorous token set covering:</p> <p>Start tags, capturing the element name, self-closing state, and raw key-value attribute pairs.<br> End tags, marking structural termination.<br> Character data, separating printable text runs from whitespace.<br> Comments, extracting developer annotations without polluting the render path.<br> Doctype nodes, identifying strict or quirks-mode document declarations.<br> End-of-file indicators, terminating state machines cleanly.<br> A critical design challenge in HTML tokenization is the handling of CDATA, raw text, and entity references. HTML is notoriously forgiving to malformed input, necessitating extensive handling for quoted and unquoted attributes, numeric entities, and named character escapes.</p> <p>Crucially, Prism implements strict RAWTEXT state management for <script> and <style> blocks. Within these elements, content cannot be tokenized as standard element markup, because characters such as < and > often represent comparison operators or JavaScript logic rather than tag boundaries. The tokenizer switches into a raw-text capture mode until it encounters a matching closing tag sequence, preserving nested code strings for the script and CSS parsers.</p> <ol> <li>HTML Parser and Stack-Based DOM Construction Tokens generated by the tokenizer are fed directly into the hierarchical document parser located in components/dom/src/parser.rs.</li> </ol> <p>The parser utilizes an explicit open-element stack to reconstruct tree hierarchies. When a start-tag token arrives, the parser instantiates a node, links it to the current stack head as its child, and pushes the new node onto the stack. When a matching end-tag token arrives, nodes are popped until the matching scope is closed.</p> <p>Because real-world markup frequently deviates from valid XML structures, the parser implements standard HTML structural recovery heuristics:</p> <p>Implicit Paragraph Termination: Opening a block-level element inside an active <p> tag automatically generates an implicit closing token for the paragraph.<br> List and Definition Management: Consecutive <li>, <dt>, and <dd> items auto-close preceding siblings without requiring explicit closing tags.<br> Implicit Table Wrapping: The HTML specification requires that <tr> elements residing directly within a <table> must be wrapped inside an implicit <tbody> element. Prism checks table child states and dynamically synthesizes <tbody> nodes on the fly. Real-world sites such as Hacker News depend heavily on this implicit wrapping behavior to ensure table geometries do not collapse.<br> Beyond full-document parsing, the subsystem provides a specialized fragment-parsing path. This allows the JavaScript engine to mutate innerHTML properties dynamically, running partial markup strings through the parser and grafting the resulting subtrees into the live DOM tree.</p> <ol> <li>The DOM Engine Prism’s in-memory document model resides in components/dom/src/lib.rs. It serves as the primary source of truth across the engine, interconnecting the HTML parser, the JavaScript execution context, the CSS style resolver, and the layout tree.</li> </ol> <p>The tree consists of element nodes, text nodes, and comment nodes. Element nodes preserve tag identities, parent pointers, sequential sibling chains, and key-value attribute maps.</p> <p>To avoid stack-overflow crashes when processing deeply nested real-world DOM trees, all critical DOM traversal, node searching, serialization, and mutation functions are implemented iteratively using heap-allocated work stacks rather than naive recursive functions.</p> <p>Prism also introduces a distinct pre-render sanitization phase. To prevent scripts and metadata from bloating layout passes, the engine runs an iterative filter that strips non-visual elements (such as <script>, <style>, <noscript>, and <template>) from the layout tree. Because asset references are harvested during initial parsing, stripping these nodes prior to layout allows the layout engine to focus strictly on structural and typographic nodes.</p> <ol> <li>JavaScript Integration and the INIX Subsystem JavaScript integration in Prism is driven by the INIX subsystem, which pairs the document model with the Boa ECMAScript runtime.</li> </ol> <p>DOM Hydration<br> A browser must bridge the memory model of its native systems language (Rust) with the object model of its scripting language. Prism solves this through an explicit hydration bridge. Rather than wrapping every single Rust node in a heavy FFI envelope during initial parse, the Rust DOM serializes its structural tree into an optimized payload. The INIX runtime consumes this payload on the JavaScript side, iteratively constructing mirrored DOM objects, populating attributes, and linking parent-child associations.</p> <p>The Mutation Interception Bridge<br> To handle dynamic client-side applications, INIX implements an event-driven mutation bridge. When scripts execute operations such as modifying element.className, mutating attributes, or appending children via appendChild, INIX catches these operations through monkey-patched prototypes and native hooks. It serializes mutation records containing:</p> <p>The unique target node identifier.<br> The property or attribute mutated.<br> The updated payload value.<br> Structural metadata for tree rearrangements.<br> These mutation batches are queued and dispatched back across the native bridge into Rust, updating the primary DOM tree and signaling the layout engine that a restyle or reflow is required.</p> <p>Parallel Custom Runtime Path<br> Alongside the integrated Boa engine, the Prism repository contains an independent, custom-built JavaScript toolchain located in src/lexer.rs, src/parser.rs, and src/compiler.rs. This subsystem consists of a hand-written JavaScript lexer, an AST parser, and an experimental bytecode compiler paired with a stack-based virtual machine. While Boa handles active webpage execution today, this internal path represents Prism’s long-term research vector toward a fully unified, zero-dependency browser runtime.</p> <ol> <li>CSS Parsing and Style Resolution The CSS architecture is split cleanly between declaration parsing and selector application.</li> </ol> <p>The stylesheet parser in components/css/src/lib.rs consumes raw CSS text, stripping comments, tokenizing at-rules, and breaking style blocks into structured rulesets containing selector lists and declaration maps.</p> <p>Style resolution takes place in components/layout/src/style.rs. Here, Prism matches the parsed rules against the live DOM tree. The selector engine contains representation logic for:</p> <p>Type selectors (element tag names).<br> ID selectors (#id).<br> Class selectors (.class).<br> Attribute matchers.<br> Combinators (parent, descendant, sibling chains).<br> The resolver constructs an intermediate StyledNode tree, applying computed values and computing basic inheritance rules (such as propagating font colors and typography defaults down from the <body> element).</p> <p>Current Limitations in the Style Engine<br> Diagnostics from production tests reveal that selector matching and cascade resolution remain incomplete. For instance, during the execution of Hacker News, the main content wrapper <table id="hnmain"> failed to receive its authored width rules (width=None), indicating that ID selector specificity weighting or attribute-matching lookups occasionally miss matches during tree walks. Correcting cascade precedence and selector specificity scoring remains an active development priority.</p> <ol> <li>The Layout Engine The layout engine in components/layout/src/lib.rs translates the abstract StyledNode tree into concrete Cartesian geometry, assigning each element an (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) coordinate along with definitive width and height bounding boxes.</li> </ol> <p>Intrinsic Display Roles<br> Prism maps HTML elements to their default structural layout behaviors:</p> <p>Block Elements: Elements like <div> expand horizontally to fill their parent container and stack vertically.<br> Inline Elements: Elements like <span> flow horizontally along the active text line, wrapping when container boundaries are reached.<br> Table Elements: Specialized display types (table, tbody, thead, tfoot, tr, td, th) enter the dedicated table constraint-solving pipeline.<br> Replaced / Inline-Block Elements: Form controls (<input>) and visual embeds (<img>) maintain intrinsic dimensions while participating in horizontal inline flows.<br> Non-Rendered Elements: Tags such as <br> emit explicit line-break commands without generating visual boxes.<br> Table Layout Resolution<br> Because legacy and data-dense websites rely on complex table formatting, Prism includes a dedicated table formatting context. The table solver operates in multi-pass stages:</p> <p>It inspects all child rows and aggregates total column counts across all row fragments.<br> It executes cell measurement passes, calculating both the minimum intrinsic content width (the smallest width an element can adopt without text overflowing) and preferred content width for every cell.<br> It resolves column widths proportionally against available space while respecting explicit author-specified dimension constraints.<br> During execution on Hacker News, Prism successfully identified the main three-column news layout, resolving column widths of approximately 31.3 pixels for ranking indices, 24.3 pixels for voting arrows, and 740.4 pixels for headline/metadata content. This multi-pass algorithm prevents columns from collapsing into equal-width divisions that ruin page readability.</p> <ol> <li>Graphics Engine and Display-List Rasterization Prism enforces a strict architectural boundary between layout computation and pixel manipulation. Located in components/graphics/src/lib.rs, the graphics subsystem does not allow the layout engine to paint directly into memory. Instead, layout generates an immutable, serializable Display List.</li> </ol> <p>Write on Medium<br> A display list is an ordered sequence of draw commands:</p> <p>Solid rectangles for element backgrounds.<br> Styled boundaries for borders.<br> Image blits containing raw pixel buffers and target coordinates.<br> Text commands carrying font handles, glyph positions, and color values.<br> The rasterizer processes these commands sequentially, drawing into an 800 by 600 32-bit RGBA software framebuffer.</p> <p>The Text Rendering Pipeline<br> Prism integrates a CSS-aware glyph rasterizer capable of measuring font metrics and applying typographic rules. While the engine successfully painted 844 glyphs across 420 text commands in production tests, text rendering remains the most visually critical issue.</p> <p>Because coordinate offsets between inline text boxes, containing block wrappers, and rasterizer baseline expectations can drift, glyphs currently exhibit coordinate displacement and overlapping text baselines. The display list is correctly generating rendering commands, but the geometry calculation within the inline layout context requires baseline alignment fixes.</p> <ol> <li>Spatial Hit Testing A browser must map hardware input events back to the appropriate DOM nodes. Prism generates a unified hit-test spatial index during the layout pass.</li> </ol> <p>Each layout object emits an axis-aligned bounding box tied to its originating node reference. During navigation and rendering of Hacker News, Prism generated 1,190 distinct hit-test bounding boxes. This spatial index allows pointer coordinates to be queried against the tree in logarithmic time, providing the foundation for click handling, link navigation, hover states, and future form-control inputs.</p> <ol> <li>Extension Sandboxing via WebAssembly Rather than implementing extensions via high-privilege JavaScript bindings that risk browser security, Prism features an extension sandbox built on Wasmtime.</li> </ol> <p>Extensions are compiled to WebAssembly targets and executed inside deterministic memory sandboxes. The host environment provides a strictly defined native shim interface, limiting extension operations to designated system calls while bounding computation via execution fuel.</p> <p>During live tests, Prism loaded and executed adblock_lite.wasm, an internal ad-blocking extension:</p> <p>The sandbox loaded the 734-byte binary.<br> It allocated an execution fuel budget of 10,000,000 instructions.<br> The extension consumed 159 fuel units, returning 9 active CSS and structural filtering rules targeting ad banners, tracking pixels, sponsored posts, and modal consent overlays.<br> These rules were injected into the layout engine’s rule list to suppress matching nodes before display lists were emitted.<br> This proves the feasibility of running isolated, memory-safe extensions natively within an independent engine core.</p> <ol> <li>The Aegis Security Pipeline Prism incorporates an internal security inspection gate called Aegis, situated directly between the network loader and the parsing pipelines.</li> </ol> <p>Aegis functions as a zero-trust payload verification boundary. Before fetched bytes are allowed to touch the HTML tokenizer or parser, the Aegis pipeline scans document streams, enforces content policies, validates resource origins, and ensures data payloads do not violate boundary constraints. In live testing runs, this clearance pipeline completed in approximately 38 microseconds, establishing an inline security verification layer that introduces near-zero latency to the content pipeline.</p> <ol> <li>Production Milestone: Loading Hacker News To prove the viability of its architecture, Prism was deployed against a live, external web destination: <a href="https://news.ycombinator.com">https://news.ycombinator.com</a>.</li> </ol> <p>The test verified that the browser could navigate the web, retrieve external HTML, download linked CSS (news.css), fetch and decode SVG/PNG image assets, sanitize DOM nodes, hydrate the JavaScript environment, fire its WASM ad blocker, resolve complex multi-column table dimensions, and rasterize a full 800 by 600 framebuffer containing 480,000 pixels.</p> <p>Pipeline Run Metrics<br> Viewport Geometry: 800 pixels wide by 600 pixels high.<br> Document Layout Height: 2,797.4 pixels of vertical content mapped.<br> Rasterized Layout Objects: 429 discrete layout elements.<br> Text Commands Executed: 420 draw calls.<br> Glyphs Processed: 844 individual characters shaped and rendered.<br> Painted Pixel Surface: 26,249 active foreground pixels rendered.<br> External Images Blitted: 2 assets loaded and painted.<br> Hit-Test Geometry: 1,190 interaction regions mapped.<br> Adblock Rules Injected: 9 structural suppression filters applied.<br> While the metrics confirm that data flows cleanly through the entire pipeline, the final rendering exposed the engine’s primary current limitations: text baselines frequently overlap due to inline cursor miscalculations, and certain CSS rules (such as #hnmain table widths) do not yet resolve correctly against the style cascade.</p> <ol> <li>Current Subsystem Status and Next Engineering Steps Prism has completed its proof-of-concept bootstrapping phase. The implementation status of the engine breaks down across its subsystems as follows:</li> </ol> <p>Browser Shell and Tab Orchestrator: Implemented and functional. Manages tabs and provides automatic fallback streaming over local HTTP when headless.<br> Network Pipeline: Functional. Concurrently fetches HTML, linked CSS stylesheets, external JavaScript, and image assets.<br> HTML Tokenizer and Parser: Implemented and functional. Supports streaming tokens, raw-text state isolation, and tree recovery including implicit table structures.<br> DOM Engine: Implemented and functional. Uses iterative traversal and sanitization mechanisms to prevent stack overflows.<br> INIX JavaScript Runtime: Functional for tested workflows. Uses Boa for ECMAScript compliance, supported by custom hydration and mutation interception layers.<br> Internal JavaScript Engine Path: Present. Standalone lexer, parser, compiler, and VM path implemented for research and future integration.<br> CSS Parser: Functional. Accurately extracts rulesets, properties, and values from stylesheets.<br> Style Cascade and Selector Engine: Incomplete. Structural tag matching functions, but ID/class specificity calculations and property inheritance need refinement.<br> Table Layout Engine: Functional. Computes minimum and preferred cell widths to generate accurate multi-column layouts.<br> Block and Inline Layout Engine: Partially functional. Block flows calculate correctly, but inline cursor tracking and text wrapping suffer from coordinate calculation issues.<br> Graphics Rasterizer: Functional. Translates display lists into memory framebuffers, drawing rectangles, borders, images, and text.<br> Hit-Testing Engine: Functional. Produces coordinate-indexed boundaries for mouse tracking and interaction.<br> Wasmtime Sandbox: Functional. Safely runs WebAssembly binaries with strict fuel budgets and native API bindings.<br> Aegis Security Gate: Integrated. Inspects incoming payloads with sub-millisecond execution times.<br> The Next Engineering Target<br> With the end-to-end rendering pipeline proven, development focus shifts away from adding high-level features and toward visual fidelity and layout correctness:</p> <p>Inline Cursor Correction: Refactor components/layout/src/lib.rs to ensure relative inline text coordinates correctly track cumulative parent offsets and baseline alignments.<br> Cascade and Specificity Rectification: Overhaul components/layout/src/style.rs so that ID selectors (#hnmain) and class selectors (.title, .subtext) take proper precedence over generic element styles.<br> Display-List Coordinate Validation: Audit the transformation path between layout box bounds and TextCommand execution in components/graphics/src/lib.rs to eliminate glyph scrambling.<br> Conclusion<br> Prism is an engineering effort to prove that a modern browser engine can still be built from the ground up without relying on the Chromium monoculture. By dividing the problem into modular, decoupled Rust crates — spanning tokenization, DOM engineering, style cascading, table mathematics, software rasterization, and WebAssembly sandboxing — the project establishes that building an independent web engine is not an impossible task.</p> <p>While substantial work remains before Prism can render arbitrary web applications with pixel-perfect standards compliance, the engine has moved past basic architectural theory. It parses real code, runs real logic, computes complex structural tables, and renders live web pages down to the pixel level through a fully self-authored pipeline.</p>

title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
description:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

title: Pre-ticked boxes are not consent: notification prompts default to off
description:
Notification permissions are usually asked for badly. The app appears for the first time, and before the user has read a single message it shows the operating system's permission dialog. If they say no, the prompt is gone for good and the app quietly decides that notifications are not for this person. If they say yes, the app now has a blank cheque for message alerts, calls, reminder emails, and whatever marketing is invented next.

We shipped the opposite last week in Folcadi, a language-exchange messenger with a Flutter client. After login, once, the app shows its own preference sheet with four channels. Every switch starts off. Nothing is pre-ticked, nothing is bundled, and "Save" with everything off is a complete, accepted answer.

This post is about why the defaults are the whole product decision, and about the code shapes that follow from taking consent seriously: tri-state columns, a fail-open call gate, and an unsubscribe link that works without logging in.

The prompt we replaced

The old app had three problems, and they are the usual three.

The first was timing. The startup path requested the OS notification permission for every user, whether or not they had ever wanted a notification. On Android 13 and later that dialog is a one-shot resource: a reflexive "don't allow" during launch is hard to undo, and a lot of users never find the settings page to reverse it.

The second was bundling. One "notifications" concept covered message alerts, incoming-call ringing, a reminder email for unread chats, and product news. Those are four different offers with four different costs to the user. A person who wants to know about a missed call may not want a marketing email, and an app that conflates them has decided that for them.

The third was the data model. There was no record of anybody's preference, because there was no preference to record. The server mailed and pushed until something errored, and the only way to stop it was to silence the app at the OS level.

Four purposes, four switches

The new sheet is one themed dialog with four rows and a matching set of toggles in Settings → Notifications:

Choice Starts What it gates
Message notifications off Push alerts for new messages; turning it on asks the OS permission and registers this device
Incoming calls off Ringing for background calls; account-level, not per device
Email reminders off One reminder email if messages stay unread for days
Product news and offers off A separate marketing consent; nothing is sent under it yet

The copy is plain, and each row says what it does rather than what it is called: "Ring for incoming calls on your devices", "Email me if messages stay unread for a few days". The footer states the deal in one line: we only send what you select, and every reminder email carries a one-click unsubscribe link.

Separating the channels is not just politeness. It is the difference between consent that is specific and consent that is a blanket. A single switch forces a user who wants call alerts to accept marketing to get them, or to refuse everything to avoid marketing. Both outcomes are worse than four honest questions.

Why pre-ticked is not consent

In the EU, consent under the GDPR and the ePrivacy rules has to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Silence, inactivity, and pre-ticked boxes do not count. That is not an interpretation; the Court of Justice said it directly in Planet49 (C‑673/17, 2019), a case about pre-ticked cookie checkboxes. Ticking a box for someone, or treating "they did not untick it" as agreement, fails every part of that test.

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. But the engineering consequence is simple, and it holds even in places where marketing consent is not a legal question at all: a default is a statement about who is making the decision. If the switch is on before the user arrives, the app made the decision and the user is only correcting it. If the switch is off, the user decides. That is also the only version that survives contact with an audit, an app-store review, or a reader asking "how do I stop this".

Marketing email is the strictest case. It gets its own switch, its own consent stamp, and its own unsubscribe path, even though we are not sending any yet. Asking for consent before you need it is fine. Assuming it is not.

Consent is a tri-state, not a boolean

Here is the part that sounds like pedantry and is not. A boolean column cannot tell the difference between "never asked" and "said no". If you treat both as false, then adding the prompt silently turns off call ringing for every existing user who has not opened the app since the release — a change nobody agreed to, discovered when somebody misses a call.

So the columns that represent a choice are nullable, and the third state is meaningful:

#   None  -> no choice recorded yet: keep the previous behaviour
#   True  -> opted in
#   False -> explicitly opted out
class NotificationConsent(Base):
    push_alerts: Mapped[bool | None] = mapped_column(nullable=True)
    call_alerts: Mapped[bool | None] = mapped_column(nullable=True)
    email_reminders: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    product_news: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)

Email reminders and product news default to false because there is no older behaviour to preserve: they are new channels, and new channels start off. Push and call alerts default to NULL, because they already worked, and a user who has not been asked must keep what they had. Only an explicit false suppresses anything:

async def opted_out_of_calls(db, recipients: list[int]) -> set[int]:
    rows = await db.execute(
        select(NotificationConsent.user_id).where(
            NotificationConsent.user_id.in_(recipients),
            NotificationConsent.call_alerts.is_(False),   # explicit no only
        )
    )
    return set(rows.scalars().all())

That single .is_(False) is the difference between honouring a "no" and inventing one.

One OS permission, hidden behind a product choice

There is only one notification permission at the operating-system level, and both message alerts and call ringing need it. Asking for it before the user has expressed an interest wastes the one shot you get.

The sequence we use is: the user picks channels in our sheet, and only if message alerts or calls are switched on do we ask the OS. If the OS says no, the switches go back to off and the app explains it instead of pretending to save:

var pushChoice = supportsPush ? _push : null;
var callsChoice = _calls;
var denied = false;

if (supportsPush && (pushChoice == true || callsChoice)) {
  final granted = await notificationService.requestOsPermission();
  if (!granted) {
    pushChoice = false;
    callsChoice = false;
    denied = true;
  }
}

The message after a denial is deliberately undramatic — "Notifications are blocked in system settings. You can enable them there later." — because a person who declined twice should not be scolded by an app they just installed.

The other half of this is unregistering. When a device ends up with no push channel on, its push token is deleted for that account, so "off" means off rather than "off in the UI, still buzzing".

Fail open where silence is dangerous

Preference lookups can fail. Databases time out, replicas lag, a migration lands mid-request. The question is what the failure means for the user.

For a marketing email, failing closed is right: if we cannot prove consent, we do not send. For an incoming call, the same logic is catastrophic. If the preference query throws and the code treats that as "not allowed", a phone stops ringing because of an unrelated hiccup. That is a missed call caused by a product decision about consent.

So the call gate fails open, explicitly:

try:
    rows = await db.execute(select(...).where(...))
    return set(rows.scalars().all())
except Exception:
    # A preference lookup must never be the reason a call stays silent.
    logger.warning("call-alert preference lookup failed", exc_info=True)
    return set()

The asymmetry is the point, and it is worth writing down next to the code: consent gates should fail closed for growth and open for safety. Marketing, newsletters, and re-engagement features can safely assume the answer is no. Calls, security alerts, and anything a user would call urgent cannot.

One more detail from that gate: cancel pushes are still sent to a user who turned call alerts off. Otherwise a device that was already ringing when the preference landed would keep ringing with no way to dismiss it.

"Not now" must not count as an answer

The sheet is shown once, and the server records both that it was completed and which version of it was shown. That gives us a cheap way to ask again if the choices materially change: bump the version, and the prompt returns once for everyone.

Dismissing is different from deciding. "Not now" closes the sheet without completing it, and the prompt can come back on a later launch — at most once per 24 hours, tracked locally per account. The cap matters: a preference that is genuinely useful deserves to be asked again later; it does not deserve to be asked on every cold start, which is how prompts become wallpaper.

The sheet also refuses to cover the wrong moment. If the app opened a chat or a call from a notification or a deep link, the prompt waits for a route where nothing is in progress, and gets offered on the next launch instead. Interrupting the one thing the user opened the app for is how you teach them to dismiss you.

There is a small implementation detail in the versioned-prompt model that is worth copying: the server is the source of truth for "this person has answered", and a local timestamp is only there to stop the sheet reappearing before the next launch. Clearing app data loses the local timestamp, not the decision.

Push is per device, calls are per account

The same sheet runs on a phone, a desktop client, and anything else signed into the account, and the four rows do not all mean the same thing on each.

Message notification is per device: a phone has a token, a desktop may have none, and a preference set on the phone should not be silently rewritten by a laptop that cannot receive push at all. So the desktop hides that row and reports "no opinion", which is the NULL state from earlier. The Calls choice is account-level, because a call should ring wherever the person is.

Getting this wrong is easy and invisible in testing. A desktop client that sends false for a channel it cannot even show looks like a clear preference in the database and a bug report in the making: "everything is off on my phone, and I never touched it".

Unsubscribing without logging in

Every channel has to be as easy to leave as it was to join, and email is the one where that is hardest, because the user may be reading it in a client that has no idea who they are.

Reminder emails therefore carry a signed link that needs no session, a visible unsubscribe link, and the standard one-click unsubscribe headers. Opening the link flips the flag off. It is the same column the in-app toggle writes, so the two cannot disagree, and the same consent stamp gets a new timestamp — a withdrawal is a decision too and deserves a record.

In the app, Settings → Notifications exposes all four channels with the same write path as the sheet. Changing your mind does not require finding the original prompt again.

What this costs

Honesty section: opt-in rates after this change are lower than they were when the permission was requested automatically. That is the intended result, not a bug.

The trade we made is a smaller list of people who actually want the alerts, in exchange for a list that means something. A push sent to a user who reflexively tapped "allow" during onboarding is worth very little; a push sent to someone who turned the switch on is worth something, and a push sent to someone who turned it off is a reason to uninstall. The same logic applies to the reminder email: it is opt-in, capped to one a week per person, and quiet for anyone who has been active.

We do not have retention numbers to show for this yet — the change is days old, and claiming a measured win would be inventing one. What we can say is that the support-shaped problem is gone: there is now one place that answers "why is this app emailing me", and it is the same place that stops it.

A checklist you can copy

If you are about to ship a notification prompt, these are the parts that mattered most:

  • Ask after the user has seen something worth notifying them about, not during the first launch animation.
  • Split the purposes. Message alerts, calls, reminder email, and marketing are four offers, not one.
  • Start every switch off, and make "all off" a real, saved answer.
  • Make consent tri-state. "Never asked" must not behave like "no".
  • Ask the OS last, once, after a product-level yes. Revert the switch and explain if the OS declines.
  • Write down which gates fail open. Calls and security alerts keep working when the preference lookup breaks; marketing does not.
  • Version the prompt so a material change can be asked about once, without becoming a nag.
  • Make leaving as easy as joining, including a link that works without a session.

None of this is exotic. It is mostly the decision to let the user answer the question instead of answering it for them, and then to build the data model that can remember the difference between "not yet" and "no".

FAQ

Is a notification prompt legally required?

Not in general, and this post is not legal advice. What is required in the EU is that consent — especially for marketing email — is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, which rules out pre-ticked boxes and silence. Separating the channels and defaulting them off is how you satisfy that while still asking for the alerts that make the app useful.

Why not just ask for notifications on the first launch?

Because the OS permission is a one-shot resource and the first launch is the worst moment to spend it. A user who has not received a message yet has no reason to say yes, and a reflexive "no" is much harder to undo than a considered "yes" is to earn.

What happens if someone dismisses the sheet?

Nothing is recorded as a decision. The sheet can be offered again on a later launch, at most once per 24 hours, and Settings → Notifications is always available. Only pressing Save writes the completion stamp.

Do existing users lose call ringing when they update?

No. The push and call preferences start empty (NULL), which keeps the previous behaviour until the person actually answers the prompt. Only an explicit "off" suppresses anything.

Does turning off message notifications still leave the account reachable?

Yes. In-app calls still arrive while the app is open and connected, and unread counts still work. The switch controls push delivery, not the account.

What does the reminder email contain?

Only a nudge that messages are waiting, with a link back to the app and a one-click unsubscribe. It never includes message content, and for encrypted chats it does not name the sender or the conversation either.
