Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

BigQuery

Feature

Conversation logging for Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now generally available (GA). You can log data agent conversations to a BigQuery table in the agent's project. For more information, see Conversation logging overview and Configure settings.

Feature

Python user-defined functions now support volume mounts, which let you access dependency files from Cloud Storage directly from your Python UDF code. This feature is in Preview.

Feature

The REGEXP_EXTRACT_GROUPS function produces substrings that match multiple capturing groups in a regular expression.

This function is in Preview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

You can also visualize the end-to-end flow of your data from BigQuery sources through the Looker semantic layer to downstream assets.

For more information, see Track data lineage with Knowledge Catalog, About data lineage, and About data lineage ingestion control.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor enforces the constraints/modelarmor.managed.requireTemplateDataResidencyCompliance managed Organization Policy Service constraint by default. When you create or update a template, this constraint prevents you from setting data_residency_compliant to false or clearing the Enforce data residency option unless an Organization Policy Administrator disables the constraint. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Disable the organization policy constraint for data residency.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

The Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server is generally available (GA) and adds tools to create and manage Database Connections and run SQL statements with database_connection_executesql. It lets you interact easily with Oracle Database@Google Cloud resources from LLMs, AI applications, and AI-enabled development platforms.

For more information, see Use the Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server.

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.

title: 👻 RepoGhost: Bringing Forgotten Codebases Back to Life with Local AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

I built RepoGhost, a local AI-powered repository analyzer designed to bring forgotten and abandoned codebases back to life.

Every repository has a story, but understanding an unfamiliar project can sometimes feel like exploring a haunted house. There may be unfinished tasks, confusing file structures, undocumented functions, and code that nobody remembers writing.

That's where RepoGhost comes in! 👻

Users can upload a repository as a ZIP file, and RepoGhost scans it to discover:

  • Repository Overview: Detects source files, programming languages, and project structure.
  • Forgotten Tasks: Finds TODO, FIXME, and HACK comments that may have been left behind.
  • Python Syntax Findings: Identifies basic Python syntax issues.
  • Chat with the Ghost: Ask questions about the repository and get AI-powered explanations.
  • Haunted Project Report: Generates an AI-assisted report to help developers understand their codebase.

I interpreted the theme Ghost in the Machine as giving a voice to forgotten codebases. RepoGhost acts like a friendly ghost that helps developers understand what is happening inside a project, even when its original developers are no longer around.

Demo

🎥 Video Demo:

Note: RepoGhost is designed primarily for local execution, so the demo can showcase the application running on your machine.

Code

💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Sourodip1804/RepoGhost

Contributions, feedback, and suggestions are welcome!

How I Built It

I built RepoGhost using a combination of open-source technologies and local AI inference.

AI Model:

  • Qwen2.5:3B – An open-weight language model used to understand repository context, answer questions, explain code, and generate reports.
  • Ollama – Runs the model locally, allowing RepoGhost to communicate with the AI without depending on a hosted AI API.

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Repository scanning and file analysis
  • ZIP extraction and processing
  • REST API endpoints for uploading repositories, chatting, and generating reports

Frontend:

  • React.js
  • Vite
  • CSS
  • Lucide React icons

How it works:

  1. The developer uploads a repository ZIP file.
  2. The FastAPI backend safely extracts and scans the repository.
  3. RepoGhost identifies programming languages, source files, and unfinished task markers.
  4. Relevant repository context is prepared for the AI model.
  5. Qwen2.5:3B processes the context through Ollama and generates explanations or answers.
  6. The frontend displays scan results, AI conversations, and the generated project report.

One of my main goals was to keep the AI workflow local. The project does not need a paid cloud AI API to perform its core AI tasks.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made this project possible in a way that would have been difficult to achieve with a closed AI API alone.

Using an open-weight model like Qwen2.5:3B with Ollama gave me the opportunity to experiment with local AI inference, understand how models interact with application backends, and build an AI-powered tool without depending on paid API access.

It also offers some important advantages:

  • Privacy: Repository source code can remain on the developer's machine when using the local setup.
  • Accessibility: Developers can experiment without needing a paid AI API subscription.
  • Customization: The model and AI workflow can be modified according to project requirements.
  • Transparency: Developers have more control over the tools and infrastructure powering their AI applications.
  • Community: Open-source models and frameworks make it easier for developers to learn, contribute, and build on existing work.

For me, open innovation is not just about using free tools. It is about having the freedom to understand, experiment, modify, and build something useful.

The Spirit of It

The most interesting part of building RepoGhost was thinking about how much knowledge gets trapped inside old repositories.

A developer might leave a project unfinished, forget how a particular function works, or return to an old codebase after months or years.

Instead of manually exploring every file, imagine asking:

"Hey Ghost, what is this project actually doing?"

And getting an explanation from the code itself.

That is the idea behind RepoGhost: every codebase deserves a second life.

Prize Categories

  • Open-Source AI Challenge – Ghost in the Machine (Week 4)

Building RepoGhost has been a great learning experience. I explored local LLM integration, Ollama, FastAPI, React, repository analysis, and the practical challenges of connecting an AI model with a real application.

There is still plenty of room to improve, and I would love to hear your feedback and suggestions!

Let's bring forgotten codebases back to life. 👻

title: Mistral Large 4 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Mistral Large 4 is now available on AI Gateway. The open-weight, natively multimodal model combines reasoning with text and image understanding. It is useful for cyber defense, manufacturing, and finance workflows.

title: My demo refused 96% of off-topic questions but only 39% of tricky ones. I know because of a test set
description:
Here are two numbers from my document Q&A demo. Ask it about something that is not in the knowledge base at all, and it refuses correctly 96.1% of the time. Ask it a question that sits close to a document but is not answered by it, and it refuses only 39% of the time.

If I had tried the demo by hand, I would have asked a few questions, seen it say "not in the docs" a couple of times, and called it good. The 39% only showed up because there was a labelled test set. That set is the subject of this post: a golden set, the cheapest acceptance test an AI feature can have.

What it is

A golden set is a list of real inputs with the answer a human accepts for each one. Nothing more. It is not training data and it is not a benchmark you publish. It is the thing you run after every change to ask one question: did it get better or worse?

Without it, every change is judged by whichever three examples someone happens to try. With it, "works pretty well" becomes a number you can argue about.

How I would build one in an afternoon

  1. Take real inputs. 100 is enough to start. Pull them from the actual process: tickets, invoices, questions people really ask. Not examples you invented to look nice.
  2. Cover the ugly cases on purpose. Roughly: most of it typical, a quarter hard or ambiguous, and a handful that must be refused or sent to a human. The ugly part is where the demo above found its 39%.
  3. Label it with the person who owns the process. The owner says what "correct" means. If two people disagree on a label, that disagreement is a finding, write it down.
  4. Freeze it. Do not tune the system on these examples. Tune on a separate split and touch the golden set only to report. In my ticket-triage demo the threshold is chosen on a validation split and the test set is used once.
  5. Write the acceptance rule before you run it. For example: "at least 97% correct on what is handled automatically, everything else goes to a person." Then the run is a pass or a fail, not an opinion.

What it showed me in my own demos

These are public demos on public datasets (test data, not client results):

  • Ticket triage. If everything were automated, accuracy would be 90.2%. Handle only the confident 75.9% and accuracy on those is 97.7%. The golden set is what made the trade-off visible.
  • Document Q&A. Out-of-base questions are refused 96.1% of the time, but near-miss questions only 39.4%. The cited answers hit 93% precision against a 95% target. I reported the gap instead of hiding it, and it points to the next fix: a reranker or an LLM for exactly those near-miss cases.

In both cases the number told me where to work next. A hand-tried demo would have told me nothing.

Pitfalls

  • Leakage. If the system has seen the golden examples while being tuned, the score is fiction.
  • Too clean. A set made only of easy cases gives 99% and a false sense of safety.
  • Never refreshed. Real inputs drift. Add new failures to the set whenever production surfaces one.
  • One number for everything. Report per category. A fine average can hide a category that fails every time.

Takeaways

  1. A golden set is real inputs plus answers a human accepts.
  2. Build it before the pilot, with the process owner.
  3. Include the ugly cases deliberately.
  4. Freeze it, and write the pass rule first.
  5. Report per category, and add every new production failure to it.

If you can only do one thing before your next AI pilot, label 100 examples. It is the cheapest hour of the project.

Portfolio and contacts: @Kotenev01_bot.

I write about practical, measurable AI adoption for business: demos on test data, no invented case studies. Telegram channel: @kotenev01_en

title: # PHANTOMTRACE: Finding the Ghosts Inside AI Agent Execution Traces 👻
description:
What I Built

AI agents can perform many tasks automatically, but sometimes something goes wrong during execution.

An agent may call the same tool repeatedly, fail to complete a task, or experience unexpected delays. Finding the exact reason inside execution logs can be difficult.

That's why I built PHANTOMTRACE.

PHANTOMTRACE is a local-first AI agent trace investigation dashboard. It helps developers inspect AI agent execution logs, identify unusual behavior, and understand possible problems.

The idea is simple:

Find the ghost hiding inside your AI agent's execution trace! 👻

🎥 Live Demo Video

Watch my PHANTOMTRACE demonstration:

In this demonstration, I show:

  • The PHANTOMTRACE dashboard.
  • Loading a sample JSONL execution log.
  • Detecting anomalies.
  • Viewing issue severity.
  • Selecting an anomaly for investigation.
  • Generating an explanation using Gemma 3 1B through Ollama.

💻 Project Repository

GitHub: https://github.com/tk1981215/PHANTOMTRACE

🛠️ Technologies Used

  • Python
  • Streamlit
  • Pandas
  • Plotly
  • Ollama
  • Gemma 3 1B
  • JSONL
  • SQLite

⚙️ How PHANTOMTRACE Works

PHANTOMTRACE follows a simple workflow:

  1. Load execution logs: Users can select bundled sample logs or upload their own JSONL agent logs.
  2. Parse events: The application reads the log records and converts them into structured events.
  3. Detect anomalies: The detection module analyzes the events and identifies suspicious behavior.
  4. Visualize traces: The dashboard displays execution events, latency, tokens, and detected issues.
  5. Investigate with AI: Users select an anomaly and ask the local Gemma model to explain what happened and suggest a possible fix.
  6. Save investigations: Runs can be stored locally using SQLite.

🤖 Open-Source AI: Ollama and Gemma 3 1B

One important part of PHANTOMTRACE is its local AI integration.

I used:

  • Ollama to run the model locally.
  • Gemma 3 1B as the local language model.

When a user selects an anomaly, PHANTOMTRACE prepares a prompt containing the issue details and nearby execution events.

The prompt is sent to Ollama's local API, and Gemma generates a short debugging explanation.

The model runs locally on my computer using CPU inference.

🔐 Why Open Innovation Matters

I believe open innovation is important because developers should have more control over their tools and data.

PHANTOMTRACE uses local inference instead of sending trace information to an external AI API.

This provides several benefits:

  • Better control over potentially sensitive execution logs.
  • No external AI API key required for local explanations.
  • Freedom to experiment with different locally installed models.
  • More control over how the AI investigation works.
  • An approach that can run without an internet connection once the model and dependencies are installed.

Open-source AI makes it possible for developers to experiment, learn, customize, and build useful tools without depending entirely on closed AI services.

👻 Challenges I Faced

Building PHANTOMTRACE was a learning experience.

Some challenges I faced included:

  • Understanding AI agent execution logs.
  • Designing an anomaly detection workflow.
  • Connecting a Python application to Ollama.
  • Running a language model locally on a CPU-only computer.
  • Keeping the application lightweight.

Working through these challenges helped me understand how local AI models can be integrated into practical developer tools.

📚 What I Learned

While building this project, I learned:

  • How to work with JSONL execution logs.
  • How to organize a Python project into modules.
  • How to build dashboards using Streamlit.
  • How to visualize execution data with Plotly.
  • How to connect Ollama with Python.
  • How to use Gemma 3 1B for local AI explanations.

🚀 Future Improvements

I would like to improve PHANTOMTRACE by adding:

  • More advanced anomaly detection.
  • Better retry and repeated-tool-call analysis.
  • Investigation reports with more context.
  • Support for additional local language models.
  • More interactive trace visualizations.

❤️ Final Thoughts

PHANTOMTRACE started with a simple idea: make it easier to understand what goes wrong inside AI agent workflows.

This project helped me explore Python, open-source AI, local language models, and application development.

I am excited to continue improving it and learning more about the open-source AI ecosystem.

Sometimes the biggest problems in an AI agent are hidden in its execution trace. PHANTOMTRACE helps find those ghosts! 👻

Thank you for reading!

title: The Hollow Horror: Every knock has a story.
description:
Github - https://github.com/VedanshVashist/hollow-horror-archive.git
Live - https://hollow-horror-archive.vercel.app/

The Hollow

An interactive midnight archive of original ghost stories and hand-drawn haunted scenes.

Open a random door to reveal a new story and illustration. Watch the night move around the page, then scroll deeper into the archive. The project is built for the web's oldest ghosts: plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Features

  • Eight original, bite-sized horror stories. Each visit to Summon another story picks a different one.
  • Locally generated SVG scenes—no image service, API key, external asset host, or tracking script.
  • Scroll-linked hero parallax and random Count Orlok sightings as you move down the page.
  • Locally bundled vampire artwork, with source and license details in ASSETS.md.
  • A flying vampire, slow-moving bats and pumpkins, a foreground spider, drifting fog, and scroll-triggered reveals.
  • A motion pause button and support for the device's reduced-motion setting.
  • Responsive layout, keyboard focus styles, skip navigation, and screen-reader announcements.
  • No build step and no runtime dependencies.

Run locally

You can open index.html directly, or serve the files locally for the most reliable browser behavior:

python -m http.server 4173

Then visit http://localhost:4173. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

Hacktoberfest

The Hollow welcomes open-source contributions all year, including during Hacktoberfest. The event format changes over time; for 2026, pull requests no longer count toward rewards. Check the official Hacktoberfest rules for the current activities and eligibility. Contributions here are welcome whether or not they qualify for an event activity.

Deploy to Vercel

  1. Push this repository to GitHub.
  2. In Vercel, choose Add New → Project and import the repository.
  3. Keep the project at the repository root. Vercel will detect a static site; leave the build command empty.
  4. Choose Deploy. The site has no environment variables to configure.

Contribute

Story ideas, new SVG scenes, accessibility improvements, responsive fixes, and documentation are welcome. Read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request. You can also start with the bug and feature-request templates under .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/.

Good first contributions include:

  • Add a story in script.js and give it one of the existing scene types.
  • Add a new scene to hauntedLandmark() in script.js and pair it with an original story.
  • Improve a small-screen layout or a keyboard/screen-reader interaction in styles.css and index.html.
  • Improve the contribution guide or add a new issue template.

Keep stories original, keep the page usable without motion, and keep the project dependency-free unless a change has a clear reason.

Project files

File Purpose
index.html Page structure and accessible controls
styles.css Theme, responsive layout, and animation
script.js Story selection and SVG scene generation
assets/vampires/ Locally bundled vampire artwork used in scroll sightings
ASSETS.md Artwork sources and license information
LICENSE MIT license for the project's original code and materials
HACKTOBERFEST_DEV_POST.md Copy-ready DEV post draft; replace the repository and demo links before publishing
favicon.svg Project icon
vercel.json Static Vercel deployment settings

License

The project's source code and original project materials are released under the MIT License. The bundled third-party artwork has separate terms listed in ASSETS.md; it is not relicensed under the project MIT license.

title: Here Lies My Toaster
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every house has a drawer of dead things: the earbuds that play on one side, the charger with the split cable, the phone with the spiderweb screen. Nobody mourns them. Halloween ends tonight and Día de los Muertos begins tomorrow, two days for remembering the departed, so I gave the drawer an obituary page.

Here Lies is a small web app that runs on your own laptop. You take a photo of something that died, and Gemma 4, running through Ollama on the same machine, writes it a straight-faced newspaper obituary: a name, a cause of death, a life of service, who it leaves behind, a request in lieu of flowers, an epitaph. You can download the card as a PNG.

The rule: the model may invent a name. It may not invent a scratch. Every physical detail on the card has to point at something the model listed when it looked at the photo, and plain Go code checks that before you see it.

Living things get a notice instead.

In my tests the cat, the dog, the monstera and the person were turned away every time.

Demo

More cards on the landing page: https://nazboyko.github.io/here-lies/


The toaster survived. Mr. Chester Golden-Crust did not: "In lieu of flowers, please wipe the crumbs from beneath the toaster tray."


Agnes Petalbrook: "Survived by a terracotta shard and the faint smell of potting mix."


Mr. Arthur Glowwick: "It shone when asked, and dimmed when done."


The app, on another run of the same toast. On the right: what the model saw, and which sentence used each detail.

Run it yourself. You need Ollama, Go 1.26 and Node 20 or newer.

ollama pull gemma4:e4b
git clone https://github.com/nazboyko/here-lies && cd here-lies
make run
open http://localhost:8787

Code

nazboyko / here-lies

Obituaries for the things that died in your house, written by a local open-weight model.

Here Lies

Obituaries for the things that died in your house, written by a model on your own laptop.

Take a photo of something that died: a cracked phone, burnt toast, shoes with holes, last week's pumpkin. Gemma 4 runs on your computer through Ollama, looks at the photo and writes the thing a straight-faced newspaper obituary. The model may invent a name. It may not invent a scratch: every physical detail on the card has to point at something the model listed when it looked at the photo, and plain Go code checks that before you see it.

Point it at a cat, a person or a healthy plant and it refuses: "Still alive. Give it a treat instead."

Landing page: https://nazboyko.github.io/here-lies/

Run it

You need Ollama, Go 1.26 and Node 20 or newer.

ollama pull gemma4:e4b
git clone https://github.com/nazboyko/here-lies && cd here-lies
make run

Then open http://localhost:8787…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Look. Gemma 4 gets the photo and returns JSON: thing, person, animal, living plant or unclear; what the object is; and what it sees, in three lists: damage, wear, features. Code numbers the details d1, d2, d3.
  • Gate. Plain code. People, animals and healthy plants get the still-alive notice.
  • Write. A second Gemma call, text only. It turns the numbered list into an obituary in JSON, and every sentence about the body carries the ids it uses.
  • Check. Plain Go, no model. The cause of death must cite a real damage or wear id, every life sentence must cite a real id, and everything must fit the column. A failing draft goes back once with the problems listed. If the rewrite fails too, code keeps what passes, rebuilds the rest from the detail texts, and the page says what it repaired.

Why two calls? The writer never sees the photo. It can only describe what the looking step wrote down, and because each reference is an id, my code can verify it. One call doing both would hand me prose I could either trust or not.

To measure it, I ran 17 photos from Wikimedia Commons through the real pipeline: 11 dead things, a cat, a dog, a healthy monstera, one person, an intact mug and a blurry shot. Then I opened every photo next to its details and marked each one true, false or unsure.

Measure Result
Photos 17
Gate decision correct 16 of 17
Obituaries printed 13
Passed the check on the first draft 12 of 13
Rewritten once after the check 1
Repaired by code after the rewrite 0
Details on printed cards 65
Really in the photo, checked by eye 53 true, 4 false, 8 unsure
Causes of death resting on a false detail 2
Median seconds 0.8 to look, 2.4 to write and check

Machine: Apple M5 Max, 64 GB, gemma4:e4b through Ollama 0.35.1. A card takes about 3 seconds. The one rejected draft was the charger's: its third life sentence cited no detail, and the rewrite fixed it.

The honest failure. My first look prompt asked for one list of details, each tagged damage, wear or feature. Gemma tagged almost everything as a feature. Burnt toast came back as "dark brown toasted surfaces", so the check found no injury and printed "Natural causes. It was simply no longer needed." Only 6 of 11 dead things had any damage or wear listed, and a split laptop charger became "white wired earbuds".

So I split the schema into three lists and asked for damage first. On the next run all 11 dead things had an injury. That run had its own bug: the model wrote "no visible damage" as an entry in the damage list, the check accepted it as an injury, and a blurred green glow was buried as Miss Petunia Bloomsworth, who "passed away due to no visible damage." Code now drops entries like that.

The table shows the check's limit. It proves that each sentence points at a listed detail, not that the detail is real. Two causes of death rested on details I could not find in the photo: a cassette adapter "suffered a missing screw hole" while its real injury, heat warping, went unmentioned, and a folded umbrella died of "torn fabric". That is why the card footer prints the model's list: you can hold the obituary up against the photo.

How it was tested:

  • 48 Go unit test cases: the check, the gate, the repair step, the HTTP routes, and the Ollama client against a fake server (bad JSON, missing model, Ollama down, timeout).
  • The live run above, plus two extra passes on three photos. The details barely moved, since the look step runs at temperature 0.2. The names changed each time, except the pumpkins, who were Mr. Josiah Gourdington twice.
  • 10 Playwright tests against the real server and model: upload, card, sentence-to-detail mapping, PNG download, still-alive notices, phone width, keyboard, missing model, Ollama down, the LAN address, and a full run that fails if any request leaves the machine.

Stack: Go 1.26 with net/http serving a React, Vite and TypeScript page; Gemma 4 E4B through Ollama; html-to-image for the PNG; Old Standard TT and UnifrakturMaguntia fonts bundled from Fontsource. The Ollama request pattern (structured JSON output, timeouts, plain-language errors) comes from my earlier project Backpack. The code here is new.

Photo credits, all from Wikimedia Commons: jack-o'-lanterns by Giulia Forsythe (CC BY 2.0), burnt toast by Sheep purple (CC BY 2.0), succulent by stephen boisvert (CC BY 2.0), light bulb by Shixart1985 (CC BY 2.0), and the shoes on the cover by Wolfmann (CC BY 4.0).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

These photos show the inside of your home: the kitchen counter, the bathroom shelf, whatever is headed for the trash. With an open-weight model on the laptop they never leave it. No upload, no account, no retention policy. The server holds the photo in memory for one request and never writes it to disk.

It works with Wi-Fi off. The browser test records every request during a full run, and the count going to any host outside the machine is zero. Each obituary costs nothing.

Because the model runs on my machine, I could cut its job into two strict steps and check the output in my own code. The schemas, the temperatures and the check live in my repository, not behind an endpoint that can change or disappear, and HERELIES_MODEL swaps in any other Ollama model.

The limit is the eyesight of a small model. Gemma called the broken mug a "creamer jug" with a spout it does not have, and 4 of 65 details were wrong. I can see those mistakes because the pipeline shows them to me, and I prefer that to a better answer I cannot inspect.

The Spirit of It

The most surprising result was a refusal. In the first run Gemma looked at a rotting succulent, translucent and black at the edges, and decided it was alive: "This plant is still with us. Water it." Once the prompt said that brown, mushy or translucent leaves mean dead, Agnes Petalbrook got her obituary.

Día de los Muertos is about remembering through stories. A dead charger is not a grandmother, but it deserves a better send-off than the trash can: a name, a cause of death, and someone to survive it. In its case, "a set of mismatched plugs and a seldom-used surge protector."

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama, does both the looking and the writing, and code checks its output against what it saw.

title: How to Learn React Hooks (and Stop Fighting useEffect)
description:
The first React app I wrote with hooks had a useEffect that fetched a user profile. It worked on the first load. Then I added the user ID to the dependency array because the linter told me to, and the network tab filled up with the same request, over and over, until the tab froze.

I fixed it by deleting the dependency array. That was the wrong fix, and it took me an embarrassingly long time to understand why.

Most people learn hooks the way I did: copy a pattern, hit a bug, paste a Stack Overflow answer. You end up knowing a dozen workarounds and none of the ideas underneath. Here's the order I'd learn them in now.

Start with what a render actually is

Before any hook makes sense, you need one mental model. Every time state changes, React calls your component function again, top to bottom. Every variable inside it is created fresh. Every function you define inside it is a new function.

That's why this logs a stale value:

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    console.log(count); // still the old number
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}

count belongs to the render that created handleClick. It isn't a live variable that updates in place. The new value only exists in the next render. Once that clicked for me, half my "hooks are weird" complaints went away. They weren't weird. I just thought my component was an object that stuck around, and it's really a function that runs again.

useState: learn the updater form early

You'll use useState constantly, so learn the one detail that bites people. If the new state depends on the old state, pass a function:

setCount(c => c + 1);

Call setCount(count + 1) three times in one handler and you get +1, because all three read the same count. Call setCount(c => c + 1) three times and you get +3. I'd also learn that objects in state get replaced, not merged, so setUser({ ...user, name }) is the habit to build.

useEffect is for syncing with things outside React

This is where most of the pain is, and the React docs rewrite at react.dev is the best thing I've read on it. The short version: an effect is for keeping your component in sync with something React doesn't control. A network request, a subscription, a timer, a DOM API, a third-party widget.

The dependency array isn't a list of "when to run". It's a list of every value from the render that the effect reads. If you lie to it, you get stale data. If you include an object or function that's recreated every render, you get my infinite loop.

The fixes I reach for, in order:

  1. Move the function inside the effect, so it isn't a dependency at all.
  2. Depend on primitive values (user.id) instead of whole objects (user).
  3. Ask whether this needs to be an effect in the first place.

That third one matters most. The docs page You Might Not Need an Effect is worth reading twice. Filtering a list, computing a total, resetting a form when a prop changes: none of these need useEffect. You can calculate them during render. A lot of my old bugs came from effects that set state that could have just been a variable.

And write the cleanup. If an effect subscribes, starts a timer or opens a socket, return a function that undoes it. In development, Strict Mode runs your effects twice on mount to flush out missing cleanups, which is why your fetch shows up twice in the console. That's on purpose.

useRef, useMemo and useCallback can wait

useRef is simple once you see it as a box that survives renders without causing one. Use it for DOM nodes and for values you need to remember but never display, like an interval ID.

useMemo and useCallback are performance tools. I'd skip them until you have a real reason, like a slow calculation or a memoized child component that keeps re-rendering. Wrapping everything in them makes code harder to read and usually doesn't make it faster.

Custom hooks come last, and they're just functions that start with use and call other hooks. The first time you pull a useDebounce or useLocalStorage out of two components that both had the same effect, you'll get why they exist.

Build small things that break

Reading about hooks only gets you so far. These four tiny projects cover almost every common mistake:

  1. A counter with a "+3" button, to learn the updater form.
  2. A search box that fetches results as you type, to learn dependencies, cleanup and race conditions.
  3. A stopwatch with start and stop, to learn useRef for the interval ID.
  4. A dark mode toggle saved to localStorage, pulled into a custom hook.

Do them without a tutorial open. When something loops or shows stale data, that's the lesson.

Then make it stick

My actual problem with hooks wasn't understanding them once. I'd read the effects docs, get it, and a month later on a different project write the same broken fetch again. The rules of the dependency array are the kind of thing you know in theory and forget in practice.

What helped was reviewing the handful of ideas that kept tripping me up: renders are snapshots, the updater form, dependencies are what the effect reads, maybe you don't need an effect. I'd look at those notes after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it works better for this than rereading a tutorial when you're already stuck.

I built Recl for exactly this kind of learning. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, say a conference talk on effects or the react.dev page itself, and it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "React", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. A plain notes file with calendar reminders does the same job if you'd rather not use an app. What matters is seeing it again before the next bug does the reminding for you.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: The night shift nobody works: what idle VMs cost, by the hour
description:
A dev VM is used from 8 to 8, five days a week. That is 60 hours. The cloud bills 168. Multiply by every VM in dev and QA and the night shift is the most expensive team you have, and it does nothing.

Control Cloud reads your clouds through the provider API with read-only credentials and puts a number on that, from your own inventory, not from a calculator with guessed inputs.

What a night costs, by the hour

The Overnight bleeding card takes the VMs that are running right now, their hourly rate, and the hours a night you choose. On this demo organization: 16 running VMs, 12 hours a night, $1.51 an hour, $18.16 a night, $127 a week, $6,627 a year. It excludes what bills 24/7 anyway (databases, load balancers, NAT gateways), so the number is what you can actually get back.

Three things that bill for nothing
