title: Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How `<Link>` Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow
description:
Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How <Link> Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers adopt Next.js App Router expecting server components to eliminate client-side waterfalls and prefetching to deliver instant navigation. The reality surprises them: links feel sluggish, dynamic routes block for seconds, and the DevTools network tab shows requests firing only after the user clicks. The prefetch happened, the data arrived, but the navigation still waits.

The confusion stems from three behaviors that collide in production: partial prefetch stops at the first Suspense boundary instead of loading the full page, the router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes, and the client cannot render anything until the server responds with the missing pieces. The result is a server-driven app that feels slower than the client-side SPA it replaced.

Next.js 16.3 introduces partial prefetching as an opt-in feature, giving developers fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. Combined with the new cache components primitive, teams can mark reusable UI as cacheable and let Next.js extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file. The client now has enough data to render an instant transition, and the server streams dynamic content as it resolves.

This post explains how App Router prefetching works under the hood, why the default behavior creates slow navigations, and how to adopt the new primitives to make every link click feel instant without breaking dynamic content.

Key Takeaways

  • Next.js App Router partial prefetch (the default) stops at the first Suspense boundary, not the full page, causing slow navigations when routes lack explicit loading shells.
  • The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes and 5 minutes for static routes, triggering re-fetches on click if the user waits too long.
  • Next.js 16.3's partial prefetching and cache components let developers mark reusable UI as cacheable and control exactly what loads before navigation.
  • Instant Insights in the Next.js DevTools automatically surfaces slow navigations during development, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.
  • Full prefetch with prefetch={true} loads the entire destination page ahead of time, but costs bandwidth and can serve stale personalized content if cached data expires.

How Next.js Link Prefetching Actually Works in App Router

The <Link> component in Next.js App Router triggers prefetching when it enters the viewport or when the user hovers over it. The exact behavior depends on the prefetch prop and whether the destination route is static or dynamic.

By default, <Link> uses prefetch="auto", which means Next.js decides what to prefetch based on the route type. For static routes, the full route loads. For dynamic routes, Next.js fetches the route down to the first loading.tsx boundary, a behavior called partial prefetch.

The distinction between static and dynamic routes matters because Next.js treats them differently at build time. A route is static if it contains no dynamic segments (like [id]), no generateStaticParams is missing, and it does not read request-specific data like cookies or headers. Everything else is dynamic.

// app/blog/page.tsx - static route
export default function BlogPage() {
  return <div>Blog posts render at build time</div>;
}

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx - dynamic route
export default function PostPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  // Reads dynamic segment, so Next.js treats this as dynamic
  return <div>Post: {params.slug}</div>;
}

When a user hovers over a <Link href="/blog/post-1">, Next.js sends a request to the server. For a static route, the server returns the pre-rendered HTML and RSC payload. For a dynamic route, the server returns only the layout and any shared UI down to the first Suspense boundary, then stops. The page component itself does not load until the user clicks.

The official Next.js documentation (as of version 16.3) describes this behavior in the prefetch prop reference: "For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a loading.js boundary will be prefetched." If no loading.tsx file exists, the prefetch ends at the layout, and the navigation blocks until the server responds with the page.

The router cache stores prefetched data with a time-to-live (TTL) that depends on the route type. Static routes cache for 5 minutes. Dynamic routes cache for 30 seconds. After the TTL expires, clicking the link triggers a new server request even if the prefetch completed successfully.

This explains why navigations sometimes feel instant and sometimes block. If the user clicks within 30 seconds of hovering, the cached data is fresh and the navigation completes immediately. If the user waits 31 seconds, the cache expires, and the client must wait for the server to re-render the route before the navigation can proceed.

Partial Prefetch vs Full Prefetch: What Gets Loaded When

The prefetch prop on <Link> accepts three values: "auto" (the default), true, and false. Each produces different behavior and costs.

prefetch="auto" defers to Next.js to decide what to load. For static routes, this means the full route. For dynamic routes, this means a partial prefetch that stops at the first loading.tsx boundary. The goal is to balance performance with bandwidth: prefetch enough to make navigation feel instant without loading content the user may never see.

prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch for both static and dynamic routes. The client downloads the entire page, including all data-fetching and rendering, before the user clicks. This guarantees instant navigation but wastes bandwidth if the user never visits the link. It also introduces stale data problems for personalized routes: if the prefetched page contains user-specific content, and the user waits long enough for the cache to expire, clicking the link shows stale content until the server responds with fresh data.

prefetch={false} disables prefetching entirely. The client requests the route only after the user clicks. This saves bandwidth but guarantees a slow navigation because the client must wait for the server to render the page before the transition can complete.

Next.js 16.3 changes the behavior when partial prefetching is enabled via partialPrefetching: true in next.config.ts. With this flag, prefetch="auto" now prefetches the route's app shell (the static and cached content) instead of stopping at the first loading.tsx boundary. The app shell includes layouts, templates, and any components marked with 'use cache', giving the client enough data to render a loading state immediately on click.

Prefetch value Static route behavior Dynamic route behavior Router cache TTL Best for
"auto" (default) Full route Partial (to first loading.tsx) Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Most links
true Full route Full route Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Critical navigation paths
false No prefetch No prefetch N/A Rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists
"auto" (with partialPrefetching: true) App shell + cached content App shell + cached content Configurable per cache tag Next.js 16.3+ apps

The tradeoff between partial and full prefetch becomes clear in a dashboard app. A sidebar contains 20 links to different reports. Full prefetch downloads all 20 pages when the sidebar renders, consuming megabytes of bandwidth and server resources even if the user only views one report. Partial prefetch downloads the shell for each page (layouts, navigation, headers) but waits to load report-specific data until the user clicks. The navigation feels instant because the shell paints immediately, and the data streams in as it resolves.

// app/dashboard/layout.tsx
export default function DashboardLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div className="dashboard">
      <nav>
        {/* Partial prefetch: loads shell, not data */}
        <Link href="/dashboard/sales">Sales Report</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/inventory">Inventory</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/analytics">Analytics</Link>
      </nav>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}

The diagram shows why partial prefetch feels faster for the initial shell render but slower for the complete page, while full prefetch either delivers the entire page instantly or serves stale content if the cache expired. Choosing the right strategy depends on whether the route contains dynamic content that changes frequently.

The Router Cache Problem: When Prefetched Data Goes Stale

The router cache in Next.js App Router exists to avoid redundant server requests. When a prefetch completes, Next.js stores the result in memory with a TTL. Subsequent navigations to the same route read from the cache instead of hitting the server, making back-and-forth navigation instantaneous.

The problem surfaces when the TTL expires before the user clicks. For dynamic routes, 30 seconds is short enough that normal user behavior (reading content, scrolling, comparing options) exhausts the cache before the navigation happens. The user clicks, the cache check fails, and the client blocks while waiting for the server to re-render the route.

This behavior surprises developers because the prefetch succeeded. The DevTools network tab shows the request completing with a 200 status. But when the user clicks 35 seconds later, a second identical request fires, and the navigation waits for that response before proceeding. The prefetch wasted bandwidth and delivered no performance benefit.

The stale data problem is worse for personalized routes. Consider a product page that shows the user's cart count in the header. If the page prefetches when the user hovers the link, and the user adds items to the cart before clicking, the prefetched page shows the old cart count until the new server response arrives. The transition looks instant, but the cart count is wrong for 200-300ms, creating a flicker as the correct data streams in.

Next.js addressed this in 16.3 by tying cache invalidation to the 'use cache' directive. When a component or function is marked with 'use cache', Next.js generates a cache key based on the function's arguments and the user's session. If the arguments or session change, the cache key changes, and the cached data is no longer valid. This lets developers opt specific components into granular caching while keeping the rest of the page fresh.

// app/dashboard/sales/page.tsx
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

async function getSalesData(userId: string) {
  'use cache';
  const response = await fetch(`/api/sales?user=${userId}`);
  return response.json();
}

export default async function SalesPage({ params }: { params: { userId: string } }) {
  const data = await getSalesData(params.userId);

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Sales Report</h1>
      {/* This data is cached per user and stays fresh across navigations */}
      <pre>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</pre>
    </div>
  );
}

The official Next.js 16.3 release notes state: "It's more explicit and composable than our previous server-side caching APIs, and now, it also brings client-side caching to Next.js for the first time." The 'use cache' directive integrates with prefetching by letting the router cache store function-level results instead of full routes. When a prefetch happens, Next.js extracts the cached data, bundles it with the shell, and sends it to the client. The user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and only the non-cached dynamic data requires a server round-trip.

The cache key mechanism solves the stale data problem but introduces a new complexity: cache invalidation. If the sales data changes server-side while the client holds a cached copy, the user sees outdated information until the cache expires or the route re-validates. Next.js provides revalidation APIs (revalidatePath, revalidateTag) to expire caches on demand, but developers must call them explicitly when data changes.

Router cache diagram showing TTL expiration and re-fetch behavior

The image illustrates how the router cache expires after the TTL and triggers a new server request, even when the original prefetch completed successfully. The gap between prefetch and click determines whether the navigation feels instant or blocks.

Controlling Prefetch Behavior: Practical Code Examples

Developers control prefetching at three levels: per-link via the prefetch prop, per-route via loading.tsx files, and globally via next.config.ts flags.

The prefetch prop is the most direct control. Setting prefetch={false} disables prefetching for a specific link, useful for links in infinite scroll lists where prefetching would waste bandwidth. Setting prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch, useful for critical navigation paths like the main call-to-action on a landing page.

// app/components/product-list.tsx
'use client';

export default function ProductList({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  return (
    <div className="grid">
      {products.map((product) => (
        <Link
          key={product.id}
          href={`/product/${product.id}`}
          // Disable prefetch for long lists to save bandwidth
          prefetch={false}
        >
          {product.name}
        </Link>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

The loading.tsx file provides a route-level loading shell that prefetching uses to render an instant transition. When a dynamic route includes a loading.tsx file, partial prefetch stops at that file and sends the loading component to the client. The user clicks, the loading state renders immediately, and the page content streams in as the server resolves data-fetching.

// app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return (
    <div className="blog-post-skeleton">
      <div className="skeleton-title" />
      <div className="skeleton-author" />
      <div className="skeleton-content" />
    </div>
  );
}

Without loading.tsx, partial prefetch has nothing to send, so the navigation blocks until the full page arrives. The Next.js DevTools Instant Insights panel highlights this as a slow navigation and suggests adding a loading file.

Next.js 16.3 adds two config flags that change prefetching behavior globally. Setting cacheComponents: true enables the new cache components primitive, letting developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache' and have Next.js extract it during prefetch. Setting partialPrefetching: true changes the default prefetch="auto" behavior from "stop at first loading.tsx" to "prefetch app shell plus cached content."

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

These flags unlock fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. A product page can mark the header, footer, and navigation as cached, while leaving product-specific content (price, availability, reviews) dynamic. The prefetch sends the shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the dynamic content streams in.

// app/product/[id]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function Header() {
  'use cache';
  return <header>Site Header</header>;
}

async function ProductDetails({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const product = await fetch(`/api/products/${id}`).then(res => res.json());

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <p>{product.price}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

export default function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading product...</div>}>
        <ProductDetails id={params.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The cache components approach solves the stale data problem by caching at the component level instead of the route level. The header never changes, so it stays cached indefinitely. The product details change frequently, so they skip the cache and fetch fresh data on every navigation. The user sees an instant shell render followed by a smooth stream of dynamic content, no flicker, no stale data.

Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations and the Future of Prefetching

Next.js 16.3 introduces Instant Navigations, a suite of features designed to make server-rendered apps feel as responsive as client-side SPAs without sacrificing the benefits of server rendering. The headline feature is partial prefetching, which builds on the cache components primitive to extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file.

The official Next.js 16.3 announcement states: "Next.js can extract this UI and load it into the client prior to a navigation, making your app feel as snappy as an SPA once users start clicking around it." The key word is "extract." Instead of requiring developers to manually define loading shells in separate files, Next.js analyzes the route's component tree, identifies cached components, and bundles them with the prefetch response. The client receives a ready-to-render shell even if the route has no loading.tsx file.

Partial prefetching also changes how prefetch payloads are structured. In prior versions, a prefetch request returned a monolithic RSC payload containing the entire route. In 16.3, the payload includes three layers: the app shell (layouts, templates, cached components), URL-specific data (dynamic segments, search params), and truly dynamic content (user-specific data, real-time updates). The client renders the app shell immediately, paints URL-specific data as it arrives, and streams dynamic content last.

This staged handoff eliminates the binary choice between instant-but-stale full prefetch and accurate-but-slow partial prefetch. The app shell is always safe to cache because it does not depend on user state or request timing. URL-specific data caches per route, so navigating between products on the same site reuses the shared shell and only fetches product-specific content. Dynamic content bypasses the cache entirely, guaranteeing freshness at the cost of a small delay.

// app/dashboard/[reportId]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function DashboardShell() {
  'use cache';
  return (
    <div className="dashboard-layout">
      <nav>Dashboard Navigation</nav>
      <aside>Filters</aside>
    </div>
  );
}

async function ReportData({ reportId }: { reportId: string }) {
  const data = await fetch(`/api/reports/${reportId}`).then(res => res.json());

  return <div>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</div>;
}

export default function ReportPage({ params }: { params: { reportId: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <DashboardShell />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading report...</div>}>
        <ReportData reportId={params.reportId} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The diagram below shows the execution flow when partial prefetching is enabled. The prefetch extracts the app shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the report data streams in as the server resolves the fetch.

The Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools automatically detects slow navigations and suggests fixes. If a route lacks a loading shell, the panel shows a warning and generates a prompt that teaches AI agents how to add one. If a route has a loading shell but still feels slow, the panel identifies which components are blocking the critical path and suggests marking them with 'use cache'.

The official documentation (Next.js 16.3 release notes) describes Instant Insights as "a new devtool that automatically surfaces slow navigations." The panel runs in development mode only, monitoring every client-side transition and measuring the time from click to first paint. If the time exceeds a threshold (currently 300ms), the panel flags the navigation as slow and logs the component stack that blocked rendering.

This eliminates the guesswork that plagued prior versions. Developers no longer need to profile every link manually or instrument their code with performance marks. The DevTools highlight the problem, explain the root cause, and provide a concrete fix. All without leaving the browser.

Instant Insights panel in Next.js DevTools showing a slow navigation warning

The image shows the Instant Insights panel flagging a navigation to /dashboard/sales as slow because the route lacks a loading shell. The panel suggests adding a loading.tsx file or marking reusable components with 'use cache' to unlock instant navigation.

Debugging Slow Navigations: Finding the Real Culprit

Slow navigations in Next.js stem from four common causes: missing loading shells, expired router cache, blocking data fetches, and oversized prefetch payloads. Identifying the root cause requires inspecting the network tab, the React DevTools profiler, and the Next.js Instant Insights panel.

The network tab shows when prefetch requests fire and how long they take to complete. A prefetch that completes in 50ms but triggers a second identical request on click indicates a cache expiration problem. The user waited longer than the TTL, so the router cache invalidated the prefetched data and fetched it again.

The React DevTools profiler shows which components are blocking the critical path. If a navigation waits 2 seconds before painting anything, the profiler flame graph reveals which component is running slow. The usual suspects are data-fetching components that call fetch without Suspense boundaries, heavy computations in the render phase, and third-party libraries that block the main thread.

The Instant Insights panel ties these signals together by showing the full navigation trace. The panel logs the click event, the prefetch check, the cache hit or miss, the first paint, and the final layout shift. If the navigation is slow, the panel highlights the step that took the longest and suggests a fix.

The diagram shows the decision tree the router follows during navigation. If the cache is valid, the render happens immediately. If the cache expired, the navigation blocks while waiting for the server response. The gap between cache check and server response is where slowness accumulates.

Fixing slow navigations requires matching the solution to the root cause. If the cache expired, either shorten the time between prefetch and click (by prefetching on hover instead of on viewport entry) or extend the cache TTL by marking components with 'use cache'. If the navigation blocks on data fetches, wrap the slow components in Suspense boundaries and add a loading fallback. If the prefetch payload is too large, reduce it by setting prefetch={false} on low-priority links or splitting the route into smaller chunks.

The useLinkStatus hook (introduced in Next.js 16.2) provides immediate feedback during navigation. When a user clicks a link, the hook returns { pending: true } until the navigation completes, letting developers show a loading indicator without waiting for the server response.

'use client';

import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link';

export default function NavigationIndicator() {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();

  if (!pending) return null;

  return (
    <div className="fixed top-0 left-0 right-0 h-1 bg-blue-500 animate-pulse" />
  );
}

The hook debounces fast navigations by adding a 100ms delay before returning pending: true. This prevents the loading indicator from flashing on screen for navigations that complete in under 100ms, reducing visual noise for instant transitions.

The official Next.js documentation (version 16.3) recommends combining useLinkStatus with CSS transitions to create a smooth loading experience: "You can 'debounce' the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. opacity: 0)." This gives the server time to respond before showing any feedback, avoiding flicker on fast networks.

For further reading on Next.js caching and performance, see the related posts Next.js 15 Caching Changes, Next.js App Router Layouts and Templates, and Next.js Caching Mental Model 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my Next.js link prefetch but still feel slow when clicked?

The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes. If the user clicks after the TTL, the client fetches the route again even though the prefetch completed. Use 'use cache' to extend the TTL or reduce the delay between prefetch and click by prefetching on hover.

What is the difference between partial prefetch and full prefetch in App Router?

Partial prefetch loads the route down to the first Suspense boundary, sending the layout and loading shell but skipping page-specific data. Full prefetch loads the entire page including all data. Partial prefetch saves bandwidth but may feel slower if no loading shell exists. Use prefetch={true} to force full prefetch on critical links.

How does Next.js 16.3 partial prefetching change the default behavior?

In Next.js 16.3, enabling partialPrefetching: true makes prefetch="auto" send the app shell plus cached components instead of stopping at loading.tsx. This gives the client enough data to render an instant transition without requiring a separate loading file for every route.

When should I disable prefetching with prefetch={false}?

Disable prefetching for rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists, and links that appear in large quantities (like a product catalog with 1000 items). Prefetching wastes bandwidth if the user never clicks the link, and disabling it has no downside if the route is not performance-critical.

How do I debug which component is blocking a slow navigation?

Use the Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools to identify slow navigations, then inspect the React DevTools profiler to see which component is blocking the critical path. The profiler flame graph shows render times per component, revealing bottlenecks like unwrapped data fetches or heavy computations in the render phase.

Making Next.js Navigations Feel Instant Without Breaking Dynamic Content

Next.js prefetching promises instant navigation but delivers slow transitions when the defaults collide with dynamic routes, expired caches, and missing loading shells. The confusion stems from partial prefetch stopping at Suspense boundaries, router cache expiration after 30 seconds, and the client blocking until the server responds with missing data.

Next.js 16.3 fixes this with partial prefetching, cache components, and Instant Insights. Developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache', and Next.js extracts it during prefetch, giving the client enough data to render an instant shell. Dynamic content streams in as the server resolves it, and the DevTools highlight any navigation that takes longer than 300ms, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.

Adopting the new primitives requires enabling two flags in next.config.ts and marking cached components with 'use cache'. The payoff is a server-rendered app that feels as responsive as a client-side SPA, with no stale data, no flicker, and no guesswork about when prefetches expire.

title: 5 Step-by-Step Ways to Integrate Email Event Notification APIs for Property Reports
description:
A step-by-step way to integrate email event notification APIs for a property-management report starts with a hard boundary: the PDF leaving the report worker is not delivery. The application must account for the handoff, the provider event, and the recipient-facing outcome. I would keep report generation and email delivery separate, then poll an event API on a schedule; that boundary is less immediate than a webhook, but it is easy to reason about and recover.

Infrai fits this specific handoff when scheduled event reconciliation is acceptable: its breadth puts email beside other backend capabilities behind one REST surface, while the event boundary remains a pull job that the application owns.

TL;DR: use the email provider to send the generated attachment, use GET /v1/email/event/list to pull event data, persist the raw response and your own processing state, and retry transport failures with backoff. A single REST surface is useful when the same service also needs storage, scheduling, or observability, but a specialist with webhook delivery is the better fit when near-real-time event intake is a hard SLO.

What does reliable delivery mean for a property report?

The incident lesson is bounded but important: a monthly owner statement can be generated correctly and still be operationally invisible. A worker can finish the PDF, an email request can be accepted, and the property manager can still have no defensible record of what happened next. The invariant is a three-part record: report identity, send attempt, and later provider event.

That is the trap.

I would put an SLO around the part the team controls: every completed report gets one recorded send attempt and one polling decision. I would not turn “the API returned” into “the owner received it.”

The five checkpoints are:

  1. Generate the report and assign a stable report ID.
  2. Hand the attachment to the email-sending boundary and record the attempt.
  3. Poll GET /v1/email/event/list on a schedule because events are exposed through API pulls rather than webhook pushes.
  4. Retry rate limits and transient transport errors without creating duplicate downstream work.
  5. Escalate ambiguous or terminal outcomes with enough evidence for an operator to act.

The first two checkpoints belong to the report and email components. The third through fifth belong to event intake. Mixing them creates a queue that can claim success before there is any event evidence.

How can you integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

Store the API key in the runtime secret store and expose it as INFRAI_API_KEY; do not put it in a repository, report payload, or log line. The base URL is https://api.infrai.cc/v1, and the event route is a GET. The route list is intentionally short here: an integration article should teach the boundary, not become an endpoint catalogue.

The worker below treats the response as opaque JSON because the verified contract establishes the event-list route, authentication, and pull model, but does not establish a safe set of event fields to hard-code into a local schema. In production, persist the response beside the poll timestamp and map fields only after checking the route’s current response schema.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os"
  "strconv"
  "strings"
  "time"
)

func main() {
  key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
  if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
  body, err := pullEvents(key)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func pullEvents(key string) ([]byte, error) {
  const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list"
  client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
  backoff := time.Second
  for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
      if attempt == 4 { return nil, err }
      time.Sleep(backoff); backoff *= 2; continue
    }
    data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body); resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
      if attempt == 4 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limited: %s", data) }
      wait := backoff
      if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value)); parseErr == nil { wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
      }
      time.Sleep(wait); backoff *= 2; continue
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data) }
    return data, nil
  }
  return nil, fmt.Errorf("event pull exhausted retries")
}

Run the worker from the service’s periodic job mechanism, with a timeout shorter than the job lease, and record a poll watermark in durable storage. If the endpoint returns the same event on two polls, the consumer must be idempotent. A retry here repeats a read; it must not send another report.

The same HTTP contract can be implemented with Node.js fetch or Axios. The operational decisions do not change: explicit GET, bearer authentication, a checked status code, 429 backoff honoring Retry-After, and a durable handoff to the event processor.

Where does a unified provider help, and where does it stop?

For a small platform team, provider breadth can remove integration seams. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with 41 routes in the comm-email-sms group; its public discovery surface describes capabilities and supplies runnable examples in 10 languages. That helps when the report workflow later needs scheduling, storage, or observability and the team wants one REST contract to inspect. Its documented idempotency convention gives write paths a common place to start, although this event pull is a read.

The boundary is real. The email and SMS event model is pull-based, so it cannot provide webhook push for this intake path. It also has no SMTP relay. This limitation is decisive if the system’s requirement is sub-minute event fan-out, or if an existing mail estate depends on SMTP; those are disqualifying constraints.

Option Event handoff Where it fits Boundary to test
Unified REST provider Pull with GET /v1/email/event/list A platform team consolidating backend capabilities behind one REST surface Polling delay and absence of webhook push
Amazon SES Commonly paired with configuration-set event publishing Teams already operating on AWS AWS-specific integration and operational ownership
SendGrid Event Webhook-oriented delivery workflows Teams needing provider-originated event delivery Webhook security, replay handling, and the wider platform stack
Mailgun Email API plus event/webhook tooling Teams wanting email-focused diagnostics Provider-specific event schema and conventions

This is not a ranking. SendGrid or Mailgun is the stronger fit when webhook intake is the primary SLO; SES is sensible when AWS event infrastructure is already the control plane. The trade-off is straightforward: the unified provider fits this workflow when a pull-based event record is acceptable and one REST surface outweighs adding a specialist integration.

What should the SLO and recovery policy say?

Start with an SLO that names the clock: report completion to recorded send attempt, then poll completion to recorded event decision. Keep those measurements separate. Otherwise a slow event poll will look like a slow PDF generator, and the on-call engineer will debug the wrong queue.

Retain the raw event response, request time, HTTP status, retry count, and your report ID. Redact authorization headers and attachment contents. For a transient failure, leave the poll eligible for the next run. For an authentication or other non-retryable client error, stop the loop and page the credential owner rather than multiplying bad requests.

Polling gives evidence from the provider, not a universal guarantee of inbox delivery. SPF is one part of sender authorization; domain authentication, suppression handling, recipient policy, and mailbox placement need their own checks. A report pipeline should expose that uncertainty in its status model.

The practical decision

Use the five checkpoints as the acceptance test: can the team identify the report, prove the send handoff, poll events, retry safely, and explain an ambiguous outcome? If yes, a pull-based API can fit property-management reports. If no, start with the missing operational control, not another SDK.

Try Infrai for the event-pull and surrounding backend handoff when one REST surface matters and scheduled reconciliation meets the workflow’s SLO. Choose a specialist when webhook delivery or SMTP relay is a hard requirement.

If that boundary fits the system, the provider documentation is the next place to inspect current discovery and email integration details.

Sources

  • Provider documentation
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide
  • Twilio SendGrid Event Webhook
  • Mailgun Events API
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework

title: React error #418: five hydration bugs I shipped
description:
This post was created with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy before publishing.

If your production console shows Minified React error #418, React is telling you that the HTML the server sent and the first render in the browser did not match. The development build spells it out ("Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client") and shows a diff. The production build gives you a number and a link to react.dev/errors/418.

It is easy to treat it as console noise, because the page still works. It is not free. When hydration fails, React throws away the server-rendered tree and renders the whole root again in the browser. On my site that one error took mobile Total Blocking Time from 0 to 420 ms and the Lighthouse performance score from 96 to 83, and pushed Largest Contentful Paint 1.2 seconds past First Contentful Paint, which had always been equal.

I have shipped this error five different ways on one Next.js site. Here is each one, how it was found, and the fix that stuck.

1. Randomness or time in a useState initializer

The games on the site generate a puzzle, a word or a board. The obvious code seeds state when the component is created:

// Wrong: the initializer runs on the server and again in the browser.
const [puzzle, setPuzzle] = useState(() => generatePuzzle());

The initializer runs twice, once during prerendering and once during hydration, and Math.random() gives a different answer each time. The same thing happened in a lorem ipsum generator, a mock data generator and a password generator. Anything that reads Date.now() or new Date() while rendering has the same problem.

The fix is a deterministic first value, with the random one set after mount:

const [puzzle, setPuzzle] = useState(INITIAL_PUZZLE); // fixed, the same everywhere
useEffect(() => {
  setPuzzle(generatePuzzle()); // runs only in the browser, after hydration
}, []);

The first frame shows the fixed puzzle for an instant. For a game that is fine. For anything where the flash matters, render a placeholder of the same size until the effect runs.

2. Formatting with the machine's locale 

// Wrong
<span>{downloads.toLocaleString()}</span>
<time>{new Date(post.date).toLocaleDateString()}</time>

With no locale argument, toLocaleString() uses whatever the current machine prefers. The server that prerenders the page (on Vercel, en-US in UTC) and a visitor in Germany or India produce different strings, so the text differs and hydration fails. It never reproduces on your own machine if your machine matches the server.

Pass the locale you rendered with, or move the formatting after mount:

<span>{downloads.toLocaleString('en-US')}</span>

To catch this class of bug, load the deployed page in a browser with a different locale and time zone. In Playwright that is two options on the context:

const context = await browser.newContext({ locale: 'de-DE', timezoneId: 'America/Los_Angeles' });

3. Browser-only APIs while rendering

Five tools on the site called something during render that only exists, or only behaves the same, in a browser: DOMParser in an XPath evaluator, document in an SVG animation tool and an HTML-to-Pug converter, and URL.createObjectURL in an SVG viewer. That last one is a good example of why this can hide: on the server it produced nothing useful, in the browser it produced a blob: URL, and the visible symptom was a broken image, not an error.

// Wrong: runs during render on the server too.
const src = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svg], { type: 'image/svg+xml' }));

The fix is to compute these only after the component has mounted:

function useHasMounted() {
  const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => setMounted(true), []);
  return mounted;
}

const mounted = useHasMounted();
const src = useMemo(
  () => (mounted ? URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svg], { type: 'image/svg+xml' })) : null),
  [mounted, svg],
);

Remember to revoke the URL when nothing can reach it any more, but that is a separate bug.

4. usePathname() in a prerendered component

This is the one that cost the most, because I fixed it and then shipped it again.

The site's navigation highlights the current page. The highlight compared the path:

const pathname = usePathname();
const isActive = pathname === href;

On the deployed homepage this logged #418 on every visit. It never happened locally, with next dev or with a local production build. The comparison for the / link came out differently in Vercel's prerender of the index route than in the browser, so the active class differed between the server HTML and the first client render.

The first time, I fixed it in one header. Later a different navigation design carried the same comparison into a new component, and it went live again. That second time is the one that took Lighthouse from 96 to 83.

The fix that stuck is a shared hook that gates only the / comparison on mount and leaves every other link server-rendered, so the other routes keep their active state from the first paint. Simplified, it looks like this:

export function useIsRouteActive(href: string) {
  const pathname = usePathname();
  const mounted = useHasMounted();
  if (href === '/') return mounted && pathname === '/';
  return pathname === href || pathname.startsWith(`${href}/`);
}

The second part of the fix was making sure it could not come back. The repository has a small script that runs before every build and fails when a client component compares usePathname() directly. A lint rule would do the same job. Writing the lesson down had not been enough.

5. A script that edits <body> before React gets there

The site sets a colour scheme and, on festival days, a few data- attributes on <body> from an inline script, so the right look paints before any JavaScript bundle loads. React then hydrates <body>, finds attributes it did not render, and complains.

This is the one case where suppressHydrationWarning is the right tool:

<body suppressHydrationWarning>

It only silences attribute and text differences on that one element, not its children, which is exactly the scope you want. Two rules keep it honest: only the element the script edits gets it (here <body>, not <html>), and the script only ever sets attributes, never content.

suppressHydrationWarning is not a fix for the first four causes. Those are real differences in what renders, and hiding the warning leaves the re-render in place.

How to find yours

  • Read the console on the deployed site, not just locally. Three of these five never reproduced on my machine.
  • Run the development build once to get the readable message and the diff React prints, which names the element and the two values.
  • Load the page with a foreign locale and time zone. It finds cause 2 and anything else that reads the environment.
  • Search the codebase for Math.random, Date.now, new Date(, toLocale, window., document., DOMParser and usePathname inside components that render on the server.

The common thread is simple: everything a component renders the first time must be computable on the server, from the same inputs, with the same answer. Anything that depends on the browser, the clock, chance or the visitor waits until after mount.

title: Sentinel-IR 0.2.1: When "eval" Hides Behind an Alias
description:
Sentinel-IR 0.2.1

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Thanks for support..
Release: "Sentinel-IR-MCP v0.2.2 on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir-mcp/-/tree/v0.2.2?ref_type=tags)

Package: "sentinel-ir-mcp@0.2.2 on npm" (https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir-mcp/v/0.2.2)

A focused improvement in AST-based analysis, six regression tests, and a closer look at two tricky JavaScript control-flow paths.

The first 30 seconds

What happens when dangerous code execution does not look like "eval()"?

Sometimes JavaScript stores "eval" in another variable and calls that variable later. A static analyzer that only looks for direct calls can miss the connection.

In Sentinel-IR 0.2.1, I focused on two situations where this can happen: "switch" fallthrough and "try/catch" control flow.

The update adds six regression tests. The goal is simple: detect the dangerous path when it is real, but avoid raising an alarm when the control flow makes that path impossible.

No magic. Just better reasoning about code.

Part 1: The 3-minute explanation for everyone

First, what does Sentinel-IR actually do?

Sentinel-IR is a small structural analysis layer for code.

Instead of sending an entire JavaScript or TypeScript source file to an AI model, it extracts structured facts using Tree-sitter.

Think of it as giving the AI a map instead of handing it an entire city.

The resulting information can include:

  • Imports and exports.
  • Routes and environment variables.
  • Filesystem, network and process operations.
  • Potentially dangerous code patterns.
  • Risk signals and their source locations.

This makes it easier for another system to reason about code without treating every line of source as equally important.

Project: "Sentinel-IR on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)

The problem: a function can have another name

Consider this:

const execute = eval;

execute("1 + 1");

A beginner might look for the word "eval" and assume the problem is easy.

But the function is being called through another variable.

That variable is an alias. The analyzer must understand what it refers to, not just what its name looks like.

And JavaScript has a few places where this gets complicated.

Problem one: switch fallthrough

Look at this example:

let execute = (value) => value;

switch (mode) {
case 0:
execute = eval;

case 1:
    execute("1 + 1");
    break;

}

Notice something?

There is no "break" after "case 0".

JavaScript continues into the next case. The alias assigned in the first case can therefore be used in the second one.

A simple analyzer may treat these cases as completely separate blocks and miss the connection.

Think of "break" as a stop sign. Without it, the baton keeps moving.

Problem two: try/catch

Another example:

let execute = (value) => value;

try {
execute = eval;
throw new Error("Something happened");
} catch (error) {
execute("1 + 1");
}

The alias is assigned before the exception.

When the exception moves execution into "catch", the analyzer needs to understand that the assignment can reach the code there.

But the opposite matters too.

An assignment that happens after an unconditional throw cannot influence the catch block. An assignment in a try block without a later explicit throw should not automatically make the catch block look dangerous either.

This is where false positives and false negatives start competing for attention.

What changed in 0.2.1?

The update improves those two control-flow situations.

It adds checks for:

  • Aliases carried through "switch" fallthrough.
  • "break" statements that stop that flow.
  • Later assignments that overwrite an alias.
  • Assignments before a throw that can reach "catch".
  • Throws occurring before an alias assignment.
  • Try blocks without a later explicit throw.

The result should be more accurate detection, not simply more things marked as dangerous.

Part 2: The developer section

What changed inside the AST analysis?

The important change is not a new search for the word "eval".

It is more accurate tracking of alias assignments and their visibility across control-flow paths.

The implementation contains dedicated helpers for:

  • Identifying equivalent AST nodes.
  • Tracking function and execution contexts.
  • Determining whether switch fallthrough is possible.
  • Checking whether a try-to-catch path is reachable.
  • Evaluating whether an alias assignment remains visible at a call site.

A parser detail worth mentioning

During the investigation, I encountered a subtle issue with Tree-sitter node wrappers.

Two JavaScript objects can represent the same logical AST node without being the same object reference.

Comparing them using:

nodeA === nodeB

is therefore not reliable for this kind of comparison.

The updated implementation compares the node type and source boundaries instead:

function evalAliasSameNode(a, b) {
return Boolean(
a &&
b &&
a.type === b.type &&
a.startIndex === b.startIndex &&
a.endIndex === b.endIndex
);
}

This gives the analysis a stable way to recognize the same logical node.

Source: "AST implementation in v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/src/ast-facts.js)

The six regression tests

The six new cases are documented in the release test suite.

Test scenario| Expected result
Alias passes through switch fallthrough| Critical
"break" blocks the alias flow| Low
Later case overwrites the alias| Low
Alias assigned before throw reaches catch| Critical
Throw happens before assignment| Low
No later explicit throw in try| Low

The tests verify more than a boolean detection result.

They also check that:

  • The source parses successfully.
  • "operations.dynamicEval" matches the expected result.
  • The risk classification is correct.
  • The "dynamic_code" risk signal agrees with the result.

Here is the core shape of the regression assertions:

const facts = AstFacts.extract(source);

assert.equal(facts.ast, true);

assert.equal(
Boolean(facts.operations.dynamicEval),
expected
);

assert.equal(
AstFacts.riskOf(facts),
expected ? "critical" : "low"
);

assert.equal(
facts.riskSignals.some(
signal => signal.signal === "dynamic_code"
),
expected
);

Full tests: "test/ast-facts.test.js, v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

Validation results

The release work was tested locally before tagging.

Validation| Result
Existing tests| 100 passed
New regression tests| 6 passed
Complete test suite| 106/106 passed
Packaged tarball smoke checks| 7/7 passed

The package was also installed into a clean consumer project for a separate smoke test.

That matters because a successful source test does not automatically prove that the packaged artifact works after installation.

What this does not mean

Sentinel-IR is not a complete JavaScript interpreter.

Its control-flow analysis is a conservative approximation, not a full simulation of every possible runtime path. It works with structural facts extracted from source code and has documented limitations.

It should be treated as an analysis component, not as a guarantee that dangerous code will always be detected.

That distinction matters, especially when an AI agent uses the output to make decisions.

Final thoughts

Version 0.2.1 is a focused release.

It does not introduce a new language or a completely new architecture. It improves one important part of the existing analyzer: understanding when an alias to dynamic code execution can actually reach a call site.

Sometimes progress in static analysis is not about detecting more patterns.

Sometimes it is about understanding why two pieces of code are connected, and when they are not.

And occasionally, the biggest bug is hiding behind a missing "break".

Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 is released.

Project links

  • "GitLab repository" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)
  • "Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 Release" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/releases/v0.2.1)
  • "Version 0.2.0 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.0)
  • "Version 0.2.1 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.1)
  • "New regression tests" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Built and tested as an independent project. Feedback, edge cases and reproducible examples are welcome.

title: How Routing Works in Next.js: Pages, Layouts and Links Explained
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

In Next.js, routing is based on your folder structure instead of a configuration file: every folder inside the app directory becomes part of the URL, a file called page.tsx inside that folder becomes the page visitors see, and a file called layout.tsx wraps pages with shared parts such as a header and footer. You do not install a router or register routes — you simply create folders and files, and Next.js turns them into web addresses.

Routing Without a Router Library

If you have used plain React, this feels pleasantly strange. In a React single-page app you normally install something like React Router and then write route definitions by hand: this path shows this component, that path shows that one. Forget a route, and your page exists but nobody can reach it — a little like building a room and forgetting the door.

Next.js took the opposite approach, called file-system routing. The framework watches your app folder and builds the route table for you. A folder named about containing a page.tsx file automatically becomes the address /about. The official Next.js documentation on layouts and pages calls a page "UI that is rendered on a specific route", and that is the whole mental model: files are routes.

Your First Routes: page.tsx

Here is a tiny site with three pages. Read the folder tree as a map of the website:

app/
  page.tsx          ->  /
  about/
    page.tsx        ->  /about
  blog/
    page.tsx        ->  /blog

Each page.tsx simply exports a React component:

export default function AboutPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>About us</h1>
      <p>We build friendly websites.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Notice what is missing: there is no route list anywhere. Add a folder, add a page file, and the URL exists. Delete the page file, and the URL politely becomes a 404. Beginners coming from other frameworks often waste an hour hunting for the routing file; in Next.js, the folder tree is the routing file. If the server/client split still feels fuzzy, our guide to Server Components vs Client Components in Next.js explains which of these files run where.

Layouts: The Frame Around Your Pages

Most pages on a site share furniture: a header, a navigation bar, a footer. Copying that furniture into every page works until the day you must change the menu in fourteen files. Next.js solves this with layout.tsx, a component that wraps the pages inside its folder:

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <header>My Site</header>
        {children}
        <footer>(c) 2026 My Site</footer>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

The magic word is children: that is where the actual page appears, framed by your header and footer. Layouts can also nest. A layout inside app/blog/ wraps only the blog pages, inside the root layout — frames within frames. Better still, when a visitor moves between two pages that share a layout, Next.js keeps the layout on screen and swaps only the page content, so your header does not flicker or lose its state on every click.

The official Next.js Docs — the sidebar shows the routing topics this article covers: Layouts and Pages, and Linking and Navigating.

Dynamic Routes: One File, Many Pages

A blog has hundreds of posts but only one post design. Next.js handles this with dynamic segments: wrap a folder name in square brackets, and it becomes a placeholder that matches any value.

app/
  blog/
    [slug]/
      page.tsx      ->  /blog/my-first-post
                        /blog/hello-world
                        /blog/any-slug-at-all

export default async function BlogPost({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <h1>Post: {slug}</h1>;
}

Your component receives the matched value as params.slug and can load the right article from a database or files. One page file now powers every post on the blog — the same trick behind product pages on shops, profiles on social sites, and documentation pages like the ones you are reading about.

Linking Between Pages with next/link

To move between routes, use the Link component from next/link instead of a plain <a> tag:

import Link from "next/link";

export default function Nav() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <Link href="/">Home</Link>
      <Link href="/about">About</Link>
      <Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>
    </nav>
  );
}

It looks like ordinary HTML, but under the surface Next.js preloads the linked pages when they appear on screen, so clicks feel instant instead of triggering a full page reload. The React documentation's Learn React guide is a good companion here, because every page and layout is still just a React component with the same rules you already know. And if you are still deciding what to learn first, our comparison of React vs Next.js lays out the honest learning order.

Special Files: Loading, Error and Not Found

The App Router has a few more reserved filenames worth knowing, because they handle the moments beginners usually dread. Add a loading.tsx file to a folder and Next.js shows it automatically while that page's data is loading — no manual spinner logic — swapping in the real page the moment it is ready. Add an error.tsx file and it becomes a friendly safety net: if the page throws an error, visitors see your message and a retry option instead of a broken screen. And a not-found.tsx file lets you design your own 404 page in the same style as the rest of the site. Each of these is optional, each lives beside the page it serves, and each follows the same rule as everything else in this article: the filename is the feature.

Route Groups and Private Folders: Organising Without Changing URLs

As a site grows, the app folder can become crowded, and Next.js offers two naming tricks to tidy it. A folder wrapped in parentheses, such as (marketing), is a route group: it organises files and can even carry its own layout, but its name never appears in the URL — so app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx is still simply /about. A folder starting with an underscore, such as _components, is the opposite: it is private, completely opted out of routing, which makes it a safe home for shared components and helpers that should never become pages. Together, these two conventions let a large project stay organised without breaking a single address.

The App Router File Conventions in One Table

File or folder What it creates
page.tsx The visible page for that folder's URL
layout.tsx Shared wrapping UI for that folder and everything inside it
loading.tsx Loading UI shown while the page prepares
error.tsx Friendly error UI for that segment
not-found.tsx Your custom 404 page
[slug] folder A dynamic route matching any value in that segment
(group) folder Organisation only — invisible in the URL
_private folder Never routed — a safe place for shared code

Keep this table nearby for your first project. After a week of building, you will stop consulting it, because the conventions start to feel less like rules to memorise and more like common sense: of course the page file is the page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need React Router in Next.js?

No. Routing is built into Next.js through the file system. Installing React Router as well would duplicate the job and confuse both tools, so let the folders do the work.

What is the difference between page.tsx and layout.tsx?

A page is the unique content for one route. A layout is shared wrapping UI — headers, footers, sidebars — that surrounds pages and stays in place while you navigate between them.

What does [slug] mean in a folder name?

Square brackets mark a dynamic segment. The folder matches any value in that part of the URL, and your page receives the value as a parameter, so one file can serve many addresses.

Why is my new page showing a 404?

Almost always, the folder is in the wrong place or the file is not named exactly page.tsx (or page.jsx). Check that the folder sits inside app and that the file exports a default component.

Conclusion

Next.js routing rewards you for tidy folders: folders become URLs, page.tsx becomes the screen, layout.tsx becomes the frame, brackets become placeholders, and Link makes moving around feel instant. Learn those five ideas and you can build the skeleton of almost any website — no routing configuration required.

title: Timestamp attributes are now supported in Vercel Flags
description:
Vercel Flags now supports timestamp attributes, so you can target entities by date and time.

Use timestamp attributes to show a campaign page only between two dates, run a Black Friday promotion, or target users who registered before a cutoff.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

Learn how to provide entities in code and release a flag at a specific time, or read the Flags documentation.

Short answer: The factors that increase LLM API spend beyond token cost are high-tier model selection, unnecessary feature usage, redundant calls, and retries that repeat accepted work; control them with token budgets, quality gates, and bounded backoff.

A gaming team answering questions from a private knowledge base should control spend at the request boundary: choose the smallest model that meets the quality target, count tokens before expensive work, and make retries deliberate. The bill grows when a high-tier model is selected unnecessarily, a failed request is retried too aggressively, or one question causes redundant calls.

This is a runbook for putting those checks around a Go service. Keep retrieval and answer generation separate, measure the input before model selection, and make every retry visible in the request budget. If a basic endpoint answers the question with acceptable quality, an advanced feature is operational waste.

For this workflow, Infrai is a concrete fit when integration friction is the cost to remove: one key and one bill cover backend services, while public discovery and consistent per-call metadata help compare model choices. It still needs the same quality evaluation and retry budget as any other API.

What factors increase LLM API spend beyond token cost?

Start with a request ledger, not a vendor price table. For each player or support question, record the original question, retrieved context size, selected model tier, number of attempts, and output length. Four cost multipliers show up repeatedly:

  • A larger-context, higher-tier model costs more per token.
  • Redundant calls multiply both input and output tokens.
  • Retries after transient failures still cost money when the upstream accepted the request before the client saw the response.
  • A broad model can consume more context or produce a longer answer than a scoped-purpose model.

The last point is easy to miss in a private knowledge base. A question about a game item does not automatically need the broadest model available. Quality is the decision axis, though. A short answer that omits a safety-critical gameplay rule is a failed result, so cost controls need a quality gate rather than a blind downgrade.

That distinction matters.

I would begin with three budgets: a token budget per request, an attempt budget, and a maximum context size. The numbers belong to the workload, not to this article. Set them from observed answer quality and review them after a representative sample.

How do model choice and redundant calls interact?

Model selection and retry policy are coupled. A high-tier model increases the cost of every attempt; a loose retry policy increases how many attempts happen. Optimizing only one leaves the other multiplier intact.

For a gaming knowledge base, classify questions before answering them: factual lookup, multi-document synthesis, and ambiguous or high-risk explanation. Use the basic endpoint for the first class when its evaluation passes. Reserve advanced capabilities for the latter two. Do not route every question to the broadest model because a few difficult questions need it.

The same discipline applies to features. If a request does not need a longer context, tool use, or a richer output shape, do not turn that feature on by default. Broader behavior often means more tokens or longer responses. The request should pay for the capability it actually uses.

Three common alternatives make different trade-offs:

Option Integration shape Useful boundary Cost-control concern
OpenAI API Direct model API and an established client ecosystem Teams already standardized on OpenAI request patterns A broad default model can make every request expensive; model selection remains your responsibility
AWS Bedrock Model access through an AWS service boundary Organizations that need Bedrock inside existing AWS governance Access configuration and provider choice add setup decisions before the first useful answer
Anthropic API Direct access to Anthropic models Workloads tuned and evaluated specifically for Claude behavior A direct vendor path does not remove the need to budget retries, context, and output
Infrai One REST API, one key, and one bill across backend capabilities, with an OpenAI-compatible surface Teams trying to reduce integration friction while keeping model routing and per-call metadata in one place It is still necessary to choose the model and validate quality; unavailable or pending capabilities must stay out of the route

This is not a claim that one surface wins every workload. OpenAI or Anthropic can be the better choice when a team already has a deeply tested provider-specific integration. Bedrock is a sensible boundary when AWS governance is the primary constraint. Infrai is the option I would try for the model-access part of this workflow when one credential and one billing surface remove real operational work, especially if the team also needs consistent discovery and call metadata across backend services.

The important limitation is capability readiness. ASR is listed but currently unavailable; real-time voice session status is pending and limited to the western region; there is no dedicated moderation endpoint; and upscale is limited to Lanc. Those boundaries matter even in a cost article. A private text knowledge-base workflow should not silently depend on one of those capabilities.

A small Go guardrail before the request

The first useful control is token counting before model selection. The verified route is POST /v1/ai/tokens/count. The example keeps the request small, reads the key from the environment, checks status codes, and backs off on HTTP 429. It does not send the platform authorization header anywhere else.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
const tokenCountURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count"

func countTokens(text string) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"text": text})
    if err != nil { return nil, err }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, tokenCountURL, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("token count failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody)
        }
        return responseBody, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("token count remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    result, err := countTokens("Where can a player find the frost key?")
    if err != nil { fmt.Println(err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The response should become an input to policy, not a number displayed and ignored. If the count is below the basic model budget, route to the basic endpoint. If the question plus retrieved context exceeds that budget, trim or summarize retrieval before choosing a higher tier. If summarization itself costs a call, include it in the ledger; otherwise the supposed optimization can cost more than the original answer.

Count first.

This route is also a good place to set a request correlation ID in your own service logs. Keep the token result, selected tier, attempt count, final status, and answer-quality outcome together. That gives an operator a usable explanation when spend rises.

What retry policy is safe?

Retry only failures that are plausibly transient, and cap the attempts. Exponential backoff with Retry-After handling prevents a rate limit from becoming a tight loop, as the example does. A retry is not free just because the first client attempt returned an error.

For answer generation, the safest application behavior is to classify the operation as read-only and make the output replaceable. If the upstream request may have been accepted, do not launch a second expensive request merely because the network response was lost. Use a request ID in the application ledger, reconcile the result when the provider surface supports it, and present a controlled failure when reconciliation is not possible. The point is to avoid turning an uncertain network event into two paid generations.

At the service boundary, keep a hard maximum such as four attempts in the retry loop, then return an error with the original request ID. The exact count needs workload testing. What should not be open-ended is the retry budget.

Four attempts is a ceiling, not a target.

The same rule applies to batch or asynchronous work: standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer needs an idempotency record keyed by the source job ID. A duplicate delivery must not create a second answer, a second embedding pass, or a second downstream write.

Verify the change, then roll it back

Verification should use a fixed evaluation set of private knowledge-base questions, not just a dashboard total. Compare answer correctness, context coverage, token count, selected model, attempts, and latency for the old and new policy. Keep the set stable while changing one control at a time: first model routing, then context limits, then retry behavior.

A useful stop condition is explicit: if the cheaper route misses a required fact, restore the previous model for that question class. If retries rise after a timeout change, revert the timeout or retry policy before investigating spend. A rollback flag in configuration is enough; it should select the previous model map and retry ceiling without requiring a code redeploy.

Infrai fits this runbook when its discovery and consistent metadata reduce the work of comparing capabilities, while one key and one bill remove credential and reconciliation overhead across backend services. Its public discovery surface exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, and its OpenAI-compatible surface can preserve existing client conventions. I would recommend trying it for the model-access layer of a gaming knowledge-base service when that integration friction is the problem to solve, not as a substitute for evaluating answer quality.

The specialist wins when provider-specific behavior is already the product requirement, or when the requested capability is outside the current readiness boundary. Keep that decision visible in the runbook. If this boundary fits your system, start with the AI cost-control guide.

References

  • Infrai AI-readable capability manifest
  • AWS Bedrock
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
