title: How to Export Google Ads Transparency Center Data (with Ad Copy) in Python
description:
I wanted something simple: every Google search ad a competitor is running, how long each one has been running, and the actual ad copy — in a spreadsheet.

Google already publishes all of this in the Ads Transparency Center (Google's answer to Meta's Ad Library). It just has no export button and no API. So I scraped it, and ran into something I didn't expect: for most big advertisers, the ad copy isn't there as text at all.

The surprise: most text ads are stored as images

When you open a text ad in the Transparency Center, Google renders it in one of two ways:

  1. A text preview — the headline and description exist as text (in a small JS preview), easy to parse.
  2. A screenshot — a PNG of the ad, nothing else. The words only exist as pixels.

I pulled the first 30 text ads of five large advertisers on Nov 1, 2026 and counted how many had a text version:

Advertiser Text ads checked With a text version
booking.com 30 0
expedia.com 30 0
hubspot.com 30 1
samsung.com 30 7
nike.com 30 21
Total 150 29 (19%)

So if a tool only reads the text preview, the best it can do here is copy for about 1 ad in 5 — and for booking.com and expedia.com, nothing. That's a big hole if "what are my competitors saying?" is the whole point.

Reading the screenshots (the DIY version)

The fix is OCR. Each ad record links to its snapshot image (tpc.googlesyndication.com/archive/simgad/...), and a basic version with Tesseract is a few lines:

import io, requests, pytesseract
from PIL import Image

def read_ad(image_url):
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(requests.get(image_url, timeout=20).content)).convert("L")
    img = img.resize((img.width * 2, img.height * 2))          # small text OCRs better when upscaled
    data = pytesseract.image_to_data(img, config="--psm 6", output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
    words = [(w, float(c)) for w, c in zip(data["text"], data["conf"]) if w.strip() and float(c) >= 0]
    text = " ".join(w for w, _ in words)
    confidence = sum(c for _, c in words) / max(len(words), 1)
    return text, confidence

That gets you a blob of text. Turning it into headline / description / display URL reliably took most of the work. The traps I hit:

  1. Not everything in the image is the ad. Many snapshots include a product thumbnail or sitelink buttons on the right. OCR happily reads those and mixes them into the description. Detect and crop them first.
  2. Headline vs. description. Google draws the headline in blue and the description in dark grey, so splitting by color before OCR works far better than guessing from line positions afterwards.
  3. Language. The same advertiser runs ads in dozens of languages. Picking the Tesseract model from the countries the ad ran in (Korean, Japanese, Thai, Arabic, Cyrillic…) fixes most of the garbage.
  4. Trust the confidence score — strictly. My first threshold was 70. At 77, one booking.com description came out as "Book a Hotel near Universal Studios. HEHHE HAHA Quick, Easy Booking." Above 90 the text was mostly clean, apart from cut-off words. Anything lower should be flagged, not trusted.
  5. Some words are simply cut off. The screenshot crops long headlines, so you'll get "Hotels in Downtown Chica…". Nothing to fix there — just know it.
  6. Be gentle with Google. The listing endpoints rate-limit quickly (429s and CAPTCHA pages). Retry a couple of times, then stop — don't hammer.

The no-maintenance version

I packaged all of this as an Apify Actor (Google Ads Transparency & Ad Library Scraper), so I don't have to babysit OCR models or rate limits. Here's how I find a competitor's long-running search ads — the ones they keep paying for:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("datalume/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["nike.com"],
    "region": "US",
    "platform": "search",
    "format": "text",
    "minDaysRunning": 30,          # skip short tests
    "sortBy": "longestRunning",
    "maxAdsPerTarget": 50,
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
good = df[df["copyStatus"] == "ok"]   # high-confidence copy only
good[["daysShown", "firstShown", "headline", "regionCount"]].head(10)

Here's what came back for nike.com (US, search, text ads, run on Nov 1, 2026) — 50 ads, copy for all 50 (38 from the text preview, 12 by OCR, all above 90 confidence). A slice of the longest-running ones:

Days shown First shown Advertiser Headline Countries
1,833 2021-10-25 WPP Media (agency) Zapatillas Air Max 90. Nike MX 8
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike - Onlineshop Deutschland 46
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike: zapatillas, ropa y más 51
1,793 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike UK - Online Store 44
1,792 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV The Official Nike Site - Nike: Shop The Collection (OCR) 39
1,735 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV NIKE — onlinebutik - Officiella Nike-webbplatsen (OCR) 29
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. Training & Gym Equipment. Nike.com (OCR) 1
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. (dynamic — Google writes it) 1

A few things jump out in under a minute:

  1. The longest-running ads weren't placed by Nike's own account but by an agency account (WPP Media). A domain search returns every advertiser whose ads point at the domain — useful, but filter by advertiser if you only want the brand itself.
  2. Nike's European "brand" ads have been running since at least October 2021, in roughly 30–50 countries each, with the same handful of lines ("The Official Website. Home Of Everything Nike. Shop The Latest Releases."). That's what a proven, evergreen brand ad looks like.
  3. In the US, 28 of the 31 ads from the Nike, Inc. account have no fixed headline — they're Dynamic Search Ads, where Google writes the headline from the landing page. Nike US leans on DSA and only controls the description. You'd never see that pattern by clicking through ads one at a time.

Also note daysShown is the number of days the ad actually ran, not just last-minus-first: three ads that all "started" on 2021-10-25 show 1,833, 1,794 and 1,688 days.

What else is in each row

  • firstShown, lastShown, daysShown, isActive — how long the ad has been running and whether it's live
  • regions — every country the ad ran in, with the last date shown there
  • headline, description, displayUrl, plus copySource (text or ocr) and copyConfidence
  • transparencyUrl — a link back to the ad on Google's site, so you can check anything by eye

You can also pass advertiser names or IDs instead of domains, filter by country / platform / date, and set onlyNewAds on a daily schedule to get just the new creatives.

Caveats (read these before you trust the numbers)

  • firstShown has a floor. The oldest ads I've seen all show 2021-10-25, which looks like where the Transparency Center's history begins. Read it as "running since at least then", not as the real start date.
  • OCR isn't perfect. Even high-confidence rows can contain a wrong letter ("Al" for "AI") or a cut-off word. Low-confidence rows are kept but marked lowConfidence.
  • Domain searches include other advertisers — agencies, resellers, or anyone whose ads link to that domain or its subdomains (like the WPP Media rows above). Use an advertiser ID if you need exactly one advertiser.

Cost

The Actor charges per ad: $2.00 per 1,000 ads, or $3.50 per 1,000 for text ads where high-confidence copy was extracted (instead of, not on top of, the $2). Countries are included, and rows Google fails to load are free. The 50-ad run above cost $0.18 (50 ads with copy × $0.0035) and took about a minute; with onlyNewAds on a schedule, you only pay for ads you haven't seen before.

Disclosure: I run datalume, the publisher of the Actor used here. Both the Actor and this article were built with AI assistance; every number above comes from real runs on Nov 1, 2026 and was checked against the raw data. Questions welcome in the comments.

title: Exploring tenant isolation with Spring Boot, OIDC, and PostgreSQL RLS
description:
A multi-tenant API needs to answer two separate questions: who is making the request, and what may that identity do inside the selected tenant?

Spring Boot SaaS Starter is an open-source backend MVP I maintain to make those boundaries easier to inspect. It provides a Projects API with tenant membership, role checks, optimistic concurrency, and audit records.

The current stack uses Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1.2, PostgreSQL, JDBC, and Flyway. Docker Compose includes Keycloak for local development.

Authentication establishes identity

The API accepts bearer tokens through Spring Security’s JWT resource server support. Its configuration validates the signature and issuer, requires an audience match, and checks for a nonblank subject and an expiration claim.

The subject identifies the caller. Memberships associate that subject with a tenant and a role in the application database.

This distinction matters: a valid token alone does not establish membership in a particular tenant. The tenant UUID in a request selects the tenant to access; authorization still happens in the service layer.

See the implementation in SecurityConfig.java.

Follow the tenant boundary into the database

The starter uses a shared schema with complementary application and database checks:

  1. A transactional service checks and locks the caller’s membership row.
  2. It verifies the role required for the operation.
  3. It sets transaction-local database context for the tenant.
  4. Queries include explicit tenant predicates.
  5. PostgreSQL enforces row-level security on projects and audit events.

TenantAccess.java activates the context using a parameterized query:

SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', ?, true)

The final argument makes the setting local to the transaction. The design therefore avoids leaving tenant state attached to a pooled connection after the transaction finishes.

The database migration enables and forces row-level security on both protected tables. Policies compare each row’s tenant_id with the current transaction’s tenant setting, including checks on writes.

Tenant and membership tables have a different role: they support onboarding and membership discovery across tenants. Their authorization boundary is enforced in services.

The application also uses restricted runtime database credentials, separate from schema migration credentials. Startup checks reject unsafe database privileges or missing RLS enforcement.

These layers help defend against accidentally omitted tenant predicates. They do not make a compromised application or arbitrary SQL execution harmless. The architecture guide explains that boundary explicitly.

Keep permissions specific to each tenant

The role model is deliberately small:

Capability OWNER ADMIN MEMBER
Read projects and list members Yes Yes Yes
Create, update, or delete projects Yes Yes No
Read audit events Yes Yes No
Manage non-owner memberships Yes No No

An authenticated identity can create a tenant and becomes its owner. Ownership transfer and owner removal are outside this MVP.

A caller who is not a tenant member receives 404 for tenant resources. A member who lacks the required role receives 403.

Make conflicting writes explicit

Projects carry a version number. Updates match the tenant, project ID, and expected version, then increment the version. Deletions also require the expected version.

For example, after updating version 0 successfully, a deletion that still supplies version 0 receives 409 Conflict.

The client should reload the project and reconcile changes before retrying. Automatically substituting the latest version would defeat the purpose of detecting a stale write.

Project mutations and their audit records occur within the same transaction. See ProjectService.java and the API walkthrough.

Run the local example

The README’s container-based path requires Git, a POSIX shell, Docker Engine with Compose v2, OpenSSL, and Python 3.9+. On Windows, use WSL with Docker access. Ports 8080, 8081, and 5432 must be available.

A host JDK is unnecessary for this path:

git clone https://github.com/chafian/spring-boot-saas-starter.git
cd spring-boot-saas-starter
./scripts/init-env.sh
docker compose up --build -d
python3 scripts/smoke.py

The setup script generates local credentials. The smoke script waits for readiness, signs in as the demo identities, and exercises the API.

It checks that an outsider cannot access the tenant’s projects, that adding the identity as a MEMBER enables reading, and that the same member still cannot create projects. It also exercises updates, stale-write rejection, deletion, audit events, and requests without authentication.

Successful completion produces:

PASS: real OIDC login, tenant isolation, membership, RBAC, CRUD, conflicts, and audit

Windows/WSL troubleshooting: On my machine, Docker could not bind host port 5432. I changed the PostgreSQL port mapping in compose.yml from 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 to 127.0.0.1:5433:5432, then reran docker compose up -d. The application’s internal database connection remained unchanged, and the smoke test passed.

Each run creates a fictional tenant and retains its audit history. Use docker compose down to stop the services while preserving the database volume.

Keycloak runs in development mode and is ephemeral. Follow the README’s reset guidance if it is recreated, because identity subjects may change.

Test and extend the example

For development, install JDK 25 and unzip, keep Docker running, and use:

./mvnw verify
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'

The documented Java verification path uses a real PostgreSQL Testcontainer. CI is configured to run verification and the Compose smoke example.

To add another tenant-owned resource, follow the extension guide and preserve the membership, transaction, tenant-context, and database-policy boundaries.

The current scope excludes billing, a frontend, email invitations, tenant deletion, and ownership transfer. Production deployment also requires environment-specific work such as TLS, production identity configuration, tenant-creation quotas or rate limits, backups, monitoring, and secret management. The local Keycloak setup is a development convenience.

If you work with Java SaaS backends, I’d welcome feedback on the isolation model and the setup experience.

Explore the repository and try the example

title: Implementing SMS OTP-Based 2FA in Node.js with API Integration Explained for Support Queues
description:
Short answer: to implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js with an API integration, keep the OTP template and verification policy in the authentication service, then let an SMS provider own delivery. For a fintech contact form, Infrai fits when SMS OTP, resend, and other backend capabilities should sit behind one REST API and one key. Pick Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when a verification specialist and its managed workflow matter more. Pick Amazon SNS when low-level delivery control is worth owning OTP generation, storage, expiry, abuse controls, and queue routing.

The boundary matters. The form service knows why a customer is signing in and which support queue should receive the request. The messaging service knows how to send a code. Mix those jobs and a small login flow becomes hard to audit.

Option Who owns the policy? Best fit Cost of the boundary
Infrai SMS OTP Your service stores and validates the challenge; the provider supplies send and resend One REST surface across backend capabilities Your app still owns limits, anti-fraud, expiry, and routing
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow A verification specialist is the priority A separate integration for the rest of the backend
Vonage Verify Managed verification workflow Teams already using Vonage Provider-specific workflow and integration
Amazon SNS Your app owns OTP logic; SNS delivers SMS AWS-centered systems wanting primitives More security state and retry code in your app

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for SMS dispatch and resend when the same service needs several backend capabilities and one HTTP contract removes integration glue. Keep the contact-form template, queue decision, and acceptance audit record in your own service.

Why does template ownership matter in an OTP flow?

A contact form is not an authentication vendor's data model. It has a customer, account, reason for contact, destination queue, and fraud signal. The OTP is one gate. It is not the workflow.

I would store a pending challenge with a server-generated identifier, timestamp, purpose, normalized phone number, and queue candidate. Store the code only in the form your security design permits; a hash is the safer default for comparison. Set an explicit validity window. Mark the record consumed after success. A second successful use should fail.

Keep the SMS body as a versioned template owned by your application or by the verification specialist you deliberately chose. That gives reviewers one place to inspect wording. It also keeps queue names, internal ticket references, and form payloads out of a message whose only job is to prove possession of a phone.

The production flow is straightforward:

  1. The contact service validates the form and selects a candidate queue.
  2. The authentication service creates a challenge and asks the SMS provider to send it.
  3. The provider returns a send result; delivery status is checked separately where needed.
  4. The authentication service validates the submitted code inside its time window.
  5. Only then does the contact service create or release the support ticket.

There is a real limitation: the relevant namespaces do not provide webhook event pushes; events are pull-based. Delivery status is not an authorization signal. The code check should depend on challenge state and user input, not an assumed instant callback.

How should I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js with an API?

Twilio Verify is the clearest specialist alternative when verification itself is the product requirement. Its managed workflow can reduce policy code. The tradeoff is architectural: the support queue and the rest of the backend remain separate integrations.

Vonage Verify is another specialist path. It makes sense for a team already standardized on Vonage or one that wants verification-specific operations. It is less compelling when the team mainly needs general SMS and already has a platform boundary to maintain.

Amazon SNS sits lower in the stack. That is useful if AWS controls, IAM, and delivery primitives are the priority. It is also the work: your Node.js service must implement challenge generation, hashing, expiry, resend limits, and fraud decisions.

Infrai occupies a different boundary. Its useful angle is breadth behind a simple surface: production modules share one REST API and one key, while the public discovery service describes capabilities and their schemas. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. Adding a backend capability can mean one more contract instead of another SDK, credential, and error vocabulary.

That does not make it universal. The platform has no hosted email OTP fallback, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geography and country-based circuit breaking remain application responsibilities. If those constraints dominate, a specialist or direct regional provider is the better choice.

What does the smallest Node.js handoff look like?

Keep the provider call narrow. Do not send queue metadata to the SMS API. Store the challenge in your database and use the returned identifier for resend. The route names below are the two SMS OTP operations in scope; confirm the live request schema before shipping.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type OtpResponse = { id: string };

async function requestOtp(phoneNumber: string): Promise<OtpResponse> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/sms/otp`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ phone_number: phoneNumber }),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const seconds = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(1, seconds) * 1000));
    return requestOtp(phoneNumber);
  }
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`OTP request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return (await response.json()) as OtpResponse;
}

async function resendOtp(id: string): Promise<OtpResponse> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/sms/resend/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`OTP resend failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return (await response.json()) as OtpResponse;
}

The retry branch needs a production cap and bounded exponential backoff. Honor Retry-After; do not let a network timeout or a 429 create an unbounded stream of messages. Use an idempotency key where the route contract supports one. After the first response, write the challenge timestamp and provider identifier with the login attempt. On submission, reject expired or consumed records and count failed attempts. Resend needs its own rate limit.

This is where the two-call shape can mislead a hurried implementation. A successful send call proves that the provider accepted a request; it does not prove that the customer received a message, that the challenge is still fresh, or that the contact belongs in the selected queue. Those are separate state transitions, and the database should show them separately.

When should the runner-up win?

Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when managed verification is the requirement and the team does not want to maintain delivery policy. Confirm regional coverage, sender rules, template review, and operational access before committing.

Choose Amazon SNS when AWS locality and low-level delivery outweigh extra application code. That design is valid, but the application boundary is larger.

Choose the broader REST platform when the strongest constraint is integration surface: SMS OTP now, then other backend capabilities under one contract and discovery model. For this form, the fit is the handoff around SMS, not ownership of the customer workflow.

That is the whole decision.

Build geographic allowlists, per-number and per-IP limits, velocity checks, and fraud review in the application layer. An SMS API can send a code; it cannot decide whether a burst is a customer or an attacker.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP and resend guide.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon SNS documentation
  • NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
  • RFC 7489: DMARC

title: Per-customer rate limits and 429s in Express and FastAPI
description:
Most rate limiting tutorials limit by IP address. That's the right tool for a login form, and the wrong one for an API that customers pay for. A customer's traffic can come from fifty servers behind fifty addresses, or from one office NAT shared with someone else's script. What you want to cap is the customer: "Acme gets 5 requests per second, however many keys or machines they use."

This post builds that in Express and in FastAPI with nothing but the framework, then covers the 429 response and the parts that tend to go wrong: ordering, retries and running more than one process.

A token bucket per customer

A token bucket is two numbers per customer: how many tokens are in the bucket, and when you last looked. The bucket holds at most capacity tokens and refills at refillPerSecond. Each request takes one token; an empty bucket means 429. A customer who's been quiet can send a burst of capacity requests, then continues at the refill rate.

You don't need a timer. Refill lazily when a request arrives:

// rate-limit.js
// One token bucket per customer. Refilled lazily when a request arrives, so no timers.
export function tokenBucket({ capacity, refillPerSecond, now = () => performance.now() / 1000 }) {
  const buckets = new Map(); // customerId -> { tokens, updatedAt }

  return function take(customerId) {
    const time = now();
    const bucket = buckets.get(customerId) ?? { tokens: capacity, updatedAt: time };
    bucket.tokens = Math.min(capacity, bucket.tokens + (time - bucket.updatedAt) * refillPerSecond);
    bucket.updatedAt = time;
    buckets.set(customerId, bucket);

    if (bucket.tokens < 1) {
      // Round up: a client that retries a moment too early just gets another 429
      return { allowed: false, retryAfter: Math.ceil((1 - bucket.tokens) / refillPerSecond) };
    }
    bucket.tokens -= 1;
    return { allowed: true, remaining: Math.floor(bucket.tokens) };
  };
}

Two details matter here. The clock is performance.now(), which is monotonic, so an NTP adjustment can't refill or drain every bucket at once. And retryAfter is rounded up, because telling a client to come back in 0 seconds produces a retry that fails again.

Express: authenticate first, then limit 

// app.js
import express from "express";
import { tokenBucket } from "./rate-limit.js";

// Stand-in for your key table. Acme has two keys but one bucket.
const KEYS = new Map([
  ["key_acme_1", "acme"],
  ["key_acme_2", "acme"],
  ["key_globex", "globex"],
]);
const CAPACITY = 5;
const take = tokenBucket({ capacity: CAPACITY, refillPerSecond: 1 });

function authenticate(req, res, next) {
  const key = req.get("authorization")?.replace(/^Bearer\s+/i, "");
  const customerId = key && KEYS.get(key);
  if (!customerId) return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid_api_key" });
  req.customerId = customerId;
  next();
}

function rateLimit(req, res, next) {
  const result = take(req.customerId);
  res.set("RateLimit-Policy", `"default";q=${CAPACITY};w=${CAPACITY}`);
  if (result.allowed) return next();

  res.set("Retry-After", String(result.retryAfter));
  res.set("RateLimit", `"default";r=0;t=${result.retryAfter}`);
  res.status(429).json({ error: "rate_limited", retry_after: result.retryAfter });
}

const app = express();
app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.send("ok")); // before the limiter: never limited
app.use("/v1", authenticate, rateLimit);
app.get("/v1/things", (req, res) => res.json({ customer: req.customerId }));

app.listen(3000);

Send six requests in a row, alternating Acme's two keys, and the sixth gets:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
RateLimit-Policy: "default";q=5;w=5
Retry-After: 1
RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=1

{"error":"rate_limited","retry_after":1}

Globex is unaffected, because it has its own bucket.

The order of authenticate and rateLimit is the whole point. Authentication runs first for two reasons:

  • The bucket key has to be the customer, not the API key string. Key it on the key and a customer with five keys gets five times the limit. You only know the customer after authentication.
  • Unknown keys should never reach the limiter. If they did, anyone could fill your Map with junk keys. Junk keys get a 401 instead. (If you're worried about key guessing, add a per-IP limit on failed authentications at the edge.)

Also note that Express middleware only applies to routes registered after it. /health above is open on purpose; a router mounted in some earlier file would be open by accident.

FastAPI: dependencies, and why they should be async

In FastAPI the natural place for this is a dependency chain: one dependency resolves the customer, the next one spends a token.

# main.py
import math
import time

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException

# Stand-in for your key table. Acme has two keys but one bucket.
KEYS = {"key_acme_1": "acme", "key_acme_2": "acme", "key_globex": "globex"}
CAPACITY = 5
REFILL_PER_SECOND = 1.0
buckets: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] = {}  # customer_id -> (tokens, updated_at)


def take(customer_id: str) -> tuple[bool, int]:
    now = time.monotonic()
    tokens, updated_at = buckets.get(customer_id, (CAPACITY, now))
    tokens = min(CAPACITY, tokens + (now - updated_at) * REFILL_PER_SECOND)
    if tokens < 1:
        buckets[customer_id] = (tokens, now)
        return False, math.ceil((1 - tokens) / REFILL_PER_SECOND)
    buckets[customer_id] = (tokens - 1, now)
    return True, 0


async def current_customer(authorization: str = Header(default="")) -> str:
    scheme, _, key = authorization.partition(" ")
    customer_id = KEYS.get(key) if scheme.lower() == "bearer" else None
    if customer_id is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, detail="invalid_api_key")
    return customer_id


# async def on purpose: a plain def dependency runs in a thread pool,
# and two threads could both spend the last token.
async def rate_limited(customer_id: str = Depends(current_customer)) -> str:
    allowed, retry_after = take(customer_id)
    if not allowed:
        raise HTTPException(
            429,
            detail="rate_limited",
            headers={
                "Retry-After": str(retry_after),
                "RateLimit-Policy": f'"default";q={CAPACITY};w={math.ceil(CAPACITY / REFILL_PER_SECOND)}',
                "RateLimit": f'"default";r=0;t={retry_after}',
            },
        )
    return customer_id


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/v1/things")
async def things(customer_id: str = Depends(rate_limited)):
    return {"customer": customer_id}

Run it with uvicorn main:app and the sixth quick request gets a 429 with the same three headers, and a body of {"detail":"rate_limited"}. FastAPI wraps HTTPException details in detail; add an exception handler if you want the same body shape as the Express version.

Two FastAPI-specific notes:

  • async def is doing real work here. FastAPI runs plain def dependencies in a thread pool. The read-modify-write in take() isn't atomic, so two threads can read the same bucket and both spend its last token. An async def dependency runs on the event loop, and take() has no await in it, so nothing else can run in the middle. If you need a sync dependency, put a threading.Lock around the bucket update.
  • A dependency can't limit what it doesn't run on. Routes that don't declare Depends(rate_limited) aren't limited. If you'd rather cover everything under a prefix, put the dependency on the APIRouter (APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(rate_limited)])). If you move the check into a middleware instead, remember that middlewares run before dependencies, so the customer has to be resolved in a middleware too.

What the 429 should carry

  • Retry-After in seconds. It tells the client how many seconds to wait before retrying. Seconds don't depend on the client's clock being right, which an HTTP date does.
  • RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit. These come from an IETF draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers). q is the bucket size and w its window in seconds; r is what's left and t is when to try again. It's still a draft and the field names have changed over the revisions, so treat them as a bonus and Retry-After as the one clients should rely on.
  • A machine-readable error code in the body, so clients can tell a rate limit apart from other 429s.

That last point matters more than it looks. If your plans have monthly quotas, "you've used this month's allowance" is often also a 429, and its Retry-After can be days away. A client that sleeps on every Retry-After will park a job for a week; one that ignores it and retries with backoff will keep hammering an answer that won't change. A reasonable client rule:

const wait = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
if (wait > 60) throw new Error(`Not retrying: ${body.error}, retry after ${wait}s`);
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, wait * 1000));

Put the same rule in your API docs, and give the two cases different error codes so people can tell them apart in their logs.

More than one process

Everything above lives in one process's memory. Put four instances behind a load balancer and a customer whose requests spread evenly gets about four times the limit. You have three choices:

  1. Accept it. A per-process cap can be enough to curb runaway scripts, as long as you can live with a customer reaching 4× the configured limit. It won't enforce a per-customer limit you've promised in a contract.
  2. Divide the limit by the number of instances, rounded up and never below 1. That keeps the total close to what you set without any shared state, but you need a reliable instance count, and a client whose keep-alive connection pins it to one instance gets only that instance's share.
  3. Use a shared store such as Redis, with the bucket update in a Lua script so it's atomic. That's exact, at the cost of a network round trip per request and a decision about what happens when Redis is down.

Decide which one you're doing before autoscaling decides for you.

Test it with a fake clock

tokenBucket() takes now as a parameter so tests don't have to sleep. Pass a function that returns a number you control, then check the edges: exactly capacity requests pass, the next one fails with retryAfter: 1, half a token isn't enough, and a long pause refills the bucket to capacity and no further.

I work on UsageRail, which does the per-customer part of this as middleware for Express (and FastAPI, Hono, Fastify, Django and Next.js), with the limits set per plan in a dashboard instead of in code: https://usagerail.com/docs/express

title: Shelf-Life Is Versioned Config, Expiry Is a Derived Field: Modelling Shelf-Life Studies, Lot Expiry and FEFO in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most food ERPs, an expiry date is a column on a lot. Someone types it at packing, or the system adds a fixed number of days to the production date, and that's the end of it. But the number of days is not a constant. It is the output of a shelf-life study, it is only valid for a particular recipe, pack and storage condition, and it should change when any of those change. If the data model can't express that, the date printed on the pack quietly drifts away from the evidence behind it.

This post walks through how we think about modelling shelf-life and expiry in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Kenya's Food Hygiene Regulations (Cap. 254), regulation 14: each container marked "to identify the producing factory and the lot", and specified products carrying a date marking. Source
  • Codex CODEX STAN 1-1985, 4.7: day and month for products lasting up to three months, month and year beyond that, and storage conditions on the label "if the validity of the date depends thereon". Source
  • Codex CXC 1-1969, 13.4: records retained "for a period that exceeds the shelf-life of the product". Source
  • FSAI Guidance Note 18 (an Irish benchmark, not Kenyan law): set shelf-life before launch, redo it on "modification or reformulation", test at least three replicates from three batches per interval where no plan is specified, apply and document a margin of safety, and verify periodically. Source

Translated into engineering terms: shelf-life is versioned configuration with provenance, expiry is a derived field on a lot, and changes to recipe or packaging are invalidation events.

Shelf-life belongs to a product version, not a product 

ShelfLifeSpec (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, pack_spec_id, storage_condition,
               date_type, days, margin_days, study_id, approved_by, valid_from, valid_to)
               date_type IN ('use_by','best_before')
ShelfLifeStudy (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, design_json, lab_id, decision_note, closed_at)

The spec points at the recipe version and the pack specification it was proven for, and at the study that justifies it. days is what goes on the label; margin_days is how much was taken off the study result and why lives in decision_note. When either the recipe or the pack spec gets a new version, the old spec doesn't silently carry over. It needs a review.

Expiry is derived at the moment the lot is made 

expiry_date = production_date(lot, factory_timezone) + spec.days

Two details matter. First, compute it from the production date in the factory's time zone, not the server's, or a lot packed at 1 a.m. in Nairobi gets the wrong date. Second, store the derived date and the spec id on the lot, so that a later change to the spec doesn't rewrite history on lots already in the market.

In FactoraERP today, stock items have a trackExpiry flag and a shelfLifeDays value, and finished-goods lots get an expiry date calculated from their production date in the factory's time zone.

Invalidation: changes that should trigger a review

FSAI lists the triggers in plain language: no evidence for an existing date, and modification or reformulation of the food or its production. That's an event rule:

on RecipeVersionPublished(item_id)  -> flag ShelfLifeSpec(item_id) as 'review_required'
on PackSpecChanged(item_id)          -> flag ...
on SupplierApproved(key_ingredient)  -> flag ...
on ComplaintLogged(type='spoilage', lot.expiry_date > complaint_date) -> attach to ShelfLifeSpec as evidence

The last rule is the one most systems miss. A spoilage complaint before the printed date is shelf-life evidence, and it should land on the spec, not only in the complaint log.

FEFO is where the date earns its keep

An expiry date nobody uses for stock rotation is just ink. Dispatch should pick first-expired, first-out, and any exception should be a recorded decision:

-- lots skipped in a dispatch that expire earlier than the lot picked
SELECT l.lot_code, l.expiry_date
FROM lot l
WHERE l.item_id = :item_id
  AND l.status = 'sellable'
  AND l.qty_available > 0
  AND l.expiry_date < :picked_lot_expiry;

In FactoraERP, dispatching out of first-expiry order needs an operations manager or admin and a written reason, and the override is stored on the sale with who and when.

Study results are measurements, not a PDF

A durability study is a grid: batch × replicate × interval × test. FSAI recommends reading it at a high percentile (90th or 95th) rather than the mean, which needs at least three replicates per time point. That's a query, not an opinion:

SELECT interval_day, test,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY value) AS p95,
       count(*) AS n
FROM shelf_life_result
WHERE study_id = :study_id
GROUP BY interval_day, test
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY interval_day;

Takeaways

  • Version shelf-life by recipe, pack spec and storage condition, and link it to the study that proves it.
  • Derive expiry at lot creation in the factory's time zone, and store the spec id with it.
  • Treat recipe, packaging and supplier changes as invalidation events.
  • Route early spoilage complaints to the shelf-life spec as evidence.
  • Enforce FEFO and record every override with who, when and why.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Kenya's food hygiene regulations, Codex CXS 1, CXC 1 and CXG 61 and FSAI Guidance Note 18, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: We put 7 frontier models on call for 100 real Kubernetes incidents. The best fixed 79.
description:
TL;DR: Tymfi Labs is a benchmark for AI SRE agents. We inject a real fault into a live Kubernetes shop, page your agent with the symptom only, and give it a sandboxed terminal. A pass means the live system works again afterwards. What the agent writes in its report doesn't count. On our current edition (100 incidents, 8 layers), the best frontier model fixed 79%. You can connect your own agent over MCP and the first 3 runs are free.

Why we built it

Most agent evals grade the transcript: did the agent mention the right root cause, run the right command, write a plausible summary? That's fine for chat. It doesn't work for operations, because production doesn't care what the agent says.

We kept seeing the same pattern while building this. An agent finds a problem, changes something, sees the error rate dip and writes "Resolved." Then a minute later the system drifts back, or a second fault is still breaking checkout, or the "fix" was deleting the thing that alerted. A text-based grader passes all of those. We wanted a grader that can't be talked into a pass.

How a run works

Every incident goes through three stages.

1. Break

A real fault is injected into a running microservices shop on Kubernetes (frontend, cart, checkout, payments, Kafka, Postgres, feature flags and the rest). Before the agent is paged, the examiner confirms the system is actually broken.

The agent gets a page with the symptom, and nothing else:

● PAGE · sev 2 · 09:14
search: 30% of requests time out since 09:12.
Traffic is normal for a Monday.

No hints, no runbook, no answer key. (This incident is a simplified illustration. We don't publish the real scenarios' answers.)

2. Investigate and fix

The agent gets a locked-down terminal with kubectl and standard Linux tools. There's no internet. Every agent gets the same command budget and the same time limit.

$ kubectl get deploy search -n prod
search   1/1   1   1
$ kubectl get hpa -n prod
search-loadtest   min 1   max 1   cpu 99%
$ kubectl delete hpa search-loadtest -n prod
horizontalpodautoscaler "search-loadtest" deleted
$ kubectl scale deploy/search -n prod --replicas=4
deployment.apps/search scaled

An agent that skips the HPA and only runs kubectl scale will see 4/4 replicas, report success, and get scaled back to 1 forty seconds later. That attempt fails.

3. Examine

The examiner checks the live system, not the report:

  • the user journey works end to end
  • the fix holds over a hold window
  • the service survives a restart
  • nothing else was changed along the way

Some shortcuts fail the attempt outright, however healthy things look afterwards:

Move Result
kubectl delete ns ... FAIL
Scaling a service to --replicas=0 FAIL
Disabling monitoring FAIL
Removing health checks FAIL
Touching the examiner FAIL

After grading, the world is restored exactly, so the next attempt starts from the same state.

Keeping the benchmark honest

A benchmark that runs live faults has its own failure modes: flaky scenarios, faults that don't reproduce, graders that pass the wrong fix. We guard against them like this:

  • Every scenario is proven 5 times before it ships: broken when injected, fixed by a known reference fix, restored exactly.
  • Every score traces to a hash of the exact scenario version that ran, so a result can't silently drift when a scenario changes.
  • Same tools, same budget for every agent and model. Nobody gets extra commands or a longer clock.
  • Your key stays with you. When you connect your own agent, your model runs on your side and we never see the API key.

Results: Edition 2

100 incidents across 8 layers, one attempt per model per incident.

# Model Fixed (verified on the live system) Cost per fix
1 Gemini 4 Argon 79% $0.35
2 Claude Opus 5.5 77% $0.26
3 GPT-6.1 Sol 75% $0.11
4 Claude Sonnet 5.5 64% $0.11
5 Kimi K3 60% $0.44
6 GLM-5.3 54% $0.26
7 DeepSeek V4 Pro 45% $0.080

A few things stand out:

  • The top three are within 4 points. With one attempt per incident that gap is small, which is why the leaderboard shows a 95% range next to each pass rate.
  • Cost varies about 3x among the leaders. GPT-6.1 Sol fixes an incident for about a third of what Gemini 4 Argon spends, and scores 4 points lower.
  • Even the best model leaves about 1 in 5 incidents broken.

The finding that worried us most came from a pilot that isn't on the public board yet. We put two independent faults on the same checkout journey, and Claude Opus 5.5 fixed 3 of 10. In 6 of the 7 misses it fixed one fault, watched the errors drop and stopped. That's the failure mode a transcript grader would never catch.

Try it with your own agent

Tymfi Labs is an MCP server, so any MCP client can run it. From Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http tymfi-labs https://tymfilabs.com/mcp

ChatGPT and Cursor connect the same way through their MCP settings. A run uses six tools:

list_benchmarks  →  pick a benchmark
start_run        →  the environment is prepared (the first incident takes a few minutes)
next_incident    →  you get the page
run_shell        →  kubectl and Linux tools inside the sandbox
submit_report    →  root cause + what you changed
get_report       →  your results

You can also skip MCP and plug in a model key (Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, or any model on OpenRouter).

The first 3 runs are free, then it's $0.001 a second.

Limits

  • Kubernetes only, one world. Every incident runs in the same microservices shop. Agents that are great on a different stack, or on bare VMs, aren't measured here yet.
  • One attempt per incident. Edition 2 is pass@1. More attempts would tighten the ranges; we're prioritising them for the incidents that separate models.
  • The multi-fault incidents aren't on the public board yet. They're built and validated, and will come in a later edition.
  • It measures fixing, not everything an SRE does. No paging etiquette, postmortems or customer comms.

What's next

We're adding harder multi-fault incidents to future editions. After that comes RL training on the same incidents, with rewards the live system verifies.

If you run AI agents anywhere near production, we'd love to hear what you'd need to see before you let one take a page on its own. Leave a comment, or put your agent on call at tymfilabs.com.

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: GPT-6.1 Terra now available on AI Gateway
description:
GPT-6.1 Terra from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast model for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, and it improves on the previous Terra model in visual reasoning, factual accuracy, and coding. It suits high-volume work in documents and desktop apps, such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, or entering invoice details into accounting software. OpenAI still recommends its larger GPT-6 models for the most complex coding tasks.

The model accepts text and images and returns text, with a context window of more than 1M tokens. It supports configurable reasoning effort, structured outputs, tool calling, and implicit and explicit prompt caching. For latency-sensitive work, fast mode is available as openai/gpt-6.1-terra-fast.

GPT-6.1 Terra works with the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, the Responses API, and coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Use openai/gpt-6.1-terra as the model name:

To use it in Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select openai/gpt-6.1-terra in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try GPT-6.1 Terra in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Handling 429 Email Rate Limit Errors in Logistics: Template Ownership
description:
Short answer: to handle 429 rate limit errors for an email API in Node.js, treat the response as a queue decision, not a send failure. Keep the verification event durable, honor the provider's Retry-After signal when present, retry with bounded jitter, and make template ownership explicit before the worker sends anything. For a logistics signup flow, I would keep the template in the application repository when its wording and variables are part of the product contract. A provider-managed template is the better runner-up when operations needs to change copy without a deploy and the application can validate the rendered result.

The important distinction is ownership. The retry loop controls when a message may leave. Template ownership controls what leaves after the delay. Mixing them creates a particularly nasty class of bugs: a verification token can be valid while the email body is stale, or a retry can send a different template than the first attempt.

The decision matrix

Template owner 429 behavior Change workflow Main risk
Application repository Queue the event and retry the same versioned render Code review and deploy Copy changes wait for release
Provider workspace Queue the event and resolve the template at send time Operations workflow A retry can observe a later template
Shared catalog service Queue the event with an immutable template version Catalog release process More coordination and another dependency

My default is application ownership for account verification. It gives the event a reproducible input: templateVersion, locale, recipient, and a token expiry. That matters more than shaving a step from the first call. A logistics signup link is a security boundary, not a newsletter.

What exactly should a 429 retry?

Retry the delivery attempt, never the HTTP request in isolation. The durable record needs an idempotency key, attempt count, next-attempt time, and the template version selected before enqueueing. A retry should not mint a second account, rotate a token by accident, or silently switch locales.

A 429 is also not permission to hammer the endpoint more politely. Respect Retry-After if the service supplies it. If it does not, use exponential backoff with random jitter and a cap. Stop after a defined deadline, then move the event to a reviewable state. The exact numbers belong in configuration for your traffic shape; the policy should be stable and observable.

This is where I usually reject clever client wrappers. A wrapper that retries every non-2xx response hides the difference between throttling, authentication failure, malformed input, and a provider outage. The caller needs a typed outcome.

Keep this boring.

The retry policy is a limitation, too: bounded backoff cannot make an expired verification token valid, and it cannot repair a bad sender configuration. Those cases need a terminal state and an operator signal, not more attempts.

How should Node.js handle 429 rate limit errors for email?

Suppose a driver signs up from a depot with a slow connection. The first request is accepted into your queue, but the downstream email API returns 429 twice. During those minutes, a copy editor changes “Verify your account” to “Confirm your dispatcher account.” With application ownership, the retry renders the recorded version. With provider ownership, it may resolve the new version unless the provider supports an immutable revision or the event stores enough information to pin one.

Neither choice is universally correct. Provider ownership is useful when a support or operations team must adjust wording quickly, especially for regional instructions. It needs a publish check, a preview test, and a rule that security-sensitive variables cannot be added by copy editors. Application ownership is easier to audit and test, but it makes copy a release artifact.

The decision criterion is not “which editor feels nicer?” It is replayability. Can an engineer reconstruct the exact body sent for a failed verification event six hours later? If the answer is no, the system has an audit gap.

A small Node.js worker with explicit outcomes

The worker below keeps transport policy separate from template rendering. It is intentionally boring. sendVerification is a generic adapter; the provider-specific SDK stays behind it.

type DeliveryResult =
  | { kind: 'sent'; providerId: string }
  | { kind: 'retry'; retryAt: number; reason: 'throttled' }
  | { kind: 'dead'; reason: 'invalid' | 'unauthorized' | 'expired' };

type SendError = {
  status?: number;
  retryAfterSeconds?: number;
  message: string;
};

function nextDelay(attempt: number, retryAfterSeconds?: number): number {
  if (retryAfterSeconds !== undefined) {
    return Math.max(1_000, retryAfterSeconds * 1_000);
  }

  const cap = 15 * 60 * 1_000;
  const base = Math.min(cap, 1_000 * 2 ** attempt);
  return Math.round(base * (0.75 + Math.random() * 0.5));
}

async function deliver(event: {
  id: string;
  attempt: number;
  templateVersion: string;
  expiresAt: number;
  recipient: string;
}): Promise<DeliveryResult> {
  if (Date.now() >= event.expiresAt) {
    return { kind: 'dead', reason: 'expired' };
  }

  try {
    const response = await sendVerification({
      idempotencyKey: event.id,
      recipient: event.recipient,
      templateVersion: event.templateVersion,
    });

    return { kind: 'sent', providerId: response.id };
  } catch (error) {
    const failure = error as SendError;

    if (failure.status === 429) {
      return {
        kind: 'retry',
        retryAt: Date.now() + nextDelay(event.attempt, failure.retryAfterSeconds),
        reason: 'throttled',
      };
    }

    if (failure.status && failure.status >= 400 && failure.status < 500) {
      return { kind: 'dead', reason: failure.status === 401 ? 'unauthorized' : 'invalid' };
    }

    throw error;
  }
}

The queue must make the state transition durable before acknowledging the job. On a retry, increment the attempt and preserve templateVersion. On a terminal result, record the provider response identifier when one exists. Metrics should separate 429, other 4xx, 5xx, queue age, and expired verification events. One counter called email_errors is not observability.

Do not use an unbounded in-process timer for this. A process restart should not erase delayed work. Use a durable queue, a database-backed schedule, or the equivalent mechanism already operated by your team. The implementation detail varies; the invariant does not.

How do provider limits affect a neutral policy?

The policy has to read the selected transport's contract instead of guessing from a status code. Amazon SES documents send rate and a rolling 24-hour sending quota as separate controls. SendGrid documents API rate limits and response headers for some endpoints. Mailgun documents API limits in its own API reference. These are different boundaries, even though all three can produce pressure that looks like “try again later.”

That difference changes what you measure. A send-rate ceiling calls for queue smoothing. A daily quota calls for admission control and an operator alert. An API-management limit may affect template lookup or status queries rather than message delivery. The adapter should translate those provider-specific signals into the small internal result type above, while retaining the raw status and headers for diagnosis.

I would test this at three levels: a pure backoff test with a fake clock, an adapter test that feeds a 429 with and without Retry-After, and a staging drill that confirms duplicate suppression after a worker restart. The last one catches the expensive bug. The code “works,” but the same verification email is sent twice when the acknowledgement is lost.

For the logistics case, choose provider-owned templates only when the team can pin revisions and review variable changes. Otherwise, keep the renderable contract beside the signup code, enqueue a versioned event, and let the worker retry delivery rather than recomputing business state. That is the runner-up's useful boundary: fast operational copy changes, at the cost of stricter release controls around template versions. Provider ownership is a poor fit when the team cannot audit revisions; application ownership is a poor fit when urgent copy changes cannot wait for deployment.

References

  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, section 4 (429): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6585#section-4
  • RFC 7231, HTTP Semantics, section 7.1.3 (Retry-After): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-7.1.3
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES sending quotas: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/manage-sending-quotas.html
  • SendGrid API rate limits: https://docs.sendgrid.com/api-reference/how-to-use-the-sendgrid-v3-api/rate-limits
  • Mailgun API reference: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/send/mailgun-messages

title: Vercel Marketplace database browser now supports Redis
description:
You can now run Redis commands, browse keys, and inspect values directly in the Vercel dashboard using the Marketplace database browser.

Both the Redis and Upstash for Redis integrations in Vercel Marketplace are supported, so you no longer need redis-cli or a separate database UI.

From your project, open Infrastructure > Storage and select a Redis database. The database page now includes two new tabs:

  • CLI: Run Redis commands and inspect the results. Run multiple commands by separating them with newlines or semicolons, with support for MULTI/EXEC transactions.

  • Browser: Browse keys in a flat list or grouped by prefix, and filter them by type or pattern. Select a key to inspect its value and metadata, including its type, TTL, encoding, and size. Supported value types include string, JSON, hash, list, set, and sorted set.

These tabs are currently available only to team members with the Owner role. Learn more in the Marketplace storage documentation.

title: Claude Opus 4.8 Fast Mode Is Retiring: A Safe Migration Playbook
description:
A production migration guide for moving Claude Opus 4.8 fast-mode workloads to Opus 5.5 without hiding compatibility, latency, capacity, or cost regressions.

Originally published on NoorYasser.com. This DEV edition is adapted for engineers planning the migration.

Anthropic is removing fast mode from Claude Opus 4.8 on November 30, 2026. After that date, requests that combine the model ID claude-opus-4-8 with speed: "fast" will return an error.

That is a feature retirement, not a November retirement of the Opus 4.8 model. Anthropic's lifecycle page still lists the model as active, with retirement no sooner than May 28, 2027.

The practical response is not a one-line model rename. If a production route depends on Opus 4.8 fast mode, move it to Claude Opus 5.5 behind a compatibility test, an offline evaluation, and a measured canary. Track the inference mode that actually served each request, not only the mode your configuration requested.

The deadline in one table

Question Documented answer Engineering consequence
What ends on November 30? Fast mode on Claude Opus 4.8 Remove speed: "fast" from every 4.8 path or migrate it
Is Opus 4.8 itself retiring then? No; it remains listed as active Do not misclassify standard 4.8 traffic as a November outage
Recommended fast target Claude Opus 5.5 Test request and response contracts before shifting traffic
Does Opus 5.5 need the old beta header? No Remove header injection after the route moves
How do you prove the serving mode? Read usage.speed Monitor actual mode, not requested intent alone
What happens at fast-mode capacity limits? 429 or 529; a 429 can include retry-after Use bounded retries or a deliberate standard-speed fallback

The dates, supported models, request fields, pricing, rate-limit behavior, and Opus 5.5 compatibility changes below come from Anthropic's official documentation, checked on November 1, 2026. The inventory, evaluation, rollout, and fallback design are engineering recommendations.

1. Find every affected request path

Searching application code for one model ID is not enough. Fast mode may be injected by an SDK wrapper, gateway policy, environment variable, managed-agent model object, feature flag, or request template.

Inventory at least these surfaces:

  • Direct Messages API payloads containing model: "claude-opus-4-8" and speed: "fast"
  • Managed Agent definitions with the same model and speed
  • Shared clients that append the fast-mode-2026-02-01 beta header
  • Internal aliases such as opus-fast or premium-low-latency
  • Fallback branches that activate only after a timeout or capacity error
  • Scheduled jobs and rarely used admin workflows
  • Dashboards, alerts, and budgets grouped by the old model or beta feature
  • Tests that validate only HTTP success instead of the response contract

A useful internal inventory record can be as simple as:

{
  "route": "support-escalation-agent",
  "model": "claude-opus-4-8",
  "requested_speed": "fast",
  "beta_header": "fast-mode-2026-02-01",
  "effort": "high",
  "tool_choice": "required",
  "fallback": "opus-4-8-standard",
  "owner": "support-platform"
}

This is not an Anthropic API schema. It is an ownership and risk record that should expose hidden compatibility work before traffic changes.

2. Treat Opus 5.5 as a contract migration

Anthropic's migration guide documents several differences that can affect an application even when prompts stay unchanged.

Thinking and effort

On Opus 4.8, thinking is off when a request omits the thinking field. On Opus 5.5, thinking runs even when that field is omitted. Anthropic also documents a default effort change: Opus 4.8 defaults to high, while Opus 5.5 defaults to medium.

Do not let defaults decide the migration implicitly. Set effort intentionally for each evaluated workload, parse thinking-aware responses, and compare both quality and token usage.

Tool contracts

The Opus 5.5 documentation lists breaking changes around forced tool use, model-linked thinking blocks, and an earlier computer-use tool version. If an agent forces a tool, replays conversations containing thinking blocks, or uses computer_20251124, include those paths in compatibility tests. A successful text-only prompt is not evidence that an agent workflow is compatible.

Prompt caching and Priority Tier

The minimum cacheable prompt on Opus 5.5 is 512 tokens, compared with 1,024 tokens for Opus 4.8. That can change cache creation and cost patterns without an obvious application change.

Anthropic also says Priority Tier is not supported on Opus 5.5. Fast mode and Priority Tier are separate capacity products; do not assume one replaces the other.

3. Measure latency correctly

Anthropic describes fast mode as the same model running with a faster inference configuration and says it can deliver up to 2.5 times higher output tokens per second. That is a provider claim about output throughput, not time to first token.

Separate the latency components:

end_to_end = queue_wait + request_setup + TTFT + generation + tool_time + post_processing
generation = output_tokens / observed_OTPS

If queueing or tool calls dominate, higher output throughput may barely change the user journey. Long streaming responses can benefit even when time to first token stays flat.

Report p50 and p95 for:

  • Time to first token
  • Output tokens per second
  • End-to-end latency
  • Tool execution time
  • Retry and fallback latency

Anthropic's current pricing page lists Opus 5.5 fast mode at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Opus 4.8 fast mode is listed at $10 and $50. These are provider prices, not a prediction of your bill. Prompt caching and data-residency multipliers can stack with fast-mode pricing, so calculate cost from real usage records.

4. Freeze an evaluation contract before the canary

Build a privacy-reviewed evaluation set that represents every affected route. Include short answers, long streaming generation, tool sequences, refusals, cacheable prompts, and peak-context requests.

Score at least:

  • Task correctness and instruction adherence
  • Tool selection, argument validity, and completion rate
  • Response parser compatibility
  • Thinking-block and stop-reason handling
  • TTFT, output throughput, and end-to-end p50/p95
  • Input, cached-input, and output tokens
  • usage.speed distribution
  • 429, 529, and other error rates
  • Retry amplification and standard-speed fallback rate
  • Cost per successful task, not cost per raw request

Use the same prompts, tools, seed data, and scoring rules for both routes. Comparing a busy Opus 4.8 production trace with a lightly loaded Opus 5.5 development request does not isolate a model or serving-mode difference.

5. Make fallback behavior explicit

A safe router distinguishes four things:

  1. The model requested by product policy
  2. The speed requested by the route
  3. The speed reported in usage.speed
  4. The fallback that actually served the response

A simplified policy might read:

if route_flag == "opus-5-5-fast":
    call Opus 5.5 with speed="fast"
    verify usage.speed
elif route_flag == "opus-5-5-standard":
    call Opus 5.5 without fast mode
else:
    keep the approved legacy route during the canary

On a 429, honor retry-after and retry within a bounded latency budget. On a 529 or exhausted budget, fall back to standard speed only when the product contract allows it. Record the fallback reason and final serving mode.

Do not silently fall back to another model merely to turn an error into a 200 response. A different model may change quality, safety, tool behavior, and cost.

6. Roll out in controlled stages

A practical sequence is:

  1. Inventory all routes, owners, headers, aliases, and fallbacks.
  2. Compatibility test request and response contracts, tool flows, and parsers.
  3. Offline evaluate quality, latency components, tokens, and cost.
  4. Shadow or replay privacy-safe traffic without affecting users.
  5. Canary a small, representative share behind a feature flag.
  6. Expand by route only after error, quality, latency, and cost gates pass.
  7. Remove the legacy path and old beta header before November 30.

Keep rollback narrow: change one route flag, preserve request evidence, and return to the last validated configuration. A rollback that also changes prompts, tools, cache boundaries, and retry rules is a second migration, not a control.

Best practices

  • Pin the model and set effort deliberately.
  • Log requested speed and usage.speed separately.
  • Treat 429 and 529 as capacity signals, not proof of model failure.
  • Alert on any remaining Opus 4.8 fast request before the deadline.
  • Measure cost per successful task.
  • Give every fallback a product-approved latency and quality contract.
  • Remove obsolete headers, aliases, dashboards, and runbook steps after cutover.

Anti-patterns

  • Changing only the model string
  • Assuming fast mode improves time to first token
  • Treating Opus 4.8 model retirement and fast-mode retirement as the same event
  • Comparing average latency while ignoring tail behavior
  • Inferring the serving mode from configuration instead of usage.speed
  • Keeping an untested standard-speed fallback indefinitely
  • Declaring success because HTTP status is 200 while tool completion or output quality regresses

Executive checklist

Before November 30, confirm that:

  • No production request combines claude-opus-4-8 with speed: "fast"
  • Opus 5.5 request, response, thinking, and tool contracts pass
  • Quality, latency, token usage, and cost gates pass on a representative set
  • usage.speed is visible in telemetry
  • 429 and 529 handling is bounded and observable
  • The standard-speed fallback is intentional and tested
  • The old beta header and internal aliases are removed
  • Rollback and route ownership are documented

Primary sources

  • Claude Platform release notes
  • Anthropic fast mode documentation
  • Claude Opus 5.5 migration guide
  • Anthropic rate limits
  • Anthropic pricing
  • Anthropic model deprecations

For the full version, related architecture notes, and the original publication context, read Claude Opus 4.8 fast mode retires: migrate without latency regressions.
