title: Building a Waitlist with Automatic Promotion in Spring Boot (and Keeping the Queue Gap-Free)
description:
🇺🇸 English version (🇧🇷 versão em português logo abaixo)

The problem: sessions with limited spots

I'm building a tutoring management system with Java, Spring Boot and PostgreSQL. Students can become tutors for a subject, and tutors open sessions with a limited number of spots.

That raised a real business question: what happens when a session is full? I didn't want to just return "Session is full". I wanted an optional waitlist:

  • if there's a free spot, the student is confirmed;
  • if the session is full and allows a waitlist, the student goes to the queue;
  • when a confirmed student cancels, the first in line is promoted automatically and gets notified;
  • the rest of the queue moves up, with no gaps (1, 2, 3... never 2, 3, 5).

Modeling the enrollment

Each enrollment has a status and an optional position in the queue:

  • CONFIRMED → has a spot, queuePosition is null
  • WAITLISTED → waiting, queuePosition is 1, 2, 3...
  • CANCELLED → left the session, queuePosition is null

In the database, I made sure an invalid position can never be saved:

CREATE TABLE enrollment (
    id             UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    status         enrollment_status NOT NULL,
    queue_position INT               CHECK (queue_position >= 1),
    session_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES session (id),
    student_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

The repository only needs two Spring Data derived queries. No SQL written by hand:

long countBySessionAndStatus(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

List<Enrollment> findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

Enrolling: confirmed or waitlisted?

After checking that the session exists, is active and the student isn't already enrolled, the enroll method decides where the student goes:

long confirmedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);

if (confirmedCount < session.getSpots()) {
    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, session, student);
    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

if (session.isAllowsWaitlist()) {
    long waitlistedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    int queuePosition = (int) waitlistedCount + 1;

    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED, session, student);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(queuePosition);

    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

throw new SessionFullException("Session is full");

If there's no spot and no waitlist, a SessionFullException is thrown, and my @RestControllerAdvice turns it into a 409 Conflict.

Cancelling: promoting the first in line

This is the most interesting part. When a student cancels, three things must happen together:

  1. the enrollment becomes CANCELLED;
  2. if that student had a confirmed spot, the first in the queue is promoted and notified;
  3. the queue is renumbered. 
@Transactional
public Enrollment cancelEnrollment(UUID enrollmentUuid, UUID userUuid) {
    // ... find the enrollment, check permission and status

    EnrollmentStatus previousStatus = enrollment.getStatus();

    enrollment.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(null);

    List<Enrollment> waitlist = enrollmentRepository
            .findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(enrollment.getSession(), EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    if (previousStatus == EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED && !waitlist.isEmpty()) {
        Enrollment promoted = waitlist.get(0);
        promoted.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);
        promoted.setQueuePosition(null);
        Notification notification = new Notification(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED,
                "You have been promoted from the waitlist", promoted.getStudent());
        notificationRepository.save(notification);
    }

    // ... renumber the queue (next section)
}

Notice previousStatus: if the student who cancelled was only waiting, no spot was freed, so nobody gets promoted. The queue still has to be renumbered, though.

Renumbering the queue without gaps

After the promotion, the list still contains the promoted student (now CONFIRMED). So I only renumber whoever is still WAITLISTED:

int position = 1;

for (Enrollment waiting : waitlist) {
    if (waiting.getStatus() == EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED) {
        waiting.setQueuePosition(position);
        position++;
    }
}

enrollmentRepository.saveAll(waitlist);
return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);

The @Transactional is what makes this safe: cancelling, promoting, notifying and renumbering are all or nothing. If anything fails halfway, nothing is saved, and I never end up with a cancelled spot and nobody promoted.

Proving it with unit tests

I tested the service with JUnit 5 and Mockito. The main scenario: a queue with positions 1, 2 and 3, and a confirmed student cancels. Expected result: the 1st becomes CONFIRMED, the others become 1 and 2, and a notification goes to the right student.

Enrollment enrollmentTest = sessionService.cancelEnrollment(enrollmentUuid, student.getId());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED, enrollmentTest.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(enrollmentTest.getQueuePosition());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, firstWaiting.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(firstWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(1, secondWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(2, thirdWaiting.getQueuePosition());

ArgumentCaptor<Notification> notification = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Notification.class);
verify(notificationRepository).save(notification.capture());

Assertions.assertEquals(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED, notification.getValue().getEventType());
Assertions.assertEquals(promotedStudent, notification.getValue().getReceiver());

ArgumentCaptor was new to me: it lets you grab the object passed to the mock and check what was saved, not only that something was saved.

What I learned and next steps

  • Modeling the states (CONFIRMED, WAITLISTED, CANCELLED) first made the code much simpler.
  • Validating in two places (service + CHECK constraint in the database) protects data even if a bug slips through.
  • @Transactional matters most when one action changes several rows.
  • A next step: enroll checks the count and then saves. Two students enrolling at the exact same moment could both see the last spot free. I want to study locking (for example, a pessimistic lock on the session) to handle that.

The full code is on GitHub: jg-abreu/tutoring-management-system

Thanks for reading! Feedback is very welcome. 🙌

🇧🇷 Versão em português

Criando uma lista de espera com promoção automática no Spring Boot (sem buracos na fila)

O problema: sessões com vagas limitadas

Estou construindo um sistema de gestão de monitorias com Java, Spring Boot e PostgreSQL. Alunos podem virar monitores de uma disciplina, e os monitores abrem sessões com um número limitado de vagas.

Isso trouxe uma pergunta de negócio real: o que acontece quando a sessão lota? Eu não queria só responder "Session is full". Queria uma lista de espera opcional:

  • se tem vaga, o aluno fica confirmado;
  • se a sessão está cheia e aceita lista de espera, o aluno entra na fila;
  • quando um aluno confirmado cancela, o primeiro da fila é promovido automaticamente e recebe uma notificação;
  • o resto da fila anda, sem buracos (1, 2, 3... nunca 2, 3, 5).

Modelando a inscrição

Cada inscrição tem um status e uma posição opcional na fila:

  • CONFIRMED → tem vaga, queuePosition é null
  • WAITLISTED → esperando, queuePosition é 1, 2, 3...
  • CANCELLED → saiu da sessão, queuePosition é null

No banco, garanti que uma posição inválida nunca seja salva:

CREATE TABLE enrollment (
    id             UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    status         enrollment_status NOT NULL,
    queue_position INT               CHECK (queue_position >= 1),
    session_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES session (id),
    student_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

O repositório só precisa de duas derived queries do Spring Data, sem escrever SQL na mão:

long countBySessionAndStatus(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

List<Enrollment> findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

Inscrevendo: confirmado ou na fila?

Depois de verificar que a sessão existe, está ativa e o aluno ainda não está inscrito, o método enroll decide para onde o aluno vai:

long confirmedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);

if (confirmedCount < session.getSpots()) {
    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, session, student);
    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

if (session.isAllowsWaitlist()) {
    long waitlistedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    int queuePosition = (int) waitlistedCount + 1;

    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED, session, student);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(queuePosition);

    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

throw new SessionFullException("Session is full");

Se não tem vaga nem lista de espera, é lançada uma SessionFullException, que o meu @RestControllerAdvice transforma em 409 Conflict.

Cancelando: promovendo o primeiro da fila

Essa é a parte mais interessante. Quando um aluno cancela, três coisas precisam acontecer juntas:

  1. a inscrição vira CANCELLED;
  2. se esse aluno tinha vaga confirmada, o primeiro da fila é promovido e notificado;
  3. a fila é renumerada. 
@Transactional
public Enrollment cancelEnrollment(UUID enrollmentUuid, UUID userUuid) {
    // ... busca a inscrição, verifica permissão e status

    EnrollmentStatus previousStatus = enrollment.getStatus();

    enrollment.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(null);

    List<Enrollment> waitlist = enrollmentRepository
            .findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(enrollment.getSession(), EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    if (previousStatus == EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED && !waitlist.isEmpty()) {
        Enrollment promoted = waitlist.get(0);
        promoted.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);
        promoted.setQueuePosition(null);
        Notification notification = new Notification(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED,
                "You have been promoted from the waitlist", promoted.getStudent());
        notificationRepository.save(notification);
    }

    // ... renumera a fila (próxima seção)
}

Repare no previousStatus: se quem cancelou estava só esperando, nenhuma vaga foi liberada, então ninguém é promovido. Mas a fila ainda precisa ser renumerada.

Renumerando a fila sem buracos

Depois da promoção, a lista ainda contém o aluno promovido (agora CONFIRMED). Por isso só renumero quem continua WAITLISTED:

int position = 1;

for (Enrollment waiting : waitlist) {
    if (waiting.getStatus() == EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED) {
        waiting.setQueuePosition(position);
        position++;
    }
}

enrollmentRepository.saveAll(waitlist);
return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);

O @Transactional é o que torna isso seguro: cancelar, promover, notificar e renumerar é tudo ou nada. Se algo falhar no meio, nada é salvo, e nunca fico com uma vaga cancelada sem ninguém promovido.

Provando com testes unitários

Testei o service com JUnit 5 e Mockito. O cenário principal: uma fila com posições 1, 2 e 3, e um aluno confirmado cancela. Resultado esperado: o 1º vira CONFIRMED, os outros viram 1 e 2, e uma notificação vai para o aluno certo.

Enrollment enrollmentTest = sessionService.cancelEnrollment(enrollmentUuid, student.getId());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED, enrollmentTest.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(enrollmentTest.getQueuePosition());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, firstWaiting.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(firstWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(1, secondWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(2, thirdWaiting.getQueuePosition());

ArgumentCaptor<Notification> notification = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Notification.class);
verify(notificationRepository).save(notification.capture());

Assertions.assertEquals(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED, notification.getValue().getEventType());
Assertions.assertEquals(promotedStudent, notification.getValue().getReceiver());

O ArgumentCaptor era novidade para mim: ele permite pegar o objeto passado para o mock e verificar o que foi salvo, e não só que algo foi salvo.

O que aprendi e próximos passos

  • Modelar os estados primeiro (CONFIRMED, WAITLISTED, CANCELLED) deixou o código muito mais simples.
  • Validar em dois lugares (service + constraint CHECK no banco) protege os dados mesmo se um bug passar.
  • O @Transactional faz mais diferença quando uma ação altera várias linhas.
  • Um próximo passo: o enroll conta e depois salva. Dois alunos se inscrevendo exatamente no mesmo momento poderiam ver a última vaga livre ao mesmo tempo. Quero estudar locking (por exemplo, um lock pessimista na sessão) para tratar isso.

O código completo está no GitHub: jg-abreu/tutoring-management-system

Obrigado por ler! Feedback é muito bem-vindo. 🙌

title: React Wheel Picker: iOS Wheels for Times and Dates
description:
TL;DR

A React wheel picker that feels native lets the browser do the scrolling: a scroll-snap list brings the phone's own momentum and rubber band, each row is turned on a 3D cylinder from scrollTop in one animation frame, and the value commits once, when the wheel comes to rest. Use wheels for times, durations and birth dates on phones, keep a typed field on desktop, and give mouse drag, the scroll wheel and the keyboard their own paths. Wingo UI's Pro Picker Wheel and Time Picker ship all of this, with a bottom sheet below 768px.

You want a React wheel picker because a phone user should not type 14:30 on a keyboard that covers half the form, and paging a calendar back 36 years to a birth date is worse. The hard part is the feel: the React wheel packages we checked replace the browser's scrolling with their own touch physics. This guide builds the wheel on a native snapping scroller with rows turned on a 3D cylinder, then covers mouse and keyboard paths, the time and date fields built on it, and the pitfalls. How wheel pickers compare across libraries is in our best React component library for mobile comparison.

When is a wheel picker the right control?

When the list is medium to long, ordered, and the user can guess what is hidden: hours, minutes, durations, quantities, a birth year. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for pickers say to "consider using a picker to offer medium-to-long lists of items", to prefer a pull-down button for "a fairly short list of choices", and a list or table for "a very large set of items". It also suggests minute steps that divide 60 evenly, such as quarter hours.

On the web that gives four rules:

  • Two to five options: a Segmented Control, so every option is visible.
  • 12 hours, 60 minutes, 1 to 99 items, the years since 1920: a wheel.
  • Hundreds of unordered names (countries, products): a searchable Select. A wheel only jumps to a typed prefix.
  • A date near today (a delivery, a booking): a calendar, because the weekday matters.

Why build a wheel on a native snapping scroller?

Because then the finger, the momentum and the rubber band at the ends are the phone's own, and a trackpad or a mouse wheel turns it with no extra code. A search for "ios picker web" in October 2026 mixed a Mendix widget, React Native packages and Flutter's CupertinoPicker in with the web answers. The two React DOM packages we found both run their own physics:

Package (as of October 2026) License, last release How it moves
@ncdai/react-wheel-picker 1.2.3 MIT, August 23, 2026 own touch, mouse and wheel handlers; rows on a 3D cylinder with CSS transforms
react-mobile-picker 1.2.0 MIT, August 3, 2025 own touchmove handler and translate3d; mouse wheel off by default

Both work. @ncdai/react-wheel-picker, which also handles arrows, Home / End and type-ahead, is the better pick if you want a free, unstyled wheel and will build the field yourself. Its feel is tuned through dragSensitivity and scrollSensitivity; a native scroller decelerates like every other list on that phone.

The native recipe has three parts. The list scrolls with scroll-snap-type: y mandatory, every row snaps to the center, and two rows of padding let the first and last rows reach it. One requestAnimationFrame per scroll reads scrollTop and writes rotateX and opacity straight to the rows, never through React state. And the value commits once, at rest: on scrollend, which MDN lists from Chrome 114, Firefox 109 and Safari 26.2, with a 120ms idle timer for older Safari.

"use client";

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

const ROW = 44; // five rows in a 220px window

export function MiniWheel({ options, onSettle }: { options: string[]; onSettle: (value: string) => void }) {
  const listRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const settleRef = useRef(onSettle);
  useEffect(() => {
    settleRef.current = onSettle;
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const list = listRef.current;
    if (!list) return;
    const rows = Array.from(list.firstElementChild?.children ?? []) as HTMLElement[];
    let frame = 0;
    let idle: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
    let last = "";

    // the turn and the fade go straight to the rows, never through React state
    const paint = () => {
      frame = 0;
      const pos = list.scrollTop / ROW;
      rows.forEach((row, i) => {
        const d = i - pos;
        row.style.transform = `perspective(400px) rotateX(${Math.max(-55, Math.min(55, -d * 20))}deg)`;
        row.style.opacity = String(Math.max(0.35, 1 - Math.min(Math.abs(d), 3) * 0.22));
      });
    };
    // one commit when the wheel is at rest, never one per row passed
    const settle = () => {
      clearTimeout(idle);
      const value = options[Math.round(list.scrollTop / ROW)];
      if (value !== undefined && value !== last) settleRef.current((last = value));
    };
    const onScroll = () => {
      if (!frame) frame = requestAnimationFrame(paint);
      clearTimeout(idle);
      idle = setTimeout(settle, 120); // Safari before 26.2 has no scrollend
    };

    paint();
    list.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
    list.addEventListener("scrollend", settle);
    return () => {
      list.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
      list.removeEventListener("scrollend", settle);
      cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
      clearTimeout(idle);
    };
  }, [options]);

  return (
    <div ref={listRef} className="h-[220px] snap-y snap-mandatory overflow-y-scroll overscroll-contain [scrollbar-width:none]">
      <div className="py-[88px]">
        {options.map((option) => (
          <div key={option} className="flex h-11 snap-center items-center justify-center text-xl tabular-nums">
            {option}
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

That is the core of the Wingo UI Picker Wheel. The sketch misses a starting value, disabled rows, looping, every input that is not a finger, and wheels mounted while hidden.

How do mouse and keyboard users turn the wheel?

A mouse wheel and a trackpad scroll it natively; dragging and keys need their own code. In the Picker Wheel only a mouse goes through pointer events: past 8 pixels of movement, snapping turns off and scrollTop follows the pointer. On release, a motion inertia animation continues from the measured velocity, and its modifyTarget rounds the landing point to a row. A click on a visible row glides it to the center.

Each column is one Tab stop with role="listbox". ArrowUp and ArrowDown move a row, PageUp and PageDown five, Home and End jump to the ends, typing jumps to the next option that starts with the text ("19", then "199" on a year wheel), and ArrowLeft and ArrowRight change column. aria-activedescendant points at the centered option, which carries aria-selected. The focus ring hugs the center row, where the edge fade cannot hide it.

What props does the Picker Wheel need?

columns (or options for a single wheel), a value and onValueChange. Everything else has a default:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { PickerWheel, pickerRange } from "@/components/ui/picker-wheel";

const hours = pickerRange(0, 12);
const minutes = pickerRange(0, 59, { pad: 2 });

export function CallDuration() {
  const [duration, setDuration] = useState(["1", "25"]);
  return (
    <PickerWheel
      aria-label="Call duration"
      value={duration}
      // once per settle, with every column's value and the id of the column that moved
      onValueChange={(value) => setDuration(value)}
      columns={[
        { id: "hours", label: "h", options: hours, align: "end" },
        { id: "minutes", label: "min", options: minutes, align: "start", loop: true },
      ]}
    />
  );
}

The props worth knowing:

  • onValueChange fires once per settle, never per row passed, so it is safe to save from it.
  • loop (on the wheel or per column) wraps 59 back to 00: the column renders extra copies and jumps silently to the middle one at rest. Only the middle copy has role="option".
  • size sets 36, 44 or 52px rows; visibleRows (odd, default 5) makes the wheel 220px tall at md; perspective tilts rows 20, 10 or 0 degrees each (ios, subtle, flat).
  • A disabled option is struck through, and a wheel that lands on one glides on to the nearest enabled row: pickerRange(36, 46, { disabled: (n) => n === 38 }) for a sold-out shoe size.
  • haptics plays a selection tick each time a finger, a mouse drag or the scroll wheel brings a new row to the center, never for keys. It works on Chrome for Android; why a scroll cannot tick on an iPhone is in our web vibration API guide.

PickerWheelField puts the same wheels in a form field: a bottom sheet with Done and Cancel below 768px, a popover that applies live on desktop.

How do you build a React time picker wheel that still types on desktop?

Use the Time Picker, which switches by width. Below 768px the field is read-only with inputMode="none", so no keyboard opens, and a tap opens a bottom sheet with hour and minute wheels. From 768px up it is a text input that reads "1430", "2:30pm" or "2p", steps minutes with ArrowUp and ArrowDown, and opens a panel of columns on click. The value is always "HH:mm" in 24 hours:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { TimePicker } from "@/components/ui/time-picker";

const lunchBreak = (time: string) => time >= "13:00" && time < "14:00";

export function PickupTime() {
  const [time, setTime] = useState("11:30");
  return (
    <TimePicker
      label="Pickup time"
      name="pickup"
      locale="en-US"
      min="09:00"
      max="18:00"
      minuteStep={15}
      disabledTimes={lunchBreak}
      value={time}
      onValueChange={setTime}
    />
  );
}

Live demo: Time Picker. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type 2:30pm or 1430 and press Enter, or click the field for the columns; at phone width a tap opens the wheels in a bottom sheet, and the lunch hour stays blocked either way). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Time Picker docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add time-picker

The sheet edits a draft: Done commits it, and dragging the sheet away keeps the old time. Times outside min and max or blocked by disabledTimes are disabled rows on the wheels too.

Should a date be a wheel or a calendar?

A wheel for a date the user knows by heart and that sits far from today, like a birth date: three flicks instead of paging through years. A calendar for dates near today, where the weekday matters. That is why the Date Picker opens a calendar, in a bottom sheet on phones.

For the birth date, useDateWheel is a React date wheel picker in one hook: day, month and year columns in the locale's order (month, day, year for en-US), month names in that language, days that follow the month (February 29 only in leap years) and years between min and max. Values are ISO dates such as "1990-05-17".

Live demo: Picker Wheel. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Flick the month, the day or the year, drag them with a mouse, or Tab to the year and type 1985: the date and the age under the wheel update when it comes to rest). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Picker Wheel docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add picker-wheel

For the wheel on phones and a typed field on desktop, render both and switch with CSS, so the server HTML matches the first paint (the mobile-first React components guide explains why a useIsMobile check would flash). One ISO string feeds both:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { DatePicker } from "@/components/ui/date-picker";
import { PickerWheelField, useDateWheel } from "@/components/ui/picker-wheel";
import { formatDate, fromISODate, toISODate } from "@/lib/date-utils";

export function BirthdayField({ initial }: { initial: string }) {
  const [birthday, setBirthday] = useState(initial); // "1990-05-17"
  const [today] = useState(() => new Date());
  const wheel = useDateWheel({ value: birthday, onValueChange: setBirthday, locale: "en-US", min: "1920-01-01", max: toISODate(today) });

  return (
    <>
      {/* phones: three wheels in a bottom sheet, Done to commit */}
      <div className="md:hidden">
        <PickerWheelField
          label="Date of birth"
          {...wheel}
          formatValue={() => formatDate(fromISODate(birthday), "en-US", { dateStyle: "long" })}
        />
      </div>
      {/* 768px and up: type 05171990, or open the calendar */}
      <div className="hidden md:block">
        <DatePicker
          label="Date of birth"
          locale="en-US"
          max={today}
          clearable={false}
          value={fromISODate(birthday)}
          onValueChange={(date) => date && setBirthday(toISODate(date))}
        />
      </div>
      <input type="hidden" name="birthday" value={birthday} />
    </>
  );
}

One catch: useDateWheel always holds a date (today when you pass none), so the field is never empty. That suits editing a profile; a required date that starts blank belongs in the Date Picker.

What goes wrong with a wheel picker on a phone?

Most bugs come from the wheel's surroundings. The Picker Wheel handles these, and you will meet them if you build your own:

  • The sheet steals the drag. A wheel at its first row hands a downward drag to the drawer. The columns carry data-vaul-no-drag, and overscroll-behavior: contain keeps a hard flick from scrolling the page.
  • A wheel mounted while hidden. Inside a closed sheet the list has no height, so setting scrollTop does nothing. A ResizeObserver scrolls to the value once the list has a size.
  • Committing per row. Saving on every row that passes floods your API and fires validation mid-spin.
  • Reduced motion. With prefers-reduced-motion the rows stay flat and programmatic moves jump instead of gliding.
  • Feedback only in the tick. Desktop and iPhone users feel nothing, so the centered row and the field text must carry the value.

Where should you start?

Open this page on your phone and flick the two demos above. The Picker Wheel, Time Picker and Date Picker are part of Wingo UI Pro; with a Pro account signed in through npx wingo-ui@latest login, npx wingo-ui@latest add picker-wheel copies the component and everything it imports into your project. A React wheel picker component is one piece of a phone-friendly form; the other patterns are in Mobile UI in React.

Components in this post

  • Picker Wheel (Pro): The iOS wheel picker for the web: columns that spin with native momentum and click into place on a 3D cylinder, inline or as a field. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add picker-wheel
  • Time Picker (Pro): A time-of-day field to type into or pick from columns, with 12 / 24 hours by locale, minute steps, limits and iOS wheels on phones. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add time-picker
  • Date Picker (Pro): A date field to type in your locale or pick from a calendar popover, with presets, limits and an optional time; a sheet on phones. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add date-picker

FAQ

Is there an iOS-style wheel picker for React web apps?

Yes. As of October 2026 the open source options are @ncdai/react-wheel-picker (1.2.3, MIT) and react-mobile-picker (1.2.0, MIT), which both run their own touch physics. Wingo UI's Picker Wheel (Pro) scrolls natively and adds a form field that opens a bottom sheet on phones, a date hook and haptic ticks.

Should I use input type=time instead of a wheel picker?

Use the native input when its look and behavior are good enough, because it costs nothing and is accessible by default. You cannot style the picker it opens, it differs between browsers and OS versions, and it cannot show blocked times such as a lunch break, which is when a custom wheel earns its code.

How do I make a wheel picker loop around in React?

Render the options several times and jump back to the middle copy whenever the wheel comes to rest, which looks identical. In the Wingo UI Picker Wheel, loop on the wheel or on one column does this, with at least 40 rows on each side of the middle copy so a hard flick never reaches the end.

Does a web wheel picker vibrate on iPhone?

No. Safari has no Vibration API, and the iPhone's one web haptic, the tick of a native switch, plays only for a tap, never for a scroll. On Chrome for Android the Picker Wheel ticks each time a new row reaches the center.

Is the Wingo UI Picker Wheel free?

No. The Picker Wheel, Time Picker and Date Picker are Pro components; the Drawer and Field they build on are free. Pro costs $8 a month, $80 a year or $150 once.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Wheel Picker: iOS Wheels for Times and Dates. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Screen recording or UI animation for your dev tool demo?
description:
Both formats show your product. They differ in control, cost and how long they stay accurate.

Screen recording

  • Pros: honest, fast, shows the real product.
  • Cons: tiny text, shaky cursor, loading delays, and it goes stale after the next release.

UI animation

  • Pros: zooms, highlights and clean transitions. You can show a feature before it ships.
  • Cons: more design and motion work, and it needs good design files.

How to choose

  • Tutorial or docs video? Record it.
  • Homepage or launch video? Animate it.
  • UI changing soon? Animate from separate layers so one screen can be swapped.

A blended video often works best: a polished animated overview, then a short real clip to prove it is the actual product.

More detail: UI animation vs screen recording.

title: Node.js Code for Verifying Property-Management Phone Numbers with SMS (Audit Evidence)
description:
Short answer: for a property-management portal, use a managed OTP boundary when the requirement is proving control of a resident's phone, but keep the decision, expiration, attempt count, recipient, and provider response in your own audit record. Send through /v1/sms/otp, validate the submitted code in your application, and treat resend as a new rate-limited action through /v1/sms/resend/{id}. That gives the platform a reviewable record without making the SMS vendor the system of record.

Infrai fits this boundary when one REST API and one key can cover the communications call alongside other backend capabilities, while the property application keeps its own evidence policy. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and does not require a key, so the request schema can be reviewed before implementation rather than inferred from an SDK.

The important distinction is between delivery and evidence. An SMS provider can create and deliver a challenge; it cannot, by itself, explain why your leasing workflow accepted a phone number, which policy version applied, or why a number was suppressed after repeated failures. Those are application decisions.

What should the property portal actually prove?

The login flow has two separate questions: did the service send a challenge to the claimed number, and did the person presenting the code satisfy the verification policy? A successful provider response answers only the first question. Your database must bind the challenge to the account, record an expiration policy, count failed attempts, and retain enough provider metadata for an auditor to reconstruct the decision.

This is also where bounces and invalid recipients matter. A failed delivery is not proof that the person lacks access to the phone, but it is a useful signal for pausing future sends. Keep a suppression decision separate from the OTP decision: a number may be temporarily blocked for abuse, permanently invalid, or merely awaiting a delivery-status check. Do not turn a transient delivery failure into an irreversible identity judgment.

For a platform team, the invariant is simple: no accepted login without a valid, unexpired challenge tied to the intended account; no retry that can create an accidental second accepted state; and no resend path that bypasses the same abuse controls as the first send. The audit trail is part of the feature, not logging polish added after launch.

Which architecture fits the evidence requirement?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a specialist verification service. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Amazon Cognito's MFA features each represent a different version of this approach: the provider owns more of the challenge lifecycle, while your application integrates at a narrower boundary. Twilio Verify is a focused verification product with a mature channel and country footprint; Vonage Verify is another managed verification option with its own regional and policy constraints; Cognito fits best when the identity system already lives in AWS and the application is willing to adopt its user-pool model. The trade-off is control. A specialist can reduce the amount of OTP machinery you operate, but it may leave your property-specific evidence model, suppression policy, and cross-channel records split across systems.

The second is an application-owned policy layer over a communications API. Your service owns challenge state, account binding, expiry, attempt limits, suppression decisions, and audit exports. The API owns SMS submission and the provider-facing delivery surface. Infrai is a deliberate option in this shape: its communications capabilities sit behind one REST contract, so adding adjacent backend capabilities does not require another SDK, key, and integration boundary. Its public discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which makes an API review easier to repeat during a control assessment.

I would choose the second architecture for a property-management platform when compliance evidence must connect the phone challenge to the resident, lease context, suppression decision, and policy version in one record. I would choose Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Cognito when the team explicitly values a more managed identity workflow and can accept the provider's lifecycle and evidence boundaries. There is no honest universal winner here; the right answer follows the ownership boundary.

Decision Application-owned policy over a communications API Specialist verification service
Evidence One property-specific audit record can contain the decision inputs Provider records are more central, application context may be separate
Operating load You own expiry, attempts, suppression, and reconciliation More challenge lifecycle is managed for you
Lock-in Communications contract is narrower, policy remains yours Identity and verification workflow can be more provider-shaped
Best fit Compliance review needs account and property context together The team wants a pre-shaped verification product

How should Node.js code verify a phone number with SMS?

The send operation should create a pending challenge before calling the provider, then mark it sent only after a successful response. The provider's identifier belongs in that record. Store a hash or otherwise protected representation of the one-time code, never the usable code in plaintext, and expire the challenge according to the policy your security review approved.

The sample below keeps the provider payload outside the example because the verified contract is discoverable and the exact request schema should be copied from that live capability definition, not guessed from a blog post. It still shows the important operational properties: explicit POST, bearer authentication from an environment variable, status checking, Retry-After handling, and a bounded exponential retry for 429 responses. The application should supply a request body generated from the discovered schema through OTP_REQUEST_JSON. It uses only the Go 1.22 standard library.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func sendOTP() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("OTP_REQUEST_JSON")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY and OTP_REQUEST_JSON are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := sendOTP()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For a real create operation, add an idempotency key derived from the pending challenge before retries, using the provider's documented convention. The same key must not be reused for a separate resend. A resend is an explicit state transition, and the application should retain its own attempt and cooldown record before invoking /v1/sms/resend/{id}.

Keep it boring.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Your application endpoint should load the pending challenge, reject an expired or already-consumed record, compare the submitted code against the protected value, and atomically mark success. Rate-limit by account and phone number as well as by source address; otherwise an attacker can rotate one of those dimensions while brute-forcing the same challenge. Keep the failure response deliberately unhelpful so it does not reveal whether a phone is registered.

The rollback story deserves equal attention. If the SMS call fails, leave the challenge in a failed-send state and make the next attempt create a fresh pending record. If delivery later proves invalid, add the recipient to the appropriate suppression workflow and stop automatic sends until a reviewed action clears it. Since the relevant event surface is pull-based rather than webhook-driven, reconciliation needs a scheduled poll and a visible freshness timestamp. A dashboard that says “verified” without showing when its delivery evidence was last refreshed is not a compliance control.

Before production, test these cases explicitly: a successful first send, an expired code, a reused code, four consecutive rate-limit responses, a resend after cooldown, an invalid recipient, and a provider error with a non-2xx body. Rollback should disable new sends behind a feature flag while preserving already-created audit records. Do not delete evidence to make a failed migration look clean.

The conditional recommendation is therefore narrow: try Infrai for the communications boundary when one consistent REST surface and a discoverable, broad backend capability set reduce integration ownership, while your service remains responsible for property-specific OTP evidence and suppression policy. Choose a specialist verification product when managed identity lifecycle is more valuable than keeping that policy layer in your application. For the Infrai boundary, start with the SMS OTP guide and verify the current request schema before shipping.

References

  • RFC 4226: HOTP: An HMAC-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • RFC 6238: TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon Cognito MFA documentation
  • Infrai SMS OTP guide

title: Browser AI Video Without Desktop Bloat — Image-to-Video vs Text-to-Video
description:
Browser AI Video Without Desktop Bloat — Image-to-Video vs Text-to-Video

Disclosure: I work on APIXO, a browser AI video and image workspace. This is a practical how-to based on how we see creators actually work—not a fake “I bought five phones” review.

If you have ever opened twelve AI video tabs, installed a 4 GB desktop app “just to try one clip,” and still ended up with a blurry product shot that refuses to move the way you wanted—this article is for you.

You do not need a local GPU farm or a timeline editor to get useful short clips for demos, social drafts, and campaign experiments. You need a clear entry point, a short generate → inspect → change one variable loop, and a human pass before anything goes live.

Two doors into AI video

Image-to-video (you already have a still)

Upload a product photo, illustration, portrait, or scene still. The model adds motion, camera feel, and atmosphere around that frame.

Good fit when:

  • Brand look must stay recognizable (logo product, hero shot, illustrated character)
  • You already paid for photography or art direction
  • The brief is “make this image move,” not “invent a new world”

Watch outs:

  • Soft edges, heavy compression, or tiny subjects make motion look mushy
  • Extreme camera moves fight the original composition
  • Text baked into the image often warps—plan to overlay type in post if you need crisp copy

Text-to-video (idea first, asset later)

Describe the scene in a prompt. Explore framing, light, camera language, and style before you have a finished source image.

Good fit when:

  • You need storyboard options from a copy line
  • Marketing wants three tones of the same idea for an internal review
  • You are exploring look-and-feel, not locking a hero asset

Watch outs:

  • Vague prompts (“cool futuristic vibe”) produce a different film every run
  • Subject, place, and motion written up front stabilize results more than adjective piles
  • Character identity across shots is still a weak spot for most models—treat early clips as drafts

Rule of thumb: still in hand → image-to-video. Only a sentence in hand → text-to-video. If both exist, start from the still; you can still rewrite the motion prompt.

A five-step browser workflow

  1. Write the job in one sentence.

    Examples: “3-second product turn for a PDP.” “Moody atmosphere clip for a landing hero.” “Social cut showing the UI flowing.” Purpose drives length, framing, and how much detail the model must invent.

  2. Pick the door. Image or text. Do not flip-flop mid-batch until you have at least two usable takes from one door.

  3. Check model controls that actually matter. Duration, motion strength, aspect ratio, seed (if exposed), and any style or camera presets. Models differ in how they interpret “slow pan” vs “orbit.” Read what the UI exposes; do not assume every slider exists everywhere.

  4. Generate → watch once → change one variable.

    Either tweak the prompt, swap the reference image, or switch model—not all three. That is how you learn what moved the needle. Save keepers in a library so you are not re-uploading the same still ten times.

  5. Human QA before publish.

    Check subject consistency, motion naturalness, warped text, brand colors, and anything that would embarrass you at 1080p on a phone. AI video is a draft engine; finishing still belongs to you (trim, captions, audio, color).

When you have three or more variants, park them in one place—canvas-style project boards help—so you stop bouncing between downloads folders.

Image-to-video vs text-to-video in practice

Situation Prefer Why
Shopify / App Store style product still Image-to-video Keeps packaging and silhouette
“Show the feeling of night commute” brief Text-to-video No locked hero frame yet
Illustrated mascot already designed Image-to-video Protects character art
Exploring three campaign moods from one headline Text-to-video Fast parallel looks
Need readable on-screen UI Neither alone Generate motion, then composite real UI or type

Neither path replaces editing. Both replace “wait for a full shoot before you can show anything.”

Pitfalls that burn credits

Prompt essay syndrome. A 120-word mood board dump often underperforms a tight subject + action + camera + lighting line. Put the noun first.

One-and-done despair. First output is a sketch. Change one knob. Log what you changed. Teams that treat runs as experiments get usable cuts faster than teams that gamble on a single “perfect” prompt.

Shipping raw generations. Morphing hands, melting logos, and scrambled captions pass casual glance and fail in a client review. Budget five minutes of human review per keep.

Fuzzy duration and channel. A 12-second cinematic wander is the wrong artifact for a 3-second story ad. Decide channel and length before you burn generations.

Ignoring source quality on image-to-video. Upscale or re-export a clean still first if the source is a WhatsApp screenshot. Garbage in still wins.

Chasing every new model name. For product work, consistency and iteration speed beat chasing yesterday’s leaderboard clip. Pick one or two models that match your look, learn their quirks, then expand.

Optional: clean stills before you animate

If night shots or high-ISO photos look grainy, a light denoise pass before image-to-video often reduces crawling noise in motion. Over-smoothing skin and fabric still ruins the look—compare against the original. If you use APIXO’s tools, denoise lives under image tools: Denoise Image.

Where APIXO fits (and where it does not)

APIXO is a browser workspace for image-to-video, text-to-video, related image tools, and cloud canvas projects. It started as a unified model API for developers; the product now emphasizes creators who want results without installing desktop bloat, while API access remains for teams wiring the same models into their own apps.

It will not replace a full NLE, a colorist, or a shoot. It will help you get short motion drafts into a library fast enough that marketing can react the same afternoon.

Takeaway

Browser AI video is not magic. It is pick a door → run a short loop → finish as a human. Image-to-video protects an existing visual. Text-to-video explores when the visual does not exist yet. Keep prompts concrete, change one variable per run, and never publish a generation you have not watched at full size.

If you want to try that loop in the browser: apixo.ai.

title: Durable workflows vs. a queue and a cron job
description:
Some work doesn't fit in a request. Moving a customer's data to new infrastructure. Onboarding a merchant across five systems. Generating, approving and sending a large batch of documents. These jobs have many steps, take minutes to days, call systems that fail, and must survive deploys and crashes.

Most teams start the same way: a queue, a cron job and a status column.

What queue + cron becomes

Version one is clean: a job row with status = PENDING, a worker that picks it up, does the work, sets DONE. Then reality adds requirements, one at a time:

  1. A step fails transiently → add a retries column and a RETRYING status.
  2. A worker dies mid-job → add locked_by and locked_at, and a cron that releases stale locks.
  3. Step 4 must not run twice → add per-step status columns.
  4. A step needs to wait for a human approval or a 24-hour cool-down → add resume_after and another cron.
  5. Step 6 fails permanently after steps 1–5 succeeded → write undo logic, scattered across the codebase.
  6. Nobody can tell where a job is → build an admin page that reads all these columns.

Each addition is reasonable. Together they're a workflow engine — one with no tests for its failure paths, state spread across columns, and behaviour that only one engineer fully understands. (The picture at the end of this post is only slightly exaggerated.)

What a durable workflow engine gives you

A durable workflow engine — Temporal is the one I've used; Cadence, AWS Step Functions and others share the idea — lets you write the process as ordinary code while the engine persists every step's progress:

@WorkflowInterface
public interface DataMoveWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void move(String accountId);
}

public class DataMoveWorkflowImpl implements DataMoveWorkflow {

    private final MoveActivities act = Workflow.newActivityStub(MoveActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder()
                    .setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(30))
                    .setRetryOptions(RetryOptions.newBuilder()
                            .setInitialInterval(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                            .setBackoffCoefficient(2.0)
                            .setMaximumAttempts(5)
                            .build())
                    .build());

    @Override
    public void move(String accountId) {
        Saga saga = new Saga(new Saga.Options.Builder().build());
        try {
            act.preflightChecks(accountId);

            String target = act.provisionTarget(accountId);
            saga.addCompensation(act::releaseTarget, target);

            act.copySnapshot(accountId, target);
            act.syncChanges(accountId, target);       // catch up writes made during the copy
            act.verifyChecksums(accountId, target);

            act.switchTraffic(accountId, target);
            saga.addCompensation(act::switchTrafficBack, accountId);

            Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofHours(24));     // soak period; costs nothing while waiting
            act.decommissionSource(accountId);
        } catch (ActivityFailure e) {
            saga.compensate();                        // undo completed steps in reverse order
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

What the engine handles for you:

  • Durability. Each completed activity is recorded. If the worker crashes after copySnapshot, a new worker replays the history and continues at syncChanges — it doesn't copy again.
  • Retries and timeouts per step, as configuration rather than columns.
  • Long waits. Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofHours(24)) holds no thread and no lock; the engine wakes the workflow when the timer fires. The same goes for waiting on a signal, such as a human approval.
  • Compensation. The Saga helper records how to undo each step and runs the compensations in reverse if a later step fails.
  • Visibility. Every workflow's current step, history and inputs are queryable — the admin page you'd otherwise build.


Steps run forward; compensations run backward. Explore the interactive diagram

The price: determinism

Workflow code is replayed to rebuild state after a crash, so it must make the same decisions every time it runs with the same history. In practice:

  • No Thread.sleep, System.currentTimeMillis(), UUID.randomUUID() or Random in workflow code — use Workflow.sleep, Workflow.currentTimeMillis(), Workflow.randomUUID().
  • No I/O in workflow code. Database calls, HTTP calls and file access go in activities.
  • Changing a running workflow's logic needs versioning (Workflow.getVersion), because in-flight workflows replay against the old history.

Activities, on the other hand, are normal code — and because they're retried, they must be idempotent (see Idempotency keys).

These rules take a week to internalise. They also force a clean separation between "what happens in what order" (workflow) and "how each step talks to the world" (activities), which tends to make the code easier to read.

When it's worth it — and when it isn't

Situation Queue + worker Durable workflow
One step, idempotent, seconds long ✅ Simple and enough Overkill
2–3 steps, no waits, rare failures ✅ Usually fine Optional
Many steps, external systems, partial failure needs undo Grows into a hand-built engine ✅
Waits of hours or days, human approvals Crons and resume_after columns ✅ Timers and signals
You must answer "where exactly is job X?" Build an admin page ✅ Built in

The real cost is operational: you run (or pay for) the engine's cluster and learn its model. For one small job, that cost dominates. For a platform that runs long, multi-step processes every day — migrations, onboarding, provisioning — it pays for itself quickly, because every new process gets retries, timers, visibility and compensation for free.

Takeaways

  • A queue + cron + status table grows into a workflow engine; decide early whether to build one or adopt one.
  • Durable workflows give resumability, per-step retries, cheap long waits, compensation and visibility.
  • The price is determinism in workflow code and idempotency in activities.
  • Use it for long, multi-step, failure-prone processes; keep simple jobs simple.

Originally published at ayushwing.com.

title: Designing a 3D Periodic Table for iPhone Duo: Reimagining Foldable UI/UX
description:
A deep dive into the UI/UX design decisions behind building an immersive, dual-screen 3D Periodic Table app optimized for foldable iPhone hardware

Designing interface layouts for dual-screen and foldable devices like the iPhone Duo requires rethinking traditional single-viewport ergonomics to maximize real estate without cluttering the visual field. In Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app, the dual-display architecture establishes a logical separation between macro navigation and micro content inspection. Opening the device reveals a balanced split workspace: the comprehensive periodic table stays pinned to one screen, while the complementary display renders interactive 3D models—such as gas balloons illustrating Helium—alongside immediate atomic and physical properties. This spatial split minimizes context switching, allowing users to study detailed element attributes while keeping the complete chemical landscape in full view.

Fluid adaptability across physical folding states is critical for next-generation mobile UX, requiring a UI that scales seamlessly whether the device is expanded or closed. When collapsed into a single display, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app transitions effortlessly into an optimized single-screen layout tailored for efficient one-handed interactions. The UI dynamically recalibrates high-density data cards and 3D visual assets—such as a battery representation for Lithium—while preserving high-contrast dark mode aesthetics, clean typography, and quick access to core metrics like atomic mass and electron configurations. This design strategy guarantees an uninterrupted user experience when moving from quick reference lookups to full dual-screen workflows.

Leveraging spanned viewports allows for rich, immersive modal presentations that turn standard educational reference tools into tactile 3D experiences. When inspecting complex elements like Protactinium, the application presents an enlarged central 3D viewport spanning across the hinge line, granting users tactile manipulation and detailed spatial rendering of elemental structures. Strategic positioning of translucent control overlays and background grids preserves visual hierarchy, ensuring navigation remains accessible without obstructing the visual focal point. By placing dual-screen ergonomics and responsive visual layout at the center of development, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app offers a template for modern, canvas-aware application design.

Designing for multi-screen foldables isn't just about handling dynamic screen bounds—it’s about crafting contextual spatial workflows that elevate everyday utility. Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app demonstrates how thoughtful layout architecture can transform complex educational data into an intuitive, visually rich 3D experience across both single and spanned displays. As dual-screen hardware continues to evolve, rethinking conventional interface boundaries opens exciting new possibilities for mobile design. title: Try a React component without creating a project
description:
You want to check how a hook behaves. The usual route is a new project: scaffold, install, start a dev server, delete the boilerplate. That's a lot of ceremony for twenty lines.

Today's twenty lines: a useDebouncedValue hook, the kind you write for a search box so it doesn't filter on every keystroke.

The hook 

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, ms = 250): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), ms);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);
  }, [value, ms]);

  return debounced;
}

How it works: every time value changes, the effect starts a timer. If value changes again before the timer fires, React runs the cleanup first, which cancels the old timer. So debounced only catches up once the input has been still for ms milliseconds.

Two details that bite people:

  • The cleanup is the debounce. Without return () => clearTimeout(id), every keystroke schedules an update and you've built a delay, not a debounce.
  • ms belongs in the dependency array. Leave it out and changing the delay does nothing until value changes too.

A component to try it in 

import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from "react";

// useDebouncedValue from above goes here

const fruits = ["apple", "apricot", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry", "grape", "mango"];

export default function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const debounced = useDebouncedValue(query, 300);

  const matches = useMemo(
    () => fruits.filter((f) => f.includes(debounced.toLowerCase())),
    [debounced],
  );

  return (
    <div style={{ fontFamily: "system-ui", padding: 24 }}>
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="Filter fruit"
      />
      <p>
        {matches.length} of {fruits.length} (typed: "{query}", filtering: "{debounced}")
      </p>
      <ul>
        {matches.map((f) => (
          <li key={f}>{f}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

Showing both query and debounced on screen is the trick: type fast and you can watch the second one lag behind, then snap into place.

Running it without a project

I ran this in JSLab, a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS. Click + in the tab bar and pick React: JSLab sets the tab's language, runtime and framework, installs the packages it needs, and opens starter code. Paste the file over it.

JSLab renders it into a Web View tile beside the console. Edit the JSX and it rerenders as you type. Change 300 to 1000 and you feel the difference on the next keystroke.

Here's a smaller component running the same way in a real JSLab Browser tab: a Counter mounted with createRoot, ticking in the Web View beside the code.

The console still works alongside it. Add a line like this inside the effect and the logs land in the output panel, tagged with their line:

console.log("debounced →", value);

Want styling? Turn on Tailwind in the status bar and the utility classes your code uses get compiled into the page, with nothing to install.

When to make it a real project

A scratchpad is for the question "does this hook behave the way I think?" Once the answer is yes, move it into your app with its tests. The point is not having to pay for a project before you know you need one.

JSLab launches Nov 15. The Web View and framework docs are here: https://js-lab.app/docs/web-view

title: The device test was there. CI never ran it.
description:
By October, our Maestro end-to-end testing setup for the mobile app looked well covered. Every one of the 99 routes expected to have automated device coverage had a flow in the repository. Then we traced what ran in CI.

Only 28 routes were reached by flows that CI executed. The other 71 depended on quarantined flows. That gap mattered more than the repository inventory: our release decisions needed evidence from tests that actually ran on mobile devices.

As the engineering manager, I needed to know why the existing flows weren't producing evidence before asking the team to write more.

Follow the call graph

Our Maestro end-to-end tests were assembled in layers. A leaf flow covered a product journey. Shared subflows handled repeated steps. Suite aggregates assembled journeys for a run. The cloud jobs called those aggregates.

That last connection mattered. A new leaf could be well written, reviewed, and tagged, yet never execute if no aggregate called it. A tag on the leaf did not put it into a cloud job. The path to evidence was:

CI job → suite aggregate → leaf flow → product route

If any edge was missing, the route was absent from that run. We began reviewing coverage through this path. Shared setup and suite entrypoints were useful, but they were not independent mobile journeys.

There was a second trap. A route could have a leaf flow that we had quarantined because it was unstable. That route looked covered in a repository search, but its flow supplied no evidence in the normal CI run. Our route audit kept those two states separate: a flow exists and a flow runs.

Make the run small enough to finish

Getting a flow into CI did not automatically make the suite useful. One flaky suite could stop later suites from producing results. We split nightly execution into a job per suite and platform so one failure would not erase the rest of the run.

Then a nine-leaf suite hit Maestro Cloud's 15-minute limit. Some leaves spent roughly two minutes just setting up their state. We split long suites into groups of no more than three leaves, keeping the jobs short enough to return evidence.

That constraint changed how I looked at coverage. A test that times out as part of an oversized batch is about as helpful to a release decision as a test that never starts.

Check reachability before review

We added a fast static check for the Maestro test definitions. It checked syntax, file paths, app identifiers, selectors that could not resolve, and whether a leaf was reachable from a CI entrypoint. It ran in the normal lint step, before anyone waited for a device run. Exceptions needed an explicit reason.

Device execution still told us whether a flow worked. The static check caught an earlier failure: work that looked like coverage in a pull request but had no route into the actual test run.

I stopped asking how many test files we had and started asking which release decisions those files could support. The audit left 71 routes with a clear next job: make their quarantined flows reliable and connect them to an executed suite. At least we were working from the run, rather than from the directory listing.

The fuller account, including the audit and rollout details, is in my Beyond the QA Bottleneck case study.

title: تصميم الموقع التعريفي للشركة: كيف تبني موقعًا يشرح نشاطك بوضوح ويقود الزائر إلى التواصل؟
Five MOSS ComfyUI Workflows: Baselines, Comparisons, Layout, and Color Control
description:
A comparison graph is useful only if you know what changes between its branches. Giving two samplers the same prompt does not make the resulting experiment a test of one variable. An added LoRA, a different guidance path, or an empty negative prompt can change what the comparison actually means.

This MOSS collection contains five separate ComfyUI workflows: a color-control LoRA experiment, a three-branch sampling comparison, a Base/SFT comparison, a structured-layout prompt example, and a simple SFT text-to-image starting point. Together they contain 70 nodes, including five documentation notes. They are separate JSON files, not five presets silently merged into one graph.

The following walkthrough is based on their saved nodes, values, and connections. It does not establish that the workflows have run successfully on a particular installation. The accompanying transcript describes the creator's image-comparison experience; that does not provide a new controlled benchmark or prove every claim about this exact set of exported graphs.

Shared preparation

All five graphs select qwen3.5_9b_bf16.safetensors through a CLIP loader with type moss_image, and flux2-vae.safetensors through a VAE loader. They configure EmptyFlux2LatentImage for width 1024, height 1024, and batch size 1. These are latent-input settings, not independently verified image outputs.

The common SFT model filename is moss_image_sft_int8_convrot.safetensors. Workflow 03 also selects moss_image_base_int8_convrot.safetensors. Other required weights are specific to the LoRA branches described below. The collection does not bundle weights, a tested dependency lockfile, or verified upstream download URLs. Resolve the matching node implementations and asset versions before queueing; do not treat filenames as proof of training method, quantization behavior, or licensing.

These are text-to-image examples. No LoadImage node is present in the five supplied graphs. Their promotional covers are not required inference inputs, and a cover's subject need not match the prompt currently stored in its corresponding JSON.

Several sampler arrays contain a control string in addition to the listed widget names. Rather than inventing a positional schema, this article distinguishes the authors' step/CFG descriptions in the notes from directly named controls and graph connections. Inspect the sampler UI against the installed node version before relying on a parameter mapping.

Workflow 05 — SFT text-to-image starting point

Purpose and assets. Start here if you want to inspect one straightforward generation path before comparing branches. It uses the common SFT model, encoder, and VAE, with SkipLayerGuidanceDiTSimple between the model loader and sampler.

Current configuration. The note describes the intended preset as 50 steps, CFG 3, Euler, simple, and SLG22. The SLG node itself stores double_layers="", single_layers="22", start_percent=0, and end_percent=1. The latent is configured for 1024×1024, batch 1. The positive text describes a misty mountain valley at sunrise; it is an input prompt, not a description of a verified output.

Use it. Load the graph, resolve dependencies, and edit positive text at node 6. Review negative text at node 7 and canvas controls at node 8. Inspect sampler 9 in the matching UI, then run only after those checks. Decode node 10 feeds save node 11, whose prefix is N01_SFT_50步_入门文生图_11.

Limitations. The note mentions 2K experiments and a separate preset document. Neither establishes a 2K default or an additional included file. No output, runtime, or compatibility result is claimed here.

Workflow 03 — Base versus SFT, with shared inputs

Purpose and assets. This graph is for comparing two selected model files, not proving that one model family always wins. In addition to the shared assets, it needs the Base filename listed above.

Current configuration. Nodes 7 and 12 load Base and SFT filenames respectively. Each model passes through its own SLG node. Both branches receive the same positive conditioning from node 4, negative conditioning from node 5, latent from node 6, and VAE from node 3. Their saved sampler arrays are identical: [777, "fixed", 50, 3, "euler", "simple", 1]. The note labels both branches as 50-step/CFG3/SLG22.

Use it. Edit the shared teapot-scene prompt at node 4 once, then confirm that both branches still receive it. Check the two model selections and corresponding SLG and sampler settings before running. Save nodes 11 and 16 provide separate destinations; label real results by branch rather than guessing from appearance.

Limitations. Matching stored arrays and shared links support a configuration comparison, not equal measured execution behavior. A pair of selected filenames does not demonstrate training history, overall quality rankings, or controlled results across many prompts.

Workflow 02 — Three named sampling presets, not one changed variable

Purpose and assets. This graph organizes the source's 50/8/4 comparison into three branches sharing one SFT model loader. The additional weights are MOSS_DMD_8STEP_QKV_FORGE_FIX.safetensors and moss_image_sft_4step_v2.0.safetensors.

Current configuration. The first model branch passes through SLG node 9. The other branches pass through LoRA nodes 14 and 19, each with strength_model=1. All three share positive conditioning and a configured 1024×1024 latent. However, the first branch receives the populated negative text from node 5, while the two LoRA branches receive empty negative text from node 6.

The note describes the first preset as 50 steps/CFG3 and the other two as 8 or 4 steps/CFG1. Their raw sampler arrays also differ. It would therefore be incorrect to write that only the step count changes: the model-processing paths and negative conditioning differ too.

Use it. Update the shared greenhouse-scene prompt at node 4. Confirm the two distinct LoRA selections and both negative-text sources. Inspect sampler nodes 10, 15, and 20 in the installed UI, then associate actual saved files with nodes 12, 17, and 22.

Limitations. The note explicitly leaves runtime acceptance pending after a structural simplification. The branch labels are not measured speed ratios. If you want a controlled experiment, record every changed setting, hardware details, elapsed time, and actual outputs; this export does not supply those measurements.

Workflow 04 — Structured layout as text input

Purpose and assets. This uses the shared SFT path but changes the form of the positive prompt. It does not add a visual bounding-box editor or a dedicated layout-validation stage.

Use it. Edit the JSON string at node 6 while retaining valid JSON syntax. Update each item's description, literal text, and box consistently. Review the canvas at node 8, then inspect the generated result after an actual run. Save node 11 uses prefix N04_JSON_Layout_结构化布局_11.

A syntactically valid JSON string does not guarantee that text will be rendered correctly or that every requested box will be obeyed. Choosing a starting point and recording results

Use workflow 05 for the simplest path, 03 for the paired model-file comparison, 02 to inspect three different presets, 04 for structured prompt input, and 01 for the additional color-control LoRA. These choices describe graph organization, not quality rankings.

For a useful first test, record the exact workflow, installed node and weight versions, prompt, canvas, effective sampler settings, and the output you actually inspected. title: The browser title was correct. The Open Graph title wasn’t.
description:
On 1 November 2026, an audit of the StackEndBox homepage found a small inconsistency that a browser-tab check had missed.

The HTML title already contained the company name. The Open Graph and Twitter titles still said “We design and build the software your business needs.” A separate page extractor returned that generic sentence as its page label. Its output matched the Open Graph field, while the browser tab remained correctly branded.

Both observations were accurate. They described different title sources.

Three fields, two answers

The initial page contained this combination:

<title>StackEndBox | Product Engineering, AI & Custom Software</title>
<meta property="og:title" content="We design and build the software your business needs.">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="We design and build the software your business needs.">

The release aligned the two share titles with the existing HTML title. It preserved the heading, design, canonical URL, robots directive and company schema.

Field Before After
HTML title Branded Branded
Open Graph title Generic sentence Same branded title
Twitter title Generic sentence Same branded title

This is a useful homepage policy when every surface should identify the same company. Other pages can legitimately use different social copy. Agree on a per-page expectation before turning consistency into a release gate.

Why checking only document.title misses the problem

A test that asserts document.title will pass for the initial page above. A test that uses querySelector for each metadata field can also overlook duplicate tags because it returns only the first match.

Collect every matching tag and keep the arrays intact:

const snapshot = await page.evaluate(() => ({
  title: [...document.head.querySelectorAll("title")]
    .map(el => el.textContent ?? ""),
  "og:title": [...document.head.querySelectorAll(
    'meta[property="og:title"]'
  )].map(el => el.getAttribute("content") ?? ""),
  "twitter:title": [...document.head.querySelectorAll(
    'meta[name="twitter:title"]'
  )].map(el => el.getAttribute("content") ?? "")
}));

This collection is read-only. It assumes an existing Playwright-compatible page handle and should run after the application has reached its rendered-ready state. Choose that state for your application instead of adding an arbitrary delay.

The arrays make four separate findings visible: a missing field, duplicate fields, an empty value and a value that differs from the reviewed expectation. DOM values have already decoded HTML entities, so compare the rendered ampersand with an ampersand rather than the source spelling &.

A runnable contract check

The public audit module and instructions contain a dependency-free function and eight synthetic example cases. The function accepts the snapshot above and an expected title:

const result = auditTitleSnapshot(
  snapshot,
  "StackEndBox | Product Engineering, AI & Custom Software"
);

if (!result.ok) {
  throw new Error(JSON.stringify(result.issues));
}

The examples cover aligned values, generic Open Graph copy, missing Twitter metadata, duplicate Open Graph tags, an empty title, three generic fields, surrounding whitespace and a malformed snapshot. All eight passed when executed in a JavaScript isolate. The public file includes the examples so readers can rerun them.

Those examples test the comparison contract. Collecting the correct page and waiting for its rendered state remain responsibilities of the browser test.

Verify the artifact that actually ships

This homepage uses a preserved static release. Editing future application source alone would leave the served artifact unchanged. The correction therefore covered the served response and future source, with validation around the known metadata structure.

The production change went through source checks, canonical release checks, provider preflight and hosted staging before publication. After publication, a browser reload showed exactly one of each title field with the branded value. A fresh independent fetch then returned the branded label too.

For another application, the implementation may simply be a shared metadata object. The acceptance question stays the same: does the response and rendered page that readers receive contain the reviewed values?

Keep search outcomes separate

Google documents Open Graph titles among the sources it can use for search-result title links. That makes the field worth checking alongside the HTML title and visible heading. Google chooses the resulting title automatically and has to recrawl and reprocess updates.

The metadata correction established a consistent page. It did not establish a ranking improvement. The ordinary company-name query still received a spelling substitution immediately after deployment. A title audit cannot measure indexability, Google’s interpretation of a brand query or search position.

A practical release checklist is therefore two-part: verify the page contract you control, then observe search behaviour separately. Passing one check should never silently mark the other complete.
