title: I added a free PDF Watermark tool with live preview (no sign-up)
description:
I just added a Watermark & Add Stamp tool to MyPDFLabs, my free set of online PDF tools. It's for marking a PDF as a draft, confidential or paid, or putting a logo on it, so I wanted to share what it does and what I focused on.

Why a watermark tool?

Marking a document comes up more often than you'd think:

  • Labeling a contract or proposal as DRAFT before sending it out
  • Marking a document CONFIDENTIAL
  • Stamping an invoice as PAID
  • Putting a logo on reports, handouts and certificates
  • Adding SAMPLE to a document you share as an example

Most of the tools I found wanted an account, added their own watermark, or gave me no way to see the result before downloading. I wanted something where you can see what you're doing as you go.

What it does

The tool has a controls panel on the left and a live preview of your pages on the right.

  • Two modes: Text Watermark and Image Stamp
  • Quick presets: Confidential, Draft, Sample, Do Not Copy, Paid and Urgent, or type your own text
  • Styling: colour, font size, font family and bold or regular weight
  • Opacity slider, so the mark doesn't make the page hard to read
  • Rotation: diagonal (45°), horizontal, vertical or reverse (-45°)
  • Position: center, tiled across the page, top or bottom
  • Page selection: all pages, first page only, or a custom range
  • Live preview that you can zoom and flip through before downloading

It needs no sign-up, adds no watermark of its own on the core tools, supports files up to 500MB, and deletes uploaded files automatically after processing.

What I thought about while building it

Watermarking looks simple, but a few design choices mattered:

  • Show the result before the download. Opacity, size and rotation are hard to judge from numbers, so a preview you can flip through saves a lot of trial and error.
  • Presets for the common cases. Most people want "CONFIDENTIAL" or "DRAFT" in a sensible default style, so one click should get them there.
  • Defaults should be readable. A strong mark can make a page unreadable, so the default opacity stays low.
  • Be honest about what a watermark is. It labels a document, it doesn't protect it. Someone determined can still copy text or try to remove it, so for sensitive files a password is the right tool.
  • Privacy matters. People mark contracts, invoices and IDs, so I decided not to keep files around and not to ask for an account.

What I'd like feedback on

The site is still new, so I'd love honest opinions:

  1. Are the controls clear, or is there too much on the panel?
  2. Is the live preview useful, or would you rather have fewer options and a simpler flow?
  3. Which PDF tool should I add or improve next?

You can try it here: mypdflabs.com/tools/watermark

Thanks for reading, and I'll reply to every comment.

title: I built db-studio, a free, open-source database studio you can run with npx
description:
I'm Hüsam, a software engineer in Istanbul and the solo developer behind db-studio. It's a free, open-source database studio you can run locally with one command.

npx db-studio

Every database. One studio.

Browse tables, edit records, run queries, and explore schema diagrams in the same app. There's also a desktop app if you prefer a dedicated window.

Start with your existing database

Run the command from your project directory. db-studio looks for a DATABASE_URL in your project's .env file or environment. If it doesn't find one, you can paste a connection URL on the Connect page.

Open the local address printed in the terminal. You don't need to create a hosted account.

Connections are saved locally, and the CLI and desktop app share the same list. Each browser tab keeps its own connection, so you can work with different databases side by side.

Edit data like a spreadsheet

The latest update adds these editing workflows:

  • Select a range of cells, copy it with headers, and paste cells from a spreadsheet.
  • Review unsaved edits, revert a single cell, or undo with Cmd/Ctrl+Z.
  • Choose explicitly between NULL, empty text, and a column's default value.
  • Copy a row as JSON or a SQL INSERT statement.
  • Duplicate a row from its menu.

Editing and schema capabilities depend on the engine. For example, ClickHouse tables are read-only in the grid, while explicit mutations remain available in the query editor. A saved connection can also open read-only when its engine supports it.

Work across nine database engines

db-studio supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, SQLite, Redis, DuckDB, Oracle, and ClickHouse.

You can also connect to MariaDB, CockroachDB, TiDB, Turso/libSQL, and Cloudflare D1 through their supported engines.

The interface follows the database's data model. MongoDB has collections, and Redis has key types. Available operations vary with the database.

Queries, schemas, and optional AI

The query editor has syntax highlighting and autocomplete. You can save queries and inspect results as a table or JSON. Import and export support CSV, Excel, and JSON.

For relational databases, schema diagrams help you see how tables connect. You can also browse related records through foreign keys.

AI assistance is optional and uses your own provider key. It can help write, explain, optimize, or fix queries.

Both screenshots show the real app running against a local demo database.

Try it and tell me what needs work

db-studio is free under Apache 2.0. I build and maintain the database adapters, API, interface, CLI, and desktop app. Contributions and bug reports are welcome.

Website and documentation · Source code

Which database would you try first, and what's one task you'd want db-studio to make easier?

title: Is Sellzivo Legit or a Scam? An Honest Look Before You Buy
description:
Is Sellzivo Legit or a Scam? An Honest Look Before You Buy

Short answer

Sellzivo is a real, live online store that sells discounted AI tools and software subscriptions. It is not a fake storefront with no product behind it: the shop at sellzivo.com/shop is live, orders go through a real checkout, and support runs through its Telegram shop. That said, it is an independent reseller, it is a relatively new store, and its products are digital — so it is worth understanding exactly what you are buying before you pay. This article sticks to verifiable facts, not hype.

What Sellzivo actually is

Sellzivo is a digital store for AI tools and software subscriptions — things like ChatGPT, Canva, Notion, Adobe, ElevenLabs and similar tools — sold as team seats and premium plans, with instant delivery and guest checkout. You can pay by card or crypto, and there is a reseller program for people who want to sell the same products themselves.

The business is based in South Jordan, Utah, United States. Its contact email is support@sellzivo.com, its shop is at https://sellzivo.com/shop, and its Telegram shop is https://t.me/sellzivobot.

Sellzivo is an independent reseller and is not affiliated with ChatGPT, Canva, Notion, Adobe, ElevenLabs, or any other brand it sells. That matters: you are buying a seat, plan, or access arrangement through a reseller, not buying directly from the brand itself.

How buying from Sellzivo works

  1. Browse the shop and open the product page for the plan you want. Read the full description on that page — it tells you what kind of access you are getting.
  2. Check out as a guest on the website, or order through the Telegram shop.
  3. Delivery is instant in the normal case, and the delivery details are shown on the product page.
  4. If anything is unclear, ask support on Telegram before you pay, not after.

That last point is the most useful habit with any reseller: a genuine seller can explain, before payment, exactly what you will receive.

Checks anyone can do in two minutes

  • Open the shop yourself: https://sellzivo.com/shop. A scam storefront usually cannot sustain a full, browsable catalog with working product pages.
  • Check the support route: https://t.me/sellzivobot. Be careful with lookalikes — only the official shop link and the official bot are Sellzivo. Anyone messaging you from a different handle claiming to be Sellzivo is not verified.
  • Read the refund policy before you buy. Sellzivo's policy is no returns and no refunds on digital products. That is a strict policy, and it is stated openly — but it also means you should be sure about the product before paying, because there is no change-of-mind refund.
  • Start small. If you are trying Sellzivo for the first time, buy one product first, confirm delivery and access work as described, and only then buy more.

The honest limitations

No honest "is it legit" article should skip the downsides, so here they are:

  • Sellzivo is a newer store, not a decade-old retailer. Newer does not mean fake, but it does mean there is less long-term track record to lean on.
  • Products are digital, so the usual "return it in the box" safety net does not exist. The no-returns, no-refunds policy is the trade-off for the lower price.
  • Some products are coupon codes or seats for your own account, and those need to be redeemed promptly after purchase. Read the product page for any activation window.
  • Because Sellzivo resells rather than owns these brands, availability and plan details can change. The product page at the time you buy is the description that counts.

None of that is, on its own, a sign of a scam. It is the normal shape of a discount reseller — and it is exactly why the "read the page, ask first, start small" advice matters.

Red flags that would change the answer

If any of these showed up, it would be a reason to stop and stay away: a seller asking you to pay to a personal wallet or account outside the official shop, a "Sellzivo" account on Telegram or social media that is not linked from sellzivo.com, pressure to pay quickly for a "today only" deal that is not on the shop itself, or a refusal to explain what access you will receive before payment. As of this writing, the official shop and bot do not work that way.

Verdict

Is Sellzivo legit? On the publicly verifiable facts — a live store, a working checkout, a named support channel, and an openly stated digital-products policy — yes, it is a legitimate reseller storefront, not a scam site. Is it risk-free? No reseller purchase is. Go in with the checklist above: use only the official shop and bot, read the product page, understand the no-refund policy, and start with a single order.

Shop: https://sellzivo.com/shop — Telegram: https://t.me/sellzivobot — Contact: support@sellzivo.com

title: Shift‑Left Testing: Bringing Quality Forward in the Development Pipeline
description:
In modern software delivery, waiting until the end of a sprint—or worse, production—to discover defects is both expensive and demoralizing. Shift‑left testing flips that model by embedding quality activities early, where they can be acted upon quickly and cheaply. Below is a practical guide to adopting the mindset and habits that make early testing effective without discarding the valuable role of dedicated QA.

The Core Idea

  • Test earlier, not just more – Quality isn’t a phase; it’s a continuous activity. Involving QA during requirements gathering and design catches misunderstandings before any code is written.
  • Cost curve argument – The classic defect cost curve shows that fixing a bug in design can be 10‑100× cheaper than fixing the same bug after release. Early detection reduces rework, shortens feedback loops, and protects the budget.

Where It Starts

  • QA in requirement reviews – Bring a QA representative into backlog refinement and requirement workshops. Their perspective highlights ambiguous language, missing edge cases, and non‑functional expectations that developers might overlook.
  • Unit tests written with the code – Encourage developers to write unit tests alongside implementation, not as an afterthought. When the same person who writes the logic also defines its verification, the test suite stays tightly coupled to the intended behavior.

Practical Habits

  • Three Amigos sessions – Regularly schedule short meetings where the developer, QA, and product owner align on acceptance criteria. Translating user stories into concrete, testable statements ensures everyone shares the same definition of “done.”
  • CI runs tests on every commit – Configure the CI pipeline to execute unit, integration, and contract tests on each push. Immediate feedback (often within minutes) lets the team correct regressions before they accumulate, keeping the codebase healthy throughout the sprint.

What It Is Not

  • Not eliminating QA – Shift‑left does not replace dedicated testing roles. QA expertise is still essential for exploratory testing, usability assessments, and complex scenario coverage that automation cannot fully emulate.
  • Not skipping later‑stage testing – Early testing complements, not substitutes, regression, performance, and security testing performed closer to release. The goal is a layered safety net, not a single checkpoint.

Do / Avoid

Do

  • Involve QA at requirements/design stage, not just before release.
  • Write acceptance criteria as testable statements up front.
  • Run automated checks on every commit, not just nightly.

Avoid

  • Treating shift‑left as “developers test, so QA isn’t needed.”
  • Skipping late‑stage regression just because you shifted left.
  • Bolting “shift‑left” onto a process where nothing else changed; the whole workflow must adapt to early feedback.

Shift‑left testing isn’t a shortcut—it’s a disciplined expansion of quality practices that saves time, money, and frustration by catching problems where they’re cheapest to fix.

title: Wire Supabase Auth and Database into Next.js App Router
description:
The Problem

Wiring Supabase into a Next.js App Router project looks simple until server components return stale sessions, middleware breaks auth refresh, or row-level security gets skipped entirely. This guide covers the full integration with the gotchas that actually bite.

Create the Supabase Project

Sign up at supabase.com and create a project in a region near your users. The free tier gives 500 MB database, 1 GB storage, 2 GB egress, and 50,000 monthly active auth users.

From the API settings grab three values:

  • SUPABASE_URL: the project's API endpoint
  • SUPABASE_ANON_KEY: public client-side key (safe to ship)
  • SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY: server-side admin key (never expose to the browser)

Install SDK and Configure Environment 

npm install @supabase/supabase-js @supabase/ssr

Add to .env.local:

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJ...your-anon-key
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=eyJ...your-service-role-key

The NEXT_PUBLIC_* prefix exposes variables to the browser. The service role key has no prefix because it must stay server-side.

Create Three Supabase Clients

Next.js 16 with the App Router needs a server client, a browser client, and a middleware client.

lib/supabase/server.ts:

import { createServerClient } from '@supabase/ssr';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';

export async function createClient() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  return createServerClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!,
    {
      cookies: {
        getAll: () => cookieStore.getAll(),
        setAll: (cookiesToSet) => {
          cookiesToSet.forEach(({ name, value, options }) => {
            cookieStore.set(name, value, options);
          });
        },
      },
    }
  );
}

lib/supabase/client.ts:

import { createBrowserClient } from '@supabase/ssr';

export function createClient() {
  return createBrowserClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!
  );
}

middleware.ts at project root:

import { createServerClient } from '@supabase/ssr';
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export async function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  let response = NextResponse.next({ request });
  const supabase = createServerClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!,
    {
      cookies: {
        getAll: () => request.cookies.getAll(),
        setAll: (cookiesToSet) => {
          cookiesToSet.forEach(({ name, value, options }) => {
            response.cookies.set(name, value, options);
          });
        },
      },
    }
  );
  await supabase.auth.getUser();
  return response;
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
};

The middleware refreshes the auth session on every request. Without it, server components see stale sessions.

Wire Auth Into the Template

Replace template auth handlers with Supabase calls.

Login handler:

'use server';
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';

export async function login(formData: FormData) {
  const supabase = await createClient();
  const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({
    email: formData.get('email') as string,
    password: formData.get('password') as string,
  });
  if (error) return { error: error.message };
  redirect('/dashboard');
}

Signup handler:

export async function signup(formData: FormData) {
  const supabase = await createClient();
  const { error } = await supabase.auth.signUp({
    email: formData.get('email') as string,
    password: formData.get('password') as string,
    options: { emailRedirectTo: `${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL}/auth/callback` },
  });
  if (error) return { error: error.message };
  redirect('/auth/check-email');
}

OAuth (Google example):

export async function signInWithGoogle() {
  const supabase = await createClient();
  const { data } = await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({
    provider: 'google',
    options: { redirectTo: `${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL}/auth/callback` },
  });
  if (data.url) redirect(data.url);
}

Callback route at app/auth/callback/route.ts:

import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server';
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

export async function GET(request: Request) {
  const { searchParams, origin } = new URL(request.url);
  const code = searchParams.get('code');
  if (code) {
    const supabase = await createClient();
    await supabase.auth.exchangeCodeForSession(code);
  }
  return NextResponse.redirect(`${origin}/dashboard`);
}

Enable OAuth providers in the Supabase dashboard under Authentication > Providers.

Query Database from Server Components

Server components run on the server, so database calls happen inside the Vercel function: no API route needed for read-only views.

import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server';

export default async function ProjectsPage() {
  const supabase = await createClient();
  const { data: projects, error } = await supabase
    .from('projects')
    .select('*, tasks(count)')
    .order('created_at', { ascending: false });

  if (error) throw new Error(error.message);

  return (
    <div>
      {projects.map((p) => (
        <div key={p.id}>{p.name}</div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

Enable Row-Level Security

This is the step most teams skip. Without RLS, your anon key gives the browser unrestricted access to every table.

For a projects table where each project belongs to a user:

-- Enable RLS on the table
alter table projects enable row level security;

-- Allow users to select only their own projects
create policy "Users can view their own projects"
  on projects for select
  using ( auth.uid() = user_id );

-- Allow users to insert projects with their own user_id
create policy "Users can insert their own projects"
  on projects for insert
  with check ( auth.uid() = user_id );

-- Allow users to update their own projects
create policy "Users can update their own projects"
  on projects for update
  using ( auth.uid() = user_id );

-- Allow users to delete their own projects
create policy "Users can delete their own projects"
  on projects for delete
  using ( auth.uid() = user_id );

Run this in the Supabase SQL editor for every table with user-specific data. Test by hitting the API with the anon key from a logged-out browser tab: every query should return empty.

File Uploads via Supabase Storage

Create a storage bucket in the dashboard. Set to "private" for user-uploaded files (avatars, attachments).

Upload from a client component:

'use client';
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/client';

async function uploadAvatar(file: File, userId: string) {
  const supabase = createClient();
  const fileName = `${userId}/${Date.now()}-${file.name}`;
  const { data, error } = await supabase.storage
    .from('avatars')
    .upload(fileName, file, { upsert: true });
  if (error) throw error;
  return data.path;
}

Get a signed URL for displaying a private file:

const { data } = await supabase.storage
  .from('avatars')
  .createSignedUrl(filePath, 3600); // 1 hour expiry

Set storage policies the same way as table policies: every bucket should have RLS scoping access to the owning user.

Realtime Subscriptions (Optional)

For live features: kanban boards, chat, presence: Supabase realtime is the fastest path.

'use client';
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/client';

export function LiveTasks({ projectId }: { projectId: string }) {
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState([]);
  const supabase = createClient();

  useEffect(() => {
    const channel = supabase
      .channel(`tasks:${projectId}`)
      .on(
        'postgres_changes',
        { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'tasks', filter: `project_id=eq.${projectId}` },
        (payload) => {
          // Handle insert, update, delete
          console.log(payload);
        }
      )
      .subscribe();

    return () => {
      supabase.removeChannel(channel);
    };
  }, [projectId]);

  return <div>...</div>;
}

Realtime requires enabling replication on the table in the Supabase dashboard. Without it, the subscription succeeds but no events fire.

Common Gotchas

Forgetting RLS. The biggest security risk. Default-deny by enabling RLS, then add specific allow policies. Never ship with RLS off.

Server vs browser client confusion. The server client uses cookies for session; the browser client uses in-memory session. Mixing them causes "user is null" bugs that look like broken auth.

Skipping the middleware. Without auth-refreshing middleware, server components see stale or expired sessions. Symptoms: random logouts, "user is null" after navigation.

Service role key in client code. The service role key bypasses RLS. It must only run on the server. Putting it in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable or referencing it from a client component is a critical security incident.

Forgetting emailRedirectTo for signups. Without it, Supabase redirects to its own confirmation page, which doesn't carry the session into your app. Always specify the redirect.

Real-time without replication enabled. Subscribing to changes on a table without replication means silent failure. Enable replication in the dashboard for every table you subscribe to.

Free tier limits. 500 MB database, 1 GB storage, 2 GB egress. Easy to hit if you store user-uploaded files without CDN caching. Plan for Pro tier ($25/month) once you have meaningful users.

title: Idempotency keys: the boring header that saves the queue
description:
Every payment API has it, and almost no internal service does. Idempotency keys are the cheapest way to make a queue safe.

The shape I use in Go:

  • the client sends Idempotency-Key with the request
  • a middleware checks a dedupe table keyed by (key, route)
  • if it exists, return the stored response
  • if not, process, store the result with a TTL, then return

The subtle parts: store the response, not just the status; set the TTL to something longer than your retry window; and make the check-and-insert atomic, or two workers will race and both process.

The win is that at-least-once delivery becomes safe without changing the queue. The cost is one small table and a header.

I'd argue every handler that touches money or email should have one. What's the smallest service where you'd skip it?

title: How to Plan a Website Structure Before Development
description:
A sitemap drawn after the design is often a record of decisions that have already been made. A useful site structure starts earlier: it connects visitor tasks to pages, content types, navigation, and the work needed to launch each part.

The output should be understandable to a designer, developer, content editor, and project owner. It need not begin as a polished diagram. A shared table, a simple hierarchy, and a few realistic task flows can expose missing content and confusing labels before they become expensive to change.

Separate the artifacts

These pieces describe different aspects of the same site:

  • A page inventory records what exists or is planned, why it exists, who owns it, and its status.
  • A hierarchy groups pages and shows their primary relationships.
  • Navigation and contextual links show how a person can move between pages.
  • A content model describes recurring objects and fields, such as services, products, or articles.
  • URLs and migration mappings identify addresses and record what should happen when an existing address changes.

A working page map is not the same artifact as an XML sitemap used by search engines. Also, an item's URL path does not need to reproduce every menu relationship. Agree on each artifact deliberately rather than using one diagram to answer every question.

Start with journeys, not department names

Write the organization's objective and the visitor's task separately. “Receive inquiries” is a business objective. “Understand the repair options and find a way to book” is a visitor task.

List the information needed to complete each task and the likely starting points. Someone may enter on a specific service page from a search result, arrive at the homepage from a recommendation, or return directly to a contact page. A design that only works when everyone starts at the homepage will miss those other routes.

Use actual questions from customer support, interviews, site search, or existing analytics when available. If those sources don't exist yet, record assumptions as assumptions. Ask stakeholders what they need the site to support, then validate the language and paths with representative users.

Build an inventory with purpose and ownership

The following is a fictional example for a bicycle workshop. It illustrates a planning method; it does not describe a real business or measured behavior.

ID Page Visitor task Related page Launch?
P01 Home Understand the offering and choose a path Services and contact Yes
P02 Services Compare available work Individual services Yes
P03 Bike inspection Understand scope and terms Booking Yes
P04 Maintenance Choose an appropriate service Booking Yes
P05 Booking Select a way to contact the workshop Services and contact Yes
P06 Contact Find location and hours Main navigation Yes
P07 Care guides Learn to maintain a bicycle Related services Later

Add the content owner, source materials, dependencies, and acceptance criteria to your real inventory. For an existing site, include the current URL and a proposed decision: keep, update, merge, or remove after review.

Ask a simple question of every row: who needs this page, and what will they do after reading it? A page with no clear purpose or owner might be unnecessary in the first release. On the other hand, a small but essential page may be missing from a diagram built only around marketing sections.

Group by visitor language

Organize content according to tasks and concepts your audience recognizes. Internal reporting lines may not be useful navigation labels. “Services,” “Delivery,” and “Contact” may be clearer than an organization's internal team names, but the right words should be checked with the people who will use them.

For the fictional workshop, one possible primary hierarchy is:

  • Home
  • Services
    • Bike inspection
    • Maintenance
  • Booking
  • Contact
  • Care guides, in a later phase

The tree describes primary relationships, not all permitted journeys. A service page can link directly to booking, and a guide can link to a relevant service where appropriate. Do not add levels merely to make a diagram symmetrical, and don't treat a particular number of clicks as proof of usability. Test whether the available choices make sense for the task.

Design paths beyond the menu

Take three important tasks and write the route from a plausible entry page to a result. For example:

  1. A visitor lands on “Bike inspection.”
  2. They can see the actual scope and terms.
  3. They follow a clearly labeled link to booking.
  4. They choose an available contact method.
  5. The system explains what happened after submission or what to do if it failed.

Now try the same task from the services listing and the contact page. Can the visitor return to compare services without losing context? Are there pages with no sensible onward route?

Main navigation should expose the stable major directions. Contextual links support a specific task within a page. Search and filters can help with larger collections, but they don't repair unclear category names or incomplete content. On narrow screens and with keyboard navigation, preserve access to the same important destinations and check the labels and focus order.

Define page types before estimating templates

A “service” might contain a title, summary, work included, terms, relevant images, and a booking link. A “product” might require a name, price, images, availability, and attributes used in filters. An “article” might have a title, body, author when applicable, date, and related content.

For every field, record whether it is required, who can edit it, where the information comes from, and what happens when it is missing. A template can serve many pages without making their content identical. List relationships too: for example, which service a guide refers to, or which categories can contain a product.

This model reveals dependencies. A category filter cannot be designed responsibly before someone agrees on the underlying product attributes. A service page may depend on approved terms. An import may require existing records to be cleaned up before development can be estimated.

Set URL rules and plan a migration

Agree on readable, stable addressing rules for new pages and on who can change them. For an existing site, prepare a mapping from old addresses to their intended new destinations. Decide which pages remain, merge, or retire; implement suitable redirects where appropriate and test the final destinations and internal links.

Similar or filtered URLs deserve a decision rather than an automatic proliferation of pages. Identify which variations have a user purpose and coordinate search requirements with the navigation design. Search visibility is one consideration; it should not override the need for a coherent visitor journey.

Test the structure before visual design is final

Give participants who resemble the intended audience a task such as “Find the conditions for a bike inspection.” Let them choose among the proposed labels without coaching them. A text-only hierarchy or simple clickable prototype is enough to reveal many naming and grouping problems.

Record where a participant starts, which labels they choose, and what they expected to find. If several people look in the same unexpected place, consider whether the label, grouping, or missing cross-link caused the confusion. Revise the specific issue and test again.

A small qualitative session helps uncover problems; it is not statistical proof that every visitor will behave the same way. Include real content lengths, narrow screens, and keyboard use when checking a more complete prototype.

Hand off a maintained decision set

Before development begins, provide the team with:

  • An agreed page inventory and hierarchy with stable identifiers.
  • Key tasks, entry points, links, and expected results.
  • Content types, required fields, relationships, and editing responsibilities.
  • URL conventions and a migration map when replacing an existing site.
  • Content sources, external dependencies, and the scope of the first release.
  • Acceptance tasks for navigation, search, forms, and smaller screens.

Assign an owner for the map and a process for new pages after launch. A structure can evolve, but unreviewed additions should not quietly create duplicate sections or leave important content unlinked.

Start with one page inventory and three real visitor tasks. A clear route through a modest first release is more useful than a large diagram whose pages have no content owner or purpose.

title: The AI Was Never the Hard Part
description:
Twenty-four articles. One agent. A lot of things I got wrong before I got them right.

This one isn't about code. It's about what I'd tell myself at article 1 if I could go back.

I thought the model was the hard part

It isn't. Spring AI handles the model. You call chatClient.prompt().user(message).call().content() and it works. Five lines.

The hard part is everything around that call. How do you pass context without spending a fortune on tokens? What happens when a tool fails mid-conversation? How do you know if the response is actually correct? How do you ship without putting your API key in git?

Those questions have nothing to do with AI. They're the same questions you'd ask about any external service you're integrating with. I wasted the first few articles thinking I needed to understand the model better. I should have been thinking about the backend.

I should have built the eval dataset first

This is the biggest regret.

I built the eval dataset in article 23. Twenty-two articles after I made my first API call. Before that, every time I changed a prompt or adjusted a tool, I was testing by hand — send a message, read the response, guess whether it was better or worse.

That's not testing. That's hoping.

The eval dataset forces you to define what "correct" means before you build anything. Once you have it, changing the system prompt goes from "seems okay?" to "pass rate held at 87%." The difference is enormous. I'd build five test cases in article 1 if I started again — even dumb ones. Anything is better than nothing.

The tool design mistake I kept making

Early tools returned verbose JSON. Something like:

{
  "city": "Mysore",
  "weather": "partly cloudy",
  "temperature": "24°C",
  "humidity": "68%",
  "lastUpdated": "2026-09-27T10:30:00"
}

That structure replays in every subsequent message in the conversation. The model doesn't need it. It can read "Mysore: 24°C, partly cloudy, 68% humidity" just as well — and that's 60% fewer tokens in every follow-up turn.

I changed this late. By the time I got to the cost optimisation article, I'd been paying for bloated tool returns for weeks. Small thing, big compounding effect.

The other tool mistake: throwing exceptions. A tool that throws NoRouteException crashes the agent and surfaces a 500 to the user. A tool that returns "No direct route found between Mumbai and Mysore" lets the model acknowledge the gap and keep going. I had to learn this the hard way — an exception in getTicketPrice that took down the whole conversation before I caught it.

Log tokens from day one

I added token logging in article 20. I should have added it in article 2.

Every request logs inputTokens and outputTokens. Without that data, you're guessing where the cost is going. When I finally queried the averages after a few days of traffic, the breakdown was immediately obvious: history was 45% of every request, the system prompt was another 25%. Together they were 70% of input tokens — and both were fixable with no change to output quality.

But I didn't know that until I measured it. If I'd been logging from the start, I would have caught it much earlier and built with more cost awareness from the beginning.

Memory architecture matters more than model choice

Swapping models changes the quality of responses. Getting memory wrong breaks the agent.

A conversation window that's too big makes every request expensive. A window that's too small makes the agent forget context three turns in. Finding the right size — 10 messages in this case — required thinking carefully about actual user behaviour, not just picking a number.

I spent more time tuning the model and its prompts than I spent thinking about memory. In hindsight, that's backwards. RedisChatMemory with a sensible window size was the most impactful architectural decision in the whole project. The model barely matters if the context management is wrong.

What I'd do differently

Build the eval dataset first. Log tokens from the first API call. Use TravelToolsPort as an interface from article 3, not article 23 — testability from the start, not retrofitted later. Think about MCP earlier — not because local @Tool methods are wrong, but because understanding the coupling between the agent and its tools changes how you design tool boundaries.

Everything else I'd keep. The bottom-up approach — one concept per article, each building on the last — was right. Spring AI's abstractions are at the right level. Starting small was right.

The short version

AI backend engineering is backend engineering. The model is the new external service — you call it, handle its failures, measure its cost, and test against it. Everything else is the same: interfaces, observability, evaluation, operational readiness.

Start small. Measure everything. Build testability in from the start. The AI-specific parts follow the same principles as the rest.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Calling an external service from Kafka Streams: size the threads, budget every call
description:
You have a Kafka Streams application, and one step needs an answer from somewhere else. It might be an AI model's decision, a fraud score, an address to geocode or a status from a provider's API. The most direct way to write it is a blocking call inside a mapValues:

stream.mapValues(value -> {
    HttpResponse<String> answer = http.send(requestFor(value), BodyHandlers.ofString());
    return withAnswer(value, answer.body());
});

This is where most applications start. It is kept bare on purpose: no timeout, no retries, no error handling.

What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams showed what such a call can do to a thread's place in the group, run by run. This post is the other half: what to do about it. A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call, so we start by sizing the threads for it. Then we give every call an upper limit, and keep the slow step from holding up the rest of the stream.

Size the threads for the call

Kafka Streams gives each input partition a task and spreads the tasks over its threads, as the previous post opens with. A thread processes its tasks' records one at a time, so a blocking call blocks the thread it runs on.

Our runs called a stub, a small HTTP server of ours that stands in for the service. It waits a set time and answers. Everything else was real: a broker, a Kafka Streams application, HTTP calls over the network, and real vulnerability records, CVEs (how we measured). The first run had three partitions and one thread, so three tasks took turns on it. The arithmetic is short: at 300 ms a call, a thread does 3.3 records a second, however fast records arrive. With 600 records arriving at 20 a second, we measured 3.2 to 3.4 a second, and the stub never saw more than one call in flight.

More partitions alone do not help. A repartition to 32 before the call gives the calling step 32 tasks, and so does an input topic of 32 partitions, which is what we measured. With the same single thread, it still did 3.3 records a second, one call at a time.

It needs threads as well: 32 stream threads (num.stream.threads), one per task of the calling step, counted across all the application's instances. At 300 ms a call, we measured 3.3 records a second with one thread, 26 with eight and 106 with 32. With 32, the stub saw 32 calls in flight at once. Of a backlog of 3,393 records, 3,247 were done after 35 seconds. The rest took until 50 seconds. The records were spread unevenly over the 32 partitions, so as the emptier ones ran out, their threads went idle and the fullest finished alone.

How many threads a stream needs follows from Little's law: calls in flight equal the input rate times the call time. What a number of threads can do, and how fast they clear a backlog, is then one division and one subtraction. With the numbers of our runs:

calls in flight = input rate × call time
                    = 25 a second × 0.3 s = 7.5, so at least 8 threads

capacity = threads ÷ call time
  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 27 a second (measured 26.4)
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 107 a second (measured 106)

backlog drains = capacity − input
  8 threads = 26.4 − 25 = 1.4 a second
  32 threads = 106 − 25 = 81 a second

service paused 45 s = 45 s × 25 a second ≈ 1,100 records
  8 threads = 1,100 ÷ 1.4 a second ≈ 13 minutes
  32 threads = 1,100 ÷ 81 a second ≈ 14 s (measured about 15)

The pause is from our last run. We paused the service for 45 seconds, and the backlog grew to about 1,100 records.

Eight threads only just keep up. The threads beyond that are headroom. Headroom is what clears a backlog, whatever builds it: a pause in the service, as in our run, a slow minute of it, a spike in the input or a restart. Headroom also covers a slower service. At 600 ms a call:

  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 13 a second, below the input
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 53 a second, above it

With 8 threads, the lag would grow by about 12 records a second. With 32, it would still drain.

Is the stream keeping up?

Once a stream runs, the consumer group's lag tells you whether that sizing still holds. With Kafka Streams the lag needs reading with care.

Operators watch a consumer group's lag: the LAG column of kafka-consumer-groups --describe, or a lag exporter's line on a Grafana dashboard. That lag comes from the group's committed offsets, and Kafka Streams commits only every commit.interval.ms, 30 seconds by default. So a stream that keeps up does not show zero lag. Between commits the committed offset stays put while records keep arriving, so the lag climbs. At each commit it drops. A stream that kept up with 25 records a second showed a lag climbing to about 750, which is 25 a second times 30 seconds. It dropped to almost nothing at each commit, every 30 seconds.

A dashboard reads this curve at its own interval. Read every 20 seconds, the dashed line, the same healthy stream jumps between about 230 and 750. A reading just after a commit could show almost zero, but most readings show hundreds.

The next chart adds a slow stream. It had a 300 ms call and received the same 25 records a second as the healthy one. It got through only 3.3 of them a second, one thread's worth at 300 ms a call. Its committed lag climbed to about 3,000 in 135 seconds and never came back down.

Lowering commit.interval.ms makes the teeth smaller, but each commit is work. The thread flushes its producer and its store caches and writes its offsets to the broker, and it processes nothing meanwhile. Raising it to commit less often has a cost of its own for slow calls, which What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams measures.

Give every call an upper limit

Sizing the threads used the typical call time. The rules in the next section start from a different number: the longest a call can take, every retry included. We call it the call’s budget. Without one, no setting keeps a thread in its group. A single call that never ends outlasts any poll interval.

The budget is the whole call, not one setting. It is the time to connect, the wait for the answer, the time to read the answer's body, every retry, and the backoff between retries. A client that tries four times with a 5-second timeout and a second of backoff between tries has a budget of about 23 seconds, not 5.

A timeout on the request is not always that budget. We checked the JDK's own HttpClient, on Java 25, against our stub, with a 5-second request timeout. When the service sent nothing for 10 seconds, the call ended at 5.01 seconds. When it sent its headers at once and its body over 20 seconds, the call did not end. It returned normally after 20.05 seconds, with the whole body. The Javadoc says only that the timeout fires "if the response is not received within the specified timeout".

What ended that call was a deadline around the whole of it:

HttpResponse<String> callWithin(HttpRequest request, Duration budget) throws Exception {
    CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> call =
            http.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
    try {
        return call.get(budget.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        call.cancel(true);
        throw e;
    }
}

The caller was free at 5.02 seconds. The cancel also closed the connection: the stub's next write, a second later, failed.

Retries go inside the same deadline. Each try gets what is left of the budget, so the budget stays one number.

With another client. We ran one client, one call per case, and no retries. Check two things. Does its timeout end a call whose body arrives slowly? If not, put a deadline around the call. Does cancelling stop the call, or only free the caller?

The arithmetic on the budget

A stream thread has to call poll() at least every max.poll.interval.ms, 300 seconds by default, or the group takes its tasks away in a rebalance. So two limits apply between two polls, and each is a number of calls times the budget:

round = tasks per thread × budget
poll's worth = max.poll.records × budget

A round is a call for each of the thread's tasks. One poll returns up to max.poll.records records, a poll's worth. How many of them the thread works through before it polls again depends on its history: while the service is fast, Kafka Streams lets it take more. A cap on max.poll.records bounds that, whatever the history. The consumer's Javadoc gives the setting this job: to bound "the maximum that must be handled within each poll interval". Keep both under half of the poll interval, 150 seconds by default. The other half is margin: when an instance goes away, its tasks move to the others, and their rounds grow.

For the stream we measured, 25 CVEs a second at 300 ms a call on 8 threads, with a 2-second budget:

round
  8 partitions = 1 × 2 s = 2 s, under 150
  32 partitions = 4 × 2 s = 8 s, under 150

poll's worth
  1,000, the default = 1,000 × 2 s = 2,000 s, far over 300
  75 = 75 × 2 s = 150 s, just half

So max.poll.records can be at most 150 s ÷ 2 s, 75. Set it there, or lower.

The bound assumes every call takes its whole budget. That is not rare: when the service slows down, it slows down for every call at once. And even at the typical 300 ms, the default 1,000 records take 300 seconds, the whole poll interval.

Tasks per thread is the calling step's partitions over its threads, all instances counted. Leave commit.interval.ms at its default. If you raise it above a round, keep the round under a third of the poll interval instead.

The table adds two more services. Their numbers are calculated, not measured: we did not run them. Their threads come from the typical call, by Little's law. Their two limits come from the budget. In the CVE column the rate, the call time and the threads are our runs, and the budget is an example.

Fraud score CVE severity, our runs AI model decision
Records a second 200 25 5
Typical call 50 ms 300 ms 3 s
Calls in flight, rate × typical call 10 7.5 15
Threads, one task each 12 8 16
Budget, retries included 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Round, with one task per thread 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Poll's worth: max.poll.records, at most 150 s ÷ budget 300 75 7

Even the fast service needs max.poll.records cut, from 1,000 to 300. The AI model allows only 7 records a poll. That is the price of a 20-second budget, short of raising the poll interval.

Break either limit and the cost is not lag. The thread is evicted, its tasks start again from the last commit, and every call since then is made again. If the service charges per call, you pay each time. We ran three tasks on one thread with a 12-second call, against a poll interval scaled down to 30 seconds. The thread was evicted four times in 210 seconds and never committed, and the output held 17 records for 7 CVEs, where each CVE should give one. What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams shows each bound run by run, and weighs the other levers, raising the poll interval among them.

Keep the slow step in its own stream

Threads are shared by all the steps of one application. So a fast step whose task lands on a thread with a slow one waits behind its calls. Two applications keep them apart. The first does the fast work and writes the records that need an answer to a topic. The second reads that topic, makes the call and routes the result. In our example, the first stream keeps the new CVEs that arrive without a severity score from their CNA, the organisation that assigned the CVE. The second asks the service for one.

The two-stream design.

The last run tested that, and the timeout, together. The first stream passed records on with no call. The second, with 32 threads, called the service. With records arriving at 25 a second, we paused the service for 45 seconds. With a 60-second timeout, the second stream simply waited out the pause, and its backlog grew to about 1,100. When the service came back, it caught up at about 100 a second in about 15 seconds. Nothing failed, and nothing rebalanced. With a 5-second timeout, 31 calls timed out together. The second stream went to ERROR, the client state that means it has stopped for good: Kafka Streams does not restart it, even after the service is back. In both runs the first stream never noticed.

The 5-second run stopped because of a default: a single call that throws sends the whole client to ERROR, with no retry, and a single connection error does the same. KIP-1033 added a handler in Kafka 3.9 that can change that policy. What to change it to, skipping the record, retrying it or sending it to a dead-letter topic, is a subject of its own. Until you have one, set the budget from what the service needs, not shorter.

Why not a separate worker

Another common way to handle a slow call is to take it out of Kafka Streams entirely. In our example, stream B would become a worker: a separate program of your own, built on a plain Kafka consumer rather than on Kafka Streams. It reads severity-requests, calls the service with many requests in flight at once, and writes the decided records to cve-decided.

Stream B needs a thread for every call in flight, because each call blocks its thread. A worker can use an asynchronous client instead: one thread sends many requests and handles each answer as it comes. For a very slow service that matters. At 25 records a second and 20 seconds a call, Little's law asks for 500 calls in flight: 500 threads and 500 partitions for stream B, a few threads for a worker.

In exchange, the worker has to do itself what Kafka Streams does for stream B, and all of it comes from the many calls it holds open. They finish in any order. So it commits an offset only when every earlier record of the partition is done, and keeps the order within a partition where that matters. And when it stops, or hands a partition to another instance, it has to finish or abandon the calls still open. Abandoned calls are made again by whoever reads the partition next.

It is also a second kind of application to watch. Its consumer group's lag shows like any other. But whatever shows you your streams, their state, threads and tasks, does not see the worker. Its health, its calls in flight and its failures need watching of their own.

Our call sits at the edge: stream B ends with it. A call in the middle of a stream, between a join and an aggregation, is harder to move out. The answers have to come back into the stream, joined to their records by key within a window. An answer later than the window needs a path of its own.

Two tools sit between stream B and a worker of your own: Confluent's Parallel Consumer and Responsive's async processor. We measured neither of them, nor a worker. The Parallel Consumer is the usual building block for a worker: more calls in flight than partitions, with order kept per key. The async processor keeps the call inside Kafka Streams and hands it to a thread pool, again with order kept per key.

The short version

  • A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call: throughput is threads over call time, up to the partitions.
  • Partitions alone do not help: a repartition without the threads to match only gives each thread more tasks.
  • Give every call a budget: the whole call, retries and backoff included. Without one, no setting is safe.
  • Keep a round, the tasks per thread times the budget, and a poll's worth, max.poll.records times the budget, under half of max.poll.interval.ms.
  • An eviction before a commit repeats the calls and writes duplicates.
  • With the defaults, one failed call stops the whole client.
  • Give the slow step its own stream, with the threads to match its partitions.

How we measured

We ran everything on one machine and one broker, against the stub, which waited a fixed time before it answered. A real service's time varies. Ours did not, so each run shows one latency at a time. The numbers describe the shape of the problem, not your cluster's. The records were real: newly published vulnerability entries, CVEs, from the National Vulnerability Database, replayed from one captured window. The runs used Kafka Streams 4.2.0 and the classic group protocol.

The stub, the replay script and the application that measured all of this are not published. If you want to run them against your own numbers, write to info@alginte.com and we will send them.

This post uses the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD.

Related reading

  • Brice Leporini, Why you should not query a database in your stream processors (2022): the same problem from the database side, with a table join and a two-stage design as the ways out.
  • KIP-442: until Kafka 2.3, Kafka Streams set max.poll.interval.ms to effectively infinite, so older advice that a slow Streams application is never evicted predates it.
  • Sébastien Viale, Loïc Greffier and Valérie Servaire, Processing error handling in Kafka Streams (2025): the handler KIP-1033 added, written by two of its authors, with the built-in choices and the dead-letter queue support KIP-1034 added later.

In the next posts of this series, the service is an AI model that makes a decision on each event. To get them, follow the blog's RSS feed or @alginte_sw on X, where we post each one.

title: I made my tmux sessions reachable from a 2002 Nokia
description:
I run my work in tmux: builds, logs, servers, and lately a lot of AI coding agents. The thing about an agent in a pane is that it stops and waits for me. "May I run this?" "Which of these three?" "Done." And I am never at that keyboard when it asks. I am in the kitchen, on the train, on a walk.

So I built muxway: a small Go agent next to tmux on each machine, a hub, and clients. The clients got out of hand. There is a browser one, an Android one with a Wear OS watch face, one for Even Realities G2 glasses, and a Java ME MIDlet that runs on a Nokia 6310i from 2002.

That phone has a 96 by 65 pixel screen, GPRS, and cannot do modern TLS. It reads Claude Code and answers it. This post is about why the Nokia was the useful one to build, not the silly one.

The agent calls you

The part I use most is the notification. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity tell muxway, through their hooks, when they ask a question, want a permission, go idle, or finish. The pane lights up in every client, the phone and the watch buzz, the glasses show a banner at the foot of whatever I am reading. Then I answer from wherever I am: a tap, Enter, y, a number, a few words, or I hold the microphone and say it. The hub transcribes, the words land on the input line, and nothing is sent until I confirm.

In the browser I get up to four tiles from any mix of machines, all live and typable. Drag a header to swap, drag a divider to resize, and tiles that are one tmux window's panes move that window on the host as I rearrange them.

A lens for tiny screens

A terminal does not fit on a watch or a pair of glasses, and certainly not on 96 by 65 pixels. What does fit is the conversation. A lens knows what an agent's screen looks like and reshapes it: the box drawing, the status line and the spinner go, the question and the prompt stay. On the glasses that is eight short lines. On the Nokia it is whatever the screen holds, and you scroll with a key. Whatever the agent suggests in its input box is offered as the first answer, so most of the time the reply is one key.

The lens is also why the Nokia was worth doing. If the API is small enough that a MIDP 1.0 phone can be a client, in under 30 KiB of JAR, then anything can. The protocol has a plain text mode: one authenticated GET returns a pane wrapped to the width you ask for. A phone of that age cannot speak current HTTPS, so it goes through a small relay that terminates TLS for it. The MIDP 2.0 build, on a Nokia 7310 from a few years later, adds colour, Unicode and the camera: take a photo of a whiteboard, it lands in an inbox on the host, and the path is typed into the reply for the agent to read.

It is a remote shell, so build it like one

Whoever can type into a tmux pane owns that machine. I did not want a "trusted network" bypass or a convenience mode that becomes the default.

  • Panes are opt-in. Nothing is reachable until its owner marks it with muxway expose.
  • A token names which hosts and panes it may read, and separately which it may type into. Read and write are different grants.
  • Input is text and a fixed grammar of named keys. Clients never send raw escape sequences.
  • Every authentication step is rate limited and locked out. Secrets are hashed, compared in constant time, never logged.
  • Every write to a pane is audit logged on the host: who, when, which pane, how many bytes.
  • The agent dials out to the hub over a signed, encrypted WebSocket. Nothing listens on your machines, and clients never reach them directly.
  • One static Go binary per role, one third party dependency, no cgo.

The hub signs people in with OpenID Connect if you have an identity provider, or with tokens if you do not. It serves the web client from files embedded in the binary, so there is nothing else to deploy.

Getting it running 

go install github.com/notmarkopadjen/muxway/cmd/muxway@latest

# on the hub
muxway hub serve --listen 127.0.0.1:7600 --public-url https://hub.example.com --trust-proxy &
muxway hub pair-code --host alice-laptop

# on the machine with tmux
muxway agent pair <code>
muxway agent run &
muxway expose -t work:1.0 --write --name build
muxway hooks claude-code

# back on the hub: a token for a client
muxway hub token create --name phone --read 'alice-laptop/*' --write 'alice-laptop/@build'

Open the hub in a browser and paste the token. For a script or your own client, a pane is one request away:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Accept: text/plain" \
  "https://hub.example.com/v1/panes/alice-laptop/@build?width=40&lines=20"

Build your own client

That last request is the whole point. The protocol is documented with examples and a diagram for every flow: bearer tokens, JSON and text mode, long polled events, the key grammar, rate limits, error codes. The four clients I wrote are proof that it holds up from a React app down to a feature phone. If you have a device I do not, a Kindle, an e-ink badge, a Game Boy with a link cable, the API will not be what stops you.

Where it is

It is young and I use it every day. Everything is Apache 2.0:

  • muxway: hub, agent, web client and the protocol. First tagged release v0.1.0, static binaries for Linux and macOS.
  • muxway-android: phone and Wear OS, APKs on the releases page.
  • muxway-glasses-even: the Even Realities G2 app.
  • muxway-midp: the Nokia, MIDP 1.0 and 2.0 JARs on the releases page.

Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are the agents I have tested the hooks and the lens with. Another CLI needs its hooks to call muxway notify on the host and a lens for its screen, and that is a pull request I would be glad to see. If you try it, the thing I most want to hear is where the security model gets in your way, because that is where I would rather hear it from you than find out later.

title: Small design systems: tokens first, components second
description:
Every design system I've built that started with components ended up with a pile of one-off variants. The ones that started with tokens survived.

Tokens are the decisions: spacing scale, type scale, radii, colors, elevation. Components are just the places those decisions show up.

The order that works for me:

  1. Name the scales. 4/8/12/16 is not a system, it's a suggestion. Pick a small set and stop.
  2. Write the tokens as CSS variables. They work in every framework and they make dark mode a variable swap instead of a refactor.
  3. Build one component at a time, and delete variants that aren't used twice.

The last part is the hard one. A variant that exists because one screen needed it is not a design system, it's a bug with a name.

Do you keep tokens in CSS variables, a JS object, or both?

title: Session Timeout UX: Show What Survives Sign-In in Your Public Demo
description:
A useful session timeout UX demo shows the work before expiry, the sign-in transition, and the exact state afterward. Make it clear which values were saved and which were still drafts. Returning to the same screen does not prove that unsaved work survived, and seeing text in a field does not prove it was stored successfully.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, that sequence gives peers a concrete continuity problem to review. It is more informative than a screenshot of a “Session expired” message or an unqualified claim that the app keeps everything safe.

The project-note editor below is fictional. All example values and states are prepared for explanation. This is a review workflow, not a report of testing a real app, and it does not recommend changing a production authentication policy for the sake of a recording.

Define the activity that should continue

Imagine a planning app with a project title and a longer meeting note. The user has saved the project title, then started editing the note without submitting the latest changes. Their authenticated session expires while that note is open.

There are several different things to inspect: the saved title, the unsaved note, the user's location in the task, and their permission to continue. Give each one an explicit expected state in your own review notes.

Do not use “restore the session” as a catch-all phrase. A new authenticated session, a restored page, and recovered draft data are separate results. A product can achieve one and fail another.

Keep the public demonstration scoped to the activity. You do not need to expose authentication tokens, internal account information, or a customer's workspace to show whether a prepared note remains available after sign-in.

Prepare a before-expiry record

Use distinctive, harmless sample values that a viewer can recognise later. The note might contain a short prepared agenda with an unfinished final line. A generic paragraph of filler makes an accidental reset harder to spot.

State whether the displayed note is already saved. If the interface has a save indicator, include it in the recording and check what that indicator actually means in the implementation. Do not call a value server-saved merely because a spinner stopped.

Record the expected outcome before triggering expiry. That prevents a successful-looking return from becoming the standard after the fact. The demonstration should answer a question you deliberately chose to inspect.

Keep a copy of the prepared values in your private review record. After sign-in, compare against that record rather than relying on memory or assuming that similar-looking text is identical.

Trigger expiry under known test conditions

Use a suitable test environment and a supported way to exercise the expired-session path. Describe the relevant conditions without publishing credentials or turning a temporary test configuration into advice for production.

Distinguish a real expiry from a mockup that displays the message. A simulated screen can help review wording, but it cannot establish that the application handles an expired credential, redirects correctly, or preserves a draft.

If you shorten a test session for the demonstration, say that the timing is a test condition. A recording with an edited pause should also say that the waiting period was compressed.

Do not claim that every expiry path behaves identically. Inactivity, an explicitly ended session, and an account change may have different consequences. Choose the path you intend to show and keep other cases in a separate check list.

Show what the person can do at the interruption

When the app asks the person to sign in again, record the available action and the explanation beside it. A viewer should be able to understand whether their work is still present, temporarily unavailable, or known to be lost.

Do not promise draft preservation in the message before the behavior supports it. If the system cannot recover a draft, the explanation needs to reflect that limit while the product team investigates the design.

Avoid replacing the whole flow with a still image of a warning. The transition matters: does the interruption cover the editor, replace it, or take the person to another page? Those choices affect what someone thinks has happened to the note.

Ask a peer to describe their next action from the visible state. Their answer can reveal unclear wording. It cannot verify the authentication or storage behavior behind the interface.

Compare the state after sign-in

Complete sign-in using a prepared test account through the normal supported flow. Return to the project and compare the saved title, unsaved note, and task location with the before-expiry record.

Show the full relevant note, including its unfinished final line. A restored first paragraph can hide lost edits farther down. Check whether the interface distinguishes a recovered draft from the last stored version.

If the note reappears, establish what that result means. It might still be an unsaved draft awaiting submission. The demo should not imply that recovery automatically completed the user's original action.

Then perform the intended save under the current authenticated state and check the supported confirmation. Treat that as a further step. Recovery, permission to save, and successful persistence each deserve their own observation.

Use accessibility guidance with its actual scope

The W3C explanation of re-authentication describes a Level AAA criterion: after an authenticated session expires, the person can continue their activity without losing data when they authenticate again. It explains why losing work can especially affect people who need more time.

That gives the review a useful goal. It does not mean a short clip proves that the whole application conforms to WCAG, or that one particular storage design is required in every system.

Review the interaction with the input methods and assistive technology relevant to your actual implementation. A pointer recording does not establish focus behavior, an accessible explanation, or a usable route back for a keyboard user.

State the checks performed and their limits. A public demo can show a specific continuity path while a separate implementation review addresses the rest of the criterion and the broader product requirements.

Keep recovered data tied to the right person

Preserving a note is not the only requirement. The application must also handle the identity and access under which that note can be viewed or submitted. Do not treat any successful sign-in as permission to attach previous work to the new account.

For the fictional editor, record an unresolved account-change case separately from the same-account demonstration. It may need a design decision about how to explain available drafts without exposing another person's content.

Do not improvise a storage workaround merely to make the public sequence look smooth. Local retention, shared devices, server storage and deletion have different implications that belong in the actual product's design and security review.

The public artifact should report what was observed under the stated conditions. A preserved sample note is useful evidence for one path, not a certificate that draft recovery is safe across every device, identity and failure condition.

Ask founder peers one continuity question

Buildside is the founder-community context for this review. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. A prepared demo gives peers a specific interaction to assess without asking them to inspect private customer work.

Choose one question: can they tell what survived, can they identify what still needs saving, or does the return location match their understanding of the task? Keep implementation findings separate from opinions about the message.

If you make a revision, repeat the relevant before-and-after sequence. A clearer sentence is a useful improvement, but it does not repair lost state by itself. Show the state comparison again when behavior changes.

Keep the version, conditions, prepared values and unresolved cases in your development notes. Your next build-in-public update can report one checked improvement and the boundary around it. That gives readers useful progress while preserving an honest account of the work still left to verify.

title: Why I Started Contributing to Open Source (and What Happened in the First Few Months)
description:
A few months ago, I made a decision. I wanted to start contributing to open source.

I work as a Java backend developer at Wipro, building REST APIs with Spring Boot. I like my work, but there is one problem with it: the code is private. Nobody outside my team can see what I build. I wanted a place where I could write real code, get it reviewed by strangers, and prove to myself that I could work on a codebase I did not write.

So I picked a few Java projects and started.

It was not easy at the start

I thought I would find an issue, fix it, send a PR, and done. It did not go like that.

  • Finding an issue that nobody was already working on took time. Many good issues already had someone on them.
  • Reading a big codebase for the first time is confusing. You open one file and it leads to ten more.
  • Maintainers are busy. Some reply in a day, some take weeks.

The most useful thing I learned early: talk to the maintainer before writing any code. It saves time for both sides, and it tells you quickly if the issue is worth your effort.

How I work now

I keep it simple.

  1. One issue at a time.
  2. Small, focused changes. A small diff is easy to review.
  3. I write the code myself and I understand every line I send.
  4. I take review comments seriously, even when they are strict. Those reviews taught me more than many tutorials.

What came out of it

Till now I have had PRs merged in:

  • Zalando Logbook: I worked on the status-code based sink and log writer.
  • Adyen Java API Library: my change shipped in SDK v42.0.0.
  • Picnic error-prone-support: my PR got merged after review.

I will write about each of these in separate posts, because each one taught me something different.

What I am building on the side

Along with open source, I am building Sionna Visualizer, a visual dashboard on top of NVIDIA Sionna (6G + AI). It is a different area from my day job, and I wanted to see if I can bring my backend skills into it. You can try it here: https://sionna-visualizer.vercel.app

What you can expect from me here

I am going to write about my work step by step:

  • the PRs I made and what happened in the reviews
  • the mistakes I made and what I learned
  • my daily work and small lessons from Java and Spring Boot
  • progress on Sionna Visualizer

If you are a Java developer who wants to start open source, I hope my posts help you start sooner than I did.

And if you are a maintainer or a team looking for someone who learns in public and likes to collaborate, my DMs are open. You can also find me on GitHub: https://github.com/Vinu2111

Next post: my Zalando Logbook PR, what the issue was, and what the review taught me.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:
