title: Stack vs Queue: What Is the Difference? (With Examples)
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

A stack and a queue are both simple ways of storing items in order, but they differ in one rule: a stack removes the last item you added (LIFO — Last In, First Out), while a queue removes the first item you added (FIFO — First In, First Out). A stack behaves like a pile of plates; a queue behaves like a line of people at a ticket counter.

What Is a Stack?

Imagine the plate pile in a kitchen. You place clean plates on top of each other, and when you need one, you take it from the top. You never pull a plate from the middle unless you enjoy washing the floor as well. That is a stack: new items go on top, and removals also happen at the top. The last plate you placed is the first one you take away — Last In, First Out.

A stack supports two main operations. Push adds an item to the top, and pop removes the item from the top. Most stacks also offer peek (or top), which lets you look at the top item without removing it — the programming equivalent of glancing at the pile before committing.

stack = []

stack.append("page A")   # push
stack.append("page B")   # push
stack.append("page C")   # push

print(stack.pop())       # page C  (last in, first out)
print(stack.pop())       # page B
print(stack)             # ['page A']

This is not a made-up classroom example: your browser's Back button works exactly like this. Every page you visit is pushed onto a history stack, and pressing Back pops the most recent page off. The Undo button in your editor, and the way programmes remember which function called which, use the same idea.

What Is a Queue?

Now picture the queue at a coffee shop. The first person who joined the line is served first, and new arrivals join at the back. Nobody (in a polite country, at least) cuts in at the front. That fairness rule — First In, First Out — is a queue. Adding an item is called enqueue and happens at the back; removing one is called dequeue and happens at the front.

from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("print job 1")   # enqueue at the back
queue.append("print job 2")
queue.append("print job 3")

print(queue.popleft())        # print job 1  (first in, first out)
print(queue.popleft())        # print job 2
print(queue)                  # deque(['print job 3'])

Queues quietly run much of the software you use daily. Printers work through documents in queue order. Websites place incoming requests in a queue so the server handles them fairly. Downloads, message apps and customer-support tickets all line up in queues. In Python, the official tutorial's Data Structures chapter shows both patterns — lists used as stacks, and queues built for first-in, first-out behaviour — in its Python documentation on data structures.

The official Python Tutorial, Data Structures chapter — its contents list both "Using Lists as Stacks" and "Using Lists as Queues".

Stack vs Queue in One Table

Point Stack Queue
Rule LIFO — Last In, First Out FIFO — First In, First Out
Real-life picture A pile of plates A line at a ticket counter
Insert happens at The top (same end) The back (rear)
Remove happens at The top (same end) The front
Main operations push, pop, peek enqueue, dequeue, front
Everyday examples Browser Back button, Undo, function calls Print jobs, waiting requests, message lines

The single most important row is the first one. If an interviewer asks you nothing else, remember: same-end versus two-ends. A stack works at one end only; a queue works at both ends — in at the back, out at the front.

Why the Removal Cost Differs in Python

Here is a detail that separates a memorised answer from an understood one. In Python, using a list as a stack is fast, because append() and pop() work at the end of the list, where nothing else has to move. A queue built from a plain list is slow, though: removing the first item with pop(0) forces every remaining item to shuffle one place forward. Do that a million times and your programme develops a noticeable limp. That is why the example above uses deque from the collections module, which is built for fast additions and removals at both ends. MDN's reference for JavaScript's Array methods shows the same pattern in another language: push/pop for stack behaviour, and shift for queue behaviour (with the same cost warning in large arrays).

If you enjoyed this comparison, our guide to array vs linked list explains where these structures actually store their items in memory, and it pairs nicely with what you have just read.

A Famous Stack Trick: Checking Balanced Brackets

Here is the example that makes stacks click for most people. Suppose you must check whether the brackets in a line of code are balanced — every opening bracket closed in the right order, as in { [ ( ) ] }. A stack solves it beautifully: walk through the characters, push every opening bracket, and whenever a closing bracket appears, pop the top and check that the pair matches. If the stack is empty at the end, the brackets are balanced.

def is_balanced(text):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in text:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in ")]}":
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
    return len(stack) == 0

print(is_balanced("{ [ ( ) ] }"))   # True
print(is_balanced("{ [ ( ] ) }"))   # False

Notice why a queue would fail here: the closing bracket must match the most recent opener, not the oldest one — and "most recent first" is exactly the stack rule. The mirror-image classic for queues is breadth-first search, where you explore a tree or a map level by level, always visiting the place that has waited longest. Same family of ideas, opposite removal rule.

How Fast Are They? A Quick Big O Note

For interviews, one line about speed is usually enough: push, pop, enqueue and dequeue are all O(1) — constant time — when the structure is built properly, because each operation touches only one end and nothing else has to move. Looking at the top of a stack or the front of a queue is also O(1). Searching for an item inside either one is O(n), because you may have to look at every element — a polite way of saying these two structures are designed for order, not for searching.

Which One Should You Use?

Choose by asking one question: which item should come out next? If the answer is "the most recent one" — undo steps, backtracking through a maze, checking that brackets in code are balanced, reversing a word — you want a stack. If the answer is "the one that has waited longest" — tasks, requests, messages, print jobs, breadth-first search through a tree or a graph — you want a queue. When in doubt, picture the plates and the coffee line; the correct structure usually introduces itself.

Stacks and queues are also the friendly front door to bigger data-structure ideas. Our explainer on what a hash table is covers the other classic beginner structure, the one that trades ordering for lightning-fast lookups by name.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does LIFO and FIFO mean?

LIFO means Last In, First Out: the newest item leaves first, as in a stack. FIFO means First In, First Out: the oldest item leaves first, as in a queue. They are simply the two removal rules written as initials.

Is a stack or a queue used for the browser Back button?

A stack. Each page you visit is pushed on top, and Back pops the latest page off, which is why you retrace your steps in reverse order.

Can one structure act as the other?

Programmers can simulate a queue using two stacks, and vice versa — a favourite interview puzzle — but in everyday code you simply pick the structure whose removal rule matches your problem.

Which is faster, a stack or a queue?

Both are fast when built correctly: their main operations are O(1), constant time. Slowness only appears when you use the wrong tool, like removing from the front of a Python list instead of using a deque.

Conclusion

A stack takes from the top; a queue serves from the front. Plates versus people in a line, LIFO versus FIFO, push/pop versus enqueue/dequeue — once those pictures stick, you will never confuse the two again, in an interview or in real code.

title: 6 Cost Factors Increasing LLM API Spend Beyond Tokens: Node.js Media Support
description:
6 Cost Factors Increasing LLM API Spend Beyond Tokens: Node.js Media Support

Route every media support ticket through a cost-aware policy before it reaches an LLM, and charge usage to a tenant at the same boundary where the request is admitted. Token count is only the visible meter; retries, model choice, context duplication, and optional features can multiply the bill while the ticket still looks like one request.

Short answer: keep a per-ticket cost ledger, cap attempts, select models by task class, and make every extra capability opt-in. The useful unit is not a monthly aggregate. It is one tenant, one ticket, one decision, and a trace of what happened to it.

This is an architecture decision record for a media company triaging incoming customer-support tickets. The decision is to put a small admission and accounting layer in front of model calls. The layer has four invariants:

  • Every admitted attempt has a tenant ID, ticket ID, model class, and reason for the attempt.
  • A retry is a new billable attempt, even when the provider eventually returns one useful answer.
  • A fallback model is recorded as a model change, not hidden inside a generic success counter.
  • Optional work, such as retrieval, tool calls, or long conversation history, must have an explicit budget and owner.

The failure boundary is the model request. Once a request leaves the service, its estimated input and output cost, attempt number, timeout policy, and tenant attribution are immutable ledger fields. That makes a later invoice explainable.

Which factors increase LLM API spend beyond token cost?

A support ticket often starts small: a subject, a few sentences, and a desired label. The runtime can quietly make it expensive by attaching the full email thread, account metadata, policy documents, and a previous draft on every attempt. A timeout then causes a retry, while a circuit-breaker fallback selects a larger model because the first model is considered unreliable. The operator sees one ticket resolved. The ledger sees several requests.

The cost model should therefore separate request count from tokens. These are the factors that increase spend beyond token cost, including unnecessary work that never changes the routing decision:

Cost driver What changes Boundary to control Evidence to retain
Retries More attempts for one ticket Maximum attempts and retryable errors Attempt number and error class
Model selection Different rates and capabilities Task policy and fallback order Requested and selected model class
Context duplication More input tokens per attempt Context builder and size limit Input token estimate and source list
Optional features Retrieval, tools, structured processing Explicit feature budget Feature flags and downstream calls
Concurrency More work in flight during a backlog Queue admission and per-tenant limits Queue wait, start, and finish times

Do not infer any of these from an invoice after the fact. An invoice can tell the finance team that usage happened; it usually cannot explain why a tenant's ticket was retried twice after a timeout or why a policy attachment was repeated across every attempt.

The invoice is the end of the story.

For a media support queue, the first routing decision can be cheap and deterministic: language, account tier, product area, and urgency. Only tickets needing semantic classification should consume a model call. That is a product decision as much as an optimization. A false negative can send a billing complaint to a general queue, so the policy needs a confidence threshold and a human review path.

How should the critical path expose tenant cost?

The critical path needs one accounting object passed through every attempt. It should not depend on a provider-specific response shape, and it should not let a background retry create an unowned request. Here is a deliberately small Python interface; the surrounding service can be Node.js, but the boundary is language-neutral.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional


@dataclass
class Attempt:
    number: int
    model_class: str
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int = 0
    status: str = "admitted"
    features: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)


@dataclass
class TicketBudget:
    tenant_id: str
    ticket_id: str
    max_attempts: int = 2
    attempts: List[Attempt] = field(default_factory=list)

    def admit(self, model_class: str, input_tokens: int,
              features: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> Attempt:
        if len(self.attempts) >= self.max_attempts:
            raise RuntimeError("ticket attempt budget exhausted")
        attempt = Attempt(
            number=len(self.attempts) + 1,
            model_class=model_class,
            input_tokens=input_tokens,
            features=list(features or []),
        )
        self.attempts.append(attempt)
        return attempt

    def record_result(self, attempt: Attempt, output_tokens: int,
                      status: str) -> None:
        attempt.output_tokens = output_tokens
        attempt.status = status

The important behavior is the admission check, not the dataclass. A retry must call admit again and receive a new attempt number. A worker that retries below the accounting layer will make its telemetry look healthy while its tenant ledger is incomplete.

The dangerous case is easy to miss: a queue worker times out locally, marks the attempt unknown, and requeues the ticket. The upstream request may still finish. If the requeued job creates a fresh ledger entry without linking the unknown attempt, the tenant is charged for work that the dashboard presents as one clean retry. The fix is to give the attempt a durable identity before dispatch, record an explicit unknown outcome, and let reconciliation close it later. That extra state looks fussy in a diagram. It is what keeps a cost report defensible when network timing is not.

Use provider usage metadata when it is available, and keep the estimate separate from the final observed count. Before admission, the estimate protects the queue from obviously oversized work. After completion, the observed usage supports reconciliation. Neither number should be silently overwritten.

Five boundaries that keep the ledger honest

  1. Retry policy

Retry only errors that are plausibly transient, such as a transport timeout or a service-unavailable response. Do not retry invalid input, a rejected safety policy, or a malformed request without changing the request. Exponential backoff reduces synchronized pressure, but it does not make retries free. Set a small per-ticket attempt budget and send the ticket to review when it is exhausted.

This is where I have seen the most misleading dashboards: success rate rises after adding retries, while cost per resolved ticket rises faster. The metric needs both values. A successful second attempt is still evidence that the first attempt consumed capacity.

  1. Model policy

Use task classes rather than a single global model setting. A short language-and-intent classifier may need less capability than a response draft that must follow a long editorial policy. The fallback rule should be explicit: which failures permit a fallback, which class is allowed, and how many total attempts remain.

Record both the requested class and the selected class. Otherwise, a configuration change can look like a tenant's demand changed when only the routing policy changed. The comparison worth making is cost per correctly routed ticket, not raw cost per call.

  1. Context construction

Treat context as a compiled artifact. Include only fields needed for the current task, deduplicate quoted replies, cap attachment-derived text, and assign a source label to each fragment. A ticket classifier rarely needs the entire customer conversation plus the final answer template. A response writer might. Those are different budgets.

A useful guardrail is a context report stored with the attempt: source names, estimated tokens, removed fields, and truncation reason. This catches a common edge case: a single unusually long customer thread consumes the normal tenant budget before the model has produced a label.

  1. Feature gates

Retrieval and tool calls should be selected by policy, not enabled because a shared prompt happens to support them. A ticket about a current subscription plan may need a controlled account lookup; a request to classify sentiment usually does not. Every feature should add a visible ledger entry and a budget owner.

Do not count a tool call as part of the model call merely because it appears in the same trace. It has its own latency, failure mode, and potentially its own charge. The accounting layer can aggregate the ticket total while retaining the component events.

  1. Queue admission

A backlog can turn a modest per-ticket policy into a large burst. Apply limits per tenant and per queue, then make the admission decision before expensive enrichment. This protects cost visibility from a noisy tenant and keeps one import job from consuming all worker capacity.

The choice is not maximum throughput. It is predictable work with a visible reason for deferred work.

Measure it per tenant.

What should the decision table reject?

The tempting rejected option is a single global monthly token cap with an alert. It is easy to operate, but it cannot tell a support lead whether the cause was retries, context growth, a model-policy change, or a feature rollout. It also creates a sharp failure at the month boundary and encourages teams to disable useful safeguards when the cap is near.

A global cap still has a valid use case: it is a backstop for the whole organization. It is not a substitute for per-tenant admission and per-attempt accounting. Keep it as the outer limit, after the local controls have produced an explainable ledger.

The decision table below makes the trade-off concrete:

Option Visibility Failure behavior Appropriate use
Global token alert Low Warns after drift Organization-wide backstop
Per-tenant request budget Medium Defers or reviews excess tickets Fair queue admission
Per-attempt ledger plus model policy High Bounds retries and records fallbacks Primary runtime control

A team can implement the ledger before it knows exact provider rates. Store usage dimensions and resolve rates in a versioned configuration outside the request path. When a rate changes, historical entries remain tied to the rate version used for reporting. The important invariant is attribution, not pretending an estimate is an invoice.

Keep the evidence durable.

How do we know the controls work?

Test the failure boundaries with synthetic tickets before production traffic reaches them. Include a one-line ticket, a long quoted thread, an attachment that expands after extraction, a timeout on the first attempt, a non-retryable rejection, and a fallback that changes model class. Assert that each admitted attempt has one ledger entry and that the ticket total equals the sum of its components.

Operational dashboards should show at least: cost estimate and observed usage by tenant, attempts per ticket, model-class mix, context size distribution, feature activation rate, deferred tickets, and correctly routed tickets. The last metric prevents cost work from turning into a silent quality regression.

For Node.js services, keep these fields in structured logs and propagate a trace ID through queue workers. The exact logging library is less important than making the event schema stable. Sample traces only after retaining the accounting events needed for reconciliation; otherwise the busiest tenant is the one most likely to disappear from the evidence.

I initially treated two attempts as a reliability setting. It is also a cost decision. Setting the default to two makes the trade-off visible in the ledger, while a critical queue can justify one additional attempt only with an owner and a quality measurement.

The decision is straightforward: bound work before the request, record every attempt, and evaluate cost against routing quality per tenant. Token pricing matters, but the architecture determines how many times you pay for the same operational intent.

References

  • https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429

title: Integrate Node.js Library for Error Tracking: Auditable 2026 Support Pricing Practices
description:
Short answer: keep the pricing decision and its audit record in the customer-support application, then put the error-tracking library behind a narrow capture boundary that carries a request ID, operation ID, rule variant, and redacted user context. Evaluate Sentry, Rollbar, Datadog Error Tracking, OpenTelemetry, and Infrai with the same failure fixtures. Choose the capture service that preserves that evidence without becoming the authority for the pricing result.

This is a governance problem disguised as a Node.js integration task. A support ticket that fails during a new pricing-rule rollout can tell the team which path failed and which cost bucket received the operation. It cannot, by itself, prove what the customer was charged. That proof belongs in the application audit trail.

What must an error record prove before it can attribute cost?

The useful event is deliberately narrow. It contains a request_id, an operation_id, the flag key, the selected variant, a pseudonymous user identifier, and the exception context needed to reproduce the failure. The support ticket body, payment credentials, and authentication material stay out of the event even if the selected library accepts arbitrary metadata.

The operation ID is the join key between two records with different responsibilities. The pricing service owns the durable decision and its idempotency key. The error service owns a report about what happened while that decision was being attempted. A repeated error report must not apply the pricing rule twice, and a failed report must not roll back or alter a successful pricing operation.

I initially treated the flag value as sufficient context for this kind of investigation. It is not. A value such as new_rule says nothing about which support action produced it, while an email address is both a weak correlation key and an avoidable privacy liability. A stable operation identifier plus a pseudonymous user key gives the investigation a join without copying the customer record into an observability system.

That distinction also sets the retention boundary. A compliance review can ask for the authoritative pricing decision, the reason for the decision, and the related error evidence, but an error tracker should not become a second ledger. Document that boundary before installing an npm library; otherwise, convenient context fields tend to become an accidental data export.

How should Node.js integrate an error-tracking library in practice?

Install the selected Node.js error-tracking library during process setup, initialize it with project-specific settings, and register its middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors. Add custom logging only around critical sections that need business context. A wrapper around every function creates a noisy record rather than an auditable one.

The integration test should use a fixed, redacted fixture instead of a production traffic dump. Give it one ordinary HTTP error, one uncaught-exception path, one duplicate report attempt, and one simulated 429 response. Assign the fixture deterministically to an old or new pricing variant, then send the identical event envelope through every candidate adapter.

The pass criteria are concrete:

  1. The receiving system contains the operation ID and variant.
  2. The business result is unchanged when error delivery is retried or fails.
  3. Sensitive support and payment fields are absent from the serialized event.
  4. A 429 response causes bounded backoff and honors Retry-After when present.
  5. A deliberately triggered sample error can be found using the operation ID.

Reject the candidate if the adapter hides a non-success response, duplicates the business operation, or requires an incident feature that it does not provide. Do not report benchmark numbers from this test. It is an acceptance test for evidence and ownership, not a performance study.

Keep the fixture boring.

The following wire-level probe uses the only verified capture route in this comparison. The 2026-11-01 discovery snapshot is the reference point for the route and capability claims here. INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD must contain the redacted JSON envelope produced by the application; keeping that envelope in an environment variable makes the route test independent of any unverified request-field names. The explicit method, bearer token, and idempotency key are visible so the request can be inspected before it is placed behind a library adapter.

set -eu

: "${INFRAI_API_KEY:?INFRAI_API_KEY is required}"
: "${INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD:?INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD is required}"
: "${ERROR_OPERATION_ID:?ERROR_OPERATION_ID is required}"

response_file="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$response_file"' EXIT

for attempt in 0 1 2; do
  status="$(curl --silent --show-error --output "$response_file" --write-out '%{http_code}' \
    --request POST 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Idempotency-Key: $ERROR_OPERATION_ID" \
    --data-binary "$INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD")"

  case "$status" in
    2*) cat "$response_file"; exit 0 ;;
    429)
      [ "$attempt" -lt 2 ] || { cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1; }
      sleep_seconds="$((2 ** attempt))"
      sleep "$sleep_seconds"
      ;;
    *) cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
done

The probe is intentionally not the pricing transaction. The application writes its own decision record with its own idempotency key, and the capture adapter reports the resulting error with the same operation identifier. That separation makes a retry safe even when the observation service is unavailable.

Which service preserves the evidence without owning the decision?

Sentry and Rollbar are reasonable choices when the dominant requirement is a focused application-error workflow with a Node.js SDK. Datadog Error Tracking is a reasonable candidate when error investigation needs to live alongside an existing Datadog operations environment. OpenTelemetry has a different role: its Logs signal defines portable telemetry concepts and correlation fields, but it is an instrumentation and collection approach rather than a complete incident-triage product.

Those distinctions matter more than a feature checklist. A specialist can be the right answer when alert routing, source-map processing, session replay, or a mature incident workspace is a release requirement. A portable signal can be the right answer when the team wants to operate the collector and choose downstream storage. The correct comparison unit is the capture boundary, not the vendor logo.

Infrai is a measured candidate for that boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key; the capability description includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. The live discovery snapshot describes 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. Those facts make it possible to inspect a contract before the Node.js adapter is deployed.

There is a second, different advantage for this support workflow: Infrai offers one key and one bill across the broader backend surface, rather than forcing the API process, queue worker, and reconciliation job to coordinate separate provider credentials and invoices. The breadth is real, while the interface remains a plain REST contract. In practical terms, a team can keep one application-owned capture method while changing the service behind it; the callers continue to depend on the boundary, not on a provider-specific SDK.

I recommend trying Infrai for the capture leg of a small, vendor-neutral error pipeline when the team values a self-describing REST contract and a replaceable backend across Node.js and worker processes. I would choose Sentry or Datadog when built-in incident workflows are mandatory, OpenTelemetry when portability and operated collection are the main requirement, and Rollbar when a focused error-monitoring product is the better organizational fit. The recommendation is conditional because the evidence boundary must remain useful even when the capture provider changes.

The limitations belong in the decision record. Threshold alert or notification routes, distributed-trace span-tree queries, source-map or crash-symbolication processing, Session Replay, and heartbeat monitoring for a job that never ran are outside Infrai's supported capability. Its flags lack change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, and a recycle bin; clients poll. Logs lack a user-deletion endpoint for a GDPR erasure workflow, or bulk export and subscription endpoints. A support platform with those obligations needs complementary systems and should not describe trace_id or span_id fields as a span-tree query system.

Option Boundary style Strong fit Boundary to verify
Sentry Node.js error-tracking SDK Context-rich application error investigation Alerting, retention, and privacy configuration still need ownership
Rollbar Node.js error-monitoring SDK A focused error workflow Confirm framework coverage and duplicate-report behavior
Datadog Error Tracking Error tracking within an operations platform Teams already using Datadog for operational analysis The wider platform becomes part of the investigation workflow
OpenTelemetry Instrumentation and collector Portable logs and correlation fields Downstream analysis and incident handling remain yours
Infrai Plain REST capture request A replaceable capture leg across runtimes Alerting, span-tree investigation, and erasure workflows need other systems

The table is a boundary map, not a ranking. The same fixture, the same redaction rules, and the same operation identifier should be used for every row.

How should rollout evidence survive a pricing-rule change?

Record the flag key, variant, operation ID, and pricing decision in the system that owns the support transaction before the rollout percentage changes. Send only the redacted diagnostic context to the error adapter. When a capture attempt is retried, reuse the operation-linked idempotency key for the report and keep the business idempotency key unchanged.

During the first rollout, inspect a deliberately triggered error from each variant and verify the join in both directions: from the support operation to its error evidence, and from the error evidence back to the authoritative operation record. A successful search is useful; it is not proof that the pricing result was correct. Reconciliation remains the authority.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error-capture discovery reference, then run the same redacted fixture against the other candidates before selecting a production adapter.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js error monitoring
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Error Tracking
  • Infrai error-capture discovery

title: 5 Website Trust Signals That Turn Small Business Visitors Into Customers
description:
Visitors decide in seconds whether a small business website is worth their trust. Here are five signals that turn browsers into buyers, why each matters, and a quick fix.

1. Real reviews with names and photos

Why it matters: Anonymous quotes look invented. Named reviews with a photo prove real people had a good experience, and social proof is one of the strongest nudges toward buying.

Quick fix: Ask your three happiest customers for a short review today, get permission to use their name and photo, and place them near your main call to action.

2. Clear phone, email and address on every page

Why it matters: Hidden contact details feel like hiding. Visible ones tell visitors a real business stands behind the site and that help is easy to reach.

Quick fix: Put your phone, email and address in the header or footer of every page, and make the phone number tap-to-call on mobile.

3. Secure HTTPS and fast loading on mobile

Why it matters: Browser "not secure" warnings scare people off instantly, and most small business visitors arrive on a phone. Slow pages lose them before they read a word.

Quick fix: Enable HTTPS through your host, compress oversized images, and test your pages on a real phone over mobile data.

4. Real photos of your team, shop and finished work

Why it matters: Stock photos are easy to spot and signal "generic". Real photos show who you are and the quality of what you deliver.

Quick fix: Spend an hour taking clear, well-lit photos of your team, space and recent projects, then replace the stock images on your home and about pages.

5. A simple guarantee or a clear "how it works" process

Why it matters: Uncertainty stops purchases. A guarantee reduces risk, and a short process explains exactly what happens after someone gets in touch.

Quick fix: Add a three-step "how it works" section and one plain-language promise you can honestly keep, such as a reply within one business day.

Start with whichever fix takes the least time, then work down the list. Small trust improvements add up quickly.

Want a second pair of eyes? ENZORA does a free website audit for small businesses: https://enzora.vercel.app

title: Reading Complex XML in SQL Server — Shredding a Thousand Attributes Generically Instead of Looping for Hours
description:
A catalog of around 3000 product configurations arrives as XML. Depending on the equipment, a configuration carries different and additional attributes, around a thousand across all variants. In an earlier project, the evaluation of such a catalog ran in application code: a loop over the object types, inside it a loop over the attributes, plus lists in memory that grew with every iteration. The program took several hours. Where exactly the time went can no longer be said in hindsight. What is certain is what the design demanded: code per type, a separate lookup per attribute, and a schema that had to be in your head beforehand. This article shows how to shred XML in SQL Server without knowing the attributes in advance: load it raw, shred it into a path/value table that holds one row per value with its path in the document, read the schema off the data, and let the database generate the views per type. In the measurement of this article that takes not hours but around 15 seconds for a catalog of the same size.

At a glance

  • Why loops over object types and attributes get so expensive with a thousand attributes, and what the database route does differently: the attributes become data rows instead of code.
  • How the catalog is loaded into SQL Server as a single XML value and then split into 3000 table rows, one per configuration. From these rows, a query in which no attribute name appears fetches every value together with its path in the document, for example /Drivetrain/Gears with the value 14. The result is 1.5 million such rows of path and value, and the whole route takes around 15 seconds in the measurement instead of hours.
  • How an inventory built from these rows makes required, optional and variant attributes per type readable, without anyone having known the attributes beforehand.
  • How the database generates views with more than 600 columns from the inventory itself, and where the limits of the method are: column limits, typing, very large files. What it requires is little: the element of the sub-documents, an upper bound for the depth, and lists that repeat uniformly in at least one configuration.

Prerequisites: Docker and SQL Server 2022 as a container (Developer Edition). The scripts run with sqlcmd, the command-line client that ships with the container. The call is at the start of the section "Load raw". The sample catalog, its generator and the scripts come in four downloads at the end of the article: the XML route and the JSON route, each for SQL Server and for Postgres. Postgres 18.6 serves for the bridge at the end.

The catalog: three types, one drivetrain with two faces

The example is a bicycle configurator with 3000 configurations. There are three object types: road bike, trekking bike and cargo bike. The three types share the groups General, Frame, Brakes and Wheels, and already here they resemble each other more than they differ. What the Drivetrain contains depends on its XML attribute kind. With kind="chain" it holds chainrings, sprockets, rear derailleur, front derailleur, gear ratios and chainline. With kind="hub" it holds gears, gear range, belt, hub type and coaster brake. The same group, but different attributes depending on the variant. The Brakes also carry their design as an XML attribute, type, and not as a child element. Lighting and Suspension are optional groups that a road bike rarely has and a cargo bike almost always. Two groups are lists. Accessories contains zero to four Part elements with name, weight and a standard-equipment flag. Wheels always contains two Wheel elements, one for the front and one for the rear, with rim, tyre and spoke count.

"Attribute" in this article means a business characteristic of a configuration, such as the number of gears or the material of the frame. In the XML such a characteristic is usually an element and only rarely an XML attribute. Where the XML construct is meant, the text says XML attribute explicitly.

To reach the order of a thousand attributes, every configuration additionally carries twelve of twenty parameter groups with 48 values each, every single one of which is present with a probability of eighty percent. These groups are simply called G01 to G20 and are filler. They are there so that the measurements have the right order of magnitude, not because they mean anything. Which type carries which groups is distributed so that the types overlap but do not coincide.

This is what one configuration looks like, shortened:

  1: <Configuration id="C000001" type="cargo_bike">
  2:   <General>
  3:     <Model>CargoBike-214</Model>
  4:     <ModelYear>2019</ModelYear>
  5:     <Weight>13.25</Weight>
  6:     <Price>4576.94</Price>
  7:   </General>
  8:   <Frame>
  9:     <Material>Aluminum</Material>
 10:     <Size>56</Size>
 11:   </Frame>
 12:   <Drivetrain kind="hub">
 13:     <Gears>14</Gears>
 14:     <GearRange>371</GearRange>
 15:     <Belt>yes</Belt>
 16:   </Drivetrain>
 17:   <Brakes type="Disc hydraulic">
 18:     <Rotor_front>160</Rotor_front>
 19:     <Pads>sintered</Pads>
 20:   </Brakes>
 21:   <Wheels>
 22:     <Wheel><Position>front</Position><Rim>584x23</Rim><Tyre>32-622</Tyre><Spokes>24</Spokes></Wheel>
 23:     <Wheel><Position>rear</Position><Rim>559x25</Rim><Tyre>47-622</Tyre><Spokes>36</Spokes></Wheel>
 24:   </Wheels>
 25:   <Lighting>
 26:     <Front_Lumen>70</Front_Lumen>
 27:     <PowerSource>HubDynamo</PowerSource>
 28:   </Lighting>
 29:   <Accessories>
 30:     <Part><Name>BottleCage</Name><Weight>275</Weight><Standard>yes</Standard></Part>
 31:     <Part><Name>Speedometer</Name><Weight>441</Weight><Standard>yes</Standard></Part>
 32:   </Accessories>
 33:   <Parameter>
 34:     <G09><P02>552.04</P02><P04>861.71</P04><P06>B</P06></G09>
 35:   </Parameter>
 36: </Configuration>

The catalog does not come from a real project but from a Python script, the generator in the download. The script rolls the dice for the type, the equipment and the values of every configuration, but starts the random generator with the same seed on every run. That is why every run produces exactly the same catalog, and all numbers in this article can be reproduced with it. The XML is 28 MB in size and contains a good 1.5 million values. The same data exists as JSON Lines, one line per configuration, in the notation produced by the Python package xmltodict: attributes as keys with @, repeated elements as arrays. Each of the two files comes with the generator in a download of its own, XML and JSON separately. The German version of this article uses the same catalog with German element names. The structure and all numbers are identical.

Why loops over variable attributes get expensive

The obvious design in application code looks like this: for every object type there is a class or a mapping table that knows its attributes. For every configuration, the code walks through the attributes of that type, looks up the node in the document, reads the value and stores it in a list. If a value turns up that the list does not know yet, the list grows. With three types and twenty attributes that is manageable. With a thousand attributes, some of which overlap and some of which exist in only one variant, it becomes code that rebuilds the structure of the catalog, line by line. Every new attribute is a code change. Every access to a node is a separate search through the document. And every list that grows with progress is searched a little more slowly with every iteration.

Where exactly the hours came from in that project can no longer be proven, and this article does not claim to know. It only claims that the design multiplies the costs: types times attributes times configurations, plus lists whose size depends on the order of processing. The general argument for why a loop per element loses against a query over the set is made in the article Set-based vs. row by row on another case study. Here it is about the special case where the loop does not even know what it is looping over, because the schema only exists in the data. The programming language is not the problem. A program that walks the tree once and emits every leaf with its path needs no schema and stays fast, and that is exactly what the twin of this article shows in Python. It only gets expensive through a design that searches the document again for every attribute.

The database route turns the task around. It does not know the attributes and does not need to. What it requires is little: the element under which the configurations sit, and an upper bound for the depth of the tree. Added to that is an assumption about lists: it recognises them only when an element name repeats within them in at least one configuration. It loads the document raw, shreds it with generic queries in which no attribute name appears into rows of path and value, and only afterwards does anyone look at which paths exist at all. The thousand attributes are then a thousand different values in one column, not a thousand lines of code. The schema is counted, not known. And the views that a consumer wants to see at the end are built by the database from this count. Architecturally this is ELT: load raw, then transform in SQL. What distinguishes that from classic ETL is explained in ETL vs. ELT.

The following diagram shows the whole route with the tables that come into being in the next sections, and with the numbers from the sample catalog.

Load raw: one row per configuration

All SQL Server scripts of this article run against a Docker container. The catalog and the scripts are copied with docker cp to /tmp in the container, which is where the paths in the scripts point. Every file is run with sqlcmd, which ships with the image: the switch -i names the file, -C accepts the self-signed certificate of the container, and -I turns on QUOTED_IDENTIFIER, which the XML methods require. For the remaining files only the file name changes.

  1: docker run -d --name 147-mssql-xml-en -e ACCEPT_EULA=Y -e MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD='S3cret!Pass' `
  2:     mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest
  3: docker exec 147-mssql-xml-en /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P 'S3cret!Pass' `
  4:     -Q "CREATE DATABASE catalog"
  5: docker cp .\configs.xml 147-mssql-xml-en:/tmp/configs.xml
  6: docker cp .\147001-mssql-xml-load.sql 147-mssql-xml-en:/tmp/147001-mssql-xml-load.sql
  7: docker exec 147-mssql-xml-en /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -I -S localhost -U sa -P 'S3cret!Pass' `
  8:     -d catalog -i /tmp/147001-mssql-xml-load.sql

The first step loads the whole file as a single value of type xml. OPENROWSET in SINGLE_BLOB mode returns the file as varbinary, and CONVERT to xml parses it once into SQL Server's internal representation. Right after that the document is split: nodes() returns one row per Configuration element, value() fetches the two XML attributes as columns, and query('.') stores the fragment as an xml value of its own.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147001: Load the catalog and split it into one row per configuration (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- The XML methods require QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON; sqlcmd starts with OFF (switch -I).
  5: SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;
  6: GO
  7: IF SCHEMA_ID('stage') IS NULL EXEC ('CREATE SCHEMA [stage]');
  8: GO
  9: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 10: -- The whole document as a single xml value
 11: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 12: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[raw_xml];
 13: CREATE TABLE [stage].[raw_xml]
 14: (
 15:     doc   xml NOT NULL
 16: );
 17: 
 18: INSERT INTO [stage].[raw_xml] (doc)
 19: SELECT
 20:    CONVERT(xml, T01.BulkColumn)
 21: FROM
 22:    OPENROWSET(BULK '/tmp/configs.xml', SINGLE_BLOB) AS T01;
 23: 
 24: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 25: -- One row per configuration: key, type and the fragment as xml
 26: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 27: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[config];
 28: SELECT
 29:     T02.n.value('@id',  'varchar(20)') AS config_id
 30:    ,T02.n.value('@type', 'varchar(20)') AS config_type
 31:    ,T02.n.query('.')                   AS node
 32: INTO [stage].[config]
 33: FROM
 34:    [stage].[raw_xml] T01
 35:    CROSS APPLY T01.doc.nodes('/Catalog/Configuration') AS T02(n);
 36: 
 37: SELECT
 38:     config_type
 39:    ,COUNT(*) AS configs
 40: FROM
 41:    [stage].[config]
 42: GROUP BY
 43:    config_type;
 44: -- cargo_bike      1025
 45: -- road_bike        995
 46: -- trekking_bike    980

The split is the most important step of the whole method, for a reason that only becomes visible later. All subsequent XQuery expressions then run against fragments of around 9 KB instead of a document of 28 MB. What that is worth is shown more drastically by Postgres than by SQL Server: there, the same generic query over the whole document was still running after 36 minutes and could not even be cancelled. More on that in the Postgres bridge section below.

One trap right at the start: the XML methods nodes(), value() and query() require QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON, alongside further session options such as ANSI_NULLS, ANSI_PADDING and ANSI_WARNINGS, which are already set in sqlcmd. The tool sqlcmd, however, starts with QUOTED_IDENTIFIER OFF, and the error message does name the option, but does not say which construct in the statement needs it. Instead it lists all the features that depend on it. The switch -I on the sqlcmd call takes care of that, alternatively the first line in the script.

Shred generically: every leaf with its path

The goal is a table with four columns: configuration, type, path and value. In the SQL Server world this breaking of a document into rows is called XML shredding, and the tools for it are the methods nodes() and value() of the xml type. The values sit in the leaves of the tree, that is, in elements without child elements, and additionally in XML attributes. An XML attribute can hang on any element, including one with children, like kind on the Drivetrain. The path is the chain of element names from the Configuration element down to the leaf. For an XML attribute it ends with @ and the attribute name. From the excerpt above this yields rows such as /Frame/Material with the value Aluminum, /Drivetrain/Gears with the value 14 or /Drivetrain/@kind with the value hub.

This happens in two passes over all 3000 fragments, called pass 1 and pass 2 in what follows. The reason for the split are the lists. A configuration with two accessory parts has two elements with the same path /Accessories/Part/Name. To tell them apart, every element would have to carry its position among its same-named siblings, that is, whether it is the first or the second part. This position is called ordinal in what follows and appears in square brackets in the path, for example /Accessories/Part[2]/Name. Computing it is expensive in SQL Server: for each of the 1.5 million leaves the XQuery engine would have to count the siblings before it, and that raises the runtime in the measurement from around two to around 40 seconds. Pass 1 therefore fetches all values with their path, but without positions. From its result, an ordinary grouping reveals at which positions elements repeat at all. In the catalog these are Part under Accessories and Wheel under Wheels. Pass 2 then computes the positions only for these positions, that is, for around 12,000 elements instead of 1.5 million. XML attributes are not elements and are skipped by both passes. They get a short pass of their own.

Pass 1: all leaves, no positions

The path expression /Configuration//*[not(*)] matches every element in the fragment that has no child element, at any depth. The names of its ancestors come from the parent axis: local-name(..) is the name of the parent element, local-name(../..) that of the grandparent, and so on. In XQuery, SQL Server supports the axes child, descendant, descendant-or-self, parent, attribute and self, but not ancestor. That is why the depth has to be chosen as a fixed number. The catalog has at most three levels below the configuration, so four name columns suffice with one column in reserve: the fourth always holds Configuration. That is exactly what can be checked. A leaf for which Configuration appears in none of the ancestor columns lies deeper than the reserve, and from the fifth level on its path would be cut off at the front without any error message pointing it out. Whoever has deeper documents adds columns.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147002: Pass 1 - every leaf element with the names of its ancestors (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- One pass over all configurations. The parent axis (..) yields the ancestor
  5: -- names; positions are deliberately NOT computed here.
  6: SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;
  7: GO
  8: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[leaf_raw];
  9: SELECT
 10:     T01.config_id
 11:    ,T01.config_type
 12:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(.)',        'varchar(100)') AS name0   -- the leaf itself
 13:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(..)',       'varchar(100)') AS name1   -- parent
 14:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(../..)',    'varchar(100)') AS name2   -- grandparent
 15:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(../../..)', 'varchar(100)') AS name3   -- great-grandparent
 16:    ,T02.n.value('.',                    'varchar(200)') AS value
 17: INTO [stage].[leaf_raw]
 18: FROM
 19:    [stage].[config] T01
 20:    CROSS APPLY T01.node.nodes('/Configuration//*[not(*)]') AS T02(n);
 21: 
 22: SELECT
 23:    COUNT(*) AS leaves
 24: FROM
 25:    [stage].[leaf_raw];
 26: -- 1516476

This single pass delivers all 1,516,476 leaf elements of the 3000 configurations in around two seconds. Lines 12 to 15 fetch the four names, line 16 the value, and that is all. What is deliberately missing is the position of an element among its siblings. It would be needed to tell the two Part elements in the accessories apart. The obvious XQuery expression for it is let $i := . return count(../*[. << $i]) + 1: count the siblings that precede me in the document. With two such expressions, one for the leaf and one for its parent element, the same query takes twenty times as long instead of around two seconds, measured 1.8 against 40.2 seconds. For each of the 1.5 million leaves SQL Server then walks the sibling list and compares document positions, and exactly this evaluation is expensive in the XQuery engine. Computing the position across the board is therefore not an option. It is computed in the second pass only where it is needed.

XML attributes

XML attributes are not elements and do not appear in pass 1, regardless of whether they hang on a leaf or on an element with children. They get a short pass of their own. In SQL Server 2022 the method nodes() also returns attribute nodes, the path /Configuration//@* matches all XML attributes in the fragment, and the parent axis leads from the XML attribute to the element that carries it. The two XML attributes of the Configuration element itself are already columns and are excluded.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147003: Attributes - nodes() also returns attribute nodes (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- The attributes of the configuration itself (id, type) are already columns in
  5: -- [stage].[config] and are excluded here.
  6: SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;
  7: GO
  8: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[leaf_attr];
  9: SELECT
 10:     T01.config_id
 11:    ,T01.config_type
 12:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(.)',        'varchar(100)') AS attr_name
 13:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(..)',       'varchar(100)') AS name1   -- element carrying the attribute
 14:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(../..)',    'varchar(100)') AS name2
 15:    ,T02.n.value('local-name(../../..)', 'varchar(100)') AS name3
 16:    ,T02.n.value('.',                    'varchar(200)') AS value
 17: INTO [stage].[leaf_attr]
 18: FROM
 19:    [stage].[config] T01
 20:    CROSS APPLY T01.node.nodes('/Configuration//@*') AS T02(n)
 21: WHERE
 22:    T02.n.value('local-name(..)', 'varchar(100)') <> 'Configuration';
 23: 
 24: SELECT
 25:     name1
 26:    ,attr_name
 27:    ,COUNT(*) AS n
 28: FROM
 29:    [stage].[leaf_attr]
 30: GROUP BY
 31:     name1
 32:    ,attr_name
 33: ORDER BY
 34:     name1
 35:    ,attr_name;
 36: -- Brakes       type   3000
 37: -- Drivetrain   kind   3000

The catalog has two further XML attributes, kind on the drivetrain and type on the brakes, and the pass takes half a second.

Pass 2: ordinals only where something repeats

Without positions, the two Part elements of a configuration fall onto the same path /Accessories/Part/Name. For the inventory in the next section that is actually fine, for a view with one column per path it is not. The solution has two steps. First, a set-based query reads off pass 1 which parent elements repeat at all: if, within one configuration, more than one leaf with the same name sits under the same parent path, then either the parent element repeats, or the leaf itself repeats within the parent element. Both need ordinals. Which of the two cases applies, the grouping does not reveal, because in pass 1 both look the same. The template below solves the first one. The second one is shown by the inventory after pass 2: the path then carries more than one value in a single configuration.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147004: Which parents repeat? Set-based, from pass 1 (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- A parent element repeats when more than one leaf of the same name sits under
  5: -- the same parent path within one configuration. The same query also finds
  6: -- leaves that repeat within a single parent.
  7: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[repeated_parent];
  8: WITH
  9: CTE_leaf_count AS
 10: (
 11:    SELECT
 12:        config_id
 13:       ,name3
 14:       ,name2
 15:       ,name1
 16:       ,name0
 17:       ,COUNT(*) AS n
 18:    FROM
 19:       [stage].[leaf_raw]
 20:    GROUP BY
 21:        config_id
 22:       ,name3
 23:       ,name2
 24:       ,name1
 25:       ,name0
 26: )
 27: SELECT DISTINCT
 28:     CASE WHEN name2 = 'Configuration' THEN ''
 29:          WHEN name3 = 'Configuration' THEN '/' + name2
 30:          ELSE '/' + name3 + '/' + name2 END AS parent_path
 31:    ,name1 AS parent_name
 32: INTO [stage].[repeated_parent]
 33: FROM
 34:    CTE_leaf_count
 35: WHERE
 36:    n > 1;
 37: 
 38: SELECT
 39:     parent_path
 40:    ,parent_name
 41: FROM
 42:    [stage].[repeated_parent]
 43: ORDER BY
 44:    parent_path;
 45: -- /Accessories   Part
 46: -- /Wheels        Wheel

The query finds two positions, /Accessories with the child Part and /Wheels with the child Wheel, and takes under a second for that. Only now does the expensive position computation come into play, and only for the nodes that this detection has delivered. For every position found, a template yields a SELECT that fetches the affected parent elements with nodes(), computes their position among their same-named siblings and reads the leaves below them with their own position. At such a position every element gets its ordinal, even when a configuration has only a single element there. A configuration with three parts gets /Accessories/Part[1]/Name to /Accessories/Part[3]/Name, one with exactly one part gets /Accessories/Part[1]/Name. If the single part stayed without an ordinal, the first element of the same list would sit on two different paths depending on the configuration. The inventory would then count one list as two things, and the path without ordinal would end up as a column in the type's view, filled only for the configurations with exactly one part. The two wheels of every configuration are accordingly called /Wheels/Wheel[1]/Rim and /Wheels/Wheel[2]/Rim.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147005: Pass 2 - ordinals only for the parents that repeat (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- For every row of [stage].[repeated_parent] the template yields one SELECT.
  5: -- At such a position every element gets its ordinal, even when a configuration
  6: -- has only a single element there: a list stays a list, and its first element
  7: -- sits on the same path in every configuration.
  8: -- The expensive position expression runs only over the few affected nodes,
  9: -- not over all leaves.
 10: -- If leaves repeat directly within one parent element, the template gets the
 11: -- same expression once more on leaf level (T03). That costs a multiple of the
 12: -- runtime of pass 2 and is not needed here. Whether the case exists is shown
 13: -- by the inventory: n_values greater than n_configs.
 14: SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;
 15: GO
 16: DECLARE @template nvarchar(max) = N'
 17: SELECT
 18:     T01.config_id
 19:    ,T01.config_type
 20:    ,''{path}/{name}''
 21:     + T02.n.value(''let $p := .
 22:                     return concat("[", string(count(../*[local-name() = "{name}"][. << $p]) + 1), "]")'', ''varchar(10)'')
 23:     + ''/'' + T03.n.value(''local-name(.)'', ''varchar(100)'') AS path
 24:    ,T03.n.value(''.'', ''varchar(200)'') AS value
 25: FROM
 26:    [stage].[config] T01
 27:    CROSS APPLY T01.node.nodes(''/Configuration{path}/{name}'') AS T02(n)
 28:    CROSS APPLY T02.n.nodes(''./*[not(*)]'') AS T03(n)';
 29: 
 30: DECLARE @sql nvarchar(max);
 31: 
 32: SELECT
 33:    @sql = STRING_AGG(
 34:              CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(@template, N'{path}', parent_path), N'{name}', parent_name) AS nvarchar(max))
 35:             ,N' UNION ALL ')
 36: FROM
 37:    [stage].[repeated_parent];
 38: 
 39: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[leaf_pass2];
 40: CREATE TABLE [stage].[leaf_pass2]
 41: (
 42:     config_id     varchar(20)  NOT NULL
 43:    ,config_type   varchar(20)  NOT NULL
 44:    ,path          varchar(400) NOT NULL
 45:    ,value         varchar(200) NULL
 46: );
 47: 
 48: INSERT INTO [stage].[leaf_pass2]
 49: EXEC sp_executesql @sql;
 50: 
 51: SELECT
 52:     path
 53:    ,COUNT(*) AS n
 54: FROM
 55:    [stage].[leaf_pass2]
 56: WHERE
 57:       path LIKE '%/Name'
 58:    OR path LIKE '%/Rim'
 59: GROUP BY
 60:    path
 61: ORDER BY
 62:    path;
 63: -- /Accessories/Part[1]/Name   2406
 64: -- /Accessories/Part[2]/Name   1831
 65: -- /Accessories/Part[3]/Name   1243
 66: -- /Accessories/Part[4]/Name    615
 67: -- /Wheels/Wheel[1]/Rim        3000
 68: -- /Wheels/Wheel[2]/Rim        3000

Pass 2 runs over 6095 Part elements and 6000 Wheel elements instead of 1.5 million leaves and takes under a second. The template applies at every position the detection reports, no matter how deep the repeated element sits in the fragment. Below it, however, it reads only the direct leaf children, the way Name, Weight and Standard sit directly under Part. If leaves repeat directly within one parent element, the template gets the same expression once more on leaf level. That costs around 15 seconds instead of one in the measurement, because navigating to the parent element from every leaf is expensive, but it stays limited to the positions found. Two forms the template does not cover. If there is a further level between the repeated element and its leaves, say Part/Product/Name, then the detection attributes the repetition to the intermediate element Product, and pass 2 assigns every Product the ordinal 1, because every Part has only one Product. The two names then land on the same path /Accessories/Part/Product[1]/Name. The same applies to lists within lists. Both cases need a further CROSS APPLY stage with the same pattern, and whether they occur is revealed by the inventory in the next section through a single metric. A third form escapes the detection itself, because it is a heuristic over the leaf names: it finds a list only when at least one leaf name repeats within it. If of two Part elements one carries only a Name and the other only a Weight, no leaf name repeats, and the two parts look like a single one in the path/value table. The inventory's metric does not show this case. It stays hidden, however, only as long as not a single configuration carries the list uniformly. As soon as one does, the detection reports the position, and pass 2 assigns the ordinals in all configurations.

One shortcut looks tempting and is not one. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) over the output of nodes() delivers the document order in practice, and in the measurement the ordinals derived from it matched the XQuery computation in all 12,095 cases. The documentation, however, does not guarantee this order, and the window function forces the optimizer into a plan that raises the runtime of pass 1 from around two to around 40 seconds. Both together are enough to leave the shortcut alone.

Merge

The path/value table comes from three sources: pass 1 without the leaves under the repeated parent elements, plus pass 2 and the XML attributes. The path is assembled from the name columns, up to the name Configuration, which marks the beginning. An index on type and path helps all the queries that now follow. At the end of the script stands a reconciliation: the number of leaves and XML attributes in the fragments must match the number of rows in the path/value table. This reconciliation only counts. Whether every value sits on the right path, it does not show.

 16:          ELSE '/' + T01.name3 + '/' + T01.name2 + '/' + T01.name1 END
 17:     + '/' + T01.name0 AS path

 32:                                     WHEN T01.name3 = 'Configuration' THEN '/' + T01.name2
