title: From a Simple "Mark as Seen" to Feedgrab & Ghostify: Story of My Life!
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

TL;DR: I keep seeing the same posts on most of the DEV home feed tabs: Discover, Following and Curated.

Wanted to fix it by implementing a simple Mark as Seen browser extension. Then one thing led to another, and I ended up building three projects: one already abandoned, and two ongoing (Feedgrab & Ghostify).

Note for users: This is still under development, so if you see errors, please look for updates: https://github.com/SweaDev/ghostify/releases

Note for judges: v1.0.0 was completed within the submission period; later releases are updates.

Backstory

These days, I spend too much time on DEV.

  • Deleted my old X/Twitter account because it gives me a headache! Created a new one only as a placeholder.
  • Deactivated my Facebook account, because it's… well, that's a story for another day!

So most of the time I spend online is here on DEV and YouTube.

But the problem with DEV (and YouTube too) is that I keep seeing the same posts in the feed!

Open DEV in the morning: there's that post. Open it at lunch: there it is again. Open it at night: guess who's back! I've read it. I've reacted to it. I may have even commented on it. Still there, staring at me like it hasn't been introduced yet.

So on October 26, I did what any sane developer would do: I opened my editor instead of closing the tab.

Attempt #1: myDEV (RIP 🪦)

The plan was simple:

  • Put a ✓ button on every post card, right next to Bookmark.
  • Click it, and the post disappears from the feed and goes into a new myDEV tab.
  • Done. Go back to reading.

And it worked! For about an hour. Then I opened YouTube and saw the same video for the 14th time this week, and realized myDEV only knew how to read one site, with selectors I hard-coded by hand. The moment DEV changes a class name, it's dead. And for YouTube, I'd have to start over.

It took me a few days to admit it, but today I finally archived it. Rest in peace, myDEV. You were too specific for this world.

Attempt #2: Feedgrab

What I actually needed wasn't a DEV plugin. I needed something that could look at any page and say: "this is a feed, these are the items, and this one is the same item you saw before, even after infinite scroll re-rendered it."

That became Feedgrab, a TypeScript library that:

  • detects feeds on a page (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), or takes CSS/XPath selectors you type;
  • lets you confirm or fix its guesses in a Shadow DOM overlay;
  • turns the feed into one de-duplicated stream of items that keeps up with infinite scroll;
  • never removes anything unless you ask it to.

It runs in browser extensions, headless browsers and on the server, with the same API.

Attempt #3: Ghostify

And then, finally, the thing I wanted in the first place. On top of Feedgrab. With a ghost. 👻

What I Built

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome + Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts.

Hover a post, click the ghost, and it's gone from the feed. For good. Reload, scroll, come back tomorrow: it stays gone.

But it's not deleted. It becomes a ghost. Ghostify keeps a copy, so you can find it again, read it later, or snooze it until the weekend.

That's my take on Ghost in the Machine: the posts you've already seen don't die, they just stop haunting your feed and move into the machine. Quietly. Politely. Until you call them back.

What it does:

  • The ghost button shows up on the post under your pointer. Click it, the post vanishes, and an Undo toast gives you 5 seconds of regret.
  • The Ghostify page keeps everything in three tabs: Ghosted, Later and Snoozed.
  • Snooze a post until later today, tomorrow, the weekend, next week, or any date. When time's up, it shows up in Back from snooze.
  • Search your ghosts by keyword, or switch on Semantic and just describe what you remember ("that post about JavaScript adding objects and arrays").
  • Auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site: "recurring weekly discussion threads I have already read". A local decision model checks new feed items against them and ghosts the matches. If it gets one wrong, Not this brings the post back, and that rule never touches it again.
  • Add any site. On any page with a feed, click Add this site. Feedgrab proposes the feeds, you confirm them in its overlay, and choose whether they're for the logged-in or logged-out view.
  • New tab flavor, if you want your ghosts on every new tab.

Demo

No store listing (yet!), so the demo is: install it, open DEV, start ghosting. It takes about a minute:

  1. Download a zip from Releases: ghostify-<version>-chrome.zip or ghostify-<version>-firefox.zip.
  2. Chrome: unzip, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked. Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, click Load Temporary Add-on… and pick the zip.
  3. Open https://dev.to/ logged out, hover a post, click the ghost.

Here's a quick tour. (The screenshots represent what a user would see.)

The toolbar popup lists your recent ghosts. Click the 👁 to unghost one, and it shows up in the feed again:

Click a ghost to see its details, the AI summary and tags:

Write auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site:

And pick a model for each job:

Code

SweaDev / ghostify

Ghostify Feed Browser Plugin (beta)

Ghostify

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome and Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts. Hover a post, click the ghost, and it disappears from the site's feed for good. Ghostify keeps a copy so you can find it again later.

v1.0.0. Ghostify works on the dev.to home feeds out of the box, and you can add any site. It has a full Ghostify page with snooze and search, and optional AI that runs locally with Ollama or with your own OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI key.

Features

  • The dev.to logged-out home feeds (Relevant /, Latest /latest, Top /top/*) are recognized automatically, through feedgrab.

  • The ghost button shows on the post under your pointer. Clicking it hides the post and saves it, and an Undo toast lets you take it back.

  • Ghosted posts stay hidden when you reload, and also when they come back…

View on GitHub

SweaDev / feedgrab

Feed Detector

Feedgrab

A TypeScript library that finds and describes content feeds in web pages (post timelines search results, product grids, article lists) and turns them into one de-duplicated stream of items with exclusion reports (ads, promoted posts, injected widgets).

  • Detect feeds automatically (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), by inspecting an element, or from CSS/XPath selectors you type.
  • Confirm/edit the proposals in a Shadow-DOM overlay, or programmatically with headless helpers.
  • Iterate a unified feed that keeps up with infinite scroll (MutationObserver) or pagination (ingest), with a report per item: kept, excluded (and why), or pending.
  • Exclude items by specificity-ranked selector rules, built-in ad rules, or plain-language LLM criteria. Nothing is removed unless you call a removal helper.

It runs in browser extensions (Chromium + Firefox, MV3), headless browsers (Playwright/Puppeteer injected bundle), and server-side (Bun/Node with a parsed DOM), using the same API everywhere.

Install

…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The open-source AI part

AI is optional and off by default. Ghostify is perfectly happy as a dumb "hide this post" button. Turn AI on, and it gets three jobs, each with its own model:

Job Default (local, via Ollama) Used for
Embeddings embeddinggemma-2 Semantic search over your ghosts
General gemma4:e2b Summaries and tags for each ghosted post
Decision d3:2b Checking new feed items against your auto-ghostify rules

All three are open-weight and small enough to run on a laptop. Start Ollama so it accepts requests from extensions, and that's it:

ollama pull embeddinggemma-2
ollama pull gemma4:e2b
ollama pull d3:2b
OLLAMA_ORIGINS="chrome-extension://*,moz-extension://*" ollama serve

If you'd rather use a hosted model, every job can switch to OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI with your own key. The plumbing is the AI SDK, so swapping providers is a dropdown, not a rewrite.

A few things I'm happy about:

  • Fallbacks everywhere. If the decision model is down, the general model handles the rule check. If embeddings fail, search falls back to keywords. Nothing breaks because Ollama isn't running.
  • Embeddings are tagged with the model that made them. Change the embedding model and Ghostify ignores the old vectors instead of mixing them up. Reindex fills the gaps.
  • One honest gap: d3's response format isn't documented (yet). Ghostify reads the shapes it knows, treats anything else as "no match", and logs it. Better to miss a ghost than to hide something you wanted to see!

The extension part

  • WXT for one codebase that builds Chrome MV3 and Firefox, plus the new-tab flavor.
  • React 19 + Tailwind v4 for the popup, the Ghostify page and settings.
  • Dexie (IndexedDB) for ghosts, embeddings and keys. Everything stays in your browser. No account, no sync, no server.
  • Feedgrab for finding feeds and items, and for hiding them. Ghostify never touches a feed node itself; it asks Feedgrab's removeItem to hide it, and its own UI lives in a separate Shadow DOM.

Security was a bit of a rabbit hole:

  • Content scripts never see API keys. They don't even open IndexedDB. Everything goes through typed messages to the background script, and the background talks to the model.
  • Keys aren't in storage.local either, because content scripts can read that. They live in a Dexie table on the extension's own origin.
  • In content scripts, Feedgrab gets a proxy instead of a model, which also shrank the bundle from 380 KB to 71 KB. Nice side effect!

The "how did you build all this in a week" part

I didn't write most of the code by hand. I used a coding agent.

But I didn't just say "build me an extension" either. I've been using a small spec-driven flow I call specx:

  1. Spec: I wrote the spec by hand. It's 17 lines. Literally a paragraph and a list of features.
  2. Plan: the agent turned it into a plan with the stack, architecture and a Decisions log.
  3. Tasks: then into 23 tasks across 4 phases, each with the spec/plan line ranges it needs, the files it touches, and a Done check.
  4. Build loop: take the first unblocked task, read only what it references, implement it, run its Done check plus lint + typecheck + tests, tick the box, commit. Repeat.
  5. Phase check: at the end of each phase, follow the README from a clean state, build, load it in the browser, fix what's broken, tag a release.

The rules live in AGENTS.md, so any agent can pick it up. Every judgment call goes into the plan's Decisions log, so I can see why something was done the way it was. And there's one commit per task, so git log reads like a changelog.

Phase 1 was "ghost a post on DEV". Phase 4 was "auto-ghostify with local AI". Each phase ended with something I could actually load and use, not a pile of half-wired modules.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the thing Ghostify reads is my browsing.

Think about what an AI feature in a feed extension actually sees: every post on every feed you scroll, what you hide, what you save for later, what you search for. That's a pretty detailed picture of a person. I don't want that going to anyone's API by default. Not even mine.

With open-weight models, it doesn't have to:

  • Gemma 4 E2B, EmbeddingGemma 2 and d3:2b run on my laptop. Summaries, tags, semantic search and the rule checks all happen locally. With Ollama, nothing leaves the machine.
  • It costs nothing per post. Auto-ghostify checks every new item in the feed. With a paid API, that's a meter running every time I scroll. Locally, it's just my fan spinning a bit.
  • It keeps working. No rate limits, no deprecation emails, no "this model will be retired on…".
  • A small, specialized model is enough. I don't need a giant model to answer "is this a weekly discussion thread?" A 2B decision model is the right size for the job, and I could only pick it because it's open.

And it's not just the models. Ghostify is built on open source all the way down: WXT, React, Dexie, the AI SDK, Biome, Vitest… and Feedgrab, which I split out because I wanted it to be reusable. If someone wants to build a "hide the reruns" extension for YouTube, or a feed reader for a site that doesn't have RSS, the hard part is already there. MIT licensed. Go for it.

A closed API would have given me a smarter summary, maybe. Open models gave me a tool I'm actually comfortable running on everything I read.

My Agent Session

The whole project was built in agent sessions, following the specx flow above. The best way to see them is the commit history: one commit per task, from Scaffold WXT React project to Add auto-ghostify rules with rescue.

The Spirit of It

I keep thinking about the name.

Most "hide this" features are really "delete this". You click, it's gone, and you'll never find it again. That always felt a bit wrong to me. I did read that post. Some of them were good! I just don't need to see them every time I open the home page.

So in Ghostify, nothing dies. It becomes a ghost. It stays in the machine, with its title, its author, a little summary, and a few tags, waiting until you call it back. A bit like Día de los Muertos for posts: not here anymore, but not forgotten either.

And somewhere in an archived repo, myDEV is resting peacefully, knowing it started all of this. 🕯️

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Ghostify uses Gemma 4 E2B (gemma4:e2b) for summaries and tags, and EmbeddingGemma 2 (embeddinggemma-2) for semantic search, both running locally through Ollama by default.

Thanks for reading! And if a post of yours disappears from my feed, don't take it personally. It just means I've probably already read it, seen it, or will read it later. 👻

title: How to design transparent AI cost controls
description:
A practical guide to choosing usage units, designing spending limits, and explaining AI costs before, during, and after the work.

Every AI response has a price. People often discover it only when a limit hits or a bill arrives.

A quick edit and a long-running agent can look almost identical in the interface. One finishes in seconds. The other might read hundreds of files, call external tools, and retry steps along the way. Yet both start with the same button.

Meanwhile, AI products keep changing what they charge for: requests, credits, tasks, usage allowances. Showing more technical numbers won’t make those costs easier to understand. People want to know what a job might use, whether it’s worth running, and what they can do to spend less.

For designers, that comes down to two decisions:

  1. The unit: what users see themselves spending.
  2. The moment: when they understand the cost — before, during, or after the work.

Under the hood: what a token is

A token is a unit a model reads or generates. A tokenizer breaks text into pieces: words, parts of words, punctuation, sometimes even spaces. For English, a useful rough estimate is that one token represents about three-quarters of a word. So a million text tokens might represent around 750,000 English words. The exact count depends on the tokenizer, language, and content.

  • Input and output cost different amounts. Model providers commonly charge more for tokens they generate than tokens they read. On several current models, output is about five times the price of standard input. Longer answers, reasoning, and repeated attempts can change the economics of what looks like one request.
  • Model choice matters. Output-token prices can differ by tens of times — or more — across models. A request that is cheap in a lightweight model can cost considerably more in a frontier model. The user’s task hasn’t changed, but the meter has.
  • Modality changes the calculation. Text, images, audio, and video don’t share one universal token conversion. A short prompt, an image attachment, and a five-minute clip may all look like inputs to the same composer, yet require very different amounts of processing. Some providers charge by tokens, others by frames, seconds, or generation settings.

For a sense of scale, a 15-word prompt might be around 20 text tokens. A 1092 × 1092 image has been estimated at roughly 1,600 image tokens using one image-accounting method. For video, Google’s published static-processing examples imply roughly 30,000–90,000 tokens for five minutes, depending on the resolution setting. Those estimates come from different systems, so they cannot be priced as though they were the same kind of token. That limitation is part of the lesson: a single input box hides very different work.

Why showing tokens fails

Tokens are the system’s currency, not the user’s. People budget in money, time, attention, and finished work. They feel the effects of tokens through longer waits, changing quotas, and unexpected charges — not by counting them.

“382,000 tokens used” may be technically precise. It doesn’t tell someone whether the next research run will fit within their allowance, which part of the job was expensive, or what to change next time.

The job isn’t just to disclose a number. It’s to translate system cost into something people can make decisions with.

Predictability beats precision

There’s a useful parallel outside AI. In a study of 10,882 internet subscribers, Lambrecht and Skiera (2006) found that many customers chose a flat-rate plan even when a metered plan would have been cheaper. In one group, nearly half made that choice; more than half of them paid at least twice what they needed to.

The researchers described two reasons:

  • Insurance effect: paying more can feel worthwhile if it removes the risk of a variable bill.
  • Taxi meter effect: people enjoy a service less when they have to watch the meter climb.

The study was about internet tariffs, not AI, so it doesn’t prove how AI subscribers behave. But it captures a tension designers know well: people want to understand what they’re spending without being forced to calculate every interaction.

A good AI cost interface gives them that predictability without pretending the underlying costs are fixed.

Decision 1: choose the unit

Before designing a meter or a pricing screen, decide what people see themselves spending.

There isn’t one perfect unit. Raw tokens expose the model’s actual consumption, which is useful in API consoles but hard to reason about in a product workflow. Dollars are easier to recognize, especially for teams managing a budget, but the amount can still change from one run to the next.

Some products charge in natural units such as minutes of audio, pages processed, or GPU time. Others use credits: a product-specific currency that lets very different AI features draw from one balance. Credits simplify billing, but people have to learn what they’re worth.

Closer to the work itself are tasks and actions — one generation, enrichment, or run — and outcomes, where a charge depends on a defined result. These are easier to count because they resemble what the user asked for. They also shift more uncertainty to the vendor: a 200-page document and a one-page email might both count as one summary, despite costing very different amounts to process.

At the other end are usage allowances, where people work within a pool or reset window, and invisible usage, where a feature is included without showing a meter at all.

The important distinction is who carries the uncertainty. Tokens and metered dollars pass more of it to the user. Tasks and outcomes put more of it on the vendor. A usage allowance protects people from per-action calculations, but can leave them guessing when they’ll hit the limit.

Neither end works for everything. That’s why many products use a hybrid approach — an included allowance for everyday work, with separate limits or paid usage for expensive actions.

When to show a price — and when to hide it

A visible cost makes people more careful. That’s helpful for an expensive batch, but exhausting for everyday chat.

For discrete, potentially expensive work — enriching 500 rows, rendering a video, or scheduling a nightly automation — show the price or a credible range before the user commits. That number matters to the decision.

For frequent, exploratory actions like chatting, small edits, or code suggestions, a usage allowance is often better. Putting a price on every interaction turns experimentation into budgeting. But when one job is unusually expensive, even inside a subscription, make an exception: show its likely cost before it starts. The goal isn’t to hide spending; it’s to show it when someone can still act on it.

Usage limits

Instead of pricing each action, the product gives users a pool and shows how much remains. It’s familiar from subscriptions and easy to understand — until the pool disappears unexpectedly.

Where it fits: Consumer and prosumer plans with frequent, exploratory actions.
What good looks like: Users can tell what’s left, when it resets, and what will happen at the limit.
Why it works. Limits remove the need to do arithmetic every time someone sends a message. The user can focus on the work, with a fairly predictable subscription price.

  • Show each time window and its reset. Claude uses short session limits alongside weekly limits. A line such as “resets in 1 hr 36 min” beside “resets Friday at 8:00 AM” gives people a plan. “Resets soon” doesn’t.
  • Separate genuinely different pools. In the examples above, Cursor distinguishes model usage categories and Claude breaks out a top-model allowance. That helps users connect a decision — using a more expensive model — to the quota it affects. Don’t split pools simply because the billing system happens to have multiple internal counters.
  • Explain the overflow order. Show what is consumed first, what happens next, whether on-demand spending is enabled, and where an actual cap applies. Users shouldn’t need to infer the order from three settings screens.
  • Give temporary promotions an end date. Claude advertises a temporary higher allowance. Stating when standard limits return avoids making the end of a promotion feel like a stealth reduction.
  • Offer an alternative to upgrading. A saved or banked reset in Codex can restore eligible usage windows, subject to plan and expiry rules. Waiting for the reset, switching modes, or reducing scope can be just as important

Tasks and outcomes

Per-action units count something users already recognize: a generation, enrichment, run, or task. The appeal is that the decision and the charge use the same language.

Where it fits: Automations and actions that are easy to count.
What good looks like: Someone can estimate a month’s workload and get close to the bill.

Zapier is a useful reference. In the captured plan, the interface shows “Included tasks: 119 / 750” and “Additional tasks ($0.05/task): 0 / 1,500.” Users can distinguish the included pool from overflow, see the unit price, and understand the potential ceiling.

The more important detail is what Zapier doesn’t count. Triggers, filters, and certain built-in steps don’t count as tasks; successful action steps generally do, while errored steps don’t. Those rules answer a question that matters as much as the price: who pays for failure?

Why it works. An action is legible. If the same action consistently costs the same amount, users can forecast and compare.

Do: Explain what counts, what doesn’t, and how failed or repeated attempts are treated. Give overages their own unit price and ceiling.

Don’t: Call something an outcome if customers can’t independently tell whether it happened.

Credits

Credits let a product use one balance across different features: chat, app building, hosting, deployments, enrichment, or external services. They’re useful, but no one arrives with an intuition for what one credit is worth.

Where it fits: Products offering several expensive AI features under one account.
What good looks like: Users understand both the credit’s approximate value and why a particular action consumed it.

Why it works. Credits make unlike actions comparable and let providers adjust underlying costs without rebuilding the subscription. The left-hand screenshot shows several pools — daily, monthly, rollover, and top-ups — with different expiry rules. The right-hand example attributes deductions to projects and jobs and maintains a running balance. That’s useful accounting.

Where it breaks. The screenshots show several familiar problems:

  • No transferable sense of value. A 50-credit pack priced at $30 works out to $0.60 per credit. A different product’s 3,000-credit pack for $500 is about $0.17 per credit. The name is the same, but the unit isn’t. These are snapshot prices from the illustrations, not a shared market rate.
  • Fractional deductions without context. “Agent Call: −0.77” is precise but doesn’t tell users what the call achieved.
  • Unexplained differences. A deployment costs 50 credits and an agent call costs 0.77. A ledger can record that difference without helping anyone understand it.
  • Promotions mixed into accounting. A “20% More” top-up offer belongs in the purchasing flow. On a usage-history screen, it competes with the reason someone opened that screen: checking where the balance went.

Decision 2: choose the moment

Choosing a unit answers what users spend. Next comes when they learn about it.

There are three chances to communicate cost: before, during, and after the work. Ignore them and the user finds out at a fourth moment: the wall, when the allowance runs out or an unexpected charge appears.

Before the work, help people judge the likely cost while they can still change the scope. Explain what drives it, use a range when the total is uncertain, and offer a cheaper mode, a smaller run, or a spending ceiling.

During the work, show meaningful progress instead of an unreliable countdown. Let long jobs run without keeping people on the same screen. Make it clear what stopping will cost, and ask before continuing if the original estimate no longer holds.

After the work, show what was delivered and what it cost. Explain unusual charges, make reused work or savings visible, say how failures are billed, and keep a history people can return to. These are the three moments the illustration brings together.

Before: model selectors, effort controls, and previews

Before a run begins, the user can still change the scope. Three controls are especially useful.

Model selectors. A dropdown of model names can force people into an engineering decision. Not everyone wants that. In August 2025, OpenAI launched GPT-5 with automatic routing, then quickly brought back clearer choices such as Auto, Fast, and Thinking alongside more detailed model controls. The lesson isn’t that model choice should disappear. It’s that most users benefit from an outcome-oriented default, while advanced users still need access to the underlying models.

Effort controls. Effort dials are becoming increasingly common in AI products, but what they actually control remains a mystery to many users. Cursor offers a scale from Low to Extra High, other interfaces use sliders, while deep-research modes make the choice more implicit. All give users some control over how much time and computation a model spends on a task. But what does High really mean compared to Medium? Will the result be noticeably better, take longer, or simply consume more of the user’s allowance? The controls are becoming more familiar, but the trade-offs behind them are still poorly explained.

Previews before large spend. Deep-research screen gives users a plan they can edit before an agent starts reading sources. That’s a strong moment to intervene. The two missing pieces are cost and consent. A plan with five steps doesn’t reveal whether cutting one will save much. And for a genuinely costly job, an auto-start countdown can turn doing nothing into agreement.

A good preflight makes the trade-off concrete: what’s included, what’s optional, what the approximate total could be, and what will happen if the job needs more.

Clay is a useful reference for pricing before execution. In the captured interface, enrichments show figures such as “0.5 / row,” “~3 / row,” or “varies by model.” A recurring signal displays its monthly cost before activation. These labels tell the truth about uncertainty rather than presenting every action as fixed-price.

The same principle applies to scheduled work. Show the likely monthly spend of an hourly or nightly automation, not just its price per execution. Small recurring charges are easy to overlook.

During: progress, cancellations, and changing forecasts

This is the thinnest part of many AI cost experiences. A run starts, a spinner appears, and all the useful controls return only when it’s finished.

Show real units of progress when they exist: 320 of 500 contacts processed, 12 sources checked, three files edited. For open-ended work, show meaningful phases instead of a percentage you’ve invented. Let long jobs move out of the foreground without losing their status.

Where costs accrue as the job runs, display usage so far and the remaining budget or cap. A forecast can change if an agent discovers extra work. When the expected cost moves well beyond the original range — or reaches an agreed checkpoint — pause and ask whether to continue. Don’t silently treat the original approval as unlimited permission.

After: receipts

The receipt connects a charge to the work it paid for. It’s also what helps people make a better choice next time.

  • Per action, right next to the result. Replit’s captured run summary lists “13 actions” and what changed; a message menu shows “Worked for 43s” and “Credits used 0.50.” The receipt is available where the work happened.
  • Per session, with cost drivers. Another captured panel shows 3,450 credits alongside context used by instructions, tools, messages, files, and tool results. The surprising insight isn’t the total; it’s what consumed the context. A Compact Conversation control gives the user a way to respond.
  • Per period, with searchable history. Clay’s usage history can be examined by time, column, run, or provider and exported. That’s what a team lead needs when someone asks why the workspace budget changed.

A breakdown with a way to act is a receipt. A breakdown without one is a report.

For most users, keep the first layer light. Put the deduction and result together; make the technical breakdown one click away; put exportable history where teams already manage billing.

Do: Attach a light receipt to the result, reveal cost drivers on demand, and record the failure policy.

Put it to work

As AI products move toward longer, more autonomous workflows, the cost of a single action becomes harder to predict. What looks like one request can involve dozens of steps, multiple models, and external tools. Traditional usage meters weren’t designed to explain that complexity.

The challenge isn’t simply to expose more information. It’s to help people understand what they’re spending, why costs vary, and which choices are within their control.

Across the examples we’ve explored, one principle stands out: cost should be visible when it matters, without becoming something users have to think about constantly.

Good cost transparency isn’t about making every charge predictable. It’s about making uncertainty understandable, so people can make informed decisions without needing to understand the system underneath.

This essay was originally published on my Substack Syntax Stream, where I write about principles of human–AI interaction.

How to design transparent AI cost controls was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: ectocheck: hunting the ghosts in an AI's answer, with a local judge that gets audited
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every AI answer is a little séance. The model channels something that sounds exactly like your data, in a calm and confident voice, and some of what comes through was never said by anyone. Those are the ghosts: claims that read as fact, cite nothing, and cost you trust the moment you repeat them.

ectocheck is a Go CLI that hunts them. You hand it an AI-generated answer and a folder of local source files (notes, logs, docs). It splits the answer into claims, retrieves candidate evidence from your files, asks a local open-weight model to judge each claim, and then - the part I care about most - it audits the judge. Every citation the judge produces must point at a real excerpt it was actually shown, or the verdict is thrown out. The exit code is 1 unless every claim checks out, so it drops straight into a script or a pipeline.

The theme pushed me here: the scariest thing about LLMs isn't that they're wrong, it's that they're wrong in the same tone of voice as when they're right. I wanted a skeptic at the table.

Demo

The repo ships a small haunted house for testing: examples/homeserver/ holds notes and a backup log for a fictional home server, and examples/answer.md is an "AI answer" about it with two invented claims mixed in - a Pi-hole that never existed and a disk failure that never happened. This is the real output of ectocheck check examples/answer.md --src examples/homeserver --model qwen2.5:1.5b, captured from my terminal, not curated:

✓ SUPPORTED  The home server is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM.
              The evidence [1] directly states that the home server is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM, which matches the claim.
              [E2] examples/homeserver/README.md:3 — The box is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM. It runs Debian 12 and liv…

? UNVERIFIED Nightly backups copy /opt/stacks to /mnt/usb/backups and verify the result.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

✓ SUPPORTED  Jellyfin serves media on port 8096.
              The evidence [1] confirms that Jellyfin services are run as docker compose stacks, which includes serving media on port 8096.
              [E3] examples/homeserver/README.md:6 — Services run as docker compose stacks in /opt/stacks. Jellyfin serves media on port 8096. …

? UNVERIFIED The server also runs Pi-hole for network-wide ad blocking on port 53.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

? UNVERIFIED Backups failed twice last week because the USB disk filled up.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

5 claims: 2 supported, 0 partial, 0 ghosts, 3 unverified
No ghosts, but not every claim could be trusted. Treat unverified claims as unchecked.

Both planted ghosts come back flagged and untrusted, and the exit code is 1. The case I like most is the middle one: a genuinely true claim (the backup schedule) also comes back UNVERIFIED, because the judge asserted support while citing evidence it was never shown. The tool refused to rubber-stamp a right answer for the wrong reason.

To be precise about what happened: the planted claims were caught by citation validation - the judge claimed support but its citations didn't survive checking - not by the judge cleanly identifying them as fabrications. That's the guard doing its job, and it's also the tool's biggest limitation: citation checking stops invented references, not a judge that misreads real evidence. The README's "Honest limitations" section keeps that distinction front and center, including the time the weaker qwen2.5:0.5b model approved an invented claim outright.

Code

DhanushNehru / ectocheck

Hunt the ghosts in an AI's answer: verify every claim against your local source files, with a local open-weight judge whose citations are themselves checked. Go CLI, runs fully offline.

ectocheck

Hunt the ghosts in an AI's answer before you trust it.

A "ghost" is a claim that cannot point to real evidence. Language models invent them constantly: plausible-sounding facts that nothing ever said ectocheck takes an AI-generated answer and your local source files (docs logs, code, notes), and checks every claim against what your sources actually contain. Claims that cannot show their evidence get marked, and the exit code tells your pipeline the answer is not to be trusted.

Everything runs locally: a small open-weight model through Ollama does the judging, and your files never leave the machine.

How it works

answer.md ──► split into claims ──► retrieve candidate evidence ──► local model judges ──► citations validated ──► report
                 (deterministic)      (token overlap, no magic)      (SUPPORTED/PARTIAL/GHOST)   (invented ones rejected)
  1. Claims. The answer is split into atomic claims, deterministically bullets and sentences, headings and boilerplate dropped.
  2. Retrieval. Each claim is matched…
View on GitHub

The full implementation (CLI, judge, citation validation, tests, examples) is on main (PR #1 and PR #2, both merged). To run the demo:

git clone https://github.com/DhanushNehru/ectocheck.git
cd ectocheck
go build -o ectocheck .
go test ./...   # 20 unit tests
ollama pull qwen2.5:1.5b
ollama serve    # if it isn't running
./ectocheck check examples/answer.md --src examples/homeserver

How I Built It

Go, one binary, standard library only. The judge is qwen2.5:1.5b served by Ollama on the same machine; there are no API keys and no network calls beyond localhost. Claim splitting is deterministic, retrieval is keyword overlap over small file chunks, and the judge must answer in a strict JSON schema with positional [n] citations into the evidence it was shown, with one format retry when it mangles the schema. After the verdicts come back, a separate validator replays every citation against the actual evidence list: a citation that points at nothing, or at an excerpt the judge never saw, downgrades the claim to UNVERIFIED with a "verdict not trusted" note. 22 unit tests cover the splitter, the citation validator, the retry path, and the exit-code semantics.

Two findings shaped the design. First, format discipline from a small model is fragile enough that the retry and the validator earn their keep immediately. Second, model size matters more than I wanted it to: the 0.5b judge once approved an invented claim, which is why 1.5b is the documented default and why SUPPORTED is only ever "worth trusting more", never "verified fact".

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The answers most worth checking quote private things: home-server logs, customer notes, internal runbooks. Shipping them to a hosted API just to verify them defeats the point. Because the judge is an open-weight model running on the same machine, the answer and the evidence never leave the laptop. The whole pipeline works with the internet off, costs nothing per run, and the judge is one flag away from being any model Ollama can run - so when a better small open model lands, ectocheck gets better with a --model flag, not a rewrite. A closed API could do the judging, but it couldn't give me any of that, and it wouldn't let me read every moving part.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos is about keeping the line to the past honest: real memories, told carefully, checked against the people who were there. ectocheck is that same instinct pointed at a machine that talks like it remembers everything. When the séance ends, the only question that matters is the one the tool asks of every single claim: show me where you saw that. If it can't point at the page, it doesn't get believed.

title: Don't Migrate Logs. Outlive Them.
description:
For two months, every log written into Shipbook was written twice.

Once into the old Elasticsearch cluster, the one we had been running for years. And once, in parallel, into a new one — a different Elasticsearch version, with a completely different way of organizing the data. Dual-write. The standard playbook for moving a database you cannot afford to lose: keep both copies, keep them in sync, prove the new one is right, then flip.

It worked. We are fully on the new cluster now; the old one is gone. But somewhere in the middle of those two months, a much smaller change — one I was forced to handle a completely different way, because dual-write was physically impossible for it — quietly showed me that I had built the entire rest of the migration the hard way.

That smaller change took one line of code and a calendar reminder. The big one took two months of machinery and a steady drip of bugs. They were solving nearly the same problem.

One Dual-Write for Two Changes

I was changing two things at once, and I folded them into a single migration.

The first was the engine: a jump from Elasticsearch 7 to Elasticsearch 9. Years of accumulated reasons — features, a saner storage-tiering model, the end of a version aging out from under us.

The second was the schema. For most of the life of Shipbook — our logging platform — we created one index per customer per day. At our scale that meant thousands of tiny indexes, most nearly empty, all of them taxing the cluster in shard count and metadata churn — the structural problem I wrote about in Driving Our Error Log to Zero. The new shape shares one index across every customer on the same plan, routes writes by account so each customer's data stays together, and gives dedicated indexes only to whale accounts — the handful pushing more than twenty million logs a day.

Both changes went into one dual-write. New cluster, new schema, all at once. Every log landed in the old per-customer index on the old cluster and in the new shared per-plan index on the new one. A backfill job scrolled the entire history across. A flag — readFromNew — kept reads coming from the old, trusted side while the new side filled, ready to flip when I believed it.

That is the textbook approach. The textbook is also where the textbook pain lives.

The Tax on Keeping Two Truths

Dual-write means every write now has two outcomes, and they can disagree.

The secondary write was fire-and-forget — I did not want a hiccup on the new cluster to block a real request on the old one. So when the new cluster pushed back under load, writes to it failed silently. Nothing surfaced, because reads were still served from the healthy old side. The gap only existed on the cluster nobody was reading from yet.

That exact failure became its own story: 1.3 million silent errors a day, accumulating on the secondary side of this very migration, invisible to every customer. It was future damage — fuel loading quietly behind a flag, waiting for the day reads flipped over to detonate as missing sessions and stale fields. We caught it only because Claude could read the production logs and a number on a histogram did not fit the story.

That is the dual-write tax. You are not running one system; you are running two systems and a promise that they match. Every write path carries a branch. Every error makes you ask which cluster it came from. The whole apparatus exists to keep two copies of the truth in sync — and keeping two copies of the truth in sync is one of the genuinely hard problems in computing. We paid the tax for two months. The commit that finally deleted the old cluster's code path is dated almost two months after the one that added the dual-write.

The One Change I Couldn't Dual-Write

In the middle of all that, I needed to add routing to the new per-plan indexes — to tell Elasticsearch to place every account's logs together on the same shard, so a query for one customer hits one shard instead of fanning out across all of them.

And I could not dual-write it. Not because of effort — because it is impossible. Routing is decided at the instant a document is written; it determines which shard the document physically lands on. The logs already written to the new indexes were already placed, scattered across shards by their id. There is no second write that fixes where the first one went. My only options were to reindex everything — expensive, and exactly the kind of bulk data movement I was trying to avoid — or to draw a line.

So I drew a line. One constant:

private static readonly RET_ROUTING_TEMPLATE_CUTOVER = '2026-04-28';

Indexes created before that date are read the old way, without routing assumptions. Indexes created on or after it carry routing. The reader checks the date in the index name and does the right thing for each. And then — because every log has a retention and a nightly job deletes the ones past it — the pre-cutover indexes simply age out. A thirty-day index is gone thirty days later. Once the last one expires, the special case is dead code.

// TODO ~2026-05-28: drop the 30d guard once pre-cutover indexes age out.

That TODO is the entire decommission plan. Not a migration. A reminder. No second write, no backfill, no flag to flip, no held breath. The only cost was patience: for a few weeks, some reads spanned both the old and new index shapes before the old ones evaporated.

It was so much calmer than the thing happening all around it that I almost did not notice it was the same kind of problem.

Where Claude Helped, and Where It Led Me Astray

I did this work in a tight loop with Claude Code, and the honest accounting cuts both ways.

It earned its keep on the hard, fiddly parts. The hot/warm storage tiering — recent data on fast NVMe, older indexes rolled down to cheaper disk — it designed cleanly. When the new per-plan indexes started rejecting writes every midnight, it worked out why: routing by account funneled a burst of high-volume accounts onto one shard the instant each fresh daily index appeared. And it caught a missing shards-per-node cap that had piled a whale's ten shards onto two machines.

It also walked me into walls with total confidence.

It opened by reasoning about Elasticsearch 7 — because it saw 7.17 in our package.json. That was the client library; the cluster was already on 9. Half its early advice applied to a system we no longer ran.

It recommended an index setting to read each index's age from its name. Reasonable, except Elasticsearch's date parser wants hyphens and our names use underscores. It did not fail in review. It failed in production, on all 325 existing indexes at once, every one stuck in an error state until I tore the setting back out by hand.

And for a stretch it argued against the hot/warm tiering I wanted — insisting it would not come out ahead, that there was nothing to gain. The argument rested on a cost calculation, and the calculation was simply wrong: my configuration cost the same either way, and the tiered shape was the right one for the workload. Not a defensible judgment built on a real number — a wrong number, stated with exactly the confidence of a right one.

The lesson is the one from every post I write about this: a confident wrong number reads identically to a confident right one. The model will reason beautifully and calculate badly in the same breath, and my job is to make it show the arithmetic before I act on the conclusion.

And the decision itself stays mine. The model can fetch, calculate, and propose — but the moment you let Claude, or any AI, do the deciding, you have handed the wheel to something that is wrong and right with the same face, and it will walk you off a cliff with perfect composure. For the moment, at least, that is the one job you do not delegate.

What I'd Do Differently

The routing change was forced into the cheap approach. I did not choose the cutoff date because it was elegant; I chose it because dual-write was off the table. And the forced move turned out to be the one I should have made everywhere.

If I ran the cluster migration again, I would not dual-write it. I would give it a cutoff date too. Stand up the new cluster, point new writes at it, leave the old cluster running and serving the logs it already holds. Read from both during the overlap and merge. Then wait — and the day the oldest log on the old cluster passes its retention, the old cluster holds nothing anyone needs, and you switch it off.

No second copy of the truth to keep in sync. No backfill dragging the whole history across the wire. No silent secondary-write failures loading future damage behind a flag. The price is real and worth naming: you keep two clusters running for as long as your longest retention tier — up to a hundred and eighty days for us — instead of cutting over in a weekend. For a dataset that deletes itself, that is almost always the cheaper trade.

I reached for dual-write because that is what you reach for when you migrate a database. But logs are not most databases. They expire. The hard part of a migration is usually moving the history — and with logs there is no history to move, only a present that, left alone, becomes the past and then becomes nothing.

The Dull Work Customers Could Feel

I have spent this whole post second-guessing how I ran the migration. I want to be just as clear about the thing I do not second-guess: running it at all.

After the new infrastructure settled, the feedback started arriving on its own — from several customers, unprompted. The server feels faster. Searches come back quicker. Nobody files a support ticket asking you to reorganize your Elasticsearch indexes — but the speed-up was real enough that they noticed it on their own and told us.

That is the part worth holding onto. Infrastructure work is the least glamorous work there is. It ships no feature, closes no requested ticket, and shows up on no roadmap anyone cheers for. It is dull — right up until you discover that the dull work was what everything visible had been quietly resting on the whole time. The plumbing is invisible until someone notices the water is suddenly faster out of the tap. The schema change I almost talked myself out of as not-worth-it turned out to be something paying customers could feel.

So both things are true at once. I would change how I did it. I would not, for a second, change that I did it.

The one change I could not force into the dual-write was the one that told me the truth. Next time I will draw the line first.

Originally published on the Shipbook blog.

title: Adaptive Concurrency Limits in Go: Dynamically Protecting Dependencies Under Load
description:
Most services eventually need a concurrency limit.

You might start with something simple:

const maxConcurrentRequests = 100

A semaphore ensures that no more than 100 requests execute simultaneously.

It works. Until the conditions change.

Your service gets more CPU resources after scaling. A downstream database becomes slower. A new deployment changes request processing time. Traffic patterns shift throughout the day.

The limit that worked yesterday might be too restrictive today. Or worse, it might be too high and allow a dependency to become overloaded.

Static concurrency limits are easy to implement, but they require continuous tuning.

What if a service could adjust its concurrency limit automatically based on how the dependency behaves?

That's the idea behind adaptive concurrency limiting.

Instead of relying entirely on a predefined number, the system observes request latency and failure signals, estimates when queueing is happening, and adjusts the number of requests it allows in flight.

In this article, we'll explore:

  • Why fixed concurrency limits eventually become difficult to maintain
  • The relationship between concurrency, throughput, and latency
  • How TCP congestion control inspired adaptive concurrency algorithms
  • How to implement a latency-aware concurrency limiter in Go
  • How to integrate it into an HTTP client
  • How adaptive limits interact with backpressure, bulkheads, and retry budgets
  • What to monitor and test before using adaptive concurrency in production

1. The Problem with Fixed Concurrency Limits

Imagine a Go service that calls an external market data API.

You initially configure a concurrency limit of 50.

limiter := NewFixedLimiter(50)

Under normal traffic, the dependency responds in 40ms.

Everything looks healthy.

Then traffic increases.

The dependency starts processing requests more slowly. Its response time grows to 150ms, then 300ms.

Your service still allows 50 concurrent requests.

The problem is that concurrency and latency are connected.

When requests take longer to complete, existing requests occupy concurrency slots for longer. New requests accumulate, queues grow, and latency increases further.

A fixed limit cannot automatically distinguish between:

  • A dependency that has additional capacity
  • A dependency approaching saturation
  • A dependency already experiencing queueing
  • A dependency recovering from an overload

You can increase the limit manually, but that risks overloading the dependency.

You can decrease it, but that might unnecessarily reduce throughput.

The challenge is finding a concurrency level that allows high throughput without creating excessive queueing.

2. Why Concurrency Matters More Than RPS Alone

Rate limiting and concurrency limiting solve different problems.

A rate limiter controls how many requests can start during a period.

A concurrency limiter controls how many requests can be in progress simultaneously.

Consider two situations:

Scenario Request rate Average latency Approx. concurrency
Healthy dependency 500 req/s 40ms 20
Slow dependency 500 req/s 200ms 100

Both scenarios have the same incoming request rate.

But the second requires five times as many concurrent requests to sustain that throughput.

This relationship is described by Little's Law:

[
L = \lambda W
]

Where:

  • (L) is the average number of items in the system
  • (\lambda) is the average arrival rate
  • (W) is the average time spent in the system

For request processing:

[
Concurrency \approx Throughput \times Latency
]

This explains why a fixed RPS limit is not always sufficient to protect a dependency.

A service can receive an acceptable number of requests per second while still accumulating too many in-flight operations because response times have increased.

Adaptive concurrency focuses on this relationship.

3. The Idea Behind Adaptive Concurrency

The central idea is straightforward:

  1. Measure request latency.
  2. Maintain an estimate of normal, unloaded latency.
  3. Compare current latency against that baseline.
  4. Increase concurrency when the dependency has spare capacity.
  5. Reduce concurrency when latency indicates queueing or failures.

This resembles congestion control in TCP.

TCP does not blindly send unlimited data. It maintains a congestion window and adjusts how much data can be in flight based on network conditions.

Adaptive concurrency applies a similar idea to service requests.

The concurrency limit becomes a dynamic window.

There are several algorithms worth understanding.

AIMD

Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease.

  • Increase the limit gradually when requests succeed.
  • Reduce it significantly when failures or overload signals appear.

For example:

Current limit: 50

Successful samples:
50 → 51 → 52 → 53

Overload detected:
53 → 37

AIMD is relatively simple and works well when the system has reliable failure signals.

However, it may react only after a dependency starts rejecting requests or timing out.

Vegas

Vegas uses latency as an early signal of congestion.

It estimates queueing using the difference between observed latency and a no-load baseline.

A simplified queue estimate is:

[
Q = L \times \left(1 - \frac{RTT_{baseline}}{RTT_{current}}\right)
]

Where:

  • (Q) is estimated queue size
  • (L) is the current concurrency limit
  • (RTT_{baseline}) is the observed no-load latency
  • (RTT_{current}) is the current measured latency

When latency stays close to the baseline, the algorithm can increase concurrency.

When latency grows significantly, it reduces the limit.

Gradient2

Gradient2 compares short-term and long-term latency averages to detect changes in the latency trend.

It is useful when latency baselines drift over time or workloads are bursty.

Instead of relying only on a minimum latency measurement, it uses smoothed averages to identify growing queueing pressure.

For a deeper implementation reference, Netflix's concurrency-limits project is worth exploring:

https://github.com/Netflix/concurrency-limits

For this article, we'll build a smaller Vegas-inspired controller. It is an educational implementation, not a complete reproduction of Netflix's Vegas or Gradient2 algorithms.

4. Building an Adaptive Limiter in Go

Let's implement a limiter that:

  • Tracks in-flight requests
  • Enforces a dynamic concurrency limit
  • Measures request duration
  • Collects latency samples in windows
  • Estimates queueing using a baseline latency
  • Increases or decreases the limit based on observed behavior

We'll use a fail-fast admission strategy.

When the current concurrency limit is reached, the limiter rejects the new request instead of allowing an unbounded queue to form.

Step 1: Define the limiter 

package adaptive

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var ErrLimitExceeded = errors.New(
    "adaptive concurrency limit exceeded",
)

type Limiter struct {
    mu sync.Mutex

    limit    int
    minLimit int
    maxLimit int

    inflight int
    peak     int

    baseline time.Duration

    sampleCount int
    sampleTotal time.Duration
    dropped     bool

    windowSize int

    alpha float64
    beta  float64
}

func New(
    initialLimit int,
    minLimit int,
    maxLimit int,
) *Limiter {
    if minLimit < 1 ||
        initialLimit < minLimit ||
        maxLimit < initialLimit {
        panic("invalid concurrency limits")
    }

    return &Limiter{
        limit:      initialLimit,
        minLimit:   minLimit,
        maxLimit:   maxLimit,
        windowSize: 20,
        alpha:      2,
        beta:       4,
    }
}

The limiter maintains two important pieces of information:

Current limit: The maximum number of requests allowed simultaneously.

In-flight count: The number of requests currently executing.

We also maintain latency statistics and a baseline.

The windowSize determines how many completed requests we collect before updating the concurrency limit.

Using a window helps avoid changing the limit after every individual request.

Step 2: Acquire a permit

The limiter needs to decide whether a new request can execute.

func (l *Limiter) Acquire() (func(bool), error) {
    l.mu.Lock()

    if l.inflight >= l.limit {
        l.mu.Unlock()
        return nil, ErrLimitExceeded
    }

    l.inflight++

    if l.inflight > l.peak {
        l.peak = l.inflight
    }

    l.mu.Unlock()

    startedAt := time.Now()

    var once sync.Once

    done := func(dropped bool) {
        once.Do(func() {
            elapsed := time.Since(startedAt)

            l.mu.Lock()
            defer l.mu.Unlock()

            l.inflight--

            l.recordSample(elapsed, dropped)
        })
    }

    return done, nil
}

The returned function releases the permit and reports the outcome.

For example:

done, err := limiter.Acquire()
if err != nil {
    return err
}

defer done(false)

return callDependency()

If the operation experiences a dependency-level overload signal, we can report that separately:

done, err := limiter.Acquire()
if err != nil {
    return err
}

defer func() {
    done(isOverloadError(err))
}()

err = callDependency()
return err

The sync.Once protects against accidentally releasing the same permit twice.

The caller must invoke the returned function exactly once in normal control flow. The sync.Once makes repeated invocations harmless.

Step 3: Record latency samples

Now we need to collect completed request samples.

func (l *Limiter) recordSample(
    latency time.Duration,
    dropped bool,
) {
    l.sampleCount++
    l.sampleTotal += latency

    if dropped {
        l.dropped = true
    }

    if l.sampleCount < l.windowSize {
        return
    }

    average := l.sampleTotal / time.Duration(l.sampleCount)

    l.updateLimit(average)

    l.sampleCount = 0
    l.sampleTotal = 0
    l.dropped = false
    l.peak = 0
}

Instead of adjusting concurrency after every request, we wait until a complete sample window is collected.

This reduces sensitivity to individual latency spikes.

A production implementation may use more sophisticated rolling windows, exponential moving averages, or percentile-based measurements.

Step 4: Implement the control algorithm

Now comes the interesting part.

We compare the current average latency against the baseline.

func (l *Limiter) updateLimit(
    currentLatency time.Duration,
) {
    if currentLatency <= 0 {
        return
    }

    if l.baseline == 0 ||
        currentLatency < l.baseline {
        l.baseline = currentLatency
        return
    }

    if l.dropped {
        l.decrease()
        return
    }

    queueEstimate := float64(l.limit) *
        (1 - float64(l.baseline)/float64(currentLatency))

    // Increase only when the previous window
    // demonstrated meaningful concurrency usage.
    if l.peak*2 < l.limit {
        return
    }

    switch {
    case queueEstimate < l.alpha:
        l.increase()

    case queueEstimate > l.beta:
        l.decrease()
    }
}

The queue estimate is an approximation of the queueing pressure observed at the dependency.

When current latency is close to the baseline, the estimated queue remains small.

When current latency increases, the estimated queue grows.

We use two thresholds:

  • alpha: Below this value, the dependency appears to have spare capacity.
  • beta: Above this value, queueing pressure is considered too high.

The gap between the thresholds creates a stability region where the limit does not change.

This helps avoid unnecessary oscillation.

Step 5: Increase and decrease concurrency

The final methods enforce the configured boundaries.

func (l *Limiter) increase() {
    if l.limit < l.maxLimit {
        l.limit++
    }
}

func (l *Limiter) decrease() {
    next := int(float64(l.limit) * 0.7)

    if next < l.minLimit {
        next = l.minLimit
    }

    l.limit = next
}

The limiter uses:

  • Additive increase: Grow gradually.
  • Multiplicative decrease: Reduce more aggressively when congestion appears.

This is intentionally conservative.

Increasing the limit by one allows the dependency to demonstrate additional capacity without creating a large traffic spike.

Reducing the limit by 30% provides a faster response to overload.

These values are configuration choices, not universal production defaults.

Step 6: Expose the current limit

We should expose the current state for observability.

func (l *Limiter) Stats() (
    limit int,
    inflight int,
    baseline time.Duration,
) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    return l.limit, l.inflight, l.baseline
}

Now we can inspect the limiter without exposing its internal synchronization.

For example:

limit, inflight, baseline := limiter.Stats()

log.Printf(
    "adaptive limiter: limit=%d inflight=%d baseline=%s",
    limit,
    inflight,
    baseline,
)

5. Integrating the Limiter with an HTTP Client

Let's apply the limiter to an external dependency.

type MarketDataClient struct {
    httpClient *http.Client
    limiter    *adaptive.Limiter
}

func (c *MarketDataClient) Fetch(
    ctx context.Context,
    symbol string,
) error {
    done, err := c.limiter.Acquire()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var dropped bool

    defer func() {
        done(dropped)
    }()

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(
        ctx,
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.example.com/market/"+symbol,
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    resp, err := c.httpClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        dropped = isDependencyOverload(err)
        return err
    }

    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests ||
        resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusServiceUnavailable {
        dropped = true
        return fmt.Errorf(
            "market data dependency returned %d",
            resp.StatusCode,
        )
    }

    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf(
            "unexpected status: %d",
            resp.StatusCode,
        )
    }

    return nil
}

The example classifies overload responses separately from other errors.

This distinction matters.

A validation error, for example, should not necessarily cause the adaptive limiter to reduce its concurrency limit.

Likewise, a network timeout might be an overload signal in one system but a network infrastructure issue in another.

The failure classifier should reflect the dependency's actual behavior.

The HTTP client should also have appropriate timeouts and connection settings. An adaptive concurrency limiter is not a replacement for transport-level protection.

6. What Happens During an Overload?

Let's walk through a simplified scenario.

Assume the limiter starts with a concurrency limit of 50.

The dependency initially responds in 40ms.

As traffic increases, the limiter observes the following:

Stage Average latency Concurrency limit
Initial 40ms 50
Increased traffic 45ms 51
Higher utilization 55ms 52
Queueing begins 120ms 36
Dependency recovers 45ms Gradually increases

The important behavior is not the exact numbers.

The limiter detects that latency is increasing relative to the baseline and reduces the amount of work it allows in flight.

As the dependency recovers, the limiter can gradually explore additional capacity again.

This is a feedback control loop.

However, it is important to understand that the limiter does not instantly discover the perfect concurrency limit. It continuously estimates a useful operating point based on observed signals.

7. Adaptive Concurrency vs. Other Resilience Patterns

Adaptive concurrency is not a replacement for the patterns we've discussed in previous articles.

It complements them.

Mechanism Responsibility
Backpressure Controls incoming work
Load shedding Rejects work when capacity is exceeded
Bulkhead Isolates resources and dependencies
Retry budget Limits additional retry traffic
Adaptive concurrency Adjusts the concurrency ceiling based on observed conditions

Consider a service that communicates with three dependencies:

  • Market Data API
  • Portfolio Database
  • Reporting Service

Each dependency has different latency characteristics and capacity.

Using one global concurrency limit would couple their behavior.

A better approach is to create an independent adaptive limiter for each dependency.

type DependencyLimiters struct {
    MarketData *adaptive.Limiter
    Portfolio  *adaptive.Limiter
    Reporting  *adaptive.Limiter
}

This gives each dependency its own feedback loop.

If the reporting service becomes slow, its concurrency limit can decrease without automatically reducing the capacity available to market data requests.

This is where adaptive concurrency and bulkheads work particularly well together.

8. Important Production Considerations

The example implementation demonstrates the core idea, but a production adaptive limiter needs additional safeguards.

Baseline latency can become stale

A latency baseline is only useful when it represents a reasonably unloaded system.

If the baseline is established while the dependency is already overloaded, the algorithm may incorrectly treat unhealthy latency as normal.

Production implementations should carefully manage baseline updates and resets.

Traffic must be representative

A dependency may expose different latency characteristics for different operations.

For example:

  • Reading a cached market price
  • Fetching historical prices
  • Calculating a portfolio
  • Executing a database aggregation

Combining all these operations into one latency signal can produce misleading results.

Consider separate limiters or traffic partitions when workloads have significantly different behavior.

The algorithm needs enough samples

Adaptive control depends on observations.

A low-traffic service might not generate enough samples to update its limit reliably.

A new instance also needs a warm-up strategy.

Slow start, conservative initial limits, and minimum sample requirements can help.

Avoid uncontrolled oscillation

A limiter that constantly increases and decreases its capacity can introduce instability.

Useful techniques include:

  • Sampling windows
  • Exponential smoothing
  • Separate increase and decrease thresholds
  • Bounded increase and decrease rates
  • Minimum and maximum concurrency limits
  • Jitter when multiple independent clients share a dependency

Local limits multiply across replicas

This is especially important in distributed deployments.

Imagine ten replicas, each with an adaptive concurrency limit of 100.

The dependency may receive up to 1,000 concurrent requests.

Each instance is making decisions based on its own observations. The aggregate behavior is not automatically coordinated.

Local adaptive concurrency is often sufficient for protecting individual instances and reacting to local conditions.

But strict global dependency quotas may require a shared dispatcher, centralized coordination, or provider-side quota enforcement.

Do not confuse concurrency with connection limits

An HTTP transport's connection pool and an application's concurrency limiter protect different resources.

A request may hold an application permit while waiting for a connection. Conversely, HTTP/2 can multiplex multiple requests over one connection.

Configure both based on the actual workload.

9. Testing Adaptive Concurrency

Adaptive algorithms should be tested as control systems, not only as ordinary utility functions.

At minimum, test these behaviors:

  • The initial concurrency limit is respected.
  • Requests are rejected when the current limit is reached.
  • Permits are released exactly once.
  • Successful low-latency windows allow gradual growth.
  • Rising latency causes the limit to decrease.
  • Overload signals trigger a decrease.
  • The limit never exceeds its configured maximum.
  • The limit never falls below its configured minimum.
  • Concurrent acquisitions are race-safe.
  • Insufficient sample windows do not trigger premature changes.

Run the race detector:

go test -race ./...

Also consider deterministic algorithm tests.

Instead of using real HTTP requests and sleeping for arbitrary durations, separate the control algorithm from the admission mechanism.

Feed known latency samples into the controller and verify the resulting limit.

For example:

Baseline: 40ms

Window 1: 42ms → increase
Window 2: 45ms → increase
Window 3: 120ms → decrease
Window 4: 130ms → decrease
Window 5: 45ms → gradual recovery

This makes algorithm behavior easier to reproduce and debug.

Finally, run load tests with changing dependency latency.

A useful test should simulate:

  1. A healthy dependency.
  2. Gradually increasing latency.
  3. Sudden overload.
  4. Partial recovery.
  5. A complete dependency outage.

Measure throughput, p95/p99 latency, rejection rate, and concurrency limit changes.

The goal is not simply to maximize throughput.

The goal is to maintain useful throughput without allowing latency and queueing to grow uncontrollably.

10. Observability

An adaptive limiter introduces a new operational component.

You need visibility into how it makes decisions.

Useful metrics include:

Metric Type Purpose
adaptive_concurrency_limit Gauge Current concurrency ceiling
adaptive_inflight_requests Gauge Active requests
adaptive_request_latency_seconds Histogram Observed dependency latency
adaptive_rejected_total Counter Requests rejected at admission
adaptive_limit_increase_total Counter Limit increase events
adaptive_limit_decrease_total Counter Limit decrease events
adaptive_baseline_latency_seconds Gauge Estimated unloaded latency

These metrics help answer important questions:

  • Is the limiter constantly operating at its maximum?
  • Is the concurrency limit frequently decreasing?
  • Is the dependency latency increasing?
  • Are requests being rejected before reaching the dependency?
  • Is the limiter recovering too slowly?

A particularly useful dashboard plots three signals together:

  1. Current concurrency limit
  2. In-flight requests
  3. Dependency latency

Looking at them independently can hide the relationship between capacity and latency.

Avoid high-cardinality labels such as raw URLs, user IDs, and request IDs.

11. When Should You Use Adaptive Concurrency?

Adaptive concurrency is not necessary for every service.

A fixed limit is often the better choice when:

  • Dependency capacity is stable and well understood.
  • Traffic patterns are predictable.
  • The service has low request volume.
  • The cost of an adaptive control loop is not justified.
  • A simple semaphore already provides sufficient protection.

Adaptive concurrency becomes more attractive when:

  • Dependency capacity changes frequently.
  • Traffic is bursty or unpredictable.
  • Services scale horizontally.
  • Latency is a reliable indicator of queueing.
  • Manual concurrency tuning is difficult.
  • You need to protect dependencies before they start rejecting requests.

Start with a fixed limit if it is sufficient. Introduce adaptive behavior when operational evidence shows that static configuration is becoming a limitation.

Conclusion

A fixed concurrency limit assumes that system capacity is relatively predictable.

In distributed systems, that assumption does not always hold.

Dependencies slow down, traffic changes, instances scale, and resource availability evolves.

Adaptive concurrency provides a feedback loop that adjusts the amount of work allowed in flight based on observed latency and failure signals.

In Go, the core mechanism is straightforward: track active requests, collect latency samples, estimate congestion, and adjust the concurrency ceiling.

The difficult part is not implementing a semaphore.

It is building a stable controller that reacts to real overload without constantly oscillating or making incorrect decisions from noisy measurements.

Don't just limit how much work your service can handle. Let it learn when it should slow down.
