title: Game Notification Bounces in 2026: Ownership Rules for Email and SMS Events
description:
TL;DR: The best practices for wiring email and SMS notification events into Node.js SaaS apps are to keep recipient suppression and delivery state in your event pipeline, while letting a delivery service own transport details. The deciding question is template ownership: if product and compliance need to change copy without a deploy, use provider-managed templates; if every message must be reviewed and versioned with code, keep templates in your repository. Either way, bounces must become durable suppression decisions, not transient send errors.

I learned to treat a notification as a state transition, not a function call. A player changes an email address, a password-reset event is emitted, the mail provider accepts the request, and the recipient still never gets the message. The dangerous part is the gap between acceptance and delivery. A retry in that gap can turn one bad address into a noisy loop, and an SMS fallback can amplify the same mistake across channels.

The bounded production scenario is a game account service sending sign-in and account-change notices. The platform receives a bounce, records the provider event, suppresses the invalid recipient, and makes the next decision from that record. The invariant is simple: transport may be asynchronous, but recipient eligibility must be durable and auditable.

The failure chain is easy to miss in a design review. An account event enters the queue while the player is online, the worker submits an email, and the provider returns an accepted result; hours later, a mailbox rejection arrives through the delivery event surface, but the original worker has already acknowledged its job. If the event consumer treats that later rejection as a notification failure only, the address remains eligible and the next account event repeats the same delivery. If it writes suppression before retaining the raw event, an operator loses the evidence needed to distinguish a bad mailbox from a temporary provider problem. The safer sequence is to retain the provider event, normalize its reason, apply the recipient-state transition idempotently, and make every later channel consult that state before it sends. This also keeps the application contract stable when the transport behind it changes, because the consumer reasons about eligibility and intent rather than a provider's vocabulary.

That is the trap.

What should own the template when a recipient bounces?

The answer is usually the team that owns the approval risk. I would keep transactional message content in versioned templates when the message is part of an authentication or account-security contract. That gives the platform team a reviewable change, a clear rollback, and one place to test variables. I would allow provider-managed templates for high-volume campaign-like notices when non-engineers need controlled edits and the provider's revision history is acceptable.

This is a real trade-off, not a branding preference. Repository-owned templates reduce vendor lock-in and make a provider swap less invasive, but they move previewing, localization, rendering checks, and approval workflow into your system. Provider-owned templates shorten that work and keep copy changes out of deploys, but a migration now includes template identifiers, variable rules, and a second source of truth.

The useful boundary is an internal notification contract. It contains an event name, a recipient reference, a channel policy, and a template version. It does not contain provider-specific status names. A worker resolves that contract, checks suppression, sends asynchronously, and records the provider identifier. A poller later translates delivery events into your states: accepted, delivered, bounced, suppressed, or needs-review.

Why are bounces harder than failed sends?

An HTTP error is immediate. A bounce is a later fact, and the two channels expose it differently. The mail event list and the SMS status resource need periodic polling because real-time push events are not available here. That means the poll interval is part of the product's notification behavior and the SLO, even if nobody put it in the service diagram.

I would set an explicit freshness objective for delivery state, then capacity-plan the poller from event volume rather than from request volume. If 2 million events can accumulate during a busy game launch, a five-minute poll target implies enough workers, pagination, storage, and provider rate-limit headroom to clear that backlog before the next poll window. The exact worker count is a measurement from your traffic and limits, not a number to borrow from a blog post.

The suppression write must be idempotent. A repeated bounce event should not create repeated tickets, repeated SMS attempts, or a race that re-enables the address. Keep the raw event for audit, keep the normalized recipient state for decisions, and make the transition monotonic unless an explicit verification flow changes it.

Bad addresses compound.

So does ambiguity.

How should Node.js SaaS apps handle email and SMS notification events?

The practical wiring is an event record, a queue, a suppression check, and a delivery poller. Node.js is a good fit for the asynchronous boundary because the web request can enqueue a notification and return while a worker performs the provider call, but that convenience does not remove the need for a durable event ID or a retry budget.

Here is the seam I want tested in a worker: the identity lookup and the mail send use the same base URL and key, while the application owns the notification decision. The request bodies shown below are application envelopes; the provider-specific body should be validated against the live capability schema before deployment.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, base, key, method, path string, body io.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, base+strings.TrimPrefix(path, "/v1"), body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    res, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("notification API returned %s: %s", res.Status, data)
    }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    ctx := context.Background()
    client := &http.Client{}

    identityPath := "/v1/auth/user/get_by_email?email=" + url.QueryEscape("player@example.test")
    identity, err := call(ctx, client, base, key, http.MethodGet, identityPath, nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    mailBody, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "event":    "account.security",
        "recipient": "player@example.test",
        "identity": json.RawMessage(identity),
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if _, err = call(ctx, client, base, key, http.MethodPost, "/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(mailBody)); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

In a production worker, replace the panic paths with durable failure records and bounded retries. Retry 429 responses with exponential backoff and the Retry-After value when present. Give every write an idempotency key derived from the event ID, recipient, channel, and template version. Log the request ID, provider status, normalized state, and suppression reason, but never log the bearer key or message body by default.

The transport behind this contract can change without changing the application call site. That is the practical value of a stable capability boundary: swapping the vendor behind it does not rewrite the event consumer, the suppression table, or the SLO dashboard. One additional benefit in this workflow is that identity lookup and dependent mail delivery can use the same account boundary, so the handoff does not require a separate credential path. The cost is just as real: one vendor becomes one trust boundary, one billing relationship, and one outage surface.

Which delivery design fits a gaming SaaS?

Option Template ownership Bounce and suppression work Best fit Boundary to accept
Amazon SES Usually application or SES templates You still need event ingestion, normalization, and suppression policy Teams already invested in AWS controls More AWS-specific integration and operational coupling
Twilio SendGrid Strong provider-managed template workflow Delivery events are useful, but your system still owns recipient eligibility Marketing and product teams changing approved copy Template migration and provider-specific identifiers
Mailgun Application or provider templates Good for teams that want event-oriented mail tooling plus their own state model Mail-heavy SaaS with a small platform team You still design the durable audit and retry contract
Self-hosted SMTP Fully application-owned All feedback, reputation, throttling, and suppression operations are yours Narrow environments with unusual control requirements Higher on-call load and a larger failure surface
A unified REST capability Application-owned contract with a replaceable transport Poll delivery events, normalize state, and suppress in your database A platform team standardizing auth and communications boundaries One provider trust and outage boundary

I would not choose solely from a feature checklist. SendGrid's template workflow can be the right answer when copy approvals are the bottleneck. SES is compelling when existing AWS identity, logging, and policy controls matter more than portability. Mailgun can suit a mail-centric team that wants provider tooling but still keeps its own event ledger. Self-hosting is defensible only when the team is prepared to own deliverability as a primary service.

For the unified option, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when one REST contract and one credential boundary matter more than having separate specialists for identity and delivery. It is not a substitute for your suppression database, compliance review, or geographic SMS controls. The business layer still needs its own anti-abuse fences, including per-country limits and geofencing.

What should the SLO measure?

Do not use “send succeeded” as the notification SLO. Measure the age of the newest delivery state, the percentage of events normalized within that objective, and the time from a confirmed bounce to suppression. Track queue age, retry count, 429 rate, provider acceptance, and the number of sends rejected by your own suppression check.

The fallback policy needs a hard stop. If email bounces, SMS is not automatically safe: the phone number may be stale, the event may not justify a second channel, and SMS abuse controls may be missing. For authentication, a self-built email-code fallback also changes the security review because there is no managed email OTP interface in this capability set. SMS cancellation is available, while scheduled email cannot be canceled, so scheduling should be conservative and tied to an event that remains valid for the whole delay.

The advice does not apply unchanged to every product. A regulated service may require a regional provider, a separate audit system, or a no-shared-vendor policy. A game with only non-critical announcements may accept eventual delivery and provider templates. The decision rule is narrower: own the recipient state and its audit trail in the system that can enforce suppression; choose template ownership according to who must approve changes; then make transport replaceable behind that contract.

Sources

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/
  • Twilio SendGrid Event Webhook documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/tracking-events/event
  • Mailgun Events API documentation: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/openapi-final/tag/Events/

title: My AI directory has 92 categories. Ten of them hold 37% of the listings.
description:
I ran one query against my AI tools directory last night, and the result explained why some of its pages get crawled while others sit ignored.

Category Tools
RIP AI 405
Video Generators 294
Image Generators 269
Productivity 253
Developer Tools 247
Education / Studies 245
Business 233
Image editing 230
LLM models 208
Life Assistants 192

Those ten categories hold 2,576 of 7,006 category assignments — 36.8% of the whole taxonomy. The directory has 4,323 tools across 92 categories.

That last number is not the problem. The tail is.

14 categories have ten tools or fewer

  • New AI Tools: 0
  • AIxploria Selection: 0
  • Programming: 0
  • AI Presentations: 2
  • AI Music: 4
  • AI Education: 4
  • AI 3D: 4
  • AI Research: 4
  • AI SEO: 5
  • AI Translation: 7
  • AI Chatbots: 8
  • AI Image Generators: 8
  • AI Social Media: 8
  • AI Customer Support: 10

Three of those are empty, and they are also the most tempting pages to publish, because the names sound valuable: "New AI Tools" and "Programming" are exactly what a searcher types. So I checked what the site actually returns for them:

$ BASE=https://aiverse.mindutil.com
$ curl -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$BASE/category/last-ai-en"
404
$ curl -s "$BASE/category/last-ai-en" | grep robots
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow"/>

And the sitemap filter is one line:

where: { tools: { some: {} } }

So 89 of 92 categories ship in the sitemap. The three empty ones do not.

Why a 404 beats an empty page

An empty category that returns 200 with "0 tools found" is a page a crawler can index. Do that twenty times and you have told a search engine your site has twenty useless URLs before it has read a single tool page. The 404 does the opposite: it says this hub does not exist yet.

None of this is free. A user who bookmarked the page gets a dead end, and the internal link from the categories index has to be removed or the link graph starts leaking 404s. The trade is simple: a little maintenance for the absence of thin pages. On a directory where the median tool page is still fighting for its first indexing, that trade is worth taking.

Category is not a tag

4,323 tools produce 7,006 category assignments, an average of 1.62 per tool. Exactly 2,100 tools (48.6%) sit in two or more categories. That overlap is real — a video editor can be "Video Editing", "Productivity", and "Business" without stretching any of those labels.

Overlap is also what keeps category pages from being template clones: each one is a different basket of results. Directory sites get flagged as doorway pages when the only unique word on 92 pages is the category name. The fix is not fewer categories. It is making each category page answer something the tool pages cannot: which five of these should I try first, and why.

The 405-tool graveyard

RIP AI is the largest bucket in the whole directory: 405 tools, 9.4% of everything, 236 of them marked free. These are discontinued or dead products. Publishing that number is useful — a directory that never deletes anything is lying by omission — but RIP AI is not a category. It is a status.

Mixing the two is how you end up with a tool that is both "RIP AI" and "Video Generators", an empty "Programming" bucket, and all three looking equally important in a sitemap.

Four rules I am adopting

  1. A category ships only if it has at least one tool. Zero-tool hub gets a 404 and noindex, never a 200 with an empty state.
  2. A category with fewer than 10 tools does not get its own indexable template until it reaches 10. Until then it is a filter on the parent listing.
  3. Statuses — dead, free, new, verified — stay filters, not categories.
  4. Every category page needs a hand-written shortlist paragraph. If I cannot write one, the category is not ready to be indexed.

Only the first rule is already live. The other three are the work for the next few weeks.

The part that surprised me

The top ten are not the categories I would have guessed. I expected "AI Chatbots" to lead; it has 8 tools. Video Generators has 294. The taxonomy drifted toward whatever the crawler found in bulk rather than toward what people actually search for. That is a data problem wearing a design problem's clothes, and it is the next thing on the list.

If you want to see the current state of the catalog, including the free and paid filters, it is here: https://aiverse.mindutil.com/free-ai-tools?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=topic

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: Balancing Centralized Cloud Computing with Individual Ownership: Addressing Underutilized Resources and User Preferences
description:
Introduction: The Clash of Computing Philosophies

The debate over the future of computing has crystallized into a fundamental conflict: on one side, proponents of centralized cloud computing, exemplified by Sam Altman, argue that underutilized consumer DRAM represents inefficiency, advocating for its consolidation in cloud ecosystems. On the other, self-hosting advocates counter that personal hardware ownership is essential for privacy, autonomy, and resistance to centralized control. Altman’s assertion that consumer DRAM operates at only 5% utilization frames idleness as waste, yet this critique overlooks the systemic implications of relinquishing hardware control—a shift that extends beyond resource allocation to the erosion of individual digital sovereignty.

Altman’s efficiency-centric argument hinges on the volatile nature of DRAM, which, while critical for active computing tasks, remains idle in personal devices during periods of inactivity. However, this idleness is not a defect but a byproduct of ownership. For instance, a self-hosted setup comprising a TrueNAS storage appliance, a Docker-based media server, and a desktop running local large language models (LLMs) exemplifies decentralized control. These systems, powered by hardware like an RTX 3080, process data locally, ensuring that sensitive information remains within the user’s domain. The 5% utilization Altman criticizes is the cost of maintaining this control, a trade-off between efficiency and autonomy.

The push for cloud centralization carries tangible risks. As hyperscale providers such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud dominate 67% of global cloud infrastructure, they accrue disproportionate control over resource allocation, dictating the terms of access and usage. Altman’s framing of idle DRAM as waste masks a strategic maneuver to subsume the last vestiges of decentralized hardware. This is not merely resource optimization but a consolidation of power, where individual computing capabilities are subsumed into corporate ecosystems.

Self-hosting, while technically feasible, faces institutional barriers. Challenges such as email deliverability from residential IPs and the complexity of security management persist, yet open-source tools like Nextcloud, Gitea, and Pi-hole have lowered technical entry points. The primary threat lies in the convenience paradigm—a gradual, often imperceptible transfer of ownership through cloud dependencies. Each service adopted cedes a degree of control, incrementally transforming the open web into a relic of the past.

The causal relationship is unambiguous: centralization begets dependency, which in turn erodes autonomy. As cloud providers extend their reach, individuals risk forfeiting not only their hardware but also the ability to compute independently. Altman’s vision of "maximum utilization" envisions a world where personal resources serve corporate interests, not individual needs. In contrast, the idle cycles of a self-hosted RTX 3080 represent a deliberate choice to retain control, prioritizing sovereignty over efficiency.

Scenario Analysis: Six Perspectives on Resource Utilization

The debate between centralized cloud computing and self-hosting transcends mere efficiency—it fundamentally concerns control, ownership, and the trajectory of digital autonomy. Below, we analyze six scenarios that illuminate these trade-offs, grounded in technical mechanisms and causal relationships.

1. The Idle DRAM Dilemma: Efficiency vs. Sovereignty

Sam Altman’s critique of underutilized consumer DRAM centers on its volatile nature: DRAM requires continuous power to retain data, rendering idle memory inefficient. In cloud environments, DRAM is pooled and dynamically allocated via virtualization and workload balancing, maximizing utilization. Conversely, self-hosted setups, such as the author’s RTX 3080-powered LLM machine, prioritize local data processing, ensuring sensitive information remains on-device. The trade-off is clear: lower utilization in exchange for enhanced sovereignty. The critical risk lies in resource monopolization: as cloud providers consolidate DRAM, individual ownership diminishes, and users forfeit the capacity for independent data processing.

2. The Email Deliverability Conundrum: Institutional Barriers in Self-Hosting

Self-hosting email in 2026 is fraught with challenges due to the fragmented nature of email protocols and the blacklisting of residential IPs. Cloud providers like ProtonMail circumvent these issues by operating from dedicated IP ranges with established reputations. The causal mechanism is straightforward: institutional barriers (ISP restrictions, spam filters) → increased technical complexity → user abandonment of self-hosting. This scenario exemplifies how convenience systematically erodes autonomy, one service at a time.

3. The RTX 3080’s Dual Role: Local LLMs vs. Cloud Rental

The RTX 3080 in the author’s setup epitomizes the utilization-ownership trade-off. In cloud environments, GPUs like the 3080 are overclocked and load-balanced across multiple tenants, optimizing efficiency but accelerating hardware degradation and generating excess heat. Locally, the GPU operates at user-defined loads, preserving its lifespan but remaining idle during downtime. The risk lies in cloud providers framing local GPU ownership as inefficient, incentivizing users to adopt rental models that centralize control.

4. The TrueNAS Paradox: Storage Centralization vs. Decentralized Control

TrueNAS, a self-hosted NAS solution, leverages local HDDs/SSDs to avoid cloud providers’ data lock-in mechanisms. However, cloud storage offers redundancy through geographic distribution and automated backups. The trade-off is data sovereignty vs. convenience. The risk lies in cloud providers’ tiered pricing and egress fees, which create economic lock-in, rendering self-hosted storage increasingly impractical over time.

5. The Pi-hole Predicament: DNS Control vs. Institutional Resistance

Pi-hole, a self-hosted DNS and ad blocker, functions by intercepting DNS queries locally, bypassing cloud-based ad networks. However, ISPs and content providers increasingly block residential DNS servers, citing security risks or policy violations. The causal chain is evident: institutional resistance → reduced functionality → user migration to cloud-based alternatives. This scenario highlights how institutional barriers systematically undermine technical solutions favoring decentralization.

6. The Open Web’s Silent Erosion: Convenience as a Trojan Horse

The author’s observation—“We lost the open web to convenience, one login at a time”—encapsulates a causal chain of dependency. Cloud services exploit proprietary APIs and vendor lock-in to consolidate control. For instance, Google Drive’s seamless integration with Gmail and Docs creates a network effect, rendering self-hosted alternatives like Nextcloud less appealing. The risk is clear: as users prioritize convenience, they incrementally surrender ownership, culminating in a centralized web dominated by a handful of providers.

Conclusion: The Mechanisms of Control

Each scenario exposes a mechanism of control: cloud providers leverage efficiency gaps, institutional barriers, and user convenience to centralize resources. Self-hosting, while less efficient, safeguards digital sovereignty through local processing and ownership. The choice is not merely technical—it is existential. As Altman targets your idle DRAM, consider: What are you willing to trade for control?

Conclusion: The Existential Clash Between Efficiency and Autonomy

The debate between centralized cloud computing and individual ownership of computing resources transcends technical considerations—it is fundamentally existential. Sam Altman’s critique of underutilized consumer DRAM underscores a legitimate efficiency concern: DRAM, a volatile memory essential for active tasks, remains idle in personal devices 95% of the time. Cloud providers address this inefficiency by pooling and virtualizing DRAM across thousands of users, achieving economies of scale unattainable by individuals. However, this efficiency is predicated on centralized control. By framing local ownership as "waste," cloud providers not only optimize resource allocation but also redefine the locus of computational ownership, shifting it from individuals to corporations.

The Efficiency Paradox: Short-Term Gains, Long-Term Dependency

Cloud computing’s promise of maximum utilization is undeniable. Hyperscale providers like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud leverage load-balancing and resource virtualization to extract peak performance from hardware. For instance, a GPU such as the RTX 3080, which might idle 90% of the time in a self-hosted setup, is overclocked and distributed across multiple tenants in the cloud. Mechanistically, overclocking accelerates thermal degradation, reducing the GPU’s lifespan, but it maximizes short-term efficiency. This trade-off commodifies individual hardware, embedding it within corporate ecosystems where users forfeit control over resource allocation and lifecycle management.

Ownership as a Bulwark Against Institutional Capture

Self-hosting champions digital sovereignty, ensuring that data processing and storage remain physically localized. By deploying services like Nextcloud, Gitea, or local LLMs on personal hardware, users retain direct control over their data and workflows. This autonomy extends beyond privacy to resisting institutional lock-in. Cloud providers employ egress fees and tiered pricing models to create economic dependency, exploiting the asymmetry between low-cost data ingestion and high-cost extraction. Mechanistically, these fees disincentivize data portability, making self-hosted alternatives like TrueNAS viable but demanding trade-offs in redundancy and convenience. Self-hosting, therefore, is not merely a technical choice but a strategic act of resistance against corporate capture.

Institutional Barriers: Eroding Autonomy by Design

The push toward centralization is as much institutional as it is technological. Email self-hosting, once a symbol of autonomy, has been rendered impractical by security-patching complexities and blacklisting of residential IPs. Mechanistically, this arises from the need to emulate the reputation of dedicated cloud IPs, a standard residential users cannot meet. Similarly, DNS solutions like Pi-hole are undermined by ISPs blocking residential DNS servers under the pretext of security risks, funneling users into cloud-based alternatives. These barriers are not accidental but deliberate, designed to consolidate control within corporate ecosystems.

Convenience as a Mechanism of Control

Convenience serves as the silent architect of dependency. Cloud providers leverage proprietary APIs and vendor lock-in to create frictionless experiences that mask the surrender of autonomy. Migrating from Google Drive to Nextcloud, for example, requires physical data transfer and workflow reconfiguration—a barrier cloud providers exploit. Mechanistically, this friction stems from the incompatibility between open protocols and proprietary ecosystems. Each interaction with a cloud service incrementally cedes ownership, eroding the open web through cumulative micro-surrenders.

The Future: Navigating the Spectrum of Control

The choice between cloud and self-hosting is not binary but exists on a spectrum. Hybrid setups, such as using Proton for email while self-hosting media stacks (e.g., Sonarr, Radarr), offer a balanced approach. However, the stakes are clear: unchecked cloud consolidation threatens to subsume individual computing capacity into corporate ecosystems. Hyperscale providers already control 67% of global cloud infrastructure, and their leadership openly advocates for greater control over consumer hardware. This is not resource optimization but strategic acquisition of the last hardware they do not yet control.

As you navigate this landscape, scrutinize the mechanisms of control: efficiency gaps, institutional barriers, and convenience traps. Self-hosting is not merely about optimizing idle DRAM—it is about preserving the ability to compute on your terms. The tools for autonomy have never been more accessible, yet the gravitational pull toward centralization has never been stronger. The open web is not being lost in a war; it is being surrendered, one login at a time. The question remains: what are you willing to trade for convenience?

title: .NET 10 + Pinecone: como integrar com um banco de dados vetorial
description:
🧭 1. Introdução

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone permite desenvolver aplicações capazes de armazenar, pesquisar e recuperar informações por similaridade semântica.

Essa abordagem é especialmente útil em projetos de:

  • Inteligência Artificial (IA).
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
  • Assistentes virtuais e chatbots.
  • Busca semântica de documentos.
  • Sistemas de recomendação.
  • Recuperação inteligente de conhecimento.
  • Aplicações baseadas em LLMs (Large Language Models).

Diferentemente dos bancos relacionais tradicionais, que normalmente consultam dados por condições e valores exatos, o Pinecone foi projetado para trabalhar com vetores (embeddings).

Esses vetores representam o significado de textos, documentos e outros conteúdos em um espaço matemático. Dessa forma, conseguimos encontrar informações relacionadas pelo contexto, mesmo quando as palavras utilizadas são diferentes.

Neste artigo, vamos implementar uma integração utilizando:

  • .NET 10 e C#.
  • Pinecone Vector Database.
  • API REST do Pinecone.
  • HttpClient e IHttpClientFactory.
  • Injeção de dependência.
  • Arquitetura organizada em camadas.
  • Operações de inserção e pesquisa vetorial.

🧠 2. O que é Pinecone?

O Pinecone é um banco de dados vetorial gerenciado, desenvolvido para armazenar e consultar embeddings em larga escala.

Seu principal objetivo é permitir pesquisas por similaridade entre vetores, oferecendo uma infraestrutura especializada para aplicações de IA.

Como funciona?

Imagine uma aplicação que armazena documentos sobre desenvolvimento de software.

Podemos cadastrar os seguintes conteúdos:

  • Documento 1: Como implementar autenticação JWT com .NET.
  • Documento 2: Como proteger endpoints de uma API.
  • Documento 3: Como configurar um banco de dados SQL Server.
  • Documento 4: Como implementar autorização baseada em políticas.

Quando um usuário pesquisa:

"Como proteger uma API desenvolvida em C#?"

Uma busca tradicional pode depender da correspondência exata das palavras.

Já uma busca vetorial pode encontrar documentos semanticamente relacionados, como o documento sobre autenticação JWT ou autorização baseada em políticas.

Principais conceitos

Conceito Descrição
Vector Representação numérica de um conteúdo
Embedding Processo de transformar conteúdo em vetor
Index Estrutura onde os vetores são armazenados
Namespace Divisão lógica dos registros
Metadata Informações adicionais associadas ao vetor
Similarity Search Pesquisa por proximidade entre vetores
Upsert Inserção ou atualização de vetores
Query Consulta por similaridade

🔄 3. Arquitetura de funcionamento

Uma integração com Pinecone normalmente envolve três etapas principais:

  1. Transformar o conteúdo em embeddings.
  2. Armazenar os embeddings no Pinecone.
  3. Gerar um embedding para a pesquisa e consultar os vetores mais próximos.

É importante entender que Pinecone e o modelo de embeddings possuem responsabilidades diferentes.

O Pinecone armazena e pesquisa vetores. O modelo de embeddings transforma textos em representações numéricas.

Fluxo de inserção 

flowchart TD
    A["Aplicação .NET 10"] --> B["Documento / Texto"]
    B --> C["Modelo de Embeddings"]

Fluxo de pesquisa

Em aplicações RAG, os documentos recuperados podem ser enviados posteriormente para um LLM, que utiliza esse contexto para construir uma resposta.

🏗️ 4. Criando o projeto .NET 10

Vamos começar criando uma Web API.

dotnet new webapi -n PineconeIntegration
cd PineconeIntegration

Para este exemplo, utilizaremos a API REST diretamente por meio do HttpClient.

Essa escolha evita acoplar a aplicação a uma biblioteca específica. O repositório do SDK oficial C# foi arquivado em julho de 2026, portanto vale avaliar cuidadosamente seu estado de manutenção antes de adotá-lo em novos projetos.

  • Api: exposição dos endpoints HTTP.
  • Application: contratos, DTOs e regras de aplicação.

  • Infrastructure: integração com serviços externos, embeddings e Pinecone.

🔑 5. Criando uma conta e configurando o Pinecone

Para utilizar o serviço, acesse:

https://www.pinecone.io/

Após criar sua conta:

  1. Acesse o painel de controle.
  2. Crie um projeto.
  3. Gere uma API Key.
  4. Crie um Index.
  5. Configure a dimensão dos vetores.
  6. Selecione a métrica de similaridade.
  7. Aguarde o índice ficar disponível.

Configuração do Index

Para nosso exemplo, considere:

Configuração Valor
Nome dotnet-documents
Tipo Dense Vector
Dimension 384
Metric Cosine
Deployment Serverless

Atenção: a dimensão 384 é apenas ilustrativa. Ela precisa corresponder exatamente à dimensão produzida pelo modelo de embeddings escolhido.

A métrica Cosine é uma opção comum para pesquisas semânticas, mas a escolha deve considerar as características do modelo e da aplicação.

Obtendo o Index Host

Depois de criar o índice, obtenha seu endereço de acesso (host).

O formato é semelhante a:

https://dotnet-documents-xxxxx.svc.region.pinecone.io

O endereço real será fornecido pelo Pinecone. Não utilize um endereço fictício na aplicação.

Em produção, prefira utilizar o host específico do índice nas operações de dados.

⚙️ 6. Configurando as variáveis da aplicação

Vamos utilizar o padrão Options do .NET para centralizar as configurações.

📦 9. Criando o serviço Pinecone com HttpClient

Agora vamos implementar a comunicação com a API REST.

O Pinecone oferece operações de Data Plane para armazenar e pesquisar vetores.

Utilizaremos:

  • POST /vectors/upsert
  • POST /query

As chamadas serão direcionadas ao host específico do índice.

PineconeService.cs 

using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

public sealed class PineconeService : IPineconeService
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;
    private readonly PineconeOptions _options;

    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOptions =
        new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);

    public PineconeService(
        HttpClient httpClient,
        Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions> options)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
        _options = options.Value;
    }

    public async Task UpsertAsync(
        string id,
        float[] embedding,
        string content,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        var request = new
        {
            vectors = new[]
            {
                new
                {
                    id,
                    values = embedding,
                    metadata = new
                    {
                        content
                    }
                }
            },
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/vectors/upsert",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    }

    public async Task<string> SearchAsync(
        float[] embedding,
        int topK,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        if (topK is < 1 or > 1000)
        {
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(topK));
        }

        var request = new
        {
            vector = embedding,
            topK,
            includeMetadata = true,
            includeValues = false,
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/query",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(
            cancellationToken);
    }

    private void ValidateEmbedding(float[] embedding)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(embedding);

        if (embedding.Length != _options.Dimension)
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                $"Expected {_options.Dimension} dimensions, " +
                $"but received {embedding.Length}.");
        }

        if (embedding.Any(value => !float.IsFinite(value)))
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                "Embedding contains invalid numeric values.");
        }
    }
}

Entendendo a implementação

UpsertAsync

Envia um vetor para o Pinecone com:

  • ID único.
  • Valores numéricos do embedding.
  • Metadata com o conteúdo original.
  • Namespace de armazenamento.

Se o ID já existir, a operação atualiza o registro.

SearchAsync

Recebe o vetor de pesquisa e solicita os registros mais próximos.

O parâmetro topK determina a quantidade máxima de resultados solicitados.

A propriedade includeMetadata permite recuperar os dados associados aos vetores.

🔐 10. Configurando autenticação e injeção de dependência

Vamos registrar o HttpClient e os serviços no container de dependências do .NET.

Program.cs 

using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Embeddings;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PineconeOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(
        PineconeOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(
        options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.ApiKey),
        "Pinecone API Key is required.")
    .Validate(
        options =>
            Uri.TryCreate(
                options.IndexHost,
                UriKind.Absolute,
                out var uri) &&
            uri.Scheme == Uri.UriSchemeHttps,
        "A valid HTTPS Index Host is required.")
    .Validate(
        options => options.Dimension > 0,
        "Dimension must be greater than zero.")
    .ValidateOnStart();

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IPineconeService, PineconeService>(
    (serviceProvider, client) =>
    {
        var options = serviceProvider
            .GetRequiredService<
                Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions>>()
            .Value;

        client.BaseAddress = new Uri(
            options.IndexHost.TrimEnd('/') + "/");

        client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "Api-Key",
            options.ApiKey);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "X-Pinecone-Api-Version",
            "2025-10");
    });

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmbeddingService, EmbeddingService>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

A versão da API utilizada no exemplo é 2025-10, conforme a documentação de referência consultada. Antes de publicar em produção, verifique a versão estável mais recente e a compatibilidade dos endpoints utilizados.

📥 11. Criando o endpoint para cadastrar documentos

Vamos disponibilizar um endpoint para receber textos e armazenar seus respectivos embeddings.

DocumentRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record DocumentRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(10000, MinimumLength = 3)]
    string Content);

DocumentsController.cs 

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Controllers;

[ApiController]
[Route("api/documents")]
public sealed class DocumentsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IPineconeService _pineconeService;
    private readonly IEmbeddingService _embeddingService;

    public DocumentsController(
        IPineconeService pineconeService,
        IEmbeddingService embeddingService)
    {
        _pineconeService = pineconeService;
        _embeddingService = embeddingService;
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
        [FromBody] DocumentRequest request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        var id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();

        await _pineconeService.UpsertAsync(
            id,
            embedding,
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        return Created(
            $"/api/documents/{id}",
            new
            {
                Id = id,
                Message = "Document successfully indexed."
            });
    }
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "content": "O .NET 10 permite desenvolver APIs modernas utilizando C#."
}

O processo será:

  1. Receber o documento.
  2. Gerar seu embedding.
  3. Criar um identificador.
  4. Enviar o vetor para o Pinecone.
  5. Retornar o resultado da operação.

🔎 12. Criando o endpoint de pesquisa semântica

Agora vamos implementar a pesquisa.

SearchRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record SearchRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(2000, MinimumLength = 2)]
    string Query,

    [Range(1, 20)]
    int TopK = 5);

Adicione o endpoint ao DocumentsController:

[HttpPost("search")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Search(
    [FromBody] SearchRequest request,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
        request.Query,
        cancellationToken);

    var results = await _pineconeService.SearchAsync(
        embedding,
        request.TopK,
        cancellationToken);

    return Ok(new
    {
        Query = request.Query,
        Results = results
    });
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents/search
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "Como desenvolver uma API moderna com C#?",
  "topK": 5
}

O Pinecone retornará os registros mais próximos do vetor da consulta.

Cada resultado pode conter:

  • ID do vetor.
  • Score de similaridade.
  • Metadata.
  • Conteúdo original, quando armazenado na metadata.

O score representa uma medida de similaridade conforme a métrica configurada no índice. Não deve ser interpretado automaticamente como uma porcentagem de confiança.

🤖 13. Integrando Pinecone com RAG

Uma das aplicações mais interessantes do Pinecone é a construção de soluções RAG.

RAG significa Retrieval-Augmented Generation e combina recuperação de informações com geração de respostas por modelos de linguagem.

Como funciona?

Imagine um chatbot corporativo que responde perguntas sobre documentos internos.

O fluxo pode ser:

  1. O usuário envia uma pergunta.
  2. A aplicação gera o embedding da pergunta.
  3. O Pinecone pesquisa os documentos mais relevantes.
  4. A aplicação recupera os conteúdos encontrados.
  5. Os conteúdos são adicionados ao contexto do LLM.
  6. O modelo gera uma resposta fundamentada nas informações recuperadas.

Arquitetura RAG 

flowchart TD
    A["Usuário"] --> B["API .NET 10"]
    B --> C["Embedding da pergunta"]
    C --> D["Pinecone Vector Search"]
    D --> E["Documentos relevantes"]
    E --> F["Construção do contexto"]
    F --> G["LLM"]
    G --> H["Resposta contextualizada"]
    H --> A

Essa arquitetura pode ser aplicada em:

  • Chatbots de atendimento.
  • Assistentes de documentação técnica.
  • Sistemas de suporte interno.
  • Pesquisa de contratos.
  • Consulta de manuais.
  • Bases de conhecimento corporativas.

Importante: a recuperação de documentos não garante, por si só, que o LLM responderá corretamente. É necessário controlar o contexto, as permissões, as fontes e a qualidade das respostas.

🧱 14. Boas práticas de arquitetura e desenvolvimento

Para utilizar Pinecone em aplicações corporativas, recomendo observar alguns pontos.

🔐 Segurança

  • Nunca exponha a API Key no frontend.
  • Utilize variáveis de ambiente ou um cofre de segredos.
  • Restrinja as permissões das credenciais.
  • Utilize HTTPS.
  • Implemente autenticação e autorização na API .NET.
  • Separe os namespaces conforme as necessidades de isolamento.
  • Não permita que o usuário escolha livremente namespaces sem validação.

⚡ Performance

  • Utilize IHttpClientFactory.
  • Configure timeout adequado.
  • Avalie operações em lote para grandes volumes.
  • Evite gerar embeddings repetidos para conteúdos que não mudaram.
  • Utilize IDs estáveis quando precisar atualizar documentos.
  • Recupere apenas os metadados necessários.
  • Avalie o custo e a latência das consultas.

📊 Observabilidade

Monitore:

  • Tempo de geração dos embeddings.
  • Tempo de resposta do Pinecone.
  • Quantidade de vetores cadastrados.
  • Quantidade de resultados recuperados.
  • Erros de autenticação e comunicação.
  • Consumo e custos associados às operações.

Evite registrar API Keys, documentos confidenciais ou informações pessoais nos logs.

🧩 Consistência dos embeddings

O modelo de embeddings utilizado na indexação deve ser compatível com o modelo utilizado na consulta.

Se trocar o modelo, a dimensão ou a estratégia de geração, considere criar um novo índice e reprocessar os documentos.

🧪 15. Estratégia de testes

Uma integração bem estruturada também precisa de testes.

Sugestões:

Cenário Resultado esperado
Inserção de documento Vetor armazenado
Atualização de documento Registro atualizado
Consulta válida Resultados encontrados
Vetor com dimensão incorreta Validação rejeitada
API Key inválida Erro de autenticação
Index Host incorreto Falha de comunicação
Pinecone indisponível Tratamento de falha
Consulta sem resultados Lista vazia
Namespace incorreto Isolamento respeitado

Uma boa estratégia é utilizar mocks para testar os serviços de aplicação e testes de integração controlados para validar a comunicação real com o Pinecone.

🏛️ 16. Evoluindo a solução

Depois de implementar as operações básicas, podemos evoluir a arquitetura para suportar cenários mais complexos.

Funcionalidades futuras

  • Upload e processamento de PDF.
  • Divisão de documentos em chunks.
  • Pipeline assíncrono com RabbitMQ.
  • Processamento em lote.
  • Integração com Azure OpenAI ou outros provedores de LLM.
  • Busca híbrida: semântica e textual.
  • Filtros por metadata.
  • Controle de acesso por usuário e organização.
  • Versionamento de documentos.
  • Estratégias de reindexação.
  • Monitoramento com OpenTelemetry.

⚠️ 17. Pontos importantes antes de utilizar em produção

O exemplo apresentado demonstra o fluxo essencial, mas uma aplicação real precisa de algumas evoluções:

  1. Implementar um provedor real de embeddings.
  2. Criar uma estratégia de chunking para documentos extensos.
  3. Implementar políticas de retry e tratamento de erros transitórios, respeitando os limites do serviço.
  4. Definir limites de tamanho e quantidade de registros por requisição.
  5. Criar uma estratégia de atualização e exclusão de documentos.
  6. Garantir isolamento entre clientes e organizações.
  7. Validar a compatibilidade entre dimensão e modelo de embeddings.
  8. Implementar monitoramento de custos e latência.
  9. Tratar indisponibilidade do serviço externo.
  10. Avaliar a retenção e proteção dos dados armazenados.

Outro detalhe importante: Pinecone não substitui necessariamente um banco relacional. Uma arquitetura pode utilizar SQL Server ou PostgreSQL para os dados transacionais e Pinecone para a recuperação semântica.

🎯 18. Conclusão

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone abre possibilidades interessantes para aplicações que precisam trabalhar com Inteligência Artificial, recuperação de conhecimento e pesquisas semânticas.

Com uma arquitetura organizada, utilizando interfaces, injeção de dependência e HttpClient, conseguimos manter a integração desacoplada e preparada para evoluções futuras.

O Pinecone pode atuar como uma camada especializada de recuperação vetorial, enquanto o .NET 10 permanece responsável pelas regras de negócio, exposição das APIs, segurança e orquestração dos serviços.

Mais do que integrar um banco de dados, estamos construindo uma base para aplicações inteligentes, capazes de recuperar informações pelo significado e não apenas pela correspondência exata de palavras.

O futuro das aplicações modernas não está somente em armazenar dados, mas também em conseguir interpretar, relacionar e recuperar conhecimento.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: **One package for the whole life of a text.**
description:
One package for the whole life of a text.

Publishing a readable article usually means wiring three separate libraries: an editor to write in, a renderer to lay the text out, and something for audio if you bother. Each with its own API to learn and its own version to keep in sync.

editorkit keeps all three in one place. The editor is where you write. The article lays the text out — typography, tables, images. And a player reads it aloud, sentence by sentence, highlighting the sentence as it goes.

That last part is the least obvious. The audio is not a bolt-on: the same document that renders also speaks. One line of code gives you a complete article page, in React, Vue, Svelte or plain JS.

It is safe by default. No reader's text ever executes code, so an article cannot run a script on its page. Multilingual, with audio optional and provided by adapter — no provider imposed.

Licensed MPL-2.0. The live playground runs at lalter.org, source on GitHub.

title: ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection and Retry Strategy
description:
ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection and Retry Strategy

Understanding R01: The Most Common ACH Return

When an ACH debit transaction bounces, the most frequent culprit is NACHA return code R01: Insufficient Funds. This occurs when the receiver's account lacks the balance to cover the transaction at settlement time. For developers building payout systems, handling R01 correctly is critical—it's not a permanent failure, but a timing and liquidity issue.

When R01 Fires

R01 triggers during the ACH settlement window (typically T+1 or T+2), when the Federal Reserve attempts to debit the destination account. The originating bank submits the return file, and your system receives notification via your ACH processor's webhook or API.

Key timing detail: R01 returns arrive 1–2 business days after the original debit attempt. This delay means your reconciliation logic must account for a multi-day window before you know the final state.

Why R01 Matters More Than Other Returns

Unlike R03 (No Account) or R04 (Invalid Account), R01 is reversible and retryable. The account exists, it's valid—the customer simply didn't have enough money at settlement time. This distinction shapes your recovery strategy.

According to Nacha data, R01 represents roughly 35–40% of all ACH returns in consumer and B2B flows. If you're processing high volume, you'll see R01 regularly.

Programmatic Detection and Routing

Here's a minimal example of detecting and categorizing an R01 return in your payout pipeline:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, transaction_id, amount):
    """
    Route ACH returns based on code.
    R01 → retry queue; R03/R04 → manual review; others → dunning.
    """
    if return_code == "R01":
        # Insufficient funds: safe to retry
        schedule_retry(
            transaction_id=transaction_id,
            retry_after_days=3,  # Give customer time to deposit
            max_retries=2
        )
        log_event("R01_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", transaction_id, amount)
        return "RETRY_SCHEDULED"

    elif return_code in ["R03", "R04"]:
        # Invalid account: manual intervention required
        escalate_to_support(transaction_id, return_code)
        return "MANUAL_REVIEW"

    else:
        # Other returns: apply dunning logic
        apply_dunning_rule(transaction_id, return_code)
        return "DUNNING_APPLIED"

Building a Retry Strategy for R01

R01 returns demand a thoughtful retry approach:

Attempt Delay Logic
Initial T+1 or T+2 Original ACH debit
Retry 1 T+4 Customer may have deposited; low cost
Retry 2 T+7 Final attempt; consider alternate rail
Fallback T+9+ Switch to Visa Direct or RTP if available

Why this cadence? R01 is often a temporary liquidity event. Waiting 3–4 days gives the customer time to deposit funds, and your retry cost is minimal (ACH retry is ~$0.25 per transaction).

Webhook Integration Pattern

Most ACH processors (Stripe, Dwolla, Treasury Prime) deliver return notifications via webhook. Here's a robust handler:

@app.post("/webhooks/ach-return")
def receive_ach_return(payload):
    """
    Webhook handler for ACH return notifications.
    Payload includes return_code, original_transaction_id, reason_code.
    """
    return_code = payload.get("return_code")
    txn_id = payload.get("transaction_id")
    amount = payload.get("amount")

    # Idempotency: check if we've already processed this return
    if Return.query.filter_by(nacha_id=payload["nacha_id"]).first():
        return {"status": "already_processed"}, 200

    # Log the return
    Return.create(
        transaction_id=txn_id,
        return_code=return_code,
        amount=amount,
        received_at=datetime.utcnow()
    )

    # Route based on code
    action = handle_ach_return(return_code, txn_id, amount)

    return {"status": "processed", "action": action}, 200

Key Takeaways

  • R01 is recoverable. It signals a timing issue, not a closed account or fraud.
  • Retry within 3–7 days. Gives customers time to resolve liquidity and keeps your success rate high.
  • Detect programmatically. Use return_code fields in your webhook payload to auto

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Most pack-opening simulators invent their pull rates — here is what ours actually look like
description:
Almost every pack-opening simulator does the same thing: the percentages are hard-coded constants. No sample size, no source date, and no way to tell whether a rate came from a published study or from someone's best guess. If the number is wrong, you cannot even tell that it is wrong.

PullSim is my attempt to build one the other way round. This post is about the awkward part: what the published samples actually support, and where they contradict themselves.

TL;DR — the three sets we model have rarest-tier rates of 0.19%, 0.56% and 0.08%. The widest is roughly 7× the narrowest. Each of those numbers rests on a single-digit count of observed packs, which is why every rate ships with the interval next to it instead of a bare percentage.

A rate without a sample size is not a measurement

Here are the three sets we model, with the sample each rate rests on:

Set Packs in the source sample Rarest modelled tier Rate Reported 95% interval
Ascended Heroes 2,000 Mega Hyper Rare 0.19% ±0.18%
Prismatic Evolutions 1,200 rarest modelled tier 0.56% ±0.41%
Phantasmal Flames 5,000 rarest modelled tier 0.08% ±0.08%

A single hard-coded table reused across every set cannot be right for all of them — 0.56% and 0.08% are the same species of claim and a factor of seven apart. That is exactly what most simulators ship.

The interval is the interesting part

Look at the Mega Hyper Rare row: 0.19% with an interval of ±0.18%. The interval is almost as large as the estimate itself. That is arithmetic, not noise. 0.0019 multiplied by 2,000 gives about 3.8 expected hits, so the entire estimate for that tier rests on roughly four packs out of two thousand.

Phantasmal Flames tells the same story from the other direction: 0.08% of 5,000 packs is also about four packs, on a sample two and a half times larger.

That is the actual state of knowledge, and printing it is the whole difference between a measurement and a number someone typed.

The per-tier schema is deliberately boring: ratePct, ciPct and samplePacks sit next to poolSize, sourceUrl and sourceDate for every tier, plus alternateRatePct wherever the source article contradicts itself. Null means not established — never zero.

Where the source articles contradict themselves

I found three cases and kept all of them visible instead of quietly picking one:

  1. Ascended Heroes, Ultra Rare — 4.81% in the main table, 20.77% in a detailed section. The main-table figure drives the simulation (it is the set-level summary); the other value is preserved as a note.
  2. Prismatic Evolutions, Double Rare — 16.51% ±2.05% in the main table, 16.94% ±0.79% in the detailed section. The main-table value drives the simulation; the alternate is preserved.
  3. Prismatic Evolutions, Specific Double Rare — the article reports 0.94%, but dividing the adopted 16.51% by its 25 cards gives about 0.66%. I could not reconcile the two, so I derive the single-card estimate myself instead of quoting the reported figure.

A dataset that hides these becomes easier to read and less true at the same time.

Normalising percentages is a bug, not a simplification

Each published tier rate is already an absolute per-pack probability inside a specific slot. The tempting fix is to divide every tier by the sum of the tiers so the numbers add up to 100%. That answers the wrong question.

Prismatic Evolutions' Special Illustration Rare rate is 2.22%. Flatten the slot so the listed hits must sum to a full outcome and that figure climbs to roughly 29%. No sample supports that. What disappeared was the ordinary reverse-holo remainder — the most common outcome in the slot. The correct model draws one random number, walks the tiers by their unmodified cumulative rates, and returns the base card when no threshold is crossed.

What the data cannot support yet

Null means not established, never zero:

  • God Packs and Demigod Packs. The Prismatic source discusses both and notes what may have been two Demigod Packs, but could not confirm them. The description is stored, the rate stays null.
  • Poké Ball Foil / Master Ball Foil. These are patterns across cards, not standalone rarity categories, so dividing by the available pool gives a deliberately conservative single-card estimate rather than an invented one.
  • Delta Reign. Listed, no confirmed rate yet.

The data is open

The whole table — per-tier sample counts, card-pool sizes, source links, and every source conflict above — is published under CC BY 4.0:

  • Dataset card: https://huggingface.co/datasets/zin294/pullsim-pull-rates
  • Source repository: https://github.com/zin294/pullsim-pull-rates

The arithmetic behind every figure, written up with the three conflicts spelled out: https://pullsim.com/how-we-calculate/

If you model pack economics, or you just want to know what you are actually buying, recompute the numbers above and tell me where they break.
