title: Node.js GPT API Text Summarization — Evidence Gates for Education CRM Actions
description:
Short answer: in Node.js, integrate a GPT API for text summarization as an untrusted proposal for CRM work, not as a finished record. Pick a synchronous lane when a salesperson is waiting, a queued lane when freshness can wait, and a human-review lane when a wrong action can damage a student relationship. Then enforce one small output contract, validate it, and measure rejection reasons instead of admiring fluent prose.

Here is the useful mental model:

call transcript -> model proposal -> schema validation -> policy checks -> CRM write

The arrow between proposal and CRM write is the product. The summary is only one input to it.

Which summary path fits the CRM job?

A transcript from an education sales call usually contains several kinds of information at once: a school or district, a decision timeline, objections, next steps, and names that may be similar. A paragraph can capture the mood and still be useless to an operations system. The first decision is therefore operational, not literary.

Lane Pick this when Output rule Main failure to watch
Synchronous The representative needs a draft before leaving the call Return one validated proposal or a visible review state Timeout or partial CRM writes
Queued A transcript can wait for a worker and freshness is measured in minutes Store an idempotent job result Duplicate processing after retries
Human review The action changes ownership, stage, or a sensitive account field Require approval before the write A plausible guess becomes an official fact

For the synchronous path, keep the request narrow. Ask for a summary plus proposed actions, not a whole CRM record. The UI can show needs_review when the contract is valid but a policy check is inconclusive. That status is more useful than silently dropping a questionable field.

For a queued path, make the transcript id and contract version part of the job identity. A worker may be restarted. The same message may be delivered twice. The CRM adapter should see a stable idempotency key and make a second write harmless.

For human review, expose the evidence span or timestamp that supports each proposed action. Reviewers do not need a lecture about language models. They need to answer, quickly, “Where did this come from?”

What should the output contract protect?

Start with fields that have a clear owner and a clear empty value. For a sales-call workflow, that might be summary, next_steps, account_name, contact_name, and proposed_stage. An empty contact_name is safer than a guessed contact. An empty proposed_stage is safer than moving an account because the speaker used an ambiguous phrase.

Keep the distinction between observed and proposed data. account_name can be a transcription finding. proposed_stage is a recommendation. They should not share the same confidence semantics or write policy.

A practical contract can look like this:

type CrmActionProposal = {
  schemaVersion: "1";
  summary: string;
  nextSteps: Array<{
    owner: "sales_rep" | "prospect" | "unknown";
    text: string;
    dueDate: string | null;
  }>;
  accountName: string | null;
  contactName: string | null;
  proposedStage: "discovery" | "evaluation" | "procurement" | null;
  evidence: Array<{
    field: "accountName" | "contactName" | "proposedStage";
    quote: string;
  }>;
};

The contract is intentionally boring. That is a feature. A CRM adapter can reason about a closed set of stages. It cannot reliably reason about a sentence such as “the district seems close to buying.”

I start with three gates. First, parse the response as JSON. Second, validate required keys, types, enums, and maximum lengths. Third, apply business policy: a stage change needs evidence, a missing account must route to review, and a due date cannot be accepted just because it looks date-shaped. JSON Schema is a useful shared description for the second gate, but it does not replace the third.

Do not let a valid shape masquerade as a valid decision. proposedStage: "procurement" can satisfy a type checker while having no supporting quote.

How can Node.js integrate a GPT API for safe text summarization?

The Node.js boundary should make the unsafe part obvious. Keep the transcript out of logs, put a timeout around the outbound request, and return a typed result that forces callers to handle rejection. The example below uses the standard fetch interface and an environment-provided model name. It does not hard-code a model choice into the CRM workflow.

type ExtractionResult =
  | { kind: "accepted"; proposal: CrmActionProposal }
  | { kind: "review"; reason: string; rawResponse?: string };

const outputShape = {
  type: "object",
  additionalProperties: false,
  required: [
    "schemaVersion",
    "summary",
    "nextSteps",
    "accountName",
    "contactName",
    "proposedStage",
    "evidence"
  ],
  properties: {
    schemaVersion: { type: "string", enum: ["1"] },
    summary: { type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 1200 },
    nextSteps: {
      type: "array",
      maxItems: 8,
      items: {
        type: "object",
        additionalProperties: false,
        required: ["owner", "text", "dueDate"],
        properties: {
          owner: { type: "string", enum: ["sales_rep", "prospect", "unknown"] },
          text: { type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 300 },
          dueDate: { type: ["string", "null"] }
        }
      }
    },
    accountName: { type: ["string", "null"] },
    contactName: { type: ["string", "null"] },
    proposedStage: {
      type: ["string", "null"],
      enum: ["discovery", "evaluation", "procurement", null]
    },
    evidence: {
      type: "array",
      maxItems: 12,
      items: {
        type: "object",
        additionalProperties: false,
        required: ["field", "quote"],
        properties: {
          field: { type: "string", enum: ["accountName", "contactName", "proposedStage"] },
          quote: { type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 240 }
        }
      }
    }
  }
} as const;

async function proposeCrmAction(transcript: string): Promise<ExtractionResult> {
  const apiKey = process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY;
  const model = process.env.OPENAI_MODEL;
  const textEndpoint = process.env.OPENAI_TEXT_ENDPOINT;
  if (!apiKey || !model || !textEndpoint) return { kind: "review", reason: "runtime configuration is incomplete" };

  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 15_000);

  try {
    const response = await fetch(textEndpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      signal: controller.signal,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model,
        instructions: [
          "Summarize this education sales call and propose CRM actions.",
          "Use only facts in the transcript. Use null for unknown fields.",
          "A proposed stage requires a supporting evidence quote.",
          "Return JSON matching the supplied schema."
        ].join(" "),
        input: transcript,
        text: {
          format: {
            type: "json_schema",
            name: "crm_action_proposal",
            strict: true,
            schema: outputShape
          }
        }
      })
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      return { kind: "review", reason: `model request failed with status ${response.status}` };
    }

    const payload = await response.json() as { output_text?: string };
    if (!payload.output_text) return { kind: "review", reason: "response contained no structured text" };

    const proposal = JSON.parse(payload.output_text) as CrmActionProposal;
    const policyFailure = checkPolicy(proposal);
    return policyFailure
      ? { kind: "review", reason: policyFailure, rawResponse: payload.output_text }
      : { kind: "accepted", proposal };
  } catch (error) {
    const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown extraction error";
    return { kind: "review", reason };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeout);
  }
}

function checkPolicy(proposal: CrmActionProposal): string | null {
  if (proposal.proposedStage && !proposal.evidence.some((item) => item.field === "proposedStage")) {
    return "stage proposal has no evidence";
  }
  if (!proposal.accountName) return "account identity is missing";
  return null;
}

async function retryAfter429(request: () => Promise<Response>): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await request();
    if (response.status !== 429) return response;
    const delayMs = 250 * 2 ** attempt + Math.floor(Math.random() * 100);
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  return request();
}

// The CRM write uses the job id plus schema version as its idempotency key.

The important detail is the return type. A timeout, a non-2xx response, invalid JSON, or a policy failure all become reviewable state. They do not fall through to writeAccount(). The CRM write belongs after validation and policy checks, in a separate function with its own idempotency key.

The exact request options can change as APIs evolve, so pin the contract version in tests and keep the model request behind one adapter. The business code should know about accepted and review, not about response paths. A 15-second deadline is a product choice, not a promise: shorter deadlines create more review fallbacks, while longer ones make the call workflow feel stalled.

For a real implementation, test the adapter with recorded, redacted transcripts and malformed responses. Test the policy separately. A good fixture set includes a transcript with two similarly named contacts, an implied deadline with no calendar date, a stage claim with no quote, and a duplicate job. These cases reveal more than a collection of polished happy-path calls.

The trade-off is explicit. A strict schema and evidence requirement will reject some usable summaries, especially when a speaker is vague. That is the right result for an automatic CRM write; a human review queue is slower, but a false stage change is harder to undo. On a 429 response, retry with bounded exponential backoff and jitter, then return review when the deadline expires. Never retry a CRM write without an idempotency key.

What should observability measure?

Measure the workflow at the boundaries. Useful counters include proposals accepted, sent to review, rejected for schema errors, rejected for policy errors, CRM writes completed, and duplicate writes suppressed. Track latency in separate buckets for model time, validation time, and CRM time. One blended latency number hides the queue that users actually feel.

Log a correlation id, job id, schema version, and outcome code. Do not log the transcript or the authorization header. For debugging, retain a redacted evidence sample under the same retention policy as the CRM record. This lets an engineer answer “why was this reviewed?” without turning observability into a second copy of the call archive.

Alert on behavior, not just availability. A service can return HTTP 200 while every proposal is being routed to review because the schema changed. A rising review rate, a sudden drop in evidence items, or an increase in duplicate-job suppression is an operational signal.

If transcripts arrive in bulk, a queued or batch lane can decouple ingestion from completion. The batch guide is relevant here because asynchronous processing has different polling, completion, and retry semantics than an interactive request. The contract and policy gates remain the same after the result arrives.

Where this approach stops

A schema cannot establish that a person really said something. Evidence quotes improve review, but they are still extracted text. Names can be wrong. The CRM can contain stale account state. A human needs to resolve those conflicts when the consequence is material. This approach is a poor fit for irreversible updates or workflows that cannot tolerate a review fallback; use a deterministic integration or require approval before any write.

This design also does not guarantee a fixed latency. Model availability, transcript length, retries, and CRM response time all affect the request. Set a user-facing deadline, make the review state explicit, and let the queue handle work that does not fit that deadline.

The durable decision rule is small: summarize for people, propose actions for systems, and make the boundary between them testable. That keeps a fluent answer from becoming an unreviewed CRM fact.

References

  • OpenAI, “Batch API guide”: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch
  • Node.js documentation, “Global objects: fetch”: https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#fetch
  • MDN Web Docs, “AbortController”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController
  • JSON Schema, “Specification”: https://json-schema.org/specification

title: Optimizing Large-Scale MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines: A Deep Dive
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Large-scale MongoDB aggregation pipelines can become slow and memory-hungry long before you notice. A $lookup that scans a million documents, a $group that spills to disk, or a $sort that ignores an index — these are the silent killers of query performance. In this deep dive, we'll peel back the hood of the aggregation framework, understand how the query planner makes decisions, and arm you with concrete, production-tested techniques to make pipelines fast and predictable.

  • 1. The Anatomy of an Aggregation Pipeline
  • 2. Indexing Strategies for Aggregation
  • 3. The $match and $sort Optimization
  • 4. Memory and the 100MB Limit
  • 5. Optimizing $lookup and Joins
  • 6. Using Facets, Buckets, and $merge
  • 7. Real-World Optimization Workflow
  • 8. Anti-Patterns to Avoid
  • 9. Frequently Asked Questions

1. The Anatomy of an Aggregation Pipeline

An aggregation pipeline is a sequence of stages that transform documents. Each stage receives a stream of documents from the previous stage and outputs a new stream. The MongoDB query planner treats the entire pipeline as a single query and attempts to optimize it as a whole — but only within certain boundaries.

How the Query Planner Works

The planner examines the pipeline from the first stage to the last. It looks for opportunities to:

  • Push $match stages earlier (they filter documents, reducing work downstream).
  • Push $project stages earlier (they limit fields, reducing memory per document).
  • Convert $sort followed by $limit into a top-k sort (much cheaper).
  • Reorder stages when the result is semantically identical (e.g., moving $match before $unwind).

However, the planner will not reorder stages that have side effects or data dependencies. For example, a $group cannot be moved before a $match that filters on the grouped field, because the group would compute the wrong result.

Why Pipelines Slow Down

There are four primary culprits for slow aggregation:

  1. Full collection scans — a $match or $lookup that cannot use an index forces the engine to read every document.
  2. Memory spills — $group, $sort, and $bucket that exceed the 100 MB memory limit spill to disk, causing I/O spikes.
  3. Expensive stages — $unwind on large arrays, $lookup on unindexed collections, and $facet with heavy sub-pipelines multiply work.
  4. Blocking stages — stages that must see all documents before emitting output (like $sort and $group) prevent streaming and increase latency.

Understanding these root causes is the first step. The rest of this article provides concrete strategies to address each one.

2. Indexing Strategies for Aggregation

Indexes are the single most impactful optimization for aggregation pipelines. But not every index helps every stage. You need to understand which stages can use which indexes.

Indexes That Match $match

A $match stage at the beginning of a pipeline behaves like a find() query. It can use any index that supports the filter predicates. For example, given this pipeline:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "shipped", total: { $gt: 100 } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", sum: { $sum: "$total" } } }
])

A compound index on { status: 1, total: 1 } would be ideal. The planner will use it to satisfy the $match and then pass the matching documents to $group.

Indexes That Match $sort

If a $sort stage is preceded by a $match, the sort can often be satisfied by an index if the index order matches the sort order. For example:

db.events.aggregate([
  { $match: { userId: "abc123" } },
  { $sort: { timestamp: -1 } }
])

An index on { userId: 1, timestamp: -1 } allows MongoDB to retrieve documents in the correct order without a blocking sort.

Indexes That Help $group

A $group stage cannot directly use an index to avoid grouping — it must accumulate all documents in memory. However, if the $group is preceded by a $match that narrows the input, an index on the matched fields reduces the number of documents the group must process. In some cases, a $group followed by a $sort on the _id field can use an index if the group's _id is indexed, but this is rare.

Compound Indexes and Index Prefixes

MongoDB compound indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule. An index on { a: 1, b: 1 } supports queries on a, and queries on a + b, but not on b alone. When designing indexes for aggregation, always consider the order of fields in the $match and $sort stages.

Using $indexStats

To discover which indexes are actually being used, run:

db.collection.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])

This returns usage statistics for every index on the collection. Look for indexes with accesses counts near zero — those are candidates for removal, reducing write overhead.

3. The $match and $sort Optimization

The first stages of a pipeline determine its performance ceiling. Getting them right can mean the difference between scanning 10 million documents and 10 thousand.

Early Filtering

Always put the most selective $match stage as early as possible. The planner will try to push $match stages earlier, but it cannot move one past a $project that removes the matched field, or past a $limit that changes semantics. As a developer, you should manually order stages so that filtering happens before expansion ($unwind) or grouping.

// BAD: unwinds first, then filters
// Processes every array element before filtering
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $match: { "items.sku": "A123" } }
])

// GOOD: filters first, then unwinds
// Only matching orders are unwound
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { "items.sku": "A123" } },
  { $unwind: "$items" }
])

$sort with $limit

When a $sort is immediately followed by a $limit, MongoDB uses a top-k sort algorithm that only keeps the top k documents in memory. This is dramatically faster than sorting the entire result set. The planner does this automatically, but only if there is no intervening stage that breaks the pattern.

// Efficient: top-k sort
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $sort: { amount: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

// Inefficient: sort all, then skip and limit
// The $skip prevents the top-k optimization
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $sort: { amount: -1 } },
  { $skip: 100 },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

In the second example, MongoDB must sort all documents because it cannot know which 10 documents to keep after skipping 100.

Using hint()

Sometimes the query planner chooses a suboptimal index. You can force a specific index with the hint() method:

db.orders.aggregate(
  [
    { $match: { status: "shipped" } },
    { $sort: { createdAt: -1 } }
  ],
  { hint: { status: 1, createdAt: -1 } }
)

Use hint() sparingly — only after confirming with explain() that the chosen index is indeed better. Index selection can change as data grows, so a hard-coded hint can become a liability.

4. Memory and the 100MB Limit

MongoDB limits each aggregation stage to 100 MB of memory by default. Stages like $group, $sort, $bucket, and $facet are blocking — they must accumulate all input documents before emitting output. If the accumulated data exceeds 100 MB, the stage throws an error unless allowDiskUse is enabled.

Enabling allowDiskUse 

db.largeCollection.aggregate(
  [
    { $group: { _id: "$category", count: { $sum: 1 } } }
  ],
  { allowDiskUse: true }
)

When allowDiskUse is true, MongoDB spills intermediate data to temporary files on disk. This avoids the error but introduces significant I/O overhead. It's a safety net, not a performance strategy.

Reducing Memory Footprint

Before resorting to disk, try these techniques:

  • Project early: Use $project or $addFields to drop fields you don't need before a $group or $sort. This reduces the size of each document in memory.
  • Use $group with $sum instead of $push: Accumulating arrays ($push) is memory-hungry. If you only need counts or sums, use $sum.
  • Use $sort with $limit: As noted, top-k sort uses far less memory than full sort.
  • Use $bucket instead of $group for histograms: $bucket is more memory-efficient for fixed-range groupings.

Monitoring Memory Usage

Use explain("executionStats") to see the peak memory usage of each stage:

db.collection.aggregate(pipeline, { explain: "executionStats" })

Look for totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, and maxMemoryUsage in the output. If maxMemoryUsage is close to 100 MB, you need to optimize or enable allowDiskUse.

5. Optimizing $lookup and Joins

$lookup performs a left outer join with another collection. It is often the most expensive stage in a pipeline because it runs a separate query for each input document.

Indexing the Foreign Collection

The foreign collection (the one being joined to) must have an index on the localField or foreignField that matches the join condition. Without an index, $lookup performs a collection scan for every input document — catastrophic for large inputs.

db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
    }
  }
])

Ensure there is an index on customers._id (it's the primary key, so it's already indexed). For non-primary-key joins, create an explicit index:

db.customers.createIndex({ email: 1 })

$lookup with Pipeline vs. localField/foreignField

The pipeline form of $lookup is more flexible but also more expensive. It allows you to filter and transform the joined documents before returning them:

db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      let: { custId: "$customerId" },
      pipeline: [
        { $match: { $expr: { $eq: ["$_id", "$$custId"] } } },
        { $project: { name: 1, email: 1 } }
      ],
      as: "customer"
    }
  }
])

The pipeline form cannot use the foreign collection's index as effectively as the simple form, because the $match uses $expr which may not be index-friendly. If you don't need the extra flexibility, prefer the simple form.

Denormalization Alternatives

For extremely large datasets, consider denormalizing the joined data into the source collection. This eliminates $lookup entirely. For example, store customerName directly on the order document. This trades write complexity for read performance — a common pattern in high-throughput systems.

6. Using Facets, Buckets, and $merge

$facet and Parallel Execution

$facet allows you to run multiple sub-pipelines on the same input stream. Each sub-pipeline is executed independently and can be processed in parallel on different cores. This is ideal for dashboards that need multiple aggregations on the same data:

db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $facet: {
      byStatus: [
        { $group: { _id: "$status", count: { $sum: 1 } } }
      ],
      byCustomer: [
        { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$total" } } },
        { $sort: { total: -1 } },
        { $limit: 5 }
      ]
    }
  }
])

$facet is memory-intensive because it buffers the entire input for each sub-pipeline. Use it with a selective $match before the facet to reduce input size.

$bucket for Histograms

$bucket groups documents into fixed ranges and is more efficient than $group for histogram-style aggregations:

db.products.aggregate([
  {
    $bucket: {
      groupBy: "$price",
      boundaries: [0, 50, 100, 200, 500],
      default: "other",
      output: {
        count: { $sum: 1 },
        avgPrice: { $avg: "$price" }
      }
    }
  }
])

$merge for Incremental Aggregation

$merge writes the aggregation results into another collection. It can be used to maintain materialized views or rollups. Instead of re-aggregating the entire dataset every time, you can incrementally update a summary collection:

db.dailySales.aggregate([
  {
    $match: { saleDate: { $gte: "2025-01-01", $lt: "2025-01-02" } }
  },
  {
    $group: { _id: { $dateToString: { format: "%Y-%m-%d", date: "$saleDate" } }, total: { $sum: "$amount" } }
  },
  {
    $merge: {
      into: "salesRollup",
      on: "_id",
      whenMatched: "replace",
      whenNotMatched: "insert"
    }
  }
])

This pattern is powerful for large-scale reporting where you can't afford to aggregate the full collection on every request.

7. Real-World Optimization Workflow

Optimizing an aggregation pipeline is not a one-off activity. Follow this workflow to systematically identify and fix bottlenecks.

Step 1: Profile with explain()

Run the pipeline with explain("executionStats") and examine the output:

db.collection.aggregate(pipeline, { explain: "executionStats" })

Key metrics to look for:

  • totalDocsExamined — number of documents read. If this is much higher than the result count, you need better filtering or indexes.
  • totalKeysExamined — number of index keys examined. If this is high but totalDocsExamined is low, you may be using an index but still scanning many keys.
  • executionTimeMillis — total time. Compare this to the time of individual stages.
  • maxMemoryUsage — peak memory per stage. Values near 100 MB indicate a spill risk.

Step 2: Use $planCacheStats

To see how the planner is caching query plans, run:

db.collection.aggregate([{ $planCacheStats: {} }])

This shows which shapes have cached plans and which indexes they use. If you see a plan using a full collection scan, you know an index is missing or not being chosen.

Step 3: Monitor with Atlas/Compass

In production, use MongoDB Atlas's Performance Advisor or the Profiler in Compass to track slow queries. Set a slow query threshold (e.g., 100 ms) and review the slow query log. This gives you a real-world view of pipeline performance under load.

Step 4: Iterate

Make one change at a time (add an index, reorder stages, reduce memory) and re-run explain(). Measure the impact before moving on. Avoid making multiple changes simultaneously, as you won't know which one helped.

8. Anti-Patterns to Avoid

$where

The $where operator runs JavaScript on the server and cannot use indexes. It forces a full collection scan and is extremely slow. Use $expr with aggregation operators instead.

// BAD: full scan
db.users.find({ $where: "this.age > 30" })

// GOOD: uses index if available
db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 30 } })

$regex Without Index

A $regex pattern that is not anchored to the beginning of the string cannot use an index. For example, /^abc/ can use an index, but /abc/ cannot. If you need substring search, consider using Atlas Search or a text index.

$unwind of Large Arrays

$unwind on a field that is an array with thousands of elements multiplies the document count. If you only need to filter on array elements, use $elemMatch or an array index instead of unwinding.

$lookup Without Index

As discussed, $lookup without an index on the foreign collection is a performance disaster. Always verify that the join fields are indexed.

$group with $push on Large Fields

$push accumulates entire documents into an array. If the documents are large, this quickly exhausts memory. Use $addToSet only when you need unique values, or project down to smaller fields before pushing.

9. Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How do I know if my aggregation pipeline is using an index?

Run the pipeline with explain("executionStats") and look for winningPlan and totalKeysExamined. If totalKeysExamined is greater than 0 and totalDocsExamined is low, an index is being used. If totalDocsExamined equals the total document count in the collection, it's a collection scan.

Q: Should I always enable allowDiskUse?

No. allowDiskUse masks memory problems and introduces I/O overhead. It should be a last resort. First, try to reduce memory usage by projecting fields, using $limit with $sort, or restructuring the pipeline. Only enable allowDiskUse when you've exhausted those options.

Q: Can I use aggregation pipelines for real-time analytics?

Yes, but for very large collections, consider pre-aggregating with $merge into a rollup collection. Real-time queries against a rollup are much faster than aggregating the raw collection on every request. You can also use change streams to keep the rollup up to date. For more insights on building scalable systems, check out Tamiz's Insights and tamiz.pro.

title: Fully local focus timer that lives in the system tray
description:
Hi everyone,

I wanted a focus timer that felt quiet and trustworthy.

Most of the ones I tried either needed an account, synced to the cloud, or lived in a browser tab I kept losing.

So I built Tempura.

It’s a small desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) that:

  • Lives in the system tray
  • Keeps the countdown accurate even if the window is closed or the computer sleeps
  • Stores everything locally in SQLite — no accounts, no cloud, no tracking
  • Comes with several focus rhythms (Classic 25/5, Sprint 15/3, Deep 50/10, 52/17, Ultradian, Flowtime, etc.) plus custom ones

I made it because I like tools that stay out of the way and respect my privacy. The whole session lives on my machine, and closing the window just hides it — quitting is a deliberate choice from the tray.

It’s free, MIT licensed, and still early (v0.1).

If a calm, local-first timer sounds useful to you, you can try it here:

https://vcostin.github.io/tempura/

I’d love to hear what you think — whether the idea resonates, or if there’s something that would make it more helpful for the way you work.

Thanks for reading.

title: Vercel applications are protected from Next.js August 2026 security vulnerabilities
description:
Summary

Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action.

Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities

Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities:

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input.

  • CVE-2026-75604 (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components.

After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service.

Impact on Vercel deployments

Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required.

  • Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path.

  • The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected.

Resolution for self-hosted applications

Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version.

For applications running Next.js 15.x or earlier:

For applications running Next.js 16.x:

In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately.

Credit

Thanks to the Hacktron team for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, and to evolutionstorm and B0RI for responsibly disclosing the Windows vulnerability.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36

title: Self-Taught Programmer Seeks Advice on Transitioning from Java to Go for Backend Development Career
description:
Introduction: The Transition from Java to Go

At 17, with no prior tech experience, a self-taught programmer stands at a crossroads: continue with Java or pivot to Go. This decision isn’t just about language preference; it’s a strategic career move. Go’s simplicity and efficiency make it a rising star in backend development, particularly in microservices and cloud-native architectures. However, transitioning from Java—a statically-typed, object-oriented language—to Go—a statically-typed, procedural language with concurrency features—requires unlearning Java-specific paradigms and adopting Go’s idiomatic style. Without a structured roadmap, this shift risks inefficiencies in learning, missed foundational skill-building, and delayed career entry.

The Problem: A Strategic Shift with High Stakes

The programmer’s attraction to Go’s philosophy is valid. Go’s goroutines, channels, and memory management offer unique advantages for backend development. However, the transition must be guided by a goal-oriented roadmap. A 1-2 year timeline demands prioritization: mastering Go’s core features, building a portfolio, and aligning skills with backend roles. Failure to structure this process could lead to superficial understanding, inability to solve complex problems, and a weak GitHub portfolio—critical for junior/internship applications.

Key Factors Driving the Decision

  • Attraction to Go’s Philosophy: Go’s simplicity and concurrency features align with modern backend demands, but require focused learning to avoid confusion with Java’s object-oriented paradigms.
  • Career Alignment: Go’s role in emerging technologies like Kubernetes and Docker makes it a strategic choice, but only if skills are mapped to backend roles and demonstrated through projects.
  • Self-Study Effectiveness: Relying on free resources (documentation, open-source projects) can be as effective as paid courses, but demands consistent practice and community engagement for mentorship and code reviews.

Typical Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Common mistakes include overlooking foundational concepts in Go, leading to an inability to solve real-world problems. For example, failing to grasp goroutines and channels can result in inefficient concurrency implementations. Another risk is neglecting networking, which limits access to mentorship and job opportunities. To avoid these, the roadmap must include:

  • Project-Based Learning: Build applications that demonstrate Go’s unique features, such as a RESTful API with goroutines for concurrency.
  • Community Engagement: Contribute to open-source Go projects to gain visibility and feedback.
  • Mentorship: Use AI tools like ChatGPT for guidance, but supplement with human code reviews to correct bad habits.

Rule for Decision-Making: If X, Then Y

If the goal is a backend developer role within 1-2 years, prioritize Go’s backend-specific features (e.g., concurrency, memory management) over Java’s object-oriented depth. Use self-study with a focus on hands-on projects and community engagement. Avoid expensive courses unless they offer mentorship or certification that directly enhances employability. This approach ensures efficient learning and a demonstrable skill set for junior/internship roles.

Evaluating the Benefits of Go for Backend Development

Switching from Java to Go isn’t just about swapping syntax—it’s a strategic pivot toward a language designed for modern backend demands. Let’s break down the mechanics of this transition, focusing on Go’s advantages, potential pitfalls, and how they align with your career goals.

Go’s Core Advantages Over Java in Backend Development

Concurrency Mechanisms: Goroutines vs. Java Threads

Go’s goroutines are lightweight threads managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. Unlike Java’s threads, which require significant memory (1MB+ per thread), goroutines start at 2KB and grow as needed. This efficiency allows Go to handle thousands of concurrent tasks with minimal overhead. For backend systems, this translates to higher throughput in I/O-bound tasks like handling HTTP requests. Mechanism: Goroutines multiplex onto OS threads via a scheduler, avoiding context-switching costs.

Memory Management: Garbage Collection Trade-offs

Go’s tri-color mark-and-sweep GC pauses execution less predictably than Java’s generational GC, but it’s simpler and faster for small-to-medium workloads. In backend systems, this trade-off often favors Go when latency isn’t mission-critical (e.g., microservices). Mechanism: Go’s GC pauses all goroutines during collection, but its efficiency in small heaps reduces pause times.

Simplicity in Syntax and Tooling

Go’s minimal syntax (no classes, inheritance) reduces cognitive load compared to Java’s object-oriented complexity. This simplicity accelerates development speed—critical for rapid iteration in backend projects. Mechanism: Fewer keywords and enforced code style (via gofmt) reduce debugging time and improve readability.

Where Go Outperforms Java in Backend Scenarios

Microservices and Cloud-Native Architectures

Go’s binary compilation produces statically linked executables, eliminating dependency hell common in Java deployments. This makes Go ideal for containerized environments (Docker, Kubernetes). Mechanism: Statically linked binaries reduce container size and startup time, critical for scaling microservices.

API Development: Speed and Efficiency

Go’s standard library includes robust HTTP handling, while Java relies on frameworks like Spring. For lightweight APIs, Go’s native tools reduce latency by bypassing framework overhead. Mechanism: Direct use of net/http avoids abstraction layers, reducing request processing time.

Potential Pitfalls of the Transition

Unlearning Object-Oriented Paradigms

Go’s procedural nature lacks inheritance and method overloading. Misapplying Java OOP patterns in Go leads to verbose, non-idiomatic code. Mechanism: Attempting to replicate Java’s class hierarchies in Go ignores its composition-over-inheritance philosophy, causing inefficiencies.

Concurrency Mismanagement

Goroutines and channels are powerful but unforgiving. Improper use (e.g., unbuffered channels in high-throughput systems) causes deadlocks. Mechanism: Unbuffered channels block sender/receiver goroutines indefinitely if not synchronized correctly.

Decision Dominance: When to Choose Go Over Java

Optimal Conditions for Go

  • If X: Your backend projects prioritize concurrency, low latency, and deployment simplicity.
  • Use Y: Transition to Go, focusing on mastering goroutines, channels, and memory management.

Suboptimal Conditions for Go

  • If X: Your target roles require deep Java ecosystem knowledge (e.g., Android backend, legacy enterprise systems).
  • Use Y: Stick with Java, but supplement with Go for side projects to test its fit.

Practical Roadmap for Go Mastery (1-2 Years)

Year 1: Foundations and Backend Basics

  1. Months 1-3: Learn Go syntax, interfaces, and error handling via The Go Programming Language (book) + small CLI projects.
  2. Months 4-6: Build a RESTful API using net/http, integrating a SQL database (e.g., PostgreSQL) and basic authentication.
  3. Months 7-9: Implement concurrency patterns (worker pools, fan-out/fan-in) in a real-time chat application.
  4. Months 10-12: Deploy a microservices project using Docker and Kubernetes, exposing Go’s deployment advantages.

Year 2: Specialization and Portfolio Polishing

  1. Months 1-6: Contribute to open-source Go projects (e.g., gin-gonic, echo) to refine idiomatic coding.
  2. Months 7-12: Build a production-grade backend system (e.g., e-commerce platform) showcasing Go’s scalability features.

Final Judgment: Is the Transition Worth It?

For a 17-year-old targeting backend roles, Go’s alignment with cloud-native technologies and its learning curve (steeper than Python but gentler than C++) make it a high-ROI choice. However, success hinges on:

  • Avoiding Java-to-Go paradigm mismatches through project-based learning.
  • Leveraging Go’s community (e.g., Gophers Slack) for mentorship.
  • Prioritizing backend-specific skills (Kubernetes, gRPC) over generalist knowledge.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is backend development in modern architectures, switch to Go now—but treat Java as a foundation, not a crutch. The transition’s efficiency depends on unlearning Java’s OOP habits and embracing Go’s procedural, concurrency-first design.

Structuring a 1-2 Year Self-Study Roadmap for Go

Transitioning from Java to Go is a strategic move for backend development, but it requires a structured, goal-oriented approach. Below is a detailed roadmap tailored to your goal of securing a junior/internship role within 1-2 years. This plan leverages Go’s strengths in concurrency, simplicity, and backend-specific features while avoiding common pitfalls.

Year 1: Foundations and Backend Essentials

Months 1-3: Master Go’s Core Syntax and Idioms

  • Mechanism: Go’s procedural nature and concurrency features (goroutines, channels) differ fundamentally from Java’s OOP. Focus on unlearning Java-specific paradigms like inheritance and method overloading.
  • Resources: Use The Go Programming Language book and official documentation. Build CLI projects to practice interfaces, error handling, and gofmt for enforced code style.
  • Risk: Misapplying Java OOP patterns leads to verbose, non-idiomatic Go code. Solution: Regularly review Go’s idiomatic style via go vet and community code examples.

Months 4-6: Build a RESTful API with Backend Integration

  • Mechanism: Go’s net/http package avoids framework overhead, making it ideal for lightweight APIs. Integrate with an SQL database (e.g., PostgreSQL) to handle data persistence.
  • Project: Create a CRUD API with authentication (JWT). Use gorm for ORM to understand database interactions.
  • Risk: Overlooking database indexing or inefficient queries leads to performance bottlenecks. Solution: Profile queries using pprof and optimize based on real-world load.

Months 7-9: Implement Concurrency Patterns in Real-Time Applications

  • Mechanism: Goroutines and channels enable efficient parallel processing. Build a real-time chat app to practice worker pools, fan-out/fan-in patterns, and deadlock avoidance.
  • Project: Use websocket for real-time communication. Implement rate limiting to prevent abuse.
  • Risk: Unbuffered channels block indefinitely if not synchronized. Solution: Use select statements with timeouts and buffered channels for controlled flow.

Months 10-12: Deploy Microservices with Docker and Kubernetes

  • Mechanism: Go’s statically linked binaries reduce container size and startup time, making it ideal for Kubernetes deployments. Learn Docker for containerization and Kubernetes for orchestration.
  • Project: Deploy a multi-service application (e.g., user service, order service) on Minikube. Use k8s.io/client-go for custom controllers.
  • Risk: Misconfiguring Kubernetes manifests leads to resource wastage or downtime. Solution: Use Helm charts for templated deployments and linters like kubeval.

Year 2: Advanced Skills and Production Readiness

Months 1-6: Contribute to Open-Source Go Projects

  • Mechanism: Engaging with the Go community provides mentorship and real-world problem-solving experience. Contribute to projects like gin-gonic or echo to understand production-grade codebases.
  • Outcome: Build a GitHub portfolio showcasing collaborative work and problem-solving skills.
  • Risk: Superficial contributions (e.g., fixing typos) add little value. Solution: Focus on meaningful issues (e.g., performance optimizations, feature additions) and document your process.

Months 7-12: Build a Production-Grade Backend System

  • Mechanism: Apply all learned skills to a complex project (e.g., e-commerce platform). Incorporate gRPC for inter-service communication, caching with Redis, and monitoring with Prometheus.
  • Project: Include features like payment gateways, inventory management, and user authentication. Deploy on AWS/GCP with CI/CD pipelines.
  • Risk: Overlooking scalability leads to system failures under load. Solution: Use load testing tools like k6 and implement horizontal scaling with Kubernetes.

Decision Dominance: Self-Study vs. Paid Courses

Optimal Choice: High-quality self-study + strong GitHub portfolio is sufficient for securing a job offer. Paid courses are unnecessary unless they offer mentorship or certifications that enhance employability.

  • Mechanism: Employers value practical skills and problem-solving ability, which are best demonstrated through hands-on projects and open-source contributions.
  • Rule: If a course offers mentorship or certification that aligns with backend roles (e.g., Kubernetes, gRPC), consider it. Otherwise, allocate resources to self-study and community engagement.
  • Typical Error: Spending on expensive courses without clear ROI. Mechanism: Lack of mentorship or certification limits the course’s impact on employability.

Final Judgment

Switching from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for modern backend development, especially in cloud-native architectures. Success hinges on:

  • Unlearning Java OOP habits and adopting Go’s idiomatic style.
  • Leveraging Go’s community for mentorship and open-source contributions.
  • Prioritizing backend-specific skills like Kubernetes, gRPC, and concurrency patterns.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is a backend developer role within 1-2 years, prioritize Go’s backend-specific features and use self-study with hands-on projects. Avoid expensive courses unless they offer mentorship or certification enhancing employability.

Real-World Applications and Case Studies

To understand the strategic value of transitioning from Java to Go for backend development, let’s examine real-world applications where Go’s unique features—concurrency, memory efficiency, and simplicity—have been leveraged effectively. These case studies not only demonstrate Go’s practical utility but also provide a blueprint for the projects you should aim to build in your 1–2 year roadmap.

1. Uber’s Transition to Go for High-Throughput Geocoding Services

Uber initially relied on Python for its geocoding services, but as the system scaled, it faced latency issues due to Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), which limits concurrent execution. Uber migrated to Go, leveraging its goroutines and channels to handle thousands of concurrent requests with minimal overhead. The result? A 30x reduction in latency and a 99% decrease in server count for the same workload. (Mechanism: Goroutines multiplex onto OS threads, enabling efficient parallel processing without the overhead of traditional threads.)

Practical Insight: In your roadmap, prioritize building a real-time geocoding API using net/http and goroutines to simulate high-throughput scenarios. This project will not only demonstrate Go’s concurrency but also align with industry demands for scalable backend systems.

2. Twitch’s Use of Go for Low-Latency Video Streaming

Twitch, a live streaming platform, adopted Go to handle its real-time chat and video streaming infrastructure. Go’s statically linked binaries and efficient memory management allowed Twitch to deploy microservices with minimal container size and startup time, critical for low-latency applications. (Mechanism: Go’s garbage collector optimizes memory usage, reducing pauses in I/O-bound tasks like video streaming.)

Practical Insight: In Months 7–9 of your roadmap, implement a WebSocket-based chat application with buffered channels and select statements to manage concurrency. This project mirrors Twitch’s use case and reinforces your understanding of Go’s backend-specific features.

3. Docker’s Foundation in Go for Containerization

Docker, the de facto standard for containerization, is written in Go. Its statically linked binaries and efficient resource utilization make Go ideal for building tools that require portability and performance. (Mechanism: Go’s compile-time optimizations and lack of runtime dependencies reduce container size and improve startup speed.)

Practical Insight: In Months 10–12 of Year 1, deploy a microservices architecture using Docker and Kubernetes. This project not only demonstrates Go’s role in cloud-native technologies but also prepares you for backend roles that increasingly require Kubernetes expertise.

4. Open-Source Contributions: Gin and Echo Frameworks

Open-source projects like Gin and Echo are widely used in the Go community for building RESTful APIs. Contributing to these projects not only enhances your GitHub portfolio but also exposes you to production-grade codebases and community best practices. (Mechanism: Engaging with open-source projects accelerates learning by forcing you to adhere to idiomatic Go and solve real-world problems.)

Practical Insight: In Year 2, focus on contributing to performance optimizations or new features in these frameworks. This aligns with the Decision Dominance rule: If your goal is to demonstrate backend expertise, prioritize open-source contributions over superficial projects.

Edge-Case Analysis: Pitfalls and Solutions

While Go’s simplicity is a strength, it can also lead to superficial understanding if foundational concepts are overlooked. For example, mismanaging concurrency—such as using unbuffered channels without timeouts—can lead to deadlocks. (Mechanism: Unbuffered channels block indefinitely if not synchronized correctly, halting goroutines.)

Solution: In your projects, always use buffered channels and select statements with timeouts. For example, in a real-time chat application, implement a worker pool pattern to manage concurrent message processing. This not only prevents deadlocks but also demonstrates a deep understanding of Go’s concurrency model.

Decision Dominance: Self-Study vs. Paid Courses

Given your resource constraints, self-study is the optimal choice for mastering Go. However, avoid the typical error of relying solely on tutorials without building projects. (Mechanism: Employers prioritize practical skills, and projects serve as tangible proof of your ability to solve real-world problems.)

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is a backend developer role within 1–2 years, use self-study with a focus on hands-on projects and open-source contributions. Invest in paid courses only if they offer mentorship or certifications that directly enhance employability (e.g., Kubernetes, gRPC).

Conclusion

Transitioning from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for aspiring backend developers, provided you follow a structured roadmap. By studying real-world applications like Uber, Twitch, and Docker, and by prioritizing project-based learning and community engagement, you can efficiently master Go’s backend-specific features. Avoid pitfalls by focusing on foundational concepts and leveraging open-source contributions to build a strong portfolio. With this approach, you’ll not only transition successfully but also position yourself for junior/internship roles within your desired timeframe.

Conclusion: Next Steps and Continuous Learning

Transitioning from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for aspiring backend developers, but success hinges on a structured, project-driven approach. Here’s how to move forward, grounded in the analytical model and practical insights:

1. Start Your Go Journey Now—But Strategically

Go’s concurrency mechanisms (goroutines, channels) and memory management (tri-color GC) outperform Java in I/O-bound tasks, making it ideal for microservices and cloud-native architectures. However, unlearning Java’s OOP paradigms is critical. Start by mastering Go’s syntax and idioms via The Go Programming Language book and official docs. Use go vet to avoid non-idiomatic code. Mechanism: Go’s procedural nature and enforced code style (gofmt) reduce debugging time, but misapplying Java patterns (e.g., inheritance) leads to verbose, inefficient code.

2. Build a Portfolio That Demonstrates Backend Proficiency

Employers prioritize practical skills over language expertise. Focus on projects like a RESTful API with net/http, a real-time chat app using WebSocket, and microservices deployed via Docker/Kubernetes. Mechanism: Go’s statically linked binaries reduce container size, enabling faster deployments. For example, Uber’s migration to Go for geocoding services achieved a 30x latency reduction by leveraging goroutines for parallel processing.

3. Leverage Self-Study Over Paid Courses—Unless Specific Conditions Apply

Decision Dominance: Self-study + GitHub portfolio is optimal for job offers. Paid courses are only justified if they offer mentorship or certifications (e.g., Kubernetes). Mechanism: Employers value problem-solving skills demonstrated through open-source contributions. For instance, contributing to gin-gonic or echo frameworks accelerates learning by enforcing idiomatic Go and solving real-world problems.

4. Stay Updated with Go’s Ecosystem and Backend Trends

Go’s role in emerging technologies (Kubernetes, gRPC) makes continuous learning essential. Follow Go’s release notes, engage with the Go community, and experiment with tools like Prometheus for monitoring and k6 for load testing. Mechanism: Go’s ecosystem evolves rapidly; for example, generics introduced in Go 1.18 enhance type safety and code reusability. Ignoring updates risks falling behind in modern backend practices.

5. Avoid Common Pitfalls by Focusing on Foundations

Typical failures include superficial understanding of concurrency (e.g., deadlocks from unbuffered channels) and neglecting networking. Use buffered channels and select statements with timeouts to prevent deadlocks. Mechanism: Mismanaging concurrency blocks goroutines indefinitely, degrading system performance. Engage with mentors or code reviews to identify and correct bad habits early.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is backend development in modern architectures, transition to Go. Focus on hands-on projects, community engagement, and unlearning Java OOP habits. Avoid expensive courses unless they enhance employability.

Start today—Go’s simplicity and efficiency will position you for junior/internship roles within 1–2 years, provided you follow this structured roadmap.

title: Cloudflare Rebuilds Its Control Plane for Selectable Data Residency
description:
Data residency requirements tend to arrive late in a project and force awkward compromises. Cloudflare has announced a beta that aims to make location a setting rather than an architecture decision. The announcement is brief, so this article covers what was said and what is still unknown.

What happened

In a post on X, Cloudflare said it is rebuilding its control plane and its logging on top of Workers and Durable Objects, its own developer platform products. According to the company, the purpose is to let customers choose where three things live: their WAF rules, their Workers, and their logs. Cloudflare describes the choice as a single click, with the option to change it again with another.

Cloudflare also opened applications for a beta program. The post links to a sign-up page.

The post does not say:

  • which regions or jurisdictions will be available
  • which plans or customer tiers can join the beta
  • what happens to existing data and configuration when a location is changed
  • pricing, or when general availability is planned

Treat those as open questions until Cloudflare publishes more detail.

Why it matters

Residency discussions usually focus on where application data is stored. In practice, security rules, serverless code and logs are also part of the picture, because logs can contain request details and rules describe how your traffic is handled. A feature that lets you place these deliberately addresses a real gap for teams in regulated environments.

The second point is architectural. Cloudflare is building its own control plane and logging on Workers and Durable Objects. That is a vendor using its developer platform for core infrastructure, which is a reasonable signal that the platform is meant for stateful, distributed workloads. It is not proof of how the beta will behave in your environment, though.

The promise of changing location with one click is attractive, but it deserves scrutiny. Moving configuration and logs between locations raises questions about data migration, retention, and audit trails. The announcement does not address those, so don't assume the experience is as simple as the wording suggests.

What you should do

  • If you have residency or sovereignty requirements: apply for the beta and test it against your actual requirements, including logs and rule configuration.
  • Write down your questions first: which regions you need, how location changes should be handled, and what your auditors expect for logs.
  • If residency isn't on your roadmap: no action is needed now. Keep it in mind if your customer base or regulatory exposure grows.
  • Don't change compliance claims yet: until Cloudflare publishes documentation, don't tell customers or auditors that your setup meets a residency requirement based on this announcement alone.

For details beyond the announcement, use the primary link below and watch Cloudflare's documentation as the beta progresses.

Sources

  • https://x.com/Cloudflare/status/2116522276988371217

title: I built a pixel-art whale that grows with your GitHub commits (Rust, SDFs, Bayer dithering)
description:
Your GitHub profile README is the one page you fully control. Most of us fill it with badges and stat cards. I wanted something alive, so I built GitTulkun: a pixel-art Tulkun (the giant whale-like creatures from Avatar's Pandora) that is generated from your real GitHub activity, swims in a seamless looping GIF, and grows up as your year goes on.

PramudithaN / git-tulkun

Procedural pixel-art Tulkun whale generated from your GitHub contributions and language colors as a looping GIF for your profile README.

git-tulkun

A procedural pixel-art Tulkun leviathan for your GitHub profile README.md that resets to a baby calf every January 1st, grows on a logarithmic scale into an armored adult bull from your contributions, and takes its colors from your top programming languages.


Live git-tulkun generated from @PramudithaN's current-year GitHub activity (1,072 contributions - Stage 3: Adolescent Tulkun)

Quick Start (1-Step Setup)

1. Add this embed snippet to your profile README.md (replace YOUR_USERNAME with your GitHub username):

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://github.com/PramudithaN/git-tulkun">
    <img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_USERNAME/output/tulkun/tulkun.gif" width="640" alt="git-tulkun swimming" />
  </a>
</p>

2. Create .github/workflows/tulkun.yml in the same repository (the action pushes tulkun.gif, tulkun.png, and share-card.png to an orphan output branch automatically so daily updates never bloat your main commit history):

name: Update Tulkun
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 0 * *
…
View on GitHub

That is my own whale, generated live from my own contributions.

What it does

  • Reads your current-year contributions and top repository languages from the GitHub GraphQL API
  • Maps your contribution count to one of five life stages, from Baby Calf to Adult Male Bull
  • Resets every January 1, so everyone starts the year as a calf
  • Tints the whale with the official GitHub colors of your top three languages
  • Renders a 48-frame, 15 FPS loop that updates daily through a GitHub Action

The five stages

Stage Contributions this year What changes
1. Baby Calf [range] Short, stubby body, blunt snout, cream belly
2. Yearling Calf [range] Longer, slimmer body; kuru whips sprout
3. Adolescent [range] Sensor crest rises; six flippers elongate
4. Adult Female [range] Dark carapace armor, sloped crest, serrated jaw
5. Adult Male Bull [range] Maximum length, hooked hammer-crest, battle scars

How the renderer works

There are no spritesheets. Every frame is computed from a handful of parameters, so one code path draws all five stages and three camera angles.

1. Shape. The body is a spline, with signed distance fields (SDFs) for the head crest, flippers, whips, jaw stripes and flukes. A stage change just moves parameters, such as the spine growing from 64 px to 186 px.

2. Lighting. For each pixel the renderer builds a surface normal from the body's cylindrical profile and lights it with a fixed directional light:

n = (nx, ny, sqrt(1 - nx^2 - ny^2))
light = [-0.30, -0.62, 0.72]

3. Pixel-art look. Brightness is quantized to a 4-shade ramp with a 4x4 ordered Bayer dither matrix, which gives the classic crosshatch of old pixel art. A 1 px dark outline (#0f121a) keeps the whale readable on both light and dark GitHub themes.

4. Language colors. Each top language's hex color becomes a 4-shade ramp (shadow, mid dark, mid light, highlight). Your top language paints the belly, skin and carapace, the second tints the sensor crest, and the third lights its tip. A TypeScript-heavy profile gets a different whale than a Rust-heavy one.

5. Swimming. The loop is 48 frames at 15 FPS (3.2 seconds). A traveling S-wave bends the torso and drives the tail, while the flippers lag behind in phase:

dy(u, t) = A_bob * sin(w*t) * (1 - u)^1.3 + A_tail * sin(2.35*pi*u - w*t) * u^0.92

Here u runs along the body from head (0) to tail (1).

6. No jitter. The camera box is precomputed across the whole stroke, so the whale never clips or bounces the frame. Output is upscaled 2x with nearest-neighbor into a 640x280 GIF, plus a PNG and an HTML preview.

Why Rust and a GitHub Action

The whole thing is one Rust binary with five dependencies (chrono, gif, png, serde, serde_json). The composite GitHub Action downloads a prebuilt binary when one exists and compiles from source otherwise. Data collection shells out to gh api graphql, so the built-in workflow token is enough.

Add your own whale

Create .github/workflows/tulkun.yml in your profile repository:

name: Update Tulkun
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 0 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  tulkun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: PramudithaN/git-tulkun@[latest tag, e.g. v1]
        with:
          view: side
          canon: "false"
      - run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add tulkun/tulkun.gif tulkun/tulkun.png
          git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m "chore: update Tulkun"
          git push

[If you shipped a commit input or an output-branch option, show the shorter workflow here instead.]

Then embed it in your README:

<img src="tulkun/tulkun.gif" width="640" alt="My Tulkun" />

Want a preview without any setup? Run the demo mode locally:

cargo run --release -- demo --commits 145 --view dive --output-dir tulkun-demo

What I learned

[Add 2 or 3 honest lessons here, for example: keeping five stages visually consistent, getting a seamless loop, or the repo bloat from daily GIF commits and how you fixed it. Real stories earn more comments than feature lists.]

What I would love feedback on

  • Should the stages scale differently, or use a rolling 365 days instead of a calendar year?
  • What else should shape the whale: pull requests, reviews, streaks?
  • Which camera angle do you like most?

Drop your whale in the comments, I would love to see them.

Repo: https://github.com/PramudithaN/git-tulkun (if you like it, a star helps others find it).

GitTulkun is an unofficial fan project. Tulkun and Avatar belong to their respective owners, and this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

title: How to Retry Email API Calls in Go: Backoff for Signup Verification
description:
Short answer: Use a bounded exponential retry policy for failed email API calls: start at 2 seconds, cap the delay at 32 seconds, stop after 5 attempts, and make every attempt idempotent.

When a signup verification email fails, the useful alarm is not “the API returned 500.” The useful alarm is “the account has not received a link after the retry budget expired.” Keep the signup state idempotent, log every attempt, and inspect the email list or event list afterward for messages that still need action.

This protects deliverability in two directions. A short-lived provider failure gets another chance without a request storm; a permanent failure stops consuming capacity and becomes visible to an operator. The verification template should remain owned by the team that can review its wording, expiry behavior, and abuse controls. Delivery infrastructure can be shared, but the decision about what the user receives should not disappear inside a vendor dashboard.

Keep it finite.

Exactly.

What should the on-call alarm actually say?

Picture the page at 03:10: signup completion is healthy, but the “verification email delivered” counter has fallen below its normal range. The first response is usually to inspect the last request, find a 503 or 429, and restart the worker. That is a noisy response if the worker immediately sends the same request again.

The earlier signal is a growing set of verification records in pending_delivery, partitioned by outcome. For example, a record that receives a 503 on attempt 1 should carry a next retry time near 2 seconds later; a second transient failure should move it toward 4 seconds, and the fifth failure should become an explicit terminal review state rather than another hidden background task. Log at least the account identifier, message identifier, attempt number, HTTP status, provider request ID when available, and the next retry time. Do not log the verification token or the full email address. Those fields help answer two different questions: did the API accept the request, and did the message later reach a useful terminal state? They also let the on-call compare the queue age with the user-facing signup state without opening a provider console and guessing which request belongs to which account. That correlation is the difference between an alert that points to a repair and an alert that merely announces traffic.

I initially treated every non-2xx response as retryable. That was a mistake in the policy, even before it became a production problem: an invalid request can be repeated five times with perfect exponential math and still remain invalid. Retry transient rate limits and server failures; surface authentication, validation, suppression, and other terminal responses for review. A backoff policy is not a substitute for classifying errors.

How should I handle retrying failed email API calls?

Use a capped schedule, not an unbounded formula. With a 2-second base, the nominal delays are 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 seconds. Five attempts give the system a finite boundary. That boundary matters because a signup flow should not keep a worker occupied indefinitely while an upstream service is unavailable.

Honor Retry-After when the server supplies it, but still enforce the local cap. A provider may ask for a delay longer than the workflow can tolerate; the application should record that fact and move the message to a later queue or an operator-visible state rather than sleeping forever. Add jitter in a real queue so many workers do not wake on the same second.

Here is a complete retry wrapper around the verified send route. It takes the request JSON from EMAIL_JSON because the exact message fields belong to the API contract you are using; the retry behavior does not need to duplicate that schema. Set EMAIL_API_BASE_URL to the service base URL in the deployment environment. The program uses a stable idempotency key for the message, checks response bodies on errors, and exits nonzero when the budget is exhausted.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("EMAIL_API_BASE_URL")
    payload := os.Getenv("EMAIL_JSON")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("EMAIL_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" || baseURL == "" || payload == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_API_BASE_URL, EMAIL_JSON, and EMAIL_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY are required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 3*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    if err := sendWithRetry(ctx, client, apiKey, baseURL, []byte(payload), idempotencyKey); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func sendWithRetry(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string, baseURL string, payload []byte, idempotencyKey string) error {
    const maxAttempts = 5
    const baseDelay = 2 * time.Second
    const maxDelay = 32 * time.Second

    for attempt := 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")+"/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("build request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == maxAttempts {
                return fmt.Errorf("attempt %d transport error: %w", attempt, err)
            }
            if err := wait(ctx, baseDelay, attempt, ""); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Printf("email accepted on attempt %d: %s\n", attempt, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            return nil
        }

        retryable := resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests || resp.StatusCode >= 500
        if !retryable || attempt == maxAttempts {
            return fmt.Errorf("email send failed on attempt %d with HTTP %d: %s", attempt, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        if err := wait(ctx, baseDelay, attempt, resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return errors.New("retry loop ended unexpectedly")
}

func wait(ctx context.Context, base time.Duration, attempt int, retryAfter string) error {
    delay := base * time.Duration(1<<(attempt-1))
    if delay > 32*time.Second {
        delay = 32 * time.Second
    }
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if delay > 32*time.Second {
            delay = 32 * time.Second
        }
    }
    // Jitter avoids synchronized retries when several workers see the same outage.
    delay += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(delay / 4)))
    timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
    defer timer.Stop()
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return fmt.Errorf("retry wait canceled: %w", ctx.Err())
    case <-timer.C:
        return nil
    }
}

The key detail is not the sleep. It is the stable Idempotency-Key. If a timeout occurs after the provider accepted the message, the next attempt must be recognizable as the same operation. Generate that key from the signup verification record, persist it before enqueueing, and reuse it on every retry. A retry without that property can create duplicate links and duplicate messages.

One small Go concern is worth calling out: the jitter expression assumes a positive delay, which this policy guarantees. If you adapt the helper to accept arbitrary durations, guard that random range before calling rand.Int63n. Tiny helpers become incident code surprisingly quickly.

Which service should own the template and delivery path?

The template owner and the transport owner can be different. For a B2B SaaS signup, I would keep the verification template in application-controlled configuration or a reviewed template store, then send through a provider with clear delivery events. The review boundary should include subject, link lifetime, locale, unsubscribe handling where applicable, and the domain authentication setup. SPF is one part of that setup, not a complete deliverability diagnosis.

The practical choices have different operational shapes:

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon SES Teams already operating on AWS and comfortable assembling their own email workflow More responsibility sits with the application for templates, event handling, and operational policy
SendGrid A managed provider with broad email tooling and a dashboard-oriented workflow Decide which template changes require code review and how provider-side edits are audited
Mailgun API-first teams that want delivery events and domain-oriented tooling Confirm regional, compliance, and event-retention requirements before making it the only path
Postmark Transactional email teams that want a focused product boundary Check whether its template and stream model matches signup verification and future message types
A unified REST layer such as Infrai A small platform team that wants one key and one bill across backend services, with email as one capability It does not provide SMTP relay or hosted email OTP; events are pull-based, so polling and the application-owned fallback remain your responsibility

There is no universal winner here. SES may fit an AWS-heavy platform; Postmark may be the clearer boundary for a narrowly transactional product; SendGrid or Mailgun may fit teams already invested in their tooling. A unified REST layer is attractive when reducing key and invoice sprawl matters across backend services, but it should not erase ownership of the verification experience.

The trade-off is concrete. A unified layer is a poor fit if your requirement is SMTP relay, hosted email OTP, webhook-driven event handling, or a domestic compliance decision based on a specific pending vendor. In those cases, choose a provider whose documented capability matches the requirement and keep the application-level retry policy anyway.

For the retry workflow, Infrai exposes the send route and list/event routes needed for follow-up inspection, while its event model is pull-based. That means the worker can retry, then a reconciler can poll for messages requiring further action. The limitation is real-time coordination: there are no webhook events in this namespace, so polling needs its own rate limit and checkpoint. It does not turn a provider response into proof that an inbox received the link.

What should happen after the fifth attempt?

Stop retrying. Mark the delivery attempt as needs_review or enqueue it in a controlled recovery queue with a new operator-visible reason. The user-facing signup state should distinguish “account created, verification pending” from “verification request rejected.” Do not silently issue a second token just because the first delivery attempt timed out; that can invalidate a link the user is already opening.

The reconciliation job should inspect the email list and event list, correlate provider IDs with the local verification record, and check suppression or bounce signals where the chosen service exposes them. Since the event surface is pull-based in this scenario, give the poller its own rate limit and checkpoint. Otherwise the recovery job becomes the next source of load during an incident.

Finally, alert on the symptoms that affect the user: pending verification age, terminal send failures by status class, duplicate idempotency keys, and the proportion of records needing review. A high retry count is a useful diagnostic, but it is not the business outcome. The business outcome is a verification link delivered once, with enough evidence to explain what happened when it was not.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide
  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Mailgun Sending Messages
  • Postmark Developer Documentation
