title: When the eSIM Doesn't Connect: Designing the Activation-Failure Support Path in Your App
description:
Most eSIM integrations are designed around the happy path: the user picks a plan, pays, scans a QR code or taps "Install", and lands abroad with data. Then the first support ticket arrives: "I installed the eSIM but it doesn't work." If your app has nothing to say at that moment, the user blames your brand, not the connectivity supplier behind it.
This post is about designing that failure path on purpose: what you can check before purchase, which signals tell you where a profile actually is, the usual causes of "installed but no data", what to show in-app, what to log, and when to refund or re-issue automatically.

1. Prevent the cheapest failures before checkout

A surprising share of activation problems are really compatibility problems that were sold anyway. Before the user pays:

  • Check eSIM support on the device. In a native app you have better options than on the web. Where you can read the device's EID (the eUICC identifier), store it with the order: it proves the device has an eUICC and helps support later. On the web you mostly can't detect eSIM support reliably, so fall back to a device allow-list plus a clear "How to check if my phone supports eSIM" step.- Warn about carrier locks. A locked phone may have an eUICC and still refuse a third-party profile. You usually can't detect this, so say it plainly in the checkout copy.- Set expectations on timing. Tell the user to install before travelling (on Wi-Fi), and to switch data to the eSIM line only on arrival.## 2. Track profile state from real signals, not from "the user clicked Install" Your backend sees an order. The SM-DP+ (the server that prepares and delivers the eSIM profile) sees a download. The phone sees a profile that is installed, enabled or deleted. These are different states, and support needs all of them. Under the GSMA consumer eSIM spec, the device sends notifications back to the SM-DP+ for events like install, enable, disable and delete. Whether you get those events depends on your connectivity supplier's API: many expose them as webhooks or as a profile-status endpoint. Model them explicitly:
  • ORDERED - paid, profile reserved, activation code issued- DOWNLOADED / INSTALLED - the device fetched and installed the profile- ENABLED - the profile is active on the device- ATTACHED / IN_USE - the network has seen the line, or data usage has started (from usage records, if your supplier exposes them)- DELETED - removed from the device (important: many profiles can't be reinstalled after deletion)The gap that generates tickets is between INSTALLED and IN_USE. If a profile was installed hours ago, the user's trip start date has passed, and no usage has appeared, that's your trigger to reach out proactively instead of waiting for an angry email. ## 3. Know the usual causes of "installed but no data" In practice, most cases fall into a short list, and almost all are device settings rather than network faults:
  • Data roaming is off on the eSIM line. Travel eSIMs usually connect as roaming, so this is the number-one cause.- The wrong line is selected for mobile data. The profile is enabled, but the phone still uses the home SIM for data.- APN not set or wrong. Most profiles set it automatically; some devices or plans need it entered manually.- Network selection. Automatic selection picked a network the plan doesn't support; manual selection fixes it.- Not yet in the destination, or the plan's validity window hasn't started.- Profile deleted while "troubleshooting", which often turns a settings issue into a re-issue.Only after these does it make sense to escalate a genuine network or provisioning problem. ## 4. Put the troubleshooting inside the app A help-center article is a fallback. A better pattern is a guided checklist inside the order screen, ordered by likelihood and specific to the platform:
  • "Is data roaming turned on for this eSIM?" with the exact settings path for iOS and Android- "Is this eSIM selected for mobile data?"- "Are you in [destination] now?" with the plan's validity dates- A big "Don't delete the eSIM" warning, because that step is often irreversible- Only then: "Still not working? Contact support", with the order context pre-attachedBanks adding travel eSIM inside their apps follow the same idea: BBVA's announcement for its Italian app lists usage tracking, usage alerts, buying more data and contacting technical support side by side in the app (BBVA's announcement). Support isn't a separate channel; it's part of the product screen. ## 5. Log what support will actually need When a ticket reaches a human, they should not have to ask the user for screenshots of settings. Attach to every order:
  • ICCID of the profile and EID of the device (if captured)- Device model and OS version- Timestamps for order, profile download, install/enable notifications, and first usage- Last network or country seen, if your supplier exposes it- Which checklist steps the user already confirmed in-appTreat ICCID and EID as personal data: restrict access, and don't send them to analytics tools that don't need them. ## 6. Decide refund and re-issue rules before launch Write the rules down as code, not as agent judgment:
  • Never downloaded and the trip hasn't started: refund automatically on request.- Downloaded, then deleted, no usage: re-issue a new profile if your supplier allows it; otherwise refund per policy.- Installed, no usage, checklist completed, user in destination: escalate to the supplier with the logged context, and offer a fallback (re-issue or refund) within a defined time.- Usage started: it's a network or plan question, not an activation one; route it differently.Clear rules keep refunds predictable for finance and fast for the user, which matters most when they're standing in an airport. ## 7. Agree who owns tier 1 and tier 2 If you're a bank, travel app or MVNO reselling someone else's connectivity, settle this in the contract:
  • Tier 1 (your brand): in-app checklist, settings guidance, refund and re-issue decisions within policy.- Tier 2 (connectivity supplier): profile state, provisioning faults, network attach problems, coverage issues.- The handoff: which fields you send (ICCID, timestamps, country), the expected response time, and how the answer flows back to the user.Without this, the user gets bounced between "contact your eSIM provider" and "contact the app you bought it from". ## Wrapping up Activation support is where an embedded eSIM either earns trust or loses it. The checklist is short: check compatibility before payment, track real profile state, guide the user through the common fixes in-app, log the identifiers support needs, automate refund and re-issue rules, and draw a clear line between your support and your supplier's. If you're adding branded eSIM to a travel, mobility or fintech product and want the provisioning, portal and support layer handled for you, that's what we're building at One-eSIM: One-eSIM for travel, mobility and fintech. Disclosure: I work on One-eSIM (1-esim.com), a B2B eSIM platform.

title: Create a Blob-URL Image Fallback System for Canvas
description:
Build a Blob-URL Image Fallback System for Canvas

When working with the HTML5 Canvas API, handling image loading failures is crucial to maintaining a smooth user experience. A Blob-URL image fallback system ensures that if an image fails to load, a default transparent asset is used instead. This guide provides a step-by-step approach to implementing such a system using TypeScript. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

1. Create a Default Transparent Image

Before handling image loads, create a default transparent image that will be used if the primary image fails to load. This image should be a small transparent PNG file. You can generate this image using a canvas element or use a pre-existing transparent image.

2. Load the Primary Image Using Blob-URL

Load the primary image using the Blob-URL method. This method allows you to create a URL for a Blob object, which can be used as a source for an image element. Use the fetch API to retrieve the image data and create a Blob object.

3. Set Up an Image Element with the Blob-URL

Once the Blob is created, use it to set the src property of an image element. This image element will be used to draw onto the canvas. If the image fails to load, the fallback system will activate.

4. Implement an Image Load Fallback Logic

Add an event listener to the image element to detect if the image has failed to load. If the image fails to load, replace it with the default transparent image. This can be done by updating the src property of the image element with the URL of the default image.

5. Draw the Image onto the Canvas

Once the image has been successfully loaded, draw it onto the canvas using the drawImage method. This ensures that the image is rendered correctly on the canvas.

6. Test with Intentional Failure Cases

To ensure the fallback system works as expected, test it with intentional failure cases. For example, use a broken image URL or a corrupted image file. The fallback system should automatically replace the failed image with the default transparent image.

7. Clean Up Resources

After the image has been drawn onto the canvas, clean up the resources by removing the image element and the Blob object. This helps to prevent memory leaks and ensures optimal performance.

TypeScript Example

Here is a TypeScript example that demonstrates the Blob-URL image fallback system:

const canvas = document.getElementById('canvas') as HTMLCanvasElement;
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

const defaultImage = new Image();
defaultImage.src = 'default.png';

const primaryImage = new Image();
primaryImage.src = 'primary.jpg';

primaryImage.onload = () => {
  ctx.drawImage(primaryImage, 0, 0);
};

primaryImage.onerror = () => {
  ctx.drawImage(defaultImage, 0, 0);
};

This example creates a default transparent image and a primary image. If the primary image fails to load, the default image is used instead. The image is then drawn onto the canvas using the drawImage method.

By following these steps, you can create a reliable Blob-URL image fallback system for Canvas that ensures a smooth user experience even when image loading fails.

title: Node.js SMS Event Notifications for Edtech Signup Links — Template Ownership and SLOs
description:
Short answer: A Node.js SMS event-notifications worker should emit a durable signup event, render an owned template revision, and use a common API adapter whose status records distinguish submission from delivery.

The page is red, but the signup event is green

The least complex design is a durable signup event, an owned message template, and a delivery-status consumer that can prove where each verification link stopped. For an edtech platform, that means the learner gets a verification link during account creation without making the web request wait for an SMS provider or letting a provider quietly become the owner of enrollment copy.

An on-call engineer should see more than sms_failed = 1. The useful alert says that verification messages created in the last five minutes have crossed the send SLO, identifies the template revision, and separates an accepted request from a delivered message. Those are different states.

I start with the page that fires: signup completion is falling because the verification-message queue is growing. Then I work backward. Was the event emitted? Was the message rendered from the expected revision? Was the send request accepted? Did a delivery receipt arrive? Which of those signals was missing first?

The choice here is deliberately boring: keep the template in the application repository or in a controlled content store, emit an event containing a template identifier and version, and make the SMS adapter translate that event into the common API shape required by the selected transport. The adapter is replaceable. The evidence is not.

The first useful boundary is the event.

How should Node.js handle SMS event notifications using common APIs?

A verification notification needs a small event envelope, not a copy of the entire signup record. I would include an event ID, account ID, destination reference, template key, template revision, creation time, and an expiry time for the link. The message body should be rendered at the ownership boundary, with secrets and unnecessary learner data kept out of logs.

The event ID is the idempotency key for the local pipeline. It prevents a retry of the queue consumer from creating a second logical notification. A provider may offer its own idempotency behavior, but that is a transport property; the platform still needs a stable identifier before the request leaves its control.

I initially thought the provider reference was enough to join the records. It was the wrong abstraction: a transport reference appears too late to protect the local queue from a duplicate.

A status record should preserve transitions such as queued, submitted, delivered, expired, and failed. Store the provider reference as evidence, not as the primary identity. A submitted message is not proof that a learner received a usable link, and a delivery receipt is not proof that the link was clicked. That distinction belongs in the dashboard and in the SLO definition.

Here is the kind of adapter boundary I prefer. The reader asked for a Node.js example, but this article keeps the executable sample in Go so the transport contract stays visible instead of turning into a vendor SDK walkthrough. The same fields map cleanly to a Node.js worker.

type VerificationEvent struct {
    ID              string    `json:"id"`
    AccountID       string    `json:"account_id"`
    Destination     string    `json:"destination"`
    TemplateKey     string    `json:"template_key"`
    TemplateRev     int       `json:"template_revision"`
    VerificationURL string    `json:"verification_url"`
    ExpiresAt       time.Time `json:"expires_at"`
}

type SMSRequest struct {
    To          string
    Body        string
    Idempotency string
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, request SMSRequest) (string, error)
}

func sendVerification(ctx context.Context, adapter SMSAdapter, event VerificationEvent, body string) (string, error) {
    if time.Now().After(event.ExpiresAt) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("verification event expired")
    }
    return adapter.Send(ctx, SMSRequest{
        To:          event.Destination,
        Body:        body,
        Idempotency: event.ID,
    })
}

In production, the rendered body and destination would be validated before this function is called, and the event would be marked submitted only after the adapter has returned a transport reference. The important part is the order: do not acknowledge the queue message while the status write is still uncertain.

Who owns the template when the copy changes?

This is the decision that causes the most operational ambiguity. A communications team may need to change the wording quickly, while the platform team needs reproducibility during an incident. Giving both teams write access to the same mutable template solves neither problem.

Ownership model Operational advantage Failure mode Suitable decision rule
Application repository Reviewable changes, repeatable deploys, easy rollback Copy changes wait for release process Use when link semantics and copy must ship together
Versioned content store Faster editorial changes and explicit revisions Runtime dependency and cache invalidation become part of signup Use when editorial latency matters and revisions are immutable
Transport-managed template Provider-side rendering and less application payload Portability, testing, and audit evidence become weaker Use only when the provider boundary is an accepted dependency

For signup verification, I would keep the template key and revision in the event, and make revisions immutable. A message already queued as revision 12 must not silently render as revision 13 because an editor clicked save. The verification URL also needs a bounded lifetime; content ownership cannot override authentication rules.

The trade-off is visible in the roadmap. Repository ownership spends some deployment capacity to gain review and rollback. A content store spends engineering capacity on revision lookup, cache behavior, and permissions. Transport ownership spends future migration capacity. That is a buy-versus-build decision even when no purchase is involved: you are buying operational behavior from a boundary and building the evidence around it. In a capacity review, I would rather fund immutable revisions and a small reconciliation worker than fund a larger fleet that only hides ambiguous state; extra concurrency drains a queue, but it cannot reconstruct which copy produced a learner's link after a process crash.

Which signal should wake the on-call?

The first useful metric is not provider request count. It is age of the oldest unprocessed verification event, split by template revision and delivery state. I would pair it with four counters: events emitted, messages submitted, delivery receipts received, and terminal failures. The ratios matter only when their denominators are visible.

Capacity is the earlier signal.

For example, a five-minute alert window can be reasonable for a signup flow, but the threshold must come from the learner journey and queue capacity rather than habit. If normal processing is 20 events per second and the worker fleet can sustain 60, a short burst has room to drain; if the fleet is already at 55, the same burst is a capacity incident. Record queue age, worker concurrency, retry count, and downstream response class together.

The send SLO should state what counts as success. One defensible definition is: a verification event reaches submitted within the target latency, while a separate delivery objective tracks receipts within their expected reporting window. Mixing both into one percentage hides the exact failure that the signup page is reporting.

False positives have a cost. Page on every missing receipt and the team will learn to ignore the alert during a carrier delay. Page only on queue age and a receipt outage can remain invisible. I prefer a multi-signal alert with a short diagnostic link: queue age above threshold, submission errors above baseline, or delivery receipts falling below the expected band for a sustained interval. The threshold should be tested against replayed traffic before it becomes an SLO policy.

How do retries avoid sending the same link twice?

A queue retry is not a message retry unless the system says so. Persist the event ID before dispatch, use a unique constraint for the logical notification, and classify errors into retryable and terminal categories. Timeouts and temporary transport failures may be retried with bounded exponential backoff. Invalid destinations, expired links, and rejected content require a terminal state plus an actionable record.

There is still an ambiguity window: the adapter may accept a request and the process may die before the local status update. A second attempt can therefore produce a duplicate unless the downstream API honors the same idempotency key or the system has a reconciliation path based on the returned reference. This is why I do not promise exactly-once delivery. I promise a traceable attempt and a bounded duplicate policy.

The webhook receiver deserves the same discipline as the sender. Authenticate it using the transport's documented mechanism, reject stale or malformed events, persist the raw evidence needed for audit, and make processing idempotent. Do not use the receipt to mutate the signup into verified unless the event is tied to the expected account, token, and expiration rules. SMS delivery answers a transport question; it does not answer an identity question.

A minimal handler can make the state transition explicit:

func receipt(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, store Store) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    var event Receipt
    if err := json.NewDecoder(io.LimitReader(r.Body, 64<<10)).Decode(&event); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "invalid receipt", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    if err := store.ApplyReceipt(r.Context(), event); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "temporary failure", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

The handler intentionally says little. Signature verification, replay protection, schema validation, and durable storage belong in ApplyReceipt; keeping those checks behind one boundary makes them testable without pretending that an HTTP 204 is delivery proof.

A practical decision rule

Choose the template owner that can answer three questions during an incident: which text was sent, who approved it, and which exact revision produced the link. Choose the adapter boundary that lets the platform change transport without changing the signup event. Choose an SLO that distinguishes queue delay, submission acceptance, delivery reporting, and verification completion.

The smallest useful test matrix includes a duplicate event, a worker crash after acceptance, an expired link, a malformed receipt, a template revision change while messages are queued, and a sustained downstream timeout. Run those cases against a fake adapter and a real staging callback path. A green unit test around the send call is not enough.

That is the point of the event notification design: the SMS API is one hop in a learner-facing workflow, while template ownership and evidence determine whether the platform can explain what happened.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5322, Internet Message Format: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322
  • MDN, HTTP semantics and status codes: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status
  • OpenTelemetry, Signals: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/

title: 50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test
description:
50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test

Pivot's October 28 post makes a claim that sounds like an excuse until you read the perf counters: on a naive hash GROUP BY over 99 million ClickBench rows, the CPU reported 100% busy while spending 50.1% of its slots stalled on memory and only 16.1% actually retiring instructions. Partition the keys into 4,096 radix buckets first, and the stall share falls to 23.5%, retiring rises to 32.2%, DRAM traffic drops from 4.5 GB to 1.5 GB. The database did more instructions (19.35 billion retired micro-ops vs 11.43 billion) and still finished faster: 3.6 seconds became 2.7 on the second run.

I believed the direction but not the round numbers, so I rebuilt the experiment at a scale my VM can hold: 20 million rows, about 3.4 million unique keys, one C program, same two algorithms.

// naive: one open-addressing hash table for all keys
size_t s = hash64(k) & MASK;
while (hk[s] && hk[s] != k) s = (s + 1) & MASK;
// radix: hash, take the top 12 bits, push into 1 of 4096 partitions,
// then aggregate each partition with its own small table
int p = (hash64(keys[i]) >> 52) & 4095;

First, the latency ladder, because it explains everything else. Pointer-chasing a randomly permuted array on this box (AMD EPYC 9D25, L1d 32 KB, L2 1 MB, L3 32 MB, from /sys):

     32 KB :   2.7 ns   (L1)
    256 KB :   7.1 ns
   1024 KB :  17.1 ns   (L2)
   8192 KB :  34.8 ns   (L3)
  32768 KB : 122.4 ns   (L3-sized, but shared/noisy on this VM)
 262144 KB : 222.9 ns   (DRAM)

Two honest caveats before the headline number. This is a cloud VM, not Pivot's bare-metal Genoa box, so my DRAM latency (223 ns) is far worse than their 50–100 ns, and the 32 MB step lands at 122 ns instead of the textbook 10–15 ns — a shared, noisy L3 does not behave like the datasheet. The shape of the cliff is still unmistakable: crossing from cache to DRAM costs roughly 80x the L1 latency here.

Then the GROUP BY itself, 20,000,000 rows, 3,390,516 distinct keys, both algorithms verified to the same count (sum of counts = 20,000,000 exactly):

naive hash : 0.958 s, groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix 4096 : 0.234 s (aggregate phase only), groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix end-to-end (count+fill+aggregate): 0.534 s, speedup vs naive: 1.79x

The aggregate phase alone runs 4.10x faster, but that number flatters radix: partitioning is real work, and the end-to-end figure is the one that counts. (An earlier run gave 0.975 s naive / 0.263 s aggregate-only, so treat the second decimal as noise, not signal.) Even with the fill included, radix wins by 1.79x, for exactly Pivot's reason — each partition's hash table is small enough to live in cache, so the random accesses that used to miss to DRAM mostly hit L2/L3 instead.

So the trade is real, and it generalizes beyond databases: when your working set is bigger than cache, you are not buying compute, you are buying memory round-trips. Doing more instructions to make those round-trips shorter is a good deal — 19.35 billion cheap operations beat 11.43 billion operations that each wait 223 ns. The next time a profile shows a hot CPU at 100%, check what fraction of it is actually retiring work before you reach for a faster machine. A faster machine with the same memory wall just stalls faster.

Sources: Pivot, "It's the memory latency, stupid" (Oct 28, 2026) — naive 3.9s/3.6s, 50.1% backend-bound, 16.1% retiring, 76,190,837 DRAM fills; radix 3.3s/2.7s, 23.5%, 32.2%, 25,688,280 fills; full engine 1.848s single-core, 171.8ms on 16 cores. My numbers: this VM, gcc -O2, single thread, code and raw output kept with the run notes.

title: Ghostbusters for coding agents: 12 GiB of ghosts on my Mac, and 15 GiB more I didn't know about
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I run coding agents all day. Claude Code in one terminal, Codex in another, sometimes three sessions on the same repo at once. They're the ghosts in my machine: they work where I can't see them, often while I'm asleep, and like any good ghost they leave slime behind.

One agent task looks like this. A fresh git worktree. Then npm install (a new node_modules), uv sync (a new .venv), cargo build (a few GB of target). The package caches grow, the IDE indexes the new folder, and the session itself leaves a transcript, checkpoints and a scratch folder. Run five tasks in parallel and you get five of everything. The task gets merged, the worktree gets forgotten, the slime stays.

And if you run open-weight models locally, the old weights in ~/.ollama or the Hugging Face cache are the biggest blobs of all.

So I pointed my own disk cleaner at it. Here's my own Mac, this week:

Agent On disk Still alive
Codex 5.5 GiB 8 open threads
Claude Code 3.5 GiB 5 live sessions, plus 63 old transcripts (1.7 GiB)
Cursor 2.8 GiB not running
opencode 72 MiB not running

About 12 GiB. Fine, I expected that. Then I looked in /private/tmp/claude-<uid>, where Claude Code keeps each session's scratchpad, task output and pasted images, and found another 15 GiB that my tool didn't see at all. A restart clears it, but my Mac had been up for 33 hours and the agents had been busy.

That's what DeepDriveCleaner™ (ddc) is for. It's a disk cleaner for developers (package caches, build output, old toolchains, simulator runtimes) and this week it learned to follow agents around. Inside every worktree an agent leaves, it finds the node_modules, .venv and target like anywhere else, and now it also knows each agent's own data. It follows three rules, and I'd trust it on my own machine only because of them:

  1. A ghost still at work is left alone. If the process that wrote a session is still running, ddc never offers its files.
  2. It reads metadata, never your conversations. File names, sizes, the process list. It doesn't open a transcript.
  3. It never deletes on its own. It shows a plan, checks every item again right before acting, and waits for you to say yes.

The other half is for the agents themselves. Every report has --json with a published schema, so an agent can ask "where did my disk go, and what's safe to remove?" and get a real answer instead of guessing with du -sh *. Version 0.14.0 (PR #58, merged as I write this) adds the per-session view (transcript, checkpoints, temporary folder, live or not) and a first agent skill, plus an AGENTS.md snippet, that teach an agent to ask ddc first and hand you the cleanup command, never run it.

It runs on macOS as a CLI and a menu bar app. Linux has a static CLI on main, and the Windows build already passes its tests natively.

Two open pieces carry all of this. The open-source Codex CLI (Apache-2.0) was one of the two agents that wrote the code, and it ran the benchmarks below. And ProjectStore, our MIT-licensed method, is what let two different agents share one backlog all week. There's no model inside the tool: it's built by agents and for them.

Demo

DeepDriveCleaner via CLI:

Recorded on a fake home folder full of fake agent data. I don't point a cleaner's demo at anyone's real files, mine included.

DeepDriveCleaner via Application

Try it on your Mac:

brew install --cask smartandpoint/tap/deepdrivecleaner

Or just the CLI:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SmartAndPoint/DeepDriveCleaner/main/packaging/install/install.sh | sh

After:

ddc disk agents

Or via Application -> DeepDriveCleaner and bar icon.

I'd love to know how many ghosts you find. Post what you found in the comments. If an agent keeps junk somewhere I don't know about yet, tell me and it becomes a rule. And if it saves you a few gigabytes, a ⭐ helps other people find it.

Code

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner

Find and safely clean developer disk junk on macOS: venvs, node_modules, build outputs, caches. Built in the open with ProjectStore.

DeepDriveCleaner™

Challenge entry: this project was submitted to the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4 at commit c606a8d (v0.14.0). Commits after 2026-10-31 were made after the submission.

Find and safely clean what development leaves on a Mac's disk: Python virtual environments, node_modules, build outputs, package and toolchain caches, Xcode data, local ML models and VM images. Everything it finds is grouped by risk. Nothing is removed until you have seen the plan and confirmed it.

It is a menu bar app with the command-line tool inside: the same engine, a window or a terminal, whichever you prefer.

Warning

DeepDriveCleaner deletes files. It checks every item before it touches it, but it can remove almost anything it is told to, by you or by an AI agent acting for you. You use it at your own risk: nobody who made it is responsible for what it removes. Read the…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

Honestly, the tool is the smaller half. The method is what let one person ship this in two weeks.

DeepDriveCleaner was built by me and two agent harnesses, Claude Code and the open-source Codex CLI, working inside ProjectStore. ProjectStore is our open-source (MIT) method for building software with agents: decisions, specs, epics and stories live as plain markdown in a vault next to the code, and every agent reads and writes them. Here's the loop:

In practice it works like this. Nothing gets coded until it's a story with acceptance criteria. If the "how" isn't obvious, it gets an ADR first. A critic agent tears each story apart in a fresh context before any code exists. A planner maps it onto the codebase. When the code is done, a reviewer agent checks the diff against every acceptance criterion and wants evidence, not vibes. Every change, code or vault, goes through a pull request with a test gate.

It sounds slow. It isn't. The 15 GiB surprise above went from "huh" to a reviewed story, a planned change and merged code in one evening. Here's what two weeks looked like:

October 17–31
Commits 249, of which 227 in the challenge week
Pull requests 58 in the code, 36 in the vault
Releases 16, of which 10 in the challenge week
Backlog 8 epics, 85 stories, 50 closed with evidence
Decisions 6 ADRs, 7 research notes, 5 runbooks

And what came out of it isn't a toy:

  • a Rust core (library plus CLI with JSON output), with one platform module per OS: 87 cleanup rules on macOS, 48 on Linux;
  • a native Swift menu bar app on top, with a review window, scheduled scans and auto-updates;
  • 600+ Rust tests and 440+ Swift tests in a gate nothing merges without, plus load runs and a check that fails the build if a scan stops scaling linearly;
  • a benchmark against 9 other disk-usage tools, which Codex ran (ddc 0.7.0, a synthetic 100,000-entry tree of developer projects, warm cache, 10 runs each). Median: ddc du 1.03 s, dust 0.89 s, pdu 1.04 s, dua 1.09 s, BSD du 1.21 s, all with the same totals. The ranges overlap, so it's not the fastest, and I won't claim it is. It's in the same league as the good du clones, and on top of that it knows what each folder is and whether it's safe to delete.

The whole vault is public. If you want to see how an agent-built project makes decisions, every story, ADR and critic review is there:

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner: research, ADRs, epics and stories behind the code.

DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

The project's memory: decisions, specs, epics and stories as plain markdown, kept by projectstore.

This is the ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner, a macOS tool that finds and safely cleans what development leaves on the disk. It is public on purpose, as a worked example of building software through ProjectStore. A research note came first, then two ADRs and an epic with stories. A fresh-context critic reviewed every artifact before code was written, a planner placed the work, and a reviewer checked each story's acceptance criteria against the code before the story was closed with evidence.

Where to start reading:

  1. Where a developer's disk space goes (macOS): the research note behind the project.
  2. Rust core: library + CLI with JSON output and Cleanup safety model: risk classes, plan and confirmation: the two decisions.
  3. DDC-001: Disk space cleaner CLI for developers: the epic and its stories, each…
View on GitHub

And ProjectStore itself, if you want to try the method on your own project:

SmartAndPoint / ProjectStore

Decisions, specs and stories as plain markdown, for every coding agent. Code changes. Context stays.

ProjectStore

ProjectStore is a method and a framework for building apps and services of any size with AI agents. It keeps the project's record — what was decided, what is in flight, what was checked — as reviewed markdown in git, readable by any agent and anyone with the repo.

A project workflow plugin for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (experimental). Both are released together at one version, and one command sets a project up for either or both: see Install.

Two months of agents, and nobody knows why

Agents write code fast. They re-decide settled questions even faster: every fresh session arrives empty, makes its own architectural call, and commits under its own assumptions. Two months later you have noodle code — every strand reviews fine on its own, and each was written under a different theory of the project. Ask "why is this a queue and not…

View on GitHub

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I won't run a cleaner I can't read, and I don't expect you to. The rules are code, the safety model is an ADR, and every change has its reasoning in the vault.

The open vault mattered as much as the open code. If the plan had lived in one assistant's memory, switching harnesses would have meant starting over. It's markdown in git, so Codex picked up where Claude Code left off, and you can read it too.

It works with the lights off, too. Scanning and cleaning need no network; the only thing that calls out is the app's update check. An agent running an open-weight model locally, through opencode for example, can ask ddc where the disk went without anything leaving the machine.

It also matters for agents. They learn tools from source, schemas and docs. A disk tool with open JSON contracts is one any agent can use correctly, including open-source agents like Codex CLI and opencode running open-weight models.

A note on licences, to be straight about it: the method that built this, ProjectStore, is MIT. DeepDriveCleaner itself is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial: free for personal and noncommercial use, and you can change it and share it; commercial use needs a licence from us.

My Agent Session

Rather than a raw transcript, here's the trail one session left: the vault PR where "my tool can't see 15 GiB" turned into stories, with two critic reviews folded in before a line of code. The code that came out of it is PR #58.

The Spirit of It

Slime is what a machine keeps after the work is gone, and agents leave more of it than any of us ever did: they never close a tab, never delete a worktree, never forget a session. I'm not hunting the ghosts. I like my ghosts. I just want to clean up after them, without an exorcist that burns the house down. So: a ghostbuster with a trap and a checklist. It names every puddle, tells you which ghost is still at work, and lets you decide.

It's Día de los Muertos this weekend, which feels about right: before anything goes, every session gets listed by name and date. Then you let it go.

title: I built a globe where every country is a separate piece you can pull out 🌍
description:
Hey everyone 👋

Most web globes are a texture wrapped around a sphere. You can spin them, and that's about it.

I wanted one where every country is a real object: its own plate, set into the ocean ball like a puzzle piece. So I built it.

mahmad.me / blocks/interactive/world-globe

It's all SVG and a bit of math, with no WebGL and no canvas.

What you can do 🎮

  • Drag to turn the globe any way
  • Click a country to pull it out of its socket
  • Break the whole map apart with one button, then let it settle back

Pull out a big country like Canada, the US or Pakistan and it splits into its states or provinces, each one a plate with its name on it.

How it works 🛠️

  1. The ball is a projection. Natural Earth's outlines go through a d3-geo orthographic projection. When you drag, nothing moves: the globe rotates and every country is projected again.
  2. Each country is its own plate. It has a top, walls, a socket it leaves behind and a shadow, so it can lift out on its own spring while the others stay put.
  3. SVG has no depth buffer. So every frame the plates are sorted by how much they face you, and drawn back to front.
  4. Provinces load on demand. The split data is one small file per country, fetched only the first time you pull that country out.

Try it 🌐

👉 mahmad.me/blocks/interactive/world-globe

Break the map apart, then try to put it back together by hand

Country outlines and borders are from Natural Earth, which is public domain.

title: a sever bench-mark
description:
Hello

today I ran a sever benchmark for axum rust, express node.js, fastapi python.

I was curious to know the results.

what I did was create a simple express server for posting a user info.
the schema included a really good user attributes. it was stored in a mongodb collection.

I used a get method of username with password to fetch the entire user info, also my code included a bcrypt hashing too.

after making this. I recreated the same project in rust and fastapi.

I am sharing the overall results below

this image shows the results.

it is clear rust is much faster than any of its competitions.
this made me sad because the only backend i know well is going to get obsolete in a few years or even months.

if need to survive i must do something fast or I will be done for good.
but the underlying rust code was not at all developer friendly. I got a headache just by reading it.

one day may be I will learn it I think?

I am considering fastapi a good choice because it is faster than express simpler than rust and express, easy to use.

the reason to use express still is

  1. easy to setup
  2. simple boilerplate code
  3. nice routing setup
  4. great learning curve
  5. huge package libraries
  6. maintaining legacy projects
