title: Context is the new interface
description:
The future of design lies in what happens between products

Imagine you receive a message from a friend recommending a restaurant. You want to check where it is, see whether you are free that evening, and reply with a time that works for both of you. You search through your messages, open the link, check the location, switch to your calendar, return to the conversation, and finally write your reply.

Each step is simple on its own, but together, they create a fragmented experience. You have to carry the context from one product to another, remembering what you were doing and what you need to do next. This is a familiar interaction. We have designed products around individual tasks for years, leaving people to connect those tasks themselves. But when AI can interpret an intention and help carry it across products, the experience starts to change.

The question becomes how we design what happens between interfaces.

From applications to context

The app became the dominant model for digital experiences because it gave software a clear structure. Each product has its own interface, features, and way of managing information. People move between them to complete a task.

The problem is that people’s intentions rarely follow these boundaries. Planning a trip involves conversations, calendars, maps, bookings, and payments. Organizing a meeting requires information about people, availability, locations, and commitments that may live in several different systems.

Each product can work perfectly well on its own while the overall experience remains fragmented. AI makes it possible to approach these activities from another direction. Instead of asking people to identify the right application and navigate its features, an assistant can start with their intention and determine which information and capabilities are relevant.

Apple’s work on Siri and Apple Intelligence illustrates this direction. Through its App Intents framework, Apple allows developers to describe actions and content that can be made available to supported system experiences. This gives Siri and other supported features a structured way to discover what an application can do.

Imagine asking Siri to find a restaurant a friend recommended in an earlier conversation, check your availability for Friday, and help prepare a reservation. Depending on the available integrations and permissions, the assistant could connect information that would otherwise require several manual searches. The applications remain responsible for their data and functionality, but their capabilities can be accessed through an experience that begins somewhere else.

This changes the design problem, because the challenge is no longer limited to helping someone navigate an application. It also involves making the right information and capabilities available in the right context, at the moment they become useful.

For a practical explanation of how this works, Apple’s developer documentation on Apple Intelligence, Siri, and App Intents describes how app entities, schemas, and onscreen context help the system interpret and use app capabilities.

Context is a design material

Context has always been part of UX. It helps a system understand what a person is trying to do, what information is relevant, and what should happen next. It can include the current conversation, a person’s preferences, previous decisions, or the state of an ongoing task. It can also include constraints, such as whether a calendar is available or whether an action requires permission.

When someone asks for a restaurant recommendation, the request alone may not be enough. The assistant may need to understand the occasion, the people involved, the location, the available time, and any preferences that matter. Some of this information may already be available. Other details may need to be requested.

Designing for context means deciding which information matters at each stage and how it should influence the experience. It also means deciding what should be remembered, what should be shared between products, and what should remain private.

Memory becomes particularly important when a task spans time or products. An assistant might remember that a friend recommended a particular restaurant, that Friday was the preferred evening, or that the user usually avoids noisy places. But remembering information is not the same as knowing whether it is still relevant. The system should be able to surface the context it intends to use, especially when that context influences a decision. Showing someone that a restaurant was recommended by a friend six months ago gives them an opportunity to confirm or correct the information before the assistant acts on it. Memory should help maintain continuity without turning past behaviour into an unquestioned assumption.

Unfortunately, context is rarely complete. A person may say, “Find somewhere nearby for dinner,” without specifying a budget, cuisine, or exact time. The system has to decide whether it has enough information to proceed or whether it should ask a question.

This has implications for how products structure their information. In Apple’s App Intents framework, developers define entities, parameters, and actions so that supported system experiences can understand what an application contains and how its capabilities can be used. These definitions influence whether a system can identify the correct item, interpret a request, and perform an action reliably.

These decisions shape the interaction as much as the interface does. They determine whether the experience feels relevant, whether the user understands what is happening, and whether the system can act without making assumptions that matter.

Context therefore becomes a design material in its own right. It is part of the structure that makes an experience coherent, and it needs to be structured, interpreted, and actively designed rather than simply collected.

UX governance defines the boundaries

When an assistant connects information and actions across products, someone needs to determine how that information can be used and what the system is allowed to do with it.

Consider an assistant arranging a meeting. It finds an available time, retrieves the participants’ contact details, and prepares an invitation. Should it send the invitation automatically, or ask for confirmation? Which calendar should it treat as authoritative? What happens if availability changes before the invitation is sent?

These are questions of UX governance: the shared principles and rules that determine how an experience behaves across products and contexts. Governance establishes who can access information, which actions can be delegated, when approval is required, and how mistakes can be identified and corrected. Without these shared rules, an experience that crosses several products can become inconsistent, even if each application behaves as intended.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a useful foundation for thinking about these responsibilities. Its four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, provide a way to identify risks, establish accountability, evaluate system behaviour, and manage issues over time.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is another relevant development. It provides a standard way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data sources. This creates opportunities for systems to work together, while making questions about access, permissions, and responsibility important parts of the design.

For designers, these questions are part of the experience itself. If an assistant can take action across products, the boundaries of that action need to be understandable. People should know what the system can access, which tools it intends to use, and when their approval is required.

This also means making tool use visible. When an assistant searches a calendar, retrieves information from a message, or sends a request to another service, people should have a way to understand what happened and why. The aim is not to expose every technical operation, but to provide enough information for people to follow the process and remain confident in the result.

Governance cannot sit with one design team alone. It requires collaboration between design, product, engineering, security, legal, and the teams responsible for the systems involved. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework Playbook can help translate these responsibilities into practical activities throughout the development process.

Designing for uncertainty

Even well governed systems can misunderstand context. An assistant might find a restaurant recommendation from six months ago and interpret it as a current preference. It might identify a date in a message but misunderstand which event it refers to. The information is available, but its meaning depends on circumstances the system may not fully understand.

This also affects how information is presented. People need enough visibility to understand what the assistant has inferred, which details it is using, and what it plans to do. They should be able to correct an assumption without having to restart the entire task.

A useful design must account for this uncertainty instead of treating every inference as fact. One practical approach is to distinguish between information explicitly provided by the user and information inferred from context. Another is to consider the consequences of an incorrect decision when determining how much confirmation is necessary.

A restaurant suggestion can be presented as an option, with a brief explanation of why it was selected. A booking should make the date, time, and party size clear before confirmation if those details have not already been authorized. A conflicting calendar entry may require a question rather than an automatic choice.

The same principle applies to how an assistant communicates its plan. Before carrying out a task that involves several steps, it can explain what it intends to do, which information it needs, and where the user may need to make a decision. For a simple request, this might require only a short explanation. For a more consequential task, it may mean presenting a sequence of actions and waiting for approval before proceeding.

Planning and visibility become especially important when the task continues across products. If an assistant is finding a restaurant, checking availability, and preparing a reservation, the user should be able to see what has been completed, what is still in progress, and what remains to be decided. Without this visibility, even a successful process can feel unpredictable.

For designers, the practical questions are straightforward. What does the system know, and where did that information come from? What assumptions is it making? What does it plan to do next? How costly would a mistake be? Can the user understand and correct the result?

These questions help teams design for the full journey, including moments when the system cannot confidently proceed, rather than treating uncertainty as an edge case. They also make the experience easier to understand and recover from when something goes wrong.

The product team no longer owns the entire experience

When a task moves across several products, no single interface necessarily contains the full experience. A user may begin in a conversation, use information from a calendar, rely on a recommendation service, and complete an action through another product.

Each product still has a role. Its value also depends on how well it participates in the wider journey. This changes the questions product teams need to ask. They need to understand which information their product makes available, which actions other systems can request, and how those actions fit into a task that may begin somewhere else.

This creates a different relationship between products and their users, because a product can contribute to a successful outcome without the person visiting its interface at all.

For product teams, that means app sessions and screen time are incomplete measures of value. A service might help someone complete a reservation through an assistant, even if the user never opens its home screen. This does not make interface design less important. It changes the scope of the work around it.

It also means that teams need to consider how their products communicate progress and responsibility to systems outside their own interfaces. If an action is started by one product and completed by another, the transition should not leave the user wondering what happened or who is responsible for the outcome.

The experience needs to remain coherent even when its parts belong to different teams. This requires shared expectations about what each product can do, how its actions are reported, and what happens when the next step cannot be completed.

What designers should work on next

Designers can begin by mapping the context a task requires. This includes the information a system needs, where that information comes from, how it changes over time, and which products are involved. They also need to define how the system should behave when context is missing, incomplete, or ambiguous.

Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction provide a useful foundation for this work. Building on these principles, we can identify a set of recurring patterns for designing agentic experiences and workflows, regardless of their specific domain.

Planning and visibility

Teams need to decide when an assistant should explain its intended steps, when it should show progress, and how people can understand the status of a task that spans several products. The level of detail should depend on the complexity and consequences of the task. People need enough visibility to understand what the system plans to do, what it has completed, and what still requires their attention.

Memory surfacing

Designers should consider how the system uses past conversations, preferences, and decisions to inform the current experience. People need ways to understand which information is influencing a recommendation or action, and to correct it when it is outdated or no longer relevant. The aim is to provide continuity without turning past behaviour into an unquestioned assumption.

Tool use disclosure

When an assistant uses external tools or accesses information across products, people should be able to understand what it has accessed and which actions it has taken. Teams need to distinguish between a suggestion, an attempted action, and a completed outcome. This makes the system’s behaviour easier to understand and helps people know when they need to intervene.

Multi step workflow tracking

A task that spans several products should feel like a continuous journey rather than a series of disconnected operations. Designers can map its stages, the information passed between them, and the decisions that require user involvement. People should be able to see what has been completed, what is in progress, and what remains to be done without having to reconstruct the process themselves.

Recovery routing

Not every task will go as planned. An assistant may encounter missing information, a failed action, or a decision it cannot confidently make. Designers need to define how the system responds in these situations, whether by asking a question, returning to an earlier step, suggesting an alternative, or handing control back to the user. Recovery should preserve the context already established and help people continue without having to start again.

Autonomy

Teams also need to decide how much autonomy to give the system. Autonomy is not a choice between a fully manual experience and an assistant that does everything independently. It is a spectrum.

An assistant might suggest a restaurant without taking any action, prepare a reservation for review, or complete a booking once it has the necessary permission. The appropriate level depends on the task, the user’s preferences, the reliability of the available information, and the consequences of a mistake.

Designing for autonomy means making the transition from recommendation to preparation and action understandable. People should be able to delegate routine steps while retaining control over decisions that matter to them. They should also be able to change their minds, interrupt a process, or take over when the system reaches its limits.

Testing

Testing should follow the task across products. Instead of evaluating each interface separately, teams can examine the full journey from the initial request to the final outcome. They can test what happens when information is unavailable, the system makes the wrong assumption, an action fails, or a user changes their mind. This helps reveal gaps between products that may not be visible when each interface is tested in isolation.

Collaboration

Designing these experiences requires collaboration across product boundaries. Designers need to work with engineers and other teams to understand system capabilities, data access, permissions, and limitations, then translate these constraints into experiences people can understand and trust.

The aim is to make the connections between products feel coherent while keeping the underlying actions visible, understandable, and under the user’s control.

Beyond the interface

The restaurant example began with a simple recommendation. Completing the task required information, decisions, and actions that lived across several products. As AI systems become able to work with more of these connections, the experience will depend on how well context is carried from one step to another.

The design challenge is to make that process useful, understandable, and respectful of the boundaries between systems. People need to know what the assistant remembers, how it plans to proceed, which tools it uses, and what happens when a task cannot be completed as expected. They also need control over how much they delegate and the ability to step in when necessary.

Interfaces remain where people see, guide, and correct what is happening. But more of the experience is shaped by the context that surrounds them, the decisions a system makes, and the rules that determine what it can do.

Designing for this future means looking beyond individual screens and considering the relationships between products. It means treating context, memory, planning, permissions, recovery, and governance as part of the experience from the beginning.

The future of design lies in what happens between products.

References

  1. Apple Developer Documentation. Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Technical guidance on exposing app content and actions, transferable entities, schemas, and onscreen context to Siri and Apple Intelligence.
  2. Apple Developer Documentation. Getting started with the App Intents framework. An introduction to making app actions and content available outside the app through system experiences.
  3. Apple Developer Documentation. Providing contextual cues to Apple Intelligence and Siri. Guidance on associating app entities with onscreen content so that Siri can interpret contextual references.
  4. Techstrong AI article on the MCP AI governance gap. The article highlights issues enterprises need to address as they connect AI systems with tools and organisational data.
  5. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0). A voluntary framework for managing AI risks and supporting trustworthy AI systems.
  6. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). NIST AI RMF Playbook. Practical suggestions aligned with the framework’s Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions.
  7. Amershi, S. et al. (2019). Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.
  8. Microsoft Research and Microsoft’s UX design for agents .

From AI × Taste

A monthly series exploring the economics of taste in the age of AI:

  • AI made everyone a creator, not a designer
    How AI made generation abundant, making design judgment and taste the new competitive advantage.
  • The organizational costs of low taste
    How weak design judgment compounds across products, teams and organizations.
  • Taste cannot be delegated
    Why AI can generate endless possibilities, but deciding what should exist remains fundamentally human.
  • Designing for the Proxy
    Why AI is changing who reads first, and what happens when we optimize for the intermediary instead of the person.
  • When the canvas starts acting, who’s really in control?
    How intelligent interfaces are changing what designers control, from interactions to agency, orchestration and attention.
  • The economics of attention in the age of AI. When machines pay attention, what deserves ours?
  • Context is the new interface. The future of design lies in what happens between products

Context is the new interface was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: When the Model Says Nothing: Failure Handling and Guardrails for an LLM in a WhatsApp ERP
description:
SokoFlow AI Build Log, Week 4 of 6: what "no tool call" really means, a daily cap with no cron job, and a black box for every question

A shopkeeper asks: "What were my sales yesterday?"

It's a perfectly clear question. The model answered with nothing: no tool call, no error, no explanation.

And the same silence can also mean "hi, how are you?", "what's the weather tomorrow?", and "how did my sales do?" Same output, completely different right responses. That's what Week 4 was about: what SokoFlow does when it can't safely give the user what they asked for.

TL;DR

  • A request that wasn't executed isn't necessarily a failed request, and a request that executed doesn't necessarily have data. Collapsing everything into one ERROR throws away the information you need to decide what to do.
  • Zero tool calls is a legitimate outcome, not an error, and the model's own explanatory text isn't trusted to classify it. The Orchestrator produces a structured outcome, and the app decides the response.
  • Retries are reserved for failures where a second model attempt has a credible chance of fixing things: an unknown tool, more than one tool call, or structurally invalid arguments.
  • The per-shop daily cap is a Redis counter whose key changes every day (shop:123:analytics_count:2026-10-31), so there's nothing to reset and no cron job.
  • For cost control I chose a query cap plus a per-call token ceiling over a full "reserve and reconcile" budget system. Cost enforcement stays a future design.
  • Every analytics question now produces one InteractionLogger record. A 25-phrasing script confirmed the defensive layer handled all of them safely.

Where we are

SokoFlow is a headless WhatsApp ERP for Kenyan SMEs. I've been building it for about five months. There's no app and no UI to learn; for a shopkeeper, the conversation is the interface. Phase 3 adds one AI feature: natural-language shop analytics. A shopkeeper asks "which products are running low?" or "how does this week compare to last week?", and an LLM, using function calling against SokoFlow's existing services, figures out which query to run.

Last week I integrated analytics into the WhatsApp conversation flow. A message the intent resolver can't classify can now be routed to analytics through a routing policy (covered in last week's post). I also used the existing session to support follow-ups like "And yesterday?", by storing the last analytics call and its arguments and building a new call from that context.

So over three weeks SokoFlow learned to interpret questions, execute tools and keep context across follow-ups. This week was driven by one question:

What happens when the system cannot safely give the user what they asked for?

Failure handling is what separates a convincing demo from a dependable backend.

Failure is not one outcome

Picture a request moving through the architecture:

The trap I first fell into: a request that wasn't executed isn't necessarily a failed request, and a request that executed successfully doesn't necessarily have data to return.

Collapsing those cases into one generic ERROR risks losing the information needed to make the right decision. But I also didn't want a special class for every imaginable failure, which would be too much abstraction. The goal was the smallest contract that preserves the distinctions that actually change system behaviour.

What does "zero tool calls" mean?

I started at the provider boundary, the LLMClient, with a thought experiment. Consider these messages:

User message Model response
"Hi, how are you?" No tool call
"What's the weather tomorrow?" No tool call
"How did my sales do?" No tool call
"What were my sales yesterday?" No tool call, despite the request being clear

All four produce the same observation: zero tool calls. But they potentially need different responses. That led to a decision from an earlier week: a model response with zero tool calls is a legitimate non-execution outcome, not automatically an error.

A second principle came out of it: the absence of a tool call tells us what the model proposed, not why it proposed it.

Who determines the reason for non-execution?

Among the fields the model returns is an optional reply text. When there's no tool call, that text can say something like "I'm not sure which sales period you mean. Could you clarify?"

Should that text decide the fallback behaviour, or should the application interpret a structured outcome? The decision was simple: model-generated prose isn't authoritative for classifying failures or choosing fallbacks. The Orchestrator detects a zero-tool-call response and produces a structured outcome.

Where does the meaning come from?

This edge case almost caused feature creep. When the model returns no tool calls, the application can't safely conclude the request is unsupported, because it might be a legitimate analytics question. It also can't safely conclude that clarification is needed. That left two choices:

  1. Treat zero tool calls as a neutral outcome. The application returns a generic, recoverable response.
  2. Add a constrained model decision alongside tool calling. The model picks from a small set of outcomes (execute_tool, clarification_needed, unresolved, and so on), and the application validates and maps it to behaviour.

I leaned toward option 2 first. It gives a better user experience. The catch: it adds another contract to validate and another source of model errors, and it was tempting to go down that rabbit hole. It was premature optimization. For reliable, read-only analytics for Kenyan SMEs, option 1 was the better call.

Retries: only where a second attempt can help

Back in Week 1 I designed a bounded retry that the Orchestrator controls. Retries are useful, since a request can recover from a transient model hiccup. But they cost latency and money, and the second response might behave differently with no guarantee of being better.

So I designed the contract around one rule: retries are reserved for failures where a new model proposal has a credible chance of fixing the problem.

Repairable model proposals (the Orchestrator allows one additional attempt, with repair feedback where appropriate):

  • Unknown tool name.
  • More than one proposed tool call.
  • Structurally invalid arguments.

No automatic LLM retry:

  • Zero tool calls.
  • A provider response that can't be normalized.
  • A provider transport failure (For the MVP and keep things simple).
  • A backend domain or business rejection.
  • A database or infrastructure failure.

Those outcomes don't justify automatically asking the model to reinterpret the same request.

The ambiguity fallback: who owns "ambiguous"?

SokoFlow has a special disambiguation branch, where the conversation parks in a waiting state while a clarification message goes back to the user. I had to decide how failures interact with it.

Last week I locked in that a pending analytics call exists for tool calls suspended while awaiting product disambiguation. The question this week: is that an ordinary analytics failure that returns a fallback, or does it hand control to the existing FSM disambiguation flow?

What I got wrong first: I had the Orchestrator notice the "ambiguous product" error in the execution result. That hid an assumption about who owns the meaning of product ambiguity.

What I settled on:

  • The Orchestrator recognizes and propagates the structured outcome.
  • The backend owns the meaning of product ambiguity.

So the Orchestrator isn't independently deciding whether a product name is ambiguous. The backend's product lookup returns a domain outcome with multiple candidates, the Orchestrator preserves it, and the analytics handler connects it to the existing disambiguation flow.

Context expiry

Last week's follow-up memory has a catch. A user asks an analytics question, SokoFlow executes it and stores the tool name, validated arguments and timestamp in last_analytics_call. Then, much later, the user sends: "And yesterday?"

That's where the 600-second TTL from last week matters. The application checks last_analytics_call freshness. If it has expired, no prior context goes to the LLM, so the model reads "And yesterday?" as a fresh request. If it proposes no tool call, the Orchestrator returns the structured non-execution outcome and the analytics handler returns a recovery message.

No stale arguments get reused, and the backend never receives a fabricated interpretation.

The edge case I chose to accept

While the fallbacks were taking shape, one edge case nearly pulled me into building a semantic interpretation system. A follow-up arrives after a sales query:

"What about the other one?"

The context is fresh, so the follow-up is allowed. But "the other one" doesn't clearly identify what should change, and the model proposes a tool call anyway. Should SokoFlow execute it if the arguments pass schema validation, or add another safeguard against semantically unsupported interpretations?

I chose to execute. The goal wasn't to eliminate every interpretation error in application code. A responsible system defines which risks it accepts and which it refuses. And semantic interpretation is exactly what the LLM is good at. Trying to rebuild every conversational reference in deterministic code would turn SokoFlow into a second, inferior language interpreter. I accepted that risk for this MVP.

What the user sees

The user shouldn't know everything that happens inside the system. Take the database being unavailable. Internally, we absolutely want to know: execution failed due to infrastructure. But telling the shopkeeper isn't helpful to them, and it leaks details that are a security risk. So the user gets a generic temporary-failure message.

Resource guardrails

The risk: LLM calls cost money per token. If a merchant, a bug or an abusive user gets into an endless chat loop, the API bill could spike.

The requirement: a per-shop daily query cap. My budget is realistically close to zero, since I chose a free provider in Week 1. But SokoFlow can change providers without touching the rest of the app, so this deserved real planning.

What counts toward the cap

Two options:

  1. Every incoming message that participates in analytics consumes one unit.
  2. Only messages that start a new analytics operation (an LLM tool call) consume a unit.

I chose option 1, for two reasons:

  • Cost alignment and protection. Every message sent to analytics incurs real token cost. Option 2 also has a loophole: if follow-ups are free, one counted trigger could carry an unbounded multi-turn conversation.
  • Simplicity. Option 1 is a plain deterministic counter in Redis. It also avoids defining when an operation "starts" versus when something is a "follow-up", which would have meant session expiry timers or FSM state checks just for rate limiting.

Making the counter safe

I avoided the classic read-modify-write approach, which is vulnerable to race conditions because the modify happens in Python memory, between the read and the write. Instead I used Redis's atomic INCR. Redis runs each command to completion before starting the next, so two concurrent requests can't interleave inside an INCR. The order matters: increment first, then check the value that came back.

Windowing: a fixed, calendar-aligned day

Next I had to choose between a fixed and a sliding window. I went with a calendar-aligned fixed window with a daily reset. A sliding window is more robust against bursts at the edge of a window, but our bounded analytics workload doesn't justify a more elaborate algorithm yet.

Why calendar-aligned? Because of a trick that spared me a cron job.

Managing time: the key that never resets

My first idea was a static key like shop:123:analytics_count. But how does it reset at the end of the day? A static key needs something running at midnight to delete it, like a cron job, and I didn't want that complexity.

The fix was to stop thinking about resetting. The key doesn't reset; the code changes which key it looks at every day. On October 31st the code generates:

shop:123:analytics_count:2026-10-31

Redis finds it, increments it, and tracks today's usage. When a merchant messages on November 1st, the date has changed, so the code generates a new key name:

shop:123:analytics_count:2026-11-01

When Redis receives INCR for a key that doesn't exist, it creates it and starts at 1.
One subtle decision. The shop's timezone still defines "today". So the date is in local timezone.

The garbage collector: a 48-hour TTL

A new key every day raises an infrastructure question: what happens to yesterday's keys? Left alone, abandoned daily records pile up and fill Redis memory indefinitely. When a key is first created, setting a 48-hour TTL acts as an automatic garbage collector. A TTL is relative to the moment of creation—so a 24-hour TTL set at 8:00 AM outlives its active calendar day and expires at 8:00 AM the next morning. However, relying on a tight 24-hour window leaves zero safety margin for clock skew across application servers, Redis, and regional timezones, while also expiring data before you can audit yesterday's metrics during the next work day.

Extending the window to 48 hours ensures yesterday's final counter remains intact for full next-day reporting, logging checks, and debugging before it automatically purges itself from RAM. To ensure a deployment restart or process crash between key creation and TTL assignment doesn't leave an orphaned key with an indefinite lifespan, the initialization check must set or verify the expiration during execution

The cap value

The number wasn't the hard part. The real question was a single limit shared by every shop, or one configurable per shop. I made it configurable from day one, with a default for the MVP baseline. The default value chosen was 100.

That broke my habit of avoiding extra design complexity, because this one costs almost nothing: fetching the value from the shop profile is cheap, and the Redis logic (current_count > limit) behaves identically. The real advantage is flexibility. If SokoFlow later has tiers, a hardcoded global cap would force a painful refactor of both the Redis middleware and the schema.

Cost control

Suppose a shop has a daily AI budget of $0.05. Before a provider call, SokoFlow estimates the next call at $0.0001, and the shop has already accumulated $0.0499. Three options:

  1. Allow the call if the estimate fits the remaining budget, and record actual usage afterwards.
  2. Reserve the estimated cost before calling the provider, block concurrent requests from spending the same remaining budget, and reconcile against actual usage afterwards.
  3. Rely on the per-shop daily query cap as a tight proxy for cost, combined with a hard token ceiling per individual call.

Option 1 eliminated itself. It fails under concurrency: if two messages hit the LLMClient at the same millisecond, both read the same remaining balance and both proceed, so the shop overspends before either records its usage.

Option 2 is the right design, with a caveat. It's a two-phase check, like how payment gateways handle authorizations:

  • Reserve: atomically check the remaining budget covers the estimate, and set that amount aside before calling the LLM API.
  • Execute: make the provider call, knowing the budget already accounts for it.
  • Reconcile: when the provider returns real token usage, adjust the ledger (refund the difference or deduct slightly more).

It needs more Redis or database transaction logic, so I kept it as a future design.

Why option 3 works at this stage:

  • Bounding the number of queries and the tokens any single call can use caps our worst-case spend without needing complex, real-time fractional-cent tracking. Rather than implementing a real-time financial escrow ledger, SokoFlow relies on a per-shop daily query cap combined with a hard token ceiling per individual LLM invocation.

Because our architecture permits a single self-repair attempt when an initial model proposal fails schema validation, one logical user message can trigger up to two physical provider calls. With our production provider Groq running gpt-oss-20b and a configured max_tokens ceiling of 256, the absolute maximum token exposure per logical interaction is roughly cap × 2 × 256 tokens. For reasoning models like gpt-oss-20b, this max_tokens ceiling restricts both the internal chain-of-thought and the final tool-call payload. While setting this limit too low could theoretically truncate a model mid-reasoning before it outputs a valid tool call, a ceiling of 256 tokens provides ample runway for structured function calling while serving as a hard safety brake against runaway token consumption.

  • Predictable cost per query. The tool surface is strict, bounded, read-only queries, not open-ended generation, so token use per query is stable.

The Interaction Logger

The last component this week is a dedicated logging component, SokoFlow's black box. Every time a merchant sends an analytics query, it captures and persists a snapshot of that transaction. Currently persisted in a JSON file store, with plans to create an actual database table schema for it.The record is written once at the end of the request.

It helps with post-mortem debugging when the LLM misbehaves, and it gives me historical telemetry on latency and cost.

How it feeds Week 5

Next week's job is an eval set that measures cost per query, among other metrics. A well-designed logger makes that easier: the raw messages and edge cases it captures can become the test cases for tuning the eval harness.

The unit of logging

What exactly counts as one log record? Three options:

  • Option A: one event per logical interaction.
  • Option B: one event per meaningful attempt, plus a final interaction event.
  • Option C: a middle ground. One final interaction record, plus separate provider-attempt records only when needed for usage and failure visibility.

I chose Option A:

  • It lines up with the eval harness: one clean record per user question lets me map the eval set directly against usage logs.
  • It's simpler to store and query: one JSON document or row per WhatsApp interaction, with no relational joins or log-aggregation pipeline.

Option B would split one conversation turn into three or four rows, exploding log volume with verbose telemetry. Option C was appealing in theory, but conditional logging means branching and state inside the logging middleware, which makes error paths harder to test and maintain.

The logging contract

What I got wrong first: I included both correlation_id and interaction_id. That was redundant. A correlation ID is for distributed, async, multi-service systems where one user action spawns background jobs or crosses service boundaries, and SokoFlow isn't that here.

The final blueprint:

Identity:     interaction_id, timestamp
Context:      shop_ref, raw_query
Outcome:      outcome, failure_category
Execution:    tool_name, selected_arguments, provider, model,
              attempt_count, repair_count
Performance:  total_latency_ms
Usage:        input_tokens, output_tokens, estimated_cost, usage_status

Hitting the KPI

To check this week's target, I wrote a custom test script that loops through 25 edge-case phrasings, generated by an LLM to represent different ways of triggering a failure inside the system.

It feeds each query to the system, captures the InteractionLogger output, and programmatically checks whether the result was handled safely, meaning it triggered the fallback text or was blocked by a guardrail. It then computes: total safe responses ÷ total queries.

The goal wasn't to test the LLM's routing accuracy. It was to test the defensive code layer. The script hit a 100% success rate.

A fair reading of that number: it shows the defensive layer handles the failure modes I thought of, using phrasings generated by one model. It doesn't say anything about failure modes I didn't think of. Week 5's eval set is where messier, real-shaped input comes in.

What I'd do differently

Looking back, the same instinct showed up in almost every decision: I reached for the elaborate version first. A constrained model-decision contract for zero tool calls. A reserve-and-reconcile ledger for cost. A correlation_id for a system that doesn't need one. Each time, the simpler option won once I wrote down what the system actually needed. Next time I would start from "what behaviour does this change?" before I design anything.

What's next

SokoFlow is taking shape. Failures are diagnosable and the system is more observable. Week 5 is the eval set: 25–40 queries with expected tool and arguments, measured properly for the first time.

title: Integrating 6 psychology frameworks in supernemawashi — 1 framework = 1 file parallel agents
description:
Introduction

supernemawashi's nemawashi-analyze skill stopped holding the profile as a single monolithic file and moved to 1 framework = 1 file × 1 parallel agent. Six psychology frameworks (defense mechanisms / Thomas-Kilmann / Transactional Analysis / Core Motivators / Cognitive Biases / Attachment Style) are each analyzed independently by an agent running in parallel. Here's why, and how I implemented it.

The first supernemawashi (v1.x) wrote the profile to a single markdown file (profile.md). The psychological analysis was one section inside it. That causes problems:

  • "I want to add one new framework" means rewriting the structure inside the monolithic file
  • Every re-run of analyze wipes and overwrites all the other frameworks' analyses too
  • The independent signals (facts) per framework get mixed, and you lose track of which judgment came from which evidence
  • Even if you want to parallelize, you get write contention on the one file

1 framework = 1 file × 1 agent

Decompose the profile per framework.

PROFILE_DIR/<person-name>/
├── profile.md                          ← slim index (Core Pattern + summary table only)
├── facts.jsonl                          ← facts (collect's output)
└── frameworks/
    ├── defense-mechanisms.md            ← per-framework classification + evidence + DO/DON'T
    ├── thomas-kilmann-tki.md
    ├── transactional-analysis-ta.md
    ├── core-motivators.md
    ├── cognitive-biases.md
    └── attachment-style.md

Each framework file is fully independent. Updating one doesn't touch the other five.

Make the framework registry the single source of truth

The frameworks' slug / display name / tier have one table as the source of truth:

Slug Display name Tier
defense-mechanisms Defense Mechanisms 1
thomas-kilmann-tki Conflict Mode (TKI) 1
transactional-analysis-ta Ego States (TA) 1
core-motivators Core Motivators 1
cognitive-biases Cognitive Biases 1
attachment-style Attachment Style 2

Tier 1 = analyzed by default; Tier 2 = analyzed only when signal density is sufficient (if thin, surfaced explicitly as a Data Gap). Steps to add a new framework:

  1. Add a row to the registry table
  2. Create frameworks/<slug>.md following the contract
  3. Update the situation→framework priority mapping in nemawashi-reply (if needed)
  4. Confirm the registry matches the actual files with scripts/check-frameworks.sh

Because a script detects drift between the registry and the real files, you can't break things by adding only one side.

Parallel agent dispatch

nemawashi-analyze's flow:

[1] Read the shared inputs (profile.md + facts.jsonl)
        ↓
[2] Dispatch one agent per framework in the registry, in parallel
    ┌─ agent: defense-mechanisms     ──┐
    ├─ agent: thomas-kilmann-tki     ──┤
    ├─ agent: transactional-analysis ──┤  run in parallel
    ├─ agent: core-motivators        ──┤
    ├─ agent: cognitive-biases       ──┤
    └─ agent: attachment-style       ──┘
        ↓ wait for all agents to finish
[3] Synthesis pass (synchronous)
    - Update profile.md's Framework Summary table
    - Re-derive the Core Pattern

Each agent only reads facts.jsonl and writes its own framework's frameworks/<slug>.md. It shares no state with the other agents. The synthesis pass only aggregates results — it doesn't re-analyze.

What goes in a framework file

Each frameworks/<slug>.md follows the same contract:

---
framework: Defense Mechanisms
tier: 1
output_label: Defense Mechanisms
---

# Defense Mechanisms

## Purpose
(what this framework reveals)

## Classification Guidance
(how to extract signals from facts)

## Reference Table
(mechanism / definition / observable signals / DO / DON'T)

## Rule Generation
(classification → situation-indexed rules)

## Signal Tags
(the tag format embedded in the facts jsonl)

As an example, two rows from the defense-mechanisms file's reference table:

Mechanism Observable Signals DO DON'T
Rationalization long explanations on failure / "because..." chains validate the reason, then redirect to the future argue directly against the justification
Passive Aggression "I'll do it" + no movement / strategic delay name the behavior neutrally call it "you're being passive-aggressive"

The agent cross-references facts against this table to tag signals, decides the dominant mechanism, and generates situation-indexed rules.

Situation categories

DO/DON'T rules are indexed by situation category. nemawashi-reply looks at the category and situation and loads only the framework files it needs:

Category Situation
When Requesting you're asking them for something
During Conflict disagreement / tension
When Reporting delivering good / bad news
Routine Collaboration day-to-day interaction

At reply time it doesn't load every framework — it narrows to the 2-3 relevant to the situation. That also cuts the context-window cost.

Gotchas

  • Drift between the registry and the real files: at first I synced by hand, and it always broke. I moved check-frameworks.sh into pre-commit for automatic detection.
  • Parallel-agent races: if each agent writes the same frameworks/<slug>.md, it obviously breaks. Strictly mapping 1 agent = 1 file avoids it.
  • The temptation for agents to share state: there are moments you want to "look at the other frameworks' results and adjust." Doing that regresses to the monolithic design, so it's banned — adjustment happens synchronously in the synthesis pass.
  • The Tier 2 threshold: attachment-style often has thin signal, so I made it Tier 2. The framework itself needs criteria to surface "I don't know" explicitly as a Data Gap.

Results

  • Adding a new framework is 3 steps (table + file + reply mapping), touching none of the existing frameworks
  • Re-running analyze doesn't break the other frameworks
  • Parallel dispatch shrank wallclock to roughly one framework's worth with all 6 agents running at once
  • Each framework file is independently readable, so you can view just the framework you want (nemawashi-show <person> --framework=defense-mechanisms, etc.)

Wrap-up

  • Drop the monolithic profile.md and decompose into 1 framework = 1 file × 1 agent
  • Make the framework registry the single source of truth, and detect drift with a check script
  • Parallel dispatch shortens wallclock; keep synthesis synchronous
  • Situation-indexed framework loading keeps the context cost down at reply time

References

  • supernemawashi (GitHub)
  • Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument
  • Transactional Analysis (Eric Berne)
  • Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan)
  • Attachment Theory (Bowlby & Ainsworth)

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.
