title: How MCP and tool calling really work: I built an AI agent from scratch in Java and traced every step
description:
I asked a local AI model to add "buy milk" to my notes file. It did. Then I traced every step to find out what actually happened.

To do that, I built the whole thing from scratch:

  • an MCP server
  • an MCP client and
  • an agent loop in plain Java and Spring Boot,

no AI frameworks and no MCP SDK, talking to Qwen 2.5 7B running locally through Ollama.

"From scratch" means no frameworks, not no help: Claude co-authored the code and this article, because writing every line by hand in 2026 would apparently make me a caveman.

Yes, I know: MCP has been around for about two years. I'm late to the party. But if even one person walks away with a new understanding, that's the best outcome I could ask for.

What we're building

One plain-text file, data/db, holds my notes. The MCP server is the only thing that touches it, through five tools: read, write (replace everything), append, update (find and replace) and clear. A simple File I/O method, ref

You ask the host in plain English ("Add buy milk"), it asks the model which tool fits, and runs it on the server.

What you need

  • Docker with Compose: runs the MCP server and the host.
  • Ollama, installed natively (ollama.com), not in Docker, so the model can use your GPU. On Linux, set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 so the containers can reach it.
  • The model: ollama pull qwen2.5:7b (about 4.7 GB; 8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB comfortable).
  • Git. No Java needed unless you run outside Docker. 
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/mcp_server
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/local_agent
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b          # with Ollama running
cd local_agent && docker compose up --build

The map

  • local_agent (port 8081) is the host. It runs the agent loop, keeps the conversation and makes every network call.
  • Ollama (port 11434) runs the model. Text in, text out.
  • mcp_server (port 8080) owns the tools. It's the only thing that touches data/db, the notes file.

Part 1: The layers

1. The model is just numbers

ollama pull qwen2.5:7b downloads about 4.7 GB of weights: billions of numbers. Together with a function that predicts the next token, that's the whole model. It doesn't listen on a port, doesn't speak JSON or HTTP, and does nothing on its own. A file of numbers can't write to your disk. Something else has to.

2. Ollama is a database server, but for models

I used to think Ollama, ChatGPT and Claude were abstractions over the model, so my own app would skip them and talk to the model directly. But the model is just numbers, and an app can't talk to numbers. Something has to load it and give you an interface to send text and get text back: a model server.

Locally that's Ollama; in the cloud it's the OpenAI or Anthropic API. That's the layer you can't bypass.

ChatGPT and the Claude app are one level higher: they're hosts like my local_agent, with a UI, history and tools on top of that API. Calling the OpenAI API isn't calling ChatGPT.

Layer Local OpenAI Anthropic
Model qwen2.5:7b on your disk GPT (private weights) Claude (private weights)
Model server (API) Ollama OpenAI API Anthropic API
Host / app local_agent, or Ollama's own chat app ChatGPT Claude app

ChatGPT is to the OpenAI API what my local_agent is to Ollama. Build on the API and you write the ChatGPT part: history, tools, the loop.

One twist: locally, Ollama sits in two rows at once. Its server (the API on port 11434) is the model-server layer, but its desktop chat window and ollama run in the terminal are hosts, thin clients of that same API. Imagine OpenAI shipping the API and ChatGPT in one download. My local_agent skips Ollama's chat window and talks to the API directly, the same way your own app would skip ChatGPT and call the OpenAI API.

3. There is no standard for talking to models (MCP vs function calling)

Every vendor has its own JSON dialect. OpenAI returns tool arguments as a JSON string, Ollama as a JSON object, and Anthropic uses tool_use content blocks instead of tool_calls. Same idea, three shapes, so every host needs an adapter.

That's also the answer to "MCP vs function calling". Function calling is the model side: you describe tools to the model and it replies with a request to use one. MCP standardized the tool side, not the model side: how a host finds and calls tools on a separate server. A real agent uses both. Since MCP's inputSchema and Ollama's parameters are both plain JSON Schema, my adapter between them is a single map().

Part 2: The illusions

4. Are LLMs stateless? Yes. Chat is an illusion

Maybe you already know this one: the model remembers nothing between calls. The host resends the entire conversation every turn, so "memory" is just a list in my Java process. That's all it ever is.

5. How tool calling actually works: it's just text

There is no special channel. Ollama's chat template renders your JSON tools into the prompt (see it with ollama show qwen2.5:7b --template). Trimmed, the model sees:

<|im_start|>system
# Tools
You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags:
<tools>
{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "append", "description": "Append content to the end of the file", ...}}
...
</tools>
For each function call, return a json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags
<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Add buy milk to my notes<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

The model predicts the most likely next tokens, which, because it was trained on this format, are:

<tool_call>
{"name": "append", "arguments": {"content": "buy milk"}}
</tool_call>

Ollama parses that text back into a neat tool_calls JSON field. The "function call" is a string that looks like one. (Start Ollama with OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 to see the full rendered prompt.)

6. The model never touches the file

Ollama returns that tool_calls JSON to my host, and it's done. It has no idea an MCP server exists. My host reads the request, calls the MCP server over HTTP, and pastes the result back into the conversation as a role: "tool" message.

Ollama and the MCP server never talk to each other. The model requests. The host decides and acts. That's why the host is the real control point for safety, not the model.

How to add your own data to an LLM (no training required)

This is what I actually set out to learn. When the model calls read, my notes come back as a role: "tool" message and sit in the conversation like any other text. The model "knows" my file because the host pasted it into the prompt.

Every popular way to give an LLM your own data is this trick, except one:

  • Prompt stuffing: paste the data in yourself.
  • Tool calling / MCP: the model asks, the host fetches (this project).
  • RAG: the host searches your documents and pastes in the relevant chunks.
  • Fine-tuning: changes the weights. Good for behaviour and style, usually wrong for "make it know my documents".

So "train ChatGPT on my own data" usually means one of the first three. Choosing what goes into the context window is context engineering, and RAG exposed as an MCP tool is agentic RAG.

Part 3: MCP on the wire

7. MCP is JSON-RPC on one endpoint, not REST

An MCP server has exactly one endpoint, POST /mcp, and the operation lives in the body's method field (JSON-RPC 2.0). Since the 2026-07-28 spec, MCP is also stateless: no initialize handshake and no session ID. Every request carries its protocol version in params._meta, and the method and tool name are copied into headers, so a gateway can route without parsing the body.

What an MCP server's API looks like

If you build REST APIs for a living, this is the light-bulb view. Here is my server's entire API, OpenAPI-style:

POST /mcp                         the only endpoint (GET, DELETE -> 405)

method            params              returns
server/discover   (none)              supported versions, capabilities
tools/list        (none)              [{ name, description, inputSchema }]
tools/call        name, arguments     { content: [...], isError }

And here is the API the model actually sees, as returned by tools/list:

tool      arguments          what it does
read      (none)             return the whole file
write     content            replace the whole file
append    content            add a line at the end
update    search, replace    find and replace text
clear     (none)             empty the file

That's the whole thing: two lists. Think of tools/list as an OpenAPI doc written for a model instead of a developer. The full spec adds the same list-and-read pattern for resources (resources/list, resources/read) and prompts (prompts/list, prompts/get), but tools are where the action is. One call on the wire looks like this:

POST /mcp
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: append

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"append","arguments":{"content":"buy milk"},
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

MCP vs API: isn't MCP just an API?

Technically, yes. The difference is who it's designed for. A normal API is designed for a developer, who reads the docs and writes a custom client. An MCP server describes itself to a model: tools/list returns every tool with a plain-English description and a JSON Schema, so any MCP host can use any MCP server with no custom code. MCP usually wraps your existing APIs rather than replacing them.

8. There are two kinds of errors

  • Protocol errors (bad JSON, wrong headers, unknown tool) come back as a JSON-RPC error. They're client bugs, for the developer.
  • Tool errors (missing argument, wrong type) come back as a normal result with isError: true. They're for the model, so it can fix its call and retry. 
// unknown tool is a protocol error, bad arguments are a tool error the model can fix
try {
    registry.validate(toolName, params);
} catch (ToolNotFoundException e) {
    throw RpcException.invalidParams("Unknown tool: " + toolName, HttpStatus.OK);
} catch (ToolArgumentException e) {
    return CallToolResult.error(e.getMessage(), resultMeta);
}

Small models make small mistakes. Hand back Param (content) is required instead of throwing, and they usually fix it on the next step.

Part 4: The full trace

One /agent request, every hop.

1. You → host

curl -s localhost:8081/agent -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"message":"Add buy milk to my notes"}'

2. Host → MCP server: tools/list (id 1) returns the five tools.

3. Host → Ollama

POST /api/chat
{
  "model": "qwen2.5:7b",
  "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" } ],
  "tools": [
    { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "append",
        "description": "Append content to the end of the file",
        "parameters": { "type": "object",
          "properties": { "content": { "type": "string", "description": "Content that gets appended" } },
          "required": ["content"], "additionalProperties": false } } },
    ... read, write, update, clear ...
  ],
  "stream": false,
  "keep_alive": "30m"
}

4. Ollama → host: the model wants a tool, and says nothing else (content is empty).

{ "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  "done": true }

5. Host → MCP server: the tools/call request shown in moment 7. This is the only moment anything touches the disk.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"resultType":"complete","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Success"}],"isError":false,
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"mcp_server","version":"0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"}}}}

6. Host → Ollama again, with the whole history

"messages": [
  { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" },
  { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  { "role": "tool", "content": "Success", "tool_name": "append" }
]

7. Ollama → host: "content": "I've added \"buy milk\" to your notes." with no tool_calls, so the loop stops.

8. Host → you: the reply, plus a list of every tool call made.

Seven HTTP calls between three processes for two words in a text file. The model was in two of them, receiving text and returning text.

Part 5: The harness

9. The agent harness matters more than people think

Everything around the model is the agent harness. Here, that's my host. The loop itself is tiny (logging trimmed):

for (int step = 1; step <= properties.maxSteps(); step++) {
    Message reply = ollamaClient.chat(messages, tools);
    messages.add(reply); // the tool_calls must stay in history

    if (!reply.hasToolCalls()) {
        return new Result(reply.content(), invocations);
    }
    for (ToolCall call : reply.toolCalls()) {
        ToolInvocation invocation = invoke(call.function().name(), call.function().arguments());
        invocations.add(invocation);
        messages.add(Message.toolResult(call.function().name(), invocation.output()));
    }
}
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not finish within " + properties.maxSteps() + " steps");

The behaviour lives in the details:

  • An iteration guard (agent.max-steps=5), because a model that calls tools forever is a real failure mode.
  • Keeping the model's own tool call in history, or the tool result makes no sense to it.
  • Tool descriptions are written for the model. My write tool says "Write all contents to file". To a 7B model asked to "add" something, that can look fine, and then your notes are gone. "Replaces the entire file. To add a note, use append." works better.

A 7B model is slow on a laptop and not deterministic, but it's good enough to learn on, because every failure is visible.

What's next

10. Frameworks hide all of this

Spring AI can do everything above with an annotation like @McpTool. I'd use it in production. But now that Claude and I built it without one, I know what it hides, and when something breaks I know which of the seven hops to check.

  • v2: the same project with Spring AI, compared line by line.
  • v3: multiple notes files, then agentic RAG with a search tool.

FAQ

Do I need to train an LLM on my own data? Usually not. Put the data in the context window with a prompt, a tool/MCP server or RAG. Fine-tuning changes behaviour, not knowledge.

MCP vs RAG? RAG retrieves relevant chunks into the prompt. MCP lets the model call tools, and search can be one. Combined, that's agentic RAG.

Does the model execute the tool? No. It writes text asking for one. The host runs the tool and sends back the result.

Is MCP the same as function calling? No. Function calling is how a model asks for a tool. MCP is how a host finds and calls tools on another server.

Do I need MCP for tool calling? No. You can define tools in your app directly. MCP pays off when tools are shared across apps or teams.

Can a local model use MCP tools? Yes, if it was trained for tool calling (Qwen 2.5, Llama 3.1, Qwen 3). The model never talks to the MCP server anyway.

What changed in MCP 2026-07-28? It's stateless: no initialize, no sessions, and context travels in params._meta plus mirrored headers.

Try it yourself

Clone both repos, run docker compose up --build in local_agent, and send the curl from hop 1. Ollama runs natively on your machine, and Docker runs the rest.

  • github.com/abir4l/mcp_server (includes a full client integration guide)
  • github.com/abir4l/local_agent

The model is just numbers. Everything else is software, and software is something we already know how to read.

Co-written with Claude. If this was useful, a star on the repo helps.

title: Stop Starting With Microservices: The Path Real Systems Actually Follow
description:
Originally published on Medium.

A new project kicks off. Someone opens a blank page and says, "Let's build it with microservices." Everyone nods. It sounds modern. It sounds scalable.

But here's the surprise: most high-scale systems don't start with microservices. They grow into them, and only when the system demands it.

This article walks through that growth one stage at a time. At each stage you'll see what breaks, why it breaks, and what teams do about it. If you'd rather watch, there's a 10-minute animated version of this article:

1. Start with a monolith

Every system starts somewhere, and the first goal isn't scale. It's correctness, speed of development and clarity. That's why most successful systems begin as a monolith.

A monolith is one application that holds every feature:

  • One backend, the code that runs on the server.
  • One deployment, so you ship it as a single unit.
  • Usually one database, where all the data lives.

Inside, each feature is a module, a separate area of the code. Modules call each other directly, as ordinary function calls with no network in between. That keeps two things easy:

  • Transactions are simple. A transaction is a group of changes that succeed or fail together, and a single database handles it for you.
  • Debugging is easy. One process, one log and one stack trace.

This leads to the first rule of architecture:

Don't add distributed complexity, meaning spreading work across many machines, until the system forces you to.

2. When the monolith feels heavy, fix coupling first

As features and engineers pile up, the monolith starts to feel heavy:

  • Builds slow down.
  • Deployments get risky.
  • A small change breaks something unrelated.
  • Teams collide in the same repository.

Many teams jump straight to microservices here. That's a mistake, because the real problem isn't the monolith. It's coupling: parts that depend too tightly on each other's insides.

The fix is a modular monolith. It still ships as one unit, but inside it's split into clean modules:

  • Each module has a defined interface, the official doorway other code must use.
  • Each module owns its data.
  • No module reaches into another's internals.
  • Each module follows a domain boundary, a business area like orders or payments.

This step matters more than it looks. If you split tightly coupled code into services, the coupling doesn't disappear. It just moves onto the network, where it's slower, harder to debug and can fail in new ways. Clean module boundaries now become clean service boundaries later.

3. When traffic grows, split into microservices

In a monolith, scaling means scaling everything. You add more running copies of the whole app, called instances. If payments get heavy traffic, the entire system gets more instances, including all the parts that were fine.

At small scale that's fine. At large scale it's inefficient and expensive, because different parts behave differently:

  • Read-heavy parts mostly fetch data.
  • Write-heavy parts mostly save data.
  • CPU-heavy parts need lots of processing power.
  • I/O-heavy parts spend their time waiting on disks or networks.

This is usually the moment to move to microservices: small, separate applications, each owning one domain. Each one can scale, deploy and fail on its own.

That solves scaling. But there's a catch. Before, everything lived in one process. Now everything lives on the network. Every section below is a consequence of that one sentence.

4. Services need to find each other: service discovery and the API gateway

Services now run on different machines, containers or pods. (A container is a packaged, isolated box for running an app, and a pod is a common way of grouping containers, for example in Kubernetes.) These instances restart, autoscale and move around, so hardcoding addresses is impossible.

The fix is service discovery. A registry tracks every available instance, and services ask it where to send each request.

The next problem is which service the app on your phone should call. With one backend there was one API. Now there are many. You don't want login checks or traffic limits copied into every service, and you don't want the frontend knowing your internal layout.

So you add an API gateway, a single entry point that handles:

  • Routing each request to the right service
  • Authentication, checking who you are
  • Logging
  • Throttling, limiting how fast a client can call
  • Sometimes combining responses from several services

5. The database becomes the bottleneck

As traffic keeps climbing, the first thing to struggle is usually the database, not the services. Services scale horizontally: you just add more machines. Databases are much harder.

The symptoms are familiar:

  • Queries slow down.
  • CPU spikes.
  • Locks appear. A lock is a hold on data while it's being changed, which makes everyone else wait.
  • Write delays grow.

Fix 1: read replicas. These are read-only copies of the database. Heavy queries move there, so reads are separated from writes. That works for a while, until the primary, the main copy that accepts writes, becomes the bottleneck itself.

Fix 2: sharding. The data is split across multiple machines, usually:

  • By user
  • By tenant, meaning a customer organization
  • By hash, a formula that assigns each record to a bucket

6. Transactions across services: the Saga pattern

In a monolith, one transaction can safely update many tables. That's an ACID transaction: a guarantee that a group of changes happens completely or not at all, and stays correct even when others are working at the same time.

Now one request, like create an order, may touch the order, payment, inventory and notification services, each with its own database. There's no easy way to wrap all of them in one ACID transaction. Forcing strong consistency, where everyone sees the same correct data at the same moment, usually hurts performance and reliability.

So high-scale systems accept eventual consistency: data may be briefly out of sync, but it catches up. They get there with three tools:

  • Events, to tell other services what happened
  • Retries, to recover from temporary failures
  • Compensation, which means undoing an earlier step

The common pattern that combines them is the Saga. Each step succeeds independently. If a later step fails, earlier steps are retried or undone. For example, if stock can't be reserved, the payment is refunded and the order is cancelled.

It's more scalable, but it's also more complex. That trade-off comes up at every stage.

7. Stop waiting: event-driven design

With a few services, synchronous calls work fine. Synchronous means the caller waits for an answer, usually over HTTP. As services multiply, these call chains become slow and fragile:

  • One slow service delays everything.
  • One failure breaks the whole flow.
  • Traffic spikes overload the services further down the line.

So high-scale systems switch to messaging. An event is a small message saying something happened. Instead of calling a service directly, you publish the event to a queue or stream, an ordered line of messages waiting to be processed. Consumers, the services that read events, handle them independently.

What you gain:

  • Services become loosely coupled.
  • Spikes are absorbed by the queue.
  • Failures can be retried.
  • Work happens asynchronously, so no one waits.

That's why large systems lean on Kafka, a popular event-streaming platform, as well as queues and pub-sub, where one sender reaches many listeners.

8. Retries are dangerous without idempotency

In distributed systems, failures are normal. Messages get retried. Requests time out, giving up after waiting too long. A consumer can crash after doing the work but before acknowledging it, that is, before telling the queue "I'm done."

So the same request may run more than once. For payments, orders, wallet updates or inventory changes, that's dangerous. Picture a customer who pays \$20 once and gets charged \$40.

The answer is idempotency: the same request produces the same result, even if it runs multiple times. Systems achieve it with two tools:

  • Idempotency keys (or unique request IDs), labels attached to each request
  • Deduplication tables, a record of which requests have already been handled

When a request arrives, the consumer checks its key. If the key isn't in the table, it processes the request and records the key. If the key is already there, it skips the work and returns the earlier result.

At scale, idempotency isn't an optimization. It's a requirement.

9. Designing to fail safely: rate limits and backpressure

At high scale, traffic isn't steady. Requests can suddenly spike, and a system that tries to handle everything at once can crash. So it has to control the flow:

  • Rate limiting restricts how much traffic is allowed in.
  • Backpressure slows down producers, the senders, when consumers can't keep up.
  • Queues buffer short spikes.
  • Dead-letter queues capture messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected instead of blocking everything else.

Sometimes the right move is to reject a request with a polite "try again later" (HTTP 429) instead of crashing the whole service.

High-scale systems aren't designed to never fail. They're designed to fail safely.

10. Observability and the CAP trade-off

In a monolith, logs are usually enough. In a distributed system, one request can pass through many services, and you need three more tools:

  • Tracing follows one request's path, so you can see which service is slow.
  • Metrics are numbers tracked over time, so you can see where load is growing.
  • Alerts tell you about problems before users complain.

Together these make up observability, the ability to see inside a running system. At this scale it has to be part of the design, not an afterthought.

Then comes the biggest trade-off, known as CAP:

  • Consistency: everyone sees the same latest data.
  • Availability: the system always answers.
  • Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when the network splits parts apart.

Networks do split in distributed systems, so partition tolerance isn't optional. When a split happens, you have to choose: keep answering, even with slightly stale data (availability), or refuse until the data is correct (consistency). You can't have all three, and different parts of the same product choose differently:

  • Payments and wallets favor consistency. A wrong balance is worse than a short wait.
  • Feeds and search favor availability. A slightly stale feed beats an error page.
  • Analytics accepts eventual consistency. Numbers that catch up in a minute are fine.

The path, in five steps

Most successful systems follow the same path:

  1. Start simple.
  2. Add structure.
  3. Split when needed.
  4. Distribute when required.
  5. Optimize when scale demands it.

Three takeaways

1. Start with a monolith. Don't add distributed complexity until the system forces you to.

2. Fix coupling first. Use a modular monolith before you split into services. Otherwise you'll just move the coupling onto the network.

3. Microservices aren't a starting point. They're a response to scale, and every stage brings new problems to solve: discovery, data, transactions, retries, traffic and visibility.

Good architecture isn't the most advanced design. It's the right design for today, plus knowing when it's time to evolve.

▶️ Watch the animated version: Stop Starting With Microservices (YouTube)

Next up: why one bad request can crash every user on a server, and how processes and threads decide the blast radius. Watch Processes vs Threads.

You can now run CI for your Turborepo with one line of configuration.

In Vercel's internal repositories, our wait time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x shorter, dramatically improving our CI's ability to keep up with our coding agents.

To get started, prompt your agent in your repo:

Each task marked with a ci tag runs on every push. Vercel CI automatically takes care of:

  • Only running CI that is affected by your code changes

  • Task caching with Vercel Remote Cache

  • Installing dependencies once per run

  • Caching dependencies across code updates

To learn more:

  • Check out our blog post

  • Visit the documentation

  • Discuss Vercel CI on the Community announcement

title: What if the history of a codebase could help explain the code nobody wants to touch?
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

NecroGit: A Little Séance for Legacy Code

Every codebase has a past.

Sometimes that past is a beautifully maintained changelog. Sometimes it is a function named do_not_delete_final2(), three deprecated imports, and a Git history that only the person who wrote it really understood.

Then that person leaves.

The code stays.

For Week 4's Ghost in the Machine challenge, I built NecroGit: a command-line tool that treats legacy-code maintenance like a bit of software archaeology. It looks for signs of bitrot, examines Git history for clues about how a project evolved, and uses an open-weight language model to help explain unfamiliar code and propose repairs.

The goal isn't to pretend a model can bring a developer back from the dead. It's to make the traces they left behind more useful to the next person who has to maintain the project.

What I Built

NecroGit is a Python CLI for developers inheriting repositories they didn't write.

It brings a few kinds of investigation into one workflow:

  • Inspect: scan Python files for known deprecated APIs and suspicious legacy patterns.
  • Summon: examine Git commits and author activity for historical context.
  • Explain: ask a language model to explain an unfamiliar function using the source and available repository context.
  • Patch: generate a proposed diff that a developer can review before applying.
  • Memory: keep a small repository dossier so useful context can carry between sessions.

The part I care about most is the connection between these steps. Finding a deprecated import is useful. Understanding why the surrounding code exists is better. Getting a proposed change that you can inspect, test, and reject if necessary is better still.

NecroGit is meant to assist the maintainer, not replace their judgment. Git history can offer clues about a previous developer's habits; it cannot tell us with certainty what that person intended. Likewise, an AI-generated patch is a proposal, not proof that the fix is correct.

Demo

Repository: github.com/avrojitduttaj/necrogit

The quickest way to see the workflow is to install the project in a Python environment, open a repository in your terminal, and try the inspection command:

necrogit inspect .

Then explore the other commands with:

necrogit --help
necrogit summon .
necrogit memory

The exact arguments for explain and patch depend on the installed CLI version; check each command's --help before running it.

Live demo / walkthrough: [Add a verified demo URL or video here]

I don't want to pass off a mockup as a working demo, so this post links to the source repository. If I add a hosted walkthrough, I'll put the verified URL here.

Code

The source is available here:

Explore NecroGit on GitHub

Live Deployment: NecroGit — The Repository Medium

A few of the implementation choices:

  • Python's ast module provides a structured way to inspect source code without executing it.
  • GitPython reads repository history and commit metadata.
  • Click provides the command-line interface, with Rich for readable terminal output.
  • HTTPX connects the engine to an OpenAI-compatible local model endpoint.
  • Repository dossiers can be stored locally, with optional Backboard integration in the project.

The intent is to keep the first step—static inspection—useful even when an AI model isn't available. The AI-assisted commands should fail clearly when inference isn't configured, rather than pretending they succeeded.

How I Built It

I built NecroGit around a simple question: what if Git history were more than a list of commits?

The scanner handles the deterministic part. It parses Python syntax and checks for patterns the tool knows about. The Git-history component gathers evidence such as authorship, commit dates, and commit messages. The AI engine can then use the available code and context to generate an explanation or a proposed diff.

For the open-model path, NecroGit is designed to work with Gemma 2 through Ollama, using a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That makes it possible to experiment with the model on your own machine rather than making a hosted, closed API the only way to run the project.

This separation matters:

  1. Rules find known patterns. They are predictable, testable, and don't need a model.
  2. Git history supplies evidence. It gives context, but it isn't a source of certainty about intent.
  3. The model helps interpret and draft. It can explain code and suggest changes, but its output still needs review and tests.

During development, I also added tests for deprecated-import detection, Git and non-Git directories, prompt construction, connection failures, local memory persistence, and CLI behavior. Those tests have been useful for catching mismatches between the intended user experience and what the command actually does.

One lesson from building a CLI is that a feature isn't finished just because the Python function works. Packaging, command registration, Windows paths, model endpoints, and readable error messages are all part of the product. I'm still tightening those edges, and I want to be honest about that rather than call the tool production-ready before it earns the label.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that reads source code, where inference happens is part of the design.

A developer may be working with a private repository, a client's code, or an abandoned internal service. Sending that code to an external API should never be an invisible default. A local model gives the developer a path to keep inference on their own machine, subject to how they've configured the rest of their environment.

Open-weight models also make the system more replaceable. Developers can experiment with different models and local runtimes instead of tying the whole experience to one provider's API, pricing, or product decisions.

And the non-AI parts remain ordinary, inspectable software. The scanner's rules can be read and tested. The Git-history analysis can be audited. A proposed patch is visible as a diff.

That doesn't mean every setup is automatically offline or private: optional integrations and telemetry need to be configured and disclosed carefully. But open tooling gives developers more control over those trade-offs—and for a maintenance tool that may touch sensitive code, that control is important.

My Agent Session

[https://dev.to/agent_sessions/finding-the-necrogit-devrelay-session-link-xmpym5]

This section is optional. I will only link a real saved session; I won't invent an embed or session URL.

The Spirit of It

There's something eerie about opening a repository and finding a whole history of decisions with nobody left to explain them.

A commit message says “temporary workaround.” The workaround is still there six years later. A function has a strange name because it once fixed a production incident. A dependency is obsolete, but nobody remembers which behavior relied on it.

The ghost isn't really the old developer. It's the missing context.

NecroGit is my attempt to make that context a little easier to recover—from the code, from the commit history, and from the tools we can run ourselves. Not to resurrect the past exactly as it was, but to help the next maintainer move forward without blindly deleting it.

🏆 Prize Categories I'm Targeting

  • [ ] Overall Challenge Winner — $250

    NecroGit aims to make legacy-code maintenance easier by combining Git-history archaeology, AI-assisted code explanations, and safer patch proposals.

  • [ ] Best Use of Gemma — $200

    Gemma 2 powers NecroGit's local AI inference workflow, helping explain historical design decisions and draft modernization patches while keeping source code on the developer's machine.

  • [ ] Best Use of Backboard — $100

    NecroGit implements persistent repository dossiers, with local JSON storage and an optional Backboard synchronization path for retaining maintainer context across sessions.

  • [ ] Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing — $100

    NecroGit includes instrumentation for tracing AI inference and memory operations, with breadcrumbs and structured context to help diagnose the resurrection workflow.

Deployment

NecroGit's web workbench is deployed on Render to make the project website accessible online. Render is used as a hosting and deployment platform, not as an AI integration.

The core NecroGit CLI remains a local developer tool, while the hosted website serves as the public-facing project experience.

Built by @avrojitduttaj.

If you've inherited a codebase that feels haunted, I'd love to know: what's the strangest piece of legacy code you've had to explain?

title: Edge Requests are now called CDN Requests
description:
CDN Requests is now the name for the usage metric previously called Edge Requests. This is a naming change only: pricing, limits, and how usage is measured are all unchanged.

The new name appears on the usage dashboard, the Observability Events chart, usage notifications, and invoice line items. It reflects that these are requests served by Vercel's CDN. Metric IDs and product aliases are unchanged, so saved queries keep working. In the billing charges API, ServiceName now returns the new name. Integrations that match charges on ServiceName should switch to the new SkuId field, which stays stable across renames.

See the CDN pricing and usage documentation for details.

title: rip: A local graveyard and ofrenda for forgotten side projects
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every developer has a drive full of abandoned side quests: half-finished prototypes, 2 AM scripts, and repos whose last commit was simply "fixing bugs please work". Usually, they just sit there until an aggressive disk cleanup wipes them out.

For Halloween and Día de los Muertos, I built rip: a local CLI tool that acts as a digital cemetery for dead code.

It scans your workspaces for dormant projects, reads strictly high-level metadata (last modified date, size, and last Git commit), and pipes it into a local Google Gemma 2 (2B) instance. Gemma acts as the gravekeeper, writing witty epitaphs for why each project died.

With the --ofrenda flag, it channels Día de los Muertos by turning the eulogy into an altar, offering actionable sparks to resurrect the project today.

Demo

The generated dark-mode visual cemetery view (cemetery.html):

In the terminal, it renders ASCII tombstones before generating the web gallery:

     .---.
    / RIP /
   |  ___  |   rust-game-engine-attempt
   | |   | |   "It chased a dream of a world built in rust, but the compiler's silence remains."
   |_|___|_|
   🌼 Ofrenda Revival: Seek the engine's heart. A compiler update might be the spark to bring it back.

Code

Razorbillworks / rip

a local graveyard for dead side projects. scans stale folders, writes obituaries, and hints at revivals with local gemma-2.

A local CLI tool and digital cemetery built for Hacktoberfest 2026: Ghost in the Machine.
Channels the spirits of forgotten scripts and abandoned repositories using local Google Gemma 2 (2B)

Overview

Every developer's drive hosts a quiet graveyard: incomplete prototypes, late-night experiments, and uncommitted scripts.

rip acts as a respectful gravekeeper. It traverses your workspaces to locate dormant projects, passing strictly metadata (modification age, sizes, and Git commit logs) to an air-gapped Gemma 2 instance. It produces witty obituaries and constructive Ofrenda sparks to resurrect your code, rendered both as ANSI terminal tombstones and a self-contained HTML gallery.

The Graveyard Gallery

Architecture & Open Innovation

  • Absolute Zero-Content Telemetry: Proprietary APIs require uploading data off your machine. rip runs an open-weight foundation model locally; source code and file contents never touch the inference pipeline.
  • Offline & Air-Gapped: Runs entirely on local compute through Ollama. No network latency…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The stack is intentionally minimal and runs 100% locally:

  • Model: Google's gemma2:2b via Ollama. Gemma 2's instruction-following at 2B parameters made it fast and consistent at returning clean, parseable JSON without hallucinated markdown fences.
  • CLI & Formatting: Python 3 with rich for terminal panels.
  • Metadata Pipeline: Standard library pathlib and subprocess to grab git log -1.

rip never reads actual code or file contents. It sends only the project name, days inactive, and the last commit message to Gemma at temperature: 0.7.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Zero-Content Privacy: Developers store credentials, draft scripts, and private code in local folders. Scanning directories using a cloud LLM is an unnecessary data risk. With an open-weight model, zero bytes leave your machine.
  • True Offline Resilience: Proprietary APIs deprecate endpoints, change pricing, and require Wi-Fi. An open-weight model on Ollama means this tool works on an airplane or 10 years from now with the Wi-Fi toggled off.
  • No Metered Costs: Scanning 200 forgotten repositories costs $0 in token fees.

The Spirit of It

Running rip against my own old folders and seeing Gemma roast a commit from months ago wasn't just fun, it was oddly motivating. Instead of feeling guilty about abandoned repos, it treats them as part of the creative process and gives a clear prompt to pick one back up.

Prize Categories

  • Ghost in the Machine (Hacktoberfest Week 4)
  • Best Use of Gemma (Local inference with Google Gemma 2 2B)

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in Singapore

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

title: My fix checker found two missing tests. Then it wrote them.
description:
In my last post, Bite checked some well-known projects and found a few small gaps: changes that no test would notice if they broke. Two of them:

  • In Rich, Markdown <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> is drawn in bold yellow, and no test checks it.
  • In chi, a Go web router, a change made XML responses get compressed by default. The commit did add a test, but that test counts the list against itself, so it still passes with the change taken out.

Finding a gap is the easy half. Someone still has to write the test. So this week Bite got a new option, --write-tests, that tries to write it.

How it works

For each change no test noticed, a fresh AI worker writes one small test on a copy of the project. Then Bite doesn't take its word for it. It runs the test itself:

  1. With the change in, the test must pass, twice.
  2. With the change taken out, the test must fail, and fail for a real reason (not just a crash on loading).

If either part goes wrong, Bite throws the test away and says so. It uses your own Anthropic API key, and --budget caps what a run spends.

What happened

Gap Bite's test With the change Without it Cost
Rich <kbd> prints <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>, checks Ctrl is bold yellow passes, twice fails: Ctrl not bold yellow $0.14
chi XML sends XML through chi's compressor, checks it comes back gzipped passes, twice fails: XML not gzipped $0.10

Total: $0.34. That's more than the two rows add up to, because of the next part.

The first chi try got thrown away, and that was Bite's fault. Go runs tests by folder, not by file, and Bite asked Go to run one file alongside the whole project. Go refused before running anything. Bite's rule caught it: a test that fails before it even runs doesn't count. So it threw the test out instead of showing a fake result. The fix is in PR #67, and the second try worked.

Did it write the right test?

Before Bite could do this, Claude had already written a test for each gap the slow way, to confirm the gaps were real. So there was an answer key.

  • Rich: Bite's test checks the same thing as the answer key: Ctrl comes out bold bright yellow.
  • chi: the answer key (chi #1246, still open) adds XML to chi's existing list test. Bite's test goes further: it sends a real XML response through the compressor and checks it gets zipped. Different route, same claim.

Here's the Rich one, exactly as Bite wrote it:

# Guards that <kbd>…</kbd> in Markdown renders its text in the markdown.kbd style.
from rich.console import Console
from rich.markdown import Markdown


def test_kbd_inline_html_is_styled():
    console = Console(
        file=__import__("io").StringIO(),
        force_terminal=True,
        color_system="truecolor",
        width=40,
    )
    console.print(Markdown("Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> now"))
    output = console.file.getvalue()
    assert "\x1b[1;93mCtrl\x1b[0m" in output

Then we tried the whole loop

On my own copy of Rich, Bite ran as a GitHub Action on a pull request. It found the <kbd> gap, wrote the test, and opened a small pull request with the test in it. I merged that pull request, and Bite's check on the original pull request turned green. Gap found, test written, test merged, without anyone typing a test.

What I took from it

  • Don't trust a test you didn't watch fail. The pass-and-fail check is the whole point. An AI can write a test that looks right and checks nothing, just like the chi commit's own test did.
  • Throwing things away is a feature. The chi test that never ran would have looked like a catch. Bite saying "no" there is what makes its "yes" worth something.
  • Two gaps is a small trial. It worked twice, on two languages. That's a start, not proof it always works.

It's in v0.7.0 (pipx upgrade bite-check). On your own computer: bite --write-tests. In GitHub Actions, the setup is in Bite's README. Since this trial, Bite also asks a second fresh check whether each test is fair before showing it.

Disclosure: I'm not a coder. Claude ran these trials, wrote Bite's code and helped me draft this post. The numbers come from the run logs.

title: Genny: Building Procedural Sounds and Music with Python
description:
Genny: Building Procedural Sounds and Music with Python

What if a game could generate its own sound effects instead of relying entirely on prerecorded audio files?

What if you could describe a material, an instrument, a physical interaction or a musical sequence in Python and turn it into an actual WAV file?

That is the idea behind Genny, an open-source Python library I have been developing to explore procedural audio synthesis and physically informed sound generation.

GitHub: https://github.com/blal1/genny

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/genny/

What is Genny?

Genny is an offline sound and music synthesis library written in Python.

It provides a collection of generators and physical models that can produce audio from parameters, code or structured JSON specifications.

Rather than simply playing prerecorded samples, Genny can generate sounds based on properties such as:

  • Instrument type and playing parameters.
  • Material and object size.
  • Physical interactions such as impacts, friction and bouncing.
  • Environmental conditions and room acoustics.
  • Musical notes, sequences and effects.
  • Random seeds for controlled variations.

The project currently includes a large catalogue of instruments, drums, sound effects, audio effects and generative layers.

Its main goal is to make procedural audio accessible from ordinary Python programs while also providing lower-level tools for people interested in sound synthesis and physical modelling.

Getting started

Install Genny with pip:

pip install genny

You can then import it directly into Python.

For example, let's generate a glass impact:

import genny
from genny.sfx import render_sfx
from genny.core import write_wav

sample_rate = 44100

audio = render_sfx(
    "impact",
    sample_rate,
    material="glass",
    size=0.2
)

write_wav("glass_tap.wav", audio, sample_rate)

The generator returns a NumPy audio array, which can be processed, mixed or saved as a WAV file.

You are not limited to glass impacts. You can generate many kinds of sounds by changing the generator and its parameters.

Generating instruments and musical sequences

Genny also provides instruments and musical synthesis tools.

For example, you can generate a short guitar sequence:

genny seq guitar "E3:1 G3:1 B3:1 E4:2" --bpm 100 -o tune.wav

You can also generate a sequence using another instrument:

genny seq cristal "A4:2 C5:2 E5:4" --bpm 60 -o cristal.wav

The command-line interface makes it possible to experiment with sounds without writing a complete Python program.

Genny also includes generated music in multiple styles, alongside instruments ranging from keyboards and strings to winds, percussion and more.

Physical sound modelling

One of the most interesting parts of Genny is its physically informed synthesis engine.

The idea is to model aspects of how sounds are produced rather than relying exclusively on generic oscillators or static recordings.

For example, the library provides models for:

  • Plucked and bowed strings.
  • Piano strings and hammer interactions.
  • Acoustic tubes, reeds and wind instruments.
  • Membranes, bars and vibrating plates.
  • Impacts and friction between physical materials.
  • Bubbles, pouring liquids, fire and environmental sounds.
  • Room acoustics and sound propagation.

Here is a small example using a physical string model:

import genny

string = genny.StringInstrument(
    body="guitar",
    position=0.18,
    brightness=0.6
)

audio = string.pluck(
    220.0,
    2.0,
    velocity=0.8
)

The library also exposes lower-level research-oriented modules under genny.physical, including waveguides, modal synthesis, particles, voice and room acoustics.

These models are reduced-order approximations designed for practical audio generation. They are not intended to replace full finite-element or boundary-element simulations.

Procedural audio for video games

Game development is one of the areas where I think procedural audio can be particularly useful.

Instead of shipping a separate audio file for every possible event, a game can generate sounds from its current state.

Imagine a game with a vehicle whose engine changes according to its RPM and load.

With Genny, you can generate an engine sound using parameters:

import genny
from genny.sfx import render_sfx
from genny.core import write_wav

engine = render_sfx(
    "pipe_engine",
    44100,
    rpm=3200.0,
    cylinders=6,
    dur=2.0
)

write_wav("engine.wav", engine, 44100)

The same principle can be used for interface sounds, footsteps, environmental ambience, machinery, impacts and other dynamic events.

Another useful feature is deterministic generation: identical arguments produce identical audio samples. This makes it possible to cache generated sounds instead of recalculating them every time.

For example, a game could maintain a cache of sound effects generated from their parameters.

Building audio directly into Python applications

Genny is not limited to command-line usage.

Its Python API allows you to integrate sound generation into an application.

A generated sound can be stored in a variable, transformed with effects, mixed with other signals or converted into WAV bytes in memory.

For example:

from functools import lru_cache
import numpy as np

from genny.sfx import render_sfx

SAMPLE_RATE = 44100

@lru_cache(maxsize=256)
def sound(name, **params):
    return render_sfx(
        name,
        SAMPLE_RATE,
        **params
    )

glass = sound("impact", material="glass", size=0.2)
wood = sound("impact", material="wood", size=0.3)

This is particularly useful when an application needs reusable sound generators or multiple variations of the same event.

The repository also contains a more complete integration example in examples/in_your_code.py, covering caching, parameter banks, interface events, effects, generated scenes and in-memory WAV conversion.

A large collection of sound generators

Genny includes a broad catalogue of sound generators and processing tools.

Some examples include:

  • Musical instruments and percussion.
  • Mechanical and vehicle sounds.
  • Environmental ambience.
  • Animals, insects and footsteps.
  • Impacts, scraping, rolling and breaking objects.
  • Speech and vocal synthesis.
  • Reverbs, filters and spectral processing.
  • Retro sound-generation engines.

You can inspect the available generators directly from the command line:

genny list

You can also inspect an existing audio file:

genny info tune.wav

The analysis tools provide information such as loudness, sharpness, brightness and spectral characteristics.

Open source and documentation

Genny is an ongoing project, and I am continuing to expand its catalogue, improve its physical models and refine its Python API.

If you want to explore the implementation, the repository contains several useful documentation resources:

Documentation What it covers
docs/README.md Documentation index and Python quick start
docs/catalog.md Instruments, effects, sound generators and parameters
docs/physics.md Physical models, references and known limitations
docs/api.md Public Python API
AGENTS.md JSON specifications, musical notation and generation recipes
examples/in_your_code.py Integration into Python applications

Important: some physical synthesis components are adapted from the Klang procedural library. If you intend to distribute Genny-generated audio in an interactive product, read THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and THIRD_PARTY_KLANG_LICENSE.txt in the repository to understand the applicable attribution requirements.

Try it and share your feedback

I would love to see what other developers, audio programmers, musicians and game creators could build with Genny.

Some interesting directions include:

  • Procedural sound effects for indie games.
  • Dynamic audio systems driven by game state.
  • Generative music experiments.
  • Physical modelling and audio research.
  • Automated sound generation pipelines.
  • Creative coding projects.

If you are interested, you can find the project here:

GitHub: https://github.com/blal1/genny

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/genny/

Contributions, bug reports, suggestions and discussions are welcome.

I'm particularly interested in feedback about the API, documentation, sound quality, physical modelling and potential applications.

Thanks for reading, and happy sound generation!

title: Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist: remembering someone with an AI that never leaves your device
description:
What I Built

When someone dies, the memories that matter most are rarely the grand ones. They are the yellow cardigan, the Sunday porch, the way someone laughed in a thunderstorm. I wanted to build a small, quiet place to put those down.

Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist is a private web app. You type or speak a few memories of someone you miss. A small open-weight model, running on your own device, turns them into a short tribute story and a poem, and builds a candlelit digital ofrenda (altar) from the things you mentioned: candles, marigolds, a favourite book, a hot mug of cider.

The theme asked for something that honors the past in the spirit of Día de los Muertos. The ofrenda tradition is much bigger than any app, so I borrowed only its simplest idea: that people stay with us while we tell their stories, and that we make small, physical places to hold them.

It has three parts:

  • Voice-to-Memory. Record a memory in the browser and it is transcribed locally with whisper.cpp. You can edit the text, or just type.
  • Story Alchemist. One tribute story and one poem, written from only what you said.
  • Altar Decorator. The model picks the objects in your memory, and each one lands on a three-tier altar and fades in, one by one.

The page says "Runs on your device" because it does. There are no accounts, no cloud APIs and no tracking. I tested it in airplane mode.

Demo

The video shows the typing path from start to finish: a memory about a fictional woman named Eleanor, then the altar, the story and the poem. I recorded it on the same phone the app runs on, and the waiting in the video is shortened, because generating a tribute takes a few minutes on this hardware.

I left voice input out of the recording. It works, but on my phone Whisper needed about two minutes for an 11-second clip, so typing is the dependable path there.

Code

nikhil-kumar-swe / virtual-ofrenda

Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist

A private web app for remembering someone you have lost. You speak or type a few memories of them, and a small open-weight AI running on your own device turns those memories into a tribute story and a short poem, then decorates a candlelit digital ofrenda (altar) with the things you mentioned: candles, marigolds, a favourite book, a bright yellow raincoat.

Nothing leaves the device. There are no cloud APIs, no accounts and no tracking. The whole project was built on a low-end device with 2 GB of RAM.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026, Week 4 challenge ("Ghost in the Machine").

  • Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wHRRkFlyoqc

What it does

  1. Voice-to-Memory. Record a memory in the browser. It is transcribed locally with whisper.cpp (tiny.en) and lands in a text box where you can edit it. Typing works just as well and is the main…
View on GitHub

The repository is MIT licensed and has setup steps, the model list and the commands to start each server. The model files are not included, so the README tells you how to download them.

How I Built It

The constraint. I built this on an Android phone with 2 GB of RAM and a 32-bit ARM processor, using Termux. My first plan was a 7 to 8 billion parameter model, and then a tiny Gemma through Ollama. Ollama does not run on 32-bit ARM, and a 7B model would not have fit in that memory anyway.

The open pieces. So I went smaller and more direct:

  • Gemma 3 270M (instruction-tuned, Q8_0, about 300 MB) writes the story, the poem and the list of altar items. It runs through llama.cpp's llama-server, built from source on the phone with -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF -DGGML_LLAMAFILE=OFF. It generates about 6.7 tokens per second.
  • Whisper tiny.en through whisper.cpp's whisper-server turns speech into text.
  • Laravel with Blade, Tailwind and SQLite runs the app. A queued job calls the model, and the browser polls for the result, so the story, the poem and the altar items appear as they arrive.

Take the model away and the app has no story, no poem and no altar choices to show. Everything else is plumbing around it.

Making a tiny model behave. A 270M model will happily make things up, and in a tribute that matters. So the app does not trust it blindly:

  • Every altar item the model suggests is checked against your own text. Candles and marigolds are always added.
  • The poem is built line by line from your own sentences. A model rewrite is used only if it passes the same check.
  • Near-duplicate items are merged, so "green shards" and "frosted green shards" become one.
  • If a server is offline, you get a clear message and a retry button, not a crash.

What still goes wrong. I tested it on three memories of different lengths (about 38, 85 and 130 words). These are the honest results:

  • The stories added no invented facts, but mostly because they repeat your own words. The small model stays very close to its input. On the Eleanor memory, the story was almost word for word what I had typed.
  • It can get who did what wrong. On a short memory about a man named Marcus, the story began "I always carried a pocketful of sea glass" instead of "Marcus always carried…". In an earlier test it wrote that someone was "always ready with a smile and a gentle touch", which no one had said.
  • The poem can add imagery. It invents no people or events, but it can add phrases like "secrets held tight" that were never in the memory.
  • Altar items are sometimes ideas, not objects. The model picked "quiet invitation" as an item for Eleanor's altar, and it shows up with the default dove icon. It is in the screenshot above.

Here is Eleanor's poem, as the model wrote it:

Yellow cardigan scent
Lavender whispers on porch
Bird wings, watercolor splashes
Ending's a quiet invitation
Remembered with love.

It is not Rilke. But every image in it came from the person who typed the memory, and I would rather ship that than something more beautiful that was made up.

I built it between Oct 29 and the morning of Nov 1 (IST), before the contest deadline, and every commit was made in that window.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A memory of someone you have lost is some of the most private writing a person will ever do. If this app had to call a hosted model, every one of those memories would leave the device and sit on someone else's server. I did not want to build that, and I would not want to use it.

Open weights made a different design possible. Gemma is small enough to run locally, and it is open enough that I could serve it myself, with no key, no account and no network. When the internet is off, it still works.

Open tools did the rest of the work. llama.cpp and whisper.cpp run on hardware that the friendlier tools do not support. My phone's 32-bit chip could not run Ollama, but it could run llama.cpp built from source. That is the difference between "this idea needs a data center" and "this idea fits in a pocket".

Openness also makes the project easy to improve. If you have a laptop, you can serve a larger open model with llama.cpp and point the same app at it by changing the model name and URL in .env. The app itself does not need to change. Nobody has to ask permission.

The Spirit of It

The constraint I started with turned out to be the idea. A small model cannot be trusted to be clever, so I made the app's promise modest: using only what you tell us. It does not try to write a beautiful eulogy for someone it never met. It gives your own words back, arranged with care, and puts a few candles around them.

There is plenty I would still like to do: a page that lists past tributes (today you return to one by its link), prompt starters for people who do not know where to begin, and a faster speech model. But the core is there, and it fits on a phone with 2 GB of RAM.

If you try it and it gets something wrong, I would like to hear about it.

Prize Categories

Gemma. The project is built around Google's open-weight Gemma 3 270M model, which does the writing and choosing in every tribute: the story, the poem and the altar items. It runs locally through llama.cpp, with no hosted API anywhere in the app.

Anti Money Laundering AI

New minor engine version released for the commercial line of business within the v004.011 version line (aml-commercial.default.v004.011.202610-000). This version extends support for the major engine version and includes no significant changes compared to the previous minor version.

Apigee hybrid

v1.16.11

On October 14, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.11.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.16.11.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
556680325 Fixed a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in URL host validation for the SemanticCacheLookup policy.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
513032450 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent control-plane connections could hang for up to 2 hours when silently dropped by a network intermediary by restoring a 15-second TCP keep-alive.
502540992 Fixed an issue where the SemanticCacheLookup policy was incompatible with Vertex AI Vector Search Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoints by adding gRPC transport support via <PrivateServiceConnect><GrpcEndpoint>.
492042425 Fixed an issue in the LLMTokenQuota policy where operation-level token quota values configured on an API product were not applied at runtime, causing product-level quota values to be enforced instead.

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

Dataform

Feature

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. For more information, see Preserve access controls metadata. This feature is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Priority PayGo support for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1

Priority Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) is available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) on the global endpoint.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.15.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Enhanced SARIF 2.1.0 reporting: Updated cm report SARIF output with standardized rule descriptors, severity properties, and repository-relative artifact locations for improved GitHub Code Scanning compatibility.
  • Model invocation metrics: Added model invocation tracking to cm stats --json, providing total, per-session, and per-turn invocation counts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed an issue where token usage from completed turns was omitted from session logs during error or cancellation exit paths.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available in Public Preview

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from DeepSeek is available as a fully managed model (MaaS) in Model Garden. The model accepts text and image input, targets agentic and coding tasks, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens.

For more information, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Google Cloud Armor

Feature

Cloud Armor supports service rate limiting. For more information, see Cloud Armor and service rate limiting. This feature is available in Preview.

Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka

Feature

Performance of the Cloud Storage Sink connector has been improved. The improvements include reduced out-of-memory errors, higher maximum throughput, and avoiding creating a large number of small files.
