title: How to Learn Rust Ownership and Borrowing (Without Fighting the Borrow Checker Forever)
description:
My first week with Rust, I spent most of an evening on one error. I had a Vec<String>, I passed it to a function that printed it, and then I tried to print it again in main. The compiler told me the value had been moved. I added & in random places until it compiled, felt clever for ten minutes, and hit the same wall the next day with a struct.

That's the usual story. People don't quit Rust because of syntax. They quit because ownership feels like a set of arbitrary rules the compiler enforces with error messages, and they try to memorize the fixes instead of the model behind them.

Here's the order I'd learn it in if I started again.

Get the three rules into your head first

The Rust Book states them plainly, and everything else follows from them:

  1. Each value has one owner.
  2. There can only be one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

That's it. Moves, borrows and lifetimes are all consequences. When an error confuses you, ask which of the three rules you just broke. Nine times out of ten the answer is obvious once you look.

Understand moves before you touch references

This is the code that got me:

fn print_all(items: Vec<String>) {
    for item in &items {
        println!("{item}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Linus")];
    print_all(names);
    println!("{:?}", names); // error: borrow of moved value
}

Passing names to print_all hands ownership to the function. When print_all returns, its parameter goes out of scope and the vector is dropped. There's nothing left in main to print.

Notice that the same thing does not happen with an i32. Integers, booleans, char and a few others implement Copy, so passing them copies the bits and the original stays usable. String and Vec own heap memory, so they move. Once that difference clicks, a lot of "why does this work here but not there" goes away.

Then learn borrowing as two kinds of permission

The fix for the code above is to borrow instead of move:

fn print_all(items: &[String]) {
    for item in items {
        println!("{item}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Linus")];
    print_all(&names);
    println!("{:?}", names); // fine
}

I find it easier to think of references as permissions rather than pointers. &T means "you can look." &mut T means "you can change it, and nobody else can even look while you hold this." You can have as many look-only borrows as you want, or exactly one mutable borrow, never both at the same moment.

The classic error that teaches this:

let mut scores = vec![10, 20, 30];
let first = &scores[0];
scores.push(40); // error: cannot borrow as mutable
println!("{first}");

It feels pedantic until you realize why. push can reallocate the vector, which would leave first pointing at freed memory. In C that compiles and crashes later. Rust refuses up front.

Since the 2018 edition, borrows end at their last use, not at the end of the block (this is called non-lexical lifetimes). Move the println! above the push and it compiles. That one detail explains a lot of code that "shouldn't" work but does.

Leave lifetimes for later

Beginners often try to learn lifetime annotations in week one, and it's a mistake. Most of the time the compiler infers them. You only need to write 'a when a function returns a reference and the compiler can't tell which input it came from:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
}

Read that as "the result lives at least as long as both inputs." Learn it when you actually hit the error. Not before.

Read the error messages slowly

Rust's compiler errors are unusually good. They point at where the value was moved, where it was borrowed and where you tried to use it again, often with a suggested fix. I used to skim to the red line and start guessing. Reading the whole message, including the notes, fixed more bugs for me than any blog post.

rustc --explain E0382 (or whatever code you got) prints a longer explanation with examples. Worth doing for the first few errors you see repeatedly.

Practice on small programs that force the issue

Toy exercises help. Rustlings has a whole section on move semantics, and it's the fastest way to get reps. After that, build something small where data has to be shared:

  • A to-do CLI that loads tasks from a file into a Vec<Task> and lets you edit them.
  • A word counter that returns a HashMap<&str, usize> borrowing from the input text.
  • A tiny linked list. It's painful on purpose, and it teaches you why Box, Rc and RefCell exist.

When you reach for .clone() to make an error go away, write down why. Sometimes cloning is the right call. Often it's a sign you wanted a borrow.

Make the model stick

My real problem wasn't understanding ownership once. I'd get it after a weekend, take two weeks off for work, and come back to the same moved-value error as if I'd never seen it. The rules are short, but the instinct for applying them fades fast if you don't revisit it.

What helped was keeping a short list of the ideas that kept tripping me up (moves vs Copy, shared vs mutable borrows, borrows ending at last use, when lifetimes need writing) and going back over them after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and for a mental model like this it beats rereading chapter four every time you get stuck.

I build Recl, and this is the kind of learning it's for. You save a Rust talk from YouTube, a chapter of the Book or a blog post about the borrow checker, it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "Rust", and brings it back on a spaced repetition schedule so you get quizzed before you forget. A plain notes file and calendar reminders do the same job if you'd rather not use an app. The point is to see it again before the compiler has to remind you.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves the videos, reels and articles you learn from, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you actually remember them.

title: Solana pre-launch security checklist: 15 checks before mainnet
description:
An audit is necessary, but it is not a launch plan. Many incidents have nothing to do with a clever exploit in the program: a leaked upgrade key, a compromised frontend, an unaudited last-minute change, or nobody noticing a drain for hours. These 15 checks cover what usually goes wrong around the code. Assign a name to each line: a check without an owner is a check nobody did.

Keys and authorities

  • [ ] 1. Move the program upgrade authority to a multisig (signers on separate devices, never the development agency).
  • [ ] 2. Decide your upgrade policy in public: upgradeable, behind a timelock or immutable.
  • [ ] 3. Review token mint and freeze authorities. Revoke what you do not need, document what you keep and why.
  • [ ] 4. Audit every admin instruction (fees, pauses, parameters, withdrawals): right signer, controlled by the multisig.

Code and deployment

  • [ ] 5. Deploy exactly the audited commit. Anything changed after the audit is unaudited code.
  • [ ] 6. Publish a verifiable build so anyone can confirm the on-chain program matches your public source.
  • [ ] 7. Test failure paths: wrong signer, wrong owner, duplicated accounts, zero and maximum amounts.
  • [ ] 8. Rehearse the launch on devnet with production settings, including multisig steps.
  • [ ] 9. Plan account migrations before you need them: reserve space or version your accounts.

Operations

  • [ ] 10. Set up monitoring and alerts for unusual outflows, failed transaction spikes, admin instructions and authority changes.
  • [ ] 11. Use more than one RPC provider, with a fallback and rate limits.
  • [ ] 12. Protect the frontend and domain: registrar lock, two-factor authentication, restricted deploy access, pinned third-party scripts.
  • [ ] 13. Write an incident response plan: who can pause, how they reach each other, who talks to users, which partners to call.
  • [ ] 14. Launch a bug bounty sized relative to the funds at risk.
  • [ ] 15. Cap risk at launch with deposit caps or rate limits, and raise them as confidence grows.

Verify that deployed code matches the audited code

Build the audited commit and compare it with the program on chain using solana-verify get-program-hash and solana-verify verify-from-repo. Once remote verification succeeds, explorers such as Solana Explorer, SolanaFM and Solscan show the program as verified.

Full article with FAQ: https://orivions.com/blog/solana-pre-launch-security-checklist
All three checklists on GitHub: https://github.com/JakeMalarczyk/solana-security-checklists

title: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them
description:
On Friday at 17:40, someone renamed one column in the orders table. The pipeline stayed green all weekend. On Monday, the revenue dashboard showed zero for Saturday and Sunday. Nothing failed, and that was the problem.

This is Part 5 of CDC in Production. In Part 4 the sink learned to survive duplicates, late events and deletes. This time the table itself changes. We'll follow a schema change through the pipeline, look at the registry rules that decide what's allowed, see what Snowflake and the lakehouse can absorb, and finish with a migration pattern that never breaks either side.

Prefer to watch? Here's the 7-minute video version with animated diagrams:

Video link: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them

How a schema change travels

Postgres logical decoding (the feature that turns the write-ahead log into row changes) doesn't carry DDL. So Debezium never sees the ALTER TABLE itself. It notices the new shape on the next row change for that table and refreshes its in-memory schema. That event goes out with the new structure.

If you use Avro, the converter then registers the new structure as a new schema version in Schema Registry, a service that stores every version of each message schema. Versions are grouped under a subject; with the default naming, the value schema for topic shop.public.orders lives under shop.public.orders-value. Before accepting a new version, the registry runs a compatibility check against what's already there.

The converter is configured on the connector (or the Connect worker):

"value.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
"value.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry:8081"

Registry compatibility modes

Compatibility is the rule the registry uses to decide whether a new version may be registered. The default is BACKWARD.

Mode Guarantee Upgrade first
BACKWARD (default) Consumers using the new schema can read data written with the old one Consumers
FORWARD Consumers using the old schema can read data written with the new one Producers
FULL Both directions Either side, independently

By default the check compares only against the latest version. The _TRANSITIVE variants (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE and so on) compare against every version, which matters if a consumer might replay old data from the start of a topic.

What does that allow in practice, with Avro?

Change BACKWARD FORWARD FULL
Add an optional field (has a default) ✅ ✅ ✅
Remove an optional field ✅ ✅ ✅
Add a required field (no default) ❌ ✅ ❌
Remove a required field ✅ ❌ ❌

All of it comes from one rule in Avro's schema resolution: if the reader's schema has a field with no default, and the data was written without that field, the read fails. With Debezium, a nullable Postgres column becomes an optional field with a null default. A NOT NULL column becomes a required field, unless Debezium can carry the column's default value into the schema (it does this for many defaults; for function defaults, see mistake 4 below).

The rename, two ways

amount_cents became total_cents. To Debezium, that's one field gone and a new one added.

If the column is NOT NULL, the new field is required, with no default. Under BACKWARD, the registry rejects it. The converter throws, and with Kafka Connect's default errors.tolerance=none, the connector task fails. That's loud, and loud is good: someone gets paged on Friday.

In the real incident, the column was nullable. Both fields are optional, so the registry accepts the change and nothing turns red. Snowflake, with schema evolution switched on, adds a TOTAL_CENTS column. The old AMOUNT_CENTS column gets NULL on every new row. Every dashboard still sums AMOUNT_CENTS, so weekend revenue reads zero.

A failed connector is the good outcome. The dangerous schema changes are the ones every system accepts.

What Snowflake absorbs

Schema evolution lets a load add columns to the target table automatically. It needs three things:

ALTER TABLE analytics.orders SET ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE;

-- The loading role needs EVOLVE SCHEMA (or OWNERSHIP) on the table
GRANT EVOLVE SCHEMA ON TABLE analytics.orders TO ROLE loader;

and a supported loading method: COPY INTO (with MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME), Snowpipe, or Snowpipe Streaming. Plain INSERT can't evolve a table.

And it does only two things:

  • it adds new columns, and
  • it drops NOT NULL from columns that are missing in new data.

It never renames and never changes a type.

Type changes through ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN are stricter still:

Change Allowed?
Make a VARCHAR longer ✅
Raise a number's precision ✅
Change a number's scale ❌
Make a VARCHAR shorter ❌
Turn a number into a VARCHAR ❌

So if Postgres moves price from numeric(10,2) to numeric(12,4), Snowflake can't follow in place. The scale changed. You add a new column, backfill it, and switch readers over, which is the pattern at the end of this post.

The lakehouse: more forgiving, not magic

Apache Iceberg tracks every column by a unique field ID, not by its name. Renames and drops are metadata changes, so no data files are rewritten. A new column gets a fresh ID, so it never reads old data by mistake, even if it reuses an old name. Type changes are limited to safe widening: int to long, float to double, or a decimal with more precision and the same scale.

Delta Lake can rename and drop columns only with column mapping enabled:

ALTER TABLE orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',
  'delta.minReaderVersion'   = '2',
  'delta.minWriterVersion'   = '5'
);

That's a protocol upgrade you can't undo, and after a rename or drop it can break readers of the table's change data feed.

Here's the catch for both formats: a CDC sink still sees a rename as a dropped field and a new one, because that's what the events say. Unless you rename the table column yourself, you get the same split as in Snowflake.

Expand, then contract

The safe pattern is expand/contract: make the schema bigger first, move everything over, and only then make it smaller. A rename becomes four steps:

-- 1. Expand: add the new column as nullable (or with a constant default)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents bigint;

-- 2. Backfill in small batches, and have the application write both columns
UPDATE orders
SET    total_cents = amount_cents
WHERE  total_cents IS NULL
  AND  id BETWEEN 1 AND 50000;

-- 3. Move every reader (views, models, dashboards) to total_cents

-- 4. Contract, weeks later, once nothing reads the old column
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN amount_cents;

Because amount_cents was nullable, every step only adds or removes an optional field, which the registry accepts in any mode. (Dropping a NOT NULL column removes a required field, which passes BACKWARD but not FORWARD or FULL.) Two practical notes:

  • The backfill is CDC traffic. Every row it updates becomes a change event, which is why it runs in batches.
  • Snowflake won't drop the old column for you. Schema evolution never removes columns. Drop AMOUNT_CENTS in the warehouse yourself once readers have moved.

Two guardrails

Test schemas in CI. Schema Registry has a compatibility endpoint that tells you whether a schema would be accepted, without registering it:

# Wrap the new Avro schema in the request body the registry expects
python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.dumps({"schema": open(sys.argv[1]).read()}))' \
  orders-value.avsc > payload.json

curl -X POST \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \
  --data @payload.json \
  'http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/shop.public.orders-value/versions/latest?verbose=true'
# {"is_compatible":false,"messages":[...]}

Fail the build when is_compatible is false. Remember that a nullable rename passes this check, so it catches only the loud kind of break.

Watch the warehouse. Alert when a new column appears on a captured table, and when a column's null rate jumps:

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', updated_at)              AS hour,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS rows_loaded,
       COUNT_IF(amount_cents IS NULL) / COUNT(*)   AS null_rate
FROM   analytics.orders
WHERE  updated_at >= DATEADD(day, -2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP  BY 1
HAVING null_rate > 0.2
ORDER  BY 1;

The threshold is yours to pick. Either alert would have caught Friday's rename on Friday night.

Five common mistakes

  1. Renaming a column with a single ALTER. Use expand/contract.
  2. Changing a numeric column's scale in place. Snowflake can't follow.
  3. Setting compatibility to NONE just to get a failed connector running again. You've switched off the only alarm.
  4. Trusting function defaults. Debezium exports a default like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) as a zero value (1970-01-01) in the schema.
  5. Changing a schema during an incremental snapshot. The Postgres connector doesn't support it.

Recap

  • Postgres doesn't send DDL, so the next event carries the new schema.
  • The registry checks compatibility, BACKWARD by default. Optional fields are safe to add or remove; required fields are not.
  • Snowflake adds columns, but never renames or changes types.
  • In the lakehouse, your sink still sees a rename as a drop and an add.
  • So expand, then contract.

This week, find the last schema change on a captured table and check what it did in the warehouse.

The CDC in Production series

  • Part 1: Change Data Capture (CDC) Explained (article · video)
  • Part 2: Debezium Postgres to Kafka: Every Setting Explained (video)
  • Part 3: The Silent CDC Bug: Data Loss With No Errors (video)
  • Previous, Part 4: CDC Deletes, Tombstones and the Idempotent MERGE (video)
  • Part 5: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them (this post · video)
  • Next, Part 6: Running CDC in Production: The WAL Slot Trap (video, out November 2)

If this was useful, the video version has the animated diagrams for every step: watch it on YouTube. Subscribe to Pipeline Whiteboard for more diagram-first data engineering explainers. Next up, in the final part: the WAL slot trap, lag, heartbeats, alerting and runbooks.

title: Designing an AI song generator: the UI states beyond the prompt box
description:
Disclosure: I work on SingMyLyrics. This article was written with AI assistance. These are design recommendations, not a claim that every safeguard described below is already implemented in the product.

A song generator can start with a single text box. The difficult part is explaining what happens after someone presses Generate, especially when they have pasted lyrics they care about and the request spends credits.

The product context is straightforward: someone brings original words, chooses a musical style and voice, and wants to hear an arrangement. The lyrics-to-song walkthrough shows that user-facing task. Here is how I would break down the interface contract behind it.

1. Model writing and generation as separate actions

An idea such as "a birthday song about our late-night road trips" is not the same input as a finished verse and chorus.

Give the composer an explicit mode: start from an idea, or use my lyrics. If an AI writes a draft, keep the draft editable before sending it to audio generation. Avoid making a user regenerate the audio just to correct a name in the text.

Treat a title as optional metadata where the provider permits it. If the provider requires one, validate that requirement before submission. The same applies to length limits: count the text that will actually be submitted, including section markers, rather than guessing from the visible number of lines.

2. Keep the user's text when a request fails

A failed request should leave the lyrics, title and musical choices intact. Store the current draft in component state and consider a local draft with a clear delete option for recovery after navigation.

Local persistence has a privacy tradeoff. Lyrics may contain personal stories. Tell users when a draft is stored on their device, avoid putting the text in URLs, and do not send full lyrics to analytics just to count form errors.

3. Separate job state from the browser's patience

The following is an illustrative UI model, not a provider API schema:

type GenerationView =
  | { kind: "editing" }
  | { kind: "submitting"; requestId: string }
  | { kind: "pending"; jobId: string }
  | { kind: "ready"; jobId: string; songId: string }
  | { kind: "failed"; jobId?: string; message: string }
  | { kind: "checking"; jobId: string };

checking matters. A browser that has stopped waiting does not prove that the provider stopped working. Keep the job identifier and offer a status refresh. Starting a new generation should be an explicit action because it may create another charge.

Use provider progress only when the provider actually reports it. Otherwise, an honest "Still generating" message is more useful than an invented percentage or a countdown that repeatedly resets.

4. Make credit handling a server responsibility

Show the credit cost before submission, but resolve the authoritative price and balance on the server. A disabled Generate button improves the interface; it does not prevent duplicate requests from another tab or a network retry.

A robust design needs a stable request identity, an atomic balance update and a durable record of the resulting job. Repeating the same request identity should retrieve the existing job rather than spend again. If the provider supports idempotency, pass an appropriate identity through that boundary too. Without that support, a timeout during submission needs reconciliation before resubmission.

Also distinguish a credit reservation, a final charge and a refund in the ledger. The appropriate policy depends on the provider's billing behavior. Whatever policy you choose, explain it in the interface and apply refunds once, even if a failure event arrives twice.

5. Make playback and download recoverable

"Job completed" and "this browser can play the file" are different checks. The player needs a visible loading state and a useful media-error state. Keep the generated song page reachable if playback fails.

If a provider returns temporary audio URLs, decide whether you will copy permitted assets into durable storage or refresh the URL through the server. Do not promise permanent downloads until the storage and retention policy supports that promise.

6. Test transitions, not just the happy path

Before polishing the waveform, try these scenarios:

  • Double-click Generate and confirm that one intended request creates one job and one credit operation.
  • Refresh while a job is pending and confirm that its status can be recovered.
  • Let a browser request time out, then let the provider finish, and confirm that the finished song remains discoverable.
  • Deliver the same completion or failure event twice and confirm that neither the charge nor refund is duplicated.
  • Return a completed job with an unavailable media URL and confirm that the UI preserves the song record and offers recovery.
  • Fail lyric generation and confirm that the original idea is still present.

These checks do not establish musical quality. They establish whether the application respects the user's input, time and credits. That is a useful foundation for any product that turns a prompt into a slower, paid generation job.

title: How long does a Postgres restore actually take?
description:
When someone asks how long it would take to get the database back, the answer is usually a guess based on the size of the dump. I wanted a real number, so we timed it: one schema at four sizes, from a 400 MB Supabase project up to a 10 GB database with 18.8 million rows, each dump restored into an empty PostgreSQL 17 on a single 2 vCPU / 8 GB VM.

The 10 GB restore took about 12 minutes. Most of those 12 minutes went to rebuilding indexes and foreign keys. Loading the rows was the smaller part, and that changes how you should estimate your own restore.

The numbers

Plain pg_restore with one job, into a fresh PostgreSQL 17 container:

Database Rows Dump Restore
396 MiB (real Supabase Free project) 723,500 74.6 MiB 19.4 s
1.03 GiB 2,172,000 226.5 MiB 65.9 s
5.04 GiB 9,222,000 1.00 GiB 379.8 s (6.3 min)
10.05 GiB 18,822,000 1.74 GiB 725.9 s (12.1 min)

Sizes are pg_database_size of the source. The schema is modeled on a multi-tenant SaaS app with an AI feature: orgs, users, projects, orders, an events table with JSONB payloads, a documents table with 384-dimension pgvector embeddings, 16 indexes, 7 RLS policies, triggers and functions. The three bigger databases are synthetic copies of that schema, and most of their size is event rows.

I also restored every dump twice through the restore drill of BackupDrill, the backup tool I work on. At every size, the restore step of those drills averaged within 5% of the single-job time above. That comparison is the restore alone; a full drill also downloads the dump, starts the database and checks every table.

Two things to keep in mind before you quote any of this:

  1. The target ran with durability turned off: fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off, wal_level=minimal, shared_buffers at 1.9 GB and maintenance_work_mem at 960 MB. That's fine for a test copy you delete afterwards. It's not how you'd run a database you're recovering production into. In a separate run earlier the same day, the 1 GB restore took 61 seconds with these settings and 110 seconds on stock PostgreSQL settings, about 1.8x slower.
  2. There's no download time in here. The dump sat in a bucket on the same VM; the 1.74 GiB dump came down in 15 seconds. If your backup lives in another region, add however long it takes to move the file.

Where the 12 minutes went

The 10 GB restore, one job, timed step by step from pg_restore --verbose:

Step Time Share
Build the pgvector HNSW index (200,000 embeddings, 384 dimensions) 184.8 s 25%
Build the JSONB GIN index on events 145.5 s 20%
Load the events table (13.5 million rows) 141.3 s 19%
Add the three foreign keys on events 102.8 s 14%
Add the primary key on events 57.7 s 8%
Build the (project_id, created_at) index on events 43.3 s 6%
Everything else: five smaller tables, their indexes and constraints, RLS policies, triggers 50.5 s 7%
Total 725.9 s 100%

Loading the biggest table, 13.5 million rows, took 141 seconds. One HNSW index over 200,000 vectors took longer than that on its own. Averaged over the two drill restores of this database, 77% of the restore (559 of 722 seconds) went to indexes, constraints and foreign keys, and 163 seconds to loading all 18.8 million rows.

That follows from what a custom-format dump contains. It has the rows and the definition of each index, not the index itself. pg_database_size counts index pages; the dump doesn't carry any. Across all four databases the compressed dump came out at 17–22% of the database size, and every index missing from the file gets built from scratch during the restore. Foreign keys get checked again against every row.

Estimate from your schema, not your dump size

Two databases with the same dump size can restore at very different speeds. One with a few large tables and a primary key on each is mostly COPY. One with GIN indexes on JSONB, trigram indexes, a vector index and a dozen foreign keys spends most of its restore in CREATE INDEX and ALTER TABLE.

You can see how much rebuilding is waiting in a dump before you restore anything:

pg_restore --list app.dump | grep -cE ' INDEX | CONSTRAINT | FK CONSTRAINT '

A count won't give you minutes, though. For that, time a restore of your own dump in a throwaway container. This one uses the same kind of tuning as our test target:

docker run -d --name restore-test -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw \
  -p 127.0.0.1:5433:5432 --shm-size=1g postgres:17 \
  -c fsync=off -c synchronous_commit=off -c full_page_writes=off \
  -c wal_level=minimal -c max_wal_senders=0 \
  -c shared_buffers=2GB -c maintenance_work_mem=1GB

Scale shared_buffers and maintenance_work_mem down on a machine with less memory. --shm-size matters because parallel index builds, HNSW builds included, use shared memory, and Docker's default 64 MB can be too small for them. wal_level=minimal only starts with max_wal_senders=0. If your tables have vector columns, swap postgres:17 for an image that ships pgvector, such as pgvector/pgvector:pg17, which is what our test used. Our target also had the extensions the schema needed (pg_trgm, pgvector) and Supabase's auth stubs created before the restore.

Then restore with a timestamp on every line of verbose output:

PGPASSWORD=pw pg_restore --verbose --no-owner --no-privileges \
  -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U postgres -d postgres app.dump 2>&1 \
  | perl -MTime::HiRes=time -ne 'printf "%.1f %s", time, $_' > restore.log

And list the slowest steps:

awk 'NR > 1 { printf "%6.1fs  %s\n", $1 - prev_time, prev_line }
     { prev_time = $1; $1 = ""; prev_line = $0 }' restore.log | sort -rn | head

With a single job, the gap between one line and the next is roughly how long the step on the first line took, so the top of that list is where your restore time goes. Use a pg_restore of the same major version as the pg_dump that made the file, or newer. If the dump came from Supabase and the restore complains about the auth schema, I wrote up the stubs a plain Postgres target needs a while ago.

What these numbers don't cover

  • More cores. Everything here ran on 2 vCPU. pg_restore --jobs can build several indexes at the same time, so a bigger machine can beat these numbers. We didn't test one.
  • Restoring into a new Supabase project. Speed then depends on the project's compute size and your connection to it.
  • Supabase's own restore from daily backups or point-in-time recovery. The Free plan has neither, so we couldn't time it.
  • Other schemas. More indexes per gigabyte, bigger vector indexes or thousands of small tables will spend the time differently.

Taking the backup was the quick part, at least for the small database: 25 seconds to dump the 400 MB Supabase Free project through the Session pooler from a VM in the same region (Ashburn to us-east-1), for a 75 MB file.

The full result tables, the drill timings, the test setup and the list of what we didn't test are on the benchmark page.

I work on BackupDrill, which runs scheduled backups and restore drills for Supabase projects. The drill timings above come from its open-source CLI; the plain pg_restore numbers don't depend on it.

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

title: Embed Sentences, Return the Section: Small-to-Big Retrieval in TypeScript
description:
• Book: AI That Reads
  • The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

A user asks your docs bot: "Can I get a refund on an annual plan after 30 days?" Retrieval works. The top hit is the sentence "Annual plans are refundable within 30 days of purchase." The model reads it and says no. The next sentence in the same section, the one that says prorated refunds apply after day 30, never made it into the prompt. It lived in a different chunk, that chunk ranked ninth, and your retriever sends the top five.

Now flip it. You chunk by whole sections instead, 800 tokens each. The refund section covers refunds, invoices, tax IDs and currency changes. Its embedding is an average of four topics, and it loses to a short FAQ entry that happens to say "refund" twice.

That is the chunk-size trade-off, and LangChain's docs for its ParentDocumentRetriever put it plainly: you want small documents "so that their embeddings can most accurately reflect their meaning", and long enough documents "that the context of each chunk is retained". The fix they describe is to search the small pieces and return the big ones. People call it parent-document retrieval or small-to-big. Below is the whole thing in TypeScript, no framework, plus a check you can run against your own docs.

The shape: children that point at parents

Two tables. Parents are sections of your docs, split on headings. Children are runs of one or two sentences cut out of a parent, and each child stores its parent's ID. You embed only the children. At query time you rank children, map each hit to its parent, drop duplicate parents, and fill a token budget with whole sections.


Search the sentence, return the page it came from.

This is the same idea frameworks ship under other names. LlamaIndex's AutoMergingRetriever builds a three-level hierarchy (2048, 512 and 128 tokens by default) and merges leaf hits into their parent once enough of a parent's leaves match. Writing it yourself takes about a page of code and means you can see every decision.

Setup, on Node 20 or later:

npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm i openai js-tiktoken
npm i -D tsx typescript

The openai client reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment. js-tiktoken counts tokens, and tsx runs the .ts files directly.

Splitting: sections and sentences

Parents come from headings. Children come from Intl.Segmenter with sentence granularity, which ships with Node, so there is no regex guessing where sentences end.

// chunk.ts
import { getEncoding } from "js-tiktoken";

const enc = getEncoding("cl100k_base");
export const countTokens = (s: string) =>
  enc.encode(s).length;

export type Parent = {
  id: string;
  title: "string;"
  text: string;
  tokens: number;
};

export type Child = {
  id: string;
  parentId: string;
  text: string;
};

Parents carry their token count so the budget check later is a lookup, not a re-encode. The two splitters go in the same file:

// chunk.ts (continued)
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("en", {
  granularity: "sentence",
});

export function splitSections(
  doc: string,
  file: string,
): Parent[] {
  return doc
    .split(/^(?=#{1,3} )/m)
    .map((t) => t.trim())
    .filter((t) => t.length > 0)
    .map((text, i) => ({
      id: `${file}#${i}`,
      title: "text.split(\"\n\")[0],"
      text,
      tokens: countTokens(text),
    }));
}

export function splitChildren(
  p: Parent,
  size = 2,
): Child[] {
  const sentences = [...seg.segment(p.text)]
    .map((s) => s.segment.trim())
    .filter((s) => s.length > 0);
  const out: Child[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < sentences.length; i += size) {
    out.push({
      id: `${p.id}/${out.length}`,
      parentId: p.id,
      text: sentences.slice(i, i + size).join(" "),
    });
  }
  return out;
}

cl100k_base is the encoding OpenAI's token-counting cookbook lists for the text-embedding-3 models. It is only used here to measure section size for the budget, so a close count is enough.

Two sentences per child is only a starting point. One sentence matches tightest; three survives pronouns like "this plan" better. The eval at the end is how you pick.

Embedding and indexing the children

OpenAI's embeddings endpoint takes an array of inputs, up to 2,048 items and 300,000 tokens summed per request, according to the API reference. Batches of 512 sentence-sized children stay well under both limits.

// embed.ts
import OpenAI from "openai";

const openai = new OpenAI();
const MODEL = "text-embedding-3-small";

export async function embed(
  texts: string[],
): Promise<number[][]> {
  const out: number[][] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < texts.length; i += 512) {
    const res = await openai.embeddings.create({
      model: MODEL,
      input: texts.slice(i, i + 512),
      encoding_format: "float",
    });
    res.data.sort((a, b) => a.index - b.index);
    out.push(...res.data.map((d) => d.embedding));
  }
  return out;
}

export function dot(a: number[], b: number[]) {
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i];
  return s;
}

A plain dot product works as cosine similarity here because OpenAI's embeddings guide states its embeddings are normalized to length 1. If you swap in a model that does not normalize, divide by the norms.

The index keeps parents in a Map and children in an array, each child carrying parentId and its vector:

// index.ts
import { readFile, readdir } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";
import {
  splitSections, splitChildren,
  type Parent, type Child,
} from "./chunk.ts";
import { embed, dot } from "./embed.ts";

export type Indexed = Child & { vec: number[] };
export type Index = {
  parents: Map<string, Parent>;
  children: Indexed[];
};

export async function buildIndex(dir: string) {
  const parents = new Map<string, Parent>();
  const kids: Child[] = [];
  for (const f of await readdir(dir)) {
    if (!f.endsWith(".md")) continue;
    const doc = await readFile(join(dir, f), "utf8");
    for (const p of splitSections(doc, f)) {
      parents.set(p.id, p);
      kids.push(...splitChildren(p));
    }
  }
  const vecs = await embed(kids.map((c) => c.text));
  const children = kids.map((c, i) => ({
    ...c,
    vec: vecs[i],
  }));
  return { parents, children } as Index;
}

In production the same shape is two tables: sections(id, title, text, tokens) and chunks(id, section_id, text, embedding), with the vector column in something like pgvector. The retrieval logic below does not change.

Retrieval: rank children, return parents within a budget 

// index.ts (continued)
export function rank(ix: Index, q: number[], k = 40) {
  return ix.children
    .map((c) => ({ c, score: dot(q, c.vec) }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, k)
    .map((h) => h.c);
}

export function smallToBig(
  ix: Index,
  q: number[],
  budget = 1500,
): Parent[] {
  const picked: Parent[] = [];
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  let used = 0;
  for (const c of rank(ix, q)) {
    if (seen.has(c.parentId)) continue;
    seen.add(c.parentId);
    const p = ix.parents.get(c.parentId)!;
    if (used + p.tokens > budget) continue;
    picked.push(p);
    used += p.tokens;
  }
  return picked;
}

A parent's rank is the rank of its best child, because the loop visits children in score order and keeps the first time each parent appears. The continue on an over-budget section matters: a 1,400-token section ranked second should not block a 200-token section ranked third from fitting.

The baseline to compare against fills the same budget with child text only:

// index.ts (continued)
export function childOnly(
  ix: Index,
  q: number[],
  budget = 1500,
): Indexed[] {
  const picked: Indexed[] = [];
  let used = 0;
  for (const c of rank(ix, q)) {
    const t = Math.ceil(c.text.length / 4);
    if (used + t > budget) break;
    picked.push(c);
    used += t;
  }
  return picked;
}


Many child hits, a few parents, one token budget.

Things to watch. A section bigger than the whole budget can never be returned, so split long sections at index time (by subheading, or every ~800 tokens). The segmenter breaks at every newline, so a heading becomes its own segment and hard-wrapped markdown splits mid-sentence; if your docs are wrapped, join single newlines inside a paragraph (text.replace(/(?<!\n)\n(?!\n)/g, " ")) before segmenting. And childOnly estimates tokens as length divided by four to stay cheap; it is the baseline, so being roughly fair is enough.

Check it on your own docs

Whether small-to-big beats plain sentence chunks depends on your docs. Short self-contained FAQ answers may not need it. Long reference pages with exceptions two sentences after the rule usually do. So measure it.

Write 20 to 30 questions in eval.json. For each one, record the section ID that answers it and a needle: the shortest exact phrase from the docs that a correct answer depends on.

[
  {
    "q": "Can I get a refund on an annual plan after 30 days?",
    "parent": "billing.md#3",
    "needle": "prorated refund for the unused months"
  }
]

Then score both strategies at the same budget:

// eval.ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { buildIndex, smallToBig, childOnly } from "./index.ts";
import { embed } from "./embed.ts";

type Case = { q: string; parent: string; needle: string };

const norm = (s: string) =>
  s.replace(/\s+/g, " ").toLowerCase();

const ix = await buildIndex("./docs");
const cases: Case[] = JSON.parse(
  await readFile("eval.json", "utf8"),
);

const s = { bigSec: 0, bigNeedle: 0, kidSec: 0, kidNeedle: 0 };
for (const c of cases) {
  const [q] = await embed([c.q]);
  const big = smallToBig(ix, q);
  const kids = childOnly(ix, q);
  const n = norm(c.needle);
  s.bigSec += +big.some((p) => p.id === c.parent);
  s.kidSec += +kids.some((k) => k.parentId === c.parent);
  s.bigNeedle += +norm(big.map((p) => p.text).join(" "))
    .includes(n);
  s.kidNeedle += +norm(kids.map((k) => k.text).join(" "))
    .includes(n);
}

const pct = (x: number) =>
  `${((100 * x) / cases.length).toFixed(0)}%`;
console.log("small-to-big section", pct(s.bigSec));
console.log("small-to-big needle ", pct(s.bigNeedle));
console.log("child-only section  ", pct(s.kidSec));
console.log("child-only needle   ", pct(s.kidNeedle));

Run it with npx tsx eval.ts. The two numbers per strategy answer different questions. "Section" asks whether retrieval found the right place at all. "Needle" asks whether the text the answer depends on is actually in front of the model. The gap between child-only's section and needle scores is the refund story from the top: the right section was touched, but the sentence that mattered stayed behind. Expect that gap to widen as the budget shrinks.

Limits. Questions you write while looking at the docs reuse the docs' wording, which flatters both strategies; real queries from your logs are a better source. The needle check is exact substring matching, so pick phrases that do not contain markdown formatting. And a 1,500-token budget is arbitrary: rerun at 800 and 3,000, because the comparison can flip as the budget changes. I haven't run this against any particular corpus, so I can't tell you which way yours will go. That is the point of the script.

If this was useful

Chunking is where a lot of RAG answers go missing, and small-to-big is one of several patterns for getting the right text in front of the model. AI That Reads is the RAG book in the AI in TypeScript series: embeddings, chunking, vector search and grounding answers in your own docs, all in TypeScript. If this post was the kind of problem you are fighting, the book is the longer version of it.

The rest of the series, from your first LLM call to agents in production, is at xgabriel.com/ai-in-typescript.

title: Discriminated Unions in TypeScript
description:
Earlier, we looked at how custom type guards (value is Type) let you manually inspect unknown data and teach TypeScript its shape. But what if you have a set of known object types that share a common property?

Enter Discriminated Unions (sometimes called tagged unions or algebraic data types). They are one of the most powerful patterns in TypeScript because TypeScript does the type narrowing for you automatically—no custom guard function required.

1. What is a Discriminated Union?

A discriminated union is a combination of three things:

  1. Types with a common property (the discriminant or "tag"), where each type has a unique literal type for that property.
  2. A union of those types.
  3. A conditional check (like a switch statement) on that discriminant property.

Let’s see it in action with a classic real-world scenario: asynchronous state management.

2. Practical Example: State Management

Imagine you are building a component that fetches data from an API. At any given moment, your state can be in one of three phases: Loading, Success, or Error.

If you lump everything into one giant interface with optional fields (data?: User, error?: string), you open the door to impossible states (like having both data and an error, or neither).

Instead, model them as a discriminated union using a status tag:

// 1. Define individual state shapes with a unique literal `status` property
interface IdleState {
  status: "idle";
}

interface LoadingState {
  status: "loading";
}

interface SuccessState {
  status: "success";
  data: { id: number; name: string }; // Only exists on success!
}

interface ErrorState {
  status: "error";
  error: Error; // Only exists on error!
}

// 2. Combine them into a Union type
type FetchState = IdleState | LoadingState | SuccessState | ErrorState;

3. Automatic Narrowing in Action

When you consume a discriminated union, you can use a simple switch or if statement checking the status tag. Watch how TypeScript's control flow analysis automatically figures out what properties are safe to access:

function renderUI(state: FetchState) {
  // TypeScript knows `state` could be any of the 4 types

  switch (state.status) {
    case "idle":
      return "<p>Press button to fetch.</p>";

    case "loading":
      return "<p>Loading data...</p>";

    case "success":
      // 🚀 MAGIC: TypeScript automatically knows `state` is `SuccessState` here!
      // You have full type safety accessing `state.data`.
      return `<div>Welcome, ${state.data.name}</div>`;

    case "error":
      // TypeScript knows `state` is `ErrorState` here.
      // You have safe access to `state.error`.
      return `<p class="error">Error: ${state.error.message}</p>`;
  }
}

No as SuccessState type assertions, no manual in checks, and no runtime ambiguity. The literal type of status tells TypeScript precisely which branch of reality your code is operating in.

4. Pro-Tip: Exhaustiveness Checking with never

What happens if you add a new state later (like RetryingState), but forget to update your switch statement? In JavaScript, your UI might silently fail or render nothing.

You can force TypeScript to catch missing cases at compile time using the never type:

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unexpected object: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

function renderUI(state: FetchState) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "idle": return "...";
    case "loading": return "...";
    case "success": return "...";
    case "error": return "...";

    // If you add a new union member and forget a case, 
    // TypeScript will throw a compile error right here because `state` 
    // won't narrow to `never`!
    default:
      return assertNever(state); 
  }
}

Summary

  • Custom Type Guards are your best tool when dealing with untrusted, unstructured data coming from the outside world (unknown inputs).
  • Discriminated Unions are your best tool when designing internal application logic, state machines, and data structures where you control the shapes.

title: My Pool Has 4 Threads, DNS Gets 2
description:
In Node, the word "asynchronous" does not describe a single thing. Some calls
really are handed to the kernel and come back when the operating system is
ready; others are placed on one of four background threads and wait their turn.
The second kind is libuv's work pool, its size is four, and that number appears
in Node's documentation in a single aside: "its current default value".

What led me to that number was my cover generator. In batch mode
generate-hero.ts drains its queue with four workers — a hard-coded 4 inside
the script — and each worker is one sharp call. In a separate run, in a
separate process, my social posting script names nine external hosts in its
source. Both are "asynchronous", both sit on their own four threads, and I had
no idea how much of those four either one was holding. I wanted to measure this
properly, once. The result was sharper than I expected: dns.lookup can never
take more than two of those four threads, and neither libuv's documentation
nor Node's mentions that limit.

Who lands in the pool

Node's command-line documentation spells out the list: all fs calls except the
file watchers and the explicitly synchronous ones, asynchronous crypto calls
such as crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes and generateKeyPair, all
zlib calls except the explicitly synchronous ones, and dns.lookup. The
warning that follows is fair: because the pool has a fixed size, if one of these
takes a long time, other "seemingly unrelated" ones get slower.

The sneakiest member of that list is dns.lookup, because you are usually not
the one deciding to call it. In Node's lib/net.js, the connect path says it in
one line: const lookup = options.lookup || dns.lookup;. So net.connect,
http, https and fetch — undici, which sits underneath fetch, uses
net.connect for plain HTTP and tls.connect for TLS, and both pass through
that same line — resolve names through dns.lookup unless you supply your own
resolver. The first step of every outbound HTTP request queues on the same four
threads as your file reads.

The dns.resolve* family is not on that list. Node's documentation draws the
line clearly: those functions do not use getaddrinfo(3), they always query
over the network, and they do not use libuv's threadpool. Keep that distinction
in mind; we will come back to it with a measurement at the end.

The lab: my own resolver, a fixed 300 ms

Measuring against a real DNS server is pointless; if the latency moves, you
cannot read the table. So I wrote a 49-line UDP server: it holds every incoming
query for exactly 300 ms, then answers 127.0.0.2, sets TTL zero (no caching),
and most importantly it counts how many distinct names are in flight at the
same time. Instead of guessing concurrency from the client side, I let the
resolver count it.

The lab ran in a node:26-alpine container: Alpine 3.24, Node v26.13.0, libuv
1.52.1, aarch64, 14 cores. /etc/resolv.conf has one line: nameserver
127.0.0.1. The client calls dns.lookup for 24 distinct names at once, with
family: 4, so each name sends a single A query and the resolver's A/AAAA
behaviour stays out of the table. The numbers below are medians of three runs.
Alpine uses musl; since the limit measured here lives in libuv, the resolver
library does not change the result, but the nsswitch.conf argument later in
this article applies to glibc setups.

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE Concurrent queries counted by the resolver 24 names, total
unset (4) 2 3,695 ms
1 1 7,414 ms
2 1 7,427 ms
3 2 3,703 ms
4 2 3,712 ms
6 3 2,480 ms
8 4 1,859 ms
16 8 934 ms

The second column is exactly half the pool size, rounded up.

What amuses me most in this table is the relationship between the second and
third rows. Going from one thread to two moves the total for 24 names from 7,414
ms to 7,427 ms — that is, nowhere. I doubled the threads and what I gained on
the DNS side is smaller than the measurement noise. But going from two to three
cuts the time in half. Adding one thread buys nothing once and a factor of two
the next time.

The reason sits in libuv's source, on line 46 of src/threadpool.c:

static unsigned int slow_work_thread_threshold(void) {
  return (nthreads + 1) / 2;
}

libuv sorts work into three kinds: UV__WORK_CPU, UV__WORK_FAST_IO and
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO. src/unix/getaddrinfo.c submits its request as
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO; src/unix/fs.c submits every file operation as
UV__WORK_FAST_IO, and user code calling uv_queue_work submits as
UV__WORK_CPU. Slow-I/O work piles up in a separate queue and only a single
"there is slow work" marker goes into the main queue. When a thread picks up
that marker and starts running slow work, a counter goes up; if the counter has
reached the threshold, the thread pushes the marker back to the tail of the
queue and looks for other work.

So this is not an accident but a deliberate guard: it exists so a slow name
lookup cannot swallow the whole pool and block file reads. I have no objection
to the logic. My objection is that the limit is written down nowhere. libuv's
own documentation covers the default, the absolute maximum, and that the pool is
global and shared across all loops; for its scope it says "all file system
operations, as well as getaddrinfo and getnameinfo requests". Not one sentence
about the half-pool threshold. Node's UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE section does not have
it either: there the advice is simply to set a value greater than 4.

Follow that advice and DNS can use at most half of whatever you set. Write 8 and
the ceiling on your name-resolution concurrency is 4. It is a ceiling, not an
allocation: when there is no DNS work those slots do not sit idle, they take
other work.

Who starves whom

The direction of the threshold matters, because it is asymmetric. Two scenarios,
both with the pool at its default four threads:

A) With 32 pending dns.lookup calls (each answered by my 300 ms resolver)
I squeezed in one fs.readFile and one pbkdf2. The fs.readFile waited 0 ms,
the pbkdf2 2 ms. Thirty-two names are queued and the file read goes straight
through. The guard works.

B) With 32 pending pbkdf2 calls — a computation that takes 208 ms on its
own — I squeezed in one dns.lookup and one fs.readFile. The fs.readFile
waited 1,719 ms, the dns.lookup 2,018 ms.

The arithmetic of that second line lands exactly: 32 × 208 ms on four threads is
a 1,664 ms queue, and the measurement is 1,719 ms. DNS's 2,018 ms comes from the
same place — 1,719 ms of queue plus my resolver's fixed 300 ms, totalling 2,019
ms. The resolver answers in 300 ms while dns.lookup takes two seconds, and 85
percent of that has nothing to do with resolving a name.

The lesson here runs the other way: some investigations that start with "our DNS
is slow" are looking in the wrong place. What fills the pool is not name
resolution but the crypto, compression or image work in the same process. The
slow-I/O threshold stops DNS from choking everyone else; nothing stops everyone
else from choking DNS.

Where the threshold sits on my own pipeline

The same question goes to my cover generator, since that is where it started.
came from. generate-hero.ts makes a single sharp call: it rasterises the SVG
at 200 dpi, fits it to 1200×630 and writes a PNG with compressionLevel: 9. On
my Mac (Node v22.16.0, libuv 1.49.2, sharp 0.35.5, libvips 8.18.7, 14 cores)
that call takes 75 ms on its own. On an idle pool an fs.readFile takes 0.2 ms.

I started the same call N times concurrently and squeezed in a read of a real
article file:

Concurrent covers How long fs.readFile waited
1 0 ms
2 0 ms
3 0 ms
4 9 ms (three runs: 1 – 31 ms)
8 62 ms (three runs: 56 – 69 ms)

The threshold is exactly at four. Up to three there is still a free thread in
the pool, so the read never waits; the moment a fourth cover enters, it starts
waiting. I will not lean on the 9 ms in the fourth row — across three runs it
wandered between 1 and 31 ms, because the instant a thread frees up is a matter
of chance. At eight the number is steady: about 60 ms.

Something caught my eye here. My script does not only write two PNGs per article
and exit; in --all mode it drains the queue with four workers, and that four
is a constant I put there myself: Array.from({ length: 4 }, ...). The comment
next to it says it "gains parallel I/O". So when I rebuild the covers for all
2,772 posts I fill the entire pool, and the fourth row of the table is exactly
that point. When I wrote that 4 I did not know the pool was also four; the two
numbers matching is a coincidence, what follows from it is not — during an
--all run every fs read and every dns.lookup in the same process queues
behind it.

The absolute values are small, I know. What interests me is not the absolute
value but that the threshold is visible at all. And one more thing: there is not
a single line in my repository that mentions UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Not in the
scripts, not in the systemd units, not in the workflows. I have been running
on four threads and until today I had not chosen that deliberately.

When exactly is the pool born

Node's documentation says that setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE "is not
guaranteed to work" and gives a reason: the pool would have been created "as
part of the runtime initialisation much before user code is run". The warning
itself is right; the reason does not hold on the Node in this lab.

libuv's pool is lazy. The first line of uv__work_submit is uv_once(&once,
init_once) — the pool is born when the first piece of work is submitted. We can
count it from outside, because since libuv 1.50.0 the threads are named
libuv-worker:

# process is up but nothing has hit the pool yet
$ ls /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm | xargs cat | grep -c libuv-worker
0

After a single dns.lookup, that same count returns whatever
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE says — 4 if you wrote 4, 128 if you wrote 128, for one
request. That is precisely libuv's sentence about preallocating the maximum
number of threads allowed. Five rows, same lab, on where the value is set:

Where it was set Concurrency counted by the resolver 24 names
nowhere (default 4) 2 3,695 ms
first line of the JS: process.env... = '16' 8 930 ms
the same line after one fs.readFile 2 3,720 ms
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 in the shell 8 923 ms
node --env-file=uv.env 8 934 ms

The third row vindicates the documentation's warning, but for a different
reason: the setting is not missed because the runtime built the pool early; it
is missed because someone submitted work to the pool before you did. A library
that reads a file with top-level await, or a dependency that calls
randomBytes, quietly makes your setting irrelevant. So the advice stands: do
not set this value from inside your code. The two honest paths in the table
above are the shell environment and --env-file; both land before the first
job.

The bill for growing it

The ceiling is 1024 (libuv 1.30.0 raised it from 128) and each thread wants an 8
MiB stack (since 1.45.0; before that it was the platform default). Readings from
the container's /proc/<pid>/status after a single dns.lookup:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE libuv-worker VmSize VmRSS Total threads
unset (4) 4 848 MiB 61 MiB 11
8 8 880 MiB 61 MiB 15
128 128 1,841 MiB 61 MiB 135
1024 1024 9,021 MiB 75 MiB 1,031

Going from four to eight adds 32 MiB to VmSize: four threads × 8 MiB, exact.
At 1024 the virtual size reaches 9 GiB while resident memory stays at 75 MiB —
the stacks are paged lazily, just as libuv's documentation says. So the thing to
worry about is not RSS; it is virtual address space in an environment capped by
ulimit -v, and a scheduler that now has 1,031 threads to deal with.

My decision: for a process like my blog pipeline, which writes a couple of
images per article and talks to five platforms, 16 is more than enough. Values
in the hundreds only make sense in a process that genuinely makes hundreds of
concurrent slow calls, and even there the real question is not the pool size but
why those calls are concurrent.

How to leave the limit behind entirely

The cleanest exit is not to grow the pool but not to use it. dns.resolve4 runs
on c-ares; the query happens on the event loop, not in the pool. I asked the
same 24 names of the same 300 ms resolver, with the default four-thread
pool:

Method Concurrent 24 names
dns.lookup 2 3,695 ms
dns.resolve4 24 312 ms

All twenty-four in flight, and the total is the duration of one query. More than
an eleven-fold difference, and I never touched the pool.

It is not free, of course. Node's documentation states the difference honestly:
dns.resolve* does not read /etc/hosts, and it does not use nsswitch.conf
and resolv.conf the way dns.lookup does. So there is no guarantee it gives
the same answer as ping. In a container, service names written into
/etc/hosts, mDNS, search domains — all of that disappears on this path. The
middle ground the documentation points to is more sensible: resolve the name
with dns.resolve() and use the address, or replace the lookup option that
APIs such as socket.connect() and dgram.createSocket() accept with your own
implementation — which is also exactly where a cache belongs.

Questions to ask about your own setup

  • How many distinct hosts does your process talk to? Each one means a default dns.lookup, and they all share at most two threads.
  • Does the same process do image processing, zlib, pbkdf2 or heavy file reads? If so, what fills the pool is probably not DNS but those.
  • Is UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE set from inside the code? If you cannot prove no work hit the pool before that line, the setting may be ignored.
  • Do you know how many threads your pool opened with? On Linux, counting libuv-worker in /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm takes two seconds (libuv 1.50.0 and above); on macOS you need sample or vmmap.
  • If you have a slow-resolver problem, should the answer be dns.resolve? Yes if you have no dependency on /etc/hosts and nsswitch; otherwise your own lookup.
  • If your traffic goes through global fetch, how do you hand it a lookup? fetch takes no such option; the path runs through undici's dispatcher — setGlobalDispatcher(new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })).
  • You opened eight worker_threads and assume you have eight pools? The thread count and the queues in threadpool.c are static: there is one pool per process. Eight workers share the same four threads and the same two DNS slots.
  • What happens when your nameserver dies? A getaddrinfo that has already started cannot be cancelled — uv__work_cancel can only pull work that has not begun off the queue — so two threads stay pinned for as long as timeout × attempts in resolv.conf says.

Limits without counters

Not one measurement in this article produces an alert. There is no counter that
goes up when the pool fills. The tooling is not entirely absent: perf_hooks
has a 'dns' entry type that tells you how long dns.lookup took, and the gap
between the node.threadpoolwork.async and .sync traces gives you the time
spent queueing. But the first one does not tell you why it took that long, and
the second is never emitted by the pool's two busiest customers — dns.lookup
and fs — because neither goes through the code that emits it. The limit is
there; in practice the only evidence is in your p99.

I ran into the same shape in the CPU quota
article: a process using
seventeen percent of its quota, throttled half a million times in ten days,
invisible to every dashboard that looks at averages. In the keepalive
article the
setting was right but almost no application read it. Here is a third variant:
the setting is documented, it is recommended, and half of the recommendation is
lost on the way — and the place it is lost is written on line 46 of the source.

Two threads out of four. If you did not choose that deliberately, libuv chose it
for you.

Official Sources

  • Node.js — UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (CLI documentation)
  • Node.js — DNS: Implementation considerations
  • libuv — src/threadpool.c (v1.x branch)
  • libuv — Thread pool work scheduling documentation
  • libuv — src/unix/getaddrinfo.c (v1.x branch)
  • Node.js — lib/net.js (main branch)

title: Make AI API Operations Idempotent
description:
Disclosure: I work on Modelflare, an OpenAI-compatible AI API gateway. The canonical version of this article lives on modelflare.dev.

Make AI API Operations Idempotent: a production guide with an explicit decision, reusable artifact, failure tests, operating signals, and source-qualified limits.

The operating rule

Make AI API Operations Idempotent should be implemented as a reliability control contract, not as a one-off configuration. Freeze the protocol, ownership, evidence, and rollback condition before traffic moves. The concrete control points in this guide are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result.

Make side-effecting AI operations idempotent at the application boundary. Bind a caller-supplied idempotency key to one authenticated principal, operation, and canonical request digest; reserve the operation atomically; persist terminal success or failure; and return the same durable result on replay. Model call IDs are correlation data, not a substitute for this ledger.

Draw the failure boundary first

Separate the reader-facing task from the control-plane work behind it. Client setup owns the local file or environment variable; the gateway owns authentication, routing, limits, accounting, and attempt records; the provider owns its native protocol and volatile capability contract. A passing text prompt proves only that one path worked once.

Reliability controls must be defined on attempts and terminal states, not on a vague notion of a request “working.” Preserve the caller deadline, distinguish overload from permanent errors, and make rejection, cancellation, retry, fallback, and settlement observable as separate outcomes.

The owner record for this page is ai-api-idempotency; its frozen controls are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result. Every value is reviewed at the wire or durable-state boundary and never inferred from a marketing label.

State and control contract: Make AI API Operations Idempotent

Use the following review record as the deployable artifact. Technical values are intentionally explicit so a reviewer can compare configuration, wire evidence, and durable state without relying on a screenshot or a successful-looking outer response.

Control point Fixed decision Evidence to retain
key_scope principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key principal_id + operation + key
request_binding canonical_digest_must_match request_digest + schema_version
reservation atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect unique_constraint + created_at + owner
replay same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result original_result_id + replay_count
conflict same_key_different_digest_rejected conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload
recovery stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write

Exercise the critical transition

The example uses placeholders and deterministic inputs. Replace identifiers with reviewed values, never with credentials or customer content. Preserve the exact configuration snapshot alongside the probe result.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO operation_ledger
  (principal_id, operation, idempotency_key, request_digest, status)
VALUES
  (:principal, :operation, :key, :digest, 'pending')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
-- only the transaction that owns the new row may perform the side effect
-- persist terminal result before returning it to the caller
COMMIT;

Verify behavior under failure

Run the ladder in order. A later check cannot compensate for a missing earlier boundary, and every attempt must remain attributable to one logical request.

  1. Freeze the current client, gateway policy, model alias, route set, and observable baseline. Evidence record for key_scope: enforce principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key and retain principal_id + operation + key.
  2. Run one deterministic positive probe and capture the client-visible response, request ID, selected route, terminal state, and usage. Evidence record for request_binding: enforce canonical_digest_must_match and retain request_digest + schema_version.
  3. Run the paired negative, limit, or disconnect case and verify that it fails in the intended layer. Evidence record for reservation: enforce atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect and retain unique_constraint + created_at + owner.
  4. Repeat the probe through the actual protocol surface; do not infer native support from a neighboring compatibility endpoint. Evidence record for replay: enforce same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result and retain original_result_id + replay_count.
  5. Roll out to a bounded cohort with an explicit owner, expiry time, stop threshold, and prepared rollback. Evidence record for conflict: enforce same_key_different_digest_rejected and retain conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload.
  6. Re-read durable configuration and accounting after the test, then remove temporary access or test data. Evidence record for recovery: enforce stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation and retain lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write.

Failure amplification to prevent

Treat each item below as a release blocker. A 200 response, attractive dashboard, or single successful demo does not override these failure conditions.

  • memory_only_deduplication — Process memory cannot protect retries after restart, failover, or concurrent execution on another node.
  • key_without_digest — Reusing a key for a different payload can return the wrong result or hide a caller bug.
  • check_then_act_race — Reading for an existing record and writing later allows two workers to perform the same side effect.
  • model_call_id_as_key — A model-generated call ID may change across retries and does not define the authenticated business operation.

Trip signals, denominators, and stop conditions

Monitor success and harm together. The threshold is a policy input, not a universal benchmark; choose it from the workload SLO and record the denominator before the observation window begins.

Signal Decision threshold Action
duplicate_side_effect_count 0 stop_operation_and_reconcile
idempotency_digest_conflicts review_each_event reject_and_alert_owner
stale_pending_age <_owned_recovery_deadline reconcile_with_external_receipt
replay_result_mismatch 0 disable_endpoint

Modelflare boundary and limitations

Modelflare can centralize OpenAI-compatible and native-protocol routing, scoped keys, groups, usage records, and failure handling. A configured channel is not proof that every optional field, model alias, retention promise, region, or fallback is supported. Verify the selected route with its native protocol, preserve explicit zero values, and use the final durable settlement as billing truth.

Idempotency does not mean every model generation becomes identical. It means the protected business operation has one durable outcome for the same authenticated request. Read-only generation may be retried under a budget, while payments, messages, database mutations, and tool actions need operation-specific keys and reconciliation.

Continue through the topic cluster

Use the linked parent for the broader decision, the sibling for the next implementation step, and the documentation route for current client configuration. These body links are deliberate because managed CMS articles do not currently carry a separate related-slug field.

  • Parent decision guide
  • Next implementation guide
  • Current setup documentation

Frequently asked questions

Is an HTTP POST automatically non-idempotent?

HTTP method semantics and application idempotency are related but different; the ledger defines replay behavior for the business operation.

Can the gateway invent the key?

The layer that understands the business operation should define it. A gateway request ID alone may not identify the user-visible side effect.

How are stale pending rows handled?

Use an owned recovery lease and external receipt lookup; never blindly repeat the side effect.

Sources and verification date

Sources were checked on 2026-08-07. They establish external contracts and engineering principles; they do not prove an untested route or future provider state.

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • OpenAI API reference: request IDs
  • OWASP: Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet

Originally published at modelflare.dev. Current models and prices: modelflare.dev/pricing · Docs: docs.modelflare.dev.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

Read more

title: OpenAI Decisions API now available on AI Gateway
description:
OpenAI’s Decisions API is now available through AI Gateway at /v1/decisions. It uses the same request and response format as OpenAI, so existing OpenAI SDK integrations can switch by changing the base URL, credentials, and model ID.

Decision models answer typed questions about shared input and return structured answers rather than generated text. In one request, you can ask a model to:

  • Estimate the probability that a condition is true with a predicate question

  • Select from supplied options with a choice question

  • Rate the input against an ordered rubric with a score question

Use these answers for tasks such as classification, routing, triage, and rubric-based scoring.

The endpoint works with any decision model on AI Gateway, including Jev, Liquid d1, and Laya. Use openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions model. This is separate from openai/gpt-6-luna, which generates text.

With OpenAI SDK 7.30.0 or later for JavaScript or 3.26.0 or later for Python, point the client at AI Gateway and call decisions.create:

The response returns answers in question order, each with the corresponding question’s name.

See the OpenAI Decisions API documentation for Python and cURL examples. To use decision models with the AI SDK or /v1/evaluate, see the decision documentation.

Read more

title: Trinity Desktop Environment R14.1.7 released with many improvements
description:
The Trinity Desktop Environment team has released R14.1.7 for the KDE 3.5-based stack, introducing Konsole bracketed paste support, KPDF AES-256 decryption, and compatibility updates for OpenSSL 4, Python 3.15, and Poppler 26.06.

Improvements to applications and tools

The Konsole terminal has gained support for a special paste function that prevents multi-line text from automatically executing before pressing Enter. New mouse capabilities, colored underlines, and bulk selection options have also been added.

The taskbar and menu now allow scrolling with the mouse wheel, while bulk management actions for grouped windows have been added. The application menu has gained keyboard navigation in search results and the ability to change the text color on the button.

The window manager has improved margins, multi-monitor support, and monitor control. PDF reading has gained AES-256 encryption support, while the image viewer has changed technology for better resizing and less distortion.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Software & Open Source

The new official Arch Linux installation version for November 2026 has been released

↗

The file manager has gained an alternative for managing RAR compressed files and fixes for TAR files. In addition, file renaming has been improved, character categorization has been added, and support for lzip compressed files has been integrated.

System stability and compatibility

A major issue that caused excessive CPU and memory usage when editing large system files has been fixed. Also addressed are unexpected shutdowns in communication, system monitoring, text and audio editing applications, and issues with scrolling and menu display after resuming from sleep.

The new release adds support for newer software, such as OpenSSL 4, Python 3.15, libical 4, libpqxx 8, and Poppler 26.06, with a minimum required version of OpenSSL 1.1. Support for Fedora 44, Mageia 10, and Ubuntu Stonking has also been added, while official support for Fedora 42, Mageia 9, Ubuntu Oracular, and openSUSE 15.6 has been discontinued.

The announcement was made by Bobby Borisov.
