title: Would You Rather Have a Dumb Component or a Smart Component?
description:
A Component Doesn't Have to Be Dumb to Be Reusable

There's a long-running idea in frontend architecture:

Keep components dumb.

Let them receive data, render the UI, and leave everything else to something higher up the tree.

It sounds clean. And often, it is.

But there's a trade-off we don't always consider:

Making a component simpler can make the surrounding architecture more complicated.

Let's look at both approaches.

🔴 The Problem

Imagine a component that displays a list of users.

It needs to fetch the data, filter the results, and render them.

One approach is to put everything inside UserList.

function UserList() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  const filteredUsers = useMemo(
    () => users.filter((user) => user.name.includes(query)),
    [users, query],
  );

  return (
    <section>
      <input value={query} onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)} />

      {filteredUsers.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

This is a smart component.

It knows where its data comes from, manages its own state, handles filtering, and decides how everything is displayed.

Using it is simple:

<UserList />

But what happens when another part of the application already has the users?

Or when the same UI needs to display data from a different source?

Now the component's built-in behavior becomes a limitation.

🟢 The Other Extreme

We could separate those responsibilities.

The container handles the data. The presentational component handles the UI.

function UserListContainer() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  return <UserList users={users} />;
}

function UserList({ users }: { users: User[] }) {
  return (
    <section>
      {users.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

Now UserList doesn't care where the data comes from.

It can render users fetched by a parent, loaded from a cache, or passed in by a test.

That's a real benefit.

But splitting components isn't free.

The container needs to pass data down. Additional behavior may require additional props. And if the presentation component is only ever used in one place, the extra layer might not make the code any easier to understand.

We haven't necessarily removed complexity. We've moved it.

🔵 Reusability Has a Cost

A dumb component is often easier to reuse because it depends on fewer things.

It doesn't need to know about an API, a router, a global store, or a particular data-fetching library.

But reusability isn't the only thing that matters.

Sometimes, keeping behavior close to the UI makes a component easier to understand.

Consider a search box.

If its value, filtering logic, and displayed results always belong together, extracting every small piece into separate components and hooks can make a simple feature harder to follow.

On the other hand, if multiple screens need the same filtering behavior or visual list, separating those responsibilities may be worthwhile.

The useful boundary isn't necessarily between smart and dumb components.

It's between responsibilities that belong together and responsibilities that benefit from being independent.

🟣 So Where Should the Logic Live?

There isn't one rule that works for every component.

A few questions can help:

  • Does the component need to work with different data sources? Separating data access from presentation may help.
  • Does the behavior only make sense for this component? Keeping it local may make the code clearer.
  • Is the component coordinating several unrelated concerns? That may be a sign it has too many responsibilities.
  • Are you extracting something just to make a component smaller? Smaller doesn't automatically mean simpler.

You can also mix the approaches.

A component can own its local interaction state while receiving data from a parent. It can use a shared hook for behavior without becoming purely presentational.

These aren't mutually exclusive architectures.

🟠 What About Consistency Across a Codebase?

So far, we've looked at individual components.

But components don't always exist in isolation. They're part of a larger codebase, often maintained by multiple developers.

Imagine a team decides that components should follow a consistent architecture:

  • Components don't fetch data directly.
  • Shared state is accessed through established abstractions.
  • Business logic lives in hooks, services, or other dedicated modules.
  • Components receive the data they need through props.

There are good reasons to do this.

Developers know where to look for things. Responsibilities are predictable. Moving between different parts of the application feels familiar.

But there's a trade-off.

Some components might genuinely be simpler if they handled their own behavior.

Forcing them into the same structure could mean creating unnecessary hooks, adding extra layers, or splitting closely related logic across several files.

You gain consistency, but potentially lose simplicity.

And that's not necessarily a bad decision.

In a large team, predictable code can be more valuable than making every individual component follow its locally simplest implementation.

The important distinction is between consistent principles and identical implementations.

A codebase can have clear architectural rules without forcing every component to have exactly the same structure.

After all, you're maintaining a codebase, not just individual components.

⚡ The Takeaway

Smart and dumb components aren't competing goals.

A dumb component can be wonderfully reusable, but separating every bit of behavior can create unnecessary indirection.

A smart component can be convenient and cohesive, but accumulating unrelated responsibilities can make it difficult to change.

Neither approach is inherently better.

Don't optimize for dumb components. Don't optimize for smart components.

Optimize for clear responsibilities.

title: October 07, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Deprecated

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. Negative values there are deprecated and will be rejected in a future release; until then, creating an API config with one returns a warning in the operation metadata. OpenAPI 3.x backends already reject a negative deadline. To use the default, omit the field or set it to 0.

For more information, see OpenAPI 2.0 extensions and OpenAPI 3.x extensions.

title: I don't have a single photo of my great-grandparents. So I built an altar for the people nobody remembers.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

There is an idea from Día de los Muertos that I keep coming back to.

A person dies three times. Once when their body stops. Once when they are buried. And a final time, when the last person who remembers them is gone.

I went looking for a photograph of my great-grandparents to put on an ofrenda. There isn't one. Nobody in my family has a single picture of them. I don't know their faces at all.

So I went to the public archives instead, and found page after page of people in the same situation as my great-grandparents. Portraits from India, a hundred years old and more, labelled with a single line:

Unidentified woman.

Milk-woman, studio photograph.

Indian Christian, India, ca. 1910.

Someone loved each of these people. Someone paid for that photograph, dressed them in their best clothes, told them to hold still. And now nobody knows their names.

So I built them an altar.

A woman photographed for a lantern slide around 1910. Her name was not recorded. Above, the photo as it survives. Below, the same photo after Living Portraits.

What I Built

Living Portraits is a digital ofrenda for old photographs. You place a photo on the altar, and it comes back to you in one short sequence I call the Return:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A thin line of candlelight passes down the photo and mends it.
  3. Colour spreads outward from the person's face, the way a memory comes back.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. Move your cursor, or tilt your phone, and it shifts gently, as if you were standing in front of a real print, while candlelight flickers brighter on whatever is nearest to you.

Under every portrait is everything we know about them, which is often almost nothing. A name if there is one. Her name was not recorded if there isn't. A link to the archive the photo came from and its licence, so you can check it is real. And a number showing how closely the restored face still matches the original.

Light a candle

If the final death comes when no one remembers you, the smallest thing we can do is remember.

Under each portrait there is one button: Light a candle. A fourth candle catches on the altar's shelf, and the server keeps count, one candle per visitor. It isn't much. But a woman whose name nobody wrote down, a hundred years ago, now has a number next to her that only goes up.

You can also place your own family's photos on the altar, and save their Return as a short video to send to the family group.

The Version I Threw Away

My first version animated the faces. One open-source model, a few lines of code, and Srinivasa Ramanujan's portrait from 1913 turned its head and broke into a wide, toothy grin.

It looked impressive for about two seconds. Then it felt scary and awkward. A man who never smiled like that for any camera was smiling at me because a model decided he should. These are real people. They can't agree to be made to smile for us, and they can't be asked.

So I deleted it. In Living Portraits the face is never moved, never re-posed and never given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth, the way a real photograph does when you carry it to a window. Every download is labelled AI-restored.

That decision changed the whole project, and I think it made it better.

Demo

Try it live: http://139.59.7.49 (light a candle for someone while you're there)

Watch the 68-second demo: demo video. A photo is placed on the altar, processed live on DigitalOcean, returns, and gets its first candle. The narration was generated with ElevenLabs.

Here is a photo being placed on the altar and processed live on the DigitalOcean server:

How It Works

Four open-source models run one after another on a single small server. The browser does the rest.

Mend. GFPGAN v1.4 repairs blur, scratches and damage on the face. I blend its output with the original at 60% instead of 100%, so the person keeps their own face rather than a polished stranger's.

Colour. DDColor predicts colour for black-and-white and sepia prints. It only predicts the colour; every bit of light and detail comes from the original photograph.

Depth. Depth Anything V2 estimates how near or far each part of the photo is. That depth map is what lets the portrait shift when you move, and what makes the candlelight fall on the face before the wall behind it.

Check. A face-recognition model (ArcFace, through facexlib) compares the face before and after restoration, and that score is printed under every portrait.

The server, a small FastAPI app, sends back three images: the photo as it was, the photo restored, and the depth map. The Return itself is a short WebGL shader running in your browser. The candlelight sweep, the colour spreading out from the face (located by the face detector), the depth and the flicker are all drawn live, so the original photo is never baked into a video.

Three Problems I Didn't Expect

1. Restoration makes everyone look like a stranger

Face-restoration models are trained to make faces look good, and "good" drifts toward young, smooth and symmetrical. For a stranger's photo, that's fine. For someone who can't tell you what they really looked like, it's a quiet kind of erasure.

So I measure it. The ArcFace check compares the face before and after for every photo. Across the eleven archive portraits I tested, ten scored 0.88 or higher, and the median was 0.94. On this scale, around 0.5 already means "probably the same person". The one low score, 0.74, was a side profile, which face models struggle with in general.

2. Sepia is not colour

Most 19th-century portraits are albumen prints: brown ink on cream paper, not black on white. My first black-and-white detector looked at saturation, decided these prints were already in colour, and skipped them. Half of my archive photos came back untouched.

The fix was to stop asking "is there colour?" and ask "does the colour depend on anything except brightness?" In a toned print, dark means brown and light means cream, and that's all. So I fit colour as a function of brightness and look at what's left over:

def is_black_and_white(img_bgr):
    small = cv2.resize(img_bgr, (256, 256))
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(small, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB).reshape(-1, 3).astype(np.float32)
    L, a, b = lab[:, 0] / 255, lab[:, 1], lab[:, 2]
    X = np.stack([np.ones_like(L), L, L * L, L ** 3], 1)   # colour as a curve of brightness
    leftover = sum(np.std(c - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, c, rcond=None)[0]) for c in (a, b))
    return leftover < 4.0   # sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing behind

Real colour photos leave a lot behind. Sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing. It now sorts every archive photo I have correctly.

3. The colours were too loud

DDColor's first results were vivid in a way old photographs never are: magenta suits, orange hands. I scale the predicted colour back by a quarter. The portraits look less like an advert and more like a hand-tinted print, which is closer to the truth of the era.

Built on DigitalOcean

The whole altar lives on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, and DigitalOcean is a big part of why one person could build and ship this in a weekend.

It sits close to the people it's for. The portraits are from India, and so are many of the families I hope will use it, so the Droplet runs in DigitalOcean's Bangalore region.

Dedicated cores, steady timing. Restoring a photo is heavy, continuous number-crunching. On a CPU-Optimized Droplet with 4 dedicated vCPUs, a photo takes about 12 seconds, every time, with no noisy neighbours slowing it down.

One machine runs everything. The four models, the FastAPI server, the candle counts and the web page itself all live on the same Droplet as a single systemd service. There is no separate GPU service, no third-party AI API, and nothing else to keep in sync.

From a blank Droplet to live with one script. setup.sh in the repo installs the models on a fresh Ubuntu Droplet, and the service file keeps the app running across restarts. Every update during the build was a copy and a service restart.

It doesn't need a GPU. I planned to rent a GPU Droplet. Then I removed the face animation, the heaviest model, and found everything else fits comfortably on CPU: about 12 seconds per photo on the Droplet, against about 5 seconds on my laptop's 4 GB RTX 3050.

The cost is small and predictable. The Droplet costs $0.125 an hour, which works out to roughly $0.0004 of compute per photo, and the whole build ran on DigitalOcean's Hacktoberfest credit.

That matters for who can use this. A family, a small local archive or a school history project can run their own altar for a few dollars a day, or switch it off when no one is visiting.

Where It Falls Short

  • Colour is a guess. DDColor doesn't know what colour her sari really was. The page says so under every portrait.
  • Side profiles are harder. Face models are trained mostly on faces looking at the camera.
  • Faded sepia prints get only a hint of colour, because the paper tone dominates.
  • Hand-tinted prints are left alone. One 1860s portrait was read as already coloured. It may well be hand-tinted, so leaving it untouched is the honest result.

Why Open Source Matters Here

Commercial apps already "bring old photos to life". To use them, you upload your family's photographs to a company's servers, usually on a subscription, and accept whatever the model decides to do to the faces of people who can't object.

Every decision that shaped this project was only possible because the models were open:

  • When face animation felt wrong, I could remove it.
  • When restoration drifted away from the real face, I could measure it and turn it down.
  • When the colours were too loud, I could change them.
  • When sepia prints were skipped, I could fix the detector that a closed API would have hidden from me.

And the photographs never leave a server the family controls. Nothing is sent to an AI company, and nothing can be taken away by a subscription ending or an app shutting down. A memory deserves at least that.

The Moment It Landed

Her first candle was lit while I was recording the demo.

The script uploaded a portrait from the 1880s, a young woman in her best sari with every ornament she owned, captioned Her name was not recorded. The Return played, the colour came back into her face, and then the button was pressed and the count changed from nothing to 1 candle lit.

It's a small number. But it's one more than she had yesterday. Her portrait is in the gallery on the live site. If you visit, light one for her.

Prize Categories

Best Use of DigitalOcean. The entire app, from the four models to the API, the candle counts and the page, runs on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, deployed with the setup script and systemd service in the repo. It shows that open-source image models don't need a GPU to be useful to a family.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The demo's narration was generated with ElevenLabs, and the repo includes the script and the tools that cut the screen recording to each narrated paragraph.

Code

Tanhaker / living-portraits

Restore, colour and give depth to old family photos for the ofrenda. Open-source AI, the face is never changed.

Living Portraits

Bring an old family photo to the ofrenda. Living Portraits mends its creases, returns its colour and gives it depth, using only open-source models on a server you control.

The face is never moved, re-posed or given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth instead.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The Return

When a photo is placed on the altar, the page plays one short sequence on a WebGL canvas:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A line of candlelight sweeps down and mends it.
  3. Colour blooms outward from the person's face.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. It shifts gently with your cursor or as you tilt your phone and candlelight flickers brighter on what is nearer.

The page can record the Return as a video to…

View on GitHub

Built with help from an AI coding assistant. Every portrait shown is public domain or CC0, from Wikimedia Commons, with sources listed in the repository README.

title: 2026 Node.js Error Tracking Library Integration: Best Practices for Silent Import Failures
description:
2026 Scheduled Import Observability: Proving Results Before Assigning Operational Cost

The constraint changes the design: a scheduled e-commerce import that produces no result may never throw, so a Node.js error-tracking library cannot prove that the job ran. Use the library for exceptions, add an explicit completion record with a stable run identifier, and have a separate heartbeat check detect a missing result before assigning the operational cost to a source or cost center.

Short answer: initialize Sentry, Rollbar, or a similar library before application work, capture uncaught and HTTP errors, and wrap the import boundary for explicit reporting. Then record successful and empty outcomes separately. A missed schedule needs a Healthchecks-style monitor or an equivalent polling check; it is not an error event.

The distinction is easy to miss.

What should the import system prove?

For every scheduled import, I want one answerable question: did the expected result arrive before the business deadline? The completion record should carry job_name, run_id, source, started_at, finished_at, rows, and cost_center. The last field is deliberate. If marketplace, catalog, and inventory feeds share workers, an error count cannot explain whose operational cost is rising.

There are three useful outcomes:

  • failed: the worker reported an exception or an HTTP failure.
  • completed_empty: the run finished, but produced zero rows where zero is suspicious.
  • missing: no completion signal arrived before the deadline.

Only the first outcome is naturally visible to an error-tracking SDK. The other two require an application event and a deadline check. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal whose records can carry attributes, which is a useful model for correlating error events, completion events, and deadline checks without pretending they are one signal.

Keep the business cost calculation outside the error tracker. A zero-row result may be a legitimate supplier response, a broken credential, or a scheduler that never fired. The tracker preserves evidence; a small attribution job applies the business rule after the run state is known.

Why does a missing import need another signal?

Absence is not an exception. Consider a nightly catalog import expected by 02:00 UTC. The worker may never start, wait behind a stuck process, or exit before it initializes the library. In all three cases, a design built only around try/catch has no event to send.

The minimum design is a pair of writes: emit an error when a failure is observed, and emit a completion event after the durable result is committed. A scheduler or Healthchecks-style service checks for the latter. Give that check a tolerance window. A deadline that is too strict converts ordinary queue delay into an incident storm, while one that is too generous delays cost attribution.

Use the same run_id in error context, completion log, queue message, and cost ledger. Trace and span fields can help correlate records when available, but this design does not depend on a distributed-trace query or a span tree.

No exception is required.

That is the awkward part. A catalog feed can return a valid response, write zero rows, and leave the error tracker quiet; the system must retain the schedule, source, row count, deadline, and cost center long enough for an attribution job to distinguish a legitimate empty feed from a missed run. I would make that distinction in the workflow, because a library cannot infer whether zero is normal for one supplier on one day. The import worker should also rethrow after reporting an exception. Swallowing it makes the scheduler believe the run succeeded, which corrupts both operational status and cost attribution.

The application contract can stay provider-neutral. This Python example shows the capture boundary for a REST capability; the Node.js worker can implement the same contract through its chosen SDK or HTTP client. The operational limits matter too: use a 10-second request timeout, make four bounded attempts, and treat HTTP 429 as a retryable response rather than a reason to loop forever. Those are explicit client choices, not promises about provider latency.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def capture_error(error_payload):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    base_url = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
    response_url = f"{base_url}/v1/errors/capture"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            response_url,
            headers=headers,
            json=error_payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"error capture failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
                )
            return response.json()

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("error capture rate limit did not clear after retries")

The key comes from an environment variable, the method is explicit, a 429 honors Retry-After, and non-success responses remain visible. The idempotency key prevents a retry after a network timeout from recording the same failure twice. Do not send this authorization header to a separate URL returned for another operation.

Which tools fit the evidence?

The comparison should follow the missing proof, not the popularity of a dashboard. Sentry is a natural fit when the main requirement is SDK-based exception capture and context. Rollbar belongs in the same shortlist for application error monitoring. Datadog is a broader observability choice when error records need to sit beside other operational telemetry. None of those labels, by themselves, answers “did this scheduled import produce a result?”

Option Strong fit Boundary for silent imports Cost attribution implication
Sentry Capturing application exceptions with project context A missing completion still needs a positive event and a deadline check Add cost_center and run_id to captured context, then calculate attribution outside the error stream
Rollbar Error monitoring for application failures A worker that never emits an error remains invisible Keep the run ledger separate so a low error count cannot be mistaken for low import cost
Datadog Joining error records with wider observability practice The monitoring design still needs an explicit import-success signal Use a common identifier and meter the workflow independently from incident volume
Healthchecks-style monitoring Detecting a missed scheduled check-in It does not replace stack traces or application context Attribute the missed run to the job and source, then link supporting error records
A plain REST error capability Sending error evidence without installing a provider SDK It is still not a heartbeat or alerting rule engine Preserve the internal event contract and assemble the missing checks separately

That last row is where Infrai can fit. Infrai's one REST API is pure HTTP: no SDK to install, and any language or runtime can send the request. Its API is also self-describing, so the discovery surface can show the request and response contract before a worker is wired to it; that reduces the friction of replacing an SDK-backed capture edge during a provider change. The internal event contract can remain stable while the service behind the capability changes, so swapping the provider does not require changing application code. Infrai also uses one key and one bill across the platform, which reduces credential and invoice sprawl without changing the observability limits. The platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but that breadth does not turn error capture into a heartbeat monitor or a notification system.

The 2026-10-29 capability snapshot also makes the limitations material. Infrai has no built-in threshold notifications, distributed span-tree query, source-map deobfuscation, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring in the stated capability boundary. Its client-side checking model is polling-based, and the observability facts do not establish a declared filter contract for log search or metric query. Choose Sentry when SDK-centered exception context is the priority, Datadog when a wider observability estate matters more, and a Healthchecks-style tool when missed schedules are the primary failure. Choose the REST capability only when a provider-neutral HTTP contract is more valuable than an integrated debugging suite; it isn't a replacement for one.

How should I integrate the Node.js library?

Install the selected library with npm and initialize it before application work begins. Configure middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors, then wrap the import worker as well; middleware catches request failures, while a scheduled worker may run outside an HTTP request entirely. Attach user information only where it is appropriate and lawful, and prefer a stable internal identifier over an email address.

The test should be repeatable. Trigger one controlled exception and verify that the report includes the import name and run_id. Run a successful import and verify the completion event. Then suppress the completion event in a test environment and confirm that the heartbeat check marks the run as missing. A green error dashboard with no missing-run test does not establish that the integration works.

The provider-specific SDK is an implementation detail. The durable contract is the useful part: error reports include the run context, successful work emits a completion record, and retries use the same idempotent run identifier. Do not use a trace tree as a substitute for this contract; the available logs may carry trace_id and span_id without providing distributed trace exploration.

A rollout rule that survives provider changes

Start with one import whose business owner can define “late.” Record the expected schedule, allowed delay, source, and cost center before enabling notifications. Compare observed exceptions, completed runs, and expected runs over a fixed test window. The gaps are the product decision.

Keep error capture, completion recording, and missed-run detection as replaceable edges around one internal event contract. This permits a move from Sentry to Rollbar, Datadog, or a plain REST capability without rewriting the import worker's business logic, while keeping the uncomfortable truth visible: an error tracker can explain a failed run, but only a positive completion signal can establish that a run occurred.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js error tracking
  • Healthchecks.io documentation

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: Twilio vs Vonage for SMS Alerts — Property Management Pricing, Features, Node.js
description:
Short answer: For property-management SMS alerts, choose Twilio when global coverage and developer tooling reduce integration work; choose Vonage when high-volume SMS economics matter more; consider a unified REST API when one signup flow must connect SMS, email fallback, and adjacent backend capabilities.

The integration decision is not “which SMS API has the longest feature list?” It is where account creation ends and message delivery begins. Twilio is the stronger default when global coverage, integrations, and developer tooling carry the most weight. Vonage deserves the lead when high-volume SMS economics and the relevant regional carrier relationships matter more. A unified REST surface is useful when the real constraint is wiring both the SMS step and its fallback without multiplying contracts.

What should the signup flow own?

For a tenant signup, the application should create the verification token, store its expiry, and enqueue a notification job. The SMS provider should accept the message and return an identifier. A worker can reconcile delivery state later. That division keeps a carrier response out of the account transaction and gives the product a stable place to decide what “verified” means.

The decision is conditional, but it is not vague. Choose Twilio when its extensive global coverage, integrations, documentation, and SDKs reduce the code your team has to maintain. Choose Vonage when volume SMS and country-specific pricing deserve more weight. Check carrier partnerships for every launch region; a general comparison does not replace that review.

Keep it boring.

For a solo team, I would also evaluate a single REST surface for the boundary between signup, SMS, and an email fallback. Infrai’s public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples without requiring a key. The documented capability set also has runnable examples in 10 languages, which turns “how do I wire this?” into a concrete inspection task rather than an SDK-selection exercise.

There is a second, different advantage: one key and one bill cover a broad backend surface. The live discovery set contains 295 routes across 20 modules, including 41 in the communication group. For this workflow, that means the same platform boundary can cover the notification step and adjacent backend work without asking a small team to collect a new credential and reconcile another provider for every capability. It does not make the specialist SMS providers irrelevant.

How should the Node.js boundary look?

Make the provider call an adapter. The signup service should deal in verificationId, providerMessageId, and expiresAt; it should not know whether the transport is Twilio, Vonage, or another REST provider. The adapter should also own status normalization, since a carrier state is evidence about delivery rather than proof that someone opened a link.

Here is the smallest useful shape. It is intentionally transport-neutral, so it can be tested without sending a real message. The production adapter supplies the provider-specific implementation and keeps credentials outside the signup code.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

function delayFor(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
  return Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
    ? Math.max(1000, retryAfter * 1000)
    : Math.min(8000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
}

async function discoverSmsBoundary(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      const manifest = (await response.json()) as {
        capabilities: Array<{ method: string; path: string }>;
      };
      return manifest.capabilities.find(
        (capability) =>
          capability.method === "GET" && capability.path === "/v1/sms/status/{id}",
      );
    }

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, delayFor(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery retry budget exhausted");
}

discoverSmsBoundary().then(console.log).catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

type Verification = {
  verificationId: string;
  providerMessageId: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

type DeliveryState = "pending" | "delivered" | "failed" | "unknown";

interface SmsPort {
  sendVerification(input: {
    phoneNumber: string;
    verificationUrl: string;
    idempotencyKey: string;
  }): Promise<{ messageId: string }>;
  readStatus(messageId: string): Promise<DeliveryState>;
}

async function createSignupVerification(
  sms: SmsPort,
  input: { verificationId: string; phoneNumber: string; verificationUrl: string },
): Promise<Verification> {
  const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 60 * 1000);
  const result = await sms.sendVerification({
    phoneNumber: input.phoneNumber,
    verificationUrl: input.verificationUrl,
    idempotencyKey: `signup-verification:${input.verificationId}`,
  });

  return {
    verificationId: input.verificationId,
    providerMessageId: result.messageId,
    expiresAt,
  };
}

The discovery call is intentionally read-only. It lets the adapter inspect the documented SMS boundary before choosing a provider-specific send implementation, and it honors Retry-After without treating a throttled response as success. The important detail in the send adapter is the idempotency key, not the syntax. A timeout after the provider accepted the message must not create a second link when the worker retries. On the read side, use bounded backoff and surface a non-success response with its body. Do not turn an unknown carrier state into a successful signup.

This also keeps the example honest about the provider boundary. The application owns the 15-minute policy shown here; it is not a claim about a provider’s delivery window. The actual adapter must use the selected provider’s documented request and response shape, and the application must store the returned message ID before it tries to reconcile status.

Is Twilio or Vonage the better SMS transport?

Twilio and Vonage overlap on the features that matter for this flow: delivery receipts and message scheduling are broadly available in both. Twilio has extensive global coverage and strong developer documentation and SDK support. Vonage can offer a cost advantage for volume SMS. Those are useful differences, but they do not answer the regional question. Carrier relationships vary, so test the countries where tenants actually receive messages.

Amazon SNS is a third option when the property platform already has an AWS-shaped operational boundary. It is a reasonable comparison point for teams that want their notification path close to existing AWS controls. It is a worse fit if introducing another cloud-specific integration is the very work the team is trying to avoid. SendGrid is relevant on the other side of the handoff: it can be considered for an email fallback, but it is not an SMS transport for the tenant signup link.

Option Where it fits What to verify before committing
Twilio Global coverage, integrations, and developer-friendly tooling Regional carrier behavior and the ongoing shape of the SDK or HTTP integration
Vonage High-volume SMS where regional pricing is a major input Country-level carrier partnerships and the complete delivery workflow
Amazon SNS A property backend already organized around AWS services Whether the added cloud-specific boundary reduces or increases integration work
SendGrid A separate email fallback owned by an email provider It does not replace the SMS provider for this signup path
Infrai A small team that values public discovery and one backend contract Pull-based status, application-owned anti-abuse policy, and regional SMS readiness

The price comparison should stay in its lane. Pricing changes, and a table of unit prices becomes stale faster than the signup code. For a large alert stream, model the actual destinations and volumes, then compare message creation, delivery-state reads, retries, and fallback work. For a product with many backend capabilities, count the credentials, SDK conventions, and operational handoffs too. Those costs are part of integration effort even when they do not appear on an invoice.

The explicit recommendation is narrow: a property-management team should try Infrai for the signup verification and email-fallback boundary when it wants to discover both capabilities from one public REST surface and keep one credential across the backend. Twilio or Vonage is the better specialist choice when carrier-level regional tooling, mature SMS integrations, or volume economics dominate the decision.

Where does the provider handoff end?

The application should own abuse policy. The available caveats matter here: geographic anti-fraud limits and country-based spend circuit breakers must be built at the business layer. Do not assume the transport provider will enforce the property product’s rules. Store an allowlist or policy decision with the signup attempt, and reject or defer suspicious requests before the send adapter runs.

That policy check is also where the comparison becomes concrete. Suppose a property manager serves several countries and the product team adds a new signup channel late in the release cycle. The transport adapter should receive a request that has already passed the country rule, rate rule, and token-expiry rule; it should not decide any of those things while talking to a carrier. A Twilio or Vonage adapter can then normalize its message identifier into the same internal record, while an email fallback can use a separate adapter with its own code and expiry. A unified REST surface can reduce the number of discovery and credential steps around this handoff, but it cannot choose the allowed geography or make an email OTP hosted for you. Those remain application decisions.

The application should also own the fallback policy. The email side does not provide a hosted OTP interface, so an email verification fallback needs an application-owned code and expiry. There is no SMTP relay, and email scheduling has no cancel route. SMS does have a cancel route, but that difference is a reason to keep cancellation semantics behind the adapter rather than exposing them as a universal notification feature.

Status is pull-based in both namespaces; there are no webhook event pushes. That makes a bounded polling worker part of the design. As of the 2026-10-31 discovery snapshot, the broader platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth does not change this constraint: the signup UI should not wait on a carrier response. Record the provider message ID, reconcile until the verification expiry, and make unresolved status visible to support without treating it as account failure immediately.

The operational checklist is short enough to enforce in code review. Store the token and expiry internally. Enqueue the send after the signup record is durable. Pass a deterministic idempotency key. Persist the message ID. Reconcile with bounded retries. Keep the token out of logs. Test every destination country and the email fallback separately.

Ship the boundary.

That is the boundary I would use: the property application owns identity and policy, the SMS provider owns transport, and a worker owns reconciliation. If the main friction is discovering and connecting adjacent backend capabilities, start with the public capability reference. If the main friction is carrier behavior in a specific country, stay with the specialist comparison and test that country first.

References

The implementation boundary follows the provider documentation and the communication constraints described above. Regional carrier behavior and current pricing should be checked again before launch.

Sources

  • Twilio SMS documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sms
  • Vonage SMS API documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_publish-to-phone.html
  • Google Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126
  • Unified API discovery and capability reference: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt

title: 5 Things Every Small Business Homepage Needs Above the Fold
description:
"Above the fold" is the part of your homepage people see before they scroll. On a phone that's a tiny space, and it's where most small business sites lose people. Here are the five things I check first on every small business homepage.

1. A headline that says what you do and where. "Welcome to our website" tells nobody anything. "Family dentist in Austin, TX" or "Same-day plumbing repairs in Tampa" tells visitors (and Google) they're in the right place.

2. One obvious call-to-action. Pick the one action that matters most — Book now, Get a quote, Call us — and make it a big, high-contrast button. Three competing buttons usually means none get clicked.

3. A tap-to-call phone number. Many local customers are on mobile and just want to call. Use a tel: link so it's one tap, and keep it visible in the header.

4. Proof. A star rating, a review count, or one short testimonial near the top builds trust instantly. Real reviews beat stock badges.

5. A real photo. Your actual team, shop, or finished work beats generic stock photos. It makes the business feel real and local. Compress it so it doesn't slow the page down.

Quick test: open your homepage on your phone and ask a friend what you do, where, and how to contact you — in five seconds. If they can't answer, the top of the page needs work.

I'm with ENZORA. We build websites for US small businesses and offer a free website and SEO audit: https://enzora.vercel.app

title: I Built PosterPilot: A Cloudinary-Powered Tool to Adapt University Event Posters Without Cropping Important Details
description:
University societies and event organizers regularly create posters for seminars, workshops, competitions, hackathons, and other campus activities.

However, sharing one poster across different platforms can become challenging. Instagram posts, Instagram Stories, and website previews all require different dimensions. Simply resizing an image can crop important information, such as event titles, dates, venue details, or sponsor logos.

To explore how image transformation can solve this problem, I built PosterPilot, a Cloudinary-powered web application that helps users adapt one uploaded event poster into multiple formats.

What is PosterPilot?

PosterPilot is a web-based image adaptation tool designed with university societies and event organizers in mind.

Users upload an event poster once and generate different output formats using Cloudinary image transformations.

The main idea is simple: make poster adaptation easier while giving users control over whether the entire image should remain visible or fill the selected dimensions.

🌐 Live Demo: https://posterpilot.vercel.app
💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/alpha5-rdx/posterpilot

The Problem I Wanted to Solve:

Imagine a university society has designed a poster for an upcoming technology event. The society wants to share it in three places:

  • Instagram Square post
  • Instagram Story
  • Website or social media preview

Each platform requires a different image size. Cropping the original poster to fit these dimensions can remove important information.

I wanted to build a simple solution that could generate these formats without requiring users to manually edit the same poster multiple times.

Technology Stack

I used the following technologies:

  1. React: Building the user interface and reusable components.
  2. Vite: Development environment and production build tooling.
  3. JavaScript: Application logic and interactions.
  4. CSS: Responsive styling and layout.
  5. Cloudinary: Image uploading, transformation, delivery, and optimization.
  6. Vercel: Deploying and hosting the application.

The project uses a frontend-only architecture. Cloudinary handles image storage and delivery, so I did not need to build a separate backend for this version.

How Cloudinary Powers PosterPilot?

Cloudinary is the central part of the application.

I integrated Cloudinary's Upload API using an unsigned upload preset. This allows the frontend to upload an image without exposing the Cloudinary API Secret. The application sends the selected image and upload preset to the Cloudinary image upload endpoint: https://api.cloudinary.com/v1_1//image/upload

After a successful upload, Cloudinary returns information such as:

  • Secure image URL
  • Public ID
  • Image dimensions
  • File format
  • File size
  • Asset version

PosterPilot uses the returned image information to generate transformed image URLs.

This approach allows the application to work with one original uploaded image and dynamically generate different versions through Cloudinary transformations.

Five Output Formats

PosterPilot currently supports five predefined formats:

Format: Innsta Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: Innsta Story Dimensions: 1080 x 1920
Format: Web/Social Preview Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: LinkedIn Portrait Dimensions: 1080 x 1350
Format: LinkedIn Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080

Users can preview the generated versions before copying their URLs or downloading the images.

*My Main Feature: No-Crop vs Crop-to-Fill
*
One of the main features I wanted to explore was the difference between preserving the complete image and filling a target canvas.

1. No-Crop Mode

For this mode, I used Cloudinary's c_pad transformation.

Example transformation: c_pad,w_1080,h_1080,b_white/q_auto/f_auto

This transformation fits the original image inside the specified dimensions while preserving the entire image. If the aspect ratios differ, padding is added to complete the canvas.

This is useful when the poster contains important information that should remain visible.

2. Crop-to-Fill Mode

For the alternative mode, I used Cloudinary's c_fill transformation with center gravity.

Example transformation: c_fill,g_center,w_1080,h_1080/q_auto/f_auto

This fills the target dimensions by cropping the image where necessary.

It is useful when users prefer a completely filled canvas and accept that some parts of the original image may be cropped.

Image Optimization and Delivery

I also used two useful Cloudinary transformation parameters:

  • q_auto: Automatically selects an appropriate image quality setting.
  • f_auto: Automatically selects a suitable delivery format based on browser support.

These transformations help optimize image delivery without requiring users to manually create multiple optimized files.

Other Application Features

In addition to image transformations, PosterPilot includes:

  1. Drag-and-drop image upload.
  2. File browsing and image validation.
  3. JPG, PNG, and WebP support.
  4. A 10 MB client-side upload limit.
  5. Upload progress and error handling.
  6. Image replacement and reset functionality.
  7. Copy transformed image URL.
  8. Download transformed images.
  9. Responsive user interface.

Testing and Deployment

After development, I tested the application locally and deployed it using Vercel. I also tested the live application to verify that:

  • Image uploads work with Cloudinary.
  • All three output formats generate correctly.
  • No-Crop and Crop-to-Fill modes update the previews.
  • Generated image URLs can be copied and opened.
  • Transformed images can be downloaded.

The live application is available here: (https://posterpilot.vercel.app)

What I Learned?

Building PosterPilot gave me practical experience with Cloudinary's image upload and transformation capabilities. Some of the important concepts I explored include:

  • Integrating an external image service into a React application.
  • Using unsigned uploads without exposing API secrets.
  • Generating image variations through dynamic transformations.
  • Understanding the difference between padding and cropping.
  • Optimizing images for web delivery.
  • Deploying a frontend application with environment variables.

I also learned that a useful project does not always need a complicated architecture. Sometimes, combining the right service with a focused real-world problem can produce a practical solution.

*What's Next?
*
PosterPilot is an initial version, and there is room for improvement. Some possible future enhancements include:

  • More social media presets.
  • Custom width and height controls.
  • Background color selection for padded images.
  • Batch poster processing.
  • Additional image editing options.

*Final Thoughts
*
PosterPilot started with a simple campus-related problem: adapting event posters into different formats without unnecessarily losing important information.

Through this project, I explored how Cloudinary can make image uploading, transformation, optimization, and delivery easier to integrate into a modern web application.

I'm excited to continue learning, building, and exploring more practical applications of Cloudinary.

I'd appreciate your feedback and suggestions!

title: Deleting files safely from a Tauri app: what I learned sending them to the Windows Recycle Bin from Rust
description:
I'm building a disk cleaner for Windows in Rust and Tauri 2. Finding junk isn't the scary part. Deleting it is. If the scanner has a bug, you see a wrong number. If the delete path has a bug, someone loses files.

So the delete path ended up with more code and more tests than anything else in the app. Here's what it does and why. All the snippets are from the real source, trimmed a bit, with the file name on top.

One thing up front: not everything my app removes goes to the Recycle Bin. I'll get to that at the end, because I only fixed how the UI talks about it this week.

1. The webview only gets to delete what a scan returned

In Tauri the UI is a webview calling Rust commands. I treat it like any other client I don't control. If a command takes a list of paths, those paths could be anything.

So the backend remembers what each scan returned, and only those paths can be trashed:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
type Approved = HashMap<ScanKind, HashSet<String>>;
static APPROVED: LazyLock<Mutex<Approved>> = LazyLock::new(Mutex::default);

/// Records the files a scan returned to the UI: only these can be trashed.
/// Protected paths are never recorded.
pub fn approve<'a>(kind: ScanKind, paths: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a str>) {
    let set = paths
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|path| !is_protected(Path::new(path)))
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .collect();
    approved().insert(kind, set);
}

trash_files checks every path against that set. Anything else is reported as failed and left alone. There's a test for it: a file no scan returned gets reported, and it's still on disk afterwards.

2. "Inside C:\Windows" means folder boundaries

The protected list is what you'd expect. %SystemRoot%, Program Files and ProgramData. $Recycle.Bin and System Volume Information anywhere. pagefile.sys, Recovery, Windows.old and friends at a drive root. Network shares get refused too.

The comparison is where it's easy to slip. A plain starts_with thinks c:\windowsill\notes.txt is inside c:\windows. So paths get normalised first (no \\?\ prefix, lower case, no trailing separator) and then compared on folder boundaries:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// `c:\data` contains `c:\data\x` but not `c:\database`.
pub fn is_within(path: &str, root: &str) -> bool {
    match path.strip_prefix(root) {
        Some("") => true,
        Some(rest) => root.ends_with(SEP) || rest.starts_with(SEP),
        None => false,
    }
}

Yes, there's a test for C:\Windowsill\notes.txt.

3. A path can change between the scan and the delete

By the time someone clicks "Move to Recycle Bin", the scan might be minutes old. In that time a folder on the path could have been swapped for a junction pointing somewhere else. Scans return resolved paths, so right before deleting I resolve the path again and refuse it if it doesn't resolve to itself anymore:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// A regular file (not a link or folder) outside protected locations whose path
/// resolves to itself. A link or junction put in the way since the scan is refused.
fn safe_size(path: &str) -> Option<u64> {
    let meta = Path::new(path).symlink_metadata().ok().filter(std::fs::Metadata::is_file)?;
    let real = normalize(&std::fs::canonicalize(path).ok()?);
    (real == normalize(Path::new(path)) && !is_protected_normalized(&real)).then_some(meta.len())
}

On Windows canonicalize also expands 8.3 short names like PROGRA~1, which is one more way two strings can mean the same folder. The check runs again for every batch, right before Windows sees the paths, since an earlier batch might have sat on a dialog for a while.

4. The trash crate and COM threads

The actual move is done by the trash crate (5.x). On Windows it initialises COM single-threaded. My app already had other commands (the program list, icons) setting COM to multithreaded on the shared command threads. Call trash on one of those and you don't get an error. You get a panic.

The fix is boring. Every Recycle Bin operation gets its own thread:

// src-tauri/src/recycle.rs
/// `trash` initialises COM single-threaded and *panics* when the thread already uses
/// the multithreaded model. A new thread has no COM state, and a panic there only
/// fails this call.
pub fn on_own_thread<T: Send + 'static>(f: impl FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static) -> Option<T> {
    std::thread::spawn(f).join().ok()
}

If you've got windows-crate COM code and trash in the same Tauri app, it's worth checking which thread each one runs on.

5. Batches, cancels, and "delete permanently?"

One shell operation per file is slow. One giant operation fails as a whole if a single path is bad. I went with batches of 64, and if a batch fails before it even starts, the code falls back to one file at a time so one bad path doesn't hold up the rest.

Windows has opinions too. If a file is too big for the Recycle Bin, Windows asks whether to delete it permanently. If the user says no, I shouldn't ask again for every remaining file:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
const TRASH_BATCH: usize = 64;
const USER_CANCELLED: [i32; 2] = [
    0x8007_04C7_u32 as i32, // HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED)
    0x8027_0000_u32 as i32, // COPYENGINE_E_USER_CANCELLED
];

for chunk in paths.chunks(TRASH_BATCH) {
    let chunk: Vec<&String> = chunk.iter().filter(|p| safe_size(p).is_some()).collect();
    match trash::delete_all(&chunk) {
        Ok(()) => {}
        Err(err) if cancelled_by_user(&err) => return, // the user stopped it
        Err(trash::Error::Unknown { .. }) => {}        // ran, but the shell skipped some
        Err(_) => { /* failed before starting: retry one by one */ }
    }
}

6. Let the disk say what moved

The shell's return value doesn't tell you what happened to each file. So after the move, the code just looks. If a path still exists, it's a failure. Only paths that are actually gone count toward "bytes freed":

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
// The file system is the source of truth for what actually moved.
for (path, size) in targets {
    if exists(&path) { report.failed.push(path); }
    else { report.bytes_freed += size; report.deleted.push(path); }
}

That's why the number the app shows can be smaller than what you picked. Files that were in use stay put and show up as failed.

7. Being honest about what doesn't go to the Recycle Bin

This is the part I got wrong.

Large files, duplicates and similar photos go through everything above. Dev build folders (node_modules, target and so on) also go to the Recycle Bin, through a similar check in recycle.rs. Temp files and caches don't. The cleanup rules in junk_rules/mod.rs delete them with std::fs::remove_file, and the confirm text says why: "These are caches and temporary files; apps rebuild them as needed." What they get instead is a couple of different guards. A rule is skipped while its app is running (the comment in the code: "deleting a live cache can corrupt it"), and One-Click Fix and the scheduler only touch files older than 24 hours.

The code was fine with that. My welcome screen wasn't. It told people deleted files go to the Recycle Bin, which just isn't true for caches.

This week (#103) I swapped the native confirm box for an in-app dialog. It lists what's about to go and shows one of two labels: "Can be restored from the Recycle Bin" or "Permanent â€” not moved to the Recycle Bin". Cancel has focus by default. The welcome text now says: "Super Cleaner always asks first. Large files go to the Recycle Bin; caches and temp files are deleted for good."

While I was in there I found 11 of my 26 confirms showing English buttons in the Chinese UI. Turns out that one was on me. My old confirmAction() wrapper defaulted to okLabel = "Continue" and cancelLabel = "Cancel", hardcoded in English, and 11 call sites never passed their own labels. Now okLabel is required and Cancel defaults to the translated string.

If you're writing your own delete path

Don't trust the UI with paths, and only delete what the backend found itself. Normalise before you compare, compare on folder boundaries, and resolve again right before the delete. If anything else in your process touches COM, give trash its own thread. Assume the user, or Windows, will cancel halfway. Count what's actually gone from the disk. And tell people plainly what they can and can't undo, because that's the part I almost shipped wrong.

The code's from Super Cleaner, a Windows cleaner I'm building in Rust + Tauri. It's not public yet. I'll post here when it is.

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

See open roles.

title: Curved text in SVG without turning your words into shapes
description:
Most ways of bending text give you a picture of text. Object to Path in a desktop editor, and the outlined export from many curved text generators, turn every letter into its own shape. It looks right, but you can no longer retype it, swap the font, or let a screen reader read it.

SVG already has the right tool for this: textPath.

The markup

Give a path an id, then point a textPath inside your text at it:

<svg viewBox="0 0 800 420" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <path id="curve" d="M 100 320 Q 400 40 700 320" fill="none" stroke="#7e9bd6"/>
  <text font-size="40">
    <textPath href="#curve" startOffset="50%" text-anchor="middle">Text that follows the curve</textPath>
  </text>
</svg>
  • href names the path. Older tools want xlink:href too.
  • startOffset is where along the curve the words start. 50% with text-anchor="middle" centres them.
  • Text runs the way the path is drawn. To flip it under a curve, reverse the path.

It is part of SVG 1.1 and renders in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

Doing it by eye in SVG Lab

Writing the curve by hand is fine for one arc. For anything you want to place by eye, SVG Lab (svglab.app), a free browser SVG editor, binds text to a path in one click. I ran it as a guest, no sign-in, on 31 October 2026. Before, one path and one line of text, both selected:

After pressing Text on path:

  1. Draw the curve with the Pen or Curve tool, or import an SVG that has one.
  2. Add the words with the Text tool.
  3. Select both (Ctrl+A).
  4. Press Text on path in the Path panel.
  5. Drag the text to slide it, or use the On path controls: Start, Side (Above or Below), Flip (Upside down) and Length (Natural or Fit path).

This is exactly what SVG Lab wrote, copied from its SVG source panel:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" viewBox="0 0 800 420" width="800" height="420">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="420" fill="#f7f3ec"/>
  <path id="path_path1" d="M 100 320 C 300 133.33 500 133.33 700 320" stroke="#7e9bd6" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="butt" stroke-linejoin="miter" fill="none"/>
  <text font-family="Arial" font-size="40" font-weight="400" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="hanging" paint-order="fill stroke" xml:space="preserve" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" fill="#1d1d1d"><textPath href="#path_path1" xlink:href="#path_path1" startOffset="15.881%"><tspan dy="-40">Text that follows the curve</tspan></textPath></text>
</svg>

The path got an id, both href and xlink:href are set, and the words are still words.

One flaw I left in: with Side set to Below at 40 px, the letters touch the line. A nudge on Start or a smaller size fixes it.

Which to use

  • Curving text in the browser and keeping it editable: SVG Lab, because it binds in one click and exports a real textPath.
  • Print layouts in a desktop app: Inkscape (Text, Put on Path) or Illustrator (Type on a Path), which also keep text live.
  • One curved line in a web page: write the textPath yourself.

The editor is free. Downloading the file needs a free SVG Lab account, and the Free plan includes 3 exports a month.

Full walkthrough with screenshots: https://svglab.app/blog/how-to-put-text-on-a-curved-path-in-svg
