title: API Gateways & the Edge
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Give your scattered services one front door. You will know what an API gateway actually handles, which managed options you will meet, and how a WAF guards the edge against the traffic you do not want.

Contents

  • You shipped three services. Now what's the URL?
  • One sentence, then a picture in your head
  • Where it sits
  • What the gateway is actually responsible for
  • What a route + rate-limit policy looks like
  • Managed options you'll actually meet
  • The WAF and the edge
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

You shipped three services. Now what's the URL?

You split your app into a few services, one for auth, one for orders, one for payments. Each runs somewhere, each has its own host and port. Now your mobile app needs to call them. Do you hand the client three different URLs? Who checks the token? Who stops a bad actor from hammering the login endpoint 10,000 times a second? Who adds CORS headers, strips the internal X-Debug header, and caches that one expensive response?

The honest answer for most teams is: an API gateway. It's the single front door that every request passes through before it reaches a backend service, and once you have one, a whole category of cross-cutting problems stops living in your application code.

📌 Who this is for: Junior cloud and backend engineers who have built an API or two and are now staring down multiple services, public traffic, and the question "where does auth and rate limiting actually go?" No prior gateway experience assumed.

One sentence, then a picture in your head

An API gateway is a reverse proxy that sits in front of your services and handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, transforms, and caching, so each service doesn't have to.

If that still feels abstract, borrow the hotel. Guests don't wander into the kitchen, the laundry, or the manager's office directly. They walk up to the front desk, and the concierge handles everything from there.

In the real world In tech
You check in once at the front desk and get a room key. You authenticate once at the gateway and get a token it validates on every later request.
The concierge sends you to the right floor and room. The gateway routes /orders to the orders service and /pay to payments.
One guest can't monopolize the concierge all day. Rate limiting caps how many requests one client can make per window.
The desk keeps printed maps ready so it doesn't reprint per guest. The gateway caches common responses instead of re-hitting the backend.
A security guard screens people at the entrance. A WAF at the edge filters malicious traffic before it even reaches the desk.

A hotel front desk is an API gateway with a uniform.

Where it sits

The gateway lives between the public internet and your private services. In front of it, at the very edge, sits a WAF and usually a CDN. Behind it, your services stay on a private network and never take traffic directly from clients.

Clients → WAF (edge) → API gateway → private backend services.

  1. Request hits the edge: The client calls one hostname over HTTPS. The WAF inspects it first and drops anything matching known attack patterns.
  2. Gateway authenticates: Clean traffic reaches the gateway, which validates the token or API key. No token, no entry, the backend never sees the request.
  3. Rate limit is checked: The gateway counts requests for this client in the current window. Over the limit returns 429 immediately, sparing the backend.
  4. Route and (maybe) cache: The path is matched to a backend route. If a fresh cached response exists, it's returned without touching the service at all.
  5. Transform and forward: The gateway rewrites headers/paths as needed, forwards to the private service, then shapes the response on the way back out.

What the gateway is actually responsible for

The pitch for a gateway is consolidation: every concern below would otherwise be re-implemented (slightly differently, slightly buggily) in each service. Centralize them once.

Responsibility What it does Why at the gateway
Routing Maps an incoming path/host to a backend service Clients get one stable URL; you can move or split services behind it freely
Authentication Validates tokens, API keys, or mTLS before forwarding Reject unauthenticated traffic once, not in every service
Rate limiting Caps requests per client per time window Protects every backend from abuse and runaway clients in one place
Caching Stores and serves common responses Cuts latency and backend load without per-service cache code
Transforms Rewrites headers, paths, and bodies in/out Hide internal shapes; add CORS; strip debug headers consistently

The five core gateway responsibilities, and why they belong here.

💡 The rule of thumb: Cross-cutting and request-shaped concerns go in the gateway. Anything that needs to know what your business does stays in the service.

What a route + rate-limit policy looks like

Most gateways are configured declaratively, you describe routes and policies, the gateway enforces them. Here's a vendor-neutral shape: a route for the orders service with JWT auth, a per-client rate limit, and a short response cache.

gateway-route.yaml

routes:
  - name: orders
    match:
      path: /orders/*
      methods: [GET, POST]
    upstream:
      service: orders-service.internal
      port: 8080
    policies:
      # 1. Require a valid JWT before forwarding
      auth:
        type: jwt
        issuer: https://auth.example.com
        audience: orders-api
        forward_claims: [sub, scope]

      # 2. 100 requests per minute, per client key
      rate_limit:
        requests: 100
        per: minute
        key: ${request.header.X-Client-Id}
        on_exceeded:
          status: 429
          body: "Rate limit exceeded. Retry shortly."

      # 3. Cache successful GETs for 30s
      cache:
        methods: [GET]
        ttl: 30s
        vary: [Authorization]

      # 4. Shape the request/response
      transform:
        request:
          remove_headers: [X-Debug, X-Internal-Trace]
        response:
          add_headers:
            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com

Read it top to bottom and you've read the request lifecycle: authenticate, rate limit, serve from cache if possible, transform, forward. No business logic anywhere in here, that's the point.

Managed options you'll actually meet

You rarely build a gateway from scratch. Each major cloud has a managed one, and Apigee is the heavyweight cross-cloud option for serious API programs. They differ in polish and price, not in the fundamentals above.

  • AWS API Gateway, deep integration with Lambda and IAM; REST and HTTP APIs; pay-per-request. The default if you're already on AWS.
  • Azure API Management (APIM), strong policy engine (XML-based transforms), a built-in developer portal, and tiered pricing. Common in enterprise Azure shops.
  • Google Apigee, full API management platform: monetization, analytics, lifecycle, and a polished portal. Heavier and pricier; chosen when APIs are the product.
  • Self-managed (Kong, NGINX, Envoy), open-source data planes you run yourself. Maximum control, you own the upgrades, scaling, and on-call.

The WAF and the edge

A Web Application Firewall sits one hop in front of the gateway, at the edge of your network. Where the gateway asks "who are you and where are you going?", the WAF asks "does this request look malicious?" It inspects requests against rules, known SQL injection and XSS patterns, suspicious user agents, traffic floods, requests from flagged IP ranges, and drops the bad ones before they cost you anything downstream.

The edge is also where your CDN lives, terminating TLS close to users and serving static content from points of presence worldwide. WAF rules typically run right there, so an attack is filtered near its origin rather than after crossing the globe to your gateway. For the CDN side of this story, see CDN & Edge Compute.

📌 Gateway vs WAF, not the same job: The WAF is about threat filtering (is this request hostile?). The gateway is about identity and traffic management (who is this, and where should it go?). You want both, in that order.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Business logic in the gateway. It's tempting to add "just one" pricing rule or order check in a transform. Now your business logic is split across two systems with different deploy cycles. Keep the gateway dumb about your domain.
  2. No rate limiting. Without it, one buggy client or one attacker can take down every service behind the gateway at once. Set sane per-client limits from day one, even generous ones.
  3. Treating the gateway as a single point of failure. Everything flows through it, so if it's one box, it's the outage. Run it across multiple instances and availability zones, and health-check it like the critical infrastructure it is.
  4. Skipping the WAF because "the gateway has auth." Auth checks identity; it does not catch injection or floods. They solve different problems.
  5. Caching authenticated responses without a vary key. Cache a logged-in user's data without varying on their token and you'll serve their data to the next person. Always vary on the auth header.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • An API gateway is the single front door: routing, auth, rate limiting, caching, and transforms in one place.
  • It lets clients use one stable URL while you reshape services freely behind it.
  • Cross-cutting concerns go in the gateway; business logic stays in the service.
  • A WAF sits one hop further out at the edge and filters malicious traffic before the gateway sees it.
  • Gateway = identity and routing; WAF = threat filtering. Use both.
  • Reach for a managed option, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, or Apigee, before building your own.
  • Always cap rate limits, run the gateway redundantly, and vary cached responses on auth.

Where to go next

The gateway handles the front door, but the contracts your services expose through it matter just as much. Pair this with the design and edge sides of the picture, then put it into practice on the path.

  • Read Secure API Design for the contract and auth patterns the gateway enforces.
  • Read CDN & Edge Compute to go deeper on what else lives at the edge.
  • Practice routing and proxy concepts in the networking lab.
  • Follow the full track on the Cloud Engineer path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Our two self-hosted fonts hold 222 and 230 codepoints, and the arrow on our homepage is in neither
description:
Two weeks ago I wrote that next/font/google broke on an ampersand, so our two fonts are 59KB in the repo now. That post was about the switch: why the build broke, what the diff looked like, and what weight: "300 700" means next to a variable font.

This one is about what is actually inside the two files, because self-hosting a font changes a subset from something a build step chose into an artifact sitting in your repository that you can open and count. So I opened them.

Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages for new listings. The site in front of it is a Next.js app, and it loads three typefaces: Space Grotesk for headings, DM Sans for body text, and Geist Mono for small labels.

const spaceGrotesk = localFont({
  src: "./fonts/space-grotesk-latin.woff2",
  variable: "--font-space-grotesk",
  weight: "300 700",
  display: "swap",
  preload: true,
});

Two of the three are files in server/src/app/fonts/: 22,320 bytes of Space Grotesk and 36,980 bytes of DM Sans. The third comes from the geist npm package.

What is in the files

Four lines of Python, with fonttools and brotli installed:

from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
t = TTFont("src/app/fonts/dm-sans-latin.woff2")
print(t["maxp"].numGlyphs, len(t.getBestCmap()))
for a in t["fvar"].axes:
    print(a.axisTag, a.minValue, a.defaultValue, a.maxValue)
Space Grotesk DM Sans
Bytes 22,320 36,980
Glyphs 291 270
Codepoints in cmap 230 222
wght axis 300 to 700, default 300 100 to 1000, default 400
Internal family name Space Grotesk Light DM Sans 9pt

Two things in that table were news to me.

The first is that our declared weight: "300 700" is accurate for Space Grotesk and a deliberate narrowing of DM Sans, whose axis actually runs from 100 to 1000. Narrowing it is harmless here, and I checked rather than assumed: the site uses font-bold 95 times, font-semibold 98 times, font-medium five times and font-light twice, so nothing on any page asks for a weight outside 300 to 700. If somebody adds font-extrabold to a heading, they will get a synthesised bold rather than the 800 the file can genuinely draw.

The second is the internal family names. The Space Grotesk file calls itself "Space Grotesk Light" with a default instance at 300, and the DM Sans file calls itself "DM Sans 9pt", which is the name of one optical size of a font whose optical size axis was dropped on the way out of Google Fonts. None of that matters to next/font/local, which generates its own font-family name and never reads those strings. It matters the moment somebody copies one of these files into a hand-written @font-face and trusts the name in it.

The 20 characters our source actually uses

Before checking coverage I wanted to know what the site asks for. Across 80 source files, the copy and markup contain 20 distinct characters above U+007F. The top one is not close:

Character Uses
U+2500 ─ box drawing 602
U+20AC € 68
U+2013 – en dash 64
U+00A3 £ 60
U+2014 em dash 56
U+00B7 · 23
U+2192 → 11

Then a long tail: …, ², ¥, ä, ó, ú, ö, ©, curly quotes, and one each of ✓, ⋮ and ⚙.

Both fonts cover £, €, the dashes, the middot, the ellipsis, the accented vowels and the quotes. They do not cover five of the characters in that list: ─, →, ✓, ⋮ and ⚙.

The 602 box-drawing characters turned out to be the easiest finding of the week to explain:

{/* ── Hero ── */}
{/* ── Feature demo rows ── spacing matches between all sections */}

They are in JSX comments. The single most common non-ASCII character in the repository never reaches a browser, which is also why nobody has ever noticed that neither webfont can draw it.

The other four do reach a browser. Our 56 em dashes are a different kind of embarrassment, documented separately, since the copy rule for this site says there are not supposed to be any.

The characters that fall back, and where you can see them

Three of the five are in rendered text, and the counts are in the HTML if you want to check them:

  • → in link text: four on the homepage, ten on the comparison hub, six on the help page.
  • ⚙ twice on the help page, in a Gmail instruction that says to click the gear icon.
  • ⋮ once on the help page, for Gmail's three-dot menu.
  • ✓ once on the post-checkout success page, which robots.txt disallows, so nobody but a buyer sees it.

Geist Mono, from the npm package, carries 889 codepoints and has the box drawing character and the arrow. It does not have the tick, the vertical ellipsis or the gear. Those three come from the operating system on every page load, in whatever the browser picks next out of ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif.

This is not a bug. Per-character fallback down the CSS font stack is exactly what should happen, and an arrow in SF Pro next to body text in DM Sans is something I only noticed because I went looking. It is still worth knowing which characters on your own site are not being drawn by the fonts you chose.

The six the repository cannot show you

Here is the part I did not expect, and the reason this is a post rather than a note in a commit message.

Notifio prices in 24 currencies, with the figure on the page being the figure charged. The symbols for those currencies are not in any source file, because Intl.NumberFormat produces them at runtime from a currency code and a locale. A grep of the repo cannot find them, so no amount of auditing the source tells you whether the fonts can draw them.

Formatting the same amount in all 24 and checking each character against both cmaps gives six that neither file covers:

Currency Rendered Missing
PLN 2499 zł U+0142 ł
CZK 2 499 Kč U+010D č
TRY ₺2.499 U+20BA ₺
INR ₹2,499 U+20B9 ₹
JPY ￥2,499 U+FFE5 fullwidth ￥
ILS 2,499 ₪ U+20AA ₪, plus two U+200F marks

The Polish and Czech ones are a subset choice: ł and č live in Google's latin-ext, and we asked for latin, both before and after self-hosting, so this is not something the switch to local files lost. Of the other four, the rupee, lira and shekel signs do fall inside latin-ext's declared unicode range, so that subset might carry them depending on what the font itself draws, and the fullwidth yen sits outside every Latin range there is.

The visible consequence is on the pricing page, where the headline price is rendered at 72px in Space Grotesk. A visitor in India gets ₹ at 72px from a system font, hard against digits at 72px from ours, with whatever difference in weight and stroke that font happens to have. The ¥ that appears three times in our own source is U+00A5, the half-width one, which both fonts do have. Japan gets U+FFE5 from Intl, which they do not.

What I am going to do about it

Not add latin-ext. It fixes two of the six for certain, maybe three more, and charges every visitor the extra bytes to find out.

The fix that matches the problem is to stop relying on the symbol for the currencies where the symbol is ambiguous or missing anyway. The line under every price already names the currency, because $39.99 needs to tell a Canadian which dollar it is. For the six above, rendering the ISO code next to the number is both a legibility win and a coverage win, and it is one branch in one formatter rather than another font file.

The thing I would take from this generally: subsetting is usually discussed as a performance decision, and it is also a decision about which of your strings are allowed to be drawn in your own typeface. The strings that catch you out are the ones your code generates rather than the ones you typed, which means you cannot audit them by reading the repository. You have to format one of everything and compare it against the cmap.

If you want to look at the pages involved, the prices are on the pricing page, the arrows are on the homepage and the comparison pages, and the gear and the three dots are in the Gmail setup steps on the help page. The per-site alert pages are at notifio.app/alerts, and the app itself is on the download page.

title: Python - Operators, Functions & Function Arguments
description:
1.Operators in Python

Operators are special symbols or keywords used to perform operations on variables and values.

Python has different types of operators.

A.Arithmetic Operators

Arithmetic operators are used to perform mathematical calculations.

B.Comparison Operators

Comparison operators are used to compare two values. They return either True or False.

C.Logical Operators

Logical operators are used to combine multiple conditions.

Python has three logical operators:

1.and – Returns True if both conditions are true.

2.or – Returns True if at least one condition is true.

3.not – Reverses the result.

Example:

age = 20

print(age > 18 and age < 30)
print(age < 18 or age == 20)
print(not(age > 18))

Output:

True
True
False

D.Assignment Operators

Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables.

E.Membership Operators

Membership operators are used to check whether a value exists in a sequence.

1.in – Checks whether a value exists.

2.not in – Checks whether a value does not exist.

Example:

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]

print("apple" in fruits)
print("orange" not in fruits)

Output:

True
True

F.Identity Operators

Identity operators are used to check whether two variables refer to the same object.

1.is – Returns True if both refer to the same object.

2.is not – Returns True if they refer to different objects.

Example:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a

print(a is b)

Output:

True

G.Bitwise Operators

2.Functions in Python

A function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task.

Functions help us avoid writing the same code repeatedly and make programs easier to understand.

Python provides two main ways to work with functions:

  • Built-in functions
  • User-defined functions

A.Built-in Functions

Built-in functions are already available in Python. We can use them directly without defining them.

Some common built-in functions are:

B.User-Defined Functions

User-defined functions are functions created by programmers to perform specific tasks.

We use the def keyword to create a function.

Syntax:

def function_name():
# Statements

Example:

def greet():
print("Hello, Welcome to Python!")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python!

Here:

  • def is used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • greet() is used to call the function.

3.Function Arguments in Python

Function arguments are values passed to a function when calling it. They allow us to send information to a function.

Let's understand the different types of function arguments.

A.Positional Arguments

In positional arguments, values are passed according to the order of parameters.

Example:

def student(name, age):
print("Name:", name)
print("Age:", age)

student("Gowtham", 20)

Output:

Name: Gowtham
Age: 20

Here, "Gowtham" is passed to name, and 20 is passed to age.

B.Keyword Arguments

In keyword arguments, we pass values using parameter names. The order does not matter.

Example:

def student(name, age):
print("Name:", name)
print("Age:", age)

student(age=20, name="Gowtham")

Output:

Name: Gowtham
Age: 20

C.Default Arguments

Default arguments have predefined values. If we don't pass a value, Python uses the default value.

Example:

def greet(name="Friend"):
print("Hello", name)

greet()
greet("Gowtham")

Output:

Hello Friend
Hello Gowtham

D.Variable-Length Arguments

Sometimes, we don't know how many arguments will be passed to a function. Python supports variable-length arguments.

1.*args

*args allows us to pass multiple positional arguments to a function.

def add(*numbers):
print(sum(numbers))

add(10, 20)
add(10, 20, 30, 40)

Output:

30
100

2.**kwargs

**kwargs allows us to pass multiple keyword arguments to a function. These arguments are stored as a dictionary.

def student(**details):
print(details)

student(name="Gowtham", age=20, city="Chennai")

Output:

{'name': 'Gowtham', 'age': 20, 'city': 'Chennai'}

title: I Got Tired of Making Study Materials Instead of Studying, So I Built Cramio
description:
An experiment in building an AI-powered study companion for students, using React, Capacitor, Supabase, and a little frustration with the way we study.

There's a funny problem with studying.

You sit down because you want to learn something. Three hours later, you've organized your PDFs, highlighted paragraphs, rewritten notes, created a few flashcards, and somehow haven't actually studied that much.

Congratulations. You've successfully procrastinated using productivity tools.

I've experienced this enough times to start questioning the workflow itself.

Why does preparing to study sometimes feel like an entirely separate subject?

That question eventually turned into Cramio.

Explore Cramio →

The real problem wasn't a lack of study materials

Students already have materials. Plenty of them, actually.

Lecture slides, PDFs, textbooks, handwritten notes, screenshots, and documents scattered across different folders.

The problem is what happens next.

A PDF contains 40 pages of information. You need to understand it, identify the important concepts, create questions, and test whether you've actually retained anything.

Most of that preparation is repetitive.

I started thinking: what if the application could handle some of that preparation, while the student focused on understanding the material?

Not another chatbot with a fancy interface. Not another application that simply summarizes everything and calls it learning.

I wanted something built around the actual studying workflow.

Building Cramio: From raw materials to active learning

Cramio is an AI-powered study application that turns existing learning materials into resources students can actively use.

The central idea is simple:

Your materials should become the starting point of your learning experience, not another thing you have to manually process.

Here's how that translates into the product.

From reading to reviewing

Instead of manually rewriting an entire lecture document, Cramio helps generate organized study notes.

The goal is to make lengthy learning materials easier to navigate and revisit.

From memorizing to active recall

Flashcards are useful because they force you to retrieve information instead of passively rereading it.

Cramio uses AI to help generate question-and-answer cards from study materials, making it easier to start practicing.

From guessing to testing

Reading something five times doesn't necessarily mean you understand it.

That's why Cramio also includes AI-generated quizzes, allowing students to test their understanding and identify areas that need more attention.

When the material gets confusing

Sometimes the problem isn't memorization. It's understanding a concept in the first place.

Cramio also includes an AI study assistant to help students work through questions and difficult topics.

The engineering behind it

I didn't want Cramio to become a collection of disconnected AI features.

The challenge was creating an application where authentication, study materials, AI generation, and the actual learning experience worked together.

The current architecture uses:

  • React for the application interface.
  • Capacitor to bring the web application into an Android environment.
  • Supabase for backend services and data management.
  • Clerk for authentication.
  • AI-powered workflows for generating learning resources.

One important engineering consideration is that AI-generated content needs structure.

Generating text is relatively straightforward. Generating useful educational material that students can actually review is a different problem.

A flashcard should test a meaningful concept. A quiz should assess understanding. Notes should be readable rather than becoming another wall of generated text.

That's the difference between adding AI to an application and designing an application around a meaningful AI-assisted workflow.

Why Android first?

I wanted to focus on making the experience accessible through an actual mobile application.

Students don't always study at a desk with a laptop open. Sometimes they're reviewing materials between classes, commuting, or studying from their phones.

Building with Capacitor gives Cramio a way to share its React application architecture while delivering an Android experience.

It also introduces its own challenges: mobile interactions, navigation, authentication flows, responsive layouts, and making sure the application feels native enough to use comfortably.

These are the kinds of details that don't always show up in a feature announcement, but they matter enormously to the actual product.

I'm not trying to replace studying with AI

This is probably the most important distinction.

AI shouldn't become another shortcut that makes students feel productive without actually learning anything.

Summarizing a chapter isn't the same as understanding it. Generating flashcards isn't the same as remembering their answers.

The interesting opportunity is using AI to reduce the friction between receiving learning materials and actively engaging with them.

Cramio is built around that idea.

What's next?

Cramio is an ongoing project, and there's still plenty to improve.

Some areas I'm particularly interested in are:

  • Improving the quality and usefulness of AI-generated study materials.
  • Making PDF processing more reliable.
  • Refining the mobile learning experience.
  • Making studying more engaging without turning the application into a distraction.
  • Building a better workflow around active recall and self-assessment.

I want to keep approaching this as an engineering problem: identify friction, understand its cause, and build something that genuinely improves the experience.

Try it yourself

If you're a student who spends too much time preparing materials instead of actually studying, Cramio might be worth exploring.

Visit Cramio

And if you're a developer interested in building AI-powered applications, I'd be interested in hearing how you're approaching the challenge of making AI genuinely useful beyond a chat interface.

Because honestly, students already have enough things to memorize. They shouldn't have to memorize an entire workflow just to start studying.

title: Temporal API in TypeScript: deadlines and time zones
description:
Being able to use the Temporal API in TypeScript was one of my favorite pieces of news around Node.js 26. Over the years I have seen plenty of code where a deadline was off by an hour because somebody wrote “plus 48 hours” instead of “plus two days” and a daylight saving change happened in between. Bugs like that don’t show up in tests. They show up in production, twice a year.

In my article on Node.js 26 LTS on Lambda I only touched on Temporal briefly. This time we go deeper: step by step, you build the deadline logic for a fictional city library, store the values cleanly in DynamoDB, deploy everything to Lambda with the Serverless Framework and deliberately test across the DST change. Afterwards you will know which Temporal type is meant for what and how to move away from Date or date-fns.

In short

Temporal replaces Date with dedicated types for instants, calendar dates and times in a time zone. Node.js 26 ships the API without a flag, TypeScript has included the types since version 6.0, and older Lambda runtimes only need a small polyfill. The biggest pitfall is choosing the wrong type: if you store a deadline as a plain date without a time zone, you only move the problem somewhere else.

What you will learn in this article

  • Which Temporal type is right for instants, calendar days and deadlines
  • How to set up Temporal in TypeScript, Node.js 26 and on Lambda with nodejs24.x
  • How to calculate and test deadlines correctly across DST changes
  • How to store Temporal values in DynamoDB, including TTL
  • How to migrate step by step from Date or date-fns

Why Date so often gets deadlines wrong

Date has been part of JavaScript since 1995 and was closely modeled on an early Java class at the time. You can still tell. Months start at 0, so new Date(2026, 9, 25) is October 25. A Date object is mutable, and if you pass it to a function you may get it back changed. On top of that, Date knows exactly two time zones: UTC and the local time zone of the machine running the code.

That last point is especially tricky in a Serverless setup. A Lambda function runs in UTC by default. Your customers, however, live in Berlin, Vienna or Zurich. Ask Lambda for “today” at 0:30 am German time and you still get yesterday. Lambda is doing everything right here. The real question is: whose “today” do you mean?

The classic example is the DST change. On October 25, 2026, clocks in Germany go back from 3:00 am to 2:00 am, so that day has 25 hours. If you create a deadline of “two days” on October 24 at 10:00 am and calculate it as 48 hours, you end up at 9:00 am on October 26. What you meant was 10:00 am. That is why Temporal clearly separates exact durations in hours from calendar arithmetic in days.

const pickup = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T10:00[Europe/Berlin]");

console.log(pickup.add({ hours: 48 }).toString());
// 2026-10-26T09:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (exactly 48 hours later)

console.log(pickup.add({ days: 2 }).toString());
// 2026-10-26T10:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (two calendar days later)

Both results are correct. They simply answer different questions. With Date you have to keep that difference in your head, while Temporal makes you write it down.

Which Temporal type for which purpose?

Temporal is a namespace like Math, not a constructor. It contains several classes, and all objects are immutable: every operation returns a new object. For everyday work you mainly need these types:

Type What it describes Typical example
Temporal.Instant Exact point on the timeline, without calendar or time zone Event timestamp, log entry
Temporal.ZonedDateTime Instant plus time zone, handles summer and winter time Return deadline “Nov 19 at 6:00 pm in Berlin”
Temporal.PlainDate Calendar date without time and without time zone Birthday, day of borrowing, holiday
Temporal.PlainTime Wall-clock time without a date Closing time “18:00”
Temporal.PlainDateTime Date and time without a time zone Form input before the time zone is known
Temporal.Duration Length of time in years, months, days, hours … Loan period, gap between two appointments

There are also PlainYearMonth (for a billing month, say), PlainMonthDay (recurring anniversaries) and Temporal.Now for the current time in various forms.

Rule of thumb for choosing a Temporal type

The rule of thumb for choosing a type

For every value I ask myself one single question: do I need to know exactly when this happens in the world? If yes, I need an Instant or a ZonedDateTime. A return deadline belongs in this group, because at 6:01 pm in Berlin it has expired, no matter where the server is. If the answer is no, a plain type is enough. A birthday is on May 3, whatever time zone you happen to be in.

A mistake I see often: deadlines get stored as PlainDateTime because it looks so simple. Then exactly the information you later need for comparisons is missing. PlainDateTime is meant for intermediate steps, for example a form before it is clear which time zone the appointment takes place in.

Setting up the Temporal API in TypeScript

Before you start, a quick look at support. Temporal has reached stage 4 in the TC39 process, the standards committee for JavaScript, which means it is fully specified. Firefox has shipped the API since version 139, Chrome since version 144 and Node.js since version 26. According to the proposal repository, Safari is still missing. TypeScript has included the matching types since version 6.0.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 26 locally (for native Temporal support) or Node.js 22/24 with a polyfill
  • TypeScript 6.0 or later; the example was tested with TypeScript 7.0.2
  • For deployment: an AWS account and the Serverless Framework v4 (npm i -g serverless)
  • Basic knowledge of Lambda and DynamoDB helps but isn’t required

Lambda runtime and polyfill

On Lambda, nodejs26.x is still a public preview, and AWS plans the regular launch for November 2026. Preview runtimes come without the Lambda SLA and are not intended for production use. Until then, use nodejs24.x and load the temporal-polyfill package (MIT license). Its entry point temporal-polyfill/global installs Temporal globally only if the runtime doesn’t already provide it. I checked this in the package’s source code: on Node.js 26 the import simply does nothing. So later you can switch the runtime without touching a single line of code.

Configuring TypeScript

You enable the types via the lib option. Either take all of esnext or only the esnext.temporal part. I prefer the more granular option because it makes clear which new features the project actually uses.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2024",
    "lib": ["es2024", "esnext.temporal"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src", "test"]
}

allowImportingTsExtensions and erasableSyntaxOnly let Node.js run the TypeScript files directly. We will use that for the tests in a moment, without any build step.

Step by step: loan deadlines for a library

Our example is a fictional city library with clear rules. A book may be borrowed for 21 days. If the last day falls on a Sunday or a holiday, the return moves to the next opening day. You can return books until 6:00 pm Berlin time. Two days before the deadline a reminder goes out at 9:00 am, and every overdue day costs 50 cents, up to a maximum of 10 euros.

Step 1: Create the project 

mkdir temporal-library-loans && cd temporal-library-loans
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm i temporal-polyfill @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb
npm i -D typescript @types/node @types/aws-lambda
mkdir src test

Then create the tsconfig.json shown above. Next comes a tiny file that loads the polyfill when needed:

// src/temporal.ts
// Loads the polyfill only if the runtime has no native Temporal
// (e.g. nodejs24.x on Lambda). On Node.js 26 this does nothing.
import "temporal-polyfill/global";

Step 2: The deadline logic as pure functions

The rules go into a file without any AWS dependencies. That makes them easy to test and independent of where the code runs later.

// src/loan-rules.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

export const LIBRARY_ZONE = "Europe/Berlin";
export const LOAN_DAYS = 21;
export const CLOSING_TIME = Temporal.PlainTime.from("18:00");
export const FEE_PER_DAY_CENTS = 50;
export const MAX_FEE_CENTS = 1000;

// Holidays when the library is closed (fictional selection)
export const HOLIDAYS = new Set(["2026-12-25", "2026-12-26", "2027-01-01"]);

function isClosed(date: Temporal.PlainDate): boolean {
  return date.dayOfWeek === 7 || HOLIDAYS.has(date.toString());
}

// Due date: day of borrowing + 21 days; on a Sunday or holiday, the next opening day
export function dueDate(borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.PlainDate {
  let due = borrowedOn.add({ days: LOAN_DAYS });
  while (isClosed(due)) {
    due = due.add({ days: 1 });
  }
  return due;
}

// Exact deadline: due date at 6:00 pm Berlin time
export function returnDeadline(due: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.ZonedDateTime {
  return due.toZonedDateTime({ timeZone: LIBRARY_ZONE, plainTime: CLOSING_TIME });
}

// Reminder two calendar days earlier at 9:00 am – wall-clock time, even across DST changes
export function reminderAt(deadline: Temporal.ZonedDateTime): Temporal.ZonedDateTime {
  return deadline.subtract({ days: 2 }).with({ hour: 9, minute: 0 });
}

// Overdue days: calendar days between due date and today (never negative)
export function overdueDays(due: Temporal.PlainDate, today: Temporal.PlainDate): number {
  const days = due.until(today, { largestUnit: "days" }).days;
  return Math.max(0, days);
}

export function lateFeeCents(due: Temporal.PlainDate, today: Temporal.PlainDate): number {
  return Math.min(overdueDays(due, today) * FEE_PER_DAY_CENTS, MAX_FEE_CENTS);
}

// "Today" from the library's point of view – not from the Lambda server's (UTC)
export function libraryToday(now: Temporal.Instant): Temporal.PlainDate {
  return now.toZonedDateTimeISO(LIBRARY_ZONE).toPlainDate();
}

A few spots deserve a second look. The due date is a PlainDate, because “21 days later” is purely a calendar question. dayOfWeek follows the ISO standard from 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday), so the Sunday-is-zero confusion of Date is finally gone. Only in returnDeadline do time and time zone come in, turning the calendar day into an actual instant.

For the reminder, we deliberately calculate in calendar days and then set the time with with(). If the DST change falls between reminder and deadline, it still stays at 9:00 am wall-clock time. That is exactly what people expect when a reminder is supposed to arrive “at nine in the morning”.

The libraryToday function looks harmless but matters a lot. It receives an Instant and converts it into the library’s time zone. As a result, “today” is always Berlin’s today, even though Lambda runs in UTC. And because the instant comes from outside, you can simulate any time you like in tests.

Step 3: Storing Temporal values in DynamoDB

DynamoDB has no date type. So you have to decide in which form to store the values, and that decision matters more than it seems. My suggestion:

  • Plain calendar dates as ISO strings like 2026-11-19. They are readable and sort lexicographically.
  • Instants as UTC strings like 2026-11-19T17:00:00Z. That way comparisons and range queries on a sort key work.
  • The time zone separately as an IANA name like Europe/Berlin, so you can restore local time for display.
  • For DynamoDB TTL, an additional number with epoch seconds, because TTL ignores anything that isn’t a Number attribute. 
// src/storage.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

export interface Loan {
  loanId: string;
  bookId: string;
  memberId: string;
  borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate;
  due: Temporal.PlainDate;
  deadline: Temporal.ZonedDateTime;
}

export interface LoanItem {
  pk: string;
  bookId: string;
  memberId: string;
  borrowedOn: string;     // "2026-10-29" – plain date, no time
  dueDate: string;        // "2026-11-19"
  deadlineAt: string;     // "2026-11-19T17:00:00Z" – UTC, sortable
  timeZone: string;       // "Europe/Berlin" – for display
  expiresAt: number;      // epoch seconds for DynamoDB TTL
}

const KEEP_AFTER_DEADLINE = { days: 180 };

export function toItem(loan: Loan): LoanItem {
  return {
    pk: `LOAN#${loan.loanId}`,
    bookId: loan.bookId,
    memberId: loan.memberId,
    borrowedOn: loan.borrowedOn.toString(),
    dueDate: loan.due.toString(),
    deadlineAt: loan.deadline.toInstant().toString(),
    timeZone: loan.deadline.timeZoneId,
    expiresAt: Math.floor(loan.deadline.add(KEEP_AFTER_DEADLINE).epochMilliseconds / 1000),
  };
}

export function fromItem(item: LoanItem): Loan {
  return {
    loanId: item.pk.replace("LOAN#", ""),
    bookId: item.bookId,
    memberId: item.memberId,
    borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate.from(item.borrowedOn),
    due: Temporal.PlainDate.from(item.dueDate),
    deadline: Temporal.Instant.from(item.deadlineAt).toZonedDateTimeISO(item.timeZone),
  };
}

Why not just store the string of a ZonedDateTime, i.e. 2026-11-19T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]? It does contain everything, but it doesn’t sort reliably once values with different offsets end up in the same column. The UTC instant doesn’t have that problem. You can read more about TTL and expiry dates in my post DynamoDB TTL: build seat holds that expire.

Step 4: Lambda handler and serverless.yml

The handler is intentionally lean. It reads the book and member from the request, calculates date, deadline and reminder and writes the record to DynamoDB.

// src/handler.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";
import type { APIGatewayProxyEventV2, APIGatewayProxyResultV2 } from "aws-lambda";
import { dueDate, libraryToday, reminderAt, returnDeadline } from "./loan-rules.ts";
import { toItem, type Loan } from "./storage.ts";

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));
const TABLE = process.env.LOANS_TABLE ?? "";

export async function createLoan(event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> {
  const body = JSON.parse(event.body ?? "{}") as { bookId?: string; memberId?: string };
  if (!body.bookId || !body.memberId) {
    return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "bookId and memberId are required" }) };
  }

  const borrowedOn = libraryToday(Temporal.Now.instant());
  const due = dueDate(borrowedOn);
  const deadline = returnDeadline(due);
  const loan: Loan = {
    loanId: randomUUID(),
    bookId: body.bookId,
    memberId: body.memberId,
    borrowedOn,
    due,
    deadline,
  };

  await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: TABLE, Item: toItem(loan) }));

  return {
    statusCode: 201,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      loanId: loan.loanId,
      dueDate: due.toString(),
      deadline: deadline.toString(),
      reminder: reminderAt(deadline).toString(),
    }),
  };
}

🎬 Flow of a book loan with Temporal – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

For the infrastructure I am using the Serverless Framework here. Since version 4 it builds TypeScript itself with esbuild, so no extra build configuration is needed.

# serverless.yml
service: library-loans
frameworkVersion: "4"

provider:
  name: aws
  runtime: nodejs24.x        # switch to nodejs26.x once it is GA
  region: eu-central-1
  architecture: arm64
  memorySize: 256
  environment:
    LOANS_TABLE: ${self:service}-${sls:stage}-loans
    TZ: UTC                  # Lambda default; library time comes from the code
  iam:
    role:
      statements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - dynamodb:PutItem
          Resource:
            - !GetAtt LoansTable.Arn

functions:
  createLoan:
    handler: src/handler.createLoan
    events:
      - httpApi:
          path: /loans
          method: post

resources:
  Resources:
    LoansTable:
      Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
      Properties:
        TableName: ${self:service}-${sls:stage}-loans
        BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
        AttributeDefinitions:
          - AttributeName: pk
            AttributeType: S
        KeySchema:
          - AttributeName: pk
            KeyType: HASH
        TimeToLiveSpecification:
          AttributeName: expiresAt
          Enabled: true

The IAM role may only call PutItem on exactly this table. The handler needs nothing more. Deploy and try it out:

serverless deploy
curl -X POST "https://<your-api-id>.execute-api.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/loans" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bookId":"book-42","memberId":"reader-7"}'

If you borrow on October 29, 2026, the response looks roughly like this (the loanId will of course differ):

{
  "loanId": "3f2c9a4e-8b1d-4c57-9e0a-5d6f7a8b9c01",
  "dueDate": "2026-11-19",
  "deadline": "2026-11-19T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]",
  "reminder": "2026-11-17T09:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]"
}

Step 5: Testing across the DST change

Now comes the part I consider most important for date logic. Tests with “today plus three days” are almost always green and prove little. They only become meaningful with fixed dates around the DST change, holidays and the day boundary between UTC and Berlin.

// test/loan-rules.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { dueDate, lateFeeCents, libraryToday, overdueDays, reminderAt, returnDeadline } from "../src/loan-rules.ts";

const day = (s: string) => Temporal.PlainDate.from(s);

test("due date is 21 days after borrowing", () => {
  assert.equal(dueDate(day("2026-10-29")).toString(), "2026-11-19");
});

test("holidays and Sundays move to the next opening day", () => {
  // Dec 25 holiday, Dec 26 holiday, Dec 27 Sunday
  assert.equal(dueDate(day("2026-12-04")).toString(), "2026-12-28");
});

test("deadline stays at 6:00 pm Berlin time, even after the DST change", () => {
  const deadline = returnDeadline(day("2026-10-26"));
  assert.equal(deadline.toString(), "2026-10-26T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.equal(deadline.toInstant().toString(), "2026-10-26T17:00:00Z");
});

test("reminder at 9:00 am wall-clock time across the DST change", () => {
  const reminder = reminderAt(returnDeadline(day("2026-10-26")));
  assert.equal(reminder.toString(), "2026-10-24T09:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]");
});

test("overdue days and capped fee", () => {
  assert.equal(overdueDays(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-23")), 4);
  assert.equal(overdueDays(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-10")), 0);
  assert.equal(lateFeeCents(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-23")), 200);
  assert.equal(lateFeeCents(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-12-31")), 1000);
});

test("“today” is based on Berlin, not UTC", () => {
  // 23:30 UTC is already the next day in Berlin
  assert.equal(libraryToday(Temporal.Instant.from("2026-10-29T23:30:00Z")).toString(), "2026-10-30");
});

You can run the tests directly with Node.js, without a compile step:

npx tsc --noEmit
node --test test/*.test.ts

Expected result: all tests pass. I ran them on Node.js 26.13 with native Temporal and on Node.js 22 with the polyfill, both times with identical results. The repository also contains a second test for the round trip through DynamoDB and the conversion from Date, which I leave out here to save space.

Summer and winter time: what Temporal decides behind the scenes

Twice a year there are times in Berlin that are ambiguous. In spring an hour is missing: on March 28, 2027 the clock jumps from 2:00 am to 3:00 am, so “2:30 am” doesn’t exist that day. In autumn an hour happens twice: on October 25, 2026, 2:30 am occurs once in summer time and once in winter time.

Temporal solves this with the disambiguation option. The default value compatible behaves like Date: inside the gap the time is pushed forward, and in the repeated hour the earlier one wins. With earlier or later you pick a variant on purpose, and with reject Temporal throws a RangeError.

// Spring gap: 2:30 am does not exist
Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2027-03-28T02:30[Europe/Berlin]").toString();
// 2027-03-28T03:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]

// Repeated hour in autumn: deliberately pick the second 2:30 am
Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2026-10-25T02:30")
  .toZonedDateTime("Europe/Berlin", { disambiguation: "later" })
  .toString();
// 2026-10-25T02:30:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]

// Often the best choice for booking systems: an error beats a silent shift
Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2027-03-28T02:30")
  .toZonedDateTime("Europe/Berlin", { disambiguation: "reject" }); // RangeError

Something similar applies to month arithmetic. January 31 plus one month gives February 28 with the default overflow: "constrain". If you prefer an error, pass { overflow: "reject" }. For subscriptions and contract terms this is a business decision that you should clarify with the domain experts instead of leaving it to chance.

Migrating from Date and date-fns

Hardly any project can switch everything overnight. It doesn’t have to. I would use Temporal first in new business logic and convert at the edges, wherever older libraries, ORMs or SDKs still expect or return Date.

// src/legacy.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

// Existing code still returns Date objects? This converts them without loss.
export function fromLegacyDate(value: Date): Temporal.Instant {
  return Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(value.getTime());
}

// For libraries that still expect Date (e.g. older SDKs)
export function toLegacyDate(value: Temporal.Instant): Date {
  return new Date(value.epochMilliseconds);
}

Going through epoch milliseconds is lossless, because Date only knows milliseconds anyway. Native runtimes and the polyfill also offer Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant(). I still prefer the explicit function, because it shows in the code where the old world ends.

With date-fns, Day.js or Luxon it pays to look at what the library is actually used for. Often it is a handful of functions like addDays, differenceInDays or format. Temporal replaces the first two directly with add() and until(). For formatting there is toLocaleString(), which uses Intl.DateTimeFormat internally. Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-11-19").toLocaleString("en-US", { dateStyle: "full" }), for example, returns “Thursday, November 19, 2026”. Running both side by side is fine for a transition period. The only important thing is that a function works either with Temporal or with Date, not with both.

Common mistakes with the Temporal API in TypeScript

A few pitfalls kept coming up while I was trying things out.

  • Comparing with === or <: Two Temporal objects with the same value are still different objects. Use equals() or the static compare() method. Comparing with < deliberately throws a TypeError.
  • Temporal.Now deep inside business logic: Then you can’t control time in tests. Get the current time at the edge, for example in the handler, and pass it on as a parameter.
  • JSON there, but not back: JSON.stringify turns Temporal objects into strings. When reading them back, you have to convert them with from() yourself, or you keep calculating with strings.
  • structuredClone and workers: Temporal objects can’t be structured-cloned, and Node.js throws a DataCloneError. Pass strings and rebuild the objects on the other side.
  • Storing an offset instead of a time zone: +01:00 is not a time zone. In summer, Berlin uses +02:00. If you only know the offset, you can’t calculate correctly into the future.

Cost, performance and security

The polyfill has a price, but it is modest. In my example, the minified handler including the polyfill weighs about 60 KB, not counting the AWS SDK, which is part of the runtime. For a Lambda cold start that hardly matters. Once nodejs26.x is generally available, you can remove the polyfill and save those bytes entirely.

DynamoDB TTL costs nothing extra. Expired items are deleted without consuming write capacity, though not immediately: according to AWS, typically within a few days. Queries should therefore filter out expired items themselves. With global tables, however, the replicated deletes in other regions do consume write capacity.

Two notes on security. Always validate date values from requests with from() inside a try block, because invalid input throws a RangeError. And don’t accept time zones from requests unchecked; compare them against a list of allowed zones. For scheduled reminders, EventBridge Scheduler is a good fit, since it understands cron expressions with a time zone. My EventBridge cron explainer shows how such expressions are built.

My take

I consider Temporal one of the most useful additions JavaScript has received in recent years. You could build correct code with Date, too. What makes Temporal valuable is that it forces the right questions. If you have to choose between PlainDate and ZonedDateTime, you automatically think about what a value means in business terms.

At the same time, I wouldn’t rebuild everything at once. Existing code with date-fns that has been running reliably for years is not an emergency. New business logic, though, I would write with Temporal starting now, on Lambda with the polyfill for the time being. For frontends that also serve Safari, the polyfill remains mandatory for a while anyway. One point where I stay skeptical: the API is large. Teams should agree on a few types and clear storage formats, otherwise you quickly end up with a new kind of sprawl, just with more modern names.

FAQ

Can I use the Temporal API in production already?

Yes. Temporal is fully standardized and available without a flag in Node.js 26, Chrome and Firefox. For Safari and older Node versions such as nodejs24.x on Lambda, use a polyfill like temporal-polyfill.

Which TypeScript version do I need for Temporal?

The types are built in from TypeScript 6.0. You enable them with "lib": ["esnext"], with "target": "esnext" or specifically with esnext.temporal.

What is the difference between Instant and ZonedDateTime?

Both describe an exact point in time. An Instant, however, has no time zone and therefore no calendar. ZonedDateTime also knows the time zone in which the instant is viewed, so it can calculate correctly with days, months and DST changes.

Does Temporal replace date-fns, Luxon or Day.js?

For arithmetic, comparisons and time zones, in many cases yes. For formatting, Temporal uses Intl.DateTimeFormat. Special features like relative times (“3 days ago”) are covered by Intl.RelativeTimeFormat or still by a library.

Your next step

Find a place in your project where a deadline or appointment is calculated with Date today, and write a test for October 25 or March 28. If it passes, great. If not, you have found your first candidate for Temporal.

How do you handle time zones in your Lambda functions so far: everything in UTC with conversion in the frontend, or do you already calculate with local time in the backend? Let me know in the comments.

Time zones matter not only for deadlines but also for triggering jobs. I show how to start cron jobs reliably at German local time in EventBridge Scheduler time zone: cron at local time.

Sources

  • TC39: Temporal proposal (stage 4, implementation status)
  • MDN: Temporal
  • Node.js: release notes v26.0.0
  • TypeScript blog: Announcing TypeScript 6.0
  • AWS: Lambda runtimes (nodejs26.x as public preview)
  • temporal-polyfill on GitHub
  • AWS: Time to Live in DynamoDB

This post was created with AI assistance.

👉 Next step: Curious what your own Lambda functions cost? Try my Lambda cost calculator – it runs right in your browser.

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports memory observability
description:
Vercel Sandbox observability now includes memory usage data.

You can access sandbox memory usage data in the dashboard and through the CLI via the vercel metrics command.

Sandbox observability memory in the dashboard

The Memory Usage card reports average, P75, and P95 memory across your sandboxes, alongside the existing CPU usage and data transfer metrics on the sandbox overview page and the project and team-level pages.

On the sandbox detail page, charts are designed to show how close a sandbox is running to its memory ceiling by:

  • Automatically scaling the y-axis to sandbox's memory limit

  • Adding a dashed reference line at 85% of that limit

Sandbox memory is also available in the Observability query builder as the memoryUsedBytes measure on the sandbox usage event. You can build custom queries against it and create alerts from the chart.

Sandbox memory observability in the CLI

Sandbox observability data is also available through the Vercel CLI via the vercel metrics command under vercel.sandbox.memory_used_bytes. Run the command in a linked project for project-specific data, or append --all to see aggregate data across all projects in your team.

The CLI returns:

  • The metric

  • The reporting period

  • The measurement interval

  • The project the sandbox is associated with

  • A graph of memory usage, with min, max and avg values

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

title: Cloudflare’s Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager Enters Closed Beta Without Attribute-Based Encryption
description:
Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, guarding geo-fenced keys with hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 instead of the attribute-based encryption used since 2022. Keys live only in kernel memory on verified regional servers, and any failed check rejects the request, a fail-closed choice practitioners ask could cause a regional outage. GA is planned for Q1 2027.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
