title: 5 Sites I Use So My Vibe-Coded Apps Don't Look AI-Generated
description:
I teach AI and web development, and the most common thing I see in vibe-coded apps is that they all look the same: same gradients, same cards, same "AI default" feel. The fix isn't a better model. It's better references and better components. Here are the five I keep coming back to.

1. 21st.dev

What it is: A large library of React + Tailwind CSS components, templates and shadcn themes made by design engineers, with a CLI (npx @21st-dev/cli add) and an MCP server so your AI agent can find and install components.
Use it when: You want polished, real-world sections (heroes, AI chat UIs, pricing, sign-ins) and you're working with Cursor, Claude Code or another MCP client.
Free vs paid: A free account can copy 2 components a day. Paid plans remove the limit.

2. React Bits (reactbits.dev)

What it is: Free animated React components: text animations, backgrounds and micro-interactions. Pick JavaScript or TypeScript, with plain CSS or Tailwind, then copy the source or install it with the CLI.
Use it when: Your UI works but feels flat and you want a bit of motion that you fully own and can tweak.
Free vs paid: The main library is free. React Bits Pro (pro.reactbits.dev) is a paid one-time purchase that adds blocks, app UI and templates.

3. Magic UI (magicui.design)

What it is: 150+ free, open-source animated components built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Motion, designed as a companion to shadcn/ui.
Use it when: You're building a landing page and already use shadcn/ui.
Free vs paid: The components are free. Magic UI Pro (pro.magicui.design) sells landing-page templates and sections for a one-time fee.

4. Uiverse (uiverse.io)

What it is: A community-made, open-source library of UI elements such as buttons, cards, loaders and inputs. Copy them as HTML/CSS, Tailwind, React or Figma.
Use it when: You need one small element that looks hand-made, even without React.
Free vs paid: The site says it's 100% free for personal and commercial use.

5. Mobbin (mobbin.com)

What it is: Not a component library. It's a UI/UX reference library of screens from real, shipped mobile and web apps.
Use it when: You need to see how real products design onboarding, paywalls or settings before you prompt your AI.
Free vs paid: Joining is free, with limited access to apps and sites. Flows, animations and search need a paid plan, and there's a student/educator discount.

Quick tip

Don't ask your AI for "a modern UI". Pick one real reference screen from Mobbin, choose one component library (mixing five libraries is how apps start looking generic), and give the AI your brand colours, font and spacing scale. Consistency is what makes an app look designed.

What's on your list? Drop it in the comments.

— KD Jayakody

title: Prompt Engineering for Beginners (Part 2): The Anatomy of a Good Prompt
description:
Part 1 of our Prompt Engineering from Scratch series, we explored how AI generates answers, what tokens and context windows are, and why the way we communicate with AI matters.

We learned one important lesson:

Getting better results from AI isn't always about using a more powerful model. Sometimes, it's about giving clearer instructions.

But knowing that we should write better prompts is one thing.

How do we actually write them?

What information should we include? How specific should our instructions be? And how do we know whether our prompt is good enough?

That's exactly what we'll explore in Part 2.

We'll break down six useful components of a well-structured prompt, understand what each one does, and learn how to combine them using simple, real-life examples.

No complicated terminology. No programming knowledge required.

Let's get started.

In Part 2, we'll learn the six useful building blocks of a good prompt, how to combine them, and how to test whether our prompts are working.

And don't worry. You don't need any technical background.

Let's begin with something we all understand.

1. Why Isn't a Simple Prompt Always Enough?

Imagine you're asking a friend to help you write an email.

You say:

Write an email for me.

Your friend would probably have a few questions.

Who is the email for?

What is it about?

Should it sound formal or friendly?

How long should it be?

Without that information, your friend has to guess.

AI faces a similar problem.

A basic prompt

Let's say you type:

Write an email asking for leave.

The AI might produce an email, but it doesn't know important details.

For example:

  • Who are you writing to?
  • Why do you need leave?
  • How many days do you need?
  • What tone should the email use?
  • Should the email be short or detailed?

Now let's make the prompt clearer.

A more detailed prompt 

Write a professional email to my manager
requesting two days of leave.

I need leave on Monday and Tuesday
because of a family commitment.

Keep the email polite and under 120 words.

Include a subject line.

This is much clearer.

You've given the AI the information it needs to create a more suitable response.

Does that guarantee the perfect email?

No.

But it reduces unnecessary guessing.

And that's the foundation of a good prompt.

A good prompt doesn't need complicated words. It needs clear instructions and enough relevant information.

2. The Six Building Blocks of a Good Prompt

When writing a prompt, there are six useful components you can think about.

These components help you explain what you need, how you want the task completed, and what the final answer should look like.

Component What it means Simple example
1. Role Who should the AI act as? Act as a helpful writing assistant.
2. Context What background information does it need? I'm writing to my manager about taking leave.
3. Examples Can you show what a good answer looks like? Here is an example of my writing style.
4. Task What exactly should it do? Write an email requesting two days of leave.
5. Constraints What rules should it follow? Keep it polite and under 120 words.
6. Output Format How should the answer be presented? Include a subject line and email body.

These six components provide a useful framework for writing clear prompts.

But here's something important: you don't need all six components every time.

For a simple question like:

What is the capital of Nepal?

A short prompt is perfectly fine.

For more complicated tasks, such as analyzing a document or writing a detailed report, additional information becomes more valuable.

The goal isn't to make every prompt longer.

The goal is to make every prompt clear enough for its purpose.

Now let's understand each component.

3. Component 1: Role - Who Should the AI Act As?

Imagine you're asking someone for advice.

If you need help preparing for an exam, you might ask a teacher.

If you need help improving your writing, you might ask an editor.

If you need help planning a trip, you might ask a travel guide.

Different roles suggest different ways of approaching a task.

You can use a similar idea when prompting AI.

Without a role 

Help me improve this paragraph.

With a role 

Act as a friendly writing tutor.

Help me improve this paragraph using
simple English.

Explain what you changed and why.

The second prompt gives the AI a clearer direction.

It suggests the type of assistance and explanation you want.

What is a system prompt?

You might hear the technical term system prompt.

In many AI applications, a system message contains higher-level instructions about how the assistant should behave.

For example, an application might instruct its AI assistant to use a particular language or follow certain rules.

However, when you type:

Act as a writing tutor.

into a normal chat, you're generally giving a role instruction as a user, not changing the application's actual system message.

You don't need to access system settings to use role-based prompting.

And a role doesn't give the model magical expertise or guarantee accurate answers.

It simply helps guide how the model approaches and presents the task.

When is this useful?

When you want a particular style of help, such as teaching, editing, planning, or reviewing.

4. Component 2: Context - Give the AI the Background Information

Imagine someone asks you:

What should I do?

You'd probably respond:

About what?

Without knowing the situation, it's difficult to give useful advice.

That's exactly why context matters.

Context is the background information that helps AI understand your situation or task.

Without context 

Write an email requesting leave.

With context 

I'm an employee writing to my manager.

I need two days of leave on Monday
and Tuesday because of a family commitment.

My manager prefers short and
professional emails.

Now the AI knows more about your situation.

It can use that information when preparing the email.

Another example

Imagine you're asking AI to recommend a laptop.

Basic prompt:

Recommend a laptop.

Prompt with context:

I'm a university student.

I mainly use my laptop for online classes,
writing assignments, browsing, and watching videos.

My budget is around $600.

Recommend suitable laptops and explain
why they would fit my needs.

The second prompt gives the model a much clearer picture of what you're looking for.

Can you provide too much context?

No.

More information isn't always better.

Imagine asking someone to help you choose a laptop, then telling them your entire life story.

Most of that information wouldn't help them.

The same applies to AI.

Provide the background details that matter for the task, and avoid including unnecessary personal or sensitive information.

Good context means relevant information, not simply more information.

5. Component 3: Examples - Show the AI What You Want

Sometimes it's easier to show someone what you want than to explain it.

Imagine you're asking a friend to design an invitation card.

Instead of describing every detail, you might show an example and say:

I want something similar to this.

AI can also use examples to understand the pattern, style, or structure you expect.

Without an example 

Rewrite this message professionally.

With an example 

Rewrite my message in a professional
but friendly tone.

Example:

Original:
"Hey, send me the report."

Improved:
"Could you please send me the report
when you have a chance?"

Now rewrite this message:

"I need the meeting details."

The example demonstrates the kind of change you want.

It shows the AI how to make a request sound more polite without changing its meaning.

A little technical detail: Zero-shot and Few-shot prompting

These are two terms you might encounter.

Zero-shot prompting means asking the AI to perform a task without providing examples.

For example:

Rewrite this sentence professionally:

"Send me the file."

Few-shot prompting means providing one or more examples before asking the AI to perform the task.

For example:

Example 1:
"Send me the file."
→ "Could you please send me the file?"

Example 2:
"Call me tomorrow."
→ "Could you please call me tomorrow?"

Now rewrite:
"Give me the document."

The examples help demonstrate the pattern.

However, examples aren't always necessary, and they don't automatically work better than clear instructions.

For simple tasks, a direct instruction may be enough.

We'll explore zero-shot and few-shot prompting in more detail in Part 3.

When should you use examples?

When you want a specific writing style, structure, classification, or repeated pattern.

6. Component 4: Task - Explain Exactly What You Need

This is one of the most important parts of a prompt.

The task tells the AI what it should actually do.

It sounds obvious, but vague tasks can lead to vague answers.

Example 1: Too vague 

Help me with my resume.

What kind of help?

Should the AI check grammar?

Improve the wording?

Shorten it?

Suggest missing sections?

Example 2: Clear task 

Review my resume.

Identify unclear sentences and
suggest improvements.

Keep my existing experience and
achievements accurate.

Do not invent qualifications or
work experience.

Now the AI knows what to focus on.

Another example

Basic:

Summarize this article.

Clearer:

Summarize this article in five bullet points.

Focus on the main findings.

Explain any difficult terms in
simple English.

Notice something?

We haven't used complicated technical language.

We've simply explained the task more clearly.

A useful habit: Before sending a prompt, ask yourself:

If someone who had never met me read this instruction, would they understand what I wanted them to do?

If the answer is no, you may need to make the task clearer.

7. Component 5: Constraints - Set Clear Rules and Limits

Now imagine you're asking someone to write a short speech.

You tell them:

Write a speech about teamwork.

They might write a ten-minute speech.

But you only have two minutes to speak.

The problem isn't necessarily the speech itself.

You forgot to explain the time limit.

That's where constraints come in.

Constraints are the rules or limitations you want the AI to follow.

They help make the output more suitable for your needs.

Example 

Write a short speech about teamwork.

Rules:
- Use simple English.
- Keep it under 200 words.
- Include one everyday example.
- Avoid difficult technical terms.
- End with an encouraging message.

Here, you've made your expectations much clearer.

Common types of constraints

Type Example
Length Keep it under 150 words.
Language Use simple English.
Tone Keep it polite and friendly.
Content Include three practical examples.
Restrictions Don't invent facts or statistics.
Structure Use short paragraphs.

Can constraints be too strict?

Yes.

If you add too many conflicting rules, the AI may struggle to follow them.

For example:

Explain this topic in detail using only ten words.

Those instructions work against each other.

So try to keep constraints realistic and relevant.

Remember: Constraints guide the AI, but they don't guarantee that every rule will always be followed.

That's why checking the final answer is still important.

8. Component 6: Output - Format Decide How the Answer Should Look

Imagine asking someone to organize your monthly expenses.

They could give you a long paragraph describing everything.

Or they could present a simple table.

Which would be easier to understand?

Usually, the table.

That's why output format matters.

Output format tells the AI how you want the final answer to be organized.

Without a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

The AI might produce several paragraphs.

With a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

Present the comparison in a table.

Include:
- Cost
- Flexibility
- Interaction
- Advantages
- Disadvantages

Finish with a short summary.

Now the structure is clear.

Common output formats

Format When it's useful
Paragraph Explanations and general writing
Bullet points Short summaries and quick ideas
Numbered steps Instructions and tutorials
Table Comparisons and organized information
Checklist Planning and reviewing tasks
Code Programming-related tasks
JSON When software needs a structured data format

A little technical detail: What is JSON?

JSON is a way to organize information using labels and values.

For example:

{
  "name": "Aarav",
  "age": 22,
  "city": "Kathmandu"
}

You don't need to use JSON in everyday prompting.

It's mainly useful when applications or programs need information in a consistent structure.

For most beginners, requesting a paragraph, table, or list is enough.

The takeaway: Choosing the right output format can make an answer easier to read, check, and use.

9. Putting All Six Components Together

Now let's combine everything we've learned.

We'll use the same email example from the beginning.

Basic prompt 

Write an email asking for leave.

This might work, but it leaves several details unclear.

Structured prompt 

ROLE:
Act as a professional writing assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm an employee writing to my manager.
I need two days of leave on Monday and
Tuesday because of a family commitment.

EXAMPLE:
Use a polite and professional tone similar to:
"I would like to request your approval
for two days of leave."

TASK:
Write an email requesting the leave.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Keep it under 120 words.
- Use simple and professional language.
- Do not invent additional personal details.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Include:
1. Subject line
2. Greeting
3. Email body
4. Closing

This prompt gives the AI much clearer instructions.

What changed?

Component What we added
Role Professional writing assistant
Context Leave dates, reason, recipient
Examples Preferred writing tone
Task Write a leave-request email
Constraints Word limit, language, accuracy
Output Format Subject, greeting, body, closing

We haven't used any magic words.

We've simply organized our instructions.

Important: Do we always need six sections?

Absolutely not.

The same request could be written naturally in a few sentences:

Write a polite email to my manager requesting leave on Monday and Tuesday because of a family commitment. Keep it under 120 words, use simple professional English, and include a subject line.

That may be enough.

A well-structured prompt doesn't have to be long or complicated. It just needs to provide the information the task requires.

The six components are a guide, not a rule that every prompt must follow.

10. Basic vs. Structured Prompts: What's the Difference?

Let's compare a few everyday examples.

Situation Basic prompt More structured prompt
Learning Explain photosynthesis. Explain photosynthesis to a 12-year-old using simple English and one everyday example.
Writing Write a birthday message. Write a short, funny birthday message for my best friend. Keep it under 60 words.
Planning Make a study plan. Create a seven-day study plan for someone who can study two hours daily. Present it in a table.
Summarizing Summarize this document. Summarize the document in five bullet points, focusing on the main findings and important numbers.
Comparing Compare these phones. Compare these phones by price, battery, camera, and storage in a table.

Notice that the improved prompts aren't necessarily much longer.

They simply explain what matters.

Does a structured prompt always give a better answer?

Not necessarily.

For straightforward tasks, a simple prompt can work perfectly.

For complicated tasks, clear instructions often help.

And sometimes the model may still make mistakes despite having a well-written prompt.

That's why we need a way to test whether our changes actually improve the result.

11. A Real-World Example: Summarizing a Long Document

This example connects closely with my work testing AI models on real documents.

Imagine you upload a 50-page report and type:

Summarize this report.

The AI might give you a useful general summary.

But suppose you actually need:

  • The report's main purpose
  • Important findings
  • Financial information
  • Major risks
  • Recommendations

Your original prompt didn't mention those expectations.

So you might have to ask several follow-up questions.

Now let's try a more structured approach.

ROLE:
Act as a research assistant.

CONTEXT:
I've uploaded a report that I need
to understand without reading every page.

TASK:
Summarize the report.

Include:
1. The main purpose of the report.
2. Five important findings.
3. Key financial figures, if available.
4. Major risks or limitations.
5. Important recommendations.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use simple English.
- Keep the summary under 500 words.
- Do not invent missing information.
- Clearly mention if something is not found.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Use headings and bullet points.

Where possible, include page references
so I can check the original information.

This prompt gives the model a clearer structure.

It also makes the output easier to verify.

For example, if the AI reports a financial figure, you can check the page where that figure appears.

Of course, the model could still overlook information or provide an incorrect page reference.

A structured prompt improves clarity and makes verification easier. It doesn't eliminate the need to check important results.

12. For the Curious: How Developers Use Structured Prompts

If you're not from a technical background, you can skip this section.

Everything we've learned so far is enough to start improving your prompts.

But if you're curious about how developers use these ideas, here's a simple example.

Suppose a developer asks:

Write code to calculate the total price.

The AI doesn't know the programming language, the calculation rules, or how to handle unusual inputs.

A clearer request might look like this:

ROLE:
Act as a Python programming assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm building a small shopping application.

TASK:
Write a function that calculates the total
price of products in a shopping cart.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Each product has a price and quantity.
- Reject negative prices or quantities.
- Explain the calculation clearly.
- Include two example calculations.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return the Python code followed by
a short explanation.

This follows the same six-component idea.

The only difference is the task.

A developer may also provide database information, existing code, error messages, or other technical details.

But the main principle remains the same:

Give the AI enough information to understand the task, and clearly explain how you want the answer.

Generated code still needs to be reviewed and tested before being used in a real application.

13. The Prompt Engineering Workflow

Now that we know how to build a prompt, what should we do if the first answer isn't good enough?

Should we rewrite everything?

Should we keep adding random instructions?

Not necessarily.

A better approach is to improve the prompt step by step.

Here's a simple workflow.

Step 1: Specify Decide What You Want

Before writing a prompt, identify:

  • Your goal
  • The information AI needs
  • The kind of answer you expect
  • Any important rules or limitations

For example:

I want a short explanation of climate change for a young student.

Step 2: Save Keep Your Original Prompt

Don't immediately replace your first prompt.

Keep a copy.

For example:

Version 1:

Explain climate change.

This is your starting point.

You can compare future versions against it.

In technical settings, saving and tracking changes is sometimes called versioning.

But you don't need special software to do this.

A notebook or text document works perfectly.

Step 3: Test Change One Thing at a Time

Let's improve the prompt.

Version 2: Change the audience

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Now compare the answer with Version 1.

Did it become easier to understand?

Next, return to Version 1 and test a different change.

Version 3: Change the length

Explain climate change in 100 words.

Now compare again.

This helps you understand whether specifying the audience or limiting the length made the answer more useful.

If you change five things at once, it becomes harder to identify which change helped.

AI responses can vary even when you use the same prompt, so repeat important tests before drawing strong conclusions.

Step 4: Improve Combine What Works

After comparing the results, you can combine useful instructions.

For example:

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Use simple English.

Keep it under 100 words.

Include one everyday example.

You now have a clearer prompt based on what you've learned.

Step 5: Reuse - Save Your Best Prompts

If a prompt works well for a task you repeat often, save it.

For example:

Explain [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE].

Use simple language.

Keep the explanation under [WORD LIMIT].

Include [NUMBER] everyday examples.

You can replace the words inside the brackets whenever you need to use the template again.

This is one of the practical benefits of prompt engineering.

Instead of starting from scratch every time, you build a collection of instructions that you can reuse and improve.

A simple workflow to remember

Specify → Save → Test → Improve → Reuse

In professional applications, teams may also track prompt versions, run repeated tests, compare results, and monitor performance after releasing an AI feature.

But for beginners, the same idea starts with something much simpler:

Keep your original prompt, change one thing, and check what happens.

14. Your Prompt Checklist

Before sending an important prompt, ask yourself:

  • [ ] Goal: Have I clearly explained what I want?
  • [ ] Context: Have I provided the necessary background information?
  • [ ] Role: Would specifying a role make the task clearer?
  • [ ] Examples: Would an example help show the result I expect?
  • [ ] Constraints: Have I mentioned important limits or rules?
  • [ ] Output Format: Have I explained how the answer should be presented?
  • [ ] Accuracy: Have I told the AI what to do if information is missing?
  • [ ] Verification: Can I check whether the result is correct?

You don't have to check every box for every question.

Use the ones that matter for your task.

15. Your 5-Minute Exercise: Build Your Own Prompt

Let's practice what we've learned.

Open your preferred AI chatbot.

We'll start with a simple request.

Step 1: Write a basic prompt 

Make a study plan for me.

Read the answer.

Is it suitable for your situation?

Does it know what subject you're studying?

Does it know how much time you have?

Step 2: Add context 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Make a study plan for me.

Compare the result with your first answer.

Step 3: Add useful constraints 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Keep the activities realistic.

Step 4: Specify the output format 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Present the plan in a table with:
- Day
- Study topic
- Duration
- Activity

Notice how the prompt becomes more specific.

The goal hasn't changed.

You've simply made your expectations clearer.

Step 5: Experiment

Now change only one part of the prompt.

For example:

  • Change the study time from two hours to one hour.
  • Or change the output format from a table to a checklist.
  • Or specify a particular subject.

Compare the results.

Ask yourself:

Which instruction changed the answer, and did that change make it more useful?

That's the habit I want you to develop throughout this series.

16. Quick Recap: The Six Components

Here's everything we've learned in one table.

Component Simple question to ask yourself
Role Who should the AI act as?
Context What does the AI need to know?
Examples Can I show what a good answer looks like?
Task What exactly do I want it to do?
Constraints What rules or limits matter?
Output Format How should the answer look?

And remember:

You don't need all six components for every prompt.

A simple question can have a simple prompt.

A complicated task may need more detail.

The purpose of prompt engineering isn't to make communication complicated.

It's to make it clearer.

What's Coming in Part 3?

In Part 3, we'll explore six useful prompting techniques:

  1. Zero-shot prompting: Asking AI to complete a task without examples.
  2. Few-shot prompting: Showing examples of the kind of answer you want.
  3. Chain-of-thought prompting: Approaches involving intermediate reasoning steps for more complicated tasks.
  4. Role-based prompting: Guiding AI through a particular role.
  5. Constraint-based prompting: Using clear rules and limitations.
  6. Meta-prompting: Using AI to help design or improve prompts.

We'll explain each one using practical examples and discuss when it might be useful.

Final Thoughts

In Part 1, we learned that language models don't automatically know what we expect from them.

Today, we learned how to communicate those expectations more clearly.

And here's the most important lesson:

A good prompt isn't measured by how long or complicated it is. It's measured by how clearly it communicates the task and how useful the result is.

You don't need to use special commands.

You don't need to memorize complicated terms.

And you certainly don't need a programming background.

Start with a simple prompt.

See what works.

Change one thing.

Compare the results.

And keep improving.

That's how you begin developing a prompt-engineering mindset.

One Question Before You Go

What's one task you regularly ask AI to help you with?

Writing emails? Studying? Summarizing documents? Planning your day?

Share your basic prompt in the comments, and let's see how we can improve it using the six components.

This is Part 2 of 6 in my "Prompt Engineering from Scratch" series. I work with and test open-source AI models on real documents, and I'm sharing what I learn along the way.

Follow the series if you'd like to understand AI and learn practical prompting techniques, one step at a time.

Further Reading

  • OpenAI: Prompt Engineering Guide
  • OpenAI: Best Practices for Prompt Engineering
  • Microsoft Learn: Introduction to Prompt Engineering

title: Looking for affordable image/video moderation API – pain points
description:
I've been evaluating content moderation APIs for a new project, and finding the right balance between cost, reliability, and data security is harder than expected.

Major cloud providers like AWS Rekognition and Google Cloud offer solid solutions, but their pricing can get steep fast, especially when processing video at scale. Smaller, specialized APIs like Sightengine and Clearview have more granular pricing, but I haven't used them extensively.

My priorities are straightforward: affordable per-image or per-video costs, reliable detection for adult content and violence, and clear data handling guarantees (no using my data for training). For indie projects, all three matter equally.

I'm leaning toward testing a couple niche providers that seem more indie-friendly, but I'd rather hear from anyone who's actually deployed these in production. What are you using, and have you run into hidden costs or reliability issues at higher volumes?

Happy to share findings once I've tested a few options.

title: Why We Built StatusNow: Stopping the $200/mo Tool Sprawl for Small Teams
description:
If you run a indie project, small SaaS, or boutique dev agency, you’ve probably hit this frustrating wall:

To properly monitor a simple web application, you end up registering for five separate tools:

  1. UptimeRobot or Better Stack to check if your site is online.
  2. Sentry or Logtail to collect application errors and stack traces.
  3. Qualys or an open-source scanner to check for exposed vulnerabilities.
  4. Statuspage.io to show customers your uptime without exposing internal infrastructure.
  5. Notion or GitHub to store server setup scripts and runbooks.

Before you know it, you’re paying $30 to $50 per month per service, managing 5 different passwords, and jumping across half a dozen tabs just to figure out why an alert fired at 2 AM.

We built StatusNow because we were tired of context-switching across fragmented tools—and tired of pricing models that punish small teams.

The Problem with Traditional Ops Tooling for Small Teams

Big enterprises have dedicated SecOps, DevOps, and SRE teams running complex Datadog dashboards. But for a team of 1–5 developers, that level of complexity is overhead you can't afford.

When an incident occurs in a small team:

  • Alerts are disconnected from fixes: An uptime alert tells you api.example.com is down, but you have to log into a separate service to view the stack trace, and a third service to find the baseline PowerShell or Bash script to restart the node.
  • Per-seat pricing scales prematurely: Adding a developer or client to view a status page or error log shouldn't cost an extra $20/month per seat.
  • Vulnerabilities go unnoticed: Small teams rarely run dedicated vulnerability scanners until something breaks or an SSL cert expires, simply because setting up security scanners feels like a separate discipline.

What We Built: 5 Core Tools, 1 Login, Zero Fluff

Instead of building another niche tool, we integrated the five core operational components every site needs into a single product with a single dashboard:

  1. Uptime & SSL Monitoring: Track HTTP 200 responses, SSL certificate expiration warnings, and TCP ports (like database ports).
  2. Vulnerability Scanning: Ownership-verified scanning for misconfigurations and known vulnerabilities, automatically prioritizing actively exploited issues (CISA KEV).
  3. Application Logs: A lightweight, Sentry-compatible log ingest with stack trace grouping and audit logs.
  4. Public Status Pages: 90-day uptime metrics and incident reports that keep your internal server details completely private.
  5. Versioned Runbooks: Store, version, and hash-check server setup scripts so your team always runs verified fixes.

Built with a "Free First, Pay Only for Extra Capacity" Model

We wanted StatusNow to be something any developer could adopt immediately without asking for management approval or putting down a credit card.

  • 10 Uptime Monitors
  • 10 Vulnerability Scan Targets
  • 1 Public Status Page
  • Application Logs & Runbooks Included
  • Unlimited Team Seats & Full API/MCP Access

All $0 forever. No feature gating, no artificial seat limits. When your application grows and you need 30 monitors or 20 scan targets, you simply add lightweight capacity packs ($5–$25/mo) as you need them.

How It Helps Small Teams Act Fast

Having an alert, a finding, and a fix in the same place changes how quickly you recover:


text
[Alert Fired] db.example.com:5432 down (TCP port closed)
 ↳ Associated finding: SSL certificate expires in 9 days
 ↳ Actionable Runbook: "02_restart_postgres_node.ps1" (Hash verified)

title: bybit-ws: a trading tool, an analyst, and an assistant
description:
bybit-ws: a trading tool, an analyst, and an assistant

A live Bybit futures system that scans, scores, argues with itself before every entry, learns from its own closed trades — and answers when I message it from my phone. Here is the machinery, including the parts that are still broken.

The entry signal is the least interesting part of a live trading system. What decides whether the thing survives is everything around it: what happens when the LLM times out, what happens when a balance reads zero and the bot quietly refuses to trade for two days.

This is a write-up of that part. No performance numbers, on purpose: I can't show you the query behind a PnL figure here, so I don't show the figure.

I built bybit-ws for one user: me. Python and asyncio, SQLite in WAL mode as the single source of truth, a systemd unit, an HTTP-RPC surface on localhost, an MCP wrapper so an agent can drive it. Boring interfaces on purpose: every clever coupling is something I'd have to debug at four in the morning.

Three jobs, one process

An execution tool, an analyst, and an assistant — in one systemd unit, over one SQLite file.

        Telegram (me, sleepy, holding a phone)
                    │
             agent layer (Hermes profile)
             │        │         │
        MCP tools  HTTP-RPC  shell
             │        │         │
   ┌─────────▼────────▼─────────▼──────────────┐
   │            bybit-ws (systemd user unit)   │
   │  async loop ──► market data (WebSocket)   │
   │      ├─► entry scoring ─► LLM judge ─┐    │
   │      ├─► regime model                │    │
   │      ├─► risk gate ──────────────────┤    │
   │      └─► order router ◄──────────────┘    │
   │  SQLite · self-learn · offline bench      │
   └───────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
              Bybit API v5

Two decisions matter:

  1. The exchange is not the database, and neither is trusted blindly. Positions are reconciled across the RPC view, the exchange and SQLite. When they disagree, the disagreement is the event worth alerting on.
  2. AI is not the decision-maker. The LLM sits inside the decision path as a veto, never as the thing that picks the trade.

The request path: what happens when I ask for a trade

I type something human into Telegram. Not a command grammar — a sentence. The agent parses intent, then works through this, reporting each step.

1. Scan. Candidates get scored on structure: band position, RSI, volume, funding, band compression, multi-timeframe confluence. If I name a symbol outside the ranking, the scanner does not pretend it looked — the symbol is either analysed from public candles or reported as skipped, never as no data. A candidate that vanishes silently looks identical to one that was never checked.

2. Size it. A sizing function maps my intent — "risk about this much of the account" — onto a quantity. Equity comes from the account level, not a per-coin balance line; the quantity is rounded to the exchange's step and formatted as a clean decimal string, because 18.900000000000002 is a valid float and an invalid order.

3. Preview, then execute. The entry endpoint is two-phase. The first call returns what would happen — side, quantity, stop, target, leverage — with confirm_required: true, and places nothing. The second, explicitly confirmed, places the order. That preview is the last point where a human catches a misparsed intent, and it's the same endpoint the automated branch uses. The caller sends an Idempotency-Key derived from the confirmed preview; a replay inside the hour returns the original response instead of opening a second position.

4. Verify, don't assume. After the order the system reads the position back and compares it with what it asked for. Fills land in the database one cycle later, so an instant check produces a false "it didn't open" — the agent waits, re-reads, and reports what it observed.

5. Mark it as mine. A manual entry is tagged as manual. That tag decides what the learner sees: self-learning excludes manual trades. My discretionary trades aren't the bot's performance, and letting the learner eat them would teach it my worst habits and call that strategy.

Two choices here look like bugs otherwise: the manual endpoint doesn't silently cap the leverage I ask for — my account, my call, discipline lives in the sizing step — and a kill switch closes everything and blocks new entries until I say otherwise.

Trust, and how it's enforced

Credibility isn't in the strategy; it's in whether the system's own reporting can be caught lying.

  • Three money flows, kept apart. Bybit's closed-pnl is net of the closing fee but not the opening one. Funding arrives as a separate ledger settlement. The transaction log carries gross and net per trade. The identity is asserted in code: net equals gross minus both fees, and account PnL equals trade flow plus funding. Sum them into one number and you report a profit that never existed.
  • Reconciliation against the exchange, not against itself. A local position the exchange doesn't have is a bug, not a rounding error — and because fills land a cycle late, the comparison carries a grace window.
  • Health checks with exit codes, after every change: service state, RPC liveness, cycle progression, the service's interpreter having its dependencies, position parity, database integrity, smoke suite. Prose lies silently; a script with an exit code doesn't.

And a watchdog with a narrow definition of silence: no entries for a window and enough block reasons inside it is an incident; a wall of "skipped, not a candidate" lines is normal filtering. The first version got this backwards — it counted a stopped bot as a quiet, healthy one.

Analysis before a trade: three kinds of "AI"

The word AI does too much work in most trading-bot descriptions. Here there are three layers, and mixing them up is how you get a bot that "decides" things nobody can explain.

Layer What it is How it fails
Deterministic Scoring, sizing, stops, targets, routing, risk limits Bugs, exchange quirks — reproducible and testable
Statistical Regime classifier, bandit parameter choice, drift detection Stale or unrepresentative sample; silently confident
Language model Pre-entry judge: pass or revise, with reasons Timeouts, drifted judgement, cost, latency

The deterministic layer owns money movement. The statistical layer only re-weights parameters — how eager the entries are, how tight a stop sits — and it can't touch the absolute limits: per-trade risk cap and the leverage the automated branch is allowed to set. The LLM only gets a veto.

The judge: fail-closed up to a threshold

Before an entry that scored high enough to be worth the tokens, the signal becomes a compact factual blob — band position, score components, proposed stop and target, funding, regime, confluence — handed to a hosted chat model with one question: is anything here contradictory?

Three choices make it something I trust more than my own opinion at 3 a.m.

  • Errors block by default. If the judge times out or returns junk, the verdict is revise and the entry does not happen. A model that is down is not a model that says yes.
  • A circuit breaker with a stated escape hatch. Consecutive failures open a cooldown instead of hammering a dead dependency. While it's open, entries stay blocked; only after an outage lasts long enough does the system drop into an explicit degraded mode — deterministic path only, low confidence, a fallback note in the log. Fail-closed by default, fail-open by announcement.
  • Caching by signal fingerprint. Identical signals don't re-bill the model; verdicts are reused for a short window.

What the judge is good at is catching what the rules can't cross-check: the score looks strong, but funding is paying the other side and the regime model has this as a downtrend on a timeframe your scanner doesn't read. What it is bad at is predicting the market. I don't ask it to.

Learning from closed trades — and its limits

Self-learning has been rewritten the most, and the hard part was never the update rule — it was telling real improvement from noise.

The learner reads closed trades from SQLite, scores them across win rate, profit factor, Sharpe, drawdown and holding time, and adjusts parameters per regime — "the right tightness for a stop" is a different question in a trend than in chop. Every closed trade produces a small update; the heavier re-selection of a parameter set runs on a sample trigger, with a time fallback so a quiet market doesn't starve it.

What survived:

  • Bandit selection with pruning. Parameters are arms, not one global setting. Losing arms get pruned; uncertainty picks what to try next, not what looks best so far.
  • Drift and change-point detection. The learner asks whether the recent distribution still resembles the one its parameters were chosen on. If not, it prefers exploration over doubling down on an outdated winner.
  • Canary comparison. A challenger runs alongside in a small, time-boxed comparison; the incumbent keeps the crown until the challenger wins on the sample, not on one good week.
  • Robust updates and versioning. Outliers are skipped instead of dragging the average, and every parameter change is a versioned artefact — so "why did it behave differently last Tuesday" has an answer that is a diff, not a memory.

And the honest part no bot post mentions: the learner cannot tell you whether the edge exists. It tunes within the space you gave it. If the space is wrong, it will find a confident local optimum and defend it.

The bench, where ideas are supposed to die

Next to the live system sits an offline bench: same strategy code, deterministic backtest engine, cached candles, and a run manifest recording code revision, parameter hash, config hash and data hash. Two runs with the same manifest produce the same equity hash — asserted in the test suite, so reproducibility is a property, not a claim.

On top sits an anti-overfitting gate: a parameter set has to survive deflated Sharpe, probability of backtest overfitting and a permutation test. Labels come from a triple-barrier scheme — hit target, hit stop, or time out — not "was the next candle up". Regime detection is a separate unsupervised model with a change-point detector beside it, because the interesting moment is when the regime stops being what the model thinks.

The gap, plainly: the bench doesn't promote a winner into the live learner automatically — promotion means touching the live loop, and I'd rather have a manual step and a boring diff than an autopilot I can't explain.

The assistant is not a wrapper

A chat over the API took an evening. Deciding what it may assume took the rest.

Every answer is fetched live — positions, balance, risk state, journal — never recalled from conversation. If the service is down, the answer is "down", not the last known number dressed up as current. Read paths are free-form; write paths are narrow, explicit, and confirmed. And the assistant carries what a human would otherwise hold in their head: which symbols the bot watches, which order type gets rejected in which position mode, why a balance line and an equity figure disagree.

That last category is most of the product: quirks nobody wrote down until they bit me.

If you build one

  1. Put the money path behind a two-phase endpoint with explicit confirmation, and give the automated branch the same endpoint. Two paths that can place orders is two bugs.
  2. Make the LLM a filter, and make it fail closed. The moment it can cause a trade, your risk model lives in someone else's weights.
  3. Separate the learner from the ledger. Tag discretionary trades, exclude them, version every parameter change — otherwise "the bot got better" is folklore.
  4. Build the watchdog before the strategy. A bot that stopped trading doesn't announce itself.

It's not a fund: one machine, my money, and every postmortem is mine.

The bot, the code, and me

  • Telegram bot: @Gridbolbot — the public side of the same engine: anyone can pull scans and signals; execution stays on my account.
  • Source: github.com/poliakarmai/bybit-ws — AGPL-3.0
  • Email: Armyanao@gmail.com

title: Immutable Offsite Backups with Restic, ZFS Snapshots & S3 Object Lock Against Ransomware
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Global DNS Propagation Checker & SSL Health Auditor, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

Comprehensive enterprise systems guide on Immutable Offsite Backups with Restic, ZFS Snapshots & S3 Object Lock Against Ransomware, covering high-availability architecture, security protocols, and production SLAs.

1. Threat Model & Ransomware Attack Vectors

Modern enterprise ransomware payloads, including variants such as LockBit, BlackCat, and Clop, specifically target secondary storage interfaces, volume shadow copies, and remote hypervisor backup paths. Once bad actors gain elevated privileges on an infrastructure node, they execute discovery scripts targeting network-attached storage (NAS) protocols, local backup repositories, and cloud API endpoints. If backup credentials grant write or delete capabilities to offsite targets, adversaries routinely purge existing backups prior to deploying encryption algorithms across primary block devices.

Mitigating this operational risk requires a zero-trust architecture where backups remain cryptographically isolated, immutable, and append-only. Local write operations must be mathematically decoupled from destruction privileges. The architecture outlined below builds a defense-in-depth pipeline utilizing three distinct enforcement boundaries:

  • Local Block Layer: Atomic ZFS read-only snapshots preventing hypervisor or root-level malware from overwriting local history.
  • Transport & Compression Layer: Restic client-side AES-256-CTR encryption and Rabin fingerprint content-defined deduplication.
  • Remote Storage Layer: AWS S3 / S3-compatible Object Lock running in strict Compliance Mode enforcing Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) immutability at the API level.

2. Local Storage Tier: ZFS Snapshot Engine & System Tuning

ZFS operates as a Copy-on-Write (CoW) file system, providing transactional atomicity. When a ZFS snapshot is generated, pointer tables freeze existing data blocks. Subsequent write operations allocate new blocks without altering historical pointers. Even if an attacker gains root access to the host operating system and attempts to encrypt files on a mounted dataset, existing ZFS snapshots remain immutable unless explicit zfs destroy commands are executed.

Storage Pool Provisioning & Tuning

Configure a enterprise ZFS storage pool using mirrored NVMe or SAS devices, explicitly setting ashift=12 for 4KiB sector alignment and enforcing record sizes optimized for large chunk processing.

# Provision ZFS pool with ZSTD compression and POSIX ACLs
zpool create -f -o ashift=12 
 -O compression=zstd-3 
 -O xattr=sa 
 -O acltype=posixacl 
 -O atime=off 
 tank mirror /dev/nvme0n1 /dev/nvme1n1

# Create dedicated datasets for production state and local backup staging
zfs create -o recordsize=1M tank/production
zfs create -o recordsize=1M tank/backup-staging

Kernel Memory & Network Tuning

High-throughput backup workloads generate heavy I/O pressure and memory page allocation churn. Apply these kernel parameters in /etc/sysctl.d/99-zfs-backup.conf to optimize memory dirty ratios and TCP buffer scales for multi-gigabit offsite transfers:

# Force memory flushing early to prevent I/O stalls during large file reads
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 5
vm.dirty_ratio = 10

# Optimize TCP buffer window scaling for long-fat network (LFN) paths
net.core.rmem_max = 16777216
net.core.wmem_max = 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 16777216
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 10000

To prevent ZFS Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) from starving Linux kernel page memory during large Restic deduplication scans, bound ARC memory consumption in /etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf:

# Limit ZFS ARC maximum memory consumption to 32GB (34359738368 bytes)
options zfs zfs_arc_max=34359738368

3. Offsite Transport Tier: Restic Configuration & S3 WORM Locking

Restic handles dataset client-side deduplication, cryptographic hashing, and chunking before data leaves the system boundary. It converts source files into encrypted blob packs stored within a content-addressable directory structure.

S3 Object Lock Configuration: Compliance vs. Governance Mode

S3 Object Lock provides WORM security guarantees. It offers two enforcement modes:

  • Governance Mode: Users with specific IAM permissions (such as s3:BypassGovernanceRetention) can override lock parameters, delete objects, or alter retention periods. This presents a vulnerability if administrative API keys are compromised.
  • Compliance Mode: Absolute immutability. No user—including the AWS account root user—can overwrite or delete locked objects until the retention period expires. Retention periods cannot be shortened, only extended.

Provision the target S3 bucket using the AWS CLI, explicitly enabling Object Lock and applying default retention in Compliance Mode for 30 days:

# Create S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled
aws s3api create-bucket 
 --bucket hostingpodium-immutable-backups 
 --region us-east-1 
 --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket

# Set strict Compliance Mode default retention policy
aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration 
 --bucket hostingpodium-immutable-backups 
 --object-lock-configuration '{
 "ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled",
 "Rule": {
 "DefaultRetention": {
 "Mode": "COMPLIANCE",
 "Days": 30
 }
 }
 }'

Least-Privilege IAM Policy

The IAM user assigned to the Restic engine requires permissions to read, put, and list objects, but must be explicitly denied delete operations. Even if an attacker exfiltrates these IAM credentials, they cannot delete backup packs or remove lock policies.

{
 "Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [
 {
 "Sid": "AllowResticOperations",
 "Effect": "Allow",
 "Action": [
 "s3:PutObject",
 "s3:GetObject",
 "s3:ListBucket",
 "s3:GetBucketLocation",
 "s3:GetObjectRetention",
 "s3:PutObjectRetention"
 ],
 "Resource": [
 "arn:aws:s3:::hostingpodium-immutable-backups",
 "arn:aws:s3:::hostingpodium-immutable-backups/*"
 ]
 },
 {
 "Sid": "ExplicitlyDenyDeleteAndBypass",
 "Effect": "Deny",
 "Action": [
 "s3:DeleteObject",
 "s3:DeleteObjectVersion",
 "s3:BypassGovernanceRetention",
 "s3:PutObjectLegalHold"
 ],
 "Resource": [
 "arn:aws:s3:::hostingpodium-immutable-backups/*"
 ]
 }
 ]
}

Initializing the Restic Repository

Initialize the encrypted remote repository using the hardened IAM credentials and password file stored under /etc/restic/repo.key with strict permissions (chmod 600):

export RESTIC_REPOSITORY="s3:https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hostingpodium-immutable-backups/prod-dataset"
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE="/etc/restic/repo.key"
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIAEXAMPLEKEYID"
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY"

# Initialize remote encrypted repository
restic init

4. Automation Architecture: Systemd Units & Snapshot Lifecycle

To ensure atomic and consistent backups without running processes against live, modifying filesystems, the backup engine must:

  • Generate an unmounted, read-only ZFS snapshot.
  • Mount the snapshot read-only under a temporary path.
  • Pass the static snapshot filesystem path to Restic.
  • Unmount and retain local snapshot based on retention schedules.

Automated Execution Script

Save the following script as /usr/local/bin/zfs-restic-backup.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

POOL_DATASET="tank/production"
SNAP_NAME="restic-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
MOUNT_POINT="/mnt/backup-target"
KEY_FILE="/etc/restic/repo.key"

export RESTIC_REPOSITORY="s3:https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hostingpodium-immutable-backups/prod-dataset"
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE="${KEY_FILE}"
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIAEXAMPLEKEYID"
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY"

echo "[INFO] Creating ZFS snapshot ${POOL_DATASET}@${SNAP_NAME}..."
zfs snapshot "${POOL_DATASET}@${SNAP_NAME}"

mkdir -p "${MOUNT_POINT}"
mount -t zfs "${POOL_DATASET}@${SNAP_NAME}" "${MOUNT_POINT}"

echo "[INFO] Executing Restic backup stream..."
restic backup "${MOUNT_POINT}" 
 --tag "scheduled-zfs" 
 --exclude=".tmp" 
 --exclude="cache" 
 --json

echo "[INFO] Unmounting snapshot path..."
umount "${MOUNT_POINT}"

# Prune local snapshot history older than 7 days
zfs list -t snapshot -o name -H | grep "${POOL_DATASET}@restic-" | while read -r SNAP; do
 SNAP_TIME=$(zfs get -H -o value creation "${SNAP}")
 # Check age logic and drop local snapshot
done

Systemd Service & Timer Configuration

Manage background execution via standard Linux systemd daemons rather than legacy cron entries to ensure structured journal logging and process monitoring.

Create /etc/systemd/system/restic-backup.service:

[Unit]
Description=ZFS Snapshot and S3 Immutable Restic Backup Engine
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/zfs-restic-backup.sh
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
IOSchedulingClass=best-effort
IOSchedulingPriority=2
Nice=10

Create /etc/systemd/system/restic-backup.timer:

[Unit]
Description=Trigger daily offsite immutable backup cycle

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# Enable and launch the systemd timer
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now restic-backup.timer

5. Operational Trade-Offs & Garbage Collection Realities

Implementing S3 Compliance Mode WORM locking alters standard repository maintenance patterns. Because object deletion is blocked by policy at the cloud provider layer, running standard restic prune commands against locked datasets will throw API permissions errors if data blocks marked for deletion remain within their WORM retention period.

Managing Remote Repository Pruning

Architects must align Restic retention parameters with S3 Object Lock retention settings. If S3 object retention is configured for 30 days, restic forget and restic prune routines must not attempt to purge index files or data blobs younger than 30 days.

Metric / Vector Local ZFS Snapshots Restic Engine S3 Object Lock (Compliance)
Ransomware Resistance Medium (Vulnerable to local root account compromise) High (Encrypted client-side, append-only) Absolute (Hardware/API WORM enforced by S3)
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) Sub-second (Local pointer swap) Minutes to Hours (Network dependent) Hours to Days (Egress & rebuild required)
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) 15 Minutes (Low local IO overhead) 24 Hours (Scheduled offsite run) 24 Hours (Aligned with transport)
CPU Overhead Negligible (Copy-on-Write pointers) High (Crypto hashing & AES-256) Zero (Offloaded to cloud S3 gateway)
Cost / GB Trajectory High (Local NVMe/SAS drives required) Low (Bandwidth efficient via deduplication) Variable (S3 Standard vs Glacier Flexible Sink)

6. Disaster Recovery Runbook & Integrity Audit

Regular validation of offsite data integrity is required to detect bit rot, payload tampering, or index corruption. Restic allows cryptographic sampling without downloading full datasets.

Verification Audit Process

Run a weekly cryptographic integrity scan against 5% of the repository volume using a dedicated worker process:

# Perform cryptographic verification check on a random 5% sample set
restic check --read-data-subset=5%

Bare-Metal Recovery Execution Flow

In the event of total site destruction or full host encryption by a threat actor, execute the following restoration sequence on an isolated, clean node:

  • Provision Node: Deploy clean RHEL 9 or AlmaLinux 9 OS host with ZFS kernel modules installed.
  • Configure Vault Credentials: Export S3 access keys and repository passphrase from secure secret store.
  • Query Remote Snapshots: Retrieve index metadata from S3 bucket without pulling full dataset blocks. 
# List available snapshots in offsite repository
restic snapshots

# Output snapshot details:
# ID Time Host Tags Paths
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# a8d93c11 2026-03-29 02:00:12 prod-host1 scheduled-zfs /mnt/backup-target
  • Execute Data Restoration: Mount target recovery dataset and restore selected snapshot directly to disk. 
# Prepare restoration directory target
zfs create tank/recovery-dataset
mkdir -p /mnt/recovery

# Trigger block stream restoration
restic restore a8d93c11 --target /mnt/recovery

# Mount recovery dataset back into production path
zfs set mountpoint=/var/www/production tank/recovery-dataset

By enforcing local Copy-on-Write storage boundaries alongside client-side encryption and remote API-level WORM Compliance locking, enterprise systems maintain structural operational resilience against advanced threat vectors and destructive ransomware strategies.

title: How long a liquor license takes in Texas, New York City and Los Angeles (data from 1,000+ applications)
description:
Disclosure: I run PourWire, which turns state liquor license and building permit filings into a daily list of restaurants and bars that are about to open. The numbers below come from that pipeline plus the states' own open data. The CSV is public under CC BY 4.0.

The question "how long does a liquor license take" has a different answer in every state, and most answers online are guesses. Here is what the filings say as of October 2026.

The short answer

Where Agency Typical time Measured on
Texas (5 metros) TABC median 24 days from submission to issue (middle half 18 to 34) 144 MB and BG applications filed since June 2026
New York City NY State Liquor Authority applications pending a median of 118 days (middle half 62 to 212); 32% over 6 months 920 restaurant and bar applications pending in the five boroughs
Los Angeles County California ABC median 67 days from application to issue (middle half 54 to 72) 23 issued type 41, 47 and 48 licenses filed since July 2026

How it was measured

Texas. TABC publishes pending applications and issued licenses as two datasets on data.texas.gov. We matched our MB (mixed beverage) and BG (wine and beer) applications in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio and Waco-Temple to the original issue date in TABC License Information by owner and permit.

New York City. The SLA queue is the story. data.ny.gov "Current SLA Pending Licenses" lists every application still in review with its received date, so the age of what is waiting today is the honest number. Of the NYC applications we have tracked since June, 25 have been issued so far, a median of 105 days after the SLA received them. That figure is capped by our start date, so the real average is higher.

Los Angeles. California ABC keeps one license number from application to issue, so filing to issue is a direct join. Every new application goes through a 30-day public notice period before ABC investigates, which is why almost nothing issues in under a month (the fastest we saw was 36 days).

Get the data

  • CSV of the wait times with sample sizes and source links: us-liquor-license-applications on GitHub (data/liquor-license-wait-times.csv), plus the last 30 days of new applications across every metro we track, refreshed weekly. Also on Hugging Face.
  • Step by step lookup guides with the license class codes explained:
    • Texas: pending TABC applications, MB, BG and FB
    • New York City: SLA wait times, classes 340, 240 and 370
    • Los Angeles: ABC wait times, types 41, 47 and 48

If you are opening a restaurant, the practical takeaway is to file early in New York, budget about two months in Los Angeles, and expect about a month in Texas. If you sell to new restaurants, the pending lists are a 1 to 4 month head start on who is about to open.

Corrections and better joins are welcome in the GitHub repo issues.

title: gRPC in the browser without grpc-web: the wire protocol over a WebRTC DataChannel
description:
grpc-web exists because browsers can't speak HTTP/2 trailers.
The usual answer is a translation proxy in front of your service.
We took a different one: run the actual gRPC wire protocol —
length-prefixed frames, HPACK-free, all four call shapes — over a
single WebRTC RTCDataChannel, and generate the runtime for it
from your .proto.

grpc-over-datachannels is that experiment, grown up:

  • Dependency-free generated runtimes for 16 languages — JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lua, C, C++, Dart, Java, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, C#, and Zig. Browser and native. The generated code is stdlib-only; there is no grpc library underneath it.
  • Our own WebRTC stack. ICE, DTLS, and SCTP written from scratch, so the native clients don't depend on a WebRTC library either.
  • Graded against stock gRPC. The generated implementations are tested against the reference implementations through a TCP↔DataChannel proxy — the oracle is the real thing, not a reimplementation of it.
  • WebRTC-Direct. A server prints one certhash multiaddr; a client dials it. No signaling server. Direct on a LAN, through a TURN relay behind symmetric NAT, or full ICE with STUN in peer mode — with runnable examples in every language.
  • A Kafka proxy in Rust. grpcdc.kafka.v1.Kafka exposes Apache Kafka as a generated gRPC service, so any generated client — including a browser tab — can produce and consume without a Kafka client library. The same generated e2e suite runs against Kafka and Redpanda in CI.

If you only have thirty seconds, the whole pitch is a 2-minute
video: https://youtu.be/LwrXpnlMlgA — and the Kafka proxy gets
its own: https://youtu.be/KJ98a4ApZ4E

The part we're proudest of is also the strangest: almost
everything in the repos is generated. The runtimes, the tests,
the examples, and the docs come from recursive generators, so
sixteen languages can't quietly drift apart. When a language
misbehaves, we fix the generator, not sixteen codebases.

Try it without installing anything — the stub generator runs in
your browser: https://browser-grpc.github.io/grpc-over-datachannels/app/

Code, releases (npm / PyPI / NuGet / GHCR / GitHub-hosted Maven):
https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels

Longer write-ups, with the design trade-offs:

  • https://c100k.blogspot.com/2026/10/introducing-grpc-over-datachannels-grpc.html
  • https://c100k.blogspot.com/2026/10/kafka-over-grpc-rust-kafka-proxy-with.html

Questions and hostile edge cases welcome — the NAT and framing ones especially.

title: Ghost Tales: Learn English Through Ghost Stories, Running Locally with Gemma
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

Ghost Tales (ভূতের কথা in Bengali) is a small web app that teaches English through ghost stories, with Bengali beside every sentence. A local model, Gemma through Ollama, writes each story and translates it on my own Mac.

You pick a place, such as an old zamindar mansion or a river ghat at dusk. You pick a mood: spooky, or a gentle "memory ghost". You can name the hero. The story is typed out one sentence at a time, and each sentence is then translated into Bengali. The two languages sit side by side.

I live in Bangladesh. I wanted a language tool that needs no account, no subscription and no constant connection. A story you enjoy is easier to remember than a list of words, and a tool that runs on your own machine is easier to trust.

The ghost in my machine is the model itself. It lives in my own computer and tells stories by lamplight.

Demo

In the video I switch Wi-Fi off on screen, and it stays off for the rest of the recording. Story writing, translation and the Listen button all worked on my Mac that way. The narration was generated with ElevenLabs. The quiet ambient sound in the middle of the video is the app's own, synthesized in the browser and captured with system audio; the Listen voice is not included. The recording is edited: some waiting time was cut or sped up.

The app has three learning helpers:

  • Side by side: English on one side, Bengali on the other.
  • Learn mode: the English is blurred. Read the Bengali, guess the English, then click to reveal it.
  • Listen: the browser reads each sentence aloud with a speech voice from my system. On my Mac both an English and a Bengali voice were available, and both sound robotic. I did not check whether every voice runs locally or online.

Here is the last pair from the run in the screenshot above, unedited:

Some memories never leave us, they just become part of the home.
কিছু স্মৃতি কখনো আমাদের ছেড়ে যায় না, সেগুলো শুধু ঘরের অংশ হয়ে যায়।

Code

https://github.com/AnamulAI/ghost-tales

One index.html file, a README and an MIT licence. No framework, no build step, no external fonts or scripts. To run it: ollama pull gemma4:12b, then python3 -m http.server 8000 in the folder, and open http://localhost:8000.

Submission snapshot: tag submission-v1 (view).

How I Built It

Gemma, locally, through Ollama. The page calls Ollama on http://localhost:11434 and uses gemma4:12b (a 7.7 GB download). I tested on an Apple M4 Mac with 16 GB of RAM. In my own testing the model writes natural Bengali, which is the main reason I chose it.

Two steps, not one. Step one streams an English story of about 12 short sentences, at level A2 to B1. Step two sends each sentence to the model on its own and asks for the Bengali only. Small models tend to be more accurate on short inputs; a whole-story translation has more room to drift, skip lines or add notes.

The think: false finding. Gemma 4 can "think" before it answers. In a manual test in the Ollama app, one short translation spent about 25 seconds thinking. That is far too slow for a dozen sentences, so the app sends think: false (and retries without it if an Ollama version rejects the field). With thinking off, three test stories took 23 to 31 seconds in total, and a single sentence took about 1.1 to 1.3 seconds on average (raw outputs are in sample-stories.md). The 25-second figure came from a different manual test, so it is not a controlled comparison, but the gap made the choice easy.

Telling the story slowly. By default each English sentence is typed out over a few seconds, then the Bengali fades in. There is a faster pace and a tap mode. In one test run at the default pace, the last sentence appeared about 50 seconds after Begin, and all twelve translations were done a few seconds later.

Local only, on purpose. The model picker reads your installed models from Ollama and hides any with "cloud" in the name, because some Ollama models run on remote servers. That keeps story writing and translation on the machine.

The look and the sound. The page is a haunted storybook by lamplight: a layered night scene with a moon, fog and fireflies that shift as you move the mouse, and a palette for each mood. Sound is synthesized in the browser with the Web Audio API, with no audio files: a quiet ambient bed for each place, and short effects triggered by words in the sentence on screen. Sound is off until you press the Sound button. I tried the visuals and sound only on my own Mac, in one browser.

Honest limits.

  • Translation mistakes happen. My AI assistant checked three test stories and found a few clear defects: a stray Russian word at the start of one line, a garbled phrase, and a stray Latin letter inside a word. Most lines looked fine, but a small model's Bengali still needs review by a person. The page says so.
  • The Listen voices are robotic, and Bengali speech needs a Bengali voice on your system.
  • I have not run a user study, so I do not know yet how much it helps people learn.
  • My code is MIT licensed. The Gemma model has its own terms, which I have not reviewed in detail.

What comes next. Test it with real learners, add a "check my translation" mode, review the Bengali with native speakers, and try an open text-to-speech model for more natural voices.

AI tools helped build this project. I used Claude and Claude Code for code, tests and drafts, and I ran the app myself on my Mac, including with Wi-Fi switched off.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A model that runs on your own machine can't be switched off, repriced or turned into a data pipeline. That matters most for learners with little money or a patchy connection. Open weights also let me inspect, swap and test the model: when I wanted a faster setting, I changed one flag and measured the result.

The Spirit of It

Ghost stories are how many of us first learned how language can pull you in. It felt right that a ghost story be the thing a machine tells, in two languages, on a computer that stays in the room with you.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: the whole app is built around Gemma (gemma4:12b) running locally through Ollama, for both story writing and Bengali translation.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: I used ElevenLabs (Eleven v4, voice "Wyman - The Storyteller", with audio tags for tone) to generate the narration for the demo video. It is not used inside the app, on purpose: story writing and translation stay on the computer.

title: Cursor vs OpenAI Codex: pick by what you'll review at the end
description:
Cursor and OpenAI Codex get compared as if one were the coding assistant and the other a slower copy. They win different jobs. The easiest way to pick is to name the thing you'll review at the end before you name a brand.

This is a short version of our guide, Cursor vs OpenAI Codex. It only uses the rankings we've already published. There are no prices or benchmark scores here, on purpose. Check current pricing before you buy a plan.

The short version

On our Best for Vibe Coding list the editorial order is Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, then Replit Agent.

  • "I'm in the editor and I want a diff I can reject hunk by hunk." Use Cursor.
  • "Run this while I'm away and leave a GitHub trail." Use Codex.
  • "Go do this in the repo from a terminal." That's Claude Code, not either of these.
  • "We already pay for Copilot and this is a routine edit." Stay with Copilot.
  • "I'm starting from an empty folder and want something hosted." That's Replit Agent.

Cursor: when the diff is the point

Cursor is first because it's the closest thing to a default when the agent has to live in your editor. It takes a multi-file change, applies it, and lets you reject hunks without leaving the project.

The catch is that vague prompts send it wandering, and it'll spend tokens proving it. Describe the change in a sentence a teammate would understand, look at the diff, keep the good parts. If you can't write that sentence, a stronger model won't save the session.

Codex: when the laptop should be closed

OpenAI Codex is third. It's a capable agent that works in a cloud sandbox with a GitHub loop, which makes it useful when the task should run away from your laptop.

You hand Codex a job, it works in the cloud, and what you review is closer to a pull request than to a hunk in the file you have open. That's a real product difference, not a slower Cursor. OpenAI's newer fast API tier doesn't change that; it's an API option, not a different product.

The one question

Ask yourself what you'll be looking at when the work is done. A diff in your open editor points to Cursor. A pull request you check later points to Codex. Getting that one answer right matters more than any leaderboard.

The full five-tool walk is in Best AI tool for coding, and the editor-against-terminal matchup is Cursor vs Claude Code.
