title: Go 1.24+ Servers Ask Linux for MPTCP: the Precondition for Claude's Root Exploit
description:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If your Go service runs on Linux and its main module targets Go 1.24 or later, it asks the kernel for a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. Anthropic wrote on October 27 that Claude, "after initial prompting," built a remote root exploit for "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Two days later the Go Security Team sent golang-announce a note on protecting Go programs against CVE-2026-98432 (archived on oss-security). Its message for Go developers: unless you told it not to, a Go 1.24+ server requests exactly that kind of listener.

The Go docs say that since Go 1.24 the multipathtcp setting "defaults to multipathtcp="2", thus enabled by default on listeners." You probably never chose that.

What changed since Anthropic's post

Anthropic's October 27 post described the bug as "a race condition-induced UAF bug in the kernel networking stack" and said it took the model's exploit "48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." The model is "an unreleased, internal research model," and Anthropic has not published the exploit.

The Go team's October 29 announcement tied the exploit's precondition to Go's default and listed mitigations. On October 30, Red Hat published RHSB-2026-016 and rated the flaw Critical for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift. It lists no fixed kernels yet and says Red Hat "is expediting the release of fixes."

The distributions have split. Debian has fixed kernels for bookworm and trixie. Ubuntu's tracker, last updated October 30, still lists the linux package as vulnerable on every release from 16.04 to 26.10, with work in progress on 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10.

The CVE itself is older. Ubuntu lists it as published on October 15 with a CVSS 3 score of 9.8, and Debian's tracker describes IP options being freed while another CPU still reads them during the IPv4 TCP handshake.

Why a Go server meets the precondition

Go 1.21 added Multipath TCP, but only when an application asked for it. Go 1.24 changed the default to multipathtcp=2: MPTCP on for listeners, off for dialers. Every net.Listen("tcp", ...) and every http.ListenAndServe in a program whose main module declares go 1.24 or later (in go.mod or go.work) requests an MPTCP socket from the kernel, unless a godebug setting says otherwise. The toolchain version alone doesn't decide it. Per the GODEBUG docs, a newer toolchain building a module that still says go 1.23 keeps the old opt-in behavior.

Whether the kernel hands one back depends on the host. The kernel switch is net.mptcp.enabled. TuxCare, which sells KernelCare, a live kernel patching service, says Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10 ship with MPTCP disabled, so a Go service on a stock RHEL host falls back to plain TCP. Don't assume. Check each host:

# 1 means the kernel will create MPTCP sockets
sysctl net.mptcp.enabled

# listening MPTCP sockets and the process that owns each
sudo ss -Mlnp

If the second command lists your Go binaries, they meet the precondition Anthropic described.

The Go team is careful about what that means. Its announcement says the bug is not specific to MPTCP, and a Go maintainer said the same on the proposal issue. Per Debian's tracker, the root cause is a use-after-free in Linux's IPv4 TCP handling. Turning MPTCP off removes the one path that has been demonstrated. Nobody has said it is the only path.


A Go 1.24+ server asks the kernel for MPTCP on its listeners. The kernel decides whether that lane is open.

Patch first. The Go switches are a stopgap

The Go team calls a patched kernel "the best fix." Debian's fixed builds are 6.12.113-1 for trixie and 6.1.190-1 for bookworm, per its tracker. A new kernel package only protects you after a reboot.

Until then, the announcement lists three ways to keep a Go program on plain TCP. The quickest needs no rebuild. Set it in the service's environment and restart:

GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 ./server

If GODEBUG already holds settings, add this one with a comma. To bake it into the binary, put it in the main module's go.mod:

module example.com/server

go 1.24

godebug multipathtcp=0

Two catches from the GODEBUG docs. Only the main module's go.mod counts, so a library can't set this for you. And when you build inside a workspace, go.mod godebug lines are ignored and go.work is read instead.

The third switch is per listener. ListenConfig.SetMultipathTCP overrides the GODEBUG value for that one socket:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"
    "net"
    "net/http"
)

func main() {
    var lc net.ListenConfig
    lc.SetMultipathTCP(false) // plain TCP, whatever GODEBUG says

    ctx := context.Background()
    ln, err := lc.Listen(ctx, "tcp", ":8080")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    log.Fatal(http.Serve(ln, http.NotFoundHandler()))
}

The Go team's own verdict on all three is "a fragile mitigation." One forgotten MPTCP listener on the host, in any language, keeps the precondition alive, and the approach assumes every working exploit needs MPTCP. Red Hat's interim nftables rule, which drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options, has the same limit: Red Hat says it "cannot fully prevent it."


GODEBUG covers a process, go.mod covers a binary, SetMultipathTCP covers one listener.

Should Go flip the default back?

A proposal to disable MPTCP by default was opened on October 29 and is still open. Maintainers disagree. One Go maintainer wrote that changing the default now would be "closing the barn door after the horse has left," and asked for a justification of the current default, noting Go seems unusual in having one. Another Go team member wrote: "I don't see any reason that a security issue should lead us to disable it." A Linux kernel MPTCP developer joined to argue for MPTCP's benefits, such as moving a connection between networks without dropping it, and to say listener-side MPTCP has no performance cost for plain TCP clients. The Go team's announcement calls a default change "premature" for now.

Some projects aren't waiting. The Lightning Network daemon lnd merged a change on October 30 that, in an lnd developer's words, "makes plain TCP the default for newly built lnd binaries." The same developer told operators that "Disabling MPTCP removes the prerequisite for the demonstrated exploit," and that they "should still install a patched kernel as soon as one is available."

What to do this week

  1. Run sudo ss -Mlnp on every Linux host that faces the internet. Note which processes hold MPTCP listeners.
  2. Check your distribution's tracker for a fixed kernel: Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat. Install it and plan the reboot.
  3. Check the go line in each service's go.mod (or go.work). At go 1.24 or later, assume the service requests MPTCP unless a godebug setting turns it off.
  4. Where no fixed kernel exists yet, set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 on Go services and restart them. Add godebug multipathtcp=0 to go.mod if you don't use MPTCP on purpose.
  5. Look at which kernel completes the TCP handshake with outside clients. If a proxy terminates TCP in front of your Go service, that proxy's host is the one an outside peer reaches first, so patch it first.

If this was useful

The fix for this one is a kernel update and a reboot on every exposed host, and the hard part is doing that across a fleet without dropping traffic. Draining a node behind a load balancer, rolling it, and bringing it back is the kind of building block the System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals walks through. I also build Hermes IDE, a free, source-available desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) that runs Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents side by side, and each one can work on its own branch; star it on GitHub if that sounds useful.

title: Should a Self-Taught Programmer Switch from Java to Go for Backend Development? A Structured Roadmap and Job Prospects
description:
Introduction: The Case for Switching Languages

At 17, with no prior tech experience, our protagonist stands at a crossroads. They’ve begun their programming journey with Java, mastering its basics and completing a small project, but now feel drawn to Go—not out of frustration with Java, but due to Go’s philosophy of simplicity and concurrency. This decision isn’t trivial. It involves unlearning Java-specific paradigms (like object-oriented design) and adopting Go’s unique features (goroutines, channels), a process that could either accelerate or derail their backend development goals. The risk? Incomplete transition, where Java-centric thinking persists, hindering mastery of Go’s memory management and concurrency model, critical for backend systems.

The stakes are high. Without a structured roadmap, they risk spreading efforts too thin or missing key backend skills (e.g., REST APIs, databases), delaying job readiness. Yet, Go’s minimalism and modern ecosystem (tools like Gin, Gorm, Docker) align with backend demands, offering a strategic advantage over Java’s verbosity. The question isn’t just about language preference but career alignment: does Go’s simplicity and concurrency model better prepare them for modern backend roles than Java’s legacy footprint?

Their plan—grind Java fundamentals until February, then switch to Go—is pragmatic. Java’s object-oriented concepts provide a transferable foundation for Go’s structural approach, reducing the learning curve. However, success hinges on self-discipline in self-study and portfolio quality. A GitHub profile with well-documented, complex projects (e.g., a RESTful API with Gorm for database interaction) is more compelling than multiple trivial ones. Community engagement (Go forums, open-source contributions) is non-negotiable; it accelerates learning and opens internship doors, mitigating the isolation risk of self-study.

The optimal path? If Go’s philosophy aligns with backend goals (simplicity, concurrency), switch, but prioritize backend concepts over syntax. Use Java’s logic as a springboard, focus on Go’s goroutines and channels for concurrency, and build projects simulating real-world backend scenarios (e.g., microservices with Docker). Avoid expensive courses; high-quality self-study (documentation, AI tools) plus a strong portfolio suffices for junior roles. However, this strategy fails if progress tracking is inconsistent or projects lack real-world applicability. Rule of thumb: If X (Go’s philosophy matches career goals) -> use Y (structured Go roadmap with backend focus).

Evaluating the Switch: Java vs. Go for Backend Development

Switching from Java to Go for backend development is a decision that hinges on aligning language philosophy with career goals, managing the learning curve trade-offs, and navigating the backend ecosystem’s demands. Let’s break this down using a causal, mechanism-driven analysis.

1. Language Philosophy Alignment: Simplicity vs. Verbosity

Go’s philosophy—simplicity, concurrency, and minimalism—contrasts sharply with Java’s verbose, object-oriented paradigm. This isn’t just a stylistic difference; it’s a mechanical shift in how you solve problems. For backend development, Go’s goroutines and channels offer a lightweight concurrency model that’s inherently suited for high-performance, scalable systems. Java’s threads, in contrast, are heavier and more resource-intensive, requiring explicit management of shared state.

Mechanism: Go’s runtime scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads, reducing context-switching overhead. This internal process translates to observable effects like faster response times and lower memory usage in backend services. If your goal is to build modern, cloud-native applications, Go’s philosophy aligns better with these demands.

2. Learning Curve Trade-offs: Unlearning vs. Transferring Skills

Switching languages involves unlearning Java-specific paradigms (e.g., inheritance, checked exceptions) and adopting Go’s idiomatic approach. This isn’t just a syntactic change—it’s a cognitive reconfiguration. For instance, Go’s lack of classes forces you to rethink encapsulation and modularity.

Mechanism: Java’s OOP concepts (e.g., encapsulation, polymorphism) can transfer to Go’s structural typing, but the risk lies in incomplete transition. Retaining Java-centric thinking (e.g., overusing interfaces) can lead to suboptimal Go code, such as unnecessary abstraction layers that bloat your codebase. Rule of thumb: If you’re drawn to Go’s simplicity, use Java’s OOP as a springboard, not a crutch. Focus on Go’s unique features (goroutines, channels) to avoid hybrid, inefficient code.

3. Backend Ecosystem: Tools and Frameworks

Go’s ecosystem is smaller but more focused compared to Java’s sprawling landscape. For backend development, tools like Gin (web framework), Gorm (ORM), and Docker are essential. Java’s ecosystem (Spring, Hibernate) is more mature but overkill for many modern use cases.

Mechanism: Go’s minimalism reduces cognitive load, allowing you to master backend concepts faster. However, the smaller ecosystem means fewer pre-built solutions, requiring you to write more code from scratch. This is a double-edged sword: it accelerates learning but demands self-discipline to avoid reinventing the wheel. Optimal strategy: Prioritize backend concepts over syntax. Build a REST API with Gin, integrate a database with Gorm, and containerize it with Docker. This project-based approach simulates real-world scenarios and solidifies your understanding.

4. Career Prospects: Market Demand and Junior Roles

Go’s adoption in backend development is growing, especially in startups and cloud-native companies. However, Java still dominates enterprise systems. For a junior role, Go’s lower barrier to entry (simpler syntax, faster onboarding) can be advantageous, but it also means higher competition due to its popularity among self-taught developers.

Mechanism: Companies adopting Go often prioritize concurrency and scalability, making Go a strategic choice for modern backend roles. However, the smaller job market for Go means you must stand out with a strong portfolio. Rule of thumb: If you’re targeting startups or cloud-native roles, Go is optimal. For enterprise roles, Java might still be necessary. Edge case: If you’re in a region with limited Go adoption, Java’s broader market presence could be a safer bet.

5. Self-Study vs. Structured Courses: Cost-Benefit Analysis

Expensive courses aren’t necessary for mastering Go. High-quality self-study (documentation, AI tools, open-source projects) combined with a strong GitHub portfolio can suffice for junior roles. However, self-study requires self-discipline and consistent progress tracking.

Mechanism: The risk of self-study lies in inconsistent progress or gaps in knowledge. For example, neglecting Go’s memory management or error handling idioms can lead to buggy, inefficient code. Optimal strategy: Use AI tools as mentors (e.g., ChatGPT for code reviews) and engage with the Go community (forums, open-source). Typical error: Overreliance on tutorials without building real-world projects. Rule of thumb: If you can’t explain your project’s architecture and trade-offs, it’s not portfolio-ready.

Conclusion: When to Switch and How

Switch to Go if:

  • You’re drawn to its simplicity and concurrency philosophy.
  • Your goal is modern backend development (e.g., microservices, cloud-native apps).
  • You’re willing to invest time in self-study and portfolio building.

Stick with Java if:

  • You’re targeting enterprise roles or regions with limited Go adoption.
  • You prefer a mature ecosystem with extensive tooling.

1-2 Year Roadmap for Go:

  1. Months 1-6: Master Go syntax, concurrency (goroutines, channels), and basic backend concepts (REST APIs, databases).
  2. Months 7-12: Build progressive projects (e.g., a blog API, a real-time chat app) using Gin, Gorm, and Docker.
  3. Months 13-24: Contribute to open-source projects, optimize for performance, and prepare a well-documented portfolio.

Final Rule: If Go’s philosophy matches your career goals, switch—but only with a structured roadmap and a focus on backend-specific skills. Avoid the trap of syntax obsession; prioritize real-world applicability.

A Structured Go Learning Roadmap: From Beginner to Job-Ready

Switching from Java to Go is a strategic move for backend development, but only if executed with precision. This roadmap leverages your Java foundation, focuses on Go’s unique strengths, and aligns with junior/internship expectations. Here’s how to avoid common pitfalls and maximize your 1-2 year journey.

Phase 1: Foundation Transfer (Months 1-3)

Mechanism: Java’s object-oriented concepts (e.g., data structures, algorithms) are transferable to Go’s structural typing. However, Go’s memory management and concurrency model require unlearning Java’s thread-based approach. Failure to address this leads to hybrid code inefficiency (e.g., overusing interfaces where goroutines are optimal).

  • Action: Complete Java Core by February, focusing on algorithms and data structures. Simultaneously, study Go’s syntax via Tour of Go to avoid syntax overload.
  • Tool: Use Go Playground for quick experiments, contrasting Java’s verbosity with Go’s minimalism.
  • Project: Rewrite a Java project (e.g., a calculator) in Go to expose differences in error handling (no checked exceptions) and memory allocation.

Phase 2: Backend Core & Concurrency (Months 4-9)

Mechanism: Go’s goroutines and channels are critical for backend scalability but require understanding scheduler mechanics (e.g., how goroutines multiplex onto OS threads). Misuse leads to deadlocks or resource starvation.

  • Action: Master REST APIs with Gin and database interactions with Gorm. Build a blog API with user authentication to integrate these.
  • Tool: Use Docker for containerized deployments, simulating production environments.
  • Edge Case: Test concurrency limits by stress-testing your API with k6. Analyze memory usage via pprof to identify goroutine leaks.

Phase 3: Advanced Backend & Portfolio Optimization (Months 10-12)

Mechanism: Junior roles prioritize problem-solving over syntax. A weak portfolio (e.g., undocumented code, trivial projects) signals inadequate real-world applicability.

  • Action: Build a real-time chat app using WebSockets and goroutines. Document design decisions and trade-offs in your GitHub README.
  • Tool: Use GitHub Actions for CI/CD pipelines, showcasing deployment readiness.
  • Rule: If a project lacks complexity (e.g., no error handling, no database), it’s not portfolio-worthy.

Phase 4: Open Source & Performance Tuning (Months 13-24)

Mechanism: Open-source contributions signal collaboration skills, a key junior role requirement. Neglecting this limits visibility and feedback loops.

  • Action: Contribute to Go projects like Gin or Gorm. Focus on fixing memory leaks or optimizing database queries.
  • Tool: Use Benchmarking tools to measure improvements (e.g., reducing API response time from 200ms to 50ms).
  • Edge Case: If your contribution is rejected, analyze the feedback for idiomatic Go violations (e.g., using mutexes instead of channels).

Decision Dominance: Self-Study vs. Paid Courses

Optimal Solution: Self-study with AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT for debugging) and community engagement is sufficient for junior roles. Paid courses are suboptimal due to:

  • Cost-Benefit Imbalance: $500+ courses rarely cover Go’s backend ecosystem better than free resources like Go by Example.
  • Lack of Portfolio Focus: Courses often prioritize theory over project-building, delaying job readiness.

Rule: If you can’t explain a Go concept (e.g., select statement) in your own words after self-study, revisit documentation or build a project around it.

Failure Risks & Mitigation

Risk 1: Incomplete Transition – Mechanism: Retaining Java’s OOP mindset leads to over-engineered Go code (e.g., unnecessary abstractions). Mitigation: Force yourself to use goroutines instead of threads for every concurrency task.

Risk 2: Weak Portfolio – Mechanism: Projects lacking real-world complexity (e.g., no error handling, no scaling considerations) fail to impress employers. Mitigation: Add rate limiting or caching to your API projects to demonstrate production thinking.

Final Rule of Thumb

If Go’s simplicity and concurrency align with your backend goals, switch now. Use Java’s logic as a foundation, prioritize backend concepts over syntax, and build a portfolio that solves real problems. Avoid paid courses; invest time in open-source and community instead.

Building a Strong GitHub Portfolio: Strategies for Success

For a self-taught programmer transitioning from Java to Go, a GitHub portfolio isn’t just a collection of code—it’s a mechanical proof of your problem-solving ability and a physical demonstration of Go’s concurrency model in action. Here’s how to build a portfolio that deforms the typical junior developer stereotype and positions you as a strategic backend candidate.

1. Prioritize Backend Concepts Over Syntax: The Causal Chain

Focusing solely on Go’s syntax expands the risk of incomplete transition, where Java-centric thinking (e.g., overusing interfaces) heats up your code with inefficiencies. Instead, leverage Go’s goroutines and channels to build projects that solve real backend problems. For example:

  • REST API with Gin: Demonstrates HTTP handling and middleware, changing how requests are processed compared to Java’s thread-based approach.
  • Real-time Chat App with WebSockets: Showcases goroutine-based concurrency, breaking the traditional thread-locking model.

Rule: If a project doesn’t highlight Go’s unique features, it’s failing to deform the Java-to-Go transition. Use concurrency as the core differentiator.

2. Document Design Decisions: The Mechanism of Risk Formation

Undocumented projects expand the risk of misinterpretation by employers, who may assume weak problem-solving skills. For each project, include:

  • README with Architecture Diagrams: Explains how components interact, preventing confusion about your design choices.
  • Commit History with Thought Process: Shows iterative thinking, changing the perception from “code copier” to “problem solver.”

Rule: If documentation is missing, the project’s complexity breaks its ability to impress. Treat documentation as part of the code itself.

3. Collaborate on Open-Source: The Optimal Solution

Contributing to open-source Go projects (e.g., Gin, Gorm) optimizes visibility and demonstrates mechanical collaboration skills. For example:

  • Fixing Memory Leaks: Shows understanding of Go’s memory management, deforming the stereotype of self-taught developers as syntax-only learners.
  • Optimizing Database Queries with Gorm: Highlights practical backend skills, changing how employers perceive your readiness for junior roles.

Rule: If you’re not contributing to open-source, you’re failing to heat up your networking and feedback loop. Start small—fix a bug or improve documentation.

4. Use GitHub Actions for CI/CD: The Causal Chain

Implementing CI/CD pipelines expands the proof of your deployment readiness, a critical backend skill. For example:

  • Automated Testing with GitHub Actions: Ensures code quality, preventing the risk of unnoticed bugs.
  • Dockerized Deployments: Demonstrates containerization, changing how your projects are perceived in a cloud-native context.

Rule: If CI/CD is missing, your portfolio breaks the illusion of production readiness. Automate everything—testing, linting, and deployment.

5. Avoid Trivial Projects: The Mechanism of Risk Formation

Simple projects (e.g., to-do lists) expand the risk of being overlooked, as they fail to deform the typical junior developer portfolio. Instead, build:

  • Microservices with Docker Compose: Shows scalability thinking, changing how employers view your backend skills.
  • Rate-Limited APIs: Demonstrates real-world problem-solving, preventing the perception of theoretical-only knowledge.

Rule: If a project doesn’t solve a real problem, it’s failing to heat up your portfolio. Complexity and applicability are non-negotiable.

Edge-Case Analysis: When Self-Study Fails

While self-study is sufficient, it breaks down if:

  • Progress Tracking is Inconsistent: Use tools like Notion or Trello to prevent knowledge gaps.
  • Feedback Loop is Missing: Engage with the Go community (e.g., forums, meetups) to deform isolation.

Rule: If self-discipline falters, use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) as a mentor to stay on track. Paid courses are suboptimal unless they focus on portfolio-building.

Final Rule of Thumb

If Go’s philosophy aligns with your career goals, prioritize backend concepts, document relentlessly, and collaborate openly. A strong GitHub portfolio mechanically compensates for lack of formal education, making self-study sufficient for junior/internship roles.

Conclusion: Navigating the Path to a Junior/Internship Role

Switching from Java to Go is a strategic move for a self-taught programmer like you, but only if executed with precision. Here’s the distilled roadmap to ensure your transition doesn’t just happen—it succeeds.

Key Takeaways

  • Leverage Java’s Foundation: Java’s OOP concepts (e.g., data structures, algorithms) transfer to Go’s structural typing, but unlearning thread-based concurrency is critical. Misusing goroutines or channels due to Java-centric thinking leads to deadlocks or resource starvation. Mechanism: Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads by Go’s runtime scheduler, reducing context-switching overhead—a feature Java’s explicit thread management lacks.
  • Prioritize Backend Concepts Over Syntax: Go’s minimalism means its ecosystem (Gin, Gorm, Docker) requires custom solutions. Focusing on syntax alone risks over-engineering (e.g., overusing interfaces). Mechanism: Go’s lack of inheritance forces structural typing, which, if misunderstood, leads to suboptimal code.
  • Portfolio Quality Trumps Quantity: Junior roles screen for problem-solving, not syntax. A weak portfolio (undocumented, trivial projects) signals inadequate real-world applicability. Mechanism: Employers assess GitHub repos for design decisions, CI/CD pipelines, and scalability features like rate limiting.

Final Advice: What to Do Next

Your 1–2 year roadmap must balance skill transfer, backend mastery, and portfolio impact. Here’s the optimal strategy:
Phase Focus Mechanism
Months 1-3 Foundation Transfer Rewrite a Java project in Go to contrast error handling and memory allocation. Use Go Playground to experiment with goroutines vs. Java threads.
Months 4-9 Backend Core Build a REST API with Gin and Gorm, stress-test with k6, and analyze memory via pprof. Mechanism: Gin’s lightweight framework reduces latency compared to Java’s Spring.
Months 10-24 Portfolio & Open Source Contribute to Go projects (e.g., fix memory leaks in Gorm). Use GitHub Actions for CI/CD to prove deployment readiness. Mechanism: Open-source contributions demonstrate collaboration and code quality under scrutiny.

Rule of Thumb: If Go’s simplicity and concurrency align with your career goals, follow this structured roadmap. Avoid paid courses—self-study with AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) and community engagement is sufficient. Edge Case: If you target enterprise roles, Java’s mature ecosystem may still be optimal, but Go’s growth in cloud-native roles makes it the better bet for startups.

Avoiding Common Pitfalls

  • Incomplete Transition: Retaining Java’s OOP mindset leads to over-engineered Go code. Mitigation: Use goroutines for all concurrency tasks, not threads.
  • Inconsistent Progress: Lack of tracking leads to skill gaps. Solution: Use Notion/Trello and set weekly project milestones.
  • Isolation: Missing feedback stunts growth. Solution: Engage in Go forums or contribute to open-source projects like Gin.

Execute this plan, and by year two, your GitHub portfolio will speak louder than any degree. The tech industry values what you build, not where you learned it. Go build it.

title: Your AI agent writes Playwright tests that pass while your API returns 500
description:
AI agents now write a lot of Playwright tests. You ask Claude Code or Copilot to "add a test for the checkout", or let an agent explore your app through Playwright MCP and turn what it did into a spec. Healer agents even fix failing tests for you.

Here is the kind of test they write:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("places an order", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/");
  await page.getByLabel("Name").fill("Ada");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Place order" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toContainText("Order placed");
});

It's a good test: role-based locators and a web-first assertion. It passes.

It also passes when the order API returns 500 and stores nothing, as long as the page still shows "Order placed". The agent checked what it could see. Nobody told it to check what the server did, and agents almost never add a network assertion on their own.

That matters more with agents than with people. A human who wrote the checkout code might remember the API can fail. An agent generating fifty tests from what's on screen won't, and a healer agent that "fixes" a red test by updating the expected text can make things worse. The suite goes green while the backend is broken.

The one-line fix

Change the import, in the tests the agent wrote or in the template it writes from:

import { test, expect } from "@vedhajs/playwright-test";

Nothing else changes. Same test, same broken app:


  ✓  1 1-playwright.spec.ts › places an order (import from @playwright/test)
  ✘  2 2-vedha.spec.ts › places an order (import from @vedhajs/playwright-test)

    Error: Vedha guard: the test's own checks passed, but the app reported a problem:
      - POST /api/orders returned 500

On a healthy app, both pass.

The failure message is also written for whoever reads it next, human or agent: what the app did, and how to accept it if it was expected. A healer agent gets a real reason instead of a green run.

What it checks

@vedhajs/playwright-test re-exports Playwright's test and expect with an automatic fixture ("guard mode") that watches the browser context while each test runs:

  • Fails the test: any 5xx from your app's own site, or a write request (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) that failed outright, even when every expect passed.
  • Warns, without failing: a 4xx answer to a write, and uncaught page errors. Validation tests expect a 422 and third-party scripts throw, so these become annotations in the report instead of failures.
  • Ignores: requests to other sites (analytics, CDNs).
  • Attaches: the findings to the test result as vedha-guard.json.

When a finding is expected, opt out per test or per endpoint:

test.use({ vedhaGuard: "strict" }); // 4xx writes and page errors fail too
test.use({ vedhaGuard: { ignore: ["/api/flaky", /\/v2\//], hosts: ["api.other-domain.com"] } });
test.use({ vedhaGuard: false }); // off, for a test that expects a 500

It is still Playwright's runner, so retries, sharding, reporters and traces work as before.

Making agents use it

Put it where the agent will pick it up:

  • Your project instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Copilot instructions): "Import test and expect from @vedhajs/playwright-test, not @playwright/test."
  • Existing specs: agents copy the patterns they find, so once your specs use the import, new ones tend to follow.
  • A lint rule that bans importing from @playwright/test in spec files, if you want to enforce it.

When the agent drives the browser itself

Guard mode is for the tests an agent writes. When the agent is the tester, driving the browser live and reporting pass or fail, Vedha also ships an MCP server that checks every step the same way. In a small pilot on held-out tasks (one model, 3 trials per task), the agent missed 9 seeded bugs with Vedha's MCP server against 26 with Playwright MCP. That's a separate setup from guard mode, covered in an earlier post.

Limits

  • A hand-written waitForResponse assertion catches this too. Guard mode is the safety net for the many tests, agent-written or not, that don't have one.
  • In Vedha's benchmark, tests with typical text and URL checks caught 0 of 140 seeded defects with plain Playwright, and 60 of 140 with Vedha's page-health check: every defect where the server rejected or failed the write. Guard mode applies the same rules to whole tests, but it hasn't been benchmarked separately yet.
  • It does not catch a write that returns 200 but stores nothing or stores the wrong value. Vedha's checked steps can read the data back, but that's opt-in and needs more than one line.

Try it 

npm install -D @vedhajs/playwright-test

Change the import in one agent-written spec and run it. If a test that used to pass now fails, look at the request it names. Either the agent's test was hiding a bug, or it's an expected error to add to ignore.

Repo, demo and benchmark data: https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA (Apache-2.0)

I'd like to hear what it finds in agent-written suites, and about any false alarm.

title: AI Agent Cancellation: Stop Work That Continues After the User Clicks Stop
description:
A Stop button can be honest in the browser and still be a lie in production. The chat stream disappears, but a model request may be generating, a browser tool may be clicking, and a background worker may be one step away from sending an email.

That is not a cosmetic bug. It is a broken contract. Users interpret “Stop” as “do not do more work for me.” Your system needs to translate that request across every layer, record what actually stopped, and make the remaining uncertainty visible. This guide gives you that contract.

The key idea is simple: cancellation is a state transition, not a boolean and not a client disconnect.

The five meanings hidden behind “Stop”

Teams often store one cancelled flag and call it a day. That collapses several different facts:

Event What it proves What it does not prove
Browser aborts a stream The browser stopped listening The server or model stopped working
API accepts a cancel request The request was recorded Every child task observed it
Worker sees the request New work should not begin An in-flight tool did not finish
Provider accepts cancellation The cancellation reached that provider No already-buffered output or usage exists
Run becomes terminal Your ledger has a final outcome An external write was reversed

Keep those facts separate. A robust lifecycle might be:

running → cancel_requested → cancelling → cancelled

with other terminal paths such as completed, failed, and needs_reconciliation. The last state is important. If a payment, ticket, or record write was in flight when cancellation arrived, pretending it is cancelled can make a later retry unsafe.

Define the cancellation contract before wiring a button

Write down the semantics your product promises. A useful default is:

  1. A user can request cancellation for a run they are authorized to control.
  2. No new model turn, tool call, or queued step starts after the durable request is observed.
  3. In-flight work gets a best-effort cancel signal and has a deadline for acknowledging it.
  4. The API never reports cancelled until the orchestrator records a terminal decision.
  5. Side effects already dispatched are reconciled, not guessed away.
  6. A cancelled run does not silently resume; resumption creates a new attempt or requires an explicit resume action.

This contract gives product, API, and operations teams the same vocabulary. It also prevents a dangerous UX pattern: changing the button label to “Stopped” the moment the browser disconnects.

Use one durable run record

Put the authoritative state in a database or workflow engine, not in a process-local abort controller. A minimal record can look like this:

type RunStatus =
  | "queued" | "running" | "cancel_requested" | "cancelling"
  | "cancelled" | "completed" | "failed" | "needs_reconciliation";

type AgentRun = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  status: RunStatus;
  cancelRequestedAt?: string;
  cancelReason?: "user" | "deadline" | "policy" | "operator";
  activeStepId?: string;
  version: number;
  terminalAt?: string;
};

The version field enables compare-and-set updates. It stops a late worker from replacing cancel_requested with running after another worker has already processed the stop request.

Your POST /runs/:id/cancel endpoint should be idempotent. It records the request once, returns the current state, and publishes a cancellation event. Repeated taps, reconnects, and retries should all produce the same outcome.

async function requestCancel(runId: string, actorId: string) {
  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const run = await tx.runs.lockForUpdate(runId);
    assertCanCancel(actorId, run);

    if (["completed", "failed", "cancelled"].includes(run.status)) return run;

    const next = await tx.runs.update(runId, {
      status: "cancel_requested",
      cancelRequestedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
      cancelReason: "user",
      version: run.version + 1,
    });
    await tx.outbox.insert({ type: "run.cancel_requested", runId });
    return next;
  });
}

The transactional outbox is not required by every stack, but the principle is: persist the decision before notifying workers. A process crash between an in-memory publish and a database write should not make a stop request disappear.

Propagate cancellation across every boundary

An agent run usually crosses more boundaries than a normal web request. Treat cancellation as a signal that travels with the run.

Browser and streaming edge

AbortController can stop fetch and response-body consumption in the browser, as MDN documents. Use it to stop rendering and then call your durable cancellation endpoint. Do not rely on disconnect detection alone: mobile networks reconnect, tabs sleep, and a user may close a page without meaning “cancel.”

const controller = new AbortController();

stopButton.onclick = async () => {
  controller.abort("user_pressed_stop"); // end local streaming now
  await fetch(`/api/runs/${runId}/cancel`, { method: "POST" });
  showStatus("Stopping…");
};

The status is “Stopping,” not “Stopped,” until the run event feed reports a terminal state. If an SSE connection reconnects, replay events from a monotonic sequence number rather than starting another run.

Orchestrator and model calls

At step boundaries, read the durable record. In long model streams, also pass a cancellation primitive that can close the network request or invoke a provider-specific cancellation API where available. A close tells your HTTP client to stop waiting; it does not automatically prove upstream inference stopped or that no tokens were billed.

Use an absolute run deadline as well. Pass the remaining time, not a fresh full timeout, to each downstream call. A run that spends 50 seconds retrieving should not receive another 60 seconds of model time merely because each layer starts its own clock.

Parallel tools

Parallelism makes cancellation interesting. If a run launches a search, an internal lookup, and a write tool together, cancellation must reach each child. But not all children have the same policy:

  • Read-only tools can normally be abandoned or cancelled.
  • A write before its commit point can be cancelled.
  • A write after dispatch needs a receipt or authoritative read-back.
  • Cleanup work may need a short shielded window so it can record the correct final state.

In Python, cancellation is cooperative: asyncio injects CancelledError at an await point, and the official guidance is to use try/finally for cleanup and generally propagate the exception afterward. Do not catch it broadly and continue doing more agent work.

async def execute_step(run_id: str):
    try:
        await assert_not_cancelled(run_id)
        result = await call_tool_with_deadline(run_id)
        await persist_result(run_id, result)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        await record_step_interrupted(run_id)
        raise

Queued and durable work

A cancellation request must invalidate queued messages too. Workers should acquire a lease, re-check the run state immediately before each externally visible action, and release the lease on exit. A message already in a queue is not permission to execute it.

For longer-running orchestration, model cancellation and external-step cancellation as explicit workflow commands. Systems such as Temporal distinguish cancellation commands from ordinary completion; the general lesson applies even if you use Postgres and workers instead of a workflow engine.

Never confuse cancellation with rollback

Cancellation prevents future work. Rollback tries to compensate for past work. They are related but not interchangeable.

Imagine an agent creates an invoice and then receives a stop request before it records the tool response. The correct terminal state is often needs_reconciliation, not cancelled. Query the payment system by a stable operation key. If the invoice exists, show it as created and offer a distinct authorized reversal. If it does not, mark the step cancelled.

This is why every write tool needs an idempotency key and an operation ledger. The full pattern is covered in AI Agent Idempotency: Prevent Duplicate Charges, Emails, and Records. Cancellation reduces how often you enter an unknown state; it never removes the need to resolve one.

Design an honest user experience

The UI should expose progress without flooding people with internals:

State User-facing message Allowed action
running Working Stop
cancel_requested Stopping work Hide or wait
cancelling Finishing safe shutdown View details
needs_reconciliation Checking an action before closing Retry check or contact support
cancelled Stopped; no new work will run Start a new run

Do not show partial generated text as a completed answer. Mark it as interrupted, keep it separate from the final result, and never automatically feed it into the next agent turn. It may have been cut off mid-instruction or before a tool result arrived.

Structured errors help clients make this distinction. An error envelope should include a stable code, whether a retry is safe, the run state, and a correlation ID. Agent Tool Error Envelopes shows a compatible pattern.

Test the race conditions, not just the button

The happy path is easy: click Stop and see the stream close. Production correctness lives in the races. Add deterministic test hooks before model calls, before a tool dispatch, after dispatch but before receipt storage, and while a worker holds a lease.

Your cancellation test matrix should cover at least:

  1. Cancel while queued: no worker starts the first step.
  2. Cancel during token streaming: client stops, provider result is recorded as interrupted or reconciled.
  3. Cancel between model output and tool dispatch: no tool begins.
  4. Cancel during two parallel tools: every child reaches a known terminal state.
  5. Cancel after a write dispatch: reconciliation runs; the write is never blindly retried.
  6. Cancel during a process crash: a replacement worker respects the durable request.
  7. Duplicate cancel calls: one lifecycle transition and no duplicate cleanup.
  8. Resume attempt after cancellation: it creates a new attempt with explicit provenance.

Capture traces for each test and replay them when the runtime changes. AI Agent Trace Replay is useful for turning an escaped cancellation race into a permanent regression test.

A practical implementation checklist

  • Store run lifecycle state durably, including cancellation reason and timestamps.
  • Make cancellation requests authorized and idempotent.
  • Send a durable signal to workers; do not trust page disconnects as intent.
  • Check for cancellation before every new turn and side effect.
  • Propagate an abort signal and remaining deadline to streams and tools.
  • Record a confirmed terminal state only after worker cleanup finishes.
  • Reconcile writes that crossed a commit boundary.
  • Preserve interrupted output as partial, never as final.
  • Emit lifecycle events that reconnecting clients can replay.
  • Test cancellation at every boundary and after simulated crashes.

A Stop button is a promise about control. Keep that promise by treating cancellation as a first-class workflow outcome, not a disappearing HTTP connection.

FAQ

Does aborting an LLM stream stop the model?

Not necessarily. It reliably stops your client from consuming the response, but the provider may stop asynchronously, may have already buffered output, and may still report usage. Record provider request IDs and reconcile their final status when the distinction matters.

Should a cancelled AI agent run be retried automatically?

Usually no. Cancellation expresses changed user intent. Create an explicit new attempt instead. Only retry internal cleanup or a clearly idempotent read when that work is necessary to reach a known terminal state.

What is the difference between a timeout and cancellation?

A timeout is a system deadline; cancellation can come from a user, policy, operator, or parent workflow. Both can use the same propagation mechanism, but record the cause separately because the correct product response differs.

How do I cancel an agent tool that has already started a write?

Request cancellation, then query the target using the operation key or receipt. If the write committed, treat it as completed and use a separate compensating action if appropriate. Never assume a network timeout means the write failed.

Can I resume a cancelled agent run?

You can, but make it explicit. Persist a checkpoint with its inputs, completed steps, and evidence. Start a new attempt that references the old one, re-checks policy, and never repeats uncertain writes without reconciliation.

What metrics show whether cancellation works?

Track time from request to terminal state, cancelled runs with work still starting afterward, orphaned tool calls, reconciliation rate after cancellation, duplicate cancellation requests, and the fraction of partial outputs mistakenly shown as final.
